# D E D I C A T I O N

*Whatever the earth holds, whatever the sea and the sky bring forth,*
*Is scarcely enough to satisfy a greedy hunger.*
*To what end will the furious lust of the belly,*
*And the wicked ambition of the throat, finally drag us wretched men?*
*This was not the image of a better world in times past,*
*While the people were simple, and the world was new.*
*When a nation led a long and happy life,*
*Unstained by the marks of innocent blood.*
*When the nourishing earth, with no farmer compelling her,*
*Gave her delights to her master of her own accord.*
*Golden ages most worthy of King Saturn <note>In Roman mythology, Saturn ruled during a "Golden Age" of peace and abundance where labor was unnecessary.</note>,*
*But our crimes forbid those times to continue for long.*
*The Silver ages soon followed, yet whoever compares them*
*To our own customs, would rightly consider them golden.*
*Although a sacrificed victim often fell, its throat cut for God,*
*It was still considered a great sin to place it upon the tables.*
*We are the Iron offspring—oh, the grief!—all things are for the belly,*
*All things have become the prey of a raving throat!*
*What did the oxen deserve—an animal without wicked deceit,*
*And patient in its labors—what did the oxen deserve? <note>The author laments the transition from a vegetarian "Golden Age" to a modern "Iron Age" where even the hardworking ox is slaughtered for food.</note>*</note>

<term>Saturn</term> <note>The ancient god of agriculture; his reign represents a lost utopia.</note>, <term>Golden Ages</term> <note>The first and best age of mankind in classical mythology.</note>, <term>Silver Ages</term> <note>The second age, less perfect than the first but superior to the present.</note>, <term>Gluttony</term> <note>Latin: gula; one of the primary vices criticized in this text.</note>, <term>Lust of the belly</term> <note>Latin: libido ventris; refers to excessive or unnatural appetite.</note>, <term>Oxen</term> <note>Symbol of innocent, productive labor.</note>

<summary>This page contains a Latin elegiac poem lamenting the moral decline of humanity through the classical framework of the Four Ages, specifically criticizing the shift from a peaceful, bloodless existence to modern gluttony and the slaughter of animals.</summary>

# D E D I C A T I O N.

*What have you deserved, you peaceful sheep, a race born*
*to protect mankind; what have you peaceful sheep deserved?*
*But it is not enough to strike down the horn-bearing bull,*
*and the cruel knife is also stained with the blood of the calf.*
*No less is the gentle lamb, snatched from the udder of its dear mother,*
*slaughtered by the hand of the executioner.*
*And you, little chick, not yet happily excluded from your egg,*
*(O truly innocent one) you fill the bellies of men.*
*Indeed, that way of life does not please the Gaetulian lions,* <note>Gaetulia was a region in ancient North Africa, famous in Roman literature for its fierce lions.</note>
*nor does that life please the Armenian tigers.*
*The fiercer beast, content with foliage and green grass,*
*surely scorns bloody feasts.*
*And that beast which is more grim and devours flesh,*
*in turn, hardly even likes to touch the sprouts of the earth.*
*But he who ought to be the rule of life for all other living things,*
*man alone devours both.*
*And if only the examples of the flocks could move him!*
*He has those whom he might imitate so that he might live more mildly.*
*Grim crows and rapacious hawks go hunting,*
*but the gentle dove seeks the charming gifts of Ceres!* <note>Ceres was the Roman goddess of agriculture and grain; her "gifts" refer to bread or seeds.</note>

# DEDICATION

*Both the wolf and the ravenous bears are sated by flesh,*
*But the doe and the gentle sheep graze upon the pastures.*
*Do not suppose that only the strong creatures feed on blood,*
*While the weaker ones enjoy the herbs and the grasses.*
*Nothing is more spirited than the crested cock <note>The rooster, often used as a symbol of courage and vigilance</note>, and what,*
*Tell me, stands stronger than the warlike horse?*
*But perhaps those bloody feasts suit common souls,*
*Yet they do not befit heroes and demigods!*
*But what was more frugal than the table of Curius <note>Manius Curius Dentatus, a Roman consul famous for his austerity; he reportedly preferred his farm's turnips to Samnite gold</note> in days of old,*
*When he conquered Kings with his strong hand?*
*And Fabricius <note>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, another Roman model of virtue who refused bribes and lived simply</note>, preparing for himself a dish of roasted turnips,*
*Remained unconquered by enemies and by bribes alike.*
*But why do I linger on the venerable examples of the ancient Romans <note>original: "Quiritum"</note>?*
*Our dear Fatherland shall provide examples no less noble.*
*O, truly they were Hollanders <note>original: "Batavi," referring to the Batavians, the Germanic tribe regarded as the ancestors of the Dutch</note> once, when by simple food*
*Strength and vigor stood firm in those fearless men!*
*And just as there was no shame in draining capacious cups,*
*Even so, a modest table was held in high esteem.*
*India had not yet sent her spices—those things which,*
*Oh, the grief!—devastate our strength and our ancestral wealth.*

<summary>A poetic dedication praising the virtues of a simple, meat-free diet by citing classical Roman heroes and the rugged ancestors of the Dutch. The author laments how modern luxuries and imported spices from the East Indies have corrupted national strength.</summary>
<keywords>dedication, frugality, Roman virtue, Curius Dentatus, Fabricius, Batavians, Dutch history, temperance, spices, luxury</keywords>

# D E D I C A T I O N.

*Why do we fools now complain of new names for diseases?*
*Those evils dwell within our fine, sumptuous dishes!*
*Use your right, you say, it is necessary that we rule,*
*It is fitting that all things pass under our laws!*
*We flatter ourselves rashly, and proud in our vanity*
*We oppress an unknown race with our nobility.*
<note>The author is likely referring to the animal kingdom or the natural world which humans exploit for food.</note>
*Which, if by chance you wished to compare to our own race,*
*Comes to be preferred by many names.*
*If, however, a more powerful enemy is able to cut the throat*
*Of the weak, and enjoy his strength instead of reason:*
*Let vile souls desire those things; let the ignoble slave*
*Of the belly consider these to be his written laws!*
*Let the peasant, so that he may endure his hard labors,*
*Prepare hard dishes for his barking stomach.*
*But if anyone, born of divine seed, rises higher,*
*Let him rejoice to have raised his head above human affairs:*
*It is fitting for this man, at least, to flee the dire contagions*
*Of foul poison, and to beware the losses of the common crowd.*
*These things my <term>PORPHYRIUS</term> <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who famously advocated for vegetarianism in his work "On Abstinence from Animal Food."</note>, noble in his learned art, strives to persuade*
*His old companion.*

<summary>A poetic dedication arguing that human diseases stem from gluttony and the consumption of meat, invoking the philosopher Porphyry to advocate for a more disciplined, "divine" lifestyle over base physical appetites.</summary>
<keywords>dedication, Porphyry, vegetarianism, gluttony, disease, Neoplatonism, temperance</keywords>

# DEDICATION

*If anyone should think these are merely the dreams of a secular philosopher,*
*And now wishes to place no faith in his books,*
*Who does not know of that man, for whom the cheaper food of locusts*
*And honey, which drips from the trees onto leaves, were enough?* <note>A reference to John the Baptist’s ascetic lifestyle in the wilderness.</note>
And that for the followers of Christ to never touch the feasts of the meat-market,
Was considered a work of holy religion!
But why should I praise things which we do not think should be imitated;
That cause does not depend upon my own judgment.
Yet if that matter were indeed within my own judgment,
I would wish to live by that law forever.
Being noble-hearted and content with the goods which the Fatherland provides,
Let the Dutch table <note>original: "mensa Batava"</note> give me its magnificent feasts.
And let me care nothing for the gifts of the Western or Eastern worlds,
Where the glutton seasons unknown foods with his art.
Truly, God cuts the regions of the heaven and the wide lands
With mountains and the sea and with rivers.
Each nation is circumscribed by its own limit, so that
It might learn to be content with the goods given within.
Whatever it may be, we praise the old ways, but we use the years
Which a good birth-fortune and God have granted us.

<vocab>Dedication, Dutch (Batavian), Western, Eastern, God, Fatherland</vocab>

<summary>A poetic dedication contrasting the extreme asceticism of biblical figures with a modern preference for the local bounty of the Dutch Fatherland. The author argues that God divided the world into nations so that people might be content with their own native resources rather than seeking exotic luxuries.</summary>
<keywords>asceticism, John the Baptist, Dutch identity, providence, nationalism, moderation, geography</keywords>

# DEDICATION.

*Now the famous city of* DEVENTER <note>original: "Daventria," the Latin name for the city of Deventer in the Netherlands</note> *has offered hospitality to the peaceful Muses,*
*and has nurtured men of the highest standing in the arts.*
*From every side, the eager student once approached this "Athenian" city on the IJssel,* <note>original: "Salicas Athenas." The river IJssel was known in Latin as the Sala; calling a city "Athens" was a common humanist compliment for a center of learning.</note>

*Europe once bore no men greater in their art*

**YOUR** *care and favor, Fathers of the Fatherland,* <note>original: "Patres patriae," referring to the city magistrates or governors.</note> *makes it so.*
*Now also... but why should my Muse be a burden to the modesty*
*of those living, when I alone am failing?*

# TO THE UNBIASED READER

->SENDS GREETINGS<-

# JACOBUS DE RHOER.

At last, therefore, I have finished weaving the web, an undertaking that seemed almost an ill-omened thing when I first approached it. For most distinguished men had indeed frequently set their hands to the "golden" books (as they are commonly called) of *Porphyry* <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>, but always with frustrated effort. Those who had pledged their labor to the Tyrian Philosopher seemed, as the saying goes, to ride the horse of Sejanus <note>A proverbial expression for something that brings ruin to its owner</note>, or to have married Fulvia, a wife fatal to her husbands. I learned that MERIC CASAUBON was among their number from his notes on DIOGENES LAERTIUS, Book II, Segment 7. That THOMAS GALE promised the same in his notes on *Iamblichus: On the Mysteries*, Section V, chapter 4, and that DAVIS, LAKEMACHER, and LA CROZE—all most excellent men—held the same intention, is a well-attested fact. But perhaps no one employed a better preparation for this matter than JOHANN FRIEDRICH THOMAS, Rector of the Gymnasium of Schweidnitz in Silesia. He certainly indicated himself that he had many collations of manuscripts ready at hand: and among them even a Vatican copy, ancient and elegant, as we know from the *Treasury of Letters* of the illustrious LA CROZE, Volume III, page 225. That same LA CROZE had shared his own observations and those of PETITUS with THOMAS. Those notes of PETITUS, however, were very few, and unless they were better than those I touched upon regarding Book I, § 42, he would have deserved little credit regarding our *Malchus* <note>original: "Malcho"; Malchus was the original Semitic name of Porphyry</note>. THOMAS also received the observations and emendations of GALE, which he had smeared with his own hand onto a copy of the Author, as the *same Treasury of Letters*, Vol. I, p. 340 and Vol. II, p. 122, informs us. Besides these, he used many aids, which can be understood from his own letters given to the most learned SIBER (which you will find at the end of this Edition). It was not permitted for me to be so fortunate as to hope for those unpublished notes; yet even so, they pointed out this path which had to be traveled if I wished to find any assistance. Receive now in a few words what I have set in motion and achieved in that matter.

Since I most vehemently desired the Vatican copy I just mentioned, I persuaded myself that it could not be better pursued than through PETER WESSELING, a man of admirable erudition, for whom we have not yet finished mourning—on account of the loss our literature suffered, and I especially in the death of an excellent Teacher, who (as they used to say of *Porphyry’s* teacher, *Longinus*) was "a certain living library and a walking museum" <note>original: "βιβλιοθήκη τις ἦν ἔμψυχος καὶ περιπατοῦν μουσεῖον"</note>. Nor had I supposed this rashly, though the outcome was not very successful. I will subjoin part of the letter in which that most kind man indicated this to me: *"I do not know if it was signaled to you that I had asked Cardinal Librarian ALBANI to order an inquiry into whether the sheets of the Porphyrian book in the Vati-"*

FELICIANUS, nothing was found there that was rare or that I lacked—even though *Thomas* testifies in the same Letter that he possessed variant readings from a Royal Paris Manuscript.

But what I had sought in vain in France, I found in Holland. I owe the greatest thanks to the most excellent Gerard MEERMANN, a man no less illustrious for his erudition and merits than for his honors, who indicated to me that in that literary treasury which he had acquired for himself from France, there was also a handwritten manuscript of Porphyry's work. With an incredible zeal for promoting literature, he offered it for my use so that I might compare it with the published editions. The manuscript is on paper, in a smaller folio size, not indeed very ancient, but of good quality. The title is as follows: *Three books of Porphyry the Philosopher on abstinence from animal food; furthermore, the Life of Pythagoras and a small volume about Alexander.* <note>original Greek: "Πορφυρίου Φιλοσόφου περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων βιβλία τρία. ἔτι δὲ καὶ Πυθαγόρου βίος καὶ περὶ Ἀλεξάνδρου μικρὸν τεῦχος."</note> You see that the subject matter is incorrectly indicated, and it is said to be three books, when there are four. That mutilated little work about Alexander the Great does not bear a name, but it is by Arrian <note>Arrian of Nicomedia, a 2nd-century historian</note>, though it contains only thirteen chapters of the first book. Then there is added: *Naulot of Coila read this in the year of Christ the Savior 1573 (1573).* <note>The original includes the date in Greek alphabetic numerals</note> and so again at the end of the manuscript, except that there he is called *Naulot of the Valley.* At the top of the page one reads: *The Paris College of the Society of Jesus.* I noticed that this manuscript agrees in most parts with the Leipzig one (of which I shall speak immediately); indeed, almost the same scholia <note>Ancient or medieval marginal notes</note> are read in the margins there. And I was often happy to see the Leipzig reading confirmed, which had seemed truer to me, and often even conjectures—born from myself or others—were confirmed, although in many matters it also left me in uncertainty.

Great Britain also provided some help. For since I believed that the most excellent DAVIS <note>John Davies (1679–1732), a Welsh classicist and editor</note> had set his hand to this work, and that he would not have attempted it without the help of handwritten manuscripts, I consulted the library catalogs to see if anything could be hoped for from there. There were, however, only two manuscript codices in the Bodleian Library which *Davis* had ordered to be compared with the printed editions. *But not without a sense of regret, which returned to him because of money spent without fruit, as HUDSON writes to J. C. WOLF in the "Treasury of La Croze," Volume II, page 99.* One manuscript, certainly, is recent...

<note>original: "Galeo"</note> Gale’s advice, in the notes to Iamblichus’ *On the Mysteries* V, 4. Most truly <note>original: "La Crozius"</note> La Croze wrote to <note>original: "Moshemium"</note> Mosheim in Volume III of the *Treasury of Letters*, page 225: *I warn again that Porphyry’s book will never be pleasing to the Learned of all nations, unless it comes forth together with the version of <note>original: "B. Feliciani"</note> Benedictus Felicianus, which will also be found very convenient in many places for correcting the Greek text.* I have followed that advice, and thus that most inept version by F. de Fogerolles, and that of Joannes Valentini—which is only slightly better—had to give way to Felicianus. For although he is said to be insufficiently concise and redundant, and not to have achieved that clarity which such length requires, by the celebrated <note>original: "P. D. Huetio"</note> Pierre Daniel Huet in *On Famous Translators*, Book II, page 222; and though I would not say he perfectly possesses all those qualities which make a true translator—namely, scrupulousness in explaining meanings, faithfulness in expressing words, diligence in showing the "color" <note>the stylistic tone or "flavor" of the original</note>, clarity, elegance, and that which corresponds to the Author and his character, and other things of this kind—nevertheless, he is commended for most of them and snatches the palm <note>wins the prize</note> from the others. He also made use of a much better manuscript than others did, though even that one was not fully cleansed of errors, and therefore he frequently bears witness to the integrity of the writing. I often grieved that, content to have expressed the sense, he left the reader in doubt as to which specific word he had found in the source. I also wish he had not followed the bad example of translators who force the Author’s verses into meter, for from that it is usually uncertain what they actually read.

I come now to the Editions. A work never sufficiently praised—to speak with <note>original: "L. Holstenio"</note> Lucas Holstenius in his *Life of Porphyry*, chapter 8—that great glory of Italy, <note>original: "Petrus Victorius"</note> Piero Vettori, brought to light at Florence in the year <term>1548</term> <note>original: "cIɔ. Iɔ. XLVIII."</note> together with the same author's <margin>Saxius, *Onomasticon*, Part III, p. 587.</margin> *Sentences Leading to the Intelligible* <note>original: "πρὸς τὰ νοητὰ ἀφορμ."</note> and Michael of Ephesus’ *Scholia on Aristotle’s Four Books on the Parts of Animals* <note>original: "σχολ. εἰς τέσσαρα τοῦ Ἀριστ. περὶ ζώων μορίων"</note>. Vettori added some observations, but these are occupied almost entirely with Eusebius, and he did not even compare all the places which that author had taken from Our Author, and sometimes did so not very accurately—for example, in Book IV, section 11—not even mentioning that Porphyry had derived all those things from Josephus into his own fields.

That First Edition was followed by F. de Fogerolles, Counselor and Physician to the King of France, who, having made a Latin version from the Greek copy, illustrated with scholia and prefaces (as he says), published it at Lyon in France (not Leiden <note>original: "Lugduni Batavorum"</note>, as <note>original: "Weinrichius"</note> Weinrich thought in *Leipzig Miscellany*, Vol. IV, p. 176) in the twentieth year of the preceding century. What he achieved he tells us in the Dedicatory Epistle (which I did not wish to prefix in its entirety to this Edition, lest I abuse your patience, Gentle Reader <note>original: "L. B." / "Lector Benevole"</note>); I will speak in his own words: "We undertook at our leisure to translate the Greek writer Porphyry, rescued from the shadows; in which version we preferred to express the flow of the meanings rather than the words. For it is difficult (says Saint Jerome) when following foreign languages not to fall away somewhere; it is also arduous to preserve the same beauty in a translation of famous sayings: something is signified by the property of a single word; I do not have the means with me to express it: and while I seek to fulfill the meaning by a long circuit, I scarcely measure out short spaces. Add to this the twists of hyperbaton <note>a figure of speech where the natural order of words is changed</note>, the dissimilarities of cases, the varieties of figures, and finally the very property of the language itself, which if I interpret word-for-word, sounds absurd; if, out of necessity, I change something in the order or the speech, I shall seem to [fail] the duty of a translator..."

Regarding the integrity of the Greek context and the diligence applied in cleansing the readings, I will not deny that <term>Petrus Victorius</term> <note>Pietro Vettori (1499–1585), a towering Italian scholar of the Renaissance known for his editions of Aristotle and other Greek classics.</note> applied so much study in emending them that he seems to have brought much aid to <term>Porphyry</term>. Nevertheless, he did not erase every stain, nor was he able to restore several mutilated passages which crept in through the ignorance of former times and the vice of the Copyists. I, however, have found a great number of errors after him, the series of which has been noted by us in the margin of the work, and we do not doubt that an even greater number can be noted by another in the future.

He had also added a *Synopsis of Pythagorean Abstinence* <note>original: "Synopsin Apoches Pythagoricae"</note> expressed in verse, and a *Double Dissertation, on Heroic Virtues, and Christian Abstinence*. Nor have I neglected these observations, as I did not think them entirely foolish everywhere. Yet, as to what should be judged of the man's industry, let <term>Holstenius</term> <note>Lucas Holste (1596–1661), a German humanist and geographer who served as the Vatican librarian.</note> speak in the passage cited: *<term>Bernardus Felicianus</term> expressed it excellently in the Latin language; neglecting this, someone or other recently in France, with a most foolish version—or rather a continuous delirium—has most foully contaminated this excellent work. So that among all the types of evils with which an angry deity has hitherto pressed upon the spirit and name of Porphyry, I would easily consider this the foremost: that he fell into the hands of such a bad physician.* <note>The "bad physician" is a scathing reference to Franciscus Fogerollaeus (François de Fogerolles), whose 1606 translation was widely mocked by scholars for its inaccuracies.</note>

The last edition, as far as I know, is that of <term>Ioannes Valentini</term>, which appeared with his new translation at Cambridge in the fifty-fifth year of the previous century <note>1655</note>. He added *Little Annotations* <note>original: "Annotatiunculas"</note>, as he calls them, which ought to also be read here; except that I have omitted one or two places in which he was merely correcting the errors of the typesetters. Incorrectly, <term>P. Petitus</term> <note>Pierre Petit (1617–1687), a French physician and scholar.</note> in *Observations*, Book 1, chapter 5, and others, attribute this version to <term>L. Holstenius</term>. Truly, what should be decided regarding Valentini's merits you will best gather from his own preface. He complains that he was destitute of all aids, and that he had not even seen the Latin interpreter mentioned by <term>Holstenius</term>. He was able to procure no manuscript codices, and used only the Florentine and French editions. Most damaging was that he everywhere stuffed into the text readings which he himself had forged, and, corrupting the healthiest passages, thrust in those things which had been born in his own brain. He was the first to divide these books into sections or paragraphs, though <term>Fogerollaeus</term> had already prefixed "arguments" <note>summaries of the content</note>, which <term>Valentini</term> mostly followed; nor were these to be erased by me, both because of the use they can provide, and because they are occasionally illustrated in the notes.

Aided by these supports, I have devoted my labor to the books which the Philosopher wrote to <term>Firmus Castricius</term>, his friend and fellow student, to recall him from error and to confute those things with which <term>Heraclides Ponticus</term>, <term>Hermachus the Epicurean</term>, and others—and specifically <term>Claudius Neapolitanus</term>—had defended <term>meat-eating</term> <note>original: κρεωφαγίαν (kreophagia), the practice of eating flesh</note>.

In establishing the text, I have followed the Cambridge Edition, yet in such a way that I might erase what he had rashly poured in, and where he manifestly erred, I might substitute truer readings—never, however, unless the authority of the manuscripts sanctioned it. I am pleased by those words of the most polished <term>D'Orville</term> <note>Jacques Philippe d'Orville (1696–1751), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> in the Preface to *Chariton*: that learned and prudent men can in no way deserve better of ancient writers today than if they oppose themselves with all their might to the license with which now the skilled and unskilled, the young and the old, [engage] in disturbing...

If anything seemed disjointed or corrupt, such as those instances where one must rely on <note>original: "solo ingenii remigio," literally "the rowing of one's own intellect alone"</note> the power of one's own intellect, I have indicated it in the notes. Regarding the changing of punctuation marks or the <term>accent</term> <note>Referring to the Greek tonal accents which were standardized long after Porphyry but were crucial for 18th-century editors.</note>, as happens not infrequently, I acted with less hesitation if the passage could thus be restored, for there is no danger to the Author from such changes.

The primary consideration had to be for the language and style. And indeed, here the style turns toward the <term>Attic manner of speaking</term> <note>A classical Greek style characterized by purity, elegance, and restraint, modeled on the writers of 5th-century BC Athens.</note>, though it is somewhat harsher, adapted to the era and the subject matter. The expressions themselves are often elegant and do not depart from the example of the best writers, as has been noted throughout the commentary. However, <term>transpositions</term> <note>original: "traiectiones," referring to the rearrangement of word order.</note> or <term>hyperbaton</term> <note>A rhetorical figure where the natural word order is disrupted for emphasis or style.</note> are exceedingly frequent. For although the Greek and Latin languages are not subject to that slavish and uniform order and sequence of words like modern languages, one is still not permitted to mix and disturb everything, unless we wish to sin against the elegance and clarity of the composition, as <term>D’Orville</term> <note>Jacques Philippe d'Orville (1696–1751), a celebrated Dutch classical scholar.</note> well noted elsewhere. Neglect of this fact has often given birth to corrections that were by no means necessary. For this reason, I do not care for those who come to these exercises to correct rather than to read. I have often transcribed the full and undiminished credit for a proposed emendation to others who saw the same thing before me, as no one of even slight refinement is ignorant that such a practice is a duty in a book of this sort. Nor have I sought out opportunities to emend other authors, unless a passage presented itself naturally which I could not do without; for I do not follow the counsel of those who love to display their <term>adversaria</term> <note>A scholar's miscellaneous notes or journals.</note> everywhere, which is truly to subject one specific author to a collection of miscellaneous observations.

With the Learned Author, I had to wander through various branches of erudition; yet I had to be careful not to linger on "commonplaces," as they call them, since those public granaries are open to everyone daily. Nor do I deny that I have engaged with these books without a sense of pleasure. To each his own is beautiful: to me, those writers who hand down things worthy of memory—customs, rituals, religions, and precepts for living—are the best, in which genre everyone knows our <term>Malchus</term> <note>The original Syrian name of Porphyry, meaning "King."</note> excels. <term>Brucker</term> <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), author of a massive and influential history of philosophy.</note> spoke well of him in his *Critical History of Philosophy*, Vol. II, p. 257: *It cannot be said how great a knowledge of ancient doctrine and history he acquired for himself, which Authors he read, excerpted, and whose fragments he preserved. If it had been permitted for him to use these correctly, rather than through a mediocrity of judgment and the vanity of superstition and the detestable and deceptive philosophy he followed, we would perhaps not have anyone in all of antiquity whom we would prefer over Porphyry.* 

Furthermore, no one will understand the rituals of our religion and the Church, such as they once were and from where they took their origin, unless he has had him and other <term>Platonists</term> <note>Specifically the Neoplatonists, who deeply influenced early Christian theology and liturgy.</note> as teachers. Truly, those who occupy themselves with great zeal in some trivial writer seem to me to manage the matter no differently than if someone, several centuries from now, were to take up some cold and tasteless <term>naenia</term> <note>A funeral dirge or a "silly trifle."</note>—of which this age is so fertile—to illustrate and explain for himself. 

However, I experienced a province more laborious than I had thought. For when you think yourself well-versed in the decrees of <term>Plato</term> and <term>Pythagoras</term>, immediately darkness is often poured over them by the "recent" Platonists, as they are called. For after the <term>Pythagorean philosophy</term> had infused itself into the Platonic, those men, although they consider nothing more divine or excellent than their own leader, often nevertheless [regard] their master...

I recall that **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the influential Christian theologian.</note> noted this somewhere regarding our Author. Indeed, even those very men not infrequently disagree among themselves, as you will see observed in the proper place. And yet, in these books you may find many things which—whether you consider the formulas of speech or the precepts themselves—might seem not much removed from our own sacred teachings. No one who knows the Author and remembers what he plotted against the Christians will wonder at this. For this was common to him along with other philosophers of this family <note>Referring to the Neoplatonists.</note>: while taking many things from the Christians (through whom, however, they did not wish to appear to have made progress), they strove to deceive them with this commentary, as if the disagreement were not so great; and to show their own followers that it was not necessary to seek from the schools of Christians those things which were praised as more wholesome in our religion, since those same things were handed down by the Philosophers. I recall this was excellently observed by the distinguished man, J. L. MOSHEIM in his *Dissertation on the Church Disturbed by the Platonists*. I wish that, besides those other things which the celebrated ERNESTI <note>Johann August Ernesti (1707–1781), a famous German rationalist theologian and philologist.</note>, that splendid light of Germany, recently advised on this matter, those who love to compare the tablets of the New Testament with writers of this kind would call it to mind; lest they allow themselves to be led into error by the similarity of words, since those authors signify entirely different things by sayings of this sort.

But I also had to compare ancient authors—**Plato**, **Josephus**, **Plutarch**—from whom Porphyry took many things, and the fragments of others which he used had to be sought out. No light labor also had to be given to the ancient Theologians who had inserted Porphyrian passages into their own works: **Eusebius**, **Cyril**, **Theodoret**, and **Jerome**. No one will wonder that the latter <note>St. Jerome.</note> took many things from our Author in his books *Against Jovinianus*, who remembers that both championed almost the same cause, but with a different purpose. Let us hear the man himself in Book II, 7: *What is it to us, whose conversation is in heaven <note>original: "quorum conversatio in coelis est" — a reference to Philippians 3:20.</note>, who [are] above Pythagoras... who subdue the resisting flesh, which drags us toward the incitements of lusts, by fasting? The eating of meat and the drinking of wine, and the filling of the belly, is the nursery of lust.* Therefore, the more frequently I found those men in citing testimonies, the more easily the true reading could be restored; if many had remembered them, they would not have rashly disturbed Porphyry's writing, or they would have healed it with a more suitable remedy.

You understand now for the most part, Kind Reader <note>original: "B. L." for "Benevole Lector".</note>, who it was who created this leisure for us. In his native tongue he was called **Malchus**, which was also his father's name. But since that fell upon Greek ears as unusual and "barbarous," **Longinus**, his teacher, called him **Porphyry**, from purple <note>The Greek "Porphyrios" means "clad in purple."</note>, a truly royal color; for that is what "Malchus" signified in the dialect of the Syrians <note>Malchus is derived from the Semitic root for "King."</note>. But I must not dwell on his life, as the most learned L. HOLSTENIUS has dealt with him with great effort in his *Dissertation on the life and writings of Porphyry the Philosopher*.

Therefore, I have not sought out judgments and testimonies, being content—as had been done by previous Editors—to prefix the Philosopher's life and the index of his Works from **Eunapius** and **Suidas**, together with the version of **Felicianus**, who added a few things from Eunapius which other Editors had left untouched.

P. VI-

to **Fabricius** <note>Johannes Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a prolific German scholar and bibliographer.</note> it was also published in Volume IV of his *Greek Library*; therefore, it was not at all necessary to increase the bulk of this edition. The distinguished man **Johann Brucker** <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), a pioneer in the history of philosophy.</note> also dealt with this subject with great diligence in his *Critical History of Philosophy*, Vol. II, p. 236. He did not leave untouched the question debated among the learned: whether the Philosopher <note>Porphyry.</note>, after he had given his name to the Christian religion, subsequently defected from it, as some writers of Ecclesiastical History seem to suggest. Reflecting on this, the learned **J. F. Thomas** had decided to prefix to his edition a *Dissertation on Porphyry’s Apostasy*, in which he intended to demonstrate that Christian rites were known and familiar to our Philosopher, but that he had not—as **La Croze** and others believed—defected from the Christian religion to Platonism. See *Thesaurus of La Croze*, Vol. I, p. 341. That attempt indeed lacked success, as was just mentioned; however, the letters survive in which Thomas and **Siber**, both eminent men, discussed this argument. These were made public in the first volume of the *New Leipzig Miscellanies*, and I wished to append them to this edition so that his plan might be honored.

I would almost believe that Porphyry simulated for a time a mind not foreign to the Christian religion—as those clever men were accustomed to do—even adapting his formulas of speech and his doctrine to the precepts of the Christians, the better to circumvent the unwary. From this arose the conviction that the Philosopher had given his name to those sacred rites, but then recoiled from them as the cause of Platonism demanded. And for that reason, perhaps, the Emperor **Constantine** wished the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who disputed the nature of Christ's divinity.</note> to be called *Porphyrians* by public edict; I see that scholars disagree on the reason for this nickname. The matter itself is recorded in **Socrates’** <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380–439 AD), a historian of the early church.</note> *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, ch. 9, and in the *Final Law* of the *Theodosian Code* regarding Heretics, and *Law 6* of the *Justinian Code* regarding Manichaean and Samaritan heretics. This is certainly true if, as it seemed to the distinguished **Heineccius** <note>Johann Gottlieb Heineccius (1681–1741), a famous German jurist.</note>, you punctuate the passage differently than is usually done: *But just as the Arians are named after Arius, so by the law of Constantine of blessed memory, they are called Porphyrians after Porphyry because of the similarity of their impiety.* The Emperor wanted to take care that the credulous were not deceived under a plausible name. To be sure, other causes might be added which can be read in Socrates, yet in that law it is expressly stated so that they might not abuse the name of "Christians." For Arius had also wished to be counted among the number of Christians, but the ancient theologians excluded him from it on every side.

Finally, there were also those who thought Porphyry had given his name to the Christian religion at the very end of his life, which they gathered from **Jerome’s** *Chronicle*; but the falsity of this opinion was long ago demonstrated.

I have detained you long enough, Best of Readers; however, I still want you to know one thing: I have placed the Latin translation next to the Greek text and added notes to each page to consult your convenience. Let the distinguished **Perizonius** <note>Jacobus Perizonius (1651–1715), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> explain the reason for this practice in the preface prefixed to *Aelian*. As for you, in the solemn formula: farewell and look with favor [on this work]. Given at **Deventer** <note>A city in the Netherlands.</note> on the very Kalends of April <term>1767</term> <note>original: cIɔ. Iɔ. CC. LXVII.</note>.

# PIERO VETTORI’S
# PREFACE.

# PIERO VETTORI
### *To those devoted to the Greek arts, written in the Greek tongue.*

Our Prince <note>Cosimo I de' Medici (1519–1574), Duke of Florence and a major patron of the arts and sciences.</note> is not of the kind of men who, captured by the brilliance of outward honor and a desire for empty glory, wish to keep distinguished and useful things for themselves alone, seeking to surpass all others by their possession. On the contrary, he believes those things to be true goods which are held in common, and which can be obtained by all who show themselves worthy of them. Just as he has often declared this to us in many ways, so now he will demonstrate it to many nations by this decision: for he has determined to publish the ancient writers sought out with the greatest diligence by his ancestors <note>The Medici family had spent generations collecting rare manuscripts from the East.</note>, and rescued at great expense from the ruins and fires of the cruel war in Greece <note>Referring to the fall of the Byzantine Empire and the subsequent conflicts that threatened ancient libraries.</note>. 

In doing so, he looks to the advantage of students and the memory of learned men, who wished to benefit posterity through their labors and excellence of mind, and who spent their entire lives in these cares and studies. Yet, having long suffered an unfair fate, these authors lay hidden in darkness; and just as they themselves were exposed to various misfortunes, so they brought no fruit—or very little—to those eager for the noble arts. 

He has decided not only to bring forth those who have not seen the light of day for many centuries, but also to issue again many works which have already been printed in a faulty and mutilated state. These are now thoroughly cleansed with the greatest care and restored to their full form with the help of the same resources and an abundance of the most faithful manuscripts. Therefore, this task is now being undertaken; work is being done so that the Prince's honorable and pious will may be brought to completion, for his own dignity and the benefit of students. 

In the meantime, desiring to give some sample of this work that is being woven, and to be the first to bring such joyful news to the ears of the learned—even though the preparation for such a great undertaking is not yet finished—I have, as it were, run ahead and seen to the publication of this small volume. 

In this volume are contained:
*   Porphyry's four books *On Abstaining from Killing and Eating Living Creatures* <note>original: *de non caedendis deuorandifque animantibus*; today commonly titled *De Abstinentia*.</note>, which are greatly celebrated even by our own authors.
*   Another short book by the same author in which certain subtle and serious questions concerning divine matters are contained, based on the decrees of Plato.
*   The declarations of Michael of Ephesus <note>An 11th-century Byzantine scholar known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note>, one of the later interpreters of Aristotle, on the four books *On the Parts of Animals*.

<summary>Piero Vettori introduces a new edition of Greek texts—including Porphyry and Michael of Ephesus—sponsored by Cosimo I de' Medici, emphasizing the recovery of lost or corrupted ancient knowledge for the common good.</summary>

# P R E F A C E.

The books of the Tyrian philosopher <note>original: "Tyrii philosophi"; referring to Porphyry of Tyre, a 3rd-century Neoplatonist</note>; and his precise discussion of those matters, once superstition is removed, will be wonderfully useful on account of the manifold and varied exposition of hidden and elegant subjects. He also makes frequent use of examples from ancient writers—now lost to the passage of time—either to confirm his own opinions or to refute the judgments and customs of those same authors. Indeed, the small book in which he wished to encourage the perception of things that are discerned only by the mind and by reason is entirely "golden" <note>original: "aureolus"; a term of high praise for a small but perfect work</note>; and it encompasses much obscure doctrine in few words. I also thought that the brief explanation by the Ephesian <note>original: "Ephesii"; likely referring to Michael of Ephesus, a 12th-century commentator</note> regarding the books of that excellent author would not be unwelcome. I am well aware that he was by no means equal to Porphyry in dignity or learning; however, because those Aristotelian books are partly obscure and very difficult, and because they are illustrated by no other Greek author that I know of—excepting the paraphrase by Metochites <note>Theodore Metochites, a Byzantine scholar and statesman</note>, which has not yet been printed—no better or more learned work should be expected in any respect.

Regarding the integrity of the text and the diligence applied in refining the reading, I will not deny that the books of Porphyry were in a terrible state due to the ignorance of former times, and were greatly corrupted by the faults of copyists. Nevertheless, by comparing many manuscripts, we have applied so much effort to correcting them that we seem to have brought them much aid. Although we were not able to erase every blemish, nor restore several places that were crippled or diminished, our faithfulness and diligence were certainly not lacking. We have also provided this same care in the scholia <term>scholia: explanatory notes or comments inserted into the margins of ancient manuscripts</term> of the Ephesian, to their great benefit. Farewell, you talented and learned men, and expect more and better things shortly from the liberality of our most humane Prince and his extraordinary love for you.

# THE PREFACE OF P. VICTORIUS,

->which he had placed before the notes.<-

### TO SCHOLARS.

Since I had consulted several excellent manuscripts to assist Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher known for his work on logic and his vegetarian treatise</note>, who was poorly preserved and neglected on all sides, and had improved his text in many parts, I attempted to see if I could bring him aid by another path, which I found to be quite useful. For I knew that Eusebius Pamphilus <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History"</note>, Porphyry's contemporary, had often taken testimonies from these works in his books <term>The Preparation for the Gospel</term> <note>original: "προπαρασκευῆς εὐαγγελικῆς" (Praeparatio Evangelica), a work by Eusebius defending Christianity against paganism</note>. Although Eusebius, not without cause, criticizes him and harasses him with every kind of insult, he was nevertheless captivated by the Author’s erudition and brings forward many passages—especially from these books—by which he either proves what he wishes to confirm or demonstrates that Porphyry thought falsely or wrongly about a certain matter.

For Porphyry was not very fair toward our piety <note>Christianity</note>, which was already spreading widely and taking firm root, and he was indeed very hostile to the Christian name. However, in these specific books, he touches on nothing that harms our faith; rather, he fits wonderfully with our institutions and customs. For just as he approved with all his soul the religion handed down from his ancestors and stood strongly by it against adversaries, he also showed himself to be a most temperate man. He was content with a very meager diet; for we can truly say that he was an enemy and the sharpest critic of the vices of the belly and the throat, and that while still living, he escaped from the prison and bonds of the body.

This character is clearly understood not only from the fact that he came from the excellent discipline of that most grave man and the most severe household of Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism and Porphyry’s teacher</note>, but also from the many most holy precepts collected by him in this work. This was the cause of salvation, I believe, for this subtle writing, filled with great learning, while his other labors have perished—deservedly, by the judgment of a more severe index <note>Likely referring to the Roman imperial or ecclesiastical bans on Porphyry's "Against the Christians"</note>—and have been erased from all human memory.

I therefore diligently examined all the passages cited by Pamphilus [Eusebius], and when I found many significant variations in those readings, I preferred—since Porphyry’s text has already been printed and the wording found in his own manuscripts retained—to note all the variations here. For even in Eusebius, not everything was preserved purely and completely, although not a few things seem to read better there. I think this happened because the writings of Pamphilus were held in great honor among Christians, since they bring much light to our history and diligently refute the empty rites of the pagans. Porphyry’s books, however, because of the justified hatred he had stirred up against himself for other reasons, lay neglected for a long time and were almost consumed by decay and filth.

Furthermore, I am well aware of the custom of the ancients, who used considerable liberty when quoting from other authors; if they retained the general meaning, they often did not care for the exact words or their order. Therefore, thinking this the safer path, I have noted whatever differences I could observe in the testimonies cited from these books by that writer [Eusebius], and I have also briefly indicated at times which reading I am more inclined to favor.

<summary>In this preface, the editor Pietro Vettori explains how he used the citations in Eusebius's "Preparation for the Gospel" to correct and restore the neglected and corrupted texts of the philosopher Porphyry. He notes the irony that while Porphyry was an enemy of Christianity, his ascetic teachings in these books align with Christian values, which helped preserve this specific work while his anti-Christian writings were destroyed.</summary>

# I. VALENTIN’S
## PREFACE.

It is not in my nature, friend Reader, to disparage the labors of others, even if they were completed under a rather unlucky omen. However, so that you may understand why I have undertaken a new version of Porphyry’s *On Abstinence* <note>original: "de Abstinentia" (On Abstinence from Animal Food), a four-volume treatise arguing for vegetarianism based on Neoplatonic philosophy</note>, listen for a moment to the illustrious Lucas Holstenius <note>Lucas Holstenius (1596–1661) was a prominent German humanist scholar and geographer who served as the librarian of the Vatican</note> complaining thus in his *Dissertation on the life and writings of this Philosopher*:

*“Four books were written by Porphyry on abstinence from eating animals, a work never sufficiently praised, which Bernardus Felicianus expressed excellently in the Latin tongue. Since that version was neglected, someone or other in France recently contaminated this excellent work with a most foolish version, or rather a continuous madness: so that among all the types of misfortunes with which an angry Deity has hitherto oppressed the spirit and name of Porphyry, I would easily consider this one the greatest—that he fell into the hands of such a bad doctor.”*

I wanted to try, good Reader, whether I could play the part of the physician somewhat more successfully. Nevertheless, I prepared this interpretation while deprived of all assistance. I did not even happen to see the Latin interpreter mentioned by Holstenius. I was unable to procure any manuscript codices, though I sought them diligently. I had only two printed editions: the Florentine, and the French edition which follows it <term>step for step</term> <note>original: "κατὰ πόδας" (kata podas), meaning to follow closely or literally</note> even where the former hallucinates most wretchedly. Nevertheless, I hope that infinite passages have been healed by us, partly from Plutarch, Josephus, and Eusebius <note>Ancient authors whose works contain overlapping quotes or themes that helped the editor reconstruct the corrupted text</note>, and partly from our own conjecture; so much so that there is perhaps only one or two places about which anyone might strongly complain. 

For the rest, I shall conclude with the words of the most learned Petavius <note>Dionysius Petavius (Denis Pétau, 1583–1652), a French Jesuit theologian and scholar</note> in his *Letter to the Reader* prefixed to Epiphanius: *“I would wish, Kind Reader, that you approach this study of ours in such a way that you understand that we have not been entirely free from error here; but if you find errors in it, you should balance them against the many good points—if indeed there are many good points in my work—or against the equal or fewer points, and enjoy those, while granting pardon for the others.”*

<summary>J. Valentin introduces his new edition of Porphyry’s "On Abstinence," explaining that he aimed to "heal" the text after previous editors had corrupted it. Despite a lack of manuscripts, he used comparisons with other ancient authors and his own scholarly intuition to correct the work.</summary>

<header>THE DEDICATION OF G. B. FELICIANO.</header>

# TO ALVISE MICHIEL

### GIOVANNI BERNARDO FELICIANO SENDS GREETINGS. <note>The "S." stands for "Salutem," a standard Latin epistolary greeting.</note>

---

How much zeal was always applied by the ancients to the regulation and composition of morals can be clear to anyone who considers the ancient method of philosophizing. Indeed, all the schools of the philosophers are seen to have been held more for the sake of establishing a way of life than for the sake of contemplation and theoretical knowledge. This is declared both by the ancient discipline of Pythagoras and later by the instruction of Socrates, from whose disputations every method of living civilly and morally emanated. Many others, and especially those two splendid lights of wisdom, Plato and Xenophon, handed this down to posterity most seriously and elegantly in their literary monuments. For since a desire is implanted in man by nature not so much for *finding* happiness as for *attaining* it, the Philosophers did not think it was enough if they labored in finding happiness, unless they also devised a way by which we might be able to reach it. 

Just as the investigation of the nature of things fortifies for us a path toward finding the first cause of all and the first author of all, God; so the integrity and purity of life, which we fashion within ourselves by imitating the goodness of God, makes us fit to possess Him. Indeed, the supreme power of goodness and uprightness can easily be perceived from this: that no action or speech—not even among the wicked—has authority unless either uprightness, or at least some appearance of uprightness, underlies it. For in truth, whatever is not stabilized and supported by the solidity of uprightness, no matter how much genius and craftsmanship it is composed with, it must eventually appear to everyone as it truly is—vain and ridiculous—and be held in contempt. 

Wherefore, most illustrious Alvise, although you excel in nobility of birth, wealth, and genius, you have nevertheless considered that your life must be established so moderately and holily that you have embraced in a wonderful manner this part of philosophy which looks toward morals—which you have been accustomed to call the "soul of philosophy"—as befits one who is truly good, and *a branch fashioned by Zeus entirely upon truth*, <note>original: "πᾶν ἐπ’ ἀλαθείᾳ πεπλασμένον ἐκ διὸς ἔρνος" — a Greek poetic fragment likely referencing Pindar or a similar lyric style, emphasizing divine and truthful origin.</note> as that famous man says. This you display both by the most tranquil type of life which you lead, and by the most noble thoughts with which you daily keep your soul raised up from the disturbances of the world and the filth of the common crowd. For this reason, since those writers have also greatly pleased you who would track down the truth not only with subtle and sharp disputations, but...

<summary>In this dedication, Giovanni Bernardo Feliciano praises Alvise Michiel for prioritizing moral philosophy and the "integrity of life" over mere theoretical study. He argues that true happiness and a connection to the divine are achieved through the imitation of God's goodness and the practice of virtue.</summary>

# D E D I C A T I O N

...[these studies] also at the same time might so instruct and purify the life of man that they might lift our minds toward that **becoming like God as far as possible** <note>original Greek: "τὴν ὁμοίωσιν τοῦ θεοῦ κατὰ τὸ δυνατόν". This is a famous concept from Plato’s *Theaetetus* regarding the goal of human life.</note>, as Plato wished. You repeatedly encouraged me, and even by your own right imposed upon me and commanded, that if I could find anything of this kind among the ancient authors, I should rescue it from the darkness and take care that it come out into the light. 

For my part, although I was distracted by other occupations and deterred by the awareness of my own modest learning, I nonetheless decided that I must not fail to obey your commands, at least in some part. This was especially so since I regard the person who gave the command with the highest respect and veneration, and I saw that the things commanded were of such a nature that being engaged in their investigation could not fail to be extremely useful. Therefore, having undertaken the task, I sought out several Greek authors of this kind, and I wished to begin this edition with this work of Porphyry, thinking that, both from the name of the author and the subject matter of which he treats, the reading of it would be pleasant to many.

For Porphyry is held in such high esteem in both Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy that he can easily attract students of philosophy by his name alone. The work itself is filled with varied and manifold learning: for since it deals with **abstinence from eating animals**, he treats this not only in the manner of Pythagoras, but also of Plato, and finally in a theological manner. 

For although he discusses the harm done to animals and the power of **unclean spirits** <note>original: "daemonum". In this context, Neoplatonists believed that consuming meat attracted lower, denser spirits to the soul.</note> which is secretly drawn in from bloody feasts of this kind—following the decrees of the Pythagorean and Platonic schools and certain others—nonetheless, everything aims toward the goal (as he himself also seems to explain) that, by reducing nourishment, the bond of the soul—which is the body—may be thinned and weakened. Thus, the mind, released from the disturbances of the passions, may be able to ascend more freely to contemplate and enjoy divine things. Furthermore, by removing more delicate feasts, a simpler diet might both prevent our care from being diverted from more serious matters and cut away every occasion for gluttony. The purpose of this argument is nothing other than to demonstrate that the principle of fasting and abstinence is approved not only by divine law but also by natural law. So that everything might be more clearly understood, we thought it would be appropriate to translate the life of the author written by Eunapius and place it before the work itself. Farewell.

# THE LIFE OF PORPHYRY.

## THE LIFE OF PORPHYRY.

### FROM THE COMMENTARY OF EUNAPIUS,
*In which he collected the lives of Sophists and Philosophers.*

Tyre was the homeland of Porphyry, the foremost city of the ancient Phoenicians, and his ancestors were not without renown. Having received a fitting education, he advanced and progressed so much that he became a student of Longinus <note>Cassius Longinus (c. 213–273 AD) was a celebrated rhetorician and philosophical critic, often called a "living library."</note> and within a short time brought honor to his teacher. At that time, Longinus was a kind of living library and a walking museum <note>original: "βιβλιοθήκη τις ἦν ἔμψυχος καὶ περιπατοῦν μουσεῖον". This phrase highlights Longinus's legendary memory and broad learning.</note>, and he had been tasked with judging the works of the ancients, just as many others had done before him—among whom Dionysius from Caria <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a famous historian and critic from the 1st century BC.</note> was the most illustrious of all. 

In the city of the Syrians <note>Referring to Tyre/Phoenicia, then part of the Roman province of Syria.</note>, Porphyry was originally called Malchus; this name signifies "king" <note>original: "Μάλχος". This is a Hellenized form of the Semitic root *m-l-k* (melek), meaning king.</note>. But Longinus renamed him Porphyry <note>original: "Πορφύριον". The name refers to the "Tyrian Purple," the royal color of imperial robes, thus preserving the "kingly" meaning of his original name in a Greek context.</note>, changing his designation to refer to the royal color of imperial clothing. Under Longinus, he received the highest education; he reached the peak of all grammar <note>In antiquity, "grammar" encompassed not just linguistics, but the deep study and criticism of literature.</note> just as his teacher had, as well as the peak of rhetoric. However, he leaned even further beyond these, absorbing every form of Philosophy. 

For Longinus was by far the best of the men of that time in all things. A great number of his books are in circulation, and those that circulate are admired; if he censured any of the ancients, the previously held opinion did not prevail, but rather Longinus’s judgment always carried the day. Having been led through his early education in this way and being admired by everyone, Porphyry desired to see great Rome, so that he might take hold of the city through his wisdom. As soon as he arrived there and entered into the circle of the great Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), the founding figure of Neoplatonism, whose teachings focused on the ascent of the soul to "The One."</note>, he forgot all others,

...and he devoted himself entirely to that man <note>Plotinus</note>. Being insatiably filled with that instruction, and with those fountain-like and divinely-inspired discourses, he was satisfied to remain a listener for some time, as he himself says. Then, overcome by the sheer magnitude of the doctrines, he came to loathe his own body and the very fact of being human. Having sailed to Sicily across the strait and the Charybdis <note>A dangerous whirlpool in Greek mythology, located in the Strait of Messina</note>—where Odysseus is said to have sailed—he could not bear to look upon a city or even to hear the sound of a human voice. In this way, he cast aside everything in him that felt pain or pleasure. Stretching himself out toward Lilybaeum <note>Modern Marsala; one of the three capes of Sicily that points toward Libya</note>, he lay there wasting away and starving himself to death, refusing food and avoiding the path of men.

But the great Plotinus did not keep a "blind watch" <note>original: ἀλαοσκοπίην — a Homeric term for failing to notice something</note> over these events. Following in his footsteps, or rather searching for the youth who had fled, he came upon him as he lay there. He provided him with a wealth of arguments to call back his soul, which was just then on the verge of flying away from the body, and he strengthened the body to retain the soul. Thus, Porphyry was restored to life and arose. Plotinus then set down the words he had spoken into a book of his writings.

While other philosophers hide their secret doctrines in obscurity—just as poets do with myths—Porphyry praised the remedy of clarity. Having tasted it through experience, he brought these matters into the light by writing a commentary. He himself then returned to Rome and applied himself to his studies with such zeal that he even appeared in public for demonstrations of his learning. The fame of Porphyry was attributed back to Plotinus by every marketplace and every crowd; for while Plotinus seemed heavy and difficult to hear because of the celestial nature of his soul and the oblique, enigmatic style of his discourses, Porphyry was like a "Chain of Hermes" <note>A metaphor for a golden chain of communication reaching from heaven to earth</note> leaning down toward men. Through his varied learning, he announced everything in a clear and pure manner. He himself says (though it seems he wrote this while he was still young) that he never encountered any of the public oracles; yet in this very book he records, and after these...

He treats many other such matters, explaining how one ought to take care of these things. He also recounts that he drove away and expelled a certain **demonic Nature** from a particular bathhouse; the locals used to call this spirit **Kausathas** <note>original: Καυσάθαν — likely a local Syrian or Semitic name for a specific demon or haunting presence</note>. According to his own records, his most distinguished fellow students were **Origen** <note>This is Origen the Pagan, a fellow student of Plotinus, not the famous Christian Church Father of the same name</note>, **Amelius**, and **Aquilinus**. While some of their writings have been preserved, not a single one of their discourses is in common circulation. This is because their style was largely unappealing <note>original: ἀκύθηρον — literally "without the grace of Cytherea (Aphrodite)"; unpolished or lacking charm</note>, even if their doctrines were sound and permeated their words.

Porphyry, however, praised these men for their intellectual power. He himself retraced every grace of thought, standing alone as the one who truly revealed and proclaimed the greatness of his teacher <note>Plotinus</note>. He left no branch of education untouched. Indeed, one might wonder and marvel at which of his pursuits was the most earnest: those tending toward the art of **rhetoric**, those bringing precision to **grammar**, those dealing with the science of **numbers** <note>Arithmetic</note>, or those leaning toward **geometry** and **music**.

As for his works on **Philosophy**, his mastery of logic and discourse is beyond easy grasping, and his own unique style is hard to rival. Let his writings on **Physics** and **Theurgy** <term>Theurgy: Literally "god-working"; a system of late-Platonic rituals intended to purify the soul and unite it with the divine</term> be reserved for the sacred rites and mysteries. Thus, the man himself became a kind of "all-mixed" vessel of every virtue. One might look upon the sheer beauty of his language even more than his specific doctrines or the raw power of his arguments.

It also appears that he participated in marriage. A book is still circulated addressed to **Marcella**, who became his wife. He says he married her—even though she was already a mother of five children—not for the sake of having children with her, but so that those she already had might receive a proper education; for these children had belonged to the woman from a previous marriage to a friend of his. He appears to have lived into a very deep old age. In his later years, he left behind many theories that contradicted the books he had written in his youth. Regarding this, one cannot conclude anything other than that as he progressed through life, his beliefs evolved. It is said that he passed away in **Rome**.

# THE LIFE OF PORPHYRY

->FROM<-

# EUNAPIUS.

**Porphyry** was a Tyrian by birth; Tyre was the leading city of the ancient Phoenicians. He was born to parents of noble status. After receiving a liberal education, he made such rapid progress that, while serving as a student of **Longinus**, he soon brought honor to his teacher. Indeed, Longinus was considered in those days a kind of "living library" and a "walking museum" <note>original: *bibliotheca & deambulans musaeum* — a metaphor for a person possessing vast, encyclopedic knowledge</note>. He had dedicated his mind to the critical study of ancient writings, much like **Dionysius of Caria** and many others before him, who was the most famous of all. 

Porphyry was originally called **Malchus** in the Syrian language of his homeland—a name that means "king" in his people's tongue. Later, the name was changed to **Porphyry** <note>meaning "the Purple One"</note> by Longinus, choosing a name associated with the royal purple of an imperial robe. Under Longinus' discipline, he devoted himself to the study of literature with the greatest effort. He reached the absolute heights of **grammar** and **rhetoric**—just as his teacher had—though his heart was not particularly inclined toward the latter. He was also highly accomplished in every branch of **philosophy**. 

For Longinus was easily the leader of all those who flourished in that time. A great number of his books survive and are held in such high esteem that if anyone found fault with an ancient writer, they would not trust their own opinion until the judgment of Longinus had also been consulted.

When Porphyry had been educated in this way and had become a figure of renown, he was seized by a great desire to see Rome, so that he might pursue wisdom in that great city. As soon as he arrived there, he entered into the company of the divine **Plotinus**. Forgetting all others, he dedicated himself entirely to him. Devoting himself to those studies with insatiable hunger, he spent some time drinking in those divine arguments from the sacred spring. 

Later, however, overwhelmed by the magnitude of his contemplations, he began to treat his own body with hatred and to loathe the fact that he was human. Consequently, he sailed to **Sicily** and crossed the strait of **Charybdis** <note>the famous whirlpool from Greek mythology</note>, where **Ulysses** <note>Odysseus</note> is also said to have journeyed. There, he would not permit himself to see a city or hear the voice of a man; so much so...

He had utterly cast off all sense of pain and pleasure; and so, having set out on a steady journey toward Lilybaeum <note>Modern Marsala; one of the three capes of Sicily</note>—which is one of the three promontories of Sicily that faces toward Libya—he cast himself down there. He lay there groaning and enduring, refusing all food, and, as the saying goes, "shunning the tracks of men." <note>A reference to Homer’s description of Bellerophon in the Iliad, wandering alone in grief.</note> Yet this empty searching did not keep the great Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism and Porphyry's teacher</note> away from these events. For he followed immediately—whether because he had a premonition of what would happen, or because he was searching for the young man who had fled—and found him lying there. He devised words for him that might both recall a soul just about to fly away from the body and strengthen the body to retain it. And so, having recovered his spirit, Porphyry rose up. Plotinus later recorded the words he had spoken in a book, among those of his writings that still exist. 

But since philosophers used to hide their secrets with obscure speech, much like poets do with myths, Porphyry—who had approved of the remedy of clarity and tasted it by experience—published these ideas to the light, illuminating them with his commentaries. He himself then returned to Rome and devoted his leisure to the study of oratory, even appearing in public for the sake of display. Nevertheless, every assembly and every gathering attributed Porphyry’s glory back to Plotinus. For Plotinus, on account of the celestial power of his soul and his hidden, enigmatic way of speaking, seemed heavy and difficult to perceive. Porphyry, however, like a kind of "Homeric Chain" <note>A metaphor for a golden chain connecting heaven and earth; here meaning he links high philosophy to human understanding</note> let down to men, expressed everything with ease and transparency through his varied learning and knowledge. 

And he himself says—though perhaps he had written these things when quite young—that he had encountered no public oracle. In the same book, he discusses many other matters regarding what care should be taken of such things: how he had put to flight and cast out a certain demonic nature from a bathhouse, which the locals call *Causathan*. <note>original: "Caufathan"</note> His fellow students, as he himself writes, were quite outstanding: Origen, Amelius, and Aquilinus. Their writings exist, yet no beauty is seen in them, even though their dogmas and opinions are correct and they persist in their words. Porphyry, however, praises the eloquence and dignity of these men, even while he himself surpasses them all in grace; he alone makes his teacher manifest and proclaims him, having omitted no branch of learning. Indeed, anyone might wonder and doubt what subject he seems to have studied most: whether those pertaining to the faculty of oratory, or those which make for the exact inquiry of grammar; those belonging to arithmetic, or those pertaining to geometry or music. Likewise, regarding philosophy, it is uncertain whether he spent more effort on the things of reason <note>Logic and theory</note> or the things of administration <note>Ethics and practical life</note>. For those matters regarding natural and divine contemplation are so sublime that they seem fit to be left to sacred rites and mysteries. Thus, that man stood out as a being perfectly harmonized for every virtue. At one moment, one might admire his words more than his dogmas; at another, his decrees and opinions more than his power of speech. He appears to have taken a wife, for a book is circulated addressed to his wife Marcella, whom—although she was already the mother of five children—

# THE LIFE OF PORPHYRY FROM THE SUDA.

Porphyry, the one who wrote against the Christians; he was properly called "Basileus" <note>original: "Basileus" (Βασιλεύς), which means "King." This was a Greek translation of his native Phoenician name, Malchus.</note>. A philosopher from Tyre <note>A major Phoenician city-state in modern-day Lebanon</note>, he was a student of Amelius (himself a student of Plotinus) and the teacher of Iamblichus. He flourished during the times of Aurelian and lived until the reign of the Emperor Diocletian. He wrote a great many books on philosophy, rhetoric, and grammar. He was also a pupil of Longinus the Critic. Among his works are:

*On Divine Names*, in 1 book.
*On First Principles*, in 2 books.
*On Matter*, in 6 books.
*On the Soul, addressed to Boethus*, in 5 books.
*On Abstinence from Animal Food*, in 4 books.
*On the precept "Know Thyself"*, in 4 books.
*On Incorporeal Things*.
*On the Unity of the Philosophy of Plato and Aristotle*, in 7 books.
*On the History of Julian the Chaldean Philosopher*, in 4 books.
*Arguments Against the Christians*, in 15 books.
*On the Philosophy of Homer*.
*To Aristotle, on the Soul being an Entelechy* <note>An "entelechy" refers to the realization or complete expression of a thing's potential; here, Porphyry debates Aristotle's definition of the soul.</note>.
*Philological History*, in 5 books.
*On Genus, Species, Difference, Property, and Accident* <note>These five terms are known as the "Predicables." This work, often called the Isagoge, became the standard introductory textbook for logic throughout the Middle Ages.</note>.
*On the Sources of the Nile according to Pindar*.
*On the Benefit of Homer for Kings*, in 10 books.
*Miscellaneous Inquiries*, in 7 books.
*On the Preface of Thucydides*.
*To Aristides*, in 7 books.
*On the Art of Minucianus*; and many other works, especially on astronomy—among which is an *Introduction to Astronomy* in three books—and *Grammatical Problems*.

This is that Porphyry who moved his insulting tongue against the Christians. Porphyry, the enemy of the Christians, from the Phoenician city of Tyre.

# AN ACCOUNT OF HIS LIFE AND A LIST OF HIS WORKS FROM THE SUDA.

Porphyry of Tyre, a city in Phoenicia, was a philosopher who was called "King" <note>original: "rex"; a translation of his Semitic birth name, Malchus</note> in his native language. He was a disciple of Amelius, a student of Plotinus, and the teacher of Iamblichus. He was also a student of the critic Longinus. He wrote a great many books, both philosophical and also rhetorical and grammatical: one *On Divine Names*; two *On Principles*; six *On Matter*; five *On the Soul*, addressed to Boethus; four *On Abstinence from Eating Animals*; four *On the Saying of the Wise Man, "Know Thyself"*; a work *On Incorporeals*; seven volumes on the fact *That the Schools of Plato and Aristotle are One and the Same*; four volumes *On the History of Julian the Chaldean Philosopher*; seven volumes *On Aristotle’s Categories*, addressed to Gedalius; and one volume *On the same Categories* in the form of questions and answers. He also wrote *On the Philosophy of Homer*; a work proving *That according to the Opinion of Aristotle the Soul is <term>entelecheia</term>*, that is, a "perfection" or "actualization" <note>original: "ἐντελέχεια"; a core Aristotelian concept describing the full realization of a potential</note>; five volumes of *Philosophical History*; a work *On Genus, Species, Difference, Property, and Accident* <note>This is the famous "Isagoge" or Introduction to logic</note>; *On the Sources of the Nile according to the Opinion of Pindar*; ten volumes *On the Utility Kings can Derive from Homer*; seven volumes of *Miscellaneous Questions*; seven volumes *On the Introduction of Thucydides*, addressed to Aristides; a commentary *On the Rhetorical Art of Minucianus*; and many other works, especially on astronomy, among which is an *Introduction to Astronomy* completed in three books, as well as grammatical questions. He flourished under the reign of Aurelian and lived until the times of Diocletian.

### THE ARGUMENT. <note>This is a summary of the book's contents provided by the editor or translator.</note>

*The first book is divided into three parts: the first of which contains the preface to Firmus Castricius, who had fallen away from the Pythagorean principles to the eating of flesh. §. 1, 2, etc. The second encompasses the arguments by which the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> and Stoics (§. 4, etc.), the Epicureans (§. 7, etc.), and Claudius of Naples (§. 13, etc.) teach that living creatures can be lawfully killed and eaten. The third part contains several points which Porphyry sets forth for a fuller understanding and clarification of the proposed subject. §. 27, etc. First...*

ANIMATE BEINGS.] *Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation* XVII. 8. <note>original: "τῶν ὄντων τοίνυν τὰ μὲν ἄψυχα, τὰ δὲ ἔμψυχα. καὶ τὰ μὲν ἄψυχα, λίθοι, καὶ ξύλα, καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα· τὰ δὲ ἔμψυχα, φυτὰ καὶ ζῶα."</note> "Of existing things, some are inanimate, others are animate. And the inanimate are stones, wood, and such things; while the animate are plants and animals." Plato's opinion is no different (see *Julian, Oration* VI. p. 193. B.) nor is Aristotle's (*History of Animals* VIII. 1). However, our author <note>Porphyry</note> and other Pythagoreans signify "animals" specifically by this word. Compare.

<column-break/>

*Samuel Bochart, Hierozoicon* I. 1. Hence the "life of a plant" <note>original: "ζωὴ φυτοῦ"</note> and the "life of an animate being" <note>original: "ἐμψύχου"</note> are distinguished by our author in his *Aphorisms on Intelligibles* <note>original: "Ἀφορμ: πρὸς τὰ Νοητ."</note> §. 12. Therefore "we shall not extend the principle of justice even to plants" <note>original: "καὶ πρὸς τὰ φυτὰ παρατενοῦμεν τὸ τῆς δικαιοσύνης"</note>, since "without them it is impossible to live" <note>original: "ὧν ἄνευ ζῆν ἀδύνατον"</note>, as is said below in Book III, chapter 18. Yet he does not teach that plants should be harmed recklessly, but he discusses this matter in another place.
