# PORPHYRY

*...it is [necessary], that he imposes this burden of abstinence not on everyone, but only on those who desire to lead an Intellectual life. <note>original: "vitam Intellectualem"; in Neoplatonism, this refers to a life governed by the higher mind or "Nous" rather than the senses.</note> §. 27, etc. The alienation of the mind from those things which move the senses and from corporeal matters promotes this life greatly. §. 30, etc. Among these, foods also have their place. §. 33, etc. For since there are various things striking our senses which disturb the soul, §. 33. one must beware, as much as possible, of the contagion of them all. §. 35, etc. Nor is it fitting for us to mix with them, following the example of the Philosophers, etc. §. 36. And since food is of no small importance in this matter, §. 38. account must also be taken of them. For what some say—that they can be mixed with sensible things and yet not be disturbed by them—is a slippery slope, §. 39, etc. And it is one by which many have been deceived and entangled in foul lusts. §. 42, 43. Provision must therefore be made against all those things which are accustomed to move the mind, §. 43, etc. And moderation must also be observed in food. §. 44, etc. Which he further proves by the example of the Epicureans. §. 49, etc. Now, since this task is not great, nor too troublesome (§. 55.), it is by no means to be refused: especially since, although we may attempt and endure all things, it ought to be considered that things have gone well for us if at length we are permitted in any way to enjoy God. §. 56. to the end.*

§ 2. For as I reason to myself the cause of this change, I would not say that you changed for the sake of health and strength, as the many and unlearned crowd might say; for on the contrary, both toward health and

---

->**Notes on the Greek and Latin Text**<-

4. *By the flight from evil...*] The ancients were accustomed to use this expression in weddings and initiations. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> says: *"I fled the evil, I found the better." It is applied to those who have come from a worse state to a better.* See Kuster there and the writers of proverbs. Presently, the Leipzig manuscript <note>original: "cod. Lipſ."</note> is faulty in reading "having flayed" instead of "having lamented," and then "returning to the better." This last is not so bad and is supported by the Meermann manuscript.

5. *According to Empedocles.*] See Book II, section 31. — VALENTINI.

6. *Found to be.*] Something seems to be missing before "found to be." For example, "for the purpose of teaching" or "for the purpose of correction." — REISKE. <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a 18th-century German scholar.</note>

7. *From what things into what things...*] A nearly identical expression occurs in Psellus' *On Demons*: "exchanging what things for what things." — VALENTINI. In Aristotle, "from what things into what things," and other formulas of this kind are very frequent. See T. Gataker on Antoninus, Book X, section 26.

1. *As I reason.*] The construction gapes and falters. For "I would say" follows. Therefore, either something is missing, or it should read "For I, reasoning to myself... I would say," or "For it appears to me, reasoning to myself..." — REISKE. Certainly, these do not respond to the rules of the Grammarians. I would almost believe this is from the number of those things which they call "confusion of syntax" or "forgetfulness," which many have taught is not infrequent among the Greeks. No one even slightly cultured is ignorant that this occasionally happened to the Latins as well: at the beginning of a longer period, they would place a case for which they intended to supply a corresponding verb, but it slipped their mind.

2. *Health.*] The words "for the sake of" or "on account of" can indeed be understood, as they are often omitted. I nevertheless think "striving for" or "desiring" is missing. — REISKE. The Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts give a different spelling for "health," which are often confused. Our author, however, prefers the former.

3. *To change.*] The Leipzig manuscript reads "to have changed." The scribe intended the past tense, which is correct, for he is speaking of a past time; although the same scribe a little later writes "to contribute." — REISKE. The Meermann manuscript also has "to have changed," but a little later "to be contributing."

# PORPHYRY

...and toward a moderate endurance of the labors of Philosophy, you yourself, while living with us, acknowledged that a meatless diet <note>Greek: τὴν ἄσαρκον δίαιταν; literally "fleshless diet"</note> contributed. And by experience you knew that this was so, so that in saying these things you spoke the truth. Either then by some deception, or by thinking it makes no difference toward Wisdom <note>Greek: Phronesis</note> whether one diets in this way or that, or perhaps for some other cause unknown to me—a Fear of committing a greater impiety <margin>4</margin> by transgressing hanging over you—it seemed you ran back to your former transgressions. For surely I would not say <margin>5</margin> that out of lack of self-control or a Fear <note>The commentator notes this should likely be "desire"</note> of gluttonous gourmet-feeding you looked down upon the laws of the Philosophy you once emulated; nor that your Nature is less than that of some <margin>6</margin> private citizens; <margin>7</margin> who, having accepted laws contrary to those they lived by before, endure the cutting of body parts <note>likely referring to ritual circumcision or castration</note>, and would sooner abstain from certain animals they previously gorged upon than from human flesh.

->§ 3.<-

<column-break/>

...that a diet free from meat contributes to the endurance of philosophy, and you yourself, while living with us, would confess: and that you spoke the truth when you affirmed these things, it is easy to recognize by experience itself. Either therefore led by deception, because you think it matters nothing to wisdom whether you feed in this or that way: or perhaps for another cause, which I do not know, which was able to strike a greater terror than the impiety of violating the established rule, you seem to me to have returned to your prior sins. For I will never assert that because of incontinence, or for the sake of gluttonous greed, you so despised the ancestral laws of philosophy which you used to admire, and that you are inferior in nature to the unskillful and common men of certain nations: who, when they have admitted laws contrary to those they used before, both sustain the cutting off of members, and would almost more readily abstain from certain animals with which they were previously filled, if necessity pressed, than from human flesh.

<margin>4. The Fear etc.]</margin> So below in section 9: "They hung an irrational Fear over them." <note>original: "Φόβον ἄλογον ἐπήρτησαν"</note> Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies* [Stromata] II, p. 412. B.: "wherefore it seems to me that the law divinely and necessarily hangs Fear over us."

Lack of self-control and desire [phobos vs pothos] etc.]</margin> In the margin of the French edition, "desire" <note>Greek: pothon</note> was substituted for "Fear" <note>Greek: phobon</note>, and the sense of the passage seems to require it. VALENT. <note>Likely the scholar Benedictus Valentinus</note> Plutarch in *Table Talk* [Symposiacs], Vol II, p. 667. Rightly Clement of Alexandria in *The Instructor* [Paedagogus], Book II, p. 146. B.: "Gourmet-feeding is nothing other than excess in the use of cooked food. The manuscripts agree in a manifest error, which gave "Fear" <note>Greek: phobon</note> here instead of "desire" <note>Greek: pothon</note>.

->§ 3.<-

Since indeed some people have even recounted the words you were accustomed to speak against those who abstain from meat, it seemed to me that I should not only feel annoyed, but even indignant and angry. ->The followers<- of Epicurus directed the bulk of their opposition against the philosophy of Pythagoras and Empedocles, which you have earnestly striven to emulate. ### ON ABSTINENCE BOOK I.

...we should consider that gods and humans have a regard for us, and that we have a kinship with them, but that we have no such fellowship with other brute animals, which have no relation to us. We should not use some for labor and others for food, as if we judged them to be utterly alien and excluded from our community and our state. For anyone who wishes to behave toward animals just as toward humans—sparing them and doing them no harm—attributes to <term>justice</term> <note>The concept of "iustitia" here refers to the legal and moral framework that binds a society together; the argument is that this framework only applies to beings capable of reason.</note> a burden it cannot bear. In doing so, he destroys that which justice *can* achieve; by introducing foreign elements into justice, he ruins what is proper to it. The result is that either we must act unjustly by not sparing them, or, if we do spare them and refuse to use them, we become unable to carry on with our lives. Ultimately, we would in a sense lead the lives of beasts ourselves if we rejected the utility we gain from beasts.

§ 5. For I shall pass over the infinite multitude of <term>Nomads</term> <note>Wandering pastoralist tribes.</note> and <term>Troglodytes</term> <note>Literally "cave-dwellers," used here to refer to "uncivilized" groups at the edges of the known world.</note>, who recognize no other nourishment except meat. But even for us, who are seen to live mildly and humanely, what work of the land, or what work of the sea, or what...

<column-break/>

...considering the gods toward us, and having a kinship toward other beasts, which have no relation to us. And not using some for work and others for food, regarding them as outside the tribe and excluded from fellowship just like a state. For he who uses these as he does humans, sparing them and not harming them, attaches to justice that which it cannot bear, and destroys and corrupts what is proper to it by what is foreign. For it becomes necessary for us either to act unjustly by not sparing them, or, if not using them, for life to be impossible and without resources; and in a certain way, we shall live the life of beasts if we let go of the uses derived from beasts.

§ 5. For I pass over the undiscovered myriads of Nomads and Troglodytes; who know meat as food and nothing else; but even for us who seem to live mildly and humanely, what work is left of the earth, what...

---

<margin>
4. **By what is foreign.**] <note>original: "Τῷ ἀλλοτρίῳ"</note> In the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts, it is written as "of foreign things" <note>original: "τῶν ἀλλοτρίων"</note>, which is incorrect.
1. **For I pass over the Nomads etc.**] You may read these things in <term>Plutarch</term> <note>A famous Greek historian and philosopher (c. 46 – 119 AD).</note>, Volume II, page 964. More will be said concerning the customs of these nations in Book IV, section 21. Instead of "numbers" <note>original: "ἀριθμῶν"</note>, the Leipzig and Meerman codices have "in number" <note>original: "ἀριθμῷ"</note>; which some also prefer in Plutarch, and which the learned Reiske restored in his *Observations on the Minor Works of Plutarch*, page 548.

4. **What manifest art.** <note>original: "Τίς ἐναργὴς τέχνη"</note> An **active** or **busy** art that is exercised. It could also be read as "some activity of art" to correspond with the following "some ornament of livelihood." — REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and scholar.</note> **Manifest** and **active** are frequently confused; some would prefer the former in St. Paul, 1 Corinthians 16:9, but against the manuscripts. Often too "activity" is used for "fate." See: Bengel on Paul’s epistle to Philemon, 6. Iamblichus also speaks of an "active art" in *On the Mysteries*, Section II: 2. Yet I would not dare to banish the common reading, which Felicianus also read. Immediately after, Reiske preferred **disposed** instead of **we are disposed**.

5. **Harmlessly — we behave.** To use **behaving reasonably** for a mild and gentle treatment is found in Diodorus Siculus IV. 53; the opposite of which is **behaving bitterly, violently**, etc., on which the great Interpreter wrote there.

"By which, according to Hesiod, Zeus" etc. or "by which" in Plutarch should be changed to "as." I had not deliberately translated Plutarch's words before, and a false punctuation in Porphyry caused me to not interpret it entirely correctly. ### From Hermarchus: the Epicurean arguments.

§ 7. 1 Those from the school of Epicurus <note>Epicureans believed that justice is a contract "neither to harm nor be harmed," made for mutual benefit.</note>, as if recounting a long genealogy, say that the ancient legislators, looking toward the social community of human life and the actions of men toward one another, decreed the slaughter of a human to be unholy and attached no ordinary punishments to it. # On Abstinence, Book I.
B 2

...between humans there is a kinship, which ensures that this kind of living being is not killed as readily as the other animals that are permitted for use. Nevertheless, they claim the primary cause for why this deed was held to be so wicked and detestable was that they <note>The early lawgivers or founders of society.</note> believed it did not contribute to the overall constitution of life. For from this origin, those who perceived the utility of this institution required no other cause to be restrained from such a crime; however, those who could not sufficiently grasp the sense of this matter were deterred from mutual slaughter by the greatness of the penalty. Both of these cases, they say, are seen to happen even now. For those who consider the utility of such a decree readily persist in their duty; those who cannot perceive it, terrified by the threats of the laws, maintain the same behavior. Some promulgated these threats for the sake of those who could not reach a consideration of utility, after the majority had accepted them.

§ 8. For from the beginning, no law, neither written nor unwritten, was violently established...

For from such a beginning, those who followed <gloss>5</gloss> the benefit of this distinction needed no other cause to keep them from this act. But those unable to obtain a sufficient perception of this, fearing the magnitude of the punishment, abstained from readily killing one another. Each of these appears to still occur even now. For those who observe the benefit of the aforementioned arrangement readily abide by it; but those not receptive to this, fearing the threats of the laws—which some defined for the sake of those who do not reason out the useful, once the majority had accepted them.

# PORPHYRIUS

<column-break/>

...writing, nor without the record of those things which still endure and are by nature suited to be passed down; but rather by the consent of those <margin>1</margin> who were to use them. For it was by the wisdom of the soul, not by bodily strength or the tyrannical <margin>2</margin> enslavement of the masses, that those who introduced such things to the multitude excelled. They brought some to a rational understanding of what is useful—those who previously perceived it without reason and often forgot it—while others they struck with awe through the greatness of the penalties. For there was no other remedy to use against the ignorance of what is beneficial than the fear of the punishment defined <margin>3</margin> by the law. Indeed, this alone even now restrains ordinary men and prevents them from doing what is unprofitable, whether publicly or privately. For if everyone were able to see and remember what is useful in a similar way, <margin>4</margin> they would not—

<column-break/>

<note>The Latin text here is a contemporary translation of the Greek column to the left, which has been integrated into the English translation above for readability.</note>

---

<column-break/>

1. *Those who use them.*] By a peculiar expression, those who observe a law, or those for whom a law is passed to be observed, are said to "use the law" <note>original: "χρῆσθαι νόμῳ"</note>. *Plato* in the *Minos*, page 565 C: "nor do they themselves always use the same laws." *Thucydides*, Book V, chapter 105: "We neither established the law, nor were we the first to use it once it was laid down." These passages shed light on those words of *St. Paul* in *1 Timothy 1:8*: "The law is good, if one uses it lawfully." Those words "now and suited to be passed down" are missing in the *Lipsius* manuscript.

2. *Enslavement*] <note>original: "Δουλεύσει"</note> Should be read as "Subjugation" <note>original: "Δουλώσει"</note>, meaning oppression. For the original term refers to the "state of slavery" which is endured, not that which is imposed upon the weak by the powerful. *REISKE* <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note>. The illustrious *Abresch* also favored this, and rightly so.

<column-break/>

3. *By the law.*] Elsewhere he uses "under" <note>original: "ὑπὸ"</note> the law. But the former is not to be condemned; it is put for the latter a hundred times, and thus one has everywhere taken the place of the other. See regarding that confusion *Wesseling* on *Diodorus Siculus IV, 46*; *D'Orville* on *Chariton VI, 4*; and many others.

4. *They would have no need of laws.*] A most true sentiment. Hence: "laws did not exist among men as long as they were happy," below in Book III, 16. And the law "left the Brahmans to be their own legislators, and was revered as something superior to itself," Book IV, Section 18. *St. Paul, 1 Timothy 1:9*: "The law is not laid down for the righteous man." Here the interpreters will measure out the sayings of others on this matter "by the whole sackful," as the saying goes. Yet *Philo* is beautiful on this...

### On Abstinence, Book I.
-> B 3 <-
<meta>catchword: ...should be [rent], / as-</meta>

...could recall what is useful to their memory, there would have been no need for laws. Instead, men would of their own accord avoid what is forbidden and perform what is commanded. Indeed, a sufficient consideration of what is beneficial and what is harmful would have prepared them both to flee from evil and to choose the good. 

But the imposition of a penalty is directed at those who are unable to perceive what is advantageous. For the impending terror of punishment compels them to master the impulses that drag them toward harmful actions, and thus, by force, keeps them to their duty.

§ 9. For this reason, legislators also willed that even involuntary homicide <note>The Greek term is *akousios phonos*, referring to accidental killing or manslaughter.</note> should not be entirely free of punishment. They did this so as not to give anyone an excuse to intentionally imitate the actions of those who acted unwillingly, and also to ensure that such occurrences did not happen frequently due to negligence or lack of caution—

<margin>
I ought to add Philemon's passage here <note>Philemon was a poet of New Comedy.</note>, because it is similar to ours. Thus he says in *Fragments*, page 290:

5. *Threat of penalty.* <note>original: "Ζημίας ἀνάστασις"</note>] Perhaps it should read *epanastasis* <note>meaning a rising up or assault</note>, and then "for it is necessary to master." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century German scholar.</note> *Anastasis* means a threat delivered with bitterness and boldness, as <term>Suidas</term> <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia.</note> says. Indeed, the word *anateinesthai* <note>to stretch upward</note> is properly said of those who raise a staff, which is the gesture of those making a threat. Hence *anastasis* and *epanastasis* are often used in reference to threats. See <term>Wesseling</term> on *Diodorus Siculus*, Book XIV, chapter 3. Next, <term>Lipsius</term> reads: "those who do not *yet* see."

</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
*to give.* <term>REISKE</term>. *Not so as* <note>original: "οὐκ ὅπως"</note> had already been added in the margin by *Fogerolles*, and our author and others are certainly accustomed to saying *oukh hopos* instead of "not only." However, in this passage, it seems to me that "not only" is suppressed through an ellipsis <note>a grammatical omission</note>. For Greek writers are accustomed to this when "but" <note>original: "ἀλλὰ"</note> follows. Consult the interpreters on *Gospel of John* 12:44 and the learned man on *Xenophon of Ephesus, Miscellaneous Observations*, Vol. X, page 201. Latin writers follow the same manner of speaking, using *non* for *non modo* [not only] when *sed* [but] follows. <term>Cortius</term> gathered a harvest of examples on *Sallust's Jugurthine War*, XIV, 23. Instead of *ekdosi* [surrender], which was a printer's error in the *Cambridge* edition, I have restored *endosi* [allow/give]; however, <term>Meermann</term> incorrectly reads "of involuntary things" <note>original: "ἀκουσίων"</note>.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s discussion on the legal distinction between voluntary and involuntary actions, specifically focusing on why even unintentional harm must be punished to maintain social order and prevent negligence.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

...so that many things truly happen involuntarily. For this was not beneficial, for the same reasons that we said it was forbidden for humans to destroy one another voluntarily. Therefore, since among involuntary acts some are committed due to an uncertain cause—the kind that cannot be avoided by human nature—while others happen due to our own negligence and a lack of care regarding the consequences; to prevent our sloth from harming others, the lawgivers did not leave even involuntary actions unpunished. Instead, through the terror of penalties, they restrained the frequency of such offenses. And—

<column-break/>

---

3. **An unmeasurable cause.** <note>original: Ἀσάθμητον αἰτίαν</note>] This "cause" can be explained as a reason for things that can neither be foreseen by the mind's insight nor guessed at through conjecture. I fear, nonetheless, that the word may be somewhat unsuitable. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774) was a pioneering German scholar of Greek and Arabic texts.</note>. The word *unmeasurable* was excellently illustrated by D'Orville in his notes on Chariton (Book VI, 4), where he showed it is very frequently applied to **fortune**, **crowds**, and **human nature**. Nothing more needs to be added to his findings.

4. **By human nature.** <note>original: Ἀνθρωπίνῃ φύσει</note>] Our author uses this phrasing more frequently below, whereas he never uses the term *human-like nature* <note>original: ἀνθρωπεία φύσις</note>. However, Monsieur Thomas <note>likely Pierre-Thomas Durand de Maillane or a similar contemporary critic</note> teaches that the latter should be used instead of the former. But the notes of the famous Duker on Thucydides (III, 40) and Wesseling’s *Observations* (I, 30) will show you by what right they teach this. There is, therefore, nothing unusual in the phrasing in James III, 7: "is tamed by **human nature**." Yet, the other term seems to carry a greater mark of antiquity. Compare the learned Pierson on Moeris, page 26.

5. **And lack of attention to the difference.** <note>original: Καὶ ἀνεπίσατον τ. δ.</note>] This "lack of attention to the difference" refers to the thoughtlessness and blindness of an angry man when he is quarreling; swept away by the heat of rage, he does not sufficiently collect himself nor foresee what he is preparing or doing, but is carried along blindly. Inflamed by the fire of a raging mind, he commits acts that he would regret when returned to his senses. <term>REISKE</term>. There is an ingenious conjecture by a learned man who preferred the reading "unstable destruction" <note>original: ἀνεπίστατον τῆς διαφθορᾶς</note>. The Cambridge editor had added the article "the" before "lack of attention." But neither the earlier editions nor the handwritten manuscripts recognize it. Often in our author and others, you may find the article sometimes added and sometimes neglected; in these cases, we must pay attention to the writer's specific habit.

6. **Harming them.** <note>original: Βλάπτουσαν αὐτοὺς</note>] Either "them" <note>original: αὐτοὺς</note> should be read simply as "the" <note>original: τοὺς</note>, or if the original is kept, it should read "them and their neighbors," as well as "quarrels" and the rest of the citizens. <term>REISKE</term>. The Leiden and Cambridge editions had substituted "the" for "them," but since all the manuscripts agree on "them" <note>original: αὐτοὺς</note>, I do not doubt that due to a scribe's error, two words were merged which should have been distinct: "again the" <note>original: αὖ τοὺς</note>. I have the Meerman manuscript in agreement. This happens quite often to this little word in our author and others, as will be discussed elsewhere. The translator rendered the word **sloth** <note>original: ῥᾳθυμίαν</note> as *inertia*. This is not wrong; however, it has a broader meaning, signifying a vice of the soul devoted to trifles, and thus it encompasses the vices that flow from that state. Consult Perizonius on Aelian’s *Various History*, IX, 9.

7. **By the fear of [penalties].** <note>original: Τῷ φόβῳ τ. ε. α</note>] The Leipzig edition reads "the penalties of the cattle," which is a **monstrous corruption** of the text. It makes no difference whether the common reading is kept and "the much" is understood as "the multitude, frequency, or commonness," or if one reads—

# On Abstinence, Book I.

Indeed, I believe that even those killings permitted by law were required to be atoned for through certain customary expiations for no other reason than this: those who first established these rites wished to distance men as far as possible from voluntary acts of violence. Since people required some form of prohibition from every side, the founders acted so that men would not slip so recklessly into committing acts that are not beneficial. Therefore, those who first observed this did not only establish legal penalties; they also introduced another kind of "irrational" terror, declaring that those who had killed a human being in any manner whatsoever were contaminated <note>original: "contaminatos"</note> unless they had purged themselves with certain sacrificial atonements. For in this way, the irrational part of the soul, being educated in various ways, arrives at a proper state of gentleness.

<column-break/>

And I, for my part, [maintain] that even killings permitted by law require the customary satisfactions through purifications for no other cause—according to those who first beautifully introduced these things—than the desire to keep men as far as possible from voluntary action. For common men everywhere needed something to prevent them from readily doing what is not advantageous. Hence, those first [legislators] who were conscious of this did not only ordain punishments, but they also suspended another irrational fear over them, proclaiming that those who had killed a man in any way were not "pure" <note>original: "καθαροὺς"</note> unless they made use of purifications. For the foolish part of the soul, having been guided like a child <note>original: "παιδαγωγηθὲν"</note> in various ways, came into a settled state of refinement.

---

<column-break/>

...they took away much <note>original: "ἀφείλοντο πολὺ"</note>; in two words, *they greatly detracted from the error.* <term>Reiske <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, 18th-century philologist.</note></term> Well said and relevant to our subject is <term>Clement of Alexandria, Miscellanies <note>original: "Stromata"</note></term> Book II, p. 376: "For those whom reason does not capture, fear tames."

8. **By those who first [introduced]... beautifully.** <term>Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius, renowned Renaissance humanist.</note></term> [suggests] "by" <note>original: "ὑπὸ"</note> (which <term>Reiske</term> approved, to vary the style) "those who first [introduced]... badly" <note>original: "κακῶς"</note>. The <term>Meermann</term> and <term>Bodleian</term> manuscripts also prefer "by" and "badly." The oldest editions also have "first" <note>original: "πρώτων"</note>, which was changed by <term>Valentin</term> to "firstly" <note>original: "πρῶτον"</note>, but I have restored it to its place. However, "badly" <note>original: "κακῶς"</note> was previously read incorrectly instead of "beautifully" <note>original: "καλῶς"</note>, unless perhaps it was "not badly." We shall mention elsewhere how these words were commonly confused.

9. **Being conscious of this.** <term>Reiske</term> says: I am unwilling to change "being conscious" <note>original: "Συνειδότες"</note> because of the multitude of examples from which I believe I have understood that the ancients were accustomed to use "being conscious" in place of "having observed" <note>original: "συνιδὼν"</note>. I shall bring forth some of these examples regarding <term>Polybius</term> if the fates allow. See the notes on <term>Polybius</term>, Book I, p. 104. Next, for "suspended over" <note>original: "ἐπήρτησαν"</note>, the <term>Bodleian</term> manuscript gave "placed above" and <term>Lipsius</term> gave "detached." Both are faulty. Our author speaks this way also above in section 2; see there.

10. **Guided like a child in various ways.** A beautiful turn of phrase. The irrational part of the soul is called a "child" <note>original: "παῖς"</note> by the Philosophers, over whom a "tutor" <note>original: "παιδαγωγὸς"</note> must preside; to rule and moderate it is "to act as a tutor" <note>original: "παιδαγωγεῖν"</note>, and the thing itself is "tutelage" <note>original: "παιδαγωγία"</note>. See below in section 44: "Some allow the child to do what he wants by himself; others leave it to the tutor." So also in Book III, 26 and elsewhere. <term>Heraclitus</term> in *Homeric Allegories*: "Just as if reason, acting as a tutor, aroused his capacity for concern." <term>The learned Palairetus</term> compares this passage with Paul's letter to the Galatians 3:24, where with similar elegance the Law is called a "tutor" <note>original: "παιδαγωγός"</note>.

11. **Devising beforehand, etc.** The construction of the words seems quite perplexed. In the translation, I believe we have followed the sense, even if not...

# PORPHYRY

->[Book I, Section 9 continued]<-

...applying various methods of taming to the irrational impulse of desire <gloss>12</gloss> from the very beginning by those who served the multitudes; among these [laws] was also the prohibition against killing one another without judgment.

### Section 10

Regarding the other animals, those who first defined what we ought and ought not to do naturally did not prevent their destruction. For in their case, utility was achieved through the opposite course of action. It was not possible for humans to remain safe unless they attempted to defend themselves <gloss>1</gloss> against the beasts while living among one another. Recalling this, some of the most refined <gloss>2</gloss> people of that time, while they abstained from killing one another because it contributed to their mutual safety, also instilled in others a memory of the outcome in their shared 

<column-break/>

[societies]... <note>The text continues the thought from the first column: early humans learned that mutual non-aggression was beneficial for survival.</note>

Indeed, they applied various modes of taming to the irrational incitement of desire—those who, from the beginning, cultivated the peoples. One of their principles was that people should not kill each other without a trial.

### Section 10

But concerning other animals, those who first established for us what things were to be done or not done rightly forbade the killing of none of them; for in their case, utility for us arose from the opposite action. For it was not possible for them to be safe unless they had attempted to repel the attacks of the beasts with whom humans lived. Since, therefore, some of those who were then the most refined remembered that they had abstained from mutual slaughter because it contributed to safety, they communicated the outcome of the matter to others in their common societies...

<margin>
*Not the form of the words.* The word "the" <note>original: "τὰς"</note> should be deleted, and thus it may be interpreted more literally as: "to those who first ruled the multitude, inventing certain things for the wild [impulses] etc." VALENTINUS. The "the" is rightly absent from the *Leipzig* manuscript, having been inserted by Valentinus. "Of desire" <note>original: "ἐπιθυμίας"</note> is in the genitive case here. REISKE. Valentinus had taken it from Fogerolles, who ineptly added that "the" in the margin; all others agree on the word "of the" <note>original: "τῆς"</note>.

12. "Taming... those who [served] the multitudes."] Perhaps "the taming [measures] of those who from the beginning ordered the multitudes." The meaning is this: *when they skillfully devised remedies and soothings for desire against the force and impetus of brute lust, those who, at the dawn of the human race, first instructed and polished the people with intellectual culture and honest laws and customs.* REISKE. I would also prefer the word "ordered" <note>original: "διακοσμησάντων"</note>, although I know what can be said in defense of the common reading "served" <note>original: "διακονησάντων"</note>. ARNTZENIUS.

Everyone knows phrases like "to serve the people." The word is quite appropriate for this kind of ministry, just as "to tame," "to act as an ambassador," and "to serve" are joined by Pollux. Here, however, another reason seems to apply. Abresch favored "governed" <note>original: "διοικησάντων"</note>, as if it were read in this order: "devising tamings (by those) who from the beginning (governed) the multitudes regarding (the impulses) of the irrational [soul] etc."

1. "Defend themselves [against this/them]."] Instead of "this" <note>original: "τοῦτο"</note>, Fogerolles had substituted "them" <note>original: "ἀυτὰ"</note> in the margin, which Valentinus adopted, but against the evidence of all the manuscripts. To Reiske, it seemed that something was missing between "defend" and "this." To me, "this" <note>original: "τοῦτο"</note> seems to have arisen from "them" <note>original: "τοὺς"</note> through a scribal abbreviation. This also pleased the learned Abresch.

2. "As they themselves abstained."] Read as "They themselves" <note>original: "Αὐτόι τε"</note> without the "as" <note>original: "ὡς"</note>, which seems to have crept in wrongly from the end of the previous word "refined" <note>original: "χαριεσάτων"</note>. REISKE. The Leipzig manuscript reads "abstained" <note>original: "ἀπέσχον"</note>. Those called "most refined" are the "civilized" men.
</margin>

### On Abstinence, Book I.
->C 2<-
<meta>catchword: ui- / θος</meta>

...be killed. For none of those animals which the laws permit to be killed is of such a nature that, if allowed to increase into excessive abundance, it would not bring harm to human beings; yet if maintained in a moderate number, it provides certain benefits for human life. For the sheep, the ox, and all such creatures, if they remain in a moderate state, offer certain utilities for the necessary conduct of our lives. However, if they were to escape into a great redundancy and exceed a fitting number, they would undermine our lives: the oxen indeed turning to aggression, as they are endowed by nature with a sufficiently strong and robust character for that; and the sheep by grazing away the nourishment that grows from the earth for our sake. For this reason, the slaughter of this kind of animal was not prohibited: so that only that multitude of them might be left which serves a practical use and which can be easily managed. For it is not as with lions, wolves, and all others called wild beasts—both small and large—where no number can be found which, if left alone, would support life...

<column-break/>

...For, so to speak, there is no creature among those permitted by the law which, if allowed to reach an excess of abundance, would not become harmful to us. But being maintained in the current quantity, it provides certain uses for life. And indeed the sheep and the ox and every such thing, being kept in moderation, brings certain benefits for our necessary way of living; but falling into every kind of plenty and having a great excess beyond what is established <note>original Greek: *tēs kathestōsēs*</note>, it would ruin our life. The one <note>the ox</note> turning even to strength <note>i.e., aggression</note>, as it partakes of a nature well-suited for this. The other <note>the sheep</note> consuming only the food sent up for us from the earth. Wherefore also for this reason it was not forbidden to destroy such animals, so that a multitude remains that is advantageous for use and capable of being easily mastered. For it is not as with lions and wolves and simply those animals called wild, similarly small and large, for there is no number that could be taken which, if left alone, [would not be harmful]...

---

<margin>The word "to harm" <note>original: *lymainesthai*</note> which follows is common in these texts; add nothing to those things noted by Wetstein <note>Johann Jakob Wetstein (1693–1754), a famous biblical critic and scholar.</note> in his commentary on *Luke's Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 8, verse 3.</margin>

3. **"Having [the character] of the established, etc."** "Having" <note>Greek: *Echousan*</note> refers back to the word "plenty" <note>Greek: *dapsileian*</note> and "established" <note>Greek: *kathestōsēs*</note> refers back to the same word for plenty. "Established plenty" means a due, opportune, fair, and moderate or convenient abundance. In a similar way, "established gentleness" is also to be understood at the end of section 9. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774) was a German physician and pioneering scholar of Greek and Arabic literature.</note>

4. **"Of a well-suited nature."** <note>original: *Physeōs euphyous*</note> Elegantly said. They properly call an innate natural dexterity "well-suited" <note>Greek: *Euphyē*</note>. The celebrated Valckenaer <note>Lodewijk Caspar Valckenaer (1715–1785), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> brilliantly explains the proper and improper use of the word in his *Critical Observations on Ammonius*, Book II, chapter 2. Hence we see "natural talent" <note>Greek: *euphyia*</note> and "natural dullness" <note>Greek: *aphyia*</note> below in Book III, section 8; see there. Recently, in place of "sent up" <note>Greek: *anetheisan*</note>, Meermann <note>likely Gerard Meerman (1722–1771), a Dutch jurist and collector.</note> erroneously has "placed against" <note>Greek: *antetheisan*</note>.

### P O R P H Y R Y
->Book 1, Section 12<-

...[abundance] which, if left to remain, would have lightened the burden of our necessary life, the same holds true for oxen, horses, sheep, and generally for all those creatures called "tame" animals. For this reason, we destroy some of them completely <note>referring to wild or dangerous animals</note>; while of the others, we remove whatever portion exceeds a balanced number.

§ 12. <gloss>1</gloss> For reasons similar to those already mentioned, one must consider that the laws regarding the eating of living beings were defined by those who originally <gloss>2</gloss> established these regulations. Regarding those animals that are considered inedible, the underlying cause is whether they are useful or harmful. Therefore, those who claim that everything noble and just exists only according to the private opinions people hold about what has been legislated <gloss>3</gloss> are full of a kind of "steep" [extreme] foolishness. For this is not the case; rather, it is just as <gloss>4</gloss> it is with other useful things—such as health and a thousand other categories—where people often miss the mark in many matters, both public and private alike. For even laws that apply in a similar manner...

<column-break/>

...could [sustain] our life: thus also it is in cattle, horses, sheep, and the rest of that kind which are called "tame." For that reason, we attempt to destroy those [wild ones] fundamentally; while of these [tame ones], we suppress their abundance if it exceeds the proper limit.

§ 12. For the same reason, one must think that those rules which concern the eating of animals were also instituted by the ancient laws. For as to why others are considered unfit for food, it is clear that utility and uselessness are the cause. Therefore, to assert that everything honorable and just arises only from each person's own opinions regarding what is sanctioned by laws is a sign of no small stupidity. For the matter is not so. But just as in other useful things—for instance, those which lead to health and innumerable other matters—we are sometimes deceived, so also in many public and private matters, error is accustomed to occur. Since indeed the institutions of laws which suit everyone...

---

1. <note>original: *Διὰ παραπλησίους*</note> *Because of similar [reasons].*] This was previously read in older editions as two words meaning "through which things," and because of this, the word "similar" had been changed to the adverb "similarly." These are all incorrect if you write it as "because of" in a single word, an emendation that the scholar *Reiske* also liked; it seemed so certain to me that I did not hesitate to restore to Malchus <note>Malchus was Porphyry's original Phoenician name</note> his own voice.

2. <note>original: *Καταλ: νόμων*</note> *Established by laws.*] Referring to those who originally sanctioned and circumscribed these things by law. REISKE.

3. <note>original: *Ἠλιβάτου εὐηθείας*</note> *Steep foolishness.*] Because manners that are too easy and simple expose a person to laughter, the Greek word *euetheia* <note>literally "good-naturedness"</note> degenerated in meaning to signify "stupidity," although it is frequently used in a positive sense. This is seen in section 23 below. The celebrated scholar *Ruhnken*, in his notes on *Timaeus' Platonic Lexicon*, shows that this word is common in Plato with this specific meaning. You may read more about its character in the "Distinguished Man’s" <note>likely referring to a contemporary scholar like Valckenaer</note> notes on *Thucydides III, 83*. The word *elibatos* <note>meaning "steep" or "high"</note> is explained by the *Etymologicum Magnum* and the notes on *Hesychius*. The celebrated *Abreschius* correctly observed that the phrase "full of foolishness" is a Platonic expression.

4. <note>original: *Τρόπον ἢ ἐπὶ*</note> *The manner or upon etc.*] Instead of the word for "if," the Leipzig manuscript has the word for "than" or "or"; with this accepted, the sentence means: "For this does not hold in any other way than as it does in the rest of [useful things]..."

Porphyry critiques the idea that justice is subjective, comparing legal errors to mistakes made in the pursuit of health.</summary>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

->C 3<-

Let everyone take notice: some people, thinking that certain matters are of no consequence, overlook them; others hold contrary opinions about these same things, and judge that which does not contribute to the universal good to be useful everywhere. From this it happens that they sometimes decree things that do not suit everyone, provided they have found things that are profitable to themselves and contribute to their mutual utility. Of such a kind are the regulations established among most nations concerning the eating and slaughter of animals <note>original: "de animalium esu & caede"</note> due to the specific nature of their region; which certainly ought not to be observed by us, since we do not inhabit the same place. If, therefore, just as among men, a certain compact <note>term: pactum — a formal agreement or social contract</note> could have been made with the rest of the animals concerning slaughter—so that they would not kill us, nor we kill them indiscriminately—justice would have been rightly extended that far; for it would have been sufficient for our security. But because it was in no way possible for those creatures which are devoid of reason <note>original: "expertia rationis"</note> to have a communication of laws and justice:

<column-break/>

...some do not perceive these things as applying to everyone. Instead, some, believing them to be among the "indifferent" things <note>term: adiaphora — in Stoic philosophy, things that are neither morally good nor bad in themselves</note>, pass them over. Others hold the opposite opinion about them, and some think that things which are not universally beneficial are beneficial everywhere. For this reason, they cling to things that are not applicable. Even if, in some cases, they discover what is advantageous to themselves and what has a common utility—among which are the regulations concerning the eating and destruction of living beings <note>original: "τὰς ἐδωδὰς τῶν ἐμψύχων"</note> ordained in most nations because of the particularity of the land. It is not necessary for us to abide by these, because we do not inhabit the same place. If, then, they were able to make a certain treaty, just as with men, so also with the rest of the animals, regarding not killing—so that they would not be killed by us without judgment—it would be well to extend justice to that point; for it would be stretched toward security. But since it was among the impossible things for those animals that do not receive reason <note>original: "λόγον"</note> to share in law...

---

<margin>
*remaining*. For it is impossible that this matter should be any different than the way other conveniences of life are. That phrase *other than* <note>original: "ἄλλονπερ-ἢ"</note> seems to have been beloved by our author, although it is redundant and lacks elegance. *per*. REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note>. Valent: had added *than*, but against the authority of all the others, and therefore we have restored the old writing. Elegant is the conjecture of *Abresch* <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch, a Dutch philologist</note>, who shortly wanted *others [discerning] other things*.
</margin>

<margin>
5. *They discover* <note>original: "Ἐξευρίσκουσι"</note>.] This is much more significant than the simple form, as such compounds usually are. Regarding our word, consult R. W. on *Hierocles: On the Golden Verses of Pythagoras*, p. 260.
</margin>

<margin>
6. *Necessary to abide by* <note>original: "Ἀναγκαῖον ἐμμένειν"</note>.] This pertains to a very frequent way of speaking, *to abide by the law*.
</margin>

# PORPHYRY

...by such a method, it is not possible to establish any utility for safety from other living beings any more than from inanimate things. # On Abstinence, Book I.

It is argued that it is according to nature for man to eat meat, just as it is contrary to nature for him to eat it raw. <note>The author is exploring the philosophical argument that humans are biologically "meant" to eat meat, but only when transformed by fire.</note> Hence, after the discovery of fire, it came about that they arrived at what was suited to their nature by admitting meat once cooking was applied. For lynxes are "eaters of raw flesh" <note>original: *crudiuori*</note>; and that famous line was spoken as a reproach: *Indeed, you would devour Priam raw* <note>Homer, Iliad 4.35</note>; and: *Tearing the raw flesh, he devoured it with a full mouth*—as if, clearly, the eating of raw flesh is attributed to the impious. But this is considered human: *The attendant placed chargers full of various meats here and there.* <note>Homer, Odyssey 1.141</note> At first, therefore, they did not feed upon animals, because

<column-break/>

it is natural for man to eat meat, but contrary to nature to eat it raw. Therefore, when fire was discovered, they reclaimed what was natural by accepting meat through boiling. For this reason, jackals are "raw-eaters," and it is a reproach to say, *You might eat Priam raw.* And, *To cut off and eat raw flesh.* As if the [practice] of [raw meat] were assigned to the godless, [the poet says] *he set before them platters of all kinds, lifting them up.* At first, then, they did not consume living things, for man was not a raw-eating animal; but when the use of fire was discovered, [they turned] to things wrought by fire, not only to meat—

---

<margin>This is discussed elsewhere.</margin> Although they permitted the use of meat, nevertheless all nations who have any dealings with literature or good morals have condemned *omophagia* <term>omophagia: the eating of raw flesh, often associated with wild Dionysian rites</term>. *Since our nature does not prevail over raw meat,* as *Artemidorus* says in *The Interpretation of Dreams, I, 72.* Therefore, when superstition had introduced this custom <note>referring to ritual raw-meat eating</note>, God by a special mandate removed raw meat from the rites of Passover, as was seen by *Spencer* in *On the Laws of the Passover, II, 4*, though he attributes too much to his own hypothesis. Immediately for *prosiemenous* <gloss>accepting</gloss>, the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts read *prosemenous*.

For example: *at the reception of Pallas [Minerva] by Telemachus, the carver set before them platters of meat.* The example seems to pertain to this: to demonstrate that it was placed in the custom of the ancients that guests were refreshed with cooked meats. Thus, when Telemachus received Minerva as a guest in his home, the distributor served not raw meats, but cooked. Because if Minerva, being a Goddess, did not disdain dishes of cooked meat, it was thus lawful to feed on cooked meat, just as it was unlawful to eat it raw. —REISKE. *Of raw-eating* is also the reading of *Felicianus*; but even then he seems to have read certain other things which, if they were present, would give us a more complete passage. ### On Abstinence, Book I

...which they began with animals. For it is according to nature for man to eat meat, just as it is against nature for him to feed on raw things. From this, it resulted that after fire was discovered, they arrived at that which was suited to their nature, as they admitted meats to their diet through the use of cooking. For lynxes are eaters of raw meat; and that saying was spoken as a reproach: *for you would eat Priam raw* <note>original: "crudum namque ederes Priamum"; a reference to the Iliad IV.35, where Hera's rage against Troy is described</note>; and, *tearing raw flesh, he devoured it with a full mouth*—as if, evidently, the eating of raw flesh is attributed to the ungodly. But this is the human way: *the attendant placed here and there dishes full of various meats.* Therefore, at first they did not feed on animals, because

<column-break/>

it is according to nature for man to eat meat, but against nature to eat it raw. Thus, when fire was found, they reclaimed what was natural by accepting meat through boiling <note>The Greek text here mirrors the Latin, using the word *hepsēsis* for boiling or cooking</note>. Because of this, while jackals <note>original: *thōes*</note> are eaters of raw meat, it is said in reproach, *You might eat Priam raw.* And, *to eat raw pieces of meat.* As if the eating of meat <note>the text implies "raw meat"</note> were assigned to the godless, *he placed dishes of all kinds, lifting them up.* In the beginning, then, they did not partake of living things; for man was not an animal that ate raw meat. <meta>This page continues Porphyry’s investigation into the history of human diet. The previous page discussed the Epicurean view that animals lack a contract of justice with humans. # PORPHYRY

...meats, but they also used, so to speak, most other kinds of foods. For the fact that man is not a raw-eater <note>original: *omophagon*</note> is shown by certain fish-eating tribes <note>original: *ichthyophaga*</note>; for they roast their fish—some whenever the rocks become especially hot from the sun, and others even in the sand. That man is a meat-eater is shown by the very fact that no nation abstains from the meat of living creatures <note>original: *empsykhōn*, meaning beings with souls</note>. Furthermore, the Greeks did not adopt this practice for nourishment alone, since the same custom exists among the barbarians <note>A term used by Greeks to describe any non-Greek-speaking people</note> as well.

§ 14. But the person who commands us not to eat meat, and considers it unjust, will also say that it is not just to kill animals or to deprive them of their souls. However, a war against wild beasts is both innate to us and just. For some attack humans of their own accord, such as wolves and lions; others do so unintentionally, such as snakes <note>original: *opheis*</note>, which sometimes bite if they are stepped on. Some attack humans directly, while others destroy our crops. For the sake of all these things, we pursue them,

<column-break/>

...because man was not an animal that ate raw meat <note>original: *crudiuorum animal*</note>. But where the use of fire was discovered, they used fire-cooked foods, not only meats but also many other edibles. For certain nations that live only on fish declare that man is not an animal meant to eat raw food. For some are accustomed to roast fish upon the rocks when they have absorbed the greatest heat from the sun, and others in the sand. Moreover, it is manifest that he is a meat-eater <note>original: *carniuorum*</note> because no nation abstains from the eating of animals; this same custom exists not only among the Greeks but also among the barbarians.

§ 14. For he who forbids feeding on them and thinks it is unjust will also assert that it is not just to kill them and deprive them of life. But against wild beasts, a war is implanted in us and is just: since some attack humans of their own accord, like wolves and lions; others do not do so of their own accord, like vipers, which bite if they are sometimes stepped on; and some range against men, while others range against the crops. For all of which things we are accustomed to take vengeance on the beasts and [them...] <note>The Latin text ends on the catchword *eas*, meaning "them."</note>

1. **The snakes; for being trodden on etc.** Only the *Florentine Manuscript* has "vipers" [*ekheis*]; I see no reason why Fogerolles did not follow this as he did in other cases.

for they differ only as genus and species. The phrase "to tread on snakes" [*opheis patein*] is a specific idiom. Therefore, this passage can be added to those used to illustrate the famous words of **St. Luke** in the Gospel 10:19: *I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions.* The author Aelian also said "to tread on scorpions" in his *History of Animals*, Book X, 23. Furthermore, the *Meermann Manuscript* reads: "some [attack] men."

<summary>Porphyry argues that humans are naturally meat-eaters who require cooked food, distinguishing them from raw-eating animals, and justifies killing wild beasts as a form of "just war" for self-defense and crop protection.</summary>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

->D<-

Whether they have attacked us or not, we kill them so that no evil may come to us from them. For there is no one who, if he sees a serpent, does not immediately kill it to the best of his ability, lest he himself or any other human at all be infested by its bite. This is done not so much out of hatred for the beast as out of the benevolence of man toward man. Since, therefore, war against wild beasts is just, we nevertheless tend to abstain from many animals that live among humans. Hence the Greeks eat neither dogs nor horses, nor likewise asses, because the tame versions are of the same genus as the wild ones; yet they eat swine, and also poultry. For the pig is useful for nothing else than

<column-break/>

<note>original: "τα, καὶ τὰ κατάρξαντα θηρία κτείνομεν..."</note>
...and we kill those beasts that have attacked us, and those that have not, so that we may suffer nothing from them. For there is no one who, seeing a serpent, has not killed it if he was able, so that neither he himself might be bitten, nor any other human simply. For it is not only hatred against the things being killed, but also affection of man toward man. While war against wild beasts is just, we abstain from many of those that live with humans. Whence the Greeks neither eat dogs, nor do they eat horses, nor indeed do they eat asses; as the tame is of the same genus as the wild; and likewise birds. For the pig is useful for nothing else than

---

<column-break/>

2. **Whoever seeing a serpent does not kill it if able.**] See below at number 20: "we kill the serpent and the scorpion even if they do not attack us." Many note that mutual hatred between serpents and humans. Consult **Samuel Bochart: *Hierozoicon* Book I, chapter 4, page 30**, who derives this from those things read in **Genesis 3:15** <note>The biblical verse regarding the enmity between the serpent and the seed of the woman.</note>. Regarding the natural instinct by which we kill harmful things, more will be said later.

3. **Affection of man toward man.**] Thus these were read in the ancient editions: all the Manuscripts I have used confirm this, and **Feliciano** <note>Giovanni Bernardino Feliciano, 16th-century translator of Porphyry.</note> also recognizes it. Therefore, **Valentini** had edited it very poorly as "affection toward men. Just—"

4. **Greeks [eat] dogs.**] **Sextus Empiricus, however, in *Outlines of Pyrrhonism* Book III, 24, page 184**, says: "Some of the Thracians are recorded to eat dogs; and perhaps this was also customary among the Greeks."

5. **As the tame is of the same genus as the wild.**] Either "as the tame being of the same genus as the wild" or "as the tame is the same genus as the wild." **REISKE** <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, 18th-century philologist.</note> says: I construe it as "they eat [the wild] as the tame [being] of the same genus," as happens a hundred times. Such *hyperbata* <note term="hyperbaton">a transposition of words from their natural order for emphasis or style</note> or transpositions are familiar both to others and especially to our author, in which he indulges himself so often that the sense becomes very difficult; many examples will occur to us in the following pages.

6. **And likewise birds.**] These words cohere poorly with those that immediately preceded. Shall we think that all those things which follow after "and we kill the beasts" were inserted as a parenthesis? But not even in this way is everything cleared up. In the [Latin] version, however, you would miss nothing. Therefore, I hardly doubt that "but they eat swine," or something similar, has fallen out of the Greek text.

7. **The pig [is for] nothing but food.**] He says this below in Book III, 20: "the pig was born for the purpose of being slaughtered and eaten." **Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams* Book I, 72**: "For a living pig is of no use to humans, but dead it is more edible than others." Hence this use is provided for those who live in luxury, as **Clement of Alexandria** says in **Book II of the *Stromata*, page 405**. Elsewhere the animal is said to be born for sacrifice. Compare **Julian, *Oration V*, page 176**, and what will be said in Book III, section 20.

# P O R P H Y R Y

->D<-

...than for eating. 8 The Phoenicians and Jews abstained from it because it was not native to those places at all; indeed, they say that even now this animal is not seen in Ethiopia. 11 Just as no one among the Greeks has sacrificed a camel or an elephant to the gods, because Greece does not produce these animals, so too in Cyprus or Phoenicia this animal <note>the pig</note> was not offered to the gods, because it was not local. 12 Neither did the Egyptians [sacrifice it] to the gods...

<column-break/>

...than for eating. Nevertheless, the Phoenicians and Jews abstained from it for this reason: because it was not born in those places at all. Even now, they claim that an animal of this kind is not found in Ethiopia. Just as no one among the Greeks has slaughtered a camel or an elephant for the gods, for the reason that Greece did not produce those animals at all: so too in Cyprus, or Phoenicia, this animal was not offered to the gods, because it was absent from those places. Neither did the Egyptians...

---

<column-break/>

8. **The Phoenicians and Jews.**] Regarding the Jews, more will be said shortly. It was also a custom for the Phoenicians to abstain from pigs. Hence, among the gifts which the Emperor Elagabalus <note>a Roman Emperor of Syrian/Phoenician origin known for bringing Eastern customs to Rome</note> used to distribute, were "all animals, as many as are tame, except for the wild ones, but excluding pigs; for he abstained from these according to Phoenician law," as found in **Herodian: Book I, 6. § 22**. But see also **Bochart: *Hierozoicon* <note>a famous 17th-century scholarly work on the animals of the Bible</note> Book II, chapter 57, page 702**.

9. **Not native to those places at all.**] Tacitus, Plutarch, and others fluctuate greatly in defining the causes of why the Jews so abhorred the pig, but we shall not discuss those here. However, **Petavius (on Julian's Oration V, p. 91)** and **Castellanus (on the eating of meat, Book IV, ch. 4)** observe that the history of the pigs into which the demons were sent—as the Holy Scripture narrates <note>referring to the "Gerasene Swine" in the Gospels</note>—proves the falsity of the claim our author <note>Porphyry</note> makes. Truly, that cannot be forced from the Gospel. Read the arguments of the incomparable **Bochart: *Hierozoicon* II, ch. 57, p. 697**. This genus of beasts was not found in Judea, not because the region was unsuitable for raising them, but because it was not permitted to raise them by religious law.

10. **Not even now in Ethiopia.**] **Samuel Bochart**, in the previously cited work, page 703, concludes from this that the Ethiopians also abstained from swine. However, **Aelian (Natural History XVII, 10)** records from Dinon that a "four-horned pig" is born in Ethiopia. **Bochart** also reviews other nations that had the same custom. To these, an eminent man adds the Comanians from **Strabo (cited in Diodorus, Volume I, p. 380)**. I add the Cretans, about whom see **Athenaeus, Book IX, 4**, and the Pessinuntine Galatians <note>a Celtic people in Asia Minor</note>, "who do not touch pigs," according to **Pausanias in *Description of Greece (Achaia)*, p. 430**.

<column-break/>

11. **Just as therefore a camel.**] Greece did not abound in camels, which is why a learned man, in his notes on **Diogenes Laertius (cited in Philostratus’ *Life of Apollonius* I, 13)**, sought to restore "apples" <note>original: "μήλοις"</note> in place of "camels" <note>original: "καμήλοις"</note>, which I see is approved by **Olearius**. Regarding other peoples, the opposite is reported. **Jerome (Book II against Jovinian, 7)** says: "The Arabs and Saracens and all the barbarians of the desert live on the milk and meat of camels; because an animal of this kind is easily born and nourished among them due to the climate and the barrenness of the regions." For the word "therefore" <note>Greek: "οὖν"</note>, **Reiske** preferred "again" <note>Greek: "αὖ"</note> from the opposite side. Just after, the Cambridge edition had wrongly omitted the word "the" before "animals," which I have restored to its place from the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts and old editions.

12. **Neither did the Egyptians.**] The Egyptians abstained from pigs, as many teachers show, but they hardly agree on the reason for the matter. See **Bochart** in the place cited a moment ago. Nevertheless, **Herodotus (Book II, 47)** says they were sacrificed to the Moon and Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note>, and I believed that those sacrifices were discussed there in chapter 45. A great man thinks that passage is corrupt and should be understood as referring to sheep, which Herodotus says the Mendesians sacrificed. This is contradicted by **Strabo (Book XVII, p. 552)** regarding the Nitriotic Nome <note>a district in Egypt</note>: "among these alone in Egypt is a sheep sacrificed." **Plutarch**, however, asserts that only the Lycopolitans eat sheep (Vol. II, p. 380 B). At any rate, Egyptian theology was not the same throughout the whole kingdom, nor through every period of time.

### ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK I.
->D 2<-
<meta>catchword: ra</meta>

The Egyptians even now sacrifice it <note>the pig</note> for the same reason. But as for why some abstain from this animal entirely, it is just as if we ourselves were to shrink from eating camel meat.

§ 15. But why then should anyone abstain from eating living beings? Does it make one's soul worse, or the body? It is clear that neither is the case. For those animals that feed on flesh are more perceptive than the rest. Indeed, they are hunters, and they practice that art by which they make life more abundant. They likewise acquire might and strength, as do lions and wolves. Thus, the eating of flesh is seen to injure neither the soul nor the body. Furthermore, proof of this can be found in the fact that athletes make their bodies stronger by eating meat, and doctors [restore] the thinned-down bodies of the sick...

<column-break/>

...to whom they sacrifice, then, for the same reason. But for some to abstain from the animal entirely is similar to us not being willing to eat camel meat.

§ 15. Why should anyone abstain from living things? Does it make the soul worse or the body? It is clear that it does neither. For carnivorous animals are more intelligent than the others; at least, they are hunters, and possess this skill from which they derive their survival; they also possess strength and courage, like lions and wolves. Thus, meat-eating harms neither the soul nor the body. This is also clear from the fact that athletes provide their bodies with greater strength through meat-eating, and from the doctors, who [restore] bodies from illness...

---

<margin>13. **Eating camel meat.** <note>original: "Καμήλια ἐσθίειν"</note>] Rather it should be *kamēleia*, meaning the flesh of the camel. But no one is unaware that such words vary everywhere, whether they are pronounced with the diphthong *ei* or a simple *iota* <note>the letter 'i'</note>. In this matter, the better manuscripts are mostly to be followed. Jacques Philippe D'Orville <note>an 18th-century Dutch philologist</note> gives a full hand of examples in his notes on Chariton, Book IV, 5. He observes that in our author, *nosēlia* is used instead of *nosēleia* <note>referring to medical care</note> further below, and in Alciphron Book III, 3, *naumation* for *naumateion*. But I would believe *naumatiaion* to be better there. Soon, Meermann’s manuscript has *aposchoi* <note>"might abstain"</note>.</margin>

<margin>1. **They make life more abundant.** <note>original: "Περιεῖναι ποιεῖται"</note>] Perhaps it should be "from which they acquire a living." <note>original: "περιποιεῖται τὸν βίον"</note>. Johann Jakob Reiske <note>a noted 18th-century German classicist</note> noted that in the Meermann manuscript, the first hand had written "acquires," but the same hand had corrected it to "makes life more abundant."</margin>

<note>Translator's note: A comment regarding the character of carnivorous animals, which was praised a little earlier, is discussed later.</note>

<margin>2. **Meat-eating.** <note>original: "Κρεωφαγία"</note>] It was written in the Leipzig manuscript such that traces of both the readings *kreēphagia* and *kreōphagia* were visible. The former way is used once or twice shortly hereafter. Henri Estienne noted in his *Thesaurus* that this is Ionic and occurs in Hippocrates. But manuscripts vary on these everywhere, as below in § 46, in Pollux Book VI, 35, and others. Only the Valencia manuscript has *kreōphagia* here, and we have that form also in Book III, 1.</margin>

<margin>3. **And from the fact that athletes.** <note>original: "Κἀκ τοῦ τοὺς ἀθλ."</note>] So below in § 46, *kan* for *kai en* <note>"and in"</note>, and quite often. In prose writers, this form is also common enough, about which the most learned D'Orville speaks in his notes on Chariton, Book IV, 7. It occurs everywhere.</margin>

...they are accustomed to restore themselves by the eating of flesh. That Pythagoras did not hold a healthy opinion is indicated by no small sign: for none of the wise men were persuaded by him, neither any of the Seven Sages, nor the Natural Philosophers who came after. Indeed, not even the wisest Socrates, nor those who followed from Socrates, accepted it.

§ 16. But come, let us suppose all men were persuaded by this doctrine. ...they have been accustomed to restore themselves by the application of meat as food. For that Pythagoras did not think rightly, there is no small evidence. ...those things which ought to have been separated have grown together into one. Regarding the fattening of athletes, more will be said later. <note>The translator is likely referring to the common argument that athletes need meat for strength.</note>

<margin>4. *The wisest Socrates.*</margin> Socrates was judged *the wisest* <note>original: "sapientissimus"</note> not only by the consensus of men, but even by the oracle of Apollo, as Valerius Maximus says in Book III, 4. Indeed, the ancients everywhere look back to that oracle:
->*Of all men, Socrates is the wisest.*<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀνδρῶν δ’ ἁπάντων Σωκράτης σοφώτατος.</note>
Consult now Markland on Maximus Tyrius, Dissertation XXXIX. It is therefore no wonder that the ancients, as they loved to distinguish each of the Philosophers by some illustrious surname, gave to Socrates the title of *The Wise*. On this matter, read Holstenius in the *Life of Porphyry*, chapter 6.

<margin>1. *For it escapes no one's notice how many young a sow or a hare produces.*</margin> Those curious about nature discuss the fecundity of the sow and its causes. Consult the learned men on Aelian's *On the Nature of Animals*, XII, 16. Regarding that of hares, see Rittershusius on Oppian's *Cynegetica*, Book III, verse 522, and the learned men on Herodotus III, 108. Clement of Alexandria traces the cause back to this lustfulness <note>original: "falacitate," likely a typo for "salacitate" (lecherousness)</note> as to why Moses excluded the hare from the food of the Hebrews, in *The Instructor*, Book II, page 188 B. Next, the Meerman manuscript reads *the other animals*.

<column-break/>

<margin>2. *They kill.*</margin> The reading *they kill* <note>original: "ἀποκτείνουσιν"</note> holds well. For we are imagining that the peasants [do not] kill the beasts. Reiske and Valentinus had inserted *they will kill*, but I do not dare to move the common reading, in which all the manuscripts agree, although Felicianus seems to have read it otherwise. Plutarch illustrates this matter beautifully, showing that the eating of flesh was introduced by necessity, lest there be an excessive multitude of living creatures, since the oracle also warned that the fruits should not be destroyed in that manner, in *Symposiacs* VIII, 8. But more on this later.

<column-break/>

...indeed, he deprives himself of all cures, who refuses to eat animal flesh.

§ 18. But if, as they say, plants also possess a soul <note>The question of whether plants had souls was a major point of debate among ancient philosophers like the Pythagoreans and Stoics.</note>, what would our life be like if we were to cut ourselves off from both animals and plants? If a person who cuts down plants is not acting impiously, then neither is the person who kills animals.

§ 19. But some might say that one must not, by nature, kill that which is of the same kind—at least if the souls of animals are of the same substance <note>original: "homoousioi" (ὁμοούσιοι). This term later became central to Christian theology regarding the nature of the Trinity.</note> as our own. However, if one grants that souls enter bodies voluntarily, one might say they do so out of a desire for youth; for in youth, the enjoyment of all things is found. Why then do they not enter again into the nature of a human—

<column-break/>

...he cuts himself off from all treatments, who refuses to consume animals.

§ 18. But if, as they say, plants are also endowed with a soul, what finally will our life be, if we perceive nothing from animals or from plants? If he who plucks and pulls up plants does not act impiously, then he who kills an animal should not be judged as guilty of a crime.

§ 19. Yet someone might say: if the souls of brute animals are of the same substance as ours, we should not act cruelly toward our own kin. But if someone admits that they join with bodies of their own accord, they might claim they do so out of a love for youth, since in youth one can enjoy every pleasure. Why then do they not enter back into the nature of man—

---

<margin>4. *The one refusing.* Perhaps *the one depriving*. I would not, however, press this point strongly. — REISKE <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774) was a famous German physician and classical scholar known for his editions of Greek texts.</note>.</margin>

<margin>1. *Plants also have a soul.* He speaks with doubt as to whether plants are animate or not. He indicates below in § 21 that the Egyptians taught this. It is no surprise, therefore, that the Pythagoreans also held that souls migrate into the bodies of plants. Diogenes Laërtius preserved the well-known verses of Empedocles <note>Empedocles was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who believed in the transmigration of souls into various life forms.</note> on this matter (Book VIII, 77). See also Plotinus, *Enneads* III, Book IV, ch. 1, 2. But our author [Porphyry] could not maintain this opinion, as he even disliked the idea that human souls take on the bodies of beasts, according to Augustine in *The City of God* (X, 30). Thus, our author distinguishes between the "life of a plant" and "having a soul" <note>original: "empsychon" (ἔμψυχον)</note>. But compare what is said below at Book III, 27.</margin>

<margin>2. *Of us cutting off plants.* Perhaps *tasting*. If we shall taste neither beasts nor plants, or *touching*. See pages 18, 24, 21, 33. — REISKE. Certainly, *cutting* fits plants better than animals.</margin>

<column-break/>

In both languages [Greek and Latin], it is common for a verb to be joined to two nouns when it can only truly apply to one of them <note>This grammatical figure is known as "zeugma."</note>. D'Orville collected a wealth of examples in his notes on Chariton (IV, 4). Who does not know that line from Florus (Book IV, 12, 37): *They cut off the eyes of some, the hands of others*? I cite this from many examples because it uses our word [cutting/amputating]. Some explain the Gospel of Luke (1:64) this way, but without necessity. The word "what" would therefore be suppressed.

<margin>1. *The same kind... if of the same substance.* After "the same kind," we should understand the phrase "as we ourselves say." — REISKE. The opposite is "of another kind," a word mentioned above. No one who remembers the upheavals stirred up among Christians is ignorant of the word <term>homoousios: a Greek word meaning "of the same substance" or "consubstantial," used in the Nicene Creed to describe the relationship between God the Father and God the Son</term>, which you might rightly call the token of the Nicene party. Suicer in his *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus* and Le Moyne in *Varia Sacra* (p. 258) show it was already in use before the Council of Nicaea.</margin>

<margin>2. *Willingly entering.* Perhaps *unwillingly*. — REISKE.</margin>

<margin>3. *Because of love.* Reiske thinks "because of" should be deleted.</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book I.

...are they driven? But if they enter into bodies voluntarily, out of a love for youth, it must be admitted that they must travel through every species of animal; thus, we should consider that the slaughter of animals is actually pleasing to them, as it procures for them a swifter return into human form. For if their bodies are eaten, it can cause them no distress, since they have already been separated from them and long to be within the nature of a man. Indeed, we must believe that just as much pain as they feel when leaving a human body, they feel an equal amount of pleasure when they are released from other bodies. This is because it allows them to return more quickly to man, who holds sovereignty over the other living creatures just as God holds it over men. Therefore, a sufficient reason for killing them is that by killing them, we prevent them from harming men. For if the souls of men are immortal while those of brutes are mortal, we do not act unjustly by killing them. But if their souls are also immortal, we actually benefit them by killing them; for we do this to grant them a swifter return into human nature.

§ 20. But if we are taking revenge, we do not offend, but rather punish those who cause offense.

->Which-<-

<column-break/>

...they entered into nature. But if they did so voluntarily, and through a love of youth <note>original: "νεότητος ἔρωτι"</note>, and through every form of living thing, then being killed would be a favor to them. For the return to the human state is swifter; and the bodies being eaten would not instill grief in the souls, as they have been released from them; and their desire would be to come into the nature of a man. Thus, as much as they might grieve leaving the human state, so much would they rejoice leaving other bodies. For the return to man is swifter—man, who rules over all irrational creatures as God rules over men. Therefore, there is sufficient cause to kill other animals insofar as they do harm by killing men. If the souls of men are immortal, but those of irrational creatures are mortal, we men do not act unjustly by killing the irrational ones; just as we benefit them, if they are indeed immortal, by killing them: for we do this to facilitate the return to human nature.

§ 20. But if we defend ourselves, we do not act unjustly, but we pursue those who act unjustly—
