Perhaps "sweet-smelling uses of incenses, and breaths that [trade] their own loves..." Indeed, the word "sweet-smelling" (*ἡδυσώδης*) is rare for "fragrant" (*ἡδύοσμος*), and the construction "sweet-smelling uses of incenses" is rare for "uses of sweet-smelling incenses." # PORPHYRY

One of the physicians once said that it is not only the medicinal preparations of the medical art, but also the daily foods and drinks we consume for nourishment, that transmit a far more deadly force to the soul than the poisons prepared by pharmacies to bring about the dissolution of the body. Furthermore, the sensations of touch—which all but turn the soul into a physical body—often provoke it to fall into inarticulate noises, as if it were already mere flesh. From these sensations, memories, fantasies, and accumulated opinions arise, stirring up a swarm of passions: they fill the soul with fears, desires, angers, loves, charms, griefs, envies, anxieties, and diseases of similar disturbances.

§. 35. Therefore, the struggle to be purified of these things is great, and the labor to be freed from the constant dwelling upon them—both by night and by day—is immense.

<column-break/>

<note>The Latin column mirrors the Greek text above, emphasizing that the "deadly power" (letifera uis) of food is more dangerous to the soul's health than physical poison is to the body.</note>

One physician said that it is not only those things compounded by medicine, but also the foods and drinks habitually taken for daily nourishment, from which a deadly power is diffused into the soul, more so than the destruction brought to the body's dissolution by poisons. Now indeed, touches—rendering the soul almost corporeal—often cause it to break out into inarticulate sounds, as if it were now becoming a body. From all these things, memories, imaginations, and opinions are gathered, and an innumerable flock of perturbations is excited, filling the soul with the diseases of fears, lusts, angers, loves, allurements, pains, emulations, anxieties, and disturbances of this kind.

§ 35. And for that reason, it is difficult to be purged of these; a very great labor must be undertaken if we wish to be liberated from the meditation upon them, since by day...

---

<margin>That this "variety of foods" is the single cause of diseases is noted in <note>original: "τῶν ἐδεσμάτων τὴν πολυειδίαν"</note> Clement of Alexandria, *The Instructor*, Book II, page 140 B.</margin>

9. **And into inarticulate noises]** I do not understand this passage. It is obscure what those "inarticulate sounds" are into which the sense of touch might run. Or, if we prefer the reading *to fall into* <note>original: "ἐμπίπτειν"</note>, it suggests being carried away and dashed against them, like a ship against rocks. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note>. I understand these as the "clatter and tumult" into which the soul falls through that sense. Jerome refers to this in *Against Jovinianus*, Book II, 8: *"The touch of foreign bodies and the burning desire for women is neighbor to insanity. Because of this sense we desire, we grow angry, we exult, we envy, we emulate, we are anxious... especially since touch depicts for itself even past pleasures, and by memory forces the soul to suffer along with it, and in a way to practice what it is not actually doing."* Lipsius does not have the word *but* <note>original: "δὲ"</note> before *touches*. Meermann wrongly reads *into articulate* <note>original: "εἰς ἄρθρους"</note>.

10. **A swarm of passions]** Below in Book II, 62, he calls it a "swarm of evils." Hesychius defines "swarm" <note>original: "ἑσμὸς"</note> as a "multitude," where learned men have noted many things of this kind.

11. **Loves, charms]** Below in Book II, 42, "erotic things" and "charms" <note>original: "Φίλτρα"</note> are also joined. The word *philtron* is used sometimes for a drug given for the sake of love, and sometimes for conjugal love or the love shown toward children. This is a well-known matter; see Wolf on Libanius, Epistle 76. Meermann mistakenly reads *fear, desire*.

I. **The labor to be freed]** Lipsius reads "a laborless labor to be freed" <note>original: "πόνος ἄπονος"</note> as a correction, for previously he had written...

...and by night the necessary connection of the senses accompanies us everywhere. ...the middle word "without toil" <note original="ἀπόνως">aponos</note> was approved, which is more tolerable, yet not necessary. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and philologist.</note> then <term>MEERMANN</term> <note>Gerard Meerman, a Dutch book collector and scholar.</note> "daily."

2. **To the multitude.** <note original="Τῷ πλήθει">To plethei</note>] Perhaps it should be "to passion" <note original="τῷ πάθει">to pathei</note>, which is not only suggested by the matter itself, but is also confirmed by a marginal scholium (a brief explanatory note) that summarizes the argument and brings it to memory; this was written in red ink in the margin of the <term>Leipzig</term> manuscript <note original="Lips.">Codex Lipsiensis</note>: "that one must stand apart from those places where we fall into passions." <term>REISKE</term>. However, the common reading is protected by the following section: "it is not changed by the multitude." <term>Meerman</term> wrongly read the preceding word as "let him depart."

1. **For thus we hear of the, etc.**] Here our author [Porphyry] continues to be followed by Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the church father, who often quoted or adapted Porphyry's arguments on asceticism despite being a theological opponent.</note> in Book 1, Chapter 9. "Invited by these reasons, many of the philosophers left the crowds of the cities and the suburban gardens... *For even the Pythagoreans, avoiding this kind of crowd, were accustomed to live in solitude and desert places. The Platonists also and Stoics spent their time in the groves and porticoes of temples...*"

<column-break/>

"...*But Plato himself, so that he might be free for philosophy, chose the villa of the Academy far from the city, which was not only deserted but even pestilential.* We read of some who gouged out their own eyes," etc. For "thus" <note original="οὕτω">houto</note> <term>Meerman</term> reads "in this way" <note original="οὕτως">houtos</note>.

2. **And far from the city.** <note original="Καὶ πόῤῥω τοῦ ἄστεως">Kai porro tou asteos</note>] This passage is quite difficult. It used to be read as "from the satiety" <note original="τῆς ἄσεως">tes aseos</note>, but we corrected it to "the city" <note original="τοῦ ἄστεως">tou asteos</note> from the <term>Leipzig</term> and <term>Meerman</term> manuscripts. This is a minor point, owed to a scribal abbreviation. But how could he say the Academy was "far from the city"? Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer.</note> rightly says in his *Attica* (p. 55) and by the consensus of all, it was separated from the city by a space of only a few paces. Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius (1579–1639), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> saw this difficulty and thus in his work *Ceramicus* (chapter 20) rewrites it as "before the city" <note original="πρὸ τοῦ ἄστεος">pro tou asteos</note>, as it is read in the author of the *Etymologicum Magnum*. And Markland <note>Jeremiah Markland (1693–1776), an English classical scholar.</note> agrees on Max. Tyr. Diss. V. p. 661. But then this error must have haunted our author for several centuries...

# PORPHYRY

...and far away, a place outside the city, but also, as they say, <note>original Greek: epinoson</note> unhealthy. Others did not even spare their eyes, out of a longing for undistracted inner contemplation. But if anyone thinks that by living among men and filling their senses with their corresponding passions, they themselves will remain unaffected, they deceive both themselves and those they persuade. Such a person does not realize that they have been greatly enslaved to these passions by the very presence of the multitude, rather than by being alienated from them. For it was not without reason, nor by lying about the nature of philosophers, that he <note>Plato</note> spoke, saying: "These men, I suppose, from their youth—"

<column-break/>

...it was deserted, and far from the city, and was considered hardly healthy, as they say. Moreover, it is known that there were some who, out of a desire for inner contemplation, so as not to be distracted, did not spare their own eyes. But if anyone thinks that by living among men and satisfying the senses with their own passions, they will remain free from suffering, they deceive both themselves and those they have persuaded; nor do they notice that by the very fact that they are not alienated from the crowd, they have surrendered most especially to the power of the passions. For it was not rashly, nor by lying about the nature of philosophers, that he who said: "These men, indeed, from their youth first [enter] the path..."

---

<note>Note 2</note> ...had occupied it, for *Jerome, Book I* reads it this way: he chose the *Academy, a villa far from the city.* I would almost believe that some such interval, however brief, is signified. Learned men have long ago noted regarding *Matthew 8:30* that the Greek word *makran* [far] and the Latin *Procul* [far] are used in this way. Indeed, the scholar Alberti observes regarding Hesychius that both *makran* and *to porrho* [the far-off], although denoting distance, can even denote a *very short* distance. Those who are "not yet washed with the copper coin" <note>A Latin idiom meaning those who are not yet educated or have not yet reached adulthood</note> know that *Astu* [The City] is used peculiarly to refer to *Athens*, just as *Urbs* refers to Rome, *Fluvius* to the Nile, and so on.

3. <note>original: Epinoson</note> *Unhealthy.*] Others also signify this. *Aelian, Varia Historia IX, 10:* "Plato, when the Academy was said to be a sickly place..." where the *Interpreters* have more on this matter. If these things are true, it must be said that Cimon gained little, who "beautified the city, showing the Academy to be a well-watered grove instead of a dry and parched one, adorned by him with clean running paths and shaded walks," according to *Plutarch, Vol. I, p. 487. C.* Just now, the word *ton* [the] had been omitted by the *Cambridge* edition, against the evidence of previous editors and my own manuscripts.

<column-break/>

4. <note>original: Polu ton p. k. etc.</note> *Greatly enslaved etc.*] It is better to read "enslaved him" and the verb should be taken in the active sense. This is customary. VALCKENAER. This latter point is most true, but I would prefer to understand "himself" as implied. The force of the middle voice verb is well known, and how uselessly it is read in *Lucian's Solecist*: "to be enslaved happens to another, but to enslave happens to oneself." *Duker on Thucydides III, 70* and others have shown this. The sense, therefore, is "that the majority of passions enslave him to it (the multitude) through non-alienation." Reiske had added to these last words: "properly not --- alienation from the common people." *Ouk-allotriosis* [non-alienation] is essentially one word, and was written as such in the *Meerman* manuscript. Note the Grammarians' figure of the *hyphen* <note>The "joining under one" or compounding of words</note>.

5. <note>original: Tes physeos katapseudomenes</note> *Lying against nature.*] "One who lies." This signifies Plato, whose famous passage on this is read in the *Theaetetus*. REISKE. Excellent. *Katapseudesthai* with the genitive is used everywhere by the Greeks for "to lie about something regarding someone" or "to rashly attribute something to someone." Thus, "to lie against human nature," below in *Book IV, 21.* Perizonius provides other examples in *Aelian, Varia Historia XII, chapter 36.*

# On Abstinence, Book I.

They do not even know the way to the marketplace, nor where the court of law, or the council chamber, or any other public assembly of the city is located. As for the laws and decrees that are spoken or written, they neither see nor hear them. Indeed, the strivings of political factions for office, the meetings, the dinners, and the revels with flute-girls <note>original: "psaltriis" (Latin) / "αὐλητρίσι" (Greek) — female musicians often present at banquets</note> do not occur to them even in their dreams. Whether something has happened well or ill in the city, or if some misfortune has befallen someone from their ancestors—whether men or women—it escapes the philosopher's notice more than the "pebbles of the sea," as the saying goes. And of all these things, he does not even know that he does not know them; for he does not abstain from them for the sake of gaining a reputation. In reality, only his body remains and dwells in the city, while his mind, considering all these things to be small and worth nothing at all—

<column-break/>

—from their youth, first of all, they do not know the way to the marketplace, nor where the courtroom or the council-chamber is, or any other common assembly of the city; and as for laws and decrees, whether spoken or written, they neither see nor hear them. Whether something has happened well or ill in the city, or if some evil has come to someone from their ancestors, whether on the side of the men or the women, it escapes his notice more than the so-called "measures of the sea" <note>original: "χόες" — a Greek unit of liquid measure, here used proverbially to mean something impossible to count, like the sands or drops of the sea</note>. 7. **The zeal of political clubs.**] We have taken care to edit it thus. Previously it was read as *spoudaite* <note>a corruption in the Greek text</note>. Not only the authority of the *Meermann* manuscript, but also *Plato*, and those whom I said described him, command it so. Instead of *hetaireiōn* (of clubs), *Clement of Alexandria* and *Eusebius* have *hetairiōn*. We have said above that "ei" and "i" were frequently confused in these matters because the sound was almost the same.

8. **In the city.**] Thus it is correct. Only the *Cambridge* manuscript had *en omi*, but *Plato* and the others go against it. Then I restored *tōi k.* (to someone) instead of *to k.* (the), which was read previously. It is correctly published as *tōi* in *Eusebius*, and it must be restored to *Plato* and others. The *Florentine* edition and the *Leipzig* manuscript command the same, except that in the latter, instead of the enclitic *tōi*, it was written as *tῷ*. This is also in the *Meermann* manuscript. Instead of "from ancestors," *Theodoret*—but he alone—has "among ancestors." *Plato* and *Eusebius*, however, have "or on the side of the men."

9. **It escapes his notice.**] Both the *Leiden* and *Cambridge* editions wanted *autous* (them, plural). But *Plato* and the rest contradict this. The editors did not remember that it is a common usage for Attic writers and others to very often transition from the plural to the singular. The *choes* (measures) are rendered as "sands of the sea" by the translator of *Plato*, p. 64. A little later, the *Meermann* manuscript has *archetai* (begins) instead of *apechetai* (abstains); this is an error.

§ 37. For through these words, Plato says that the philosopher does not descend into the aforementioned affairs, remaining unaffected by them, but rather remains one who does not lower himself into any of them. <gloss>1</gloss> Therefore, he says, he knows neither the way to where the court or the council chamber is, nor any other specific matter of this kind. <gloss>2</gloss> It is not that he knows them and encounters them, but in encountering them fills his senses with them so that he "knows nothing"; on the contrary, Plato says that by abstaining from them and being ignorant of them, he does not even know that he does not know. § 37. By these words, Plato says that by not involving himself in the things mentioned before, the philosopher remains unaffected by them, being one who involves himself in none of these things. Therefore, he says, he knows neither the way to the street, nor where the forum, the court, or the council-chamber is, nor anything else of this specific sort. He does not say that he knows and encounters them, and by encountering them and filling his senses from them, he is unaware that he does not know; but on the contrary, while he abstains from them and is ignorant of them, he then says he does not even know whether he is ignorant. He says it occurs to him. Much less, then, will he be indignant if he is deprived of some broth or a small piece of meat; instead, he will apply a certain care to these matters: not considering them small or insignificant if he abstains, but rather great and harmful if he partakes in them. Since he holds examples within the nature of reality—that the divine is the most blessed state, while the godless is the most miserable—he will show himself similar to the former and dissimilar to the latter. He will establish a life consistent with the one he wishes to resemble, a life content with a very meager diet and one that is least filled with mortal affairs.

# PORPHYRY

§ 38. For as long as someone is troubled <note>original: "διαφορῆται" - to be distracted or anxious</note> about foods, and argues that this or that must be eaten, and does not consider that—if it were possible—one should abstain from all nourishment entirely, such a person is merely advocating for their own passions. They are "hunting for reputation" <note>original: "δοξοκοπεῖ" - to seek vain glory or be obsessed with mere opinion</note>, acting as if there were no difference in the very things they are disputing. Now, the philosopher will not take himself out by force <note>This refers to the Neoplatonic prohibition against suicide; one must wait for the soul to be naturally released.</note>. For he who is forced out nevertheless remains in that place from which he is being violently removed. Yet, he will not think it a matter of indifference if he makes his bond <note>The "bond" refers to the physical body which chains the soul.</note> thicker. Therefore, granting only what is necessary to nature, and ensuring that even this is light and provided through lighter foods, he will reject everything beyond this as tending toward pleasure.

<column-break/>

§ 38. For as long as anyone disputes about foods, and contends that this also must be eaten, and is not of the opinion that, if it could be done, one should assert that all nourishment whatsoever must be abstained from; he seems to patronize his passions boastfully and in vain: as one who thinks it matters nothing in those things about which he disputes. But he who practices philosophy will not withdraw himself from these things by force: for he who is compelled by violence is nonetheless accustomed to resist in that place from whence he is unwillingly led away: yet he will not think, if he renders the bond thicker for himself, that he is doing something that matters nothing. Wherefore, exhibiting to nature only that which is necessary, and that being exceedingly light, and by the lightest foods possible, he will refuse whatever exceeds this limit, as if for the sake of pleasure.

---

<margin>
It is the same, and has just as much value as *accommodating oneself to another*, or finally, adopting the reading of the *Leipzig manuscript*, *being filled*, one should read *being filled with mortal things*, or *being filled with mortal food*. REISKE. A little before, instead of *likely*, the Meerman manuscript wrongly has *yielding*.
</margin>

1. *Is troubled.*] To be troubled <note>original: "διαφορεῖσθαι"</note> in this place is not *to disagree*, but to be distressed in mind, to labor, not to be at peace whether a thing exists or not, or whether it happens in this way or another, but to think it matters much to oneself how a thing happens or does not happen. Therefore, *to be troubled* is the same as *to differ* <note>original: "διαφέρεσθαι"</note> a little later. REISKE. The illustrious Abresch preferred *both to be troubled and* or *to differ and*. Instead of *foods* <note>original: "βρωτῶν"</note>, the Meerman manuscript has *mortals* <note>original: "βροτῶν"</note>, by a frequent error, as we saw above.

2. *That this also must be eaten.*] *That this must also be eaten*. REISKE.

3. *Hunting for reputation*] This is a rarer word. It is said of a vain opinion which occupies someone fruitlessly, like other compounds of this origin. In *Plutarch's Life of Pericles*, p. 154 E, instead of *hunting for reputation* and *reputation-seeking*, some manuscripts prefer our word and *reputation-seeking*. Several authors use this latter term, as does our author below in Book II, 52, which see.

<column-break/>

4. *The philosopher [will not take] himself out.*] Holstenius in *The Life of Porphyry*, chapter 8, and the learned editor of *Hierocles on the Golden Verses*, p. 260, as well as others, explain *to lead oneself out* as *to take one's own life*, in which sense our author is accustomed to use it, as we shall say regarding Book II, § 46. It could be understood here as *detachment*, when one withdraws oneself from the senses and leads the soul out, as it were, from the body, so that it is not hindered by its mass and passions—a doctrine he emphasizes everywhere. Nevertheless, the nature of the expression is the same.

5. *Making the bond thicker.*] See above, § 34, and below in § 47 he calls it the *thickness of the bond*.

6. *Through lighter [foods].*] Perhaps *nourishing through the lightest [foods]*, namely *nature* or *the body*. REISKE. Soon, instead of *tending toward*, the Bodleian manuscript wrongly has *stretching together*.

...making [the soul] abstinent, he will reject them. For he is persuaded, as that famous man said <note>original: "inquit ille" — referring to Plato in the *Phaedo*</note>, that sensation is a "nail" to the soul. This nail, through the multitude of things it perceives, penetrates the soul and glues it to the body, fastening it there through enjoyment. For if the senses were not an obstacle to the pure activity of the soul, what difficulty would there be for a person to remain unaffected by the motions of the body even while living within it?

# PORPHYRY

...another thing is to think that one is not present by withdrawing oneself <note>original: "ἄλλο δὲ, ᾧ τῷ ἀφισάντα νομίζειν ἑαυτὸν μὴ παρεῖναι"</note>. Certainly, no one will show that Plato grants this, unless they wish to demonstrate that he was deceiving himself. For he who willingly descends into the acceptance of food, and into sights perceived by the eyes, and into social gatherings and laughter, is—by that very descent and attachment—present there where the emotion is. But he who is intent on other things and stands apart from these, is the one who, through his lack of worldly experience, provides laughter not only to Thracian maidservants but to the rest of the crowd; and when he is forced into such situations, he falls into every kind of confusion—not because he truly lacks sensation, nor because he perceives with exactness, but because he perceives only with the irrational part of his soul.

<column-break/>

...it is another thing to think that one is not present by attending to and standing by a thing. Certainly, no one can show that Plato concedes this point, unless one wishes to argue that he was deceiving himself. Therefore, the person who voluntarily gives himself over to the consumption of food, to spectacles, to social meetings, and to laughter, is—by that very surrender and approach—present in the place where the feeling exists. But he who is focused on other things and stays away from these, is that famous figure who, due to his lack of skill in worldly matters, offers a reason for laughter not only to Thracian maidservants but to the common mob. When he is compelled to join them, he falls into total hesitation; not because he is devoid of his senses, or because he perceives things exactly, but because he functions only by the irrational sense.

---

3. *The one withdrawing...*] It would be better to read *the one applying focus* <note>original: "τὸ ἐφισάντα"</note>. VALENTINUS. Reiske was of the same opinion, and rightly so, although I know what might be said in defense of the common reading. The Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts also have *the* <note>original: "τὸ"</note>. The Bodleian manuscript is very faulty here... and then the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts have *encountering* <note>original: "ἀπαντῶντα"</note>, which Fogerolles had published.

4. *Into the sights of the eyes willingly, etc.*] The word *through* <note>original: "διὰ"</note> is missing in the Leipzig manuscript. I am troubled by this passage and cannot easily explain it. For what does it mean? Are there other sights <term>theai: spectacles or contemplations</term> that are not made *through the eyes*? Is the word *sight* as ambiguous as *thing heard* <note>original: "akroama"</note>? Just as the latter signifies any kind of performance (though properly it refers only to things delighting the ear), perhaps *sight* refers to every spectacle, even if it does not delight the eyes alone. I do not like the word *social gatherings* <note>original: "homilias"</note>; I would prefer *jesting* <note>original: "samylias"</note>, which fits better with *laughter*. I also wonder if *of the sight* <note>original: "opseos"</note> hides the word *of a taunt* <note>original: "skopseos"</note>. REISKE. I understand these *sights* to be those mentioned above in § 33, which are very different from that contemplation described in Book II, § 34, where he says of the Gods: *that they truly nourish us through the sight of them.* The word *socializing* <note>original: "homilia"</note> has a very broad meaning and encompasses all meetings and almost everything that usually happens in daily life. Compare those cited by Alberti on Paul's First Epistle to the Corinthians 15:33: "Bad company ruins good morals."

5. *Providing laughter.*] This refers to the famous story told about the philosopher Thales and his clever maidservant <note>Thales was so busy looking at the stars that he fell into a well; a Thracian maid laughed at him for knowing the heavens but not what was at his feet</note>. I have Plato as a witness for this, who, after narrating that story, continues in the *Theaetetus*: *he provides laughter not only to Thracian maids but to the crowd.* Eusebius excerpted this from Plato, as he did other things. That woman is commonly said to have been Thracian by birth, but Origen suggests this was her proper name. Since it was common for maidservants to take their names from their homelands, there is no reason to worry about this reading.

6. *But not lacking sensation.*] Instead of *but* <note>original: "ἀλλ'"</note>, it seems *since* <note>original: "ἅτε"</note> should be read. But this passage is somewhat complex. What if the author meant: *as one not perceiving with precision, nor again perceiving with precision, but by the irrational part*—insofar as he shows himself neither completely foolish and slow, nor on the other hand a spectator and judge of common things.

...then act with that faculty: for Plato never dared to say this. ### PORPHYRII
5.

§ 41. But what was the need both to wither the passions <note>original: "marainein ta pathe"</note> and to die from them, and to practice this daily, if it were possible for us to act according to the intellect while being joined to mortal things without any oversight from the intellect—as some have declared? For "it is the intellect that sees and the intellect that hears." <note>A famous maxim by the poet-philosopher Epicharmus, suggesting that without mental attention, the physical senses are useless.</note> But if, while eating costly foods and drinking the sweetest wine, you are able to be present with immaterial things, why can you not also frequently be present and act,

<column-break/>

§ 41. But what need would there be to cause the passions to waste away and to die as far as they are concerned, and to meditate on this daily: if it were possible that we might work by the intellect, and yet dwell upon mortal things without any inspection of the intellect, as some assert? For "the intellect sees, and the intellect hears," as that man says. If indeed, while eating very sumptuously and drinking the most pleasant wine, you can direct your mind to things lacking matter: why can you not also do the same while you possess the thing and act upon it,

---

pertinere <gloss>to pertain to</gloss>. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and philologist known for his editions of Greek texts.</note> As below in § 41. *for it is not possible*, with which place in the *Gospel of Luke* XIII, 33 the illustrious <term>Elsner</term> <note>Jakob Elsner, a theologian who compared classical Greek usage with the New Testament.</note> compares: and so throughout.

1. **To wither the passions, and to die.**] **To wither** is used metaphorically regarding the passions. Our author [Porphyry] uses "through withering" below in III, 26 and IV, 3—and "death" above in § 32, just as in this place it is joined with "to die." Elsewhere he calls it the **death of the Philosophers**, which by others, such as Pythagoras in the *Golden Verses*, is called the "release from evils." This philosophical death is recommended throughout at the end of Book II: "we who have made the daily practice of dying our way of life." What kind of death that is, he teaches in *Sentences Leading to the Intelligible* § 9: "Death is indeed twofold: one well known [physical death]... the other that of the Philosophers, when the soul is released from the body." Pythagoras took this custom of subduing and taming the body like an enemy from the Egyptians, and from them it was propagated to other nations, especially the Indians, where it has not yet fallen into disuse; on this matter see La Croze's *History of Christianity in India*, Book VI. Truly, as for the fact that interpreters are accustomed to crowd these sorts of passages when they find something similar in the New Testament (for example, in the *Epistle to the Romans* VI, 2), those who have experience in ancient philosophy understand by what right this is done.

2. **Some declared.**] Perhaps *as some declared*. The word "as" <note>original: "hos"</note> was lost in the collision with the end of the word "inspection" <term>REISKE</term>. This is very true, and thus the translator has it. Previously it was read as "Who were declaring?"; however, traces of the true reading were in the Leipzig manuscript. <term>Meermann</term> <note>Gerard Meerman (1722–1771), a Dutch scholar and book collector.</note> reads it more correctly as "some declared." Unless it was in the singular "someone declared," which <term>Marsilio Ficino</term> <note>The 15th-century philosopher who translated Plato and Porphyry into Latin.</note> seems to have read, for he translates: "as someone declared," so that it refers back to the following saying of Epicharmus. But the preceding syllable had absorbed the "as," as happens a hundred times. You could also read "of some inspection," which pleased <term>Abresch</term>.

3. **For the intellect sees etc.**] A famous saying of Epicharmus: "The Intellect sees, and the Intellect hears; all else is deaf and blind." Jerome, in *Against Jovinian* II, 9: "That the mind sees, and the mind hears, and that we can neither hear nor see anything unless our sense is focused on those things we discern and hear," is also an ancient opinion. We will say more at Book III, 21, where Plutarch praises the saying, but with the author’s name suppressed.

4. **Why not also etc.**] "Frequently" in this place is not "often," but "for example," so that I may use this. <term>REISKE</term>. For the word "you are," the Leiden edition had substituted "it may be," which I do not know where they got. For the Florence edition also has "you are." But both are wrong in the word "being with." <term>Abresch</term> preferred "frequently being with." Those things which follow, "things which are not even beautiful to speak of," are frequently used in cases of this kind; <term>Wetstein</term> <note>Johann Jakob Wetstein (1693–1754), a theologian and scholar of the Greek New Testament.</note> teaches this, and does not forget our author in his notes on Paul’s *Epistle to the Ephesians* V, 12.

<column-break/>

# PORPHYRY

->and being carried toward that place, while being here, to be there. For we do not direct our attention with a part of ourselves, but with our whole being.<-

**§ 42.** 1. The belief that one can be affected according to the senses and yet simultaneously act toward the intelligible <note>Greek: *noētois*; things understood by the mind rather than the senses</note> has led many, even 2. among the barbarians <note>A term used by Greeks/Romans for non-Hellenic peoples, often including Jews and Christians</note>, to fall headlong into ruin. These people, out of a spirit of negligence, have advanced into every form of pleasure, claiming 3. that it is possible for one who is occupied with other things to allow themselves to use the irrational part of their nature. Indeed, I have already heard some who, in defense of their own misfortune, argue in this manner—

<column-break/>

—it is possible that we are carried here and there at the same time, and while we are here, we are also able to be present there. For attentions are not made by a part of us, but by the whole.

**§ 42.** For this opinion—that anyone, while all their senses are being affected, can still be free for intelligible things—has carried many even of the barbarians headlong and destroyed them. These people, poured out into every kind of pleasure through negligence, asserted that they were indulging themselves because, while they were attending to other things, they could also use their irrational faculties. Now indeed I have heard some, when they were patronizing their own unhappiness, in this—

***

<margin>Venetian Miscellaneous Observations, chapter 16.</margin>
—it is necessary: because we are born such that we cannot help but indulge ourselves in this. <small>REISKE.</small> So above in § 31: *the necessity of generation* <note>original: "hē anankē tēs geneseōs"</note>. Plato and others very often speak this way. Our author calls it *the necessity of mortal nature* <note>original: "tēs thnētēs physeōs anankēn"</note> in § 45. Just before "to perceive" <note>original: "noein"</note>, the word "of the" <note>original: "tou"</note> was wrongly missing in the Florence and Leiden editions.

1. *The belief that etc.*] Jerome expressed this in *Against Jovinianus*, Book II, chapter 9: *But if anyone thinks that he can enjoy an abundance of food and drink and still be free for wisdom—that is, to live in luxury and not be held by the vices of luxury—he deceives himself.*

2. *Led many of the barbarians headlong.*] *P. Petit, Miscellaneous Observations, book 1, chapter 5*, is excessive in explaining and amending this passage. He says it was badly translated by Holstenius (note a frequent error, about which I speak elsewhere) and that he could not amend or complete it. He thinks it refers to Solomon, King of the Hebrews, and that he is called a "barbarian." He suggests Porphyry had read those words of Solomon: "vanity of vanities" etc., and had also seen the passage where Solomon boasts of his wealth and magnificence. From this, he concludes that Solomon held the heresy that a wise man could be free for mental contemplation and bodily pleasures at the same time. He thinks that after the word "saying" <note>original: "legontes"</note>, Solomon's words "vanity etc." were lost and the passage should be reconstructed in that sense.

<column-break/>

Who does not see that these ideas are far-fetched, and there is no need for such circuitous reasoning? Nor do I subscribe to the learned *Thomasius*, who (*Treasury of Lacrozian Epistles, Vol. I, p. 341*) thought the Epicureans were being touched upon here. I would hardly think he wished to include them under the name of "barbarians," for he usually speaks of them more mildly. As that word is used most widely, and pertains peculiarly to the Jews and Christians, it should be taken here in that broad sense. *Led headlong* <note>original: "Exetrachēlisen"</note> is a term taken from the wrestling school. The word was excellently illustrated by *Perizonius on Aelian's Varia Historia XII, 58* and *V. D. Miscellaneous Observations Vol. III, p. 242*. From there, it means in any way to *cast someone down headlong, to ruin them.* "To lead youth headlong" <note>original: "ektrachēlizein tēn neotēta"</note>—*Plutarch, Vol. II, p. 13. A.; Alciphron III, 40; Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book IV, p. 173. D.: "they led the multitudes and the common people headlong."* Compare also *Wetstein on the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. IV, 13*, though that passage does not belong here. *Meermann*, with the order of letters disturbed, wrote "exetrachilēsen." Just now I have restored "hou" <note>of which</note> on the faith of the *Leipzig* manuscript; previously it was read as "hoi" <note>who</note>.

3. *And to be able etc.*] In the *Leipzig* manuscript it is "tōn," which leads us to the tracks of the true reading. By deleting "kai" <note>and</note>, which seems to have been born from the "s" of the word "legontes" <note>saying</note>, and changing "tōn" to "tō," I think it should be read: *saying, that by being able to perceive* (understand "someone") *even while being occupied with other things, they allow themselves to use the irrational part* (understand "themselves"). <small>REISKE.</small> "Tōn" was also in—

### ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK I.

...this way, they say, foods in no way pollute us: just as the sea is not defiled by filthy flows. For we dominate all things, just as the sea is superior to all fluids. But if the sea closed its mouth so as not to admit those things that flow in, it would indeed be great in itself, but in relation to the world it would be considered small, as if it were unable to contain filth. If it were careful not to be defiled, it would certainly not admit them. But since it recognizes its own greatness, it receives everything, and turns away nothing that flows into it. Thus we, they say, if we avoid the eating of some things, we are reduced to slavery, being subject to fear; for us, it is necessary that all things be subjected. For if a small amount of water collected anywhere admits something filthy, it is immediately polluted by...

<column-break/>

...way: 4 For foods do not defile us, they say, just as the filthy flows do not defile the sea. For we are masters of all things, just as the sea is of all liquids. If it were cautious about being defiled, it would not receive them. But because of this, it receives everything, knowing its own greatness, and does not turn away what comes into it. And so we also, they say, 6 if we are cautious about eating, have become enslaved to the 7 mindset of fear. But it is necessary that all things be subjected to us. Indeed, these words are often used interchangeably. Consult D'Orville's notes on Chariton, Book V, chapter 10. However, *stexai* properly means to take in such a way that you hold it, and therefore it is said of vessels that have no cracks, and thus hold what has been poured in. Many things are noted by...

</margin>

6. **If we are cautious.** <note>Greek: *ean eulabēthōmen*</note> Perhaps it should be "we were cautious" <note>Greek: *eulabēthēmen*</note> because of the following "we were enslaved." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske was a 18th-century German scholar known for his corrections of Greek texts.</note>

7. **To the mindset of fear.** <note>Greek: *tou phobou phronēmati*</note> In place of "mindset" <note>*phronēmatos*</note>, the Leipzig manuscript has "thread/thought" <note>*nēmati*</note>. It seems it should be read as "we were enslaved to the **stain of slaughter**" <note>Latin: "serviremus piaculo vel sceleri caedis"; Greek: *tou phonou miasmati*</note>, that is, we would never be free from the fear of the slaughter to be carried out in some animal, and thus of contracting guilt. Since no one can be careful enough to prevent themselves from sometimes killing an animal even against their will, this matter would keep every one of us always anxious. <term>REISKE</term>. **Mindset** <note>*phronēmati*</note> here means a thought, or as commonly said, a *presumption*.

# PORPHYRY

...is immediately defiled, and <margin>8</margin> is enslaved by that filth; but the deep abyss is not defiled. In this same way, the eating <margin>9</margin> of a few things <note>referring to restricted or specific types of food</note> overcomes [the soul]. But where there is a depth of power, <margin>10</margin> they receive all things and are defiled by nothing. Deceiving themselves with such arguments, they acted in ways consistent <margin>11</margin> with their own deception; and instead of achieving freedom, they threw themselves into the abyss of misery and were drowned. This is also what made some of the <margin>12</margin> "all-craving" Cynics <note>Greek: *pantorektas*, meaning those who reach for or eat everything</note> cling to the very cause of their sins—that which we are accustomed to call "indifferent" <note>Greek: *adiaphoron*; a Stoic and Cynic term for things that are neither morally good nor evil, such as food or wealth</note>.

§ 43. But a man who is cautious and suspicious toward the enchantments of nature...

<column-break/>

...and is oppressed by it, and overcome, but the abyss is not defiled. Thus, eating overcomes and oppresses those who are small; but to those in whom there is a "depth" and immense breadth of liberty, all things are taken as nourishment and bring no defilement. These people, therefore, deceiving themselves with such follies, also acted according to their errors: and having pushed themselves from freedom into the deep abyss of unhappiness, they were suffocated. This was also what led some of the Cynics to desire and devour all things, when they applied their minds to the cause of errors—that which we have become accustomed to call "indifferent."

§ 43. But a cautious man, who holds the deceptions of nature in suspicion...

---

...as *Abreschius* <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch (1699–1782), a Dutch philologist</note> rightly noted. It is well known how widely the use of this word extends.

8. **And is enslaved.**] The French translator noted "is muddied" <note>original: *tholoutai*</note> in the margin. But "is enslaved" <note>original: *douloutai*</note> is read correctly enough, as it seems to me. — VALENTIUS. Either it should read "is muddied," or "is revealed" is a corruption. — REISKE. *Valentius*, however, had placed "is muddied" in the text. "Muddy water" is said a thousand times. This could be confirmed by a beautiful passage suited to our subject from *Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation XXXIII, 5*: "Just as the winter floods of rivers muddy the safety of works and the order... so also the soul is unsettled by the immoderation of passions," etc. I would prefer not to dare condemn the beautiful metaphor of "being enslaved," especially since that word preceded it.

9. **The eating of a few things overcomes.**] The eating of a few (namely, of impurities or defilements) does not overcome; that is, *the eating of a few kinds cannot overcome impurities.* This means that when we dread many kinds of foods but stop within a few, we cannot help but contract filth from the eating of those few. — REISKE.

10. **They receive all things.**] In the *Florence* and *Leyden* editions, it was wrongly "they received" <note>original: *dechonto* instead of *dechontai*</note>. Instead of "authority" <note>original: *exousias*</note>, *Abreschius* preferred "excessive" <note>original: *exaisios*</note>.

11. **With which they deceived.**] Namely "themselves," which preceded. *Valentius* preferred "they were deceived" or "they suffered," which would agree with "they acted." In the *Florence* and *Leyden* editions, it was "deception." Meermann has "they had been deceived." He meant "they deceived themselves," which I think is true.

12. **Made them all-craving, as they clung etc.**] Reiske reads "clinging to the cause." I was reshaping it to: "the causes of errors clinging persistently to them." In Greek, this is *prosplékesthai* <note>to be entangled or entwined</note>, a word the lexicons are ignorant of, but which *Gataker* supports with suitable authority in his notes on *Marcus Aurelius, Book X, 7*. But you would not find the word "all-craving" <note>original: *pantorektēs*</note> in those authors either, though it is used by others like *Anacreon, Ode X, 11*.

# On Abstinence, Book I.

Whoever observes the nature of the body and understands that it has been fitted to the powers of the soul like an instrument, is not ignorant that its harmony is such that if it is struck from without, and that very stroke is perceived, the emotions will resonate whether we wish it or not. For perception is nothing other than the sound itself. But the soul cannot resonate unless it has been turned entirely toward the sound, and has directed its presiding eye toward it. For since the irrational faculty is by itself unreflecting, and is in no way able to judge to what extent, or how, or from where, or toward whom it acts, but wherever it leans it is very much like horses without a charioteer, it is impossible for it to manage anything properly with external things, or to know the occasion and measure of nourishment, unless the eye of the charioteer is present, who mo- <note>The text breaks mid-word; "mo-" likely continues as "moves" or "moderates" on the next page.</note>

<column-break/>

<note>original: Greek</note>
...of [perception], having examined the nature of the body, and knowing how it has been joined like an instrument to the powers of the soul, he knows that the passion is ready to speak, <gloss>1</gloss> whether we wish it or not, when the body is struck by things from without, and the stroke arrives at the point of perception. For perception happened to be the "speaking"; but it is not possible for the soul to speak unless it is turned entirely <gloss>2</gloss> toward the sound, and shifts its presiding eye toward this. In general, since the irrational part has no power to judge the "how much," and "how," and "from where," and "toward whom," being by itself unobservant, wherever it might lean, <gloss>3</gloss> it is like horses without a charioteer; it is impossible to manage anything fittingly toward <gloss>4</gloss> external things, or to know the timing and measures of food, unless the <gloss>5</gloss> charioteer...

---

<column-break/>

<gloss>1. Whether we wish it or not.]</gloss> Rather, it should read <note>original: "ante boulometha ante me"</note>. So the most ancient editions command, as do all the Bodleian manuscripts I use. However, a little before, the Bodleian reads very poorly <note>original: "hermosan"</note> instead of <note>original: "etoimon"</note> [ready].

<gloss>2. Toward the sound.]</gloss> Perhaps "toward the stroke." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note>

<gloss>3. Like horses without a charioteer, etc.]</gloss> A beautiful type of comparison, and not unknown to those who know the Platonic school. They compare the part of the soul devoid of reason to a horse, over which they place a charioteer, as will be said immediately. <term>Clement of Alexandria, The Instructor, Book III, p. 245. D. "He who, pulling back the reins, leads and carries the human horse—the irrational part of the soul—toward salvation."</term> and <term>The Miscellanies, Book V, p. 572. E. Philo, On Agriculture, p. 153. F. Jerome, Against Jovinianus, II. 10. "The senses of the body are like horses, running without reason; but the soul, in the manner of a charioteer, holds the reins of those running."</term> And because just now the horses without a ruler rush headlong, so the body without the reason and command of the soul is carried to its own destruction. That line of <term>Virgil, Georgics I. 514</term> fits this place beautifully:
> The charioteer is carried away by the horses, and the chariot hears not the reins.

Instead of <note>original: "hyparchouses ---- epibrisei"</note> it was poorly written in the <term>Leipzig</term> edition as <note>original: "hyparchouse ---- epibrose"</note>. This latter error is also in the <term>Meerman</term> manuscript, which also has <note>original: "eoikyias"</note>, and so the Lyon and Florentine editions; and this corresponds to the preceding words.

<gloss>4. External things.]</gloss> So the <term>Cambridge</term> manuscript. Prior editions and the <term>Leipzig</term> and <term>Meerman</term> manuscripts read <note>original: "tas exo"</note>.

<gloss>5. The eye of the presiding charioteer.]</gloss> The "presiding eye" is the charioteer. This is customary for the Philosophers. <term>The Golden Verses of Pythagoras.</term>

# P O R P H Y R Y

...of the presiding eye, which regulates the movements and acts as the charioteer of that which is, by its own nature, blind irrationality. But the person who removes the oversight of reason from this irrational part, and allows it to be carried along according to its own nature—whoever that might be—and who indulges desire so that it proceeds as far as it wishes in its own movements, and does the same with anger: such a person would surely make the virtuous man <note>original: σπουδαῖον (spoudaion) - a term for a person of serious moral character</note> and his deeds appear "rational" by making them uncurbed by presiding reason in the activities of the irrational part.

...moderates and rules its motions which are blind of themselves. # ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK I.
## K 2
->catchword: of the<-

§ 44. For in this, the honorable and upright man seems to differ from the base man: that the former everywhere has reason <note>original: "rationem"</note> sitting by him, which restrains and governs the faculty that lacks reason. The latter, however, having cast aside reason, acts without it in whatever he does. For this reason, the base man is called "ill-advised" and "irrational," and is said to be dragged along by his irrational faculty. The former, by contrast, is "well-advised" and "rational," being one who masters every reckless appetite. Indeed, the reason why most people fail in speech, in action, in their desires, and in anger—while the good act rightly—is that the former have permitted the child within them to do whatever it wishes by itself. The good have handed over the leadership to the tutor <note>original: "paedagogo" (the household slave responsible for a child's moral upbringing)</note>, and they govern their actions according to his precepts. From this it follows that both in taking food and in other bodily functions—

<column-break/>

§. 44. And yet, in this respect, the virtuous man <note>original: "ὁ σπουδαῖος" (ho spoudaios) - the serious or excellent person</note> appears to differ from the base, in that the former everywhere has reason standing by, ruling and driving the irrational part like a charioteer. But the latter allows the irrational part to do much, neglecting reason, and does what he does without it. Therefore, the one is called "unreasoning" and "carried away by irrationality," while the other is "rational" and "self-controlled over all that is unreasoning." Thus, failing in speech, in action, in desires, and in anger happens to the many; but acting rightly happens to the virtuous, because the former have allowed the child to do as he pleases by himself, while the latter have allowed the tutor, and with him they govern their own affairs. So it is both in the matter of food and in other things pertaining to the—

<margin>
[Note on the Greek text:] ...by doing these things; namely, the actions themselves. If you adopt "the" <note>original: τὸν (ton)</note>, the sense seems to stand well. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts agree on "the" <note>original: τὸ (to)</note>, and it can be explained in this way: "He will perform the virtuous deed beautifully" <note>original: "καλὸν [or καλῶς] ποιήσει τὸ σπουδαῖον"</note>. "To do beautifully" <note>original: "καλῶς ποιεῖν"</note> is a well-known formula for those praising a thing, used by Demosthenes and others. I remember this being shown by philologists regarding the New Testament on more than one occasion. These words, however, are to be taken ironically, as "beautifully" <note>original: "καλῶς"</note> is often used in ironies. "The virtuous thing" <note>original: "τὸ σπουδαῖον"</note> denotes any excellent thing worthy of our zeal. See Perizonius on Aelian’s *Various History*, Book II, 13.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s philosophical argument regarding the soul's control over the body, specifically focusing on the metaphor of the charioteer and the necessity of abstinence from meat and bodily pleasures.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

In the activities or enjoyments of the body, when the charioteer <note>The "charioteer" is a Platonic metaphor for the rational mind or intellect (Logos) governing the soul.</note> is present, he defines what is proportionate and timely. But when he is absent and—as some say—occupied with his own affairs, if he keeps our attention with him, he does not allow the irrational part of the soul to be affected by passion or to act at all. However, if he allows this attention to remain with the "child" <note>The "child" refers to the lower, irrational part of the soul that requires constant supervision.</note> without his guidance, he destroys the man, who is then dragged away by <margin>4</margin> the folly of the irrational.

§ 45. Therefore, for serious men, abstinence from both meats and the pleasures and actions of the body is more appropriate than engagement with them. For in touching bodily things, one must descend from one's own character to the training of the irrational element within us. This is even more necessary regarding food, for the irrational part is not capable of calculating what will result from it. By its very nature, the irrational is unable to recognize what is not immediately present. If it were possible to be as free from foods as we are from visible objects when they are removed (for it is possible to be occupied with other things by putting to <margin>1</margin> sleep...

<column-break/>

...in the operations or functions, let the present charioteer prescribe the measure and the opportunity. But when he is absent and, as some say, vacant in his own thoughts, if he has held our attention with him, he permits the irrational faculty neither to be moved nor to work anything at all. But if he should allow our attention to be present with the "child" without himself, he loses the man, since he is dragged headlong by irrational madness.

§ 45. Wherefore it is fitting for upright men that, regarding the pleasures and actions which exist through the body, they should abstain from foods more than from touch. This is because, although while we touch bodily things it is necessary to descend from our own habits to instruct the irrational faculty which is in us, the same must be done even more in the taking of food. For the irrational part cannot consider what will happen because of them; it is of such a nature that it perceives absent things in no way at all. For if we could be as free from nourishments as we are from things exposed to the sight when they are withdrawn—since, when the images of those things are put to sleep...

---

<margin>4. *The folly of the irrational.*] I confidently restore the reading "of the irrational" (*tou alogou*), whereas previously it was read as "of the reason" (*tou logou*). Someone might perhaps want "ignorance of the reason," as these words are swapped a hundred times; but since he says below "the irrational is unable to recognize what is absent," and the *Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts* as well as the translator agree on "irrational," I do not doubt this came from our pen. Next, do not wonder that "more" (*mallon*) is joined with a comparative; the Greeks do this a hundred times: see *Wetsten* on Paul's Epistle to the Philippians 1:23, and the Latins do no differently. "More clearer" and similar things, on which see the learned men on *Justin, Book III, chapter 2.* Then, in the phrase "and of those through the body," the *Leipzig manuscript* had wrongly omitted "and." Then also "of enjoyment" and "of touch," both erroneously.</margin>

<margin>1. *Putting to sleep from them.*] So it was read, but I have restored "putting to sleep" (*koimisanta*). The matter itself, as well as the authority of the Translator and the *Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts*, absolutely demands it.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument that the rational mind must act as a guardian over the body’s physical needs. It specifically addresses the biological "delays" of digestion and sleep as obstacles to the soul's freedom.</meta>

# ON ABSTINENCE BOOK I.

->K 3<-

...to direct the mind to other things would be permitted: it could happen quite conveniently that once we had indulged the necessity of our mortal nature for a little while, we would immediately emerge free. But since a delay of time is stretched out while food is both concocted <note>In ancient medicine, "concoction" refers to the process of "cooking" or ripening food in the stomach through heat to turn it into nutrients.</note> and digested, and while—even before that—help is sought from sleep and rest and other leisure, and after digestion a certain balance and the removal of waste is effected: it is necessary that a pedagogue <note>In Greek culture, a *paedagogus* was a tutor or guardian who supervised a child’s behavior; Porphyry uses it as a metaphor for Reason guiding the irrational body.</note> be present. Choosing for himself light things that bring no hindrance, he grants those to nature. For since he foresees what is to come, and how great a hindrance the matter would be if he obeyed desires, he judged it not fair that for the sake of a brief pleasure, which is perceived in swallowing while we take in food, such a heavy burden should overwhelm us.

§ 46. Not without merit, therefore, does reason [logos] secrete that which is excessive and superfluous—

<column-break/>

...[putting to sleep the phantoms arising from them] it would have been moderate, yielding to the necessity <gloss>2</gloss> of mortal nature for a little, to be immediately set free. But since there is also a need for a drawing out of time, and for digestion, and for distribution of nutrients <gloss>3</gloss>, and for the cooperation toward these things from sleep and rest, and other idleness, and after these things for the particular temperament resulting from the distribution, and the passage of waste, it is necessary for the pedagogue to be present. Having selected for himself the light things and those that offer no hindrance, <gloss>4</gloss> he will permit these to nature, foreseeing what is to come, and <gloss>5</gloss> how great an impediment it would be if he conceded to the desires, to introduce to us a burden <gloss>6</gloss> not easily carried <note>original: *ouk euankalon* — literally "not easy to hold in one's arms."</note> for the sake of a little pleasure, which they perceive <gloss>7</gloss> during the acceptance of these things in swallowing.

§ 46. Not without reason, therefore, does reason [logos] separate the much and the superfluous—

---

<margin>
1. They command. With the same elegance "to lull the strife to sleep" <note>original: *koimēsai tēn stasin*</note> [is used by] Dionysius of Halicarnassus Book 9, page 596. Reiske <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and philologist known for his editions of Greek texts.</note>. To me, "before" <note>original: *pro*</note> seemed the right reading, and I see that confirmed in the Meermann manuscript.

# PORPHYRY

->78<-

...having judged [this], he limits what is necessary to a small amount, so that he might neither <gloss>1</gloss> face troubles by needing more things, nor, by preparing elegant meals, need more servants; nor, by eating, be caught by more pleasures; nor, by being filled, be filled with much idleness; nor, by stuffing himself with a heavier burden <gloss>3</gloss>, become sleepy; nor, by filling himself with things that fatten the body, make the bond <note>The "bond" refers to the Neoplatonic idea of the soul being "chained" or "tethered" to the physical body.</note> stronger, and himself lazier and weaker for his proper duties. Let some man, then, <gloss>4</gloss> show us—one striving as much as possible to live according to the mind, and to be undisturbed by the passions of the body—how [a diet of meat] is more easily provided...

<column-break/>

...excluding [excess], he contracts what is necessary into a small and narrow space: lest by supplying [excess] he undergo troubles while requiring more; or by preparing rich meals he need more who might serve him; or by eating he be affected by more pleasures; or by being sated he be filled with much leisure; or by stuffing himself with a heavier load he fall into sleepiness; or by filling himself with things that fatten the body he render the bond stronger and himself lazier and weaker for performing his own duties. Therefore, let someone show us—one who seeks as much as possible to lead a life according to the intellect, and desires to be disturbed and distracted as little as possible by the affections of the body: how [meat-eating]...

---

<column-break/>

1. <note>original: "Ἔξειν πράγματα"</note> *To have troubles.* "Troubles" here refers to *business* or *annoyances*. Thus, "to have troubles" is to be involved in annoying affairs; just as "to provide troubles" is to cause annoyance to someone. This is called "providing labor" in *Matthew 26:10* <note>In the Gospel of Matthew, this refers to the disciples "troubling" the woman who anointed Jesus.</note>. Hence, "having troubles" and "providing them" are elegantly joined by *Alciphron* in *Book III, Letter 30*. *Bergler* notes: Epicurus in *Diogenes Laertius, page 795* says: "The blessed and incorruptible being neither has troubles itself, nor provides them to another." In some bad editions, "because of this" was written instead of "because of [the need]."

2. <note>original: "Μήτε εὐπρεπῆ ποιῶν"</note> *Nor by making elegant meals.* The learned *Abresch* (in his *Illustrations of Thucydides, page 381*) contends we should read *euprepē* ("elegant" or "becoming"). This is also preferred by the *Leipzig manuscript* and *Reiske*. These words [in Greek] could easily be confused, as often happens. In *Diodorus Siculus Book I, 45*, some manuscripts wrongly have *euprepesi* instead of "elegant temples." In *Euripides' Suppliants*, *Markland* wanted to read *euprepēs*. Likewise in *Lucian's Dialogues, page 84*, the famous *Hemsterhuis* excellently illustrates the power of this word. *Euprepē* refers to things that are *splendid* and *magnificent*, such as an "elegant table" meaning a table furnished with magnificent and rich feasts, as already noted by *Henri Estienne* in his *Thesaurus*.

<column-break/>

3. <note>original: "Ἐμπιμπλάμενος"</note> *Being filled.* The *Bodleian manuscript* reads "having been filled." The *Leipzig manuscript* reads "being filled" [with a spelling variation]. Spelling often varies in this word; sometimes it is written *empimplasthai*, sometimes *empiplasthai* [with or without the 'm']. This happens with other words where the letter M is sometimes added and sometimes not. See *D’Orville’s* notes on *Chariton, Book V, chapter 2*. Our author [Porphyry] loves to add that letter to the word.

4. <note>original: "Τὶς ἀνὴρ, σπεύδων κ.τ.λ."</note> *Some man, striving etc.* We have punctuated the text this way for the first time. The [Latin] translator does the same, as does the *Leipzig manuscript*, which however mistakenly gave "who" instead of "as." Based on the authority of that same manuscript, I have restored the word *aperispastos* ("undistracted"), for which "unstable" was previously read, though *Foggerolles* had already corrected this in the margin. *Meermann* wanted the same, giving the word "unavoidable." The word in...

# On Abstinence, Book I.

...the eating of all fruits and vegetables is either more abundantly available or more cheaply prepared; it brings less pleasure and is lighter in concoction <note>The ancient physiological process of "cooking" or ripening food within the stomach via heat</note> and digestion. It irritates the desires less, and contributes less to the passions and the physical strength of the body than a diet sought from inanimate things <note>original: "inanimatis," referring here to plants/fruits which lack a "sensitive soul" in Neoplatonic thought</note> and those which require no labor from cooks.

§ 47. But if neither a physician, nor a philosopher, nor a trainer <note>original: "alipta," a specialist in a gymnasium who oiled and trained athletes</note>, nor—

<column-break/>

—meat-eating <note>original: "ἡ κρεωφαγία"</note> [is compared to] dishes made from tree-fruits and vegetables, the preparation of the latter is cheaper than that of inanimate things <note>The commentator Reiske suggests this should perhaps read "animate things" (meat) to make sense of the comparison</note>, and they generally do not require cooks. It is, in itself, unpleasant when compared to the inanimate diet, but lighter in digestion than the other, and in the distributions <note>The process of nutrients being sent from the stomach to the rest of the body</note> to the body, it is faster than the distribution from vegetables. It excites the desires less and contributes less to the thickness <note>or "passion"</note> and strength of the body than the inanimate diet.

§ 47. But if neither any of the physicians, nor of the philosophers, nor a trainer—

---

<margin>
*Wetstein* illustrates this: on 1 Corinthians 7:35.
</margin>

5. **Meat-eating** ----.] *Florence, Lipsius, &amp; Meerman manuscripts:* "meat-eatings" (plural). We have seen these terms vary frequently.
§ 15. **Tree-fruits** <note>original: "’Ακρόδρυα"</note> properly refers to those covered with a harder shell (nuts), but from there, all fruits of trees are generally so named. See *Bodaeus à Stapel* on Theophrastus's *History of Plants*, Book III, chapters 12 &amp; 15; and this usage is frequent in *Diodorus Siculus*, as noted by *Wesseling* on Book V, chapter 43.

6. **And the preparation is cheaper etc.**] *Jerome*, *Against Jovinian*, Book II, 10: *“The preparation of vegetables, fruits, and legumes is both easier and does not require the art and expense of cooks; it sustains the human body without care, and when taken moderately (since that which has no stimulants for the throat is not greedily devoured), it is concocted with a lighter digestion.”*

7. **Of the inanimate.**] Perhaps it should be "of the inanimate, fire, and cooks." This is a comparison and adaptation of the eating of foods sought from inanimate things, which need neither fire nor cooks. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century German scholar</note>.

8. **In itself compared.**] Perhaps "unpleasant both in itself and when compared." Both viewed on its own and compared with. <term>REISKE</term>. It seems it should read "compared to the *animate*" <note>meat</note>, and at the end "than the *animate* diet." This was pleasing to *Abresch*, a distinguished man,

<column-break/>

unless in this place you prefer "unpleasant." I shall speak of this immediately.

9. **And in the distributions.**] *Valentin* had given "and in the distributions" against the evidence of all others. See on § 15. However, *Valentin &amp; Lipsius* correctly have "those into the body," for which the *Florence &amp; Leiden* manuscripts had "of that into the body."

10. **Faster.**] Thus *Valentin* is correct, from whom *Lipsius* does not differ. *Meerman* gives "faster than that of vegetables." In the *Florence &amp; Leiden* manuscripts, it was "faster." Soon after, *Reiske* preferred "into thickness" <note>original: "πάχος"</note> referring to the *thickness and mass of the flesh*, because a little later he calls it the "thickness of the bond" <note>referring to the body as a bond to the soul</note>. But in the previous sections, he had called them "the passions of the body."

11. **Of the inanimate diet.**] Either it must be read as "animate diet," and a little before "compared to the animate." For as these are now read, they do not provide a suitable sense. They could easily have been confused, for since the ancients wrote *ampsychos* for *empsychos* <note>living/animate</note>, it happened that one occasionally took the place of the other. See *D’Orville* on *Chariton* VIII, 1. Or perhaps a little before, "unpleasant" for "unpleasant." *Let someone show me how meat-eating is joined with pleasure or sweetness if it is contended against an inanimate diet, and how that is lighter... contributing [less] than the inanimate diet.* The word "but" is then repeated, as is often the case among the Greeks.

# PORPHYRY

->[Book 1, Section 47 continued]<-

...[nor has] any ordinary man <gloss>1</gloss> dared to say: why do we not voluntarily withdraw from this bodily burden? Why do we not free ourselves, together with our <gloss>2</gloss> departure from many things (for it was not from one thing, but from ten thousand, that he who accustomed himself to be satisfied with the least was set free), from a surplus of money, the service of many slaves, a multitude of household goods, a sleepy state, the severity and multitude of diseases, the need for doctors, the irritations toward sexual matters, thicker vapors, a multitude of excrement, <gloss>3</gloss> the thickness of the bond <note>A Neoplatonic metaphor for the physical body which "binds" the soul</note>, a strength that rouses one toward external actions, and finally <gloss>4</gloss> an Iliad of woes. From all of these, an inanimate <note>In this context, "inanimate" refers to a diet consisting of plants and fruits rather than "animate" meat</note> and simple diet, easily provided for all, delivers us, preparing peace for the <gloss>5</gloss> reasoning power that provides us with salvation. For Diogenes says <gloss>6</gloss> it is not from the bread-eaters that thieves and enemies come, but from the meat-

<column-break/>

...nor has anyone from the common crowd ever dared to affirm: why do we not voluntarily abstain from this burden of the body? Why do we not finally free ourselves from the slavery of many things by such abstinence? For he who has grown accustomed to be content with the smallest things can be liberated not from one thing, but from six hundred <note>The Latin "sexcentis" (six hundred) is often used idiomatically to mean an indefinitely large number</note>. From an overabundance of money; from the service of many slaves; from a wealth of furniture; from a sleepy constitution; from the violence and multitude of diseases; from the lack of doctors; from irritation toward sexual pleasures; from thicker exhalations; from the abundance of excrement; from the thickness of the bond; from the strengths that rouse one to external actions; and finally from an Iliad of woes. From these things, a frugal, thin, and easily obtained nourishment leads us away and draws us back; while it prepares peace and tranquility for the reason which suggests healthy things to us. For Diogenes says it is not from the bread-eaters that thieves and enemies arise, but from the meat-

---

<margin>
1. **Ordinary man.** <note>original: "Ἰδιώτης" / "idiota"</note> In these types of passages, "ordinary men" are those who live according to common custom and do not organize their lives by any particular rational principle to care for their own well-being. See: *Casaubon’s notes on Athenaeus, book II, chapter 8.*

2. **Departure from many things.** Perhaps this refers to "those" many things which he lists immediately afterward. —REISKE.

3. **Thickness of the bond.** See Section 38. <note>This refers to the density or "coarseness" of the physical body hindering the soul</note>

4. **Iliad of woes.** <note>A classical idiom meaning a vast, overwhelming number of troubles, referencing the length and tragedy of Homer's Iliad</note> *Diodorus Siculus in the Eclogues, page 534:* "All of Sicily was possessed by confusion and an Iliad of woes." See also *Wesseling's* notes there. To the Latins, it is an *Ilias malorum*. *Cicero, Letter to Atticus, Book VIII, 2:* "An Iliad of woes hangs over us." Compare with the proverb collectors.

5. **Providing us with salvation.** In the *Lipsius* manuscript, it read "to the reasoning power living healthily." The word "living" likely arose from the following word "providing."

6. **From the bread-eaters... says Diogenes.** *Jerome, Book II against Jovinian, chapter 2:* "Diogenes asserts that tyrants, the subversions of cities, and wars—whether foreign or civil—are stirred up not for a simple diet of vegetables and fruit, but for meat and the delicacies of banquets." Regarding how content he was with the cheapest kind of food, see *Aelian, Historical Miscellany, XIII, 26*, where *Kuhn* thought the word "bread" <note>original: "μᾶζαν"</note> had fallen out of the text because of this passage in our author. This saying is also mentioned, though in a slightly different way, by *Julian, Oration VI, page 198 D.*
</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book I.
**L**

<column-break/>

...from meat-eaters, slanderers and tyrants arise. Indeed, once the cause of our needing many things is removed, and the abundance of those things taken into the body is reduced—with the weight of the things being digested likewise lightened—it follows that the eye emerges free, tranquil, and clear of the bodily waves and smoke.

§ 48. This is a point that requires neither proof nor demonstration, because of the self-evident clarity inherent in the matter. Thus, not only those who strive to live according to the intellect—and who establish such a life as their goal—consider this abstinence necessary for achieving that goal; but also every philosopher, I believe, judging that frugality is suitable for conducting a life of civic virtue, would more highly approve of a life satisfied with few things than one [satisfied with many...]

<column-break/>

...from meat-eaters, the slanderers and tyrants [arise]. But when the cause <gloss>7</gloss> of needing many things is lifted, and the mass of things brought <gloss>8</gloss> into the body is stripped away, and the weight of those things distributed [through the system] is lightened, the eye <gloss>9</gloss> becomes free, anchored far away from the smoke and waves of the body.

§ 48. And this needs neither reminder nor proof, because of the evidence present in the thing itself. Wherefore not only those who are eager to live according to the intellect, and have established the life according to it as their goal, see this abstinence as necessary toward that goal; but also nearly every philosopher, I think, preferring simplicity <gloss>1</gloss> over extravagance, would rather accept the one who is satisfied with little than the one [satisfied with more...]

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument regarding the virtues of a simple diet, specifically citing the unexpected support of the Epicureans for frugal living.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

...content with little, rather than that which requires much. Furthermore (and this might seem incredible to most people), we find that those who believe pleasure to be the goal of philosophy <note>Porphyry is referring to the Epicureans, who are often misunderstood as gluttons, but here he defends their actual practice of moderation.</note> actually assert and value this principle. For most of the Epicureans, beginning with their founder himself, appear to have been satisfied with a simple barley cake and fruits; they have filled their writings with descriptions of how little Nature truly requires, demonstrating that her necessary needs are sufficiently healed by a thin and easily obtainable diet.

§ 49. For he says, "The wealth of Nature is limited and easy to procure..." <note>A famous quote from Epicurus's *Principal Doctrines*.</note>

<column-break/>

...although it may seem common, it is nonetheless not better. It appears Porphyry gave it this way, comparing **frugality** with **extravagance**, and would rather approve of a life lived with little and satisfied with little, than one requiring more. Certainly, in the *Leipzig* manuscript, instead of "a life with little," it reads "a life in words." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske was a 18th-century German scholar known for his editions of Greek texts.</note> The word "before" was also in the oldest edition and the *Meermann* manuscript, and I have therefore restored it to its proper place.

2. **Those saying this etc.**] Perhaps: "We find those very people saying and valuing this who otherwise state and embrace the exact opposite." <term>REISKE</term>

3. **Those who think pleasure is the goal etc.**] He means Epicurus and those who followed him. They established **Pleasure** as the highest good, which for them was "cheerfulness" and "freedom from disturbance"—neither suffering in the body nor being troubled in the soul. Not a bad thing in itself, but they used the word poorly, since in common usage it signified a different kind of pleasure, as is well known. See, however, *Perizonius on Aelian's Varia Historia IV, 13 and Book IX, ch. 12.* *Reiske* preferred the reading "those who, by Zeus, think pleasure is the goal." In earlier editions, "those who philosophized" was written as "those who played the sophist."

4. **Satisfied with barley cake and fruits.**] Epicurus himself used to say that he was ready to compete with Jupiter for happiness, provided he had "barley cake and water." See *Aelian, Varia Historia IV, 13* and *Julian, Oration VI, p. 195 B*: "not even a barley cake, of which Epicurus says that if he has plenty, he does not fall behind the gods in terms of happiness." *Jerome* refers to our author in *Against Jovinian II, 11*: "**And what is wonderful, Epicurus, the defender of pleasure, filled all his books with vegetables and fruits, and says we must live on cheap foods.**" I am not surprised. For in this way, the body and mind can best be kept to their duty, and thus "freedom from disturbance" <note>original: *ataraxia*</note> could be promoted. Recently, the *Meermann* manuscript mistakenly gave "citizens" instead of "thin/simple."

1. **For he says.**] The *Leipzig* manuscript does not do badly with "He says." Epicurus, I suppose, whose saying this is, taken from his *Principal Doctrines*. A little later, however, it has "They say," in which it deviated from consistency. <term>REISKE</term> Excellent. Such is that saying of Epicurus...
