<meta>This page continues the discussion of Epicurean philosophy regarding human desires. The previous page established that the Epicureans, despite their reputation for seeking pleasure, actually practiced extreme frugality. Here, the text distinguishes between natural, necessary desires and those born of "empty opinions."</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book I.
L 2

arise from empty opinions; these are infinite and of such a kind that they can hardly be compared. For those things which are easily available, having a simple nature of both fluids and solids <note>The "simple nature of fluids and solids" refers to basic food and drink, like water and bread.</note>, are accustomed to remove well and abundantly all the bodily distress that comes from deficiency. All other things, whatever fall into luxury, they [the Epicureans] say do not stem from a necessary desire, nor are they of the kind that arises necessarily from some actual pain. Instead, they arise either from distress alone <gloss>taken from the absence of the thing desired</gloss>, or entirely from joy in its presence, or from empty and false opinions. None of these things pertain to a natural deficiency, which, if left unsatisfied, would be able to dissolve our physical constitution. For the things already mentioned are sufficient to obtain—

<column-break/>

—procured; but that which [comes] from empty opinions is both undefined and difficult to procure. For that which troubles the flesh according to need is removed well and sufficiently by things easy to obtain, having a simple nature of both fluids and solids. But the rest, as much as has fallen into <gloss>2</gloss> extravagance, they say does not have a necessary appetite, nor is it necessarily produced from something painful. Rather, one kind arises from that which <gloss>3</gloss> either causes pain or merely stings in its absence; another entirely from that which brings joy; <gloss>4</gloss> another entirely from empty and false dogmas, <gloss>5</gloss> or is not reduced to any natural deficiency, nor to that which dissolves the constitution through its absence. For even the most ordinary things are sufficient—

---

<margin>In Diogenes Laertius, Book 10, page 798: "The wealth of nature is both limited and easy to procure, but the wealth of empty opinions falls away into infinity." And page 790: "That which is natural is all easy to procure, but that which is empty is hard to procure." <note>Diogenes Laertius was a 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers; his Book 10 is the primary source for the lost writings of Epicurus.</note></margin>
Since it was also read this way in the *Florentine* and *Leiden* editions, and this was confirmed by the translator and the *Meermann manuscript*, I did not hesitate to restore this reading to the author. Immediately after, instead of "if," <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774) was a pioneering scholar of Greek texts who often suggested "conjectures" or corrections to corrupted manuscripts.</note> conjectured "of us," or "at the same time," or "together."

2. **Has fallen into extravagance.**] I would prefer "has fallen away into" <note>original: "ekpeptoken"</note>. This usage is known to everyone. And thus in the saying of Epicurus, which I just cited: "it falls away into infinity." Our author [Porphyry] clearly has that in mind. Instead of "they say they have," Reiske preferred the phrase "to have by nature."

3. **Either grieving or stinging.**] Perhaps "either not (or lest) grieving." The word "on the one hand" is sadly missing in the *Leipzig* edition. <term>REISKE</term>. The metaphorical use of the word "to sting" <note>original: "nyttein"</note> is very frequent. Diodorus Siculus (13.58) says "to receive stings in the soul," just as Themistius (Orat. 14, p. 171) says "it stung the mind." To these can be compared "to be stung in the heart" from the Acts of the Apostles (2:37). Often "to sting" and "to grieve" are synonyms. This was beautifully demonstrated by <term>D’ORVILLE</term> <note>Jacques Philippe d'Orville was an 18th-century Dutch philologist.</note> in his notes on the novelist Chariton (6.5), where he did not forget to mention our author.

<column-break/>

4. **Another entirely from —**] The latter "entirely" is missing from the *Leipzig* edition. If "entirely" must be absent, it would be better omitted in the first instance. <term>REISKE</term>. However, the *Meermann manuscript* also does not have the second "entirely," nor did the previous translator include it.

5. **Or to no natural deficiency...**] Either "or which" should be read, or rather "if or." Both, together with the verb "is reduced," refer back to "appetite." <term>REISKE</term>. I have corrected what was previously written as "she" into "or," as the *Meermann* manuscript correctly has it. In the *Florentine* edition it was faultily written as "deficiency" <note>original: "eleimma," misspelled with one 'l'</note>, an error which the *Leiden* edition followed, as is its custom.

# PORPHYRY

...consequent disturbances. Indeed, it is necessary for the Philosopher that the hope <gloss>3</gloss> that nothing will fail him throughout life be present. This hope is sufficiently preserved by things that are easily procured, while luxury makes one hopeless. Many people, for this reason, although they possess much, toil without end <gloss>4</gloss> as if things will fail them. But remembering that nothing, not even all the wealth in the world gathered together, is naturally able to provide any significant release from the soul's disturbance, makes one content with what is easily procured and most simple. However, even very moderate and ordinary things remove the body's distress; and possessing such easily obtained things, even if they should fail, does not disturb the one who practices for death. Furthermore, the pain <gloss>5</gloss> caused by great want...

<column-break/>

...which follow from it, might compensate in any way. Add to this that since it is also necessary for the philosopher to be in such hope that he thinks nothing will be lacking to him in life: simple things preserve this kind of hope, while sumptuous and luxurious things weaken and diminish it. For this reason, it happens that most people, although they possess many things, never cease to labor as if wealth will always be lacking to them. However, that we may be content with the cheapest things and those most easily obtained, it helps most if we keep in mind that there is nothing which has any power to bring about the calming of the soul's disturbances—which is of any importance—even if all the riches were collected. To calm the body's distress, however, any things, even quite modest ones and those which can most easily be supplied from everywhere, are sufficient. Even if these are lacking a little, they cannot disturb him who [meditates on] death...

---

<column-break/>

<margin>"To one contemplating" <note>original: "θεωροῦντι"</note> or something similar. "It becomes useless" is the same as "it appears to be so." When thinking about impediments, it immediately appears that the preparation of so many great things is not worth the effort. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske was a 18th-century German scholar famous for his editions of Greek texts.</note></margin>
<margin>3. "That nothing be lacking." <note>original: "Τοῦ μηδὲν ὑπολ."</note> Later writers often use this verb to mean "to fail" or "to cease to be supplied." This precept corresponds excellently to our own religion. We have the warnings of the Lord Christ against vain worry about the future in **Matthew, Chapter 6.** <term>REISKE.</term></margin>
<margin>4. "They toil endlessly." <note>original: "Ἀνήνυτα μοχθοῦσιν."</note> That is, "in vain." Thus "vain and endless labor" is found in Plato. Alciphron (Book I, Letter 2) uses the same formula: "we toil fruitlessly and endlessly." See Bergler. <term>REISKE.</term></margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>5. "Through much want, gentleness, etc." The **Leipzig Manuscript** <note>original: "Cod. Lips."</note> gives "or that through fulfillment." As this is true, it sheds a great and clear light on the sentence, which without that lamp we would have always found obscure. One should read "much more" or "simply more" instead of "great." Thus the passage is established: "furthermore, the pain which exists from want has much more mildness than that which follows fulfillment." Besides, the pain arising from poverty has much more of a kind of madness or gentleness than that which follows over-filling. <term>REISKE.</term> The distinguished man followed his manuscript excellently. It was no different in the Meermann manuscript and the oldest editions. I do not know by what authority **Valentini** removed the phrase "or that." It may be understood...</margin>

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK I

...meditates constantly. Add to this that the pain which arises from a lack [of food] is much milder than that which comes from over-fullness, unless someone deceives themselves with empty opinions. Furthermore, a variety of foods not only fails to remove the soul’s disturbance, but it does not even increase the pleasure of the body; for pleasure reaches its limit as soon as the pain [of hunger] is removed. Thus, the eating of meat does not resolve any natural distress, nor does it provide anything that, if left undone, would lead to pain. Instead, it offers a fleeting and intense pleasure <note>original Latin: "violentam gratiam"</note> which is quickly mixed with its opposite. For it does not contribute to the preservation of life, but only to a variety of pleasures—much like sexual acts or the drinking of foreign wines, without which nature can still persist. Those things without which nature cannot endure are very few, and of the kind that can be easily obtained with justice, freedom, and much peace and leisure.

<column-break/>

...of extreme mildness, or that which comes from fullness, unless one deceives themselves with empty opinions. The variety of foods does not at all release the disturbances of the soul; it does not even <gloss>6</gloss> increase the pleasure in the flesh. For this pleasure also has its limit as soon as the pain [of hunger] is removed. So too, the practice of meat-eating did not solve any troublesome thing in nature, <gloss>7</gloss> nor did it accomplish anything that would have resulted in pain if not completed. It provided a violent pleasure that was quickly mixed with the opposite. For it did not contribute to the <gloss>8</gloss> duration <term>duration: 'symmone' in Greek, referring to the continuity or preservation of life</term> of life, but rather to the variety of pleasures; it is similar to sexual pleasures or the drinking of foreign wines, which nature can do without. The things without which nature could not endure are quite few and can be provided easily, with justice, freedom, stillness, and much ease.

Thus, I have restored to Malchus <note>Malchus was Porphyry's original Phoenician name; the editor is asserting a correct reading of the text</note> what is his. 1. *For by those means through which health is recovered &c.*] Jerome expressed this in Latin in *Book II against Jovinian, 11*: <note>original: "Quibus ergo cibis recipitur sanitas..."</note> "By whatever foods health is regained, by these it can also be kept, lest anyone think that diseases are stirred up by vegetables: But if vegetables do not provide the strength of that famous Milo of Croton &c." Regarding the strength of Milo, all things are well known. <meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument from Book I of *On Abstinence*. # On Abstinence, Book I.
->M<-

no certainty or stability of philosophy and contemplation is found in the majority of people. Nor are common men fit to take up wisdom, or any part of it that possesses some excellence: they do not sufficiently perceive what it contributes either to private or public life, nor are they able to judge which customs are depraved and which are honorable. Moreover, much petulance and intemperance exists within them: so that it is not at all to be feared that there will not be people found to eat animals.

§ 53. For if everyone were to think the best thoughts, we would have no need for bird-catchers, fowlers, fishermen, or swineherds. But if the animals, governing themselves, had no one by whom they were cared for and ruled, they would easily perish; they would be attacked by other animals that would thus diminish their numbers, and be—

<column-break/>

for <gloss>5</gloss> there is nothing faithful or permanent of friendship and goodwill <note>original Greek: Φιλίας καὶ εὐνοίας (philias kai eunoias)</note> among the many. Nor are they receptive to these things, nor to wisdom, <gloss>6</gloss> nor to the parts of wisdom that possess anything noteworthy. <gloss>7</gloss> The multitude is wise neither in what is useful, nor in private matters, nor in common affairs; nor are they able to make a judgment between <gloss>8</gloss> base and refined habits. In addition to these things, there is much lewdness and a fullness of intemperance among the many. Therefore, one must not fear <gloss>9</gloss> that there will never be those who will eat animals.

§ 53. For if everyone should think the best thoughts, there would be no use for <gloss>1</gloss> bird-catching, fowlers, fishermen, or swineherds. But the animals, managing themselves and not having one to care for and oversee them, are quickly destroyed and consumed by those who attack them, and their multitude is re— <note>original catchword: λι- (li-), likely completing the word "reduced" or "diminished"</note>

---

<margin>What is this to you? It certainly pertains. "Nothing to me," <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν πρὸς ἐμὲ (ouden pros eme)</note> and similar expressions appear a hundred times in other authors. I cite no one specifically, because it has been abundantly done by Philologists who vindicated the Gospel of John (21:22) from the suspicion of being a Latinism.</margin>

5. **Friendship and goodwill.** *Felicianus* reads "Philosophy," but this is supported by no manuscript. But should it also be "goodwill"? I should not think so. *Hesychius* explains the word "well-minded" <note>original: εὔνουν (eunoun)</note> not only as "friend" but also as "wise," though for him "goodwill" is "friendship." This word is also translated as "prudence" in Pollux’s *Onomasticon* (IV, 33); see the notes by *Jungermann*.

6. **Nor of those noteworthy...** Previously it was read as "the" (singular), but *Fogerolles* and *Valentinus* have already corrected it. I was persuaded to adopt the plural form <note>original: τῶν (tōn)</note> in the text by the authority of the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts.

<column-break/>

7. **Neither of the useful, etc.** *Cicero, For Plancius, chapter 4: "For there is no counsel in the common people, no reason, no judgment, no diligence."* Much has been written on this sentiment, which is confirmed by experience; see *Gataker on Antoninus* [Marcus Aurelius], Book IV, § 3.

8. **Base and refined.** These are well-contrasted. See what the celebrated *Hemsterhuis* noted on the character of the word "refined" <note>original: ἀσεῖος (asteios)</note> in Pollux (Book IX, 17), which illustrates the passage we have at hand excellently.

9. **That there will never be.** Previously it was read as "neither," but the Leiden and Cambridge editor corrected it in its place; the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts read "and not" <note>original: οὐδὲ (oude)</note> instead of "neither."

1. **Bird-catching.** This word is sought in vain in the Dictionaries—

Health must be preserved, not out of fear of death, but so as not to be hindered from those goods that come from contemplation <term>theoria: the act of intellectual vision or meditation</term>. The primary preservation of health is an undisturbed state of the soul and a disposition of the mind toward that which truly exists <note>original Greek: τὸ ὄντως ὄν (to ontos on), referring to Platonic ultimate reality</note>. For much [benefit] reaches even to the body from this, as our associates have demonstrated by experience. <gloss>4</gloss> Indeed, they drove away a disease of the joints <term>arthritis</term> in both feet and hands—which was so severe that for <gloss>5</gloss> eight whole years they had to be carried—at the same time as they renounced their wealth and looked toward the divine. <column-break/>

...will be consumed. This is what usually happens with countless animals that humans do not eat. But if this various and all-encompassing foolishness persists among men, there will also be countless people who, devoted to gluttony, will gorge themselves on these things.

Furthermore, health is not to be maintained out of fear of death, but for this reason: so that we are not hindered from attaining those goods which arise from contemplation. Its chief preserver is the undisturbed and tranquil constitution of the soul, and the attention of our mind to that which truly is. For there is much that flows from here even to the body: just as our friends have shown by experience. Though they suffered from a disease of the joints <term>arthritis</term> which had so violently seized their hands and feet that for eight full years they had to be carried about, they expelled it as soon as they cast aside their wealth and turned themselves to the contemplation of divine things. They were <note>referring to those who recovered from illness through simple living</note>. Therefore, a great power, and indeed almost the entire means of bringing about health, descends into the body from a certain good constitution of the soul. Nevertheless, a reduction in food also generally contributes to the same end. In general, however, as **Epicurus** <note>The Greek philosopher (341–270 BCE) who taught that pleasure is the absence of pain and advocated for a simple life</note> rightly said, we must avoid that food which we desire and pursue in order to enjoy it, but which, once consumed, we judge to be unpleasant. Of such a kind, certainly, is all luxurious and heavy food. ...increase the intensity of desire for each thing, just as life itself is set in motion. For we must nowhere wander without limits, but we must everywhere hold to a boundary and a measure in such matters. One must consider that he who fears abstinence from living creatures <note>original: "ἐμψύχων ἀποχὴν", referring to a vegetarian diet</note>—if he partakes in meat-eating for the sake of pleasure—is actually afraid of death. For immediately, along with the deprivation of meat, he associates the presence of some undefined evil, from which death arises. It is from these and similar causes that an insatiable desire for living, for riches, for money, and for glory arises; for people think that along with these things they will increase their total good over a longer period of time, and they always dread the evil of death as something <column-break/> infinite. They act no differently than those for whom great riches have already been acquired. Indeed, we must never wander indeterminately, but a limit and a mode must be predefined in all these things. It must be considered that the man who fears abstaining from animals, if he allows the eating of meat for the sake of pleasure, fears death: because he immediately adds to the removal of foods the presence of some unbounded evil, from which death exists. From these and similar causes, a certain insatiable desire for living, for riches, for money, and for glory is born: while they think that together with these things they will increase every good over a longer time, and they fear the evil of death as if it were forever unbounded.

<note>The following section contains scholarly commentary on the Greek and Latin philology of the text.</note>

...nothing would be lacking. *Life is set in motion* <note>original: "βίος γε κίνηται"</note>, or rather *Life has been set in motion* <note>original: "βίος κεκίνηται"</note>, as it appears in the Meerman and Claromontanus codices <note>handwritten manuscript copies</note>. To Abrescibius, this seemed a lovely metaphor that could be said of those for whom ample means have been produced and prepared, as the metonymic meaning of "producing" often occurs. He therefore says the same thing as **Horace** <note>original: "Flaccus", the Roman poet</note> in *Odes*, Book III, 16: *Care follows increasing money, and a hunger for greater things.* This sentiment is widely known. But if you contend the passage is mutilated, the loss could be repaired in various ways; however, since one must use the "oars of one's own wit," no one can define with dictatorial authority what were the original words of **Malchus** <note>Porphyry’s original name was Malchus</note>. For this reason, I do not wish to "strike a light in the dark," and with **Pyrrho** <note>The Greek skeptic philosopher</note> I say: *I define nothing.*

3. *But hold to a limit and measure.* After the word *measure*, the word "necessary" or "proper" either must be understood or, better yet, added. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century German scholar</note>. The Emperor <note>Marcus Aurelius</note> says beautifully in *To Himself* <note>The Meditations</note>, Book V, § 1: *Nature gave measures even for this. It gave them, indeed, for eating and drinking.* **Gataker** <note>Thomas Gataker, a 17th-century English scholar</note> aptly compares this passage with our Author, where many other things are said to this effect.

4. *If indeed for the sake of pleasure.* I have restored this, following the authority of all printed editions and manuscripts. Only the Valentinian edition had *if*.

5. *And of glory.* The Leipzig Codex gives *and of glory* <note>original: "καὶ δόξης"</note>. I approve of that. But then the word *the* <note>original: "τὸ"</note> must be read instead of *of the* <note>original: "τοῦ"</note>, so that the construction is *and the thinking that all good will increase*. Or rather, both words should be deleted. <term>REISKE</term>. All others agree on *of glory*. Therefore, the Author’s own word had to be returned, as the Valentinian edition had given *to glory*.

6. *Infinite.* The Scholiast <note>ancient commentator</note> on **Aristophanes** in *The Clouds*, line 2: *Infinite (aperanton) is that which has no limit (peras); those who write "infinite" with a "u" (aperauton) are mistaken.* You may read the same in **Suidas** <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> under the entry *Aperaton*. They rashly condemn that which occurs a hundred times among both more recent and more ancient writers.

Indeed, the pleasure that arises from the luxury of banquets does not even come close to that which a person experiences from frugality <note>original Latin: "parsimonia"</note> and from having what is sufficient. These would not only be useless and bring us no benefit, but like a state of over-filling <term>repletio: the physical discomfort of eating too much</term>, they would actually become a burden. From such necessary satisfaction, true and pure pleasure arises. However, the body must also be trained,

7. *Regarding "the one who has experienced it."*] The *Bodleian* manuscript reads "pleasure indeed." In place of "experienced," the *Lipsius* manuscript has "attempting." It is doubtful, as *Reiske* pointed out, whether the author intended "the one trying" or "the one who has already tried." We have already noted above that the phrase "to come close to" <note>original: "ἐγγὺς τείνειν"</note> is a Platonic expression.

8. *Regarding "does not have. For once [luxury] is removed, etc."*] The *Lipsius* manuscript incorrectly omits "and not" (which is also missing in the *Meermann* manuscript) and the subsequent "For once luxury is removed." The error arose from the repetition of the word "removed." I approve of the reading "ambition for external things" <note>original: "τῆς ἔξω Φιλοτιμ."</note> which was found in earlier editions and the *Bodleian* and *Meermann* manuscripts, though the latter omitted the second "removed." *Reiske* preferred "ambition toward those outside."

9. *Regarding "Not that of poverty, so that..."*] I would gladly insert "moderation" <note>original: "μετριότης"</note> to fill the gap in the text. —VALCKENAER. The *Lipsius* manuscript reads "to become," which contributes nothing to the sense; in other respects, this book is just as faulty and contaminated as the others, and contains a gap, an indicator of a defect. Perhaps "and" should be read instead of "not." As far as I can see in these dark and rocky passages, the author calls the "fullness of poverty" <note>original: "τὴν κατὰ πενίαν πλησμονὴν"</note> the voracity and desire of the poor to taste every delicacy with a greedy mouth. Perhaps you might fill the spot this way: *and of the fullness of poverty, which yearns to be filled with everything and to taste everything, so that it may go through all things.* We must train our desire so that it shrinks from *that familiar voracity of the poor, which flies at everything set before it, engorges itself on everything, and tastes everything, so that it leaves nothing unexperienced.* —REISKE. There is also a gap in the *Meermann* manuscript after "so that." *Felicianus* translates as if we had a complete text, except that he seems to have read "hunger" instead of "poverty," which is only a transposition of letters. Then, for "to be," he reads "truly necessary." "Not (or lest) the indefinite..." *Maussac*, in his French version, translates similarly: *not the repletion of hunger, but the pleasure of that satisfaction, so that he can reach all those things; and that he sets as a limit not that which is undefined, etc.* Thus everything fits together well. Or the words, as they lie, could be explained in this way: *But the body must be called away from that pleasure which is born from an excessive abundance of food, not from that satiety which pertains to hunger—that is, which belongs only to the driving away of famine (or "poverty," which is content with the smallest things, so that the poverty of nature is relieved. See Book III, 27)—and thus to experience it, so that true pleasure (pure pleasure) may extend itself through all things, and permeate the entire mind and body—*

**§ 55.** Come now, how, I ask, is it not absurd? If a man who is afflicted, or oppressed by some heavy external calamity, or caught in chains, does not even think of food, nor labor for how it might be provided; but if it is set before him, he takes only what is necessary: yet he who is truly a prisoner, and is afflicted by internal calamities <note>Porphyry refers here to the passions and the soul's entanglement with the body</note>, seeks out the preparation of banquets, and procures a variety of dishes? By these very things, he strengthens his bonds and makes them thicker. <note>original: "crassioraque efficiat"</note> In what way is this the behavior of men who have recognized what they have suffered? Is it not rather the behavior of those who delight in their suffering, and are ignorant of the evils in which they are placed? For them, the calamity surely results in the opposite way than it does for those who, since they are bound, recognize their misery...

<column-break/>

...should it not remain for a longer time. <note>original: "μὴ τὸν πλείονα χρόνον παραμένειν"</note>

**§ 55.** In addition to these things, how, by Zeus, is it not strange? One who is suffering, or who is in a powerful external crisis <term>peristasis: a surrounding circumstance, often used by Stoics to mean a trial or hardship</term>, or caught in bonds, has no thought of food, nor worries about from where it will be provided; but even when it is served, <gloss>2</gloss> he takes <note>original: "παρατίθεσθαι"</note> only what is necessary. Certainly, all the manuscripts agree on this word.

# P O R P H Y R Y

For surely, it is not merely for the sake of being freed from a physical illness that we must endure all things—being cut, bled, cauterized, drinking bitter medicines, and being purged through the bowels, through vomiting, and through the nostrils, while also paying fees to those who treat us in this way. Should we not then reasonably endure everything for the sake of curing the internal illness? We are, after all, contending for immortality and for communion with God <note>original: "θεοῦ συνουσίας" (theou synousias) — literally "being with God," a central goal of Neoplatonic philosophy</note>, a union from which we are barred because of our close association with the body. Even if it were necessary to endure these things with great pain, we should certainly not follow the laws of the body, which are violent and stand in opposition to the laws of the mind and the paths of salvation. But since our philosophical inquiry here is not even about enduring pain, but simply about rejecting unnecessary pleasures, what excuse remains for those who wish to shamelessly defend their own lack of self-control?

->§ 57.<-

<column-break/>

...must be done? For surely, it is not simply to be freed from a disease of the body that we must endure so many things, such as being cut, being made to bleed, being burned, swallowing bitter medicines, and being purged through the bowels, vomiting, and nostrils—all while paying fees to the very people who cause us this distress. Rather, it is for the sake of the internal disease, where our struggle is for immortality and for the privilege of keeping company with God. We are currently prohibited from this because of our habit of following the body; therefore, we ought to endure everything, even if it meant suffering pain and affliction. We should not follow the laws of the body, which are violent and oppose the laws of the mind and the ways of salvation. But since we are now philosophizing not about tolerating pain, but about rejecting pleasures that are not even necessary, what further excuse is left for those who impudently wish to protect their own lack of restraint?

# P O R P H Y R Y

The more one is established far from every material manifestation, the more it is fitting for the person approaching him to be in every way pure and holy, beginning from the body and ending at the inner self, assigning to each part, or to all things present, the purity that is natural to each. But perhaps no one would speak against these points; yet one might wonder how we place abstinence in the category of purity, even though in sacrifices we are accustomed to slaughtering sheep and oxen, considering this sacred rite to be both holy and pleasing to the gods. Therefore, since a long discourse is needed for the resolution of this problem, we must take up the subject of sacrifices from a different starting point.

->§ I.<-

# PORPHYRY THE PHILOSOPHER
### ON ABSTINENCE FROM ANIMAL FOOD
### BOOK TWO.

# P O R P H Y R Y
### ON ABSTINENCE FROM THE EATING OF ANIMALS.
### *BOOK TWO.*

->S U M M A R Y.<-

*Porphyry first provides a preface; he briefly describes the order in which the matters of this second book are to be treated. § 1. Afterward, he addresses the refutation of an argument considered by some to be of the greatest importance: that because animals are used in sacrifices, the lawful use of them for food is thereby proven. § 2, etc. He then explains the entire business of sacrifices. § 5, etc. Namely, by what steps the practice eventually arrived at the immolation of animals. § 6, 7, etc. For what reasons this practice was introduced. § 9, 10, etc. He reviews several arguments of Theophrastus <term>Theophrastus: A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle who wrote extensively on botany and ethics</term> against the slaughter of animals. § 12, etc. He proves that the nature of animals and fruits is different. § 13. He shows that God is most delighted by things easily obtained and of little expense. § 15. Nor does any of the reasons for which we perform sacred rites to the Gods have a place regarding animals. 24. Therefore, the true cause for why we sacrifice them is our own lack of self-control and our pursuit of pleasure. § 25. He returns afterward to show the beginnings of sacrifices. § 27, etc. How, starting from fruit, the license of sacrifices eventually progressed to humans. § 27, 28, etc. He then adds several reasons why it is necessary to abstain from animals. § 31, etc. He teaches most excellently what things and what kind of things it is proper to offer. § 33, etc. He illustrates his own view by reviewing the opinions of the Pythagoreans § 36, and the Platonics. § 37. Wherein he runs through the various types of Gods, their natures, and their duties. § 37, & 38. He records much concerning good and evil Spirits <note>original: Geniis; referring to intermediate divine beings or daemons</note>. § 39, etc. Indeed, that the evil spirits are most delighted by the smell <note>original: nidore; the smoke and fumes of roasting meat</note> of sacrifices made from animals. § 42. Therefore, a pious man ought to refrain from them. § 43. To which he finally and seriously exhorts the reader, since it contributes greatly to chastity and holiness. § 44, etc. These things are even imitated by sorcerers. § 45. They are hinted at by the external symbols of all sacred rites. § 46, 47, etc. Arguments for ani-*

### PORPHYRY

...they say. For not even in the life of the city did the legislators define the same duties for private citizens and for priests; instead, while they conceded <gloss>2</gloss> to the masses matters of food and their general way of life, they forbade the priests from following those same practices, setting death or heavy fines as the penalties.

§ 4. For if <gloss>1</gloss> these things are not confused, but are distinguished in the proper manner, most of the arguments of our opponents are found to be empty. For most of them argue either that because it is necessary to kill animals that cause harm, the act of eating them follows as a consequence; or they reason that because animals were included in sacrifices, they must therefore be eaten by humans. And again, if certain animals must be removed because of their wildness, they think it follows that even tame animals must be killed. And if meat must be eaten by some, <gloss>2</gloss> such as athletes, soldiers, and those who perform manual labor, they think it must also be eaten by philosophers; and if for some of these—

<column-break/>

—since indeed neither did the legislators in the communal life of the state decree that the same things were to be done by both the common people and the priests: but while they allowed many things to most people both in their diet and the rest of their lifestyle, they forbade the priests from using these same things, having proposed the penalty of death or some heavy fine.

§ 4. If, therefore, these things are not confused, but are accepted with that distinction which is proper, most of the arguments brought forward by those who contradict us will be found to be empty. For most things are assumed either because some animals must be killed on account of the damage they cause, as if eating follows from the killing; or because animals are also accustomed to be used for sacrifices, they reason from this that they must also be eaten by humans: and likewise, if certain animals are to be removed from our midst on account of their wildness, they judge it to follow from this that tame animals must also be killed: and if it is permitted for some to feed on flesh—of which kind are athletes, soldiers, and those who labor with their bodies—that this is also permitted for philosophers: and if for some of all these it is permitted—

# On Abstinentia, Book II

...they consider it to be necessary: since all consequences of this sort are both faulty and bring no necessity for establishing any rule. The faults of all these things can be easily seen by those who are not prone to being argumentative. Therefore, since we have already refuted some of these errors, and will convict others in the course of the following discussion, we will now turn to a detailed explanation of this investigation into sacrifices. We will explain where they originated in the beginning: what they were like at first, how and when they were changed. Then, we will consider whether the philosopher should offer all types of sacrifices; to whom animal sacrifices are offered; and finally, we will report everything related to these matters—partly through our own reasoning and partly from what we have received from ancient sources, [remaining within the bounds of proportion]—

<column-break/>

...and for everyone, all these consequences are faulty, and are unable to establish any necessity for the position taken. And that <gloss>3</gloss> all these are faults is immediately obvious to those who are not <gloss>4</gloss> contentious. We, however, having already corrected some points and being about to refute others as the discourse proceeds, will now clarify the <gloss>5</gloss> investigation concerning sacrifices. We will explain the origins from which they arose, and who started them, and of what kind the first ones were; <gloss>6</gloss> how they changed and from where, and whether the Philosopher <note>Porphyry refers to the "Philosopher" as an ideal figure seeking spiritual purity.</note> should sacrifice all things; and to whom sacrifices involving animals are made; and generally every <gloss>7</gloss> related matter, partly discovering them ourselves and partly receiving them from the ancients...

---

<column-break/>

3. **All faults.** <note>original: "Πᾶσαι μοχθηρίαι"</note> Thus all the manuscripts say, except for the Bodleian which has "wicked things," which was noted in the margin by Fogerolles and approved by Valentinus. Shortly before, after "being," the Lipsiensis manuscript had mistakenly omitted "and."

4. **Occurs to the contentious.** <note>original: "Ἐριστικοῖς προπίπτει"</note> Fogerolles and Valentinus restored "encounters" <note>original: "προσπίπτει"</note>. It is well known that these words are confused a thousand times, as seen below in Book III, chapter 26, where I nevertheless defend the common reading. In this place, "occurs" <note>original: "προπίπτει"</note> means to fall forward or to run into one's eyes spontaneously. The word carries a meaning that suggests something sudden and appearing of its own accord. Hence, in a bad sense, "rashly" <note>original: "προπετῶς"</note> means precipitously or inconsiderately, and the verb signifies a certain recklessness in the heat of action. See Gataker on Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius</note> I, 17, and Wesseling on Diodorus XV, 65.

5. **We shall clarify the investigation.** <note>original: "Σκέμμα διευκρινήσομεν"</note> This is correctly rendered by the earlier editions

<column-break/>

and also the Lipsiensis and Meermann manuscripts. Valentinus, for some unknown reason, changed it to "we shall distinguish." Gataker illustrates this very word in his notes on Antoninus X, 12. Cicero, in his letter to Atticus VII, 8, says: "we shall clarify this in a more philosophical manner" <note>original: "id philosophōteron dieukrinēsomen"</note>, where some editors wrongly suggest "we shall distinguish."

6. **How they changed, etc.** The Lipsiensis manuscript reads "And how they changed and when," which Reiske rightly approved. "When" is also found in the Meermann manuscript. Shortly after, instead of "are made," the oldest editions and the manuscripts suggest we should read "occur."

7. **Related matter.** <note>original: "Παρακείμενον"</note> I do not disapprove of this word, though "proposed matter" <note>original: "προκείμενον"</note> is more common. Furthermore, in the sentence "to whom sacrifices are made," something seems to be missing, unless we want to understand "to which gods or spirits" after the word "whom." —REISKE.

# PORPHYRY

...[as we proceed] we shall record; aiming as much as possible for a symmetry and style appropriate to the subject. The matter stands thus:

§ 5. It seems an almost immeasurable time has passed since that most learned race of all mankind—as **Theophrastus** says—who inhabit the most holy region created by the **Nile**, first began to sacrifice to the celestial gods, starting from the hearth...

<column-break/>

...maintaining that proportion, as far as possible, which is most suited to the proposed argument. The matter, therefore, is as follows:

§ 5. It is a nearly countless time since the race of men, the most learned of all (as Theophrastus says), who inhabited the most holy region founded by the Nile, first began to sacrifice to the celestial gods from the hearth and home, not...

---

<margin>
To aim for symmetry: *Diodorus Siculus* said this quite often, as the great *Commentator* <note>likely referring to Peter Wesseling</note> teaches regarding Book I, ch. 8, who did not forget our author [Porphyry].
</margin>

1. **An immeasurable time...** — These words and those following, up to the phrase "but the antiquity etc." near the end of this section, were transcribed from our author by **Eusebius** in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book I, p. 28. Eusebius partly provides help in reading Porphyry and partly expects it from him. In the *Meerman* margin it is noted: "Note that Theophrastus speaks of bloodless sacrifice."

<margin>
2. **Most learned race.**
</margin>
He means the **Egyptians**, whose wisdom is praised everywhere. He calls them "the most learned of all" below in § 26. The term *logioi* <note>original: λογιωτάτοι</note> refers to those who are wise and skilled in a particular matter. Thus, "the most learned of the priests" and similar phrases are found in **Plutarch** and others. **Wesseling** (on Diodorus II, 4) and the **Philologists** (on Lucian) will satisfy you on this point.

<margin>
3. **As Theophrastus says.**
</margin>
He praises Theophrastus frequently in the following parts of this book, which I suspect were taken from the same work. But out of the many books he wrote, I will discuss which one is meant at § 11.

<margin>
4. **By the Nile.**
</margin>
The *Lipsian* manuscript lacks the article "the." It signifies **Egypt**, but why does he say it was "founded by the Nile"? Does he mean the King, who is called *Neileus* in Diodorus Siculus (I, 63) and *Nilus* by others, from whom the city of Nilus in Egypt also took its name? So it seems to **Fabricius**. But although I would easily grant that this king deserved well of the Egyptians, 

<column-break/>

it cannot be conveniently said that he "founded the region." I would prefer, therefore, to understand it as the **river**. The Author speaks from the conviction of the ancients (though the reasons of the great **Bochart** suggest this is false), who believe that Egypt, or rather its lower part, was born from the alluvial deposits and accumulated silt of the river; hence they call it the *gift of the Nile*. **Heliodorus** says the river itself is "the savior of the upper part, and both the father and creator of the lower." See **Olear** on Philostratus and **Wesseling** on Diodorus, who shows that the expression "to found a region" <note>original: κτίζειν χώραν</note> was used very broadly among the Greeks.

<margin>
5. **From the hearth.**
</margin>
In Eusebius it is "at the hearth," where the most learned **Vigerus** translates it as "at the domestic hearth." And certainly more correctly than I did with "from Vesta." **VALENTINUS**. See the *Scholiast on Aristophanes' Wasps*: the meaning is that the first of all to whom sacrifices were made were the celestial gods, and in these very acts, the beginning of the sacrifice was made from **Vesta** <note>The goddess of the hearth</note>. **REISKE**. Excellent. **Phurnutus** <note>Cornutus</note> says: "Wherefore the Greeks began from her as the first in sacrifices, and ended with her as the last." Therefore, it should also be restored in Eusebius, where Vigerus did not see how this proverbial "from the hearth" <note>original: ἀφ’ ἑστίας</note> fit here. It fits because of where the proverb originated. **Plato** in *Cratylus*: "Let us begin from Vesta according to the law." Read the cause explained there.

6. ...not of myrrh, nor of cassia, nor the first-fruits of frankincense mixed with saffron; for these too were adopted many generations later. 7. This was the step of error, when man, being deprived of necessary life, with many labors and tears, 8. offered drops of these things as first-fruits to the gods. They did not sacrifice these things previously, 9. but rather...

---

6. **Not of myrrh nor of cassia.**] We ought not to dwell upon "commonplaces," as they say <note>Refers to rhetorical tropes or well-known moral arguments</note>. Yet I cannot restrain myself from adding those lines from **Ovid, Fasti Book I, 337**:
> *Grain and a sparkling grain of pure salt*
> *Were enough to win over the gods for man.*
> *Not yet had the foreign ship carried over the sea*
> *The myrrh that wept from the bark.*
> *The Euphrates had not sent frankincense, nor India the costus,*
> *Nor were the threads of red saffron yet known.*
> *The altar gave off smoke content with Sabine herbs,*
> *And the laurel was burned with no small crackle.*

7. **Step of error.**] In **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century Christian historian who preserved many fragments of Porphyry</note>, who cites this passage in the first book of his *Preparation for the Gospel*, we read "the investigator of error, *mazer*." <note>The word "mazer" is a difficult term, possibly derived from Hebrew, which commentators here are trying to reconcile with the Greek text</note> However, I would not advise anyone to correct Porphyry in this way. For I fear that these notes might belong to someone who was not very skilled, who believed that the word "step" (*klimakter*) meant what he expressed in those two words. I myself feel differently, and I think that "step" (*klimakter*) here—if this reading is intact—signifies the origin of error, serving as a kind of ascent or grade. Since, however, it is read in that manner in the magnificently printed Paris codices of Pamphilus, I have seen a manuscript in which only the latter of those words was read. <term>VICTORIUS</term> <note>Pietro Vettori, a 16th-century Italian philologist</note>. In Eusebius, it is read differently: *and man, becoming a searcher of error, mazer, offered the first-fruits to the gods from necessary life with many labors and tears.* The translator rendered it thus: *when man, having become a curious investigator of error, offered the first-fruits of necessary life to the gods after the drops of many labors and tears.* The words as they are read in Porphyry can be conveniently rendered as I have already interpreted them, if "overcoming" were written instead of "becoming." <term>Vigerus</term> <note>François Viger, a Jesuit scholar</note> thinks that "investigator" in Eusebius is an interpretive gloss explaining the term *mazer*. <term>VALENT</term>. Either "overcoming" or "becoming self-controlled." <term>REISKE</term>. <term>MEERMANN</term>. *Klimater*. Long ago I had reconstructed it as "error and *mazer*," which <margin>Suidas III, 336. <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note></margin> anyone can see how easily it could have been born from the word for "step" (*klimakter*). I was much delighted when I noticed this was confirmed by **Eusebius**, in whose work, however, the word "investigator" must be considered a gloss (as the troublesome tribe of scribes often tends to substitute a more frequent word for a less frequent one, which then creeps into the text). I conclude this especially from our author—not as **Viger** preferred, that *mazer* is the same as "investigator," for otherwise those two words are also usually joined. See **Bergler** on *Alciphron* I, 11 and **Sylburg** on *Clement of Alexandria* p. 814. But if the phrase "and *mazer*" displeases you, at any rate "step" (*klimakter*) is preferable. Not what **Valent.** had given as *klimater*. And indeed the older editions of **Felicianus** and the **Leipzig Manuscript** agree on the reading "step" (*klimakter*).

8. **Drops of these.**] So it is printed in the same author: *he offered drops as first-fruits to the gods.* Although the word "of these" is missing there, it is found in the written manuscript, in which part it agrees with Porphyry. <term>VICTORIUS</term>. I restored the phrase "to the gods" from **Eusebius**: it used to read "to the divine things." The Greeks usually say "the divine" <note>original: το θείον</note> in the singular to mean the Godhead, not "the divine things" in this sense.

9. **But just as if someone...**] **Eusebius** also refers to this in the *Proof of the Gospel*, chapter 10.

# PORPHYRY
<meta>catchword: 6.</meta>

...but of grass itself, as if they had plucked with their hands a kind of down of fertile Nature. 10. For the earth brought forth trees before animals; 11. and much before trees, she produced the annual-growing grass, the leaves and roots and entire shoots of which they gathered 12. and burned: by this 13. sacrifice welcoming the visible celestial gods, and 14. through the fire consecrating honors to them for immortality. For to these gods also we 15. maintain the immortal fire in the temples, because it is most similar to them. From the burning of incense... <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ χλόης... τοῦ πυρὸς; Latin: herba ipsa... Ex suffitu</note>

<column-break/>

...but of grass itself, as if they had plucked with their hands a kind of down of fertile Nature. For the earth brought forth trees before animals; and she brought forth the grass—which arises in annual germination—much before trees. Gathering its leaves and roots, and indeed the entire stalks themselves, they consumed them in flames. Welcoming the celestial gods who were visible by this sacrifice, and by fire consecrating honors to them for immortality. For to these gods also we are accustomed to maintain the immortal fire in the temples, seeing as it is most similar to them. From the burning of incense...

---

<margin>10. Page 34. B. and *Theodoret* <note>Theodoret of Cyrus, a 5th-century bishop and theologian</note> in his *Sermon on Sacrifice*: where he is intent on showing that Porphyry thought sacrifices were far removed from true piety, and that Porphyry had stolen these ideas from the sacred scriptures: "but of grass itself, as if they had plucked with their hands a kind of down of fertile Nature," etc. *Diodorus Siculus* (Book I, 43) also touches on this most ancient Egyptian custom: "Therefore, even to the present day, men, remembering the usefulness of this plant, whenever they approach the gods, they take some of it in their hand and pray." *Wesseling* <note>Peter Wesseling, an 18th-century scholar</note> touches on these Porphyrian matters there.</margin>

10. **For the earth brought forth trees—**] Just as Empedocles <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher</note> says in *Plutarch* (Volume II, page 910. C.): "Empedocles says trees were the first of living things to emerge from the earth."

11. **And much before trees—**] I have reconstructed "much before trees" as it was in the *Florentine editions*; it is read no differently in the *Eusebius Leipzig* and *Meermann Codices*. I think it better to follow the word Porphyry uses, "being generated," rather than Eusebius's word "becoming," though that too could be defended. Instead of "annual," the *Bodleian* manuscript very poorly has "flying." <note>The scribe likely confused the Greek word *epeteion* (annual) with *epeteinon* (flying)</note>

12. **They burned: by this.**] Thus these ought to be distinguished, as the *older editions* had distinguished them. However, all had mistakenly given "in this way" instead of "by this."

<column-break/>

<margin>13. **Welcoming with sacrifice.**] An elegant word, just as "to welcome with gifts" appears in *Aelian* (Historical Miscellany, Book I, chapter 32) and other places. *Hesychius* <note>A 5th-century lexicographer</note>, regarding this usage, says: "to welcome is to bring near." See the celebrated *Alberti* there.</margin>

14. **Through the fire [consecrating] honors.**] "Through" is not found in *Eusebius*; *Viger* rightly notes there that while both versions can be approved, our reading is easier to understand. *P. Wesseling*, in his notes to *Diodorus Siculus* (Book II, 20), excellently explains the force and power of the word "to make immortal," and teaches that "to be made immortal" is said of all those who achieve immortality in any way; from this he illustrates our phrase "to consecrate honors for immortality."

15. **We maintain [the fire] etc.**] Thus in Pamphylus: "they maintained [the fire] immortal in the temples as being..." VICTORIUS. In *Eusebius*: "they used to maintain." VALENT. These things ought to be explained according to the custom of the ancients, who nourished eternal fires in honor of the Gods. Thus, besides hanging lamps, *Spanhem* shows from this passage (in *On Vesta and the Greek Prytaneion*, Volume V of *Greeve’s Antiquities*) that an altar and a fire always burning were consecrated to Vesta <note>The Roman goddess of the hearth</note> by the ancients. But our author does not restrict these things to Vesta alone.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

From those things which were burned from the earth—that is, from *incense-burning* <note>original: "thymiasi"</note>—they named the altars *incense-burners* <note>original: "thymiatēria"</note>, as if you were to say "vessels for fumigation," and they called the act *to sacrifice* <note>original: "thyein"</note> and the offerings *sacrifices* <note>original: "thysias"</note>. We, however, do not interpret these terms correctly, as if they surpassed the later sin <note>The "sin" refers to the later introduction of animal slaughter</note>; for we call that worship which appears to be offered to the gods through the slaughter of animals a *sacrifice* <note>original: "thysian"</note>. Indeed, those ancients had such great care that the old custom should not be violated, that against those who neglected the old ways and introduced new ones, they employed a curse <note>original: "execratione"</note>, and named those things with which we are now accustomed to fumigate *aromatics* <note>original: "arōmata"</note>, which is to say, "cursed things" <note>The author suggests a folk etymology linking 'aroma' to 'ara' (a curse)</note>. And anyone might observe this use of ancient fumigations from the fact that many even now [offer] chopped pieces of fragrant wood...

<column-break/>

...most similar. And from the burning of the products of the earth, they called them both *incense-burners* and the act *to sacrifice* and *sacrifices*. We, however, misinterpret these, as they deviate from the later error, by calling the service that seems to be done through animals a *sacrifice*. So much did the ancients care not to transgress the custom, that against those who left behind the ancient way and brought in another, they uttered curses, and called the things now used for fumigation *aromatics* <note>original: "arōmata"</note>. One might see the antiquity of the aforementioned incense-offerings by looking at the fact that many even now still sacrifice chopped pieces of fragrant [woods]...

---

<margin>16. **Sacrifices — deviate.** There, the printed text had "sacrificing" and "signifying." However, the manuscript I saw does not differ at all from the author's reading in the first part. **VICTORIUS.** I conjectured it ought to read "revealing." **Eustathius** confirms this, where "signifying" is found. **VALENTINUS** also cites "revealing," as does **Graevius** in *Notes on Hesiod* ch. 8. But I do not dare to proscribe a beautiful metaphor in "deviating" and similar words. To **Reiske**, "as" here seems to be the same as "towards," and he reads: "those deviating." Or if "as" is taken for "as if," he reads: "confirming," as if confirming and stabilizing the more recent impiety.</margin>

<margin>17. **Having cursed.** Better there "having cursed" <note>original: "arasamenous"</note>. **VICTORIUS.** In other editions it was "about to curse," and so also in the Leipzig and Meerman Codices, whence **Reiske** conjectured it should read "cursing." This scholium was added in the margin of the Leipzig manuscript: *Why incense-offerings are called "aromatics" and how those sacrificing through them were either cursing or praying. For from this they say prayer is a "curse" <note>original: "aran"</note>.* And so also the Meerman, except that there it is "sacrificing" instead of "having sacrificed." Where "aromatics" were so named should not be investigated here. **Bodaeus à Stapel** on Theophrastus' *History of Plants* IV, 6, derives it from "I pray," but such is the infirmity of human memory that at IX, 7, being inconsistent with himself, he fetches it from elsewhere. A little before, instead of "having introduced," the Leipzig Codex has "introducing," which **Reiske** deservedly preferred because of the preceding "neglecting." It is no different in **Eusebius**.</margin>

<margin>18. **Fragrant woods.** Secular writers record that trees, especially fragrant ones, were used in sacred rites in olden times; the use of frankincense is more recent for them. **Pliny**, *Natural History* XIII, 1: *In the times of the Trojan War, supplication was not made with frankincense; they only knew the smell—or rather the soot—of cedar and citrus wood rolled in smoke during sacrifices.* We know of an older use of this from the Sacred Scriptures. But this is not the place for dealing with these matters. As for the fact that **Spencer** [claims] the law by which God ordered cedar wood to be burned with the heifer...</margin>

...certain fragrant woods. From this 19 **once the earth—which at first produced only grass—began to bring forth trees, and humans first ate the fruit of the primary oak <note>acorns</note>, they offered a few of the fruits to the gods in sacrifice due to the scarcity of food, but offered more of the leaves. But later, when human life transitioned to a more civilized <term>civilized: literally "tame" or "mild"</term> diet, and they had said 21 "Enough of the oak," 20 they began to sacrifice nuts.**

§ 6. **However, when 1 barley appeared as the first of the fruits of Demeter <note>The goddess of agriculture, known as Ceres to the Romans</note> after the legumes, the human race used this from the beginning 2 for the sacrificial sprinkling of grain according to the first**

They were accustomed to burn certain things to the gods. Wherefore, when after that first sprouting of herbs the earth had already begun to produce trees, and humans first fed upon the fruits of the oak, they offered a few of the fruits to the gods in sacrifice because of the penury of food, but offered more of the leaves. But afterward, when life had already transitioned to a milder form of nourishment, and had said, "Enough of the oak," they sacrificed with nuts.

§ 6. But when, among the fruits of Ceres, barley first emerged after the legume, the human race used it whole from the beginning, sprinkled with water for sacrifices—

<margin>
[The commentator] draws this from that ancient rite, in *On the Hebrew Ritual Laws*, chapter 8; this is indeed to be a slave to a hypothesis. A little earlier in the *Bodleian manuscript* it was written: "that many even now."
19. *After the grass from the beginning.*] Perhaps it should read: "after the grass of the beginning." and soon, instead of "of the leaves for them," the *Leipzig manuscript* correctly reads "of the [oak] itself." Reiske thinks it refers to the oak. The *Meerman Codex* also confirms "of itself." The same source soon says "incense" <note>original: "thymiata"</note> rather than "sacrifices" <note>original: "thyata"</note>.
20. *From the nuts.*] Perhaps "from the fruits." REISKE. Excellent. "From the beginning, sacrifices of fruits were made to the gods." See below, section 27: "But in ancient times it was through sacrificial cakes and fruits, as we have demonstrated." Also section 59. *Nut* <note>original: "Karyon"</note> has a very wide application, like the Latin *nux*. It denotes every fruit covered by a hard shell, and hence even *Walnuts*; because humans were for a long time nourished by acorns, when they finally found the tree that bore nuts and tasted the sweet flavor, they called them "Jupiter's acorns" <note>the etymological origin of the Latin word for walnut, 'iuglans'</note> because of their excellence. But see *Bodaeus a Stapel* on *Theophrastus's History of Plants*, book 3, chapter 15. I ought to mention this because of what follows. *Nuts* <note>original: "Karya"</note> encompasses every kind of tree-fruit, as *Casaubon* also teaches in his notes on *Athenaeus*, book 2, chapter 12.
21. *Enough of the oak.*] A well-known proverb, often explained by ancient critics. He uses it again in book 4, chapter 2. Compare *Casaubon* on *Theophrastus's*
</margin>

*Ethical Characters*, page 313. *Eusebius* against Marcellus, book 1, chapter 3, who explains the origin of the saying. *Libanius*, Epistle 1082, and there see *Wolf* and *Alberti* on *Hesychius* under the letter V. But "there is enough of those things, just as of the oak," to speak with *Julian the Apostate* in the *Misopogon*, page 346 A.
1. *The fruit of Demeter after the legumes, etc.*] Elsewhere they usually use the plural: *legumes* <note>original: "chedropa"</note>. And so our author does below in book 3, chapter 18. They call by this name all pod-vegetables which are gathered and plucked by hand, from which bread is not made. By another name they are called *pulses* <note>original: "ospria"</note>. *Pollux*, book 6, section 60: "there are also the pulses which they also named legumes." Some indeed distinguish them, but without necessity. See *Bodaeus a Stapel* on *Theophrastus's History of Plants*, book 8, chapter 1. Indeed, whenever "legumes" are mentioned simply, "pulses" seem to be understood, for you may find them added sometimes. *Suidas* shows from *Thucydides* that the ancients used the singular form as well, as is done in this place. Our author says that barley was found first after the legumes; therefore, mortals first fed on barley. *Artemidorus*, book 1 of the *Interpretation of Dreams*, chapter 71: "barley breads are good for all, for legend holds that this was the first food given to humans by the gods." Next, *Reiske* preferred "of the first appearing of the barley" [in a different grammatical case].

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK II

...used, which they called the "sprinkling of whole barley" <note>original: οὐλοχυτεῖσθαι</note>. Then, when they had broken it and crushed it for food, they hid the tools of its manufacture in a secret place—viewing them as objects that had brought divine aid to human life—and venerated them as if they were sacred. Moreover, from this ground nourishment, which they considered "blessed" <term>blessed: a reference to the Greek 'makarios,' implying a life of abundance and ease compared to the primitive past</term> above previous diets, they made offerings into the fire for the gods. From this practice, even now at the conclusion of sacrifices, we are accustomed to use ground offerings, thereby testifying to that ancient increase in the use of incense, and not

<column-break/>

the human race [offered] the sacrifices. But later, when they had crushed the grains and ground the food, they hid the tools of the labor—having provided divine help to their lives—in a secret place, and approached them as if they were sacred. Since the "ground life" <note>original: ἀληλεσμένου βίου; a metaphor for the civilized life that uses flour</note> was considered blessed in comparison to the previous one, they first offered a portion of the ground food to the gods in the fire. For this reason, even now toward the end of the sacrificial rites, we use ground offerings; thus testifying to the practice established from the beginning...

---

<margin>
*Theophrastus* is praised; I ought to add a short note <note>original: scholion</note> which is read under the name of *Didymus* <note>A famous Greek scholar and grammarian of the 1st century BCE</note> regarding the *Iliad*, Book I, line 449, on the word *oulochytai* <note>sacrificial barley</note>: "Oulae: these are barley grains mixed with salt which they poured upon the animals being sacrificed before they were killed, either for the sake of a great calling-forth, or to keep the memory of the ancient way of eating. For as *Theophrastus* says in his book *On Discoveries*, before humans learned to grind the fruit of Demeter <note>grain</note>, they ate the grains in this manner." From this you might almost guess the passage was taken from that book by *Theophrastus*, though it does not seem so. I will speak on this further at paragraph 11.
</margin>

3. **When they had crushed—ground the food.**] The term *Ereikesthai* <note>to bruise</note> is said of fruits or legumes that are *only lightly bruised*; from this come terms for "bruised" or "crushed." However, *Psaiestai* means *to be reduced to flour by a mill*. Immediately after, he calls them "ground offerings," which by another name are called elliptically *psaista*, meaning ground fruits. To the Latins, these are *molae* or *liba* <note>sacrificial cakes</note>: handfuls soaked in flour and oil, which the poor offered to the gods in place of libations. *See Kuster* on *Aristophanes' Plutus*, 138, and *D'Orville* on *Chariton*, VI, 7.

4. **As if to sacred things.**] I would prefer "to the [tools] themselves as sacred things." <note>VALENT: This was an error of the typesetter, who in the *Vittorius* edition had given 'priests' (hiereis) instead of 'sacred things' (hieroîs); it was foolishly propagated into subsequent editions. *Felicianus* and the manuscript codices have it correctly.</note>

<column-break/>

5. **Of the ground life.**] See *Casaubon* on *Athenaeus*, Book XIV, chapter 12. <note>VALENT: In previous editions and the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts, it was written as 'ground' (alēlemenou). However, the "ground life" (alēlesmenos bios), meaning "a life using milled grain," was so frequent among the ancients that it became a proverb. It is contrasted not only with the life of the first humans, who are believed to have lived on acorns, but also with those who came immediately after them, who ate the first fruits not milled, but only lightly bruised. This is certain from what *Paullus Leopardus* taught in his *Emendations* XI, 4, and *Petrus Wesseling* on *Diodorus*, I, 17.</note>

6. **In comparison to the previous... blessed.**] *In comparison to the previous.* Meaning: the previous life. Then, after "fire," it seems that a word like "placing," "sending," or "giving" is missing. <note>REISKE</note>

7. **Of the sacrificial offerings.**] *Reiske* preferred "of the sacrifices." He uses the word again below in paragraph 59; see there. This passage matches that of the poet in the *Iliad*, Book IX, line 220:
> "And he cast the sacrificial offerings into the fire."

8. **With ground offerings**] What these were has just been said. Since the most ancient people reconciled themselves to the gods with these alone, that honor was thereafter held for antiquity, so that after everything else, they offered ground meal as a gift most pleasing to the gods. Go to *Casaubon* on *Theophrastus's Ethical Characters*, page 231, who explains these things beautifully. It was incorrectly written in the *Florentine* edition and the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts as *opsaistheisi*.

# PORPHYRY

...the increase of the nine types of incense <note>original: "θυμιαμάτων αὔξησιν"</note>; yet they did not perceive for what reason we perform each of these acts. Starting from these beginnings, as fruits and even wheat became more abundant for us, the first-fruits of cakes <term>pelanoi: sacrificial cakes made of meal and honey</term> and all other remaining things were added to the sacrifices for the gods. People gathered many flowers, and mixed in no fewer of these, if they possessed anything beautiful in life or fitting in scent for divine perception. Some of these they used for wreaths <note>original: "σέφοντες" - literally 'honoring' or 'crowning'</note>; others they gave to the fire, offering other divine drops of wine and honey. Furthermore, having discovered oil for human needs, they offered the first-fruits of this as well to the gods who were the causes of it.

§ 7. To all these things, the procession of the Sun and the Hours, which is performed in Athens even to this day, seems to bear witness—

<column-break/>

—not understanding, however, for what reason we were doing each individual thing. Proceeding from here, as other fruits and now wheat were supplied more abundantly, the first-fruits of wheat porridge and all other things were employed in sacrifices to the gods: while men culled flowers from many sources and mixed in other things, if they seemed to have anything beautiful in life, and which excelled in scent for the divine sense: and of these, some they used for garlands, others they burned having been cast into the fire. Where they had also found divine drops of both wine and honey, and likewise oil for human uses, they made a sacred offering from these also to the gods who were the authors of them.

§ 7. To all of which, the procession of the sun and the hours which to this very day at Athens—

---

<margin>9. *The increase of incense.*] Either there is a fault in the word "increase" <note>Greek: αὔξησιν</note>, or rather something seems to be missing. "The simplicity of the incense (or sacrifices, as in the Leipzig Manuscript) from the beginning, which afterwards proceeded and grew into an increase of luxury." Thus testifying by that rite to the original meager nature of the offerings, which later advanced and grew into sumptuosity and splendor. REISKE. "Sacrifices" <note>Greek: Θυμάτων</note> appears in the Meermann Manuscript, whereas conversely at the end of § 5 it is "incense" <note>Greek: θυμιάματα</note> where others have "sacrifices."</margin>

<margin>10. *For us, and of the... etc.*] It would be easy to substitute "at the same time" <note>Greek: ἅμα</note> for "but" <note>Greek: ἀλλὰ</note>, which are exchanged for each other a hundred times. One might also think of adding "not only." But the common reading holds well, and the simple "but" has the same value as "not only... but also." I have compared examples of this matter in Polybius. Therefore the fault does not seem to be here, but in the word for "wheat" <note>Greek: πυρῶν</note>, and one should read "means/resources" <note>Greek: πορῶν</note>. REISKE. Clearly the Cambridge Editor had rashly inserted "on the one hand" <note>Greek: μὲν</note> after "us"; Reiske has skillfully explained the "but also," unless you prefer "nay even" or "furthermore."</margin>

<margin>11. *Now of cakes.*] In the Leipzig and Meermann Manuscripts, this Scholion <note>ancient marginal explanation</note> was added: "Pelanoi: cakes made of fine flour, or it is the thinnest meal, suitable for sacrifice. Or fruits softened with honey. Or certain first-fruits for the gods. Or the foam solidified around the body, and the solidified and dried gummy tear, such as frankincense and gum, and the obol <note>small coin</note> which is the seer's fee." You may read almost the same things in Suidas under "Pelanoi," which the celebrated Ruhnken illustrates in his Lexicon to Timaeus, suspecting they were taken from Boethius’s Platonic Lexicon.</margin>

<margin>12. *Some they used for wreaths.*] See § 16 near the end. VALENTINI. "Some," namely the flowers. It is said not only "to honor a statue with flowers," but also "to honor flowers," meaning to place wreaths on the head. Therefore this reading seems to hold well here. But in the next line I approve the reading of the Leipzig Manuscript, "those," namely the "drops." But in such a way that the punctuation at line 23 and the "but" <note>Greek: δὲ</note> are omitted according to the prescription of that same manuscript, and a comma is placed after "oil." And yet even so, the sentence is a little harsh and more intricate. For which reason—</margin>

### On Abstinence, Book II.
->P<-

...is celebrated, seems to bear witness: in which not only other herbs but also grass, as well as oak and the berries of the strawberry tree, service-berries, tri-

<note>original Greek: "πομπῇ, Ἡλίου τε καὶ Ὡρῶν. πομπεύει γὰρ εἰλυσπόα ἄγρωσις ἐπὶ πυρηνίων ἡγηρίας, ὄσπρια δρῦς"</note>
...procession of the Sun and the Hours. For there is carried in procession a "rolled-up grass" <note>likely a specific bundle of couch-grass</note> upon kernels of "guidance" <note>referring to a ritual object called a *hegeteria*</note>, along with legumes, oak...

---

I would prefer to stick with the common reading on this condition: that we read "crowning" and "giving" <note>original: "σεφόντων & δωρουμένων"</note>, on account of the preceding word "flower-gathering." Once this is admitted, everything in this passage will be clear and straightforward. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and celebrated philologist</note>. The punctuation has made the passage obscure. I have followed the distinctions of the first <term>EDITIONS</term> <note>original: "Edd."</note>, which <term>VALENTINUS</term> <note>Benedictus Valentinus, a commentator</note> had disturbed by inserting a "but" <note>Greek: "δὲ"</note> after the word "divine."

1. **The Sun and the Hours.** Many believe the *Thargelia* <note>An ancient Athenian festival held in May to honor Apollo and Artemis, where first-fruits were offered</note> were celebrated at Athens in honor of the Sun and the Hours, during which the first-fruits of the crops were carried around. However, those cannot be the ones under consideration here; rather, the *Horaea* are meant, in which we read of solemn feasts dedicated to the Hours, who stood by the Sun and presided over the seasons of the year. This is argued by <term>CASAUBON</term> <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a famous classical scholar</note> regarding <italic>Athenaeus</italic> XII, 20. Yet there is nothing there to illustrate the rituals that follow. We read that such sacred rites were celebrated during the *Pyanepsia* <note>An autumn harvest festival</note>. See the <italic>Scholiast on Aristophanes</italic> regarding *The Knights* 725 and *Plutus* 1056, and the great <term>HEMSTERHUIS</term> <note>Tiberius Hemsterhuis, a Dutch philologist</note> on that passage.

2. **Rolled-up grass.** This passage has certainly caused me more trouble than any other. <term>MEURSIUS</term> <note>Johannes Meursius (1579–1639), a Dutch historian and Greek scholar</note> cites these words in his *Greek Festivals* under "Thargelia" as: "for there is a procession of mud, grass, and couch-grass upon the suppliant branch of kernels, legumes, oak, etc., and the 'guide-cake' <note>original: "παλάθη ἡγητυρία"</note>." This is how I have seen it printed. Meursius proves in that place that this procession was made to the Sun and the Hours during the Thargelia and Pyanepsia. In the Pyanepsia, an olive branch <note>original: "θάλλος ἐλαίας"</note>, which <term>EUSTATHIUS</term> calls a "suppliant branch" <note>original: "ἱκετηρία"</note>, was carried forward. Meursius says this branch apparently had berries, around which Porphyry says the grass was wound, although everyone else says it was wool. Therefore, perhaps it is better read as: "wool wound around the suppliant branch of kernels." The "guide-cake" <note>original: "Παλάθη"</note> is perhaps a marginal explanation <note>glossēma</note> for "the leader." Concerning the use of the pot in the same festival, see Meursius on the Pyanepsia. That the "upright cake" <note>original: "ὀρθοσάτης"</note> is the name of a pastry, and that it was named for its shape, is clear from <term>POLLUX</term> <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century grammarian</note>. <term>VALENTINUS.</term> I find it necessary to leave this passage to those who have more leisure. To me, in my haste, these few thoughts occur spontaneously; they will be, unless I am mistaken, plain and open. Within "rolled-up grass" <note>original: "εἰλυσπόα"</note> lies a hidden scholium <note>marginal note</note>. It seems someone wrote in their manuscript next to "grass" this

<column-break/>

reminder: "a species of grass" <note>original: "εἶδος πόας"</note>, to teach that couch-grass is a certain *genus* of herb. It happened later that this "eidos poas," deformed into "eilypspoa," was shoved into the main text. The second "hegerias" [or "hegerias" as it is in the Leipzig Code] should be removed from line 32, as it is a faulty spelling of the word "hegeteria" in line 35. This later spelling of the same word is just as erroneous as the first. But while in line 33 it has invaded a foreign place, in line 35 it holds its own place, and is easily corrected. Read "then" <note>original: "εἶτ’"</note> (that is, "then there was carried in procession") "the hegetria." Then they carried the *hegetria*, a type of very thin cake made from the finest flour. If I knew for certain that a *pyrenion* was once the name for a wooden dish or carrier, made in the shape of a pine cone or pyramid, I would suspect we should read "upon the pyrenion." But let this conjecture vanish into thin air. <term>REISKE.</term> I notice my own manuscripts offer no help here, and the <term>BODLEIAN</term> <note>The library at Oxford</note> omits everything from the word "grass" to "wheat." <term>ABRESCH</term> <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch, a 18th-century philologist</note> conjectures it was "winding grass" <note>citing Theocritus</note> upon a "leader of wheat-kernels." <term>VALENTINUS</term> had corrected it to "being wound." The <italic>Attic Lexicon</italic> says "wound up" <note>iluspomenos</note> is Attic, while "enveloped" <note>eiloumenos</note> is Greek. On this word, see Heringa. Was it "eiloumene," meaning "woven"? For this word, see also Albertus on Hesychius. Or rather, "a bundle, a herb, couch-grass"? In Hesychius, "eile" means the stalk of legumes. That certainly comes close to the writing and the subject matter. But enough of conjectures. Choose for yourself. "Herb" <note>original: "πόα"</note> and "couch-grass" <note>original: "ἄγρωστις"</note> are well distinguished: the former is grass that cattle and four-legged animals eat; the latter is what physicians use—though this distinction is not always kept, as <term>WESSELING</term> correctly observes.

3. **Upon kernels of guidance.** I think it was written "hegetrias" for "hegetorias" <note>both words for 'leader' or 'guide'</note>. As for "pyrenion," I would prefer "pyrenon" or "pyrinon" <note>kernels or wheat</note>. For "pyrenas" and "pyrinas" are frequently confused. They call "pyrenas" the kernels in fruits which support the exterior surrounding flesh...
