# PORPHYRY
->10.<-

oak, <note>original Greek: "μιμαίκυλα"</note> 4 strawberry-tree fruits, barley, wheat, 5 pressed fruit-cake, guidance-cake, of wheat and barley flour 6 a *phthois* cake, *orthostatai* cakes, 7 a pot. 8 But when men moved far away from the first-fruits of sacrifices which took precedence among them, the adoption of the most terrible sacrifices was introduced, so that—

<column-break/>

wheat, barley, bundles of dried figs, and cakes made from wheat and barley flour, sweets, and also pots of legumes were customarily brought. But while the offerings made in sacrifices kept men far from injustice, the adoption of wicked victims was introduced, of cruelty—

---

<margin>
...found in cherries, olives, etc. Read *Bodeus à Stapel* <note>Johannes Bodaeus à Stapel (1602–1636), a Dutch physician known for his botanical commentaries</note> on *Theophrastus: History of Plants III, 17.* Indeed, everything in a nut or cone or other thing that is fit for eating, as *Casaubon* <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar</note> teaches on *Athenaeus II, 16.* Thus it signifies what kind of "guidance-cake" <note>original: "ἡγητορίαν"</note> he wants to be understood here.
</margin>

4. **Strawberry-tree fruits.** <note>original Greek: "Μιμαίκυλα"</note>] What these are is well known from the Lexicographers. Regarding the varied spelling of the word, see Valckenaer on *Pollux VII, 144.*

<margin>
5. **Pressed fruit-cake [palathe], guidance-cake [hegeteria].** <note>original Greek: "Παλάθη ἡγητηρία"</note>] Unless this is a single phrase, *palathe* and *hegeteria* can be distinguished. The former belongs to the custom of the ancients, who, when they had dried figs, plums, and other things of that sort, were accustomed to thicken them into a single mass and arrange them in various shapes, calling them *palathae*. Consult *Wesseling* on *Diodorus XVIII, 67.* However, in *Suidas*, *palathe* is also *a kind of herb*. And the *Etymologicum Magnum* (under the entry "Hegetores"): *the palathe of figs; palathe is a mass of figs.* Certainly *hegeteria* or *hegetoria* is the name usually given to the mass of dried figs that was carried in the procession, *because they considered this the first civilized food.* See *Kuster* on *Suidas* and *Casaubon* on *Athenaeus III, 2.* For at Athens the fig was first discovered (while others previously fed themselves on acorns and other fruits, on which matter see *Aelian: Varia Historia III, 39*), and thus a better way of living was introduced. See *Aelian: V. H. III, 38* and *Meursius: Attic Lectures II, 13.*
</margin>

<margin>
6. **phthois cake —** <note>original Greek: "φθόϊς"</note>] This seems to be the nominative plural; and instead of "orthosatais," read "orthosatai kai" [and], and instead of "chutros" [pot], read "chutroi" [pots]. Thus three types of cakes are designated, all included under the general name of "rams" <note>original: "κριῶν" - likely referring to sacrificial cakes shaped like animals</note>. *Phthois, orthosatai, chutroi.* What the differences between them were is not easy to say. Thus, having removed extraneous matters, the order of the passage runs roughly like this: *in the procession... of wheat [or wheat-flour]... legumes, acorns of oak, strawberry-tree fruit, barley, wheat, pressed fruit-cake, crumbs [etria] of wheat and barley flour, phthois cakes, orthosatai cakes, and pots.*
</margin>

<column-break/>

...it seems the last kind took its name from the oil and honey poured over those cakes. These are the things that extemporaneous reflection suggested to a person in haste; if they are not so polished and perfected as to leave no doubt or obscurity remaining, they nonetheless do not seem entirely useless or irrelevant. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and philologist</note>. I distinguish between "phthois" and "orthos." The ancient critics teach us that the former word is spoken by the Attics as one syllable, while for others it is two syllables. I therefore read *phthois* (in the plural, as the Attics usually do). See *Suidas* and *Spanheim* on *Aristophanes' Plutus 676.* Then "orthosatai" is *a kind of sacred bread*, as *Pollux* says (*VI, 73*), which is certainly just as good as *Valentinus's* "orthosates," which he had substituted in the text.

7. **Pot.** <note>original Greek: "Χύτρος"</note>] I would by no means dare to condemn this reading, on account of the manifold use of pots in sacred rites. See *Suidas* and the *Scholiast on Aristophanes' Plutus 1198*, where a very timely note for this passage occurs in the margin of the Leiden manuscript, which *Hemsterhuis* <note>Tiberius Hemsterhuis (1685–1766), a Dutch philologist</note> published: *those who dedicate something in temples, or establish them, were accustomed to offer pots full of gruel and fine flour, or of cakes and ground legumes.*

8. **But when [men moved far away]...** <note>original Greek: "Πόῤῥω δὲ τῶν"</note>] Read this until the end of this section also in *Eusebius: Preparation for the Gospel, Book I, p. 29 and Book IV, p. 151.* *Theodoret* <note>Early Christian bishop and theologian</note> also has part of them in his *Sermon on Sacrifices.*

9. **Standing out [or advancing].** <note>original Greek: "Προεχουσῶν"</note>] In *Eusebius* it is printed as well as written in two places as *proiouson* [advancing]: namely in the first and fourth of those books. <term>VICTORIUS</term> <note>Piero Vettori (1499–1585), a leading Italian humanist</note>. It is better in *Eusebius III, 14: proiouson.* <term>VALENTINUS</term> <note>Benedictus Valentinus, a 16th-century editor</note>. *Reiske* preferred *proelthouson* [having come forward]. The common reading *proechouson* can be defended—that is, *taking precedence*—however *Theodoret* also has *periouson* [surpassing] in addition to *Eusebius*. Next, the meaning of *epeisagesthai* [to be introduced] in this context is illustrated by *Wetstein* <note>Johann Jakob Wetstein (1693–1754), a theologian and textual critic</note> on the author of the *Epistle to the Hebrews 7:19*.

It seems almost like a play of wit that the inhabitants are called **Thoes** <note>A name meaning "jackals" in Greek, here used for a specific tribe.</note> by the author, with respect to the name of that city, in much the same way that the Trojans are compared to "Thoes" (jackals) in *Homer's Iliad, Book 11, line 474*. There, the commentator **Didymus** <note>An ancient scholar from Alexandria.</note> says: "He spoke of Thoes and Trojans as equal and rhyming." This is even more likely because Porphyry had already spoken of this carnivorous animal earlier in Book I, section 13. However, if anyone should discover a tribe actually named the "Thoes" on this coast, I will very quickly strike out this conjecture. The barbarian King of the Tauri, **Thoas**, is well known from *Euripides' Iphigenia in Tauris, line 30*.

<margin>2. Snatched away—they were.]</margin> A people is said to be "snatched away from men" <note>original: "Ἀνάρπαστος ἐξ ἀνθρώπων"</note> when they are utterly destroyed. These phrases are common—to be "snatched away" or "to be made vanished"—regarding cities that are not only captured but suddenly overturned from their very foundations. There is a sense of violence and speed in this expression. The nature of this word was beautifully examined by the scholar **D’Orville** in his notes on *Chariton, Book III, 7 and IV, 6*. The Greeks also say "to be plucked up" or "to be made desolate," which we saw above in Book I, section 26; the distinction between these words is often scarcely 

<column-break/>

noticed. Compare the notes of the celebrated **Valkenaer** <note>A famous 18th-century Dutch classical scholar.</note> on *Herodotus, Book IV, chapter 204*.

For insolence &c.]</margin> Those verses from **Hesiod’s** *Works and Days*, line 133 <note>original: "Hes. ἔργ. 133"</note>, were previously corrupted in this way: "nor to see the blessed ones" and "as is the law for the immortals." **VALENTINUS** <note>Likely referring to a previous editor of the text.</note>. These were also found corrupted in the same manner in the *Bodleian, Leipzig, and Meermann manuscripts*. **Theodore Canter** had already corrected these from Hesiod in his *Various Readings, Book II, 24*.

<margin>4. But of the Bassarae.]** Valentinus does not have the particle "de" (but). This is contrary to all other editions, both printed and manuscript. I have printed "Tauri" with a capital letter, as **Feliciano** <note>An early editor of the text.</note> correctly did, though it was not usually done. He means the Tauri, a people of Scythia, who were once infamous for the human sacrifices they performed for the goddess Diana. This fact is very well known from ancient authors and the writings of Christians, who often throw this back at the pagans. See **Minucius Felix**, *Octavius, chapter 6*, and the commentators there.

<margin>5. To the frenzy of human sacrifices &c.]</margin> The *Leipzig manuscript* reads "to these," and it was also thus in the *Florence edition*, which the *Lyons edition* followed.

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK II
->P 3<-

...they were steaming <note>original: "fumebant"</note>, just as we do now with other animals, when we set aside the remaining meat of the sacrifices for feasts. Who is unaware of how they were driven into such a fury against one another, attacking each other with bites, and did not truly cease from feeding on blood <note>original: "cruore uesci"</note> until they had destroyed the very race of those who had first introduced such sacrifices among them?

§ 9. Therefore, the sacrifice offered through animals is a later and very recent development. It did not arise from a grateful cause, as did the offering of fruits, but rather from hunger or some other onset of calamity. Indeed, the origins of specific slaughters among the Athenians are traced back to either ignorance, or anger, or fear. For example, they attribute the slaughter of a sow to the involuntary error of Clymene <note>A figure in Greek myth; here used to illustrate that killing animals was originally seen as a mistake.</note>, who had killed the animal after striking it unintentionally with her weapons.

<column-break/>

...[steaming] <note>original: "νων"</note>, (just as we do now with the animals; for after offering the first-fruits, we set out the rest for a feast). Who has not heard that, falling upon one another with madness <gloss>6</gloss> and biting one another—and moreover, truly feasting on blood—they did not stop until they had utterly consumed the race of those who first among them took up such sacrifice?

§ 9. <gloss>1</gloss> Therefore, sacrifice through animals is later and most recent; it took its cause not from gratitude, like the sacrifice from fruits, but from a circumstance of famine or some other misfortune. Immediately, the causes of the particular killings <gloss>2</gloss> among the Athenians have their origins in either ignorance, or fits of rage, or fears. For they attribute <gloss>3</gloss> the slaughter of sows to an involuntary error of Clymene, she having struck the animal <gloss>4</gloss> without intent, and thus killed it.

---

<margin>6. Biting one another <note>original: "Δάκνοντες ἀλλήλους"</note>.] "To bite" <note>original: "Δάκνειν"</note> is a metaphor taken from biting animals; it is used a hundred times regarding men who inflict injury and harm upon others. As the saying goes, "with the whole bag," the learned men will provide examples in their notes on Paul’s Letter to the Galatians 5:15; to add more here would be silly.</margin>

<margin>1. Later then, etc. <note>original: "Ὑστέρα μὲν τοίνυν"</note>] Perhaps it should be "last" <note>original: "ὑσάτη"</note>. REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note>. Cyril <note>St. Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father.</note> transcribed our author in his work *Against Julian*, Book X, page 348, where you may read these same things in the same way.</margin>

<margin>2. The causes <note>original: "Αἱ αἰτίαι"</note>.] This is also found in the Leipzig Codex, but from a correction by the same hand that had previously written something else. It seems "yearly" <note>original: "ἐνιαυτοῖς"</note> might fit, or "the most part" <note>original: "αἱ πλεῖσαι"</note>. REISKE.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>3. The slaughter of sows, etc. <note>original: "Τῶν συῶν σφαγὴν"</note>] The ancients frequently teach that this was the oldest form of victim, as we saw above. But I do not remember others handing down this particular case. Potter <note>John Potter, author of *Archaeologia Graeca* (1697).</note> in *Greek Antiquities*, Book II, chapter 4, page 228, suspects that the reason why this animal was so hated by the Jews is to be sought here, though to investigate that is not the purpose of this passage.</margin>

### On Abstinence, Book II.

Furthermore, they first killed a goat in Icarus, a district of Attica, because it had nibbled at a vine. Likewise, Diomus, who was a priest of Jupiter Polieus <note>original: "Jupiter of the City"</note>, is said to have been the first to slaughter an ox under the following circumstances: while the Diipolia <note>the festival of Jupiter</note> was being celebrated, and the fruits had been prepared for it according to ancient custom, an ox approached and tasted the sacred grain-paste. Among the Athenians, these specific reasons are offered; different accounts are told among other peoples; yet all are full of wretched— <note>The text breaks off mid-sentence here; "miserorum" (wretched/miserable) is the start of a description of the myths' tragic nature.</note>

§ 10. They first laid hands on a goat in Icarus of Attica because it cropped the vine. Diomus was the first to slaughter an ox; he was a priest of Zeus Polieus <note>original: "Zeus of the City"</note>. While the Diipolia was being conducted and the fruits had been prepared according to ancient custom, the ox approached and tasted the sacred cake <note>original: "pelanos" - a thick, liquid-and-flour offering</note>. Taking as helpers the others who were present, he killed it. Among the Athenians, such specific causes are assigned, while others are told among other peoples. But all are full of—

<margin>
—wretchedness. <note>original: "erorum"</note> *Chernips* <note>original: "χέρνιψ"</note> refers to "water for the hands." However, in this passage, as frequently in others, it is to be understood as lustral water <note>holy water used for purification</note>. See the notes by Duker on Thucydides, Book IV, 97. What they called the basin (*chernibon*) and the water (*cherniba*) will also be excellently explained by the learned Pierson in his notes on the Attic writer Moeris, page 414.

1. *In Icarus.*] Meursius corrects this to *Icarium*. See "Icarium" in his *Peoples of Attica*. VALENTINUS. This is correct, and Reiske agrees.

2. *They laid hands on/killed.*] Felicianus correctly translated this as *interemerunt* (they killed). Compare Xenophon’s *Expedition*, Book VII, page 403: "but if anyone resists, we shall try with your help to lay hands on <note>subdue or kill</note> them." Elsewhere, "to lay hands on" animals means to subdue or tame them, a usage discussed by Wesseling in his notes on Diodorus, Book V, 39.

3. *Cropped the vine.*] This was correctly restored by Valentinus and, before him, Fogerolles. Suidas defines "cropped" <note>original: "ἀπέθρισεν"</note> as "shorn" or "cut off." In that entry, Kuster did not act with the best faith; read Abresch's *Observations on Aeschylus*, Book II, 8, for a more skillful restoration. See also Barnes on Euripides’ *Helen*, 1204, regarding this word.

4. *Of Jupiter Polieus.*] There was no city among the ancients that did not have some specific God or Goddess to whose care it primarily committed itself. Hence, "Gods of the City" <note>original: "θεοὶ πολιεῖς"</note> and "City-Keepers" <note>original: "πολιοῦχοι"</note>

<column-break/>

are mentioned throughout the literature. Jupiter, in particular, was called by this name, as he performed the general protection of cities. I will give one rich testimony: Hemsterhuis on Pollux, IX, 26.

5. *While the Diipolia was being conducted.*] See Meursius’s *Greek Festivals*. VALENTINUS. This matter is very well known from those who have explained Greek antiquities. They commonly call it the *Diipolia*. See Hesychius under this letter, and the learned editors there, though it is also written *Dipolia*. Below, in section 30, our author calls it the *Diospolia*; if it ever goes by that name, it is certainly very rare. Because this is a very ancient festival, it happened that in Aristophanes, "Diipolia-like" <note>original: "διϊπολιώδη"</note> is a term for things that are very old and obsolete. They also called it the *Bouphonia* (Ox-slaying), because of those things our author narrates about the ox in the following section. See Pausanias on Attica and others cited by the learned editors on Aelian’s *Various History*, Book VIII, 3. More on this matter below. Some wish for these events to have happened during the festival of Dionysus, but most say the Diipolia. See the Scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Clouds*, 979. "To hold a festival" is a very common expression, concerning which see the Scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Plutus*, 621, and Hemsterhuis in the same place.

6. *Prepared.*] The *Leipzig* and *Meermann manuscripts* more correctly read *pareskeuasmenon* (having been prepared). And here, it immediately says "taking helpers" without the word "for."

...of explanations that are not at all holy. 8 Most people blame famine, and the injustice that arises from it, as the cause. They argue that because humans were forced by hunger to taste the flesh of living beings, they also began to offer these animals as first-fruits <note>original: "aparchai" — the first portion of a harvest or hunt dedicated to the gods</note>, even though they had previously been accustomed to abstain from such food. 9 Therefore, since the custom of these sacrifices is shown to be no older than the time when eating animals became a necessity, it should be clear to people that animals ought to be excluded from what is considered edible. It follows that although they tasted and sacrificed animals, we are not obliged to accept this as a "pious" act, because they did not offer those initial sacrifices to the gods in a pious spirit.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book II of Porphyry's "On Abstinence," specifically focusing on the historical and utilitarian reasons why certain ancient cultures, like the Egyptians, forbade the eating of cows while allowing the sacrifice of bulls.</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

There was a great scarcity among them of this animal, which is otherwise very useful. Therefore, while they both ate bulls and slaughtered them in sacred rites, they spared the females for the sake of breeding. They ordained it as a <term>piaculum</term> <note>an act requiring expiation or a religious crime</note> if anyone should lay hands upon them. In this matter, it was undoubtedly utility and practical use that determined what was considered piety and impiety within one and the same species of cattle. Since these things are so, Theophrastus—who truly wishes to act with piety—rightly forbids the sacrifice of animals for these and other similar reasons.

<column-break/>

<note>original: Greek text of the passage above</note>
...this animal being useful, it was scarce among them. Therefore, they both tasted and offered first-fruits of the bulls. But sparing the females for the sake of offspring, they legislated that touching them was a defilement; and indeed, based on utility, they defined the pious and the impious act regarding one and the same genus of oxen. Since these matters stand in this way, Theophrastus reasonably forbids those who wish to be truly pious from sacrificing living creatures, employing these and other such arguments.

->§ 12.<-

<column-break/>

->§ 12.<-

Our author <note>referring to Porphyry</note> mentions the Egyptians and Phoenicians quite often. See the end of this book, and Book IV, 7. *Jerome, in his second book against Jovinian, chapter 7: "In Egypt and Palestine, because of the rarity of cattle, no one eats a cow."* *Herodotus* testifies that the Barcaeans, Cyrenaeans, and the nomadic Africans from Egypt as far as Lake Tritonis abstain from eating the cow. Others say the same of different groups. See *Bochart, Hierozoicon II, 32.* It is therefore not surprising that even today the Brahmins of India—disciples of the ancient Egyptians, as some believe—abstain from cows, for which reason they abominate European Christians. See *Jablonski in the Prolegomena to the Egyptian Pantheon, p. 20.* Learn from our author the "secret of the State," the true cause of this abstinence. For since Egypt was not very fertile in animals, greater consideration was rightly given to the females than the males (not unlike how, during the recent plague, the most provident Fathers of our Country took measures). A matter useful to the public was later turned into a superstition, and thus gave occasion for the worship of beasts. It will not be a regret to have read *Mosheim's notes on Cudworth’s System, p. 918*, which our author could have defended excellently. *Wesseling, in his notes on Herodotus II, 41*, observes that this superstition lasted until the times of the Emperor Constantius. We ought not to dwell here on the opinion of *Spencer (Ritual Laws II, 15)* that God once willed a cow to be slaughtered so that the Hebrews might be led to contempt and hatred of the Egyptian cow-worship.

But "pious" and "utility" can be well connected. The *Cambridge edition* wrongly gave *diorizan*; the others are correct. The words "pious and the" are not found in the *Meerman manuscript*.

It is well known, and already mentioned above, that the negative particle is often added unnecessarily to verbs of forbidding. This passage of *Theophrastus* seems to be taken from the same book as the one occurring in § 5, and below in § 20 and 26; for in all of those, he treats of sacrifices. I will speak of this later.

### PORPHYRY

->§ 12.<-

First, it was because a greater necessity, as we have said, overtook us that they began these [sacrifices]; for famines were the cause, and wars, which also brought about the necessity of tasting [meat]. Therefore, since fruits are available to us, what need is there to employ a sacrifice born of necessity? Furthermore, one must return favors and thanks to others in different ways, according to the value of their beneficence; to those who have done us the greatest good, we must return the greatest thanks, chosen from the most precious things—especially if they themselves are the providers of these very things. Now, the most beautiful and precious things the gods bestow upon us are the fruits of the earth. For it is through these that they preserve us and allow us to live according to the law. Consequently, it is with these fruits that we ought to honor them. And indeed, one must sacrifice—

First, because a certain greater necessity was pressing upon us, as we have said, they performed these sacrifices: for famine and wars were the cause, which brought about the necessity of eating those things. Secondly, because since the repayments of benefits and thanks should be rendered to some in one way and to others in another, according to the dignity of the beneficence: to those who have bestowed the greatest benefits upon us, the greatest returns must be made, and from the most precious things, especially if they themselves have provided those things to us. § 13. But perhaps someone will say that we also take something from plants when we make offerings of fruits to the gods. But that taking is not similar: for it is not done to the unwilling. For even if we leave the plants alone and apply no force, they release their fruits of their own accord. Moreover, the removal of fruits is not accomplished with the death of the stalks, as when animals pour out their soul. Furthermore, because the fruit of the bees exists also from our labors, it is fitting that a common benefit be perceived from it. For they themselves, sipping here and there, collect honey from flowers: but we have the care of them, so that the utility ought to be divided justly, lest they themselves be affected by any loss. For what is not an advantage to them provides many uses for us: so that it seems it should be taken as a kind of wage from them.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument from Section 13. While the previous page established that harvesting plants does not harm them in the same way killing an animal harms its "soul," this page moves into the practical and economic reasons why plant-based sacrifices are superior to animal sacrifices.</meta>

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK II

-> Q 3 <-

Therefore, we must abstain from animals in sacrifices. There is also the fact that while all other things belong to the gods, fruits seem to belong to us, since we are the ones who sow them, plant them, and nourish them through our various labors. Thus, one should sacrifice from what is our own, and not from what belongs to another. Furthermore, that which can be obtained at a small cost is more holy and more pleasing to the gods—as well as to those performing the sacrifice—than that which requires great expense; it is easier to provide and allows for the continuous practice of piety. However, that which is neither holy nor obtainable at a low cost, even if it is available, should by no means be employed in sacrifices.

§. 14. Now, that animals are not among those things which are easily or cheaply obtained can be best seen if we look at the majority of humanity. For even if there are some people who have many sheep or many cattle, we must not consider them for our present purpose. This is first because there are many nations that possess none of the animals suitable for sacrifice, except perhaps the most lowly; and second, because even among those who live in cities, the majority suffer from a scarcity of these—

<column-break/>

Therefore, we must keep away from animals in sacrifices. For in other respects, while all things are of the gods, the fruits seem to be ours; for we sow them and plant them, and we raise them with our other cares. One must therefore sacrifice from our own things, not from those belonging to others. Since that which is inexpensive and easy to provide is holier than that which is difficult to provide, and it is more pleasing to the gods, and it is ready for those who sacrifice for the sake of continuous piety. <gloss>4</gloss> Therefore, that which is neither holy nor inexpensive should not be sacrificed at all, even if it were present.

§ 14. That animals are not among the things easy to provide or inexpensive must be observed by looking at the greater part of our race. For we must not consider this based on the fact that some men are <gloss>1</gloss> "rich in sheep and rich in cattle." First, because many of the nations possess none of the animals used for sacrifice, unless one speaks of those that are without honor. Second, because most of those who live in the cities themselves are in want—

---

<column-break/>

<gloss>4. Therefore, that which is neither—]</gloss> This appears again in the passage of <term>Eusebius</term> <note>Eusebius was a 4th-century Christian historian who preserved many fragments of earlier pagan philosophers like Porphyry.</note> cited previously.

<gloss>1. Rich in sheep and rich in cattle among men.]</gloss> Perhaps it should read "among men, and all are such, but this must be considered in this way." Because there are some among men who abound in herds and flocks, *therefore all excel in these resources; but here the matter must be looked at.*—<term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and philologist known for his editions of Greek texts.</note>. He seems to refer to those words of <term>Homer</term> in the *Iliad* I, 154:
> "Therein dwell men rich in sheep and rich in cattle."

See the <term>Scholia</term> <note>Ancient marginal notes or commentaries.</note> there. A little earlier the <term>Bodleian</term> and <term>Meerman</term> manuscripts <note>Reference to specific historical copies of the text used to compare variations.</note> incorrectly read "looking" <note>original: ὁρῶντες (horontes)</note>.

<vocab>Porphyry, On Abstinence, Eusebius, Homer, sacrifices, animals, frugality</vocab>

<summary>Porphyry argues that animal sacrifices are inappropriate because animals do not belong to humans in the same way cultivated plants do, and because true piety should be accessible and inexpensive for all people, not just the wealthy. He cites the scarcity of livestock in many nations and among the urban poor as evidence that animal sacrifice is not a universal or practical path to holiness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument from Section 14. Having established that animal sacrifices are often prohibitively expensive and difficult to obtain, Porphyry now argues that the "ease of provision" of plant offerings makes them more suitable for a life of constant, universal piety. He concludes the page with a famous anecdote from the Oracle at Delphi.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

-> ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK II <-

<column-break/>

...they struggle with scarcity. For even if someone should say that there is a scarcity of certain <gloss>2</gloss> cultivated crops, there is certainly no scarcity of the other things that grow from the earth; nor is it as difficult to obtain these crops as it is to procure animals. Therefore, the provision of crops and things from the earth is easier than that of animals. That which is inexpensive and easy to provide contributes toward a continuous state of piety, and indeed toward the piety of all people.

§ 15. Experience itself bears witness that the <gloss>1</gloss> gods take more joy in this than in that which is very expensive. For when that <gloss>2</gloss> certain Thessalian <note>A man from Thessaly, a region in northern Greece famous for its wealth and cattle.</note> brought oxen with gilded horns and hecatombs <note>A massive public sacrifice, literally of a hundred oxen.</note> to the Pythian Apollo, the Pythia <note>The high priestess of the Oracle at Delphi who delivered the prophecies of Apollo.</note> said that the <gloss>3</gloss> man from Hermione had pleased the god more, even though he had only sacrificed <gloss>4</gloss> some of the cakes...

---

<margin>2. *Of the cultivated crops.*] Perhaps it should be "some" <note>original: τινὰς</note>. REISKE. The translator read it as "our" crops <note>original: ἡμετέρων</note>, and it is also found this way in the Bodleian and Meermann manuscripts; but nothing should be changed, because these are being contrasted with "things that grow from the earth." Where the Lipsian and Meermann manuscripts have "from the earth," it is not a bad reading.</margin>

<margin>1. *The gods [take more joy in this] than in the expensive.*] The word "more" <note>original: μᾶλλον</note> is understood; its absence in this kind of word order is not unusual. We encountered examples in Book I, 54 and elsewhere. Needham provides more on this in his notes on Hierocles' *Golden Verses*, p. 138, as does Wesseling on Diodorus, XI, 11. Many other examples could easily be added. It is surprising that such a frequent occurrence, often unobserved, has repeatedly led learned men into error. I will not list the examples here.</margin>

<margin>2. *That Thessalian with the gilded-horn oxen.*] Perhaps it should read "that man who [brought] the gilded-horn [oxen]" <note>original: ἐκείνου τοῦ τὰς χρυσόκ.</note> REISKE. He is called "Thettalos," which others spell "Thessalos." See the discussion on this spelling by Wasse in his notes on Thucydides, I, 20.</margin>

<margin>3. *The man from Hermione had pleased [the god].*] "Had pleased" <note>original: κεχαρίσθαι</note> means to have done something grateful and acceptable. REISKE. Most excellent. We have the response of the Pythia in Hierocles' *Golden Verses*, p. 26:
> "But the grain of the far-famed man from Hermione was pleasing to me."

Note where Needham shows that Bentley restored the word "pleased" <note>original: κεχαρίσθαι</note> in our text, than which nothing is more true. It is confirmed by the words that follow: "he was one who had pleased." Abresch was of the same opinion.</margin>

<column-break/>

...struggle with scarcity. For if someone says they have a lack of our fruits: yet they will not lack the others which arise from the earth: nor will it be as difficult to obtain fruits as to provide animals. Therefore, the acquisition of fruits and those things born from the earth is easier than that of animals. But that which is easier and considered of less cost, leads to a constant piety for anyone at all.

§ 15. And indeed, the outcome of the event itself testifies that these things please the gods more than those which require great expense. For when long ago that Thessalian was sacrificing oxen with gilded horns and hecatombs to the Pythian Apollo, the Pythia asserted that the man from Hermione had been more pleasing to her—

---

<margin>4. *The cakes from the small bag.*] We saw above what "cakes" <note>original: ψαιστὰ</note> were, where he calls them "crushed offerings." These were the sacrifices of the poorer people, almost no different from those mentioned below in Section 17. The wealthy would cast frankincense and other offerings of that kind onto the altar, and they observed the custom of offering either the incense or the grain with the tips of their fingers, as Casaubon writes in his notes on Theophrastus' *Characters*, p. 232. Indeed, it was customary to do this with three fingers. Ovid, *Fasti* II, 573.</margin>

<summary>Porphyry argues that plant-based sacrifices are superior because they are accessible to everyone, promoting a continuous and universal practice of piety. He cites a famous Delphic oracle where the humble grain offering of a poor man was preferred over a wealthy man’s sacrifice of a hundred gilded oxen.</summary>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

...sin, who had offered cakes from a small basket using only three fingers. When that man, because of what had been said <note>referring to a previous oracle or divine statement praising the small gift</note>, threw all the rest of his belongings into the fire upon the altar, the divinity spoke again, saying that he had made himself twice as unwelcome by doing so as he had previously been pleasing. Thus, that which is easily provided is dear to the gods; the divine power looks more to the spirit and character of those who sacrifice than to the abundance of the victims.

§ 16. Theopompus <note>A Greek historian of the 4th century BCE</note> has also recorded similar things. He says there was a certain man of Magnesia in Asia, who was exceedingly wealthy. Since he possessed a great abundance of cattle, he was accustomed to perform many magnificent sacrifices to the gods every year, partly because of his great wealth and partly because of his piety—

<column-break/>

—cakes from the small bag with his three fingers. But when he, because of what was said, cast all the rest into the fire upon the altar, the voice said again that he was twice as much hated for doing this as he was formerly favored. Thus, the inexpensive is dear to the gods, and the divine looks toward the character <term>ethos</term> of those who sacrifice rather than the quantity <term>plethos</term> of the things sacrificed.

§ 16. Theopompus relates similar things, saying that a man of Magnesia from Asia came to Delphi; he was very rich and owned many flocks. He was accustomed to make many grand sacrifices to the gods every year, partly due to his prosperity—

---

<margin>
*And he places three grains of incense with three fingers beneath the threshold.*
Compare Bodaeus à Stapel on Theophrastus's *History of Plants*, Book IX, chapter 4. Therefore, the man from Hermione was content with that kind of sacrifice which the wealthy were accustomed to add to others, and which they properly called "to sacrifice additionally" <note>original: ἐπιθύειν (epithyein)</note>, as will be discussed in another place.
</margin>

</margin>

<margin>
6. *Twice as much hated.*] Either "by twice as much" or "twice as much." The syllable *ma* (in the word *soma*, "body") was born from the final letter *n* of the word *toson* ("so much") and the *a* from the start of the following word *apechthoito* ("he might be hated"). REISKE. Excellent. Fogerolles and Valentinus have already corrected it to "twice as much." It was no different in the Bodleian Codex. Rightly, therefore, Needham restored it thus. I was unwilling to allow "the body" <note>original: τὸ σῶμα (to soma)</note>, which used to be read, to remain any longer.
</margin>

<margin>

</margin>

—ancient sages repeat a hundred times. I will only bring forward Plato in the *Alcibiades* (page 459 B) because it is a most beautiful passage: *For it would be a terrible thing if the gods looked to our gifts and sacrifices, and not to the soul, if one happens to be holy and just. Much more so, I think, than to these costly processions and sacrifices.* And consider that which happened to the widow in the Gospel, Mark 12:43. Note also the elegant wordplay <term>paronomasia</term> between "character" <note>original: ἦθος (ethos)</note> and "quantity" <note>original: πλῆθος (plethos)</note>, which ancient authors often like to pursue. Among others, Alberti has much on this matter regarding Luke 8:30. Such is the case in § 19: "dear to God" <note>original: θεοφιλεῖς (theophileis)</note> and "costly" <note>original: πολυτελεῖς (polyteleis)</note>.

Besides those, there is Theopompus, a Pythagorean philosopher mentioned by Libanius in Epistle 1526, whom Wolf wants added to the list of Pythagoreans given to us by Fabricius in volume 1. ...of his possessions, and others out of piety and a desire to please the gods. Being thus disposed toward the divine, he went to Delphi, having conducted a procession with a hecatomb <note>original: *hekatomben*, a massive sacrifice of 100 oxen</note> for the god and having honored Apollo magnificently, he approached the oracle <gloss>3</gloss> to consult it. Thinking that he served the gods most beautifully of all men, he asked the Pythia <note>The high priestess of the Temple of Apollo who delivered the oracles</note> who most excellently and eagerly honored the divinity, and <gloss>4</gloss> who performed the most pleasing sacrifices, assuming that the first prize for this would be given to him. But the priestess answered that Clearchus, who lived in Methydrium of Arcadia, served the gods best of all men. Greatly astonished <gloss>5</gloss> at this, he desired to see the man and, having met him, to learn in what manner he performed his sacrifices.

<column-break/>

...and because he studied to please the gods to the highest degree. Being thus affected, he set out to the god at Delphi with sacrifices, and when he had worshipped Apollo there with a magnificent procession of hecatombs, he entered to consult the oracle. Since he believed that he exhibited the most distinguished worship of the gods among all men, he asked the Pythia who it was that most excellently and promptly worshipped the god, and offered him the most pleasing sacrifices, thinking it certain that the palm <note>a symbol of victory or the first prize</note> in this matter would be granted to him without doubt. But the prophetess replied that Clearchus, who lived in Methydrium (which is a town in Arcadia), worshipped the gods best of all. He, marveling in a wonderful manner, resolved in his mind to travel there and meet the man, and to inquire from him by what method he offered sacrifice.

1. <note>This note refers to a word for</note> piety, which is mentioned in the *Scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds*, line 1354, and following him, *Vossius in his "On the Greek Historians"*, Book I, chapter 7, and others, who attribute this story to Chios, unless they were deceived by a corrupt reading, a matter which is discussed below.

2. **Of his possessions.** <note>original: *Ton hyparchonton*</note> This phrase is used hundreds of times in this sense by the Greeks. Hence *Wetstein* illustrates this passage in his commentary on *Luke's Gospel* 8:3; it was certainly worth the effort for him to heap up thirteen examples of this specific meaning.

3. **Consulting the oracle.** <note>original: *Chresteriazomenon*</note> By an error of the typesetters, I believe, the *Cambridge edition* had *chreseriazomenon*. What the terms "to consult an oracle" and "to be consulted as an oracle" properly mean has been beautifully taught by "the great one" <note>likely referring to a renowned scholar like Wesseling</note> in his notes on *Diodorus Siculus*, Book XVI, chapter 26.

4. **Performing the sacrifices.** <note>original: *Poionta tas thusias*</note> Perhaps it should be "making for himself" <note>suggesting the middle voice form *poioumenon*</note>.

5. **To desire.** <note>original: *Epithymeisthai*</note> This should be "To have desired" <note>original: *epithymesai*</note>. Toward this also leads the reading of the *Leipzig Manuscript*, in which "to desire" is indeed read by the same hand; however, the letters are so distorted that it easily appears the scribe was up to something, having previously written something else. # ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK II.

And when he had quickly traveled to Methydrium, at first indeed, having seen the smallness and humble nature of the town, he so despised the place that he could not believe that any private person there, nor even the whole city, could worship the gods more excellently and magnificently than himself. Nevertheless, he approached the man and asked him to explain the manner in which he worshipped the gods. And Clearchus spoke thus: "I indeed always sacrifice to the gods with the greatest diligence at the appointed times; while every single month at the new moons I crown and adorn Mercury <note>original: *Mercurium*, referring to the Greek god Hermes</note>, and Hecate, and the rest of the gods whom our ancestors left to us, and [I honor] them with incense, and cakes, and—"

<column-break/>

When he had quickly arrived at Methydrium, he first looked down on it, as the size <gloss>6</gloss> of the place was small and humble, thinking it impossible not only for any individual, but not even for the city itself to be able to honor the gods more magnificently or more beautifully than he did. But nevertheless, having met the man, he asked him to tell him in what way he honors the gods. And Clearchus said that he performs and diligently sacrifices at the proper times, <gloss>7</gloss> every month at the new moons, crowning and cleansing [the statues of] Hermes and Hecate, and the rest of the shrines which the ancestors left behind, and <gloss>8</gloss> honors them with incense and bar- <note>The word breaks off; the following page will complete it as 'barley-cakes'</note>

***

I should have warned here that we have the same form in *Plato*: in the *Gorgias* page 327. E. concerning other teachers: *Abresch*: *Dilucidations on Thucydides* page 282. In this place, the *Meermann* manuscript more correctly has "to desire" <note>original: *epithymesai*</note>.

6. **Small — of magnitude of the place.**] The word *magnitude* <note>original: *megethos*</note> here signifies nothing other than the *space and extent* of the town, and is a term common to both large and small things. Therefore, the comma is rightly absent from the word "being" <note>original: *ontos*</note> in the *Leipzig Codex*; however, I will not hide that it seems to me *Theopompus* gave it thus: "being humble in the magnitude of the place." **REISKE** <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century German scholar</note>. "Methydrium, no longer a city, but a village belonging to the district of Megalopolis," says *Pausanias* <note>A 2nd-century AD geographer</note>: Book VIII, pages 475 and 512. For since Megalopolis was founded, it degenerated into a village. Compare the learned commentator on *Thucydides*: V, 58. "Small magnitude" seems to be a species of **oxymoron** <note>a figure of speech that combines contradictory terms</note>, about which type of speaking the learned have said much. The opposite, "cities greatest in magnitude," was elegantly said by *Aelian*: *Various History* III, 18. Other examples

<column-break/>

can be read in *Wesseling*: on *Herodotus* I, 19.

7. **Every month etc.**] A most ancient Athenian law: to sacrifice at the New Moons, which were called "monthly sacrifices" <note>original: *epimenia*</note>. See *Petit*: *Attic Laws* Book I, 1. page 158. Hence *Plato* in *The Laws*: Book VIII. page 905. B. "there are twelve festivals for the twelve gods... for each of these there are monthly sacrifices." Therefore, since this custom was very frequent among the Gentiles long before the age of Moses, God once willed that victims be immolated to Himself at the new moons, lest the Israelites, being too addicted to ancient customs, should sacrifice to the deities of the Gentiles, as it seemed to *Spencer* <note>John Spencer, a 17th-century theologian who argued that some Jewish rituals were adaptations of existing customs</note>: *On Ritual Laws* III, 4.

8. **To honor with incense.**] There was added in the margin of the *Leipzig & Meermann Codices*: "<margin>Incense <note>original: *libanotos*</note> is the spice produced from frankincense. Barley cakes <note>original: *psaista*</note> are meal-flour moistened with oil and wine from the grinding of the mill, which they burned for the gods; and *popana* are flat, thin, and circular cakes.</margin>"

# PORPHYRY

...and with round sacrificial cakes. <note>original: "ποπάνοις" / "placentis"</note> Every year I perform public sacrifices, omitting no solemn festival. In these very festivals, I worship the gods not by slaughtering oxen, nor by cutting up sacrificial victims, but by offering whatever happens to be at hand. I make it a point, however, to offer the firstfruits to the gods from all the seasonal fruits <note>original: "καρπῶν καὶ τῶν ὡραίων"</note> that are received from the earth; some of these I set before them, and others I consecrate by fire. <note>original: "καθαγιάζειν" / "adolere"</note> Because I am devoted to self-sufficiency, I have never even considered the sacrifice of oxen.

§ 17. It has been recorded by certain historians that when the tyrants, after defeating the Carthaginians, <note>A reference to the Battle of Himera (480 BCE) where Gelon of Syracuse defeated the Carthaginian forces.</note> [offered] a hecatomb... <note>A hecatomb is a grand sacrifice, literally of a hundred oxen.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>9. *And with sacrificial cakes.*] See the celebrated Rhunken’s notes on Timaeus’s Platonic Lexicon under *Popana*, where the reading matches the cited scholium, except that "pastries" <note>original: "πέμματα"</note> is used instead of "flat-cakes." Suidas and Photius also prefer this in their manuscript lexicons. Compare Suidas under *Anasatoi*, where the interpreter incorrectly says *popana* are also called *placentae* (cheesecakes), an error corrected by the elegant Toup in his *Emendations of Suidas*, p. 36. The word migrated into Latin; see Juvenal, Satire VI, 540: *"Osiris corrupted by a thin sacrificial cake."* Frankincense and the *popanon* cake are joined in Menander, below at section 17, where more is said.

10. *Of fruits and seasonal things.*] REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century philologist.</note> notes that *seasonal things* <note>original: "ὡραῖα"</note> also includes those things produced annually from animals at fixed times. However, *seasonal fruits* are properly all fruits coming from the earth which were used according to the season of the year—spring, summer, etc.—as they were born in their own hour <note>original: "ὥρᾳ"</note> or rather reached maturity. For the text speaks of mature fruits, not immature ones as the Learned Gentleman <note>original: "V. D." - Vir Doctus</note> suggested in his notes on Diogenes Laertius II, 32. This is certain from what Graevius and Wesseling have taught.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>11. *To consecrate.*] Perhaps it should read *kathagizein*: to burn to ashes, to consume by fire. REISKE. Felicianus also translated this as *adolere* (to burn/worship), and certainly *kathagizein* is frequently used for victims placed on the altar and consumed by fire. See Wesseling on Diodorus IV, 23. These words are very often confused with one another. For an example, see what the Learned Gentlemen observed on Pollux I, 26.

12. *Considered the sacrifice of oxen.*] REISKE notes that before "considered" <note>original: "προνοεῖσθαι"</note> the word "not" or "nothing" is missing. Unless you take "considered" in the sense of "taking precautions against" or "avoiding," as found in Henri Estienne’s Thesaurus.

1. *The tyrants.*] I believe Porphyry is referring to the history found in Diodorus Siculus, Book XI, and Herodotus, Book VII, concerning Gelon and his allies. VALENTINI. Diodorus (XI, 24) records Gelon’s affairs with the Carthaginians, but nothing there fits this specific passage. Herodotus (VII, 65) relates that Gelon reported a victory over the Carthaginians and sent money to Delphi.

2. *Having presented hecatombs.*] "To present" <note>original: "Παραστῆσαι"</note> is the proper technical term for sacrifices. We saw this in section 25...</margin>

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK II.

## R 2

...among themselves, and in a spirit of rivalry after they had conquered the Carthaginians, they had brought extraordinary hecatombs <note>A hecatomb is a massive sacrifice, traditionally of one hundred oxen.</note> to Apollo and asked which of them he delighted in most. The god, contrary to all their expectations, replied that the sacrificial cakes <note>original: "liba" / "ψαιστοῖς"</note> of Docimus were most acceptable to him. This Docimus was a man of Delphi <note>A citizen of Delphi, home of the famous Oracle of Apollo.</note> who cultivated a certain rugged plot of ground. Having come from his field into the city on that day, he had offered a few handfuls of meal from a small sack hanging [from his shoulder]. With these, he pleased the god more than those who had presented sacrifices with the most magnificent display. For this reason, one of the poets, because of the clarity of the matter, seems to have asserted such things, just as Antiphanes discusses in the play *The Woman of the Mysteries*:

> For the gods delight in the simplicity of inexpensive things.

3. *And this man was a Delphian.*] The citizens were called "Delphians" just as the city itself was. The ethnic name is the same as the city’s, as *Stephanus of Byzantium* writes. You will find examples in *Perizonius's notes on Aelian's Various History, VI, 9* and *Bossius's Critical Observations, chapter 2*. Here, just as he speaks of "those who farm rocky ground" <note>original: "γεωργῶν πετρίδια"</note>, so in *Isocrates's On the Peace, page 362*, "farming the rocks" occurs.
</margin>

<margin>
4. *He offered handfuls.*] You might perhaps prefer the reading "he offered sacrificial cakes." <note>A technical correction of the Greek verb from "ebulēsato" to "ethulēsato."</note> The word *thylēsthai* is rarer; it denotes offering *thylēmata* (sacrificial offerings). See *Casaubon's notes on Theophrastus's Characters, p. 231*. We have seen in section 6 what these *thylēmata* were among the ancients. More frequent is *thylēsashai*, concerning which see *Pollux, I, 27*, though the manuscripts vary there, and some have *thylēsashai*. In the *Bodleian* and *Meerman* manuscripts, it was incorrectly written as *ethulēsato*. What they called "handfuls" <note>original: "drakas"</note> is taught by the learned men in their notes on *Hesychius* under the entry *Drax*. Instead of "having pleased" <note>original: "τερψάς"</note>, which
</margin>

...hecatombs <note>original: "ἑκατόμβας"</note> with much rivalry against one another, and then asked which he was most pleased with, he answered, contrary to all their expectations, that he was most pleased with the sacrificial cakes <note>original: "ψαιστοῖς"</note> of Docimus. 3. This man was a Delphian, farming a harsh, rocky plot; and coming down from that place on that day, he **offered a few handfuls** <note>original: "δράκας ἐβυλήσατο"</note> 4. of barley-meal from the pouch hanging around him, pleasing the god more than those who performed magnificent sacrifices. 5. 6. *As by Antiphanes etc.*] We owe the translation of those verses of Antiphanes to the illustrious Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch humanist and jurist.</note> in excerpt 617. He reads the second and third lines as follows:

> As proof: for whenever some

> As proof: for whenever some

# PORPHYRY
<meta>catchword: IV</meta>

As evidence: for whenever some sacrifice hecatombs <note>A massive sacrifice of one hundred oxen.</note>, upon all these, last of all, even incense <note>original: "libanotos"</note> is placed.

> Just as many other things are consumed at the same time,
> Their expense being a vain thing for their sake.
> But this small thing itself is pleasing to the gods.

And Menander says in *The Bad-Tempered Man* <note>original: "Dyskolos," a famous play by the Greek comedian Menander.</note>:
> The incense is a pious thing, and the sacrificial cake <note>original: "popanon"</note>;
> This the god received when the whole was placed upon the fire.

<column-break/>

Submitting a proof of this matter, he says:
"For when someone has made a sacrifice from a herd of oxen,

After all things, the vapor of incense is added to the altars
Last: so that the vast abundance of the other things
May seem to offer nothing but the glory of the givers
And empty expense; whereas that which is brought in the final place,
May be seen to please the gods, even if it be very small."

Indeed, even Menander in *The Bad-Tempered Man*—that is the name of the play—speaks thus:
"From this, a pious offering of incense and libations,

Which, when cast into the flames, the god received in its entirety."

---

->§ 18.<-

<margin>From the meter of the poem it appears that either the ancients wrote *libanotos* <note>incense</note> with an 'o' [short vowel], or in poetry they used 'o' and 'a' interchangeably. The argument of the matter is this: when they have sacrificed hecatombs, incense is offered last of all and placed on the altar. REISKE. <note>Johann Jakob Reiske was a prominent 18th-century German classicist.</note></margin>
*As in Antiphanes, etc.*] There were various men of this name: here is signified the one whom most think was a Rhodian, concerning whom see *Fabricius, Bibliotheca Graeca* II, 22. *Athenaeus* also praises this comedy in Book X, 11 (where he shows it concerned the conversation of women, and there was no reason why Dalecampius should think we should read *Amystiden*) and Book 13. This *Mysis*, or *The Woman of the Mysteries* <note>original: "memuēmene," referring to a woman initiated into religious mysteries.</note>, seems to have taught a form of divine worship which was celebrated not with pomp and immense costs, but with a pure and holy mind. For it is credible that the Comic poet in this play wished to sting and scrub at the corrupt laws and ceremonies of sacred rites, as was well observed by the distinguished Tiberius Hemsterhuis <note>A famous Dutch philologist.</note> in his notes on *Pollux* X, 67, who did not forget this fragment. Now as for the verses themselves, what the opinion of Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, the famous legal scholar and humanist.</note> was, Valentin has stated; yet it is not for nothing that in that place, instead of "was placed" <note>original: "epetethē"</note>, one reads

<column-break/>

->§ 18.<-

"was sacrificed additionally" <note>original: "epethuthē"</note>. To "sacrifice additionally" <note>original: "epithuein"</note> would certainly be most fitting here. Compare what is said in § 59. In any case, it does not seem probable to me that all those words are by Antiphanes, which the Author [Porphyry] introduces until he reaches Menander. I am persuaded that most of them are taken from the poet, but not expressed in a continuous series. If my ear does not deceive my judgment, those words "as evidence" <note>original: "tekmērion de"</note> certainly seem to belong to the philosopher rather than the Comic poet. I will not be anxious about the meter for that reason; if you note that Grotius is not always consistent in these matters, I would like you to remember that this Great Man everywhere took greater care for the meaning than for the musical measure. Moreover, the word "the" <note>original: "ta"</note> before "such things" was missing in Meermann's manuscript, in which the code was added: "Sopater also says this in his *Excerpts of Histories*." And thus also the Leipzig manuscript, but there instead of "says," it is "brings forward."

7. *Menander in The Bad-Tempered Man, etc.*] In *Menander's Fragments*, page 52, it is read thus:
- - - - - - incense is a pious thing
And the sacrificial cake. This the god received when the whole
Was placed upon the fire.
And thus says Grotius in his *Excerpts*, page 719, and Athenaeus.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

§ 18. For this reason, indeed, they were accustomed to use vessels of earthenware, wood, and wickerwork, especially for public sacrifices, believing that the gods themselves took delight in such things. Whence even now, the most ancient vessels, which were made of clay or wood, are considered more divine both because of their material and because of the simplicity of their craftsmanship. For they say that when Aeschylus <note>The famous Greek tragedian (c. 525–456 BC).</note> was asked by his brothers to write a paean <note>original: "paeana" — a hymn of praise or triumph, specifically to Apollo.</note> to the god, he said that the best had already been composed by Tynnichus; therefore, if his own works were compared to the hymns of Tynnichus, they would be received in the same way as new statues are when compared to ancient ones. For the old ones, although they are fashioned in a simple manner, are held to be divine; whereas the new ones, however accurately—

<column-break/>

§ 18. Because of this, they also used <gloss>1</gloss> ceramic vessels, and those made of wood, and woven ones, and more so for the public sacred rites, being persuaded that the Divine rejoices in such things. Whence even the oldest ceramics and wooden items that exist are thought to be more divine because of the material and the plainness of the art. They say at least that Aeschylus, <gloss>2</gloss> when his brothers requested him <gloss>3</gloss> to write a paean to the god, said that the best <gloss>4</gloss> had been made by Tynnichus. And comparing his own to that man's, he said he would experience the same thing as new statues compared to the ancient; for these, although simply made, are considered divine; but the new—

---

<column-break/>

<note>The following section contains critical commentary by 18th-century scholars regarding the Greek text and historical references.</note>

IV, 11. Where see: the great Commentator. Regarding the integrity of the verses, the interpreters ought to be consulted. The Latin phrase *pious incense* <note>original: "tus pium"</note> is well-suited, as the celebrated *Burman* <note>Pieter Burman the Elder, a Dutch classicist.</note> contends with this type of expression in his notes on *Ovid's Fasti, Book I, line 672.* And just as in this place, so in *Aelian's Various History, XI, 5*, the sacrificial cake <note>original: "πόπανον" (popanon)</note> and frankincense <note>original: "λιβανωτός" (libanotos)</note> are joined, where *Perizonius* <note>Jacobus Perizonius, a Dutch scholar.</note> says more concerning these sacred rites.

1. Ceramic vessels.] Others are usually accustomed to suppress the noun through ellipsis <note>Omission of a word.</note>. *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> defines "kerameion" as a vessel. But the proper term is "keramion"; the word "vessel" is not added when spelled with the diphthong *ei*. Thus *Our Author* <note>Porphyry</note> immediately calls them "keramia." Certainly, it should have been read here as "kerameiois," but we have said elsewhere that *ei* and *i* are confused a hundred times in this sort of thing.

2. Of the brothers.] Read: "Of the Delphians" <note>original: "Τῶν Δελφῶν" (Ton Delphon)</note>. He was asked by the people of Delphi to celebrate their god Apollo, specifically the Delphic one, by composing a paean. REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a German physician and philologist.</note>. The same was seen by *Faber in his Letters, Book I, page 187*, nor does *Fabricius* seem to disagree in *Greek Bibliography, II, 6, 8.* If only the manuscripts would confirm it! Certainly, through the sluggishness of scribes, a "head" <note>The Greek letter 'alpha'</note> was often added to "Delphi," which they ought to lack, as in *Plutarch, Volume II, page 965 C*, and others cited by *Wesseling* in his notes on *Herodotus, V, 72.*

<column-break/>

3. To write a paean.] Correct, for a "paean" is properly a hymn to Apollo or Diana, although it may extend more broadly and be transferred to any kind of praise. See: *Wolf* in his notes on the *Letters of Libanius, 1333.*

4. Made by Tynnichus.] No one of this name has been found. We have therefore restored "Phrynichus," a tragedian contemporary with Aeschylus. VALENTI. Perhaps it was "made by Ibycus." But see Fabricius, *Greek Bibliography, Volume I, page 615*, who defends the common reading from Plato. REISKE. And so also *Menage* in his notes on *Diogenes Laertius, II, 42*, and rightly so. Indeed, a certain Phrynichus is praised by *Plato in Minos, page 569*, but he is another person. There were several of this name, as can be clear from *Fabricius* and the *Learned Men* on *Aelian, XI, 8*, but since we have the true author, it is not necessary to look around for others.

# P O R P H Y R Y

...new things, elaborately worked <note>original: "περιέργως εἰργασμένα" (periergōs eirgasmena) — referring to overly ornate or "fussy" craftsmanship.</note>, may be wondered at for their art, but possess less of the glory of god. And thus Hesiod <note>Ancient Greek poet, c. 700 BC, known for "Works and Days."</note> was right to say, when praising the law of ancient sacrifices:

> As the city performs its rites; the ancient law is best.

§ 19. Those who have written about sacred ceremonies and sacrifices command that precision regarding sacrificial cakes <term>popana: round, flat sacrificial cakes offered to the gods as a bloodless alternative to animal sacrifice</term> should be maintained, as this is more pleasing to the gods than the sacrifice performed through animals. And Sophocles <note>The Athenian tragedian (c. 497–406 BC).</note>, describing a sacrifice dear to the gods in his play *Polyidus*, says:

> For there was the fleece of a sheep, and there were the fruits of the vine.
> A libation and a grape-cluster well-stored;

<column-break/>

...though elaborately worked, they are admired for their craftsmanship, yet they carry in themselves a far smaller estimation of divinity. And for that reason Hesiod, rightly commending the law of ancient sacrifices, said:

> *For the people to perform a sacred rite, the ancient law is best.*

§ 19. But those who have written on the performance of sacred rites and sacrifices prescribe that diligence must be observed in libations <term>libamina: liquid offerings, often wine, honey, or oil, poured out to a deity</term>, since these are far more pleasing to the gods than the sacrifice which is offered from the slaughter of animals. Likewise, Sophocles, setting forth a sacrifice pleasing to the gods in his *Polyidus*, speaks thus:

> *For a sheep's fleece was offered, there was the vine's*
> *Libation, and grapes and well-preserved juice:*

---

5. **Elaborately worked.**] You will easily understand what kind of things these were if you consider the force and power of the word *periergazesthai*. It is, in fact, to *elaborate* something with care. Hence it is commonly said of extreme and immoderate zeal spent on some matter, from which *periergon* began to denote whatever involves excessive and superfluous labor. Let students <note>original: "tirones" — literally "recruits" or beginners in study.</note> consult Perizonius on Aelian's *Miscellaneous History* II, 44; and the prefix *peri* is usually used this way in other compounds.

6. **Hesiod.**] See *Hesiod: Fragments*, verse 169. But there these lines are poorly praised, as if they were sought from the *Cave of the Nymphs* <note>A reference to Porphyry's other famous work, "On the Cave of the Nymphs."</note>. A little later, because of the phrase *dia tēn*, the words were transposed in the older editions of Lipsius, the Codex, and Meerman.

1. **Sophocles describing.**] The verses of Sophocles cited there were interpreted by the same Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch scholar and jurist.</note>. VALENT.

2. **For there was, etc.**] You may find these lines taken from Sophocles also among others, but in a different way. And first, I have reshaped the verse thus: *and there were the vines*, whereas previously it was read *and of the vines*. Both the logic of the meter and the authority of Clement of Alexandria <note>A Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who often quoted Greek poets.</note> in *Miscellanies* Book IV, page 476, and Grotius in *Excerpts* page 139, who expressed it this way, encouraged this change. These things ought to be explained by the use of wool in the sacrifices of the ancients, just as *wool and fleece* are often joined together. See Hemsterhuis <note>Tiberius Hemsterhuis (1685–1766), a Dutch philologist.</note> on line 1055 of the comic poet [Aristophanes'] *Plutus*, very skillfully restoring *fleece* <note>original: "μαλλοῦ" (mallou)</note> for *branch* <note>original: "θαλλοῦ" (thallou)</note>, and surrounding Porphyry with excellent light. Compare also Castellanus, *On Greek Festivals* regarding the *Eiresione* <note>An olive branch wound with wool and hung with fruits, used in festivals.</note>, and how Spencer in *On the Hebrew Ritual Laws* II, 15, uses these things for his own purpose, though by his own judgment.

3. **And there were the vines.**] Perhaps *it was from the vines*. Soon *olais*, that is *oulaies*, for the ancients used the letters *o* and *ō* and *ou* interchangeably; and *oulai* are the same as *barley grains*: grains of barley not yet crushed by the millstone. REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and philologist.</note>.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->**Table of Ancient Offerings**<-

| | |
|---|---|
| *A mixture of all kinds of fruits was there:* | 4 There was a mixture of all fruits together, |
| *And the rich liquid of the olive, and most skillfully* | The oil of the olive and the most varied |
| *The wax-molded honeycomb, the work of the tawny bee.* | 5 Wax-molded instrument of the tawny bee. |

Venerable monuments of the ancients were in Delos <note>A sacred island in the Aegean, legendary birthplace of Apollo and Artemis.</note>, brought by the Hyperborean <note>A mythical people from the far north who were said to live in a land of perpetual sunshine and piety.</note> sheaf-bearers. It is necessary, therefore, that we approach the gods with purified character to perform sacrifices.

6 There were sacred 7 memorials of the men of old in Delos, from the Hyperborean sheaf-bearers. 8 It is necessary, then, for those who are purified in character to go to sacrifice, to those...

---

4. *There was a mixture of all fruits* etc.] This is poorly rendered in the edition of **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and scholar.</note> as: 
*In which a mixture of all fruits was among the scales.*
The version by **Clement of Alexandria** <note>A Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who often quoted Greek literature.</note> is better, although the order is slightly disturbed: *There was a mixture of all fruits together.* This might seem more "poetic." Perhaps the term <term>pagkarpia: an offering of all types of seasonal fruits</term> displeased the scribe, who was unaware that many words of this kind can be expressed in two ways. The lexicographers teach us what the <term>oulai: sacrificial barley-groats mixed with salt</term> were. It amounts to the same thing whether you write it this way or as "whole" (*holai*). Neglecting this observation led a learned scholar to blame **Lucian** <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist of the 2nd century AD.</note>, from which charge **D’Orville** <note>Jacques Philippe d'Orville (1696–1751), a Dutch classicist.</note> clears him. In this later passage, the meter requires the specific form.

5. *the tawny bee* etc.] In **Clement**, "of oil" is published instead of "of the olive," and "yellow" (*xanthēs*) instead of "tawny" (*ksouthēs*). But poets prefer the latter, as seen in a fragment of **Antiphanes** in **Athenaeus** and below in section 21. In the **Scholia on Euripides**, which praises this little verse, it is read as "of the tawny bee," and **Valckenaer** <note>Lodewijk Caspar Valckenaer (1715–1785), a Dutch philologist.</note> thought this originated from **Sophocles**, and not without reason. He elegantly calls honey the "instrument of the bee," using "instrument" in place of "work." Poets everywhere call honey the "works of the bees." Note also the use of honey in sacred rites, which they believed was most pleasing to the gods. See **Wesseling** on **Diodorus Siculus**. This was different from what pleased the Hebrew lawgiver <note>Moses; Leviticus 2:11 forbids the use of honey in offerings made by fire to the Lord.</note>, but that does not pertain to this passage.

6. *There were sacred [memorials] of those* etc.] In the most ancient times, it was customary for the sacred objects of the Hyperboreans—sheaves of grain—to be sent to the island of Delos with solemn pomp and dance. <term>Amallai</term> signifies sheaves of grain, and we read that the Athenians performed sacrifices to **Amallophoros** 

<column-break/>

**Ceres** <note>The Roman name for Demeter, the goddess of agriculture and grain.</note>. Specifically, however, these are understood to be sheaves of barley, the first-fruits of the barley. For what our author calls "sheaf-bearers," **Servius** <note>A 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Virgil.</note> calls "groat-bearers" (*oulophorous*). But you may read quite different accounts of these things, depending on whether the authors drew from the ambitious stories of the Athenians or from elsewhere. Distinguished men, whom I see cited by the interpreters of **Herodotus**, have spared me further effort on this matter. However, since Delos was previously devastated and perhaps recovered some splendor under **Hadrian** <note>Roman Emperor (reigned 117–138 AD) known for his love of Greek culture.</note>, it could be doubted whether that rite had already fallen into disuse by **Porphyry’s** time or not. You might conclude the former from this passage, and yet below in section 28, he speaks of those rites as if they were still celebrated in his own time. Hence, it may be probable that while the other Delian monuments were in poor condition, the altar mentioned there had not been violated. See the arguments of the learned scholar in the *Miscellaneous Observations*. Certainly, I do not know from where it can be proven that the Emperor Hadrian granted the Athenians the right to administer those sacred rites according to the ancient ritual. **Plutarch** says that in ancient times those rites were sent to Delos with the use of flutes, pipes, and lyres. Therefore, when **Aelian**, who is later than him, speaks of this matter as something still observed in his time, it should be understood as referring to the preceding century.

7. *Of the men of old.*] Supply "customs" or "laws," unless you prefer to add them. <term>REISK.</term> <note>Note by Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and philologist.</note>

8. *It is necessary then* etc.] Perhaps it should be "It was necessary" (*edei*). This corresponds to "but now" (*nyn de*) which follows. And soon...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the nature of true piety and sacrifice, specifically contrasting external cleanliness with internal purity of the soul. The text is presented in parallel Greek and Latin columns, which I have unified into a single English translation for readability.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

...offering these sacrifices as dear to the gods, rather than those that are merely expensive. But as it stands, people believe that if they are clothed in a splendid garment over a body that is not <gloss>9</gloss> clean, it is not sufficient for the purity required of sacrifices. Yet, when some have <gloss>10</gloss> brightened their bodies along with their clothing, while possessing a soul that is not clean of evils, they go toward the sacrifices and believe it makes no difference. This is as if God does not rejoice most in the most divine element within us when it is in a pure state, seeing as it is of a nature akin to His own. At least in Epidaurus <note>A major religious center in ancient Greece, famous for the sanctuary of Asclepius</note>, this inscription was posted <gloss>11</gloss> for those entering within the fragrant temple:

->One must be pure who enters the fragrant temple;<-
->And purity is to think holy thoughts.<-

->§ 20.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>The word "most slender" <note>original: λετάτας</note> is treated as a single word by Reiske. Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a Church Father</note> took these passages from our author in Book IX *Against Julian*, page 310, where he gave the phrase "sacrifices dear to God." Regarding the matter itself, see § 15. Just as Porphyry does, Clement of Alexandria says in *Stromata* VII, page 719: "It is necessary, therefore, to offer sacrifices to God that are not expensive, but dear to God."</margin>

<margin>9. **Clothed in a clean [garment].** Valentinus had given "clothed in a clean [thing]" <note>original: καθαρὸν</note>. But the earlier editions and the Lipsius and Meermann manuscripts have "clothed in a clean [garment]" <note>original: καθαρὰν, feminine to match 'veste'</note>. In Cyril it is "having been clothed." This is a slight matter, but it makes a great difference whether you read "clean" in the feminine or masculine. The older editions and the Meermann manuscript gave the former, except that the scribe wrote "lyre" <note>original: κιθάραν</note> by a slip of the pen. The translator of Cyril does not differ: "now if we have been clothed in a splendid garment, *not a clean one*." Certainly, a "splendid" garment and a "clean" one differ, just as "white" and "clean" are distinguished below in § 45. The Pythagoreans used clothing that was "white and clean." See Iamblichus in *Life of Pythagoras*, chapter 21. The former refers to the color and external brilliance, the latter to the material,</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>or if it were polluted by any other thing that did not suit the sacred rites. The Latins call the former "white," "bright," etc., and the latter "pure" or "chaste." Both are used in sacred rites. See Broukhusius on Tibullus I, II, 27. The words that follow prove that "clean" <note>original: καθαρὰν</note> is the true reading here.</margin>

<margin>10. **Having brightened, not...** Cyril has "Being brightened, or clean," where one should rewrite "not clean," and then "being disposed" instead of "of those being disposed." Also, "was inscribed" <note>original: προσεγέγραπτο</note> is wrongly placed there for "was posted" <note>original: προεγέγραπτο</note>; for those words differ. Note also the construction "clean of evils." The Greeks are accustomed to use that mode so that the thing signified by that case is excepted and excluded. We have the phrase "a place clean of evils" in Plato's *Theaetetus*, page 129, from which Plotinus took it in *Enneads* VI. 9, page 768, and Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel*, page 606. Read other things of this kind in R. W. on Hierocles' *Golden Verses*, page 252. A little after, "just as not even to the divine." Meermann manuscript.</margin>

§ 20. But that God is delighted not by the abundance and magnitude of sacrifices, but by a pious frugality <note>The Latin 'tenuitate' and Greek 'tychonti' both imply a sense of "slender" or "ordinary" offerings versus "bulky" ones</note>, can be clear from this very fact: that from our daily food, whatever happens to be served, we are all accustomed to offer a first portion to the gods before we taste anything.
