We think that instead of "we say" <note>original: ἐμφάμεν (emphamen)</note>, "to enter" <note>original: ἐμβάμεν (embamen)</note> should be read. "Purity" etc. were separated from the rest. Unjustly indeed, in my opinion. Therefore, I have restored it to its place. VALENTINUS. Since many have recorded the inscription, we can restore the true writing with greater certainty. As we present it, so also does Clement of Alexandria: *Stromata* Book V, page 551, although the meter was not preserved there; and Cyril: Book IX, page 310, *Against Julian*, where instead of "of the temple" <note>original: ναοῖο (naoio)</note>, which has occupied all editions of Porphyry, you should restore "of the temple" <note>original: νηοῖο (neoio)</note>. For that, and "purity" <note>original: ἁγνείη (agneie)</note> (for previously it was read as <note>original: ἁγνεία (agneia)</note>), belongs to the dialect. In the Leipzig manuscript it was "things being said, purity" <note>original: ἐμφάμενα ἁγνεία</note>. In the Bodleian and Meermann manuscripts it was "things being said" <note>original: ἐμφάμεναι</note>. This almost agrees with that old "we say" <note>original: ἔμφαμεν</note> that was read before. Learned men have illustrated this matter in notes to Clement and Aelian: *Various History* II, 31, and many others.

1. **It is clear from etc.** This "from" <note>original: τοῦ</note> is suited to the infinitive "to begin" <note>original: ἄρχεσθαι</note>, or rather, as I think it should be read, "to be content" <note>original: ἀρκεῖσθαι</note>. I would also prefer "clear" <note>original: δῆλον</note>, for "to be content" would better suit the verb "it makes clear" <note>original: δηλοῖ</note>, but "from the" <note>original: ἐκ τοῦ</note> responds more aptly to the word "clear." I will therefore arrange the passage thus: "It is clear from the fact that he is entirely content with the daily food, of whatever kind is set before him, even before the enjoyments (or before this and the enjoyments)." (That is, the thing offered to God each time is small.) This is established by the fact that whatever kind of daily food is proposed or offered to him (God), he is certainly more content with it than even with delicacies that are set aside. Let it be so; let the thing that is repeatedly served be small. But. — REISKE. In place of "of this" <note>original: ταύτης</note> in the older Leipzig and 

<column-break/>

Meermann editions (which have "before the" <note>original: προτῶν</note> instead of "before the" <note>original: πρὸ τῶν</note>), the Manuscript had "these" <note>original: ταύτας</note> and instead of "the daily" <note>original: τῆς καθ’</note> it had "those daily" <note>original: τοὺς καθ’</note> which Fogerolles supplemented in the margin as "touching." And here both he and Valentinus replaced "to begin" <note>original: ἄρχεσθαι</note> with "to offer first-fruits" <note>original: ἀπάρχεσθαι</note>. But "to begin" is often said instead of "to offer first-fruits." Moreover, "it makes clear" <note>original: Δηλοῖ</note> refers to God. The phrase "the fact that from" <note>original: τὸ ἐκ τοῦ</note> pleased the celebrated Abresch. It is a known custom, derived even from the heroic ages, that before the guests filled themselves with food, they would offer first-fruits to the Gods.

2. **Theophrastus.** Does this refer to Theophrastus’s books *On History* or *Historical Memoirs* of which Diogenes Laërtius speaks (V, 47) and others? I would prefer the books *On Piety*, the same ones mentioned above in § 5 and 11 and below in 26; in all of those, he speaks of sacrifices. Fabricius (*Bibliotheca Graeca* III, 9, 16) thinks the *History of Divine Matters* is meant, but I will show from Photius's Lexicon under the word "Mito" that those things which follow shortly after at the beginning of § 21 are sought from the monuments I mentioned.

3. **Ancestral customs of various peoples.** It is common for the word "customs" <note>original: ἔθη (ethe)</note> to be suppressed in this formula of speaking. The Bodleian manuscript gives "ancestral" <note>original: πατρῴων (patroon)</note>, as those words are usually confused since they mean almost the same thing. Certainly, authors much more rich than the grammarians often ignore the grammarians' rules about the distinction between them, saying both "ancestral laws" <note>original: πατρῴους νόμους</note> and "ancestral laws" <note>original: πατρίους νόμους</note>. However, Porphyry also uses "ancestral" <note>original: πατρίους</note> below in IV, 22; and they certainly tend to call the manners and institutions of the ancestors "the ancestral" <note>original: τὸ πάτριον</note> rather than "the hereditary" <note>original: πατρῷον</note>. See the learned notes on Thucydides VIII, 76.

4. **That the ancient.** The word "the" <note>original: τὸ</note> is not in the Leipzig Manuscript.

# On Abstinence, Book II

...which are indeed, in truth, like certain copies of the Corybantic rites from Crete: but these things are also confirmed by Empedocles <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher who famously argued against animal sacrifice</note>: who, when speaking of sacrifices and the nature of the gods, sings thus:

> For among them there was no god Mars <note>original: "Mars" (Ares), the god of war</note>, nor any tumult of battle,

<column-break/>

...of the [pillars], which are truly like copies of the Corybantic rites from Crete; but also from Empedocles, who, in explaining matters concerning sacrifices and the genealogy of the gods, indicates this by saying:

> Nor was there any god Ares among them, nor the din of war,

---

<margin>
Strabo says the city was founded by Corybas (Book X, p. 325), but it is clear that the word *kyrbeis* <note>triangular wooden tablets for laws</note> came to our author's pen from Theophrastus, as cited in Photius's unpublished Lexicon: "*kyrbeis* are triangular axles or... it is said to be named from being peaked (*kekoryphōsthai*) at the top... but Theophrastus says they are named after the Cretan Corybantes. For they are, as it were, copies of the Corybantic rites." This passage is of great value to us, because it teaches that these are also the words of Theophrastus, from whom Porphyry draws much both just before and in the preceding sections. These were taken from Theophrastus's book *On Piety*, as the most learned David Ruhnken—a distinguished man—kindly pointed out to me in correspondence. I learned this from the Scholiast on Aristophanes' *Birds* (line 1354): "*Kyrbeis* are named from the Corybantes, for they were their invention, as Theophrastus says in *On Piety*." Do not say that I act in bad faith by writing "Theophrastus" in the Scholiast, when in all editions "Theopompus" is read. It is clear enough from my arguments that there is no place for Theopompus here. Therefore, the book *On Piety* should be deleted from the catalog of the works of the historian Theopompus, where Meursius, Vossius, and others—deceived by a corrupt reading—placed it. Thus far the celebrated Ruhnken. To the same scholar, it seemed that the word "pillars" (*stēlōn*) should be ejected from the text, as it had crept in from a gloss <note>a marginal explanation that accidentally entered the main text</note>. If the decision were mine, I would rewrite it: "by the [sacrifices] from the *kyrbeis* and pillars." Plato joins them thus in the *Statesman* (p. 555 B): "writing on *kyrbeis* and pillars." Eusebius in *Life of Constantine* (I, 1): "others engraving lines on *kyrbeis* and deep pillars." The illustrious Abresch, who held the same opinion as I, added from Themistius (Oration 30): "how it is necessary to perform sacrifices, those from the *kyrbeis* and the pillars, according to the writings." For so Taylor established it in his work on the *Cyrbe*.
</margin>

From Pollux, Suidas, and a hundred others, all these things are widely known: among later writers especially, all monuments testifying to the memory of some matter are called thus. See Hemsterhuis on Pollux (VIII, 128). Furthermore, in the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts, it was written: "*kyrbeis*: triangular tablets in which the laws concerning sacred and civil matters were kept; *axones* were square ones, in which private laws were kept." In the margin of the Bodleian manuscript, it was corrected to "on the *kyrbeis*." Regarding the most ancient custom of handing down famous discoveries, laws, and other things to posterity on columns, stones, walls, and bronze tablets, nothing need be said here. However, let the student note that by *stēlas* <note>pillars</note> one should not understand columns properly so-called, but stones which were mostly square, artistically polished and smoothed. Their use spread from the Egyptians to other nations, on which matter see Jablonski in *Egyptian Pantheon* (V, 5).

2. **The ones from Crete, etc.**] Who the Corybantes <note>armed, rhythmic dancers who worshipped the goddess Cybele</note> were has been excellently investigated and demonstrated by learned men; see Wesseling on Diodorus (III, 55). *Antigrapha* are copies. Attic writers love the plural number even when speaking of a single copy. On this matter, see Thomas Magister and other grammarians. See Wolf on Libanius (Epistle 1044). However, more recent writers do not always reject the singular number. Plutarch in *Life of Alexander* (Vol. I, p. 668 B): "he writes a letter of which there is a copy (*antigraphon*)." But see the learned men on Moeris the Atticist (p. 7). As our author uses it, "copies of a pillar" in Demosthenes (*Against Leptines*, p. 378). Instead of the word "the" (*ta*), the learned Ruhnken preferred "certain" (*hatta* or *tina*).

3. **Nor was there any, etc.**] These seven continuous verses of Empedocles are also cited by Athenaeus in the *Deipnosophistae* (Book XII), near the beginning of the book, where he discourses on pleasure. In his version, these are varied, because the third verse is halved, thus:

### On Abstinence, Book II.
S 3

...considering. After Mars <note>The god of war; original: "Mars"</note> and tumult, and all battles, and the occasion of wars invaded: then for the first time it happened that no one abstained from the slaughter of their own kind. Indeed, these things must be considered in this manner. For just as we believe that, although there is a kinship between us and other men, those evildoers who—driven by a certain impulse of their own nature and depravity—are led to inflict harm on anyone, should all be killed and punished: so among the animals lacking reason it is perhaps appropriate to kill those which are unjust by their own nature and malicious, and incited to harm and attack the human race. However, to kill the others, which are endowed with no such cruelty or inclination to harm, is undoubtedly unjust, no differently than it is to kill humans who are not injurious. This very fact suggests that we have no right over the rest of the animals—

<column-break/>

—the rest of the animals. <gloss>1</gloss> But when Ares <note>The Greek god of war; original: "ἄρης"</note>, and tumult, and every battle, and the beginning of wars took hold, then first <gloss>2</gloss> no one truly spared any of their kin. And these things must still be considered. <gloss>3</gloss> For just as there is a kinship between us and other men, those who do evil—and as if carried by some <gloss>4</gloss> breath of their own nature and wickedness toward harming those they meet—we think it necessary to destroy and punish them all; so also of the irrational animals, those unjust in nature and evildoers, driven by nature to harm those who approach them, it is perhaps fitting to destroy. But to kill and murder the rest of the animals that do no wrong, nor are driven by nature to harm, is surely unjust, just as it is with such men. This also seems to indicate that there is no justice between us and the rest of the animals, because—

---

<column-break/>

<gloss>1. But when Ares.]</gloss> *Leipzig Manuscript:* Strife <note>original: "ἔρις" (Eris)</note>. Did he intend Mars <note>Ares</note> or Strife? A little later, instead of "beginning" <note>original: "ἀρχὴ"</note> perhaps it should be "disturbance" <note>original: "ταραχὴ"</note>. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist</note>.

<gloss>2. No one truly [spared] any.]</gloss> The illustrious *Abresch* preferred: "no one, as if there were nothing [of kinship] existing, spared their kin." And indeed, "existing" <note>original: "ὄντος"</note> is also in the <term>Meerman manuscript</term>.

<gloss>3. For just as there is a kinship etc.]</gloss> The Author often speaks in these books about this natural instinct by which we kill harmful things; and *Grotius*, who did not leave these Porphyrian passages untouched, discusses this in *On the Law of War and Peace, II. 20. 9.* Pythagoras himself says in *Ovid*:

> - - - - - - *and we admit that bodies*
> *seeking our destruction are sent to their death*
> *without violating our piety.*
<note>Original Latin: "nostrumque petentia letum / Corpora missa neci salva pietate fatemur."</note>

This passage did not escape the diligence of <term>Grotius</term>.

So below in III, 26: "and they are carried along... by some breath of their own nature and wickedness." To be said to be "carried along" <note>original: "φέρεσθαι"</note> is a metaphor for those who are driven and moved by their passions. A little later, the <term>Meerman manuscript</term> has "the things doing no wrong" with the "but" <note>original: "δὲ"</note> omitted.

...because <margin>5</margin> some of these are harmful and injurious by nature, while others are not, just as is the case among human beings.

§ 23. Should we then sacrifice to the gods those animals that deserve to be slaughtered? And how could that be right, if they are evil by nature? For it is no more fitting to offer such things than to offer those that are mutilated <note>original: ἀνάπηρα (anapēra) - referring to animals with physical defects which were traditionally forbidden in sacrifice</note>. <margin>1</margin> Indeed, by doing so, we would be making an offering of evils <margin>2</margin> rather than performing sacrifices for the sake of honor. But if animals must be sacrificed to the gods, then we should sacrifice those that do us no harm. <margin>3</margin> Yet we have already agreed that we must not kill any of the other animals that do us no harm; therefore, we must not sacrifice them to the gods either. If, then, neither these nor the harmful ones should be immolated, is it not clear that above all else we must abstain from animals, and that none of the other animals should be sacrificed—

<column-break/>

...it by no means seems to signify in the case of animals, because some of them are noxious and harmful, others not at all, just as is also the case among men.

§ 23. Therefore, should those things which ought to be killed be sacrificed to the gods? But in what way is that lawful, since they are of a depraved nature? For it is no more fitting to offer them than those which are lame and damaged. For we would be making first-fruits of evils, not sacrifices for the sake of honor; but if animals are to be slaughtered for the gods, those that do no harm should be slaughtered. But it is well-established that those doing no harm are not to be killed: therefore they are not to be sacrificed to the gods. But if neither these nor the harmful ones ought to be immolated, is it not evident that one must abstain from animals most of all, and that sacrifice should not be made from them, even...

---

<margin>5. Some of these are harmful.]</margin> Perhaps "some certain harmful things" <note>original: βλαβερὰ ἔνι’ ἄττα</note>. And then "towards those that are not such." Namely, that there is some justice for us. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a famous German physician and philologist known for his commentaries on Greek texts.</note>. In the following section, "certain other things." The Grammarians have much to say about this little word, distinguishing between *atta* meaning "whichever" and *atta* meaning "certain ones." See <term>Duker</term> on <term>Thucydides</term> II, 100 and <term>Alberti</term> on <term>Hesychius</term> under the letter V.

<margin>1. In this way, or the mutilated.]</margin> Just as God formerly removed such things from the altars, so did the Greeks and others, among whom the overseers of sacred rites diligently examined whether the victims were "disapproved or maimed" <note>original: ἀδόκιμα καὶ πηρὰ</note>. Often, however, by some mystical reasoning of the rites, they would immolate victims mutilated in some part. The Spartans also did this, but for another reason, concerning which see <term>Wesseling</term> on <term>Petit's</term> *Attic Laws*, Book I, page 74. Instead of "in this way" <note>original: οὕτω</note>, <term>Reiske</term> preferred "these" or "them."

<column-break/>

<margin>2. First-fruits of evils in this way.]</margin> The word "in this way" <note>original: οὕτως</note> is "being" <note>original: ὄντων</note> in the <term>Leipzig Manuscript</term>. The meaning is not sufficiently clear, nor does the passage seem intact; you might repair and explain it thus: "making a first-fruit of things that are evil, out of contempt for the gods, let us not perform sacrifices for the sake of honor." <term>REISKE.</term>

<margin>3. But it must not be killed ---]</margin> "The things that [do] nothing." There is a fault in the word "having agreed" <note>original: ὡμολογηκότες</note>, or something is missing after "animals." For example: "how shall we say this?" <term>REISKE.</term> The structure is rather intricate due to the use of *hyperbaton* <note>a rhetorical figure where the natural word order is disrupted</note>, which our author is too fond of. If you construe it as "having agreed that we must not kill those doing us no harm... nor sacrifice," then the word "so that" <note>original: ὥστε</note> is redundant or implies a consequence. If you use "so that," then the word "but" <note>original: δὲ</note> is vacant. Furthermore, for the word "if" <note>original: εἰ</note>, the <term>Florentine</term> edition had "who" <note>original: οἳ</note>, which <term>Fogerolles</term> had also corrected, but whose dullness failed to see it was a typesetter's error.

4. *Yet it is proper ---*] Read *ge* <note>a Greek particle emphasizing the previous word</note> instead of *te*. The word *me* <note>"not"</note> was wrongly inserted by the translator. *Meanwhile, however, it is fitting to kill some of the animals.* <term>REISKE.</term> The illustrious <term>Abresch</term> also preferred *ge*. Regarding this particle, which is often abundant in the middle of a sentence or takes on the force of "and" and is confused with *ge*, read <term>D’Orville</term> in his notes on *Chariton*, Book IV, chapter 4, page 419. The earlier editions also did not recognize the "not," and so it has been deservedly sent into exile. <term>Valentini</term> wanted "not" to be read after the word *atta* <note>"some"</note>.

1. *Three reasons for which one must sacrifice...*] <term>Iamblichus</term>, *On the Mysteries*, Book V, chapter 5: <note>original: ἐγὼ δέ σοι λέγω... "But I tell you my own doctrine concerning sacrifices, that they should never be performed for the sake of honor alone, just as we honor benefactors; nor for the sake of acknowledging favors for the good things the gods have given us; nor for the sake of first-fruits or the repayment of certain gifts."</note> He says these reasons are common and derived from ordinary human custom. You see, therefore, by what right the Illustrious Man <note>likely referring to a previous editor or critic</note> writes that these views of <term>Iamblichus</term> are refuted by our Author <note>Porphyry</note> in this place. Rather, Porphyry confirms them, but argues that it does not follow from them that living creatures must be slaughtered.

2. *Having previously received a benefit.*] The verb *Paschein* <note>"to be affected" or "to suffer"</note> is of a neutral middle sense. It is said either simply for *to be affected*, or for *to suffer something evil*, but with the addition of the particles *well* or *badly*, etc., it is reduced to a specific meaning. Often

<column-break/>

our Author <note>Porphyry</note> uses it this way, but never simply to mean "to be affected by good." Nor is it usually spoken of so by others; and if ever it seems to be said, it is understood from the context in what sense it should be taken, as in <term>Dionysius of Halicarnassus</term>, Book VII, page 456. In that place, the Learned Man <note>V.D. - Vir Doctus</note> uses it to prove the opposite, even though "to suffer something" is frequent in <term>Dionysius</term> for "to be affected by a thing." It is no different in <term>Josephus</term>, *Antiquities*, Book III, chapter 13. I shall therefore expect more certain things from the interpreters of <term>Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians</term>, chapter III, verse 4, to establish that usage.

3. *Or in order that we might obtain etc.*] The words *or in order that we might obtain* seem like they should be deleted. For their force is already present in the preceding words *seeking the preparation of good things*. Soon after, one or the other instance of the word *the* <note>the Greek article "tēn"</note>—but preferably the second one—seems like it should be deleted. <term>REISKE.</term>

4. *Thus even of the animals etc.*] In <term>Eusebius</term>, in the fourth book of his work on the same subject <note>The *Preparation for the Gospel*</note>, where this entire passage is cited, the word *of these* is missing from these words. However, the written manuscript retains it. Below, where the text here says *we shall acknowledge that we act unjustly*, it is written there as *to act unjustly*. In the following *must not be sacrificed*, the negative particle is added in the third word from this, *repaying*. In the second to last, *certain* is indeed read, and the number is varied in that word in the edition of <term>Eusebius</term>. Mixed with <term>Porphyry</term>, it makes sense. <meta>This page continues Porphyry’s systematic dismantling of the justifications for animal sacrifice. Following the previous page's introduction of the three reasons for sacrifice (honor, gratitude, and need), he now argues that killing innocent animals fails the first two categories.</meta>

-> ### PORPHYRY ### <-

<column-break/>

If animals 5 are to be offered to the gods as first-fruits, they must be sacrificed for one of these reasons. For whatever we sacrifice, we do so for one of these specific reasons. [6] Would our god then think he was receiving honor from us when we clearly act unjustly right from the very start of the offering? Or would he not rather think such an act—offering a first-fruit—is a dishonor? [7] For in the very act of sacrificing, by killing animals that have done no wrong, we admit we are acting unjustly. Therefore, none of the other animals should be sacrificed for the sake of honor. [8] Nor indeed should they be sacrificed to return thanks for benefits received. [9] For he who wishes to give a just return for a benefit and an equivalent for a kindness ought not to provide these by doing harm to others.

<column-break/>

If animals are to be offered to the gods, they must be sacrificed for a reason of this kind: since we are accustomed to perform sacrifices to the gods for one of these purposes. Would God then consider himself to have obtained honor from us if we appear to behave unjustly from the very moment of the offering? Or will he not rather think that he is being treated with indignity by such a sacrifice? But if, in sacrificing, we slaughter animals that cause no offense, it is admitted that we act unjustly. Therefore, for the sake of honor, none of the other animals should be sacrificed to the gods. Nor should they be sacrificed to return thanks for benefits. For he who wishes to return worthy thanks for a benefit and kindness ought not to return them through the injury of another. For in no way—

---

<margin>
The phrase <note>original: "doxei e"</note> "it will seem that..." appears in the first part, but the following <note>original: "oude charin tinos"</note> "nor for the sake of..." is faulty, as is evident. **VICTORIUS.** <note>Pietro Vettori, a 16th-century Italian philologist.</note> This material up to the end of section 24 was harvested by Eusebius into his own fields in Book IV, page 151 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*.
</margin>

5. **Offered as first-fruits to the gods.**] This should be punctuated as "offered; these to the gods." <term>REISKE.</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske was a 18th-century German scholar famous for his work on Greek texts.</note>

<margin>
6. **Our God.**] The Leipzig manuscript gives "the goddess" <note>original: "he theos"</note>. That is incorrect, yet it suggests that Porphyry might have written "either a God or a good man." **REISKE.** Eusebius has "whether any of us, or a god," but Vigerus has already noted that it is more correct to delete "any" <note>original: "tis"</note> and "us" <note>original: "he"</note> in our text. For "we appear" <note>original: "phainometha"</note>, the Meerman manuscript repeats "we appear."
</margin>

7. **In the act of sacrificing.**] I have inserted the word "in" <note>original: "en"</note>. The Eusebius manuscript confirms this. Later, I substituted "to return" <note>original: "apodidonai"</note> instead of "they return" <note>original: "apodidontai"</note>. Eusebius has "those returning." **VALENTINUS.** <note>Presumably the editor or a previous commentator.</note> Perhaps the sense is: "Therefore, by such a first-fruit, do we not act unjustly?" Or do you deny that an injury is committed by offering such first-fruits? In the act of sacrificing, when we offer things slaughtered by us that do not harm us, we ourselves voluntarily confess that we are inflicting an injury upon them. **REISKE.** Eusebius does not have the phrase "through the first-fruits." Valentinus had substituted "if" <note>original: "ei"</note> in the text after "in," but the old editions and Eusebius have "in the act of sacrificing," as does the Meerman manuscript. Therefore, read "in the act of sacrificing" or "in the [specific] act of sacrificing," which was preferred by Abresch. <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch, a Dutch philologist.</note>

<margin>
8. **Nor indeed... returning.**] "Returning" <note>original: "apodidontas"</note> is the correct reading, as the common phrase "we must sacrifice them to the gods" is understood. **REISKE.** Eusebius reads the same. Previously it read "they return" <note>original: "apodidontai"</note>, which Fogerolles and Valentinus had corrected to the infinitive "to return." The former also wanted to change "of the" <note>plural</note> to "of the" <note>singular</note>, but incorrectly.
</margin>

9. **Return... return.**] We discussed what "to give a return" <note>original: "amoiben apodidonai"</note> properly means in section 12; that passage should be compared with this one. There is also a discussion there on the word "kindness" <note>original: "eupoia"</note>. Just now, I restored "it will seem" <note>original: "doxei"</note> in place of "to be about to seem" <note>original: "doxein"</note>, which was previously read and is also in the Leipzig manuscript.

<summary>Porphyry argues that animal sacrifice is fundamentally unjust and therefore cannot serve as a valid way to honor the gods or express gratitude. He contends that killing harmless creatures to thank a deity is a contradiction, as true gratitude should not involve harming others.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument against animal sacrifice from Book II of Porphyry's "On Abstinence." The previous page likely established that sacrifices are intended to show gratitude or seek favor, which the author now refutes.</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->**Column 1**<-

...he will appear to act with no more grace than a man who, having stolen something from another, wishes to honor a third party with the loot. <note>original: "furatus, eo honeſtare alium uelit"</note> Likewise, it is not fitting to slaughter animals for the sake of obtaining some protection from the gods. For he who seeks to obtain a benefit from another by acting unjustly falls under the suspicion that he will feel no true gratitude for any benefits received. Thus, even for those desiring some favor, animals are not to be sacrificed at all. For although we might perhaps be able to act in such a hidden way that it remains undiscovered by any man, it is in no way possible for us to remain hidden from God. If, therefore, one must sacrifice for the sake of one of these reasons, yet for none of these reasons should animals be slaughtered, it is manifest that animals are not to be sacrificed.

**§. 25.** But while we attempt to erase the truth of these matters through the pleasures we enjoy from the sacrifices, we hide the truth from ourselves, not from God. For—

<column-break/>

->**Column 2**<-

—for he will no more seem to make a return, than if someone, having snatched the property of his neighbor, should crown certain people <note>original: "στεφανοίη τινὰς"</note> as if returning thanks and honor. But neither is it for the sake of some need for good things. For he who hunts for good treatment through an unjust action is suspected of not being likely to feel gratitude even after receiving the good. So that even when a benefit is hoped for, one must not sacrifice animals to the gods. And indeed, one might perhaps hide this action from men, but it is impossible to hide from God. If, therefore, one must sacrifice for the sake of something, but it must not be done for the sake of any of these things, it is clear that one must not sacrifice animals.

**§ 25.** For by trying to wipe out the truth about these things with the enjoyments derived from the sacrifices, we hide it from ourselves; for certainly not from—

***

<margin>
The *Meermann* manuscript reads "it would seem." But *Eusebius* left the reading to us as it stands, followed by "or even if." Instead of "to do certain things," the same author has "to do a certain thing."
</margin>

**10. Should crown certain people.** "To crown" <term>stephanoun: to bestow a crown or prize</term> is generally to give or affect with a reward; or properly to give for the sake of honor. See *Xylander* on *Plutarch* Vol. I p. 22 and *Wesseling* on *Diodorus* XIV, 53. Those words which follow, "as if returning thanks etc.," seemed deservedly useless to *Reiske*, unless "he acts philanthropically" or something similar is added. They are, however, protected by the authority of *Eusebius*.

<margin>
**11. But neither for the sake of some need.** *Eusebius* reads: "but not even for the sake of anyone." But our reading responds to the preceding points. Since that word had just preceded, it seems to have been repeated by mistake.
</margin>

<column-break/>

**12. Impossible to hide.** Either something is missing, or "and" <note>Greek: "καὶ"</note> should be exchanged for "is" <note>Greek: "ἐστὶ"</note>. REISKE. Presently *Eusebius* reads: "one must sacrifice for the sake of some of these." Then the *Meermann* manuscript incorrectly has "for the sake of whom" instead of "for the sake of these."

**13. Animals. For by...** In *Eusebius*, several other words are inserted here: "animals at all to the gods, for..." and what follows. VICTORIUS. On the contrary, *Eusebius* ends the testimony there which he had taken from our author. Those words "For by..." etc. are not read there. Let students note the phrase "to wipe out the truth" <note>original: "ἐξαλείφειν ἀληθὲς"</note>. Properly it means *to smear over*: to scrape away the wax with which tablets were covered, and hence in a general sense *to cancel, to delete*.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument from the previous section. # P O R P H Y R Y

->**Column 1**<-

...God. Of the dishonored animals, then, which provide no use for our life <gloss>1</gloss> and offer no enjoyment, we sacrifice nothing to the gods. For who ever sacrificed snakes and scorpions and monkeys, <gloss>2</gloss> or any such animal? But of those that provide some use for our lives, or have something in them for enjoyment, we abstain from none, truly slaughtering and skinning them <gloss>3</gloss> under the pretext of the divine. 

For cattle and sheep, and besides these, deer and birds—and even those who share in no cleanliness but provide us enjoyment, such as fattened pigs—we slaughter to the gods. Some of these assist our lives by laboring alongside us, while others provide help for food or other needs. Those that do none of these things are likewise destroyed by men in sacrifices, just like the useful ones, because of the pleasure derived from them. But we do not sacrifice donkeys, nor elephants, nor...

<column-break/>

->**Column 2**<-

For from those animals which provide no human use for life, and bring no delight in their enjoyment, we offer none in sacrifice to the gods. For who ever sacrificed either snakes, or scorpions, or monkeys, or any such thing to the gods? 

But from those which are of some use to our life, and which have something in themselves for enjoyment, we do not abstain from any of them; rather, under the pretext of the deity, we truly slaughter and skin them. For cattle and sheep, as well as deer and birds, and even those who are partakers of no cleanliness but yet bring us pleasure in their enjoyment—pigs—we kill for the gods. Some of these are a support for human life by laboring; others supply us with food and other comforts; others provide none of these. But for the sake of the desire for enjoyment alone, no differently than those which are useful, they have become accustomed to being killed by men in sacrifices. But donkeys, and elephants, and all...

---

<margin>1. **"Better, and of those that have no enjoyment."** The scholar Reiske notes that the beginning of this Greek word seems to be a faulty repetition of the preceding word "use" <note>original: "chreian"</note> and contains clear traces of the omitted words "or of those." Therefore, he suggests the passage should read, "or of those that have no..." <note>original: "ἢ τῶν οὐδεμίαν"</note>. Another scholar, Abresch, suggests "Better, and of those that have no enjoyment." The scholar Meermann notes that "we sacrifice nothing" and "or monkeys" also appear in the Bodleian Manuscript.</margin>

<margin>2. **"Or any such."** Reiske suggests it might read "Or any other such." He also notes that our author, Porphyry, is fond of using the plural form for the word "lives." This usage was discussed in depth by P. Leopard in his *Emendations*, Book XI, chapter 4.</margin>

<margin>3. **"Under the pretext of the divine."** Reiske suggests the text might be understood as: "truly slaughtering and skinning them for our own enjoyment, but pretending <note>original: "prospoietos"</note> that it is under the pretext of the divine." The phrase "under the pretext" <note>original: "epi prophasia"</note> means using something as a false excuse or cover.</margin>

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK II

->T 2<-

...other animals which, though they may be helpful through their labor, are unsuitable for enjoyment, we do not sacrifice at all. Furthermore, even if sacrifices were set aside, we would not abstain from these useful animals, but we kill them simply for the sake of eating. And even among those animals which are deemed suitable for sacrifice, we are accustomed to slaughtering not those that might be more pleasing to the gods, but those that are more delightful for our own appetites to enjoy. Thus, we testify against ourselves that we persist in the observation of sacrifices for the sake of enjoying our own pleasure, not for the sake of the gods.

§ 26. Now, among the Syrians, the Jews—who, from that ancient first sacrifice, still sacrifice animals even now, as <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BCE) was Aristotle’s successor; his lost work on piety is a major source for Porphyry.</note> Theophrastus says—if they were to [command us to sacrifice] in the same manner as they themselves...

<column-break/>

...but another of those who labor with us, yet provide no enjoyment, we do not sacrifice. And indeed, even without the act of sacrificing, we do not abstain from such animals, slaughtering them for the sake of our enjoyments; and we sacrifice from among the sacrificial animals themselves, not the things pleasing to the gods, but much more the things that are agreeable to the desires of men. Thus we bear witness against ourselves: that for the sake of enjoyment <gloss>4</gloss> we abide by the gods, but not the victims. <note>original: "ἐμμένομεν τοῖς θεοῖς, οὐ τοῖς θύμασιν" — a difficult phrase suggesting we stick to the gods only as a pretext for the meat.</note>

§ 26. <gloss>1</gloss> And yet, among the Syrians, the Jews, on account of the <gloss>2</gloss> sacrifice from the beginning, even now, <gloss>3</gloss> says Theophrastus, sacrifice living beings; if in the same way...

---

<column-break/>

<gloss>4. We abide by the gods, not the victims.]</gloss> Perhaps: "we sacrifice to the gods for the sake of [pleasure], not for the honor." <note>original: "χάριν θύομεν τοῖς θεοῖς οὐ τῆς τιμῆς"</note> That is, we make these things sacred to the Gods so that we may feed on the victims, not so that we might hold the Gods in honor. Or perhaps: "we abide by the victims, not the gods." <note>original: "ἐμμένομεν τοῖς θύμασιν, οὐ τῶν θεῶν"</note> We cling to the ancient religious rites of sacrifices for the sake of our own pleasure, not for the sake of the Gods. This conjecture seems to be confirmed by what follows more than the previous one. <term>Reiske</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and celebrated philologist.</note> In place of "not" <term>Valerius</term> had substituted "and." Perhaps he wrote "we do not abide by the gods," or "not of the gods," in the same way that <term>Felicianus</term> understood it. If you retain "abide in the gods," the passage from the <term>Gospel of John 6:56</term> could be beautifully compared: "he abides in me," which the illustrious <term>Abresch</term> had noted; and he explained "in the victims" as "on account of the victims and the sacrifices," or "for the sake of the victims." To "abide in the victims" was perhaps said just as "to abide in the ways of the fathers" in <term>Book IV, 8</term>, or "in abstinence" in <term>section 16</term>, or "in law, in faith," and similar expressions. The Latins say "to remain in faith," etc. See <term>Staveren's notes on Cornelius Nepos XVII, 2.</term>

<gloss>1. And yet, among the Syrians, the Jews etc.]</gloss> This passage, up to the words "one might learn by looking," etc., was copied by <term>Eusebius</term> in <term>Preparation for the Gospel, Book IX, p. 404 A.</term> From this you may gather that it pertains to the Essenes (an observation that will soon be useful to us), for he immediately joins to them the statement: "and in the fourth book... he records the same things concerning them." There, it is beyond doubt that the discussion concerns the Essenes. In <term>Eusebius</term> it says "and yet because," but <term>Vigerus</term> says "because" is rightly erased from our text and the manuscripts. Regarding the passage from Theophrastus, it was discussed above.

<gloss>2. Sacrifice from the beginning.]</gloss> Either read "holy rite" <note>original: "ὁσίαν"</note> on account of the antiquity of the ceremony, or rather "on account of the original sacrifice of Abraham." <italic>Because of that sacrifice of Abraham, the primal example of this religion.</italic> <term>Reiske.</term>

<gloss>3. Sacrificing living things...]</gloss> The passage does not seem to be free of error. # PORPHYRY

...if they were to command us to sacrifice, we would surely abandon the undertaking. 4 For they do not feast upon the flesh of the sacrificed animals, but burning them entirely as whole-offerings <note>original: "holocausts"</note> at night, and pouring much honey and wine over them, they consume the sacrifice quickly, so that the all-seeing one <note>The Sun</note> might not become a spectator of the dread deed. And they do this while fasting during the intervening days; and throughout all this time, being philosophers by race, they converse with one another about the divine. But at night they perform the contemplation of the stars, looking toward them, and through...

<column-break/>

...if they wished us to sacrifice, we would undoubtedly desist from the business. For they do not banquet on the flesh of the sacrificed victims, but they consume the entire host—having been cast into the fire—quickly at night, with much honey and wine additionally poured on, lest the sun, who gazes upon all things, be made a spectator of the crime. And they do this while occupying themselves with fasts on the intervening days, and through that whole time, as they are philosophers by race, they talk among themselves concerning God; but at night they contemplate the stars, while they look up at them, and with certain...

<column-break/>

...which I later saw Vigerus <note>François Viger, a 17th-century scholar</note> agreeing with me. I had also supplied the word <term>manner</term> <note>Greek: τρόπον</note>. Eusebius confirms this. VALENT. The reading <term>sacrificing living things</term> <note>Greek: ζωοθυτοῦντες</note> is also in the Bodleian and Meerman manuscripts, and truly so, in my opinion. Then, after the word <term>itself</term> <note>Greek: αὐτὸν</term>, if you adopt <term>manner</term> from Eusebius, everything is explained. However, instead of <term>if</term> <note>Greek: εἰ</note>, the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts had <term>into</term> <note>Greek: εἰς</note>; and in the former, <term>sumon</term> instead of <term>suron</term>. Both are incorrect.

4. **For they do not feast, etc.** Vigerus writes that Theophrastus (quoted in Eusebius) speaks of unknown and false things, but I doubt if he is correct. I admit these details poorly suit all Jews. Learned men have long ago shown that it was their custom to prepare feasts from the remaining parts of the victims. But these remarks of our author—or rather of Theophrastus—seem to pertain solely to the **Essenes** <note>An ascetic Jewish sect of the Second Temple period</note>. I said so immediately, and the following parts confirm it. No one who has investigated their affairs is ignorant of the fact that they differed greatly from other Jews in matters of religion. The celebrated Mosheim uses this passage in his notes on Cudworth to settle the controversy that has long exercised scholars: whether the Essenes sacrificed victims or not? In this matter, Josephus and Philo seem to disagree. They did indeed offer victims, but not in the Temple, because they avoided all use of meat. Furthermore, Philo speaks of the Essenes who lived in Egypt, others of those in Syria, as our author does here, which he explicitly indicates at the start of the section. Finally, it must be noted that these men were divided into many classes and sects, and not all taught the same things. I would wish more to be read in Mosheim. I only add now that they departed from the religion of their ancestors in many ways, and while living among the Gentiles, they adopted certain ideas of the Philosophers—especially of **Pythagoras**—which recommended themselves by an appearance of sanctity.

5. **Honey and wine.** We have the Divine Law which forbade this to the Jews in Moses, Leviticus 2:11. Regarding them, see also Plutarch, *Symposiacs* IV, 5: <note>original: "furthermore, they do not offer honey in their sacrifices, because it seems to spoil the wine when mixed."</note> This was different from the custom of other nations, as mentioned above.

6. **The all-seeing one might become a spectator.** This signifies the Sun, <note>original: "who sees all and hears all"</note> as the poet says in *Odyssey* XII, 323; and the man from Sulmo <note>Ovid</note>, "who hears and sees us." *Metamorphoses* IV, 769. The term <term>all-seeing</term> <note>Greek: πανόπτης</note> is often used by Aeschylus and others. See Cuper, *Harpocrates* p. 114. It seems the Essenes thought of the sun somewhat more magnificently than was proper, which you may also gather from the testimony of Josephus below (IV, 12), where there is more.

7. **During the intervening days.** Eusebius and the Meerman and Leipzig manuscripts read <term>of these days</term>.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->**On the transition from plant offerings to animal sacrifice**<-

...they were led by greed to taste and eat everything. This is exactly what commonly happens now with food derived from all kinds of fruits. For when they have relieved their natural hunger by consuming them, they seek an excessive fullness and prepare many things for food that exceed the limits of temperance. Hence, as if they were presenting no mean sacrifices to the gods, they proceeded to eat them; and from the beginning of this practice, the eating of animals was added by men to their nourishment from fruits. For just as in ancient times they offered fruits to the gods, and after the sacred rite <note>original: "sanctimoniam" / "hosian"</note> they joyfully ate of those same things: so when they had sacrificed animals, they thought they ought to do the same for themselves. Although in ancient times, holiness <note>The author argues that true ancient piety did not involve blood sacrifice.</note> was not thus...

<column-break/>

...leaving nothing untasted or uneaten. This is what now happens among all people regarding food from fruits. For when they have eased their necessary want by the offering, seeking the excess of satiety, they labor to produce many things for eating that lie outside the bounds of self-control. Hence, as if making these things no dishonorable sacrifices to the gods, they were led to taste them. And through the beginning of this practice, the eating of animals became an addition to the food from fruits for men. Just as, therefore, in the old days they offered the first-fruits to the gods and gladly tasted of the offerings after the sacred rite, so having begun the sacrifice of animals, they thought they should do the same thing, even though in the ancient time holiness did not thus...

### On Abstinence, Book II.
V
<meta>catchword: me-</meta>

§ 28. This can be observed from the altar that is still preserved even now at Delos: because no animal is brought to it or slaughtered upon it, it is called the "Altar of the Pious." Thus, they not only abstained from animal sacrifices themselves, but they also considered those who had established the altar, and likewise those who used it, to be participants in piety. For this reason, the Pythagoreans, having adopted this tradition, abstained from eating animals throughout their entire lives. However, whenever they did set aside a portion of an animal for the gods as a first-fruit offering in place of themselves, they would taste only that portion, but in truth, they lived without touching any other meat. But we do not act in this way; instead, being filled beyond measure in our—

<column-break/>

§ 28. 1 This can be observed from the altar concerning Delos that is still preserved even now; because nothing is brought to it by them, nor is any animal sacrificed upon it, it has been called the Altar of the Pious. Thus, 2 they not only abstained from animals when sacrificing, but they also shared the quality of piety with those who founded it and those who used it. Wherefore the Pythagoreans, having received this, abstained from the eating of animals throughout their whole life. But whenever they might distribute a portion of an animal to the gods as a first-fruit offering instead of themselves, 3 having tasted only this, they lived in truth untouched by the rest. But not so with us; 4 being filled—

*Suidas* and the *Scholiast on Homer: Iliad: N.* 103. and *Odyssey: B.* 289. should be consulted.
1. **This can be observed &c.**] This is the correct reading. The *Florentine* edition and the *Lyon* edition which follows it incorrectly have *theōrizai* <note>original: θεωρίζαι</note>. *Cyril, the Meermann Codex, and the Leipzig Codex* agree with our reading. We spoke of the Delian Rites above in § 19. It is well known that the altar of Apollo Genitor <term>Apollo Genitor: "Apollo the Ancestor" or "The Begetter," a title under which he was worshipped at Delos with bloodless offerings</term> was never stained with the blood of victims (and therefore it should not be confused with the "horn altar" of Apollo, concerning which there is an elegant discussion by the illustrious H. I. Arntzen in *Miscellany ch. 2*). Iamblichus relates in chapters 5 and 7 that Pythagoras visited and honored that altar; for it was his custom to worship at bloodless altars, as is clear from the same chapter 24. I omit Clement of Alexandria and others who discuss this altar, cited by Spanheim in his notes on *Callimachus: To Apollo* 60 and *To Delos* 266; also Lomeier in *On Lustrations* 24, and others, who abundantly explain why it was called *eusebōn*, or the "Altar of the Pious." In that place, offerings were made of wheat, barley, and cakes without the use of fire, as we know from Diogenes Laertius.
</margin>

...such as the "fireless" or "bloodless" altars, which are mentioned as being different from "fire-altars," though they need not be discussed here. There is an ingenious conjecture by the celebrated Michaelis in *Exercise I on the Victims of the Heart and Cerebrum* § 30: that Pythagoras imitated Delian Apollo and composed the laws of the table according to the customs of that altar, so that he might demonstrate he was procreated from Apollo.

2. **Not only.**] The phrase *Ou monōs* <note>original: Οὐ μόνως</note> is in the *Leipzig Codex*, which is slightly better than what is in the common speech. However, Reiske would prefer *ou monon* <note>original: οὐ μόνον</note>. To be sure, *monos* was in the older Cambridge editions; the older sources agree with the *Leipzig Codex*, but *Cyril* has *ou monon*. Iamblichus in *On the Mysteries IV, 7* and others also use *monas*.

3. **Distribute to the gods.**] Perhaps it should be "apportion" <note>original: ἀπομερίσειαν</note>, and the comma should be moved immediately and placed after the phrase "in truth." Reiske says: *if we wish the truth, the Pythagoreans did not eat their victims, but only took a small taste.* And the *Meermann* manuscript distinguishes the text in this way.

4. **Being filled.**] The *Bodleian and Meermann Codices* read *empimplamenoi*. See Book I, 46.

# PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

...and having arrived at this point, we have proceeded into a most lawless custom in these matters throughout our lives. For neither should the altars of the gods be stained with slaughter, nor should men touch such food, just as they must not feed upon the flesh of their own bodies. Instead, that lesson for all of life must be adopted, which is still preserved in Athens.

§ 29. For in ancient times, as we also said previously, when men offered the fruits of the earth to the gods, but did not sacrifice animals nor consume them for their own nourishment, it is said that during a certain public sacrifice being celebrated at Athens, a certain Diomus or Sopatrus—who was not a native by birth, but farmed land in Attica—witnessed an event. While the <term>pelanos</term> <note>A thick, sacrificial cake made of grain and liquid</note> and the offerings were lying clearly upon the table so that they might be sacrificed to the gods, one of the oxen coming in from work...

<column-break/>

...proceeded into a most lawless custom. For neither are the altars of the gods to be imbued with slaughter: nor should men use food of this kind, in the same way that they must not eat the flesh of their own bodies. But that example of life must be made, which even yet is accustomed to be observed at Athens.

§ 29. For anciently, as we have also said above, when men offered fruits to the gods, but neither sacrificed animals nor took them for food, while a certain public rite was being celebrated at Athens, they say a certain Diomus or Sopatrus—who was not indeed a native, but cultivated fields in Attica—because an ox, coming from its labor, approached the table where the sacred meal and other libations had been placed to be sacrificed, [ate] some of them...

---

<margin>
1. *But not animals.*] See what we noted regarding those words "but not," Book I, 41.
2. *Abusing for food.*] The Greeks use the compound verb <note>original: *katachresthai*</note> for the simple "to use," although you may see translators everywhere incorrectly rendering it as "to abuse," as in Paul, 1 Corinthians 7:31, and others. So also Worth in his edition of Tatian, p. 6. See also Huet on Origen’s Select Works on the Psalms, p. 528. It is true, however, that it is often turned toward a worse sense, as in this place and elsewhere.
3. *Diomus or Sopatrus.*] Above in § 10 he calls him *Diomus*. The Scholiast on Aristophanes' *Clouds* 979 calls him *Bauwon*, but there it should be rewritten as *Thaulon*. See Suidas under *Bouphonia* and *Thaulon*. Meursius had already corrected the name in *Attic Readings* VI. 22.
4. *Of the cake and the offerings.*] The Lyon and Cambridge editions had given *thymematon* <note>incense-offerings</note>. Often indeed the tribe of copyists perverts the more unusual form *thyema* <note>sacrificial offering</note>; see this excellently supported and explained by the illustrious Ruhnken in his notes on Timaeus' Lexicon under *Thuyemata*. Here, however, nothing should be changed, for all the manuscripts agree on *thylemata* <note>sacrificial cakes</note>. And so Victorius himself gave it, but the laziness of editors had not noticed the error of the typesetters. Regarding the word itself, it was discussed above. Those *thylemata* were placed "upon the table." "For there are tables in the temples on which they place the offerings," as the Scholiast on Aristophanes' *Plutus* 678 says.
5. *One of the oxen coming from work.*] Pausanias in his *Description of Attica* p. 43 says it was an ox "which they keep ready, having prepared it for the sacrifice." You might easily think the animal was killed with the best justification. But if you remember that the ox was a plowman...
</margin>

The marginal notes provide philological commentary on Greek terms for offerings and historical variants of the protagonist's name.</summary>

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK II.

V 2
<meta>catchword: that</meta>

...[the ox] had eaten some of the offerings and trampled others. In a rage, he rushed forward, seized an axe that happened to be being sharpened by a neighbor, and struck the beast. When the ox died from the wound and his anger had cooled, he realized the crime he had committed. Having buried the ox, they say he took upon himself a voluntary exile and fled to Crete due to the charge of impiety. But when a drought and a great barrenness of crops struck Attica, they decided to consult the oracle publicly. The Pythia <note>The high priestess of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi</note> replied that the exile in Crete would solve these things: if they both punished the killer and "raised up the dead" in the same fat in which he had died: that

<column-break/>

...entering from his labor, it devoured some of the things and trampled others. He, being excessively indignant at what had happened, seized an axe <note>original: *pelekys*</note> that was being sharpened nearby and struck the ox. When the ox had died, and he had calmed from his anger, he reflected on what a deed he had done. He buried the ox. But taking up a voluntary flight, as one who had acted impiously, he fled to Crete. When droughts took hold and a terrible barrenness occurred, they inquired of the god in common. The Pythia proclaimed that the fugitive in Crete would release them from these things, if they punished the murderer and raised up the dead in the very fat <note>original: *sialos*, a word that can mean fat, grease, or a hog-trough</note> in which he had died.

---

<margin>Returning from work; you will judge otherwise. It is well known how diligently the Athenians and others took care that this should not happen. See § 31. *Work* here refers to "rustic labor," just as the farmer is said to "work," and the "plow-ox" below in § 30. Who has not illustrated this?</margin>

6. **An axe.** <note>Greek: *Pelekeōs tinos*</note> Perhaps it should be "the axe" <note>Greek: *pelekun*</note>, for the word "being sharpened" is not passive here, but in the middle voice, meaning *someone not far from there was sharpening his own double-axe for himself.* — REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century German scholar</note>.

<margin>7. **Taking up a voluntary flight.** He says the ritual arose from this, because that first man who killed the ox had fled. I note this because Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note>, in describing it, adds: "I do not write the cause alleged for these things." Therefore, he should be illustrated by our author.</margin>

8. **They inquired of the god.** This is the proper expression for those who consult an oracle. Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> (Book III, ch. 59) uses a similar phrase regarding a disaster: "And the earth becoming barren, they inquired of the god concerning the deliverance from these evils." Also in the *Excerpts* (p. 550): "Upon these calamities, he inquired at Delphi." And Thucydides (I, 118): "Sending to Delphi, they inquired of the god." More examples are at hand, which I will not use now.

<column-break/>

9. **In the fat in which he died.** <note>The text here is corrupted and difficult to translate</note> Perhaps it should read: "It would be better <note>Greek: *loion esesthai*</note> if they resurrected the dead and set him to that work <note>Greek: *ergasia*</note> in which he had expired." — REISKE. An Oedipus <note>A metaphor for someone who can solve a great riddle</note> is needed to explain the oracle of the Loxian <note>A title for Apollo, referring to his "ambiguous" or "crooked" oracles</note>. Instead of "he died" <note>Greek: *apethanen*</note>, the Florence, Leiden, Leipzig, and Meerman codices had "they died" <note>Greek: *apethanon*</note>, but Fogerolles correctly amended it. For the phrase "would be," the same scholar restored it, and Valentinus followed: "would be benefited by the threshing floor" <note>Greek: *alō onēsesthai*</note>, in which I confess I find much charm. But since "in the fat" <note>Greek: *sialō*</note> is found in all copies, I suspected it meant "this man would be the one in the fat in which he died" — that is, the one who would expiate the crime. Or "this would be the way," meaning the disaster could be removed in that manner. Abresch attempted: "there would be a harvest <note>Greek: *alōēn*</note> in the fat/trough in which he died." Or "a harvest in the iron/sword." Or "a harvest in the coffin." Whichever you choose, there will be ambiguity <note>Greek: *loxotēs*</note>. If you choose the first, one must think of the rich sacrificial feasts which the ox had devoured, and which had become the cause of its death.

Scholarly notes debate the exact wording of the Pythia's cryptic oracle regarding the "fat" or "trough" involved in the ox's death.</summary>

# P O R P H Y R Y

<column-break/>

...would come to pass, if they both tasted of the dead ox and did not hold back the murderer. Therefore, when an inquiry was held and Sopatrus was found along with the evidence of the deed, Sopatrus—believing he would be freed from the distress <note>original: *dyscholias*</note> surrounding him as one under a curse if everyone performed this act in common—told those who had come to fetch him that an ox must be slaughtered by the city. When they were at a loss as to who would be the one to strike the blow, he offered to do it for them, provided they would make him a citizen and share in the guilt of the slaughter. When these terms were granted, they returned to the city and arranged the performance of the deed in the same manner that is still observed among them today.

->§ 30.<-

---

...and the hay and herbs by which oxen are distended and fattened. The notion of *fatness* <note>original: *pinguedinis*</note> is established from *Hippocrates* <note>The famous Greek physician</note> and *Foesius's Oeconomicon* under the word *sialos* <note>original: σίαλος; meaning fat or hog-grease</note>. If the word for "iron" <note>original: *sidērō*</note> lies hidden in the syllable *si*, the oracle may have intended that the ox fall by iron, and thus, having been stuffed with hay, be raised onto its feet by some iron instrument. If the word *sera* <note>meaning a rope or a bolt</note> is used, it indicates the *skin*, and it is finally suggested that it must be eaten—not buried in the earth as Diomus had done. If they did this, there would be a "threshing floor" <note>original: *aloe*; implying a harvest/abundance</note>. See *Hesychius* <note>A 5th-century lexicographer</note> under *Aloē* and the *Scholiast on Theocritus* cited there. Or finally, the author perhaps left it as "in the very trough" <note>original: *pyalos*</note> there would be a threshing floor. The syntax of "those having punished" and "those having tasted and not held back" seems to be the same as that discussed in the *Dilucidations on Thucydides*, page 833. These are the views of that Illustrious Man; for my part, being of a doubtful mind in these trifles, I do not wish to waver or fluctuate any longer, leaving the learned reader to choose what he prefers. I have restored *geusamenois* <note>meaning "having tasted"</note> because the older editions and all my manuscripts demanded it.

10. **And not holding back.** "And not holding back the murderer." —REISKE. *Fogerolles* had earlier corrected this to "and not the murderer."

11. **Sopatrus with...** Instead of "discovered" <note>original: *aneurethentos*</note>, the Leipzig manuscript reads "discovered," but there is doubt

<column-break/>

none regarding the word *meta* <note>meaning "with" or "after"</note>. The phrase "Sopatrus being found together with the deed" or "apprehended" can easily produce the meaning that Sopatrus was the one guilty of the deed, and the whole crime was carried out in that order. However, I would prefer to read *metaitio* <note>meaning "accessory" or "sharer in the guilt"</note>. —REISKE. I have removed a most shameful error that had occupied all editions regarding the word "discovered." The reading of the *Leipzig* and *Meermann* manuscripts is correct. The word *meta* can denote "after," in which sense it occurs with the genitive in our author and others. See *D’Orville on Chariton*, III, 4. But nothing prevents him from saying simply that while they were busy searching, Sopatrus was found.

12. **Distress.** <note>original: *Dyscholias*</note> Perhaps *dyschorias* <note>meaning "narrowness of space"</note>? *Hesychius* defines *dyschoria* as "distress of place." But perhaps the reading in the *Leipzig* and *Meermann* manuscripts, *dyskolias* <note>meaning "difficulty" or "peevishness"</note>, is better; this was also a conjecture by *Abresch*, who cited a passage from *Pausanias*. Nevertheless, the common reading has enough to defend itself. The word is not found in the lexicons I consult. But neither do they have *dyscholon*, even though *Theophrastus* joins "bitter and difficult" <note>original: *pikron kai dyscholon*</note> in *On Odors*.

13. **As one under a curse.** <note>original: *enagous*</note> Or "as a matter of pollution" <note>original: *agous*</note>, which...

# On Abstinence, Book II.
->V 3<-

§ 30. They selected water-carrying virgins to bring water for those who were to sharpen the axe and the knife. Once the axe and knife were sharpened, one person handed over the axe, another took it and struck the ox, and yet another slaughtered it. After they had flayed it, everyone feasted upon its flesh. Afterward, however, having sewn the hide back together and stuffed it with hay and straw, they raised the ox up in the same form it had when it was alive, and they yoked it to a plow as if it were working. When this was done, they summoned all who had participated in the act to a trial for murder. When the water-carriers accused those who had sharpened the tools, and those who had sharpened them accused the one who had handed over the axe, and he in turn accused the one who— <note>The Latin text breaks off mid-word: "iu-" for "iugulavit" (slaughtered).</note>

<column-break/>

§ 30. 1. They selected water-carrying virgins; these bring the water so that they may sharpen the axe and 2. the knife. When they had sharpened them, 3. one person handed over the axe; another struck the ox, and another slaughtered it. After those who followed had flayed it, everyone tasted of the ox. When these things were performed, they sewed up the hide of the ox and, 4. having stuffed it with hay, they stood it up, having the same appearance it had when living, and yoked it to a plow as if it were working. 5. Holding a trial for the murder, they called all those who shared in the deed to a defense. When the water-carriers blamed those who had sharpened the tools more than themselves, and those who sharpened them blamed the one handing over the axe, and he blamed the one who slaughtered— <note>The Greek text breaks off mid-word: "σφά-" for "ἐπισφάξαντα" (the one who slaughtered).</note>

---

<margin>
*What the crime was*, consider that which he had committed, or rather *as if being under a curse* <note>original: "ὡς ἐναγὴς ὢν"</note>. On account of the preceding *Sopatrus the lawgiver* <note>original: "Σώπατρος νομ."</note> or *as if not being under a curse*. Or, as I would prefer, *as if the whole people were under a curse, since the entire population would contract the guilt of the crime.* <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist.</note>
</margin>

1. **They selected water-carrying virgins.**] Carrying water was the work of women. *Xenophon: Expedition of Cyrus, Book IV, p. 330* mentions "women carrying water." The same custom existed in the Orient, as the sacred scriptures show, and today among the tent-dwelling Arabs. Compare *The Learned Man on the Gospel of John IV, 7.* You may observe everywhere that this was the work of virgins, as in this place; see *Homer: Odyssey VII, 20; Athenaeus XIII, 6, etc.* That our word is common and of good repute is shown by *Hemsterhuis on Pollux VII, 130.*

2. **The knife.**] *Felicianus* rightly translates this as "knife" <note>Latin: "cultrum"</note>; others wrongly as "sword." It often happens with this word <note>Greek: "μάχαιραν"</note> that it signifies a larger knife. See *Xylander on Plutarch’s Theseus p. 3* and *Alberti on the Gospel of Matthew XXVI, 51.*

<column-break/>

3. **One person handed over the axe.**] The common reading can be defended. I would prefer, however, "someone handed over the axe, and another struck," or "they handed over the axe, and another struck." <term>REISKE</term>. The older writers preferred "to give back" <note>Greek: "Ἀποδιδόναι"</note>, but our word is also correct, as these terms are confused a hundred times. See *D’Orville on Chariton VIII, 4*, who did not forget this passage. Recently, instead of "of those" <note>Greek: "τῶν δὲ"</note>, the earlier *Leipzig and Meermann editions* had "of those indeed."

4. **Having stuffed.**] The vocabulary of *Henri Estienne* <note>A famous 16th-century lexicographer.</note> can be increased by this word. It is the same as if he had said "sufficiently swollen," as the prefix "apo-" often functions in compounds. So below in IV, 8, "to bear witness," "to marvel at," concerning which see *The Illustrious Abresch: Readings on Aristaenetus p. 290, and elsewhere.* Recently, instead of "having it," *Reiske and Abresch* rightly preferred "the same thing which..."—that is, "the same."

5. **A trial.**] There was a note in the margin of the *Leipzig and Meermann Manuscripts*: "A strange and playful trial."

From that time until the present day, during the <term>Diipolia</term> <note>A festival in honor of Zeus Polieus, "Zeus of the City."</note> at Athens on the Acropolis, those designated for the task perform the sacrifice of the ox in this same manner. For having placed grain and cakes upon a bronze table, they lead around the oxen that have been selected; the one that tastes the offerings is the one they slaughter. There are families who still perform these deeds today: those descended from Sopatros, who struck the first blow, are all called <term>Boutypoi</term> <note>Literally "ox-strikers."</note>; those descended from the one who drove the animal around are called the <term>Kentriadai</term> <note>Literally "goaders," from the "kentra" or goad used to drive cattle.</note>. For once the meal and cakes are placed on a bronze table, they drive the grazing oxen around: of these, they slaughter whichever one tastes the offerings from the table. And the families of those who perform these acts remain even now: from Sopatros, who wounded the animal, come those called the "ox-strikers"; from the one who drove it around, they are called the "stimulators"; and from the slaughterer come those they call "dividers," named for the banquet which was established from the division of the meat. # P O R P H Y R Y
## On Abstinence, Book II.

...the judgment is reached, and they sink the knife, which has been cast into the sea.

§ 31. Thus, in ancient times, it was not considered holy to kill animals that were helpers to human life; and now the same must be avoided. And just as previously it was not pious to slaughter these for sacrifices, so now it must not be thought holy to kill animals of this kind for the sake of eating. If indeed this must be done for the sake of expiation toward the gods, yet all this pollution from the bodies must be rejected, lest the nourishment—

<column-break/>

...they are brought to judgment, and they sink the knife into the sea.

§ 31. Thus neither in the olden days was it holy to kill animals that cooperate with our lives, and now this must be guarded against. And just as before, it was not holy for men to touch these, so now for the sake of food it must not be considered holy to touch animals. If then this must be done for the sake of sacred ritual <note>original: ἁγισείαν (hagiseian)</note> toward the divine, yet certainly this entire suffering <note>original: πάθος (pathos); referring to the physical remains or the trauma of the act</note> from the bodies must be cast out from oneself, so that the nourishment—

---

<margin>
11. <gloss>Brought to judgment.</gloss> <note>original: Κρίσιν ἀχθῶσιν</note> This is the specific term for those who are led to plead a case or are led to punishment. In Latin, this is *ducere* ("to lead"). Examples are found everywhere. See Staveren on Nepos XIX, 4.
12. <gloss>They sank the knife.</gloss> <note>original: Κατεπόντωσαν τὴν μάχαιραν</note> We just spoke of the judgment. Herodotus and others use this form of the word. More often it is said as *katapontizein* ("to cast into the sea"). See D'Orville on Chariton I, 5. Much rarer is the usage by Nicolaus of Damascus in the Valesian Excerpts, p. 445: "the men... he sank them as if they were godless." Compare Wesseling on Diodorus XIV, 112. A gentler judge is encountered by the double-ax in Pausanias, Book I, p. 53: "the ax, having been judged, was immediately acquitted."
1. <gloss>To kill the helpers etc.</gloss> <note>original: Κτείνειν τὰ συνεργὰ</note> Pliny says in Book VIII, 45, "We have this animal <note>the ox</note> as a partner in labor and the cultivation of the field." Aelian in *Varia Historia* V, 14, calls it "a farmer and a sharer in human toils." It is no wonder, then, that the Athenians and others were so careful not to rashly slaughter the ox, the primary plowman, although later this was not always so rigidly observed in sacred rites. Regarding this, see the learned editors on Aelian. Hence, poets of the Golden and Silver Ages say humans did not eat oxen; they attribute it finally to the Bronze or, as others say, the Iron Age. I will not linger on this well-known matter. As for what was done in the Diipolia—
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
—our author says, "the Thebans anciently sacrificed bulls to the Gray Apollo." See Pausanias, Book IX, p. 559.
2. <gloss>Must be guarded against doing.</gloss> <note>original: φυλακτέον ἐστὶ πράττειν</note> *Phylattein* means to observe someone or something, so that they do not do something, or that it does not happen, or even that they do something. I add nothing to illustrate the use of the word beyond what has long been observed. See D'Orville on Chariton V, 2, p. 442.
3. <gloss>To men...</gloss> <note>original: Τοῖς ἀνθρ.</note> REISKE suggests: "For the sake of holiness (or sacrifice or first-fruits) to men to touch animals." *Haptesthai* means to eat or feed upon. It is said elsewhere, "he touched food" in Chariton I, 13, where the celebrated commentator says more. But the Greek word, like the Latin *tangere* ("to touch"), generally means to harm or injure, specifically by touching. See the learned editors on 1 John 5:18, in which sense it can be conveniently explained here.
4. <gloss>Sacred ritual/Expiation.</gloss> <note>original: Ἁγισείαν</note> Felicianus translated this as "expiation"; further down in Book IV, 8, it is "sanctification." The word has a very broad scope and includes the worship of the gods and also sacrifices. See Rittershuis on Porphyry's *Life of Pythagoras*, 6, and Valesius on Sozomen's *Ecclesiastical History*, V, p. 102.
5. <gloss>But that indeed...</gloss> <note>original: Ἀλλ’ ὅτι γε</note> The phrasing is short and abrupt; the full meaning of this sentence would be: "But this at least, one must know and observe, that..." or more briefly, "But remember that..." according to REISKE.
</margin>

# PORPHYRY

-> On Abstinence from Animal Food <-

...sustenance obtained from sources where it was not fitting <note>original: *proseke*</note>, we would have this act of violence as a constant companion in our own lives. For indeed, if nothing else, we would all benefit greatly at least in terms of a mutual truce <note>original: *ekecheiria* — a cessation of hostilities</note> toward one another. Certainly, for those whose senses recoil from touching animals of other species, it is evident that their minds will abstain from harming those of their own kind. Perhaps, then, it would be best of all to abstain immediately from now on. But since no one is without sin, it remains for us to heal <note>original: *akeisthai* — to remedy or medicate</note> our previous errors concerning food through purifications for the future. This would likewise happen if, having placed the horror before our eyes,

<column-break/>

...from where it is not appropriate, it becomes a kind of provocation for us to inflict violence upon one another. For even if the matter held no other evil in itself, it would certainly bring it about that we are rendered more ready to invade one another. For those whose feelings turn away from harming foreign creatures, it is clear that their minds will refrain from injuring their kinsmen. Therefore, it would perhaps be best of all if we abstained immediately for the future: but since there is no one who is free from sins, it remains that the sins of our ancestors in the taking of food be at least left behind for posterity through expiations. This, moreover, would be achieved if, with the crime before our eyes...

---

<margin>
6
</margin>
6. *It was fitting to provide.*] In the *Leipzig & Meerman Manuscripts* it reads "it is fitting." These are confused a hundred times. But the Grammarians have often taught that the imperfect is used for the present. Above at the end of section 12: "it was not fitting to take away." So too "it reached," "it was proper," and similar terms, concerning which see *D’Orville on Chariton, Book VIII, 2. p. 670.*

<margin>
7
</margin>
7. *The act of violence.*] For *biasma* (violence), the French translator had substituted *miasma* (pollution/defilement). This change does not seem necessary to me, yet I did not want to omit it. Perhaps it will please others more. — VALCKENAER. It does not please me. The common reading is, as they say, "healthier than a fish" <note>a Latin idiom meaning perfectly sound</note>. He understands the impulse to inflict force. Felicianus translated it well.

<margin>
8
</margin>
8. *For indeed if etc.*] The translator rendered this with little accuracy. Instead of "against one another" <note>Greek: *kat’ allēlon*</note>, my dearest friend Abresch restored "reciprocal" <note>Greek: *katallēlon*</note>. The word *ekecheiria* (truce) is very well known from *Suidas* and other lexicographers. Learned men have illustrated its proper and improper use in notes on *Thucydides IV, 58.*

<margin>
9
</margin>
9. *To abstain for the future.*] "For the future" <note>Greek: *loipon*</note> should be deleted. For it holds its place afterward. — REISKE.

<margin>
10
</margin>
10. *It remains to heal...*] Valckenaer would prefer "to be removed for the future." REISKE: "To be dedicated" <note>Greek: *anakeisthai*</note> is fine, provided it is understood as coming not from the verb "to lie" <note>keisthai</note>, but from the verb "to heal" <note>akeisthai</note>—*to repair, to amend, to cure, to correct.* A little later, "concerning food." *Akeisthai* and *iasthai* (to heal) are not infrequently used this way, and that word alone must find a place here; it is confirmed by what follows, "remedy" <note>akos</note>, and below, "to heal injustice." Rightly, therefore, Abresch in *Diluc. Thuc. Auct. p. 390* reads "it remains to heal." And Ruhnken in his *Humane Letters* emends it to "to heal." He himself in section 60 imitates "to heal the injustice," as he does everywhere, following Plato’s *Republic II, p. 424 C*: "by sacrifices and incantations, if any injustice... to heal." Phrynichus in the manuscript notes on Timaeus p. 84 looked to this passage of Plato. $^+$ Thus says the Learned Man. Since, therefore, not even a letter was changed, I have separated what was previously read as one word (*anakeisthai*) into two words (*ana keisthai*). The translator did not understand the passage. I would not dare to condemn those words "concerning food." The Greeks are accustomed to using the second and fourth cases <note>Genitive and Accusative</note> indiscriminately in such matters. See *Abresch, p. 387.*

<margin>
11
</margin>
11. *Having placed before the eyes.*] What our author calls "to make before the eyes," others call "to place before the eyes."
