# PORPHYRY

-> On Abstinence, Book II <-

...with this purpose, we should deplore our misery along with Empedocles <note>Empedocles was a 5th-century BC Greek philosopher who taught that souls migrate between humans and animals, making meat-eating a form of murder.</note>.

> *Woe is me, that the lot of fate did not destroy me before*
> *my lips had defiled themselves with wicked deeds of food.* <note>original Latin: "dapibus patres temerassent ora scelestis"</note>

For to be so affected by one's own sense of sin belongs to those seeking some remedy for present evils: so that each person, offering pure and chaste sacrifices to the divinity with holiness, may do so and obtain benefit from the gods.

§ 32. The first and foremost benefit, however, comes from the fruits of the earth, from which alone the first fruits <term>primitiae: the first portion of a harvest dedicated to the gods</term> are to be offered to the gods and to the earth itself which produced them. For the earth is common to both gods and men—

<column-break/>

...we might lament according to Empedocles, saying:

> 12 *Woe is me, that the pitiless day did not destroy me before,*
> *Before I devised wicked deeds of food upon my lips.* 13

For feeling pain for sins in one's own perception <note>original: "oikeian aisthesin"</note> is characteristic of lives seeking 14 some remedy for the evils that are present; so that each human, offering 15 pure sacrifices as first fruits to the divine, might obtain holy 16 benefit from the gods.

§ 32. But most of all and first is the benefit of the fruits, of which alone one must offer first fruits to the gods and to the earth that gave them up. For this is common 1 to both gods and men—

---

<margin>
& "To take before one’s eyes" <note>original: "pro ophthalmon lambanein"</note> was said several times by Polybius <note>A Greek historian</note> in those passages which Raphel collected to illustrate Paul’s letter to the Galatians (3:1). "We might lament" <note>original: "aneuphemesaimen"</note> is well interpreted as "we should deplore." Following Plato’s example, this word means the same as "to wail." See Kuhn’s Index to Aelian’s *Various History*.

12. *Woe is me, etc.* Stephanus did not neglect these lines in his *Poetry of Philosophy*, page 30. "Pitiless day" <note>original: "neleës emar"</note> is a Homeric phrase from the *Iliad* (11.484, 587; and 13.514).

13. *Upon my lips.* The word "upon" <note>original: "peri"</note> should not refer to "lips," but to the verb "devised." Reiske <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note> suggests this means "to cleverly and artfully commit crimes with the lips."

14. *To find some [remedy]...* Either "something is found" or "it is possible to find something." Reiske suggests the word "is" <note>original: "esti"</note> should be added (as the famous Abresch preferred) or understood. There is no need for the asterisk Valentinus placed before "lives"; we just need to consider Porphyry's way of building a sentence. All manuscripts, however, have the word "life" <note>original: "bion"</note>.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
Manuscripts. Other scholars have already corrected the error of Phrynichus <note>A 2nd-century grammarian</note>, who thought the word for "to find" <note>original: "eurasthai"</note> was not pronounced with an 'a' but with an 'e'. See Alberti on the Epistle to the Hebrews (9:12).

15. *Pure sacrifices.* <note>original: "Agna thumata"</note> These are usually contrasted with "bloody" sacrifices. Plato says in the *Laws* (Book 6, p. 875C): "Sacrifices to the gods were not animals, but grain-cakes and fruits soaked in honey, and other such pure sacrifices." I see these and many other examples have already been gathered by the learned editors of Pollux (1.26).

16. *And benefit from the gods.* In fact, the earlier editions and the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts more correctly say "and [the] benefit from the gods." Those same manuscripts have "only" <note>original: "mones"</note> instead of "alone," as if it referred to the word "benefit."

1. *The substance of gods and men.* Just as the author of *On the Universe* (p. 20) calls the earth "the substance and mother of all kinds of animals." This earth is certainly the common mother of all mortals, as Livy says (1.56), which is very well known.
</margin>

<meta>This page concludes Porphyry’s summary of the philosopher Theophrastus's views on the origins of sacrifice. It emphasizes the Earth as a nurturing mother and argues that vegetable offerings are the only appropriate way to honor the divine, as animal sacrifice is a later, "wicked" corruption.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

...the hearth and home of mankind. We all ought to recline upon her as our nurse and mother, celebrating her with songs of praise, and loving her dearly as the one who gave us birth. For if we lived our lives in this way, having reached the end of our life <note>original: "katatrophe," literally an overturning or conclusion</note>, we might again be deemed worthy of returning to heaven and to the entire company of the gods in heaven. Since these gods are the joint-providers of our crops, we ought to honor them by looking up to them and offering the first fruits of our harvests. While everyone should do this, we must not assume that every person is fit to perform sacrifices to the gods. For just as not everything is suitable to be sacrificed, so too, perhaps, sacrifices are not welcomed by the gods from every individual. This, then, is the summary of the arguments—excluding the myths that were inserted and a few brief additions and abridgments of my own—from the works of Theophrastus regarding why animal sacrifice is not necessary.

->§ 33.<-

<margin>2. **Having reached the end of life.** The translator Felicianus gave "the change of life." This is what the exit from life, or death, is called. A commentator on Thucydides (II, 42) says: "*katatrophe* is death." Aelian in his *Miscellaneous History* (I, 14) says: "whenever the end of life approaches," and in IV, 14, "to finish life," and he uses it thus quite often.</margin>
<margin>3. **We might be deemed worthy of heaven, and... etc.** Reiske suggests: "Perhaps we might be deemed worthy to *ascend* again into heaven to the whole race of the gods. These gods, whom we do not now see, we must or should honor, since they are the co-causes of our benefits." Use this to smooth out this rough passage. Reiske explains: "For it would happen that we return to heaven to the whole race of celestial gods, whom, although we do not yet see them, we ought to honor with those things which they help produce for us."</margin>

<column-break/>

...the hearth and Vesta <note>Vesta is the Roman goddess of the hearth, equivalent to the Greek Hestia mentioned in the left column.</note> of mankind. We ought all to recline on her as our nurse and mother, celebrate her with praises, and love and cherish her as a parent. For thus having reached the conclusion of life, we would be made worthy so that the path back to heaven and to the whole assembly of celestial gods might lie open to us. Those whom we now look up to, we ought to venerate with the fruits which they supply to us, and everyone should worship them with first-fruits; yet we should not think that everyone is suitable to perform the sacred rites. For just as not everything is to be sacrificed to the gods, so it must be thought that perhaps sacrifices are not made pleasing to the gods by everyone. This, then, is the summary of the reasons why animals should not be sacrificed, taken from Theophrastus, excluding the stories that were inserted and a few things briefly added by us.

->§ 33.<-

<margin>The structure here is confused, which is typical of our author, and perhaps obscures the sense. It could be explained this way: "worthy of heaven (or *in* heaven) and to honor again the whole... those (instead of 'the ones', as is common) whom we now see (Valentinus mistakenly substituted 'they see'). With these things (Fogerolles and Valentinus rightly corrected it to mean 'we should honor them') of which they are the co-providers of fruits, everyone offering first-fruits," etc. This "and" is missing from the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts and the old editions. And instead of "fruits," there was previously something else in the Leipzig manuscript, in place of which another hand seemingly substituted "fruits," the earlier reading having been obscured.</margin>

He asserts that animal sacrifice is not universally pleasing to the gods and marks the end of his summary of Theophrastus's core arguments.</summary>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

§ 33. For my part, I would not attempt to dissolve the established customs that have prevailed among various peoples; for it is not my present purpose to discourse upon the nature of the state. However, since the laws under which we live permit us to honor the Divine even through the simplest and inanimate things, we shall choose that which is most frugal. Thus, we shall sacrifice according to the law of the city, and we ourselves shall take care to offer a fitting sacrifice, approaching the gods pure in every respect. For in general, if sacrifice holds the status of "first-fruits" <note>original: "ἀπαρχῆς" (aparchēs) - the first portion of a harvest dedicated to a deity</note> and an expression of gratitude for those things we have received from the gods for the uses of life, it would seem most absurd if we, who abstain from living beings, were to make offerings to the gods from them. Surely the gods are not inferior to us, such that they should require things which we ourselves do not need. Furthermore, it is not holy to offer first-fruits from a food from which we ourselves abstain. For we have understood that such is also the custom of men—

<column-break/>

§ 33. <note>This column contains the Greek source text for the Latin passage provided on the left.</note> I do not come to destroy the prevailing customs among each people. For it is not set before me now to speak concerning the constitution. But since the laws in which we live as citizens have granted us the right to honor the Divine even through the most simple and soulless things, choosing the most simple, we shall sacrifice by the law of the city, and we ourselves shall be diligent to make the <gloss>1</gloss> fitting sacrifice, approaching the gods pure from all sides. And altogether, if the value of sacrifice is that of <gloss>2</gloss> first-fruits, and a thanksgiving for what we have from the gods for our needs, it would be most irrational for those who themselves abstain from living things to offer first-fruits of these to the gods. For the gods are not worse than us, <gloss>3</gloss> so that they themselves should need these things, while we do not need them; nor is it holy to give a first-fruit of food from which we ourselves abstain. Since we have also understood such a custom of men—

---

<column-break/>

1. *Fitting sacrifice... approaching.*] In the Leipzig manuscript it is *to make the fitting [sacrifice] to approach*; regarding those who approach the gods for the sake of religion, it is a frequent expression, as with the Latin *adire* <note>to approach/address</note>, or *to approach the Gods*, as I shall say later.

2. *From the beginning...*] These two words are to be contracted into one, and joined in a single embrace, so that it is <term>aparchēs</term> <note>first-fruits</note>; the sacrifice has the value of an offering of first-fruits. Or, the force and meaning of sacrifice is this: that by offering it, we wish to declare that we are returning to God the first-fruits of a thing received from Him. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and philologist</note>. <term>Felicianus</term> <note>Giovanni Bernardino Feliciano, 16th-century translator of Porphyry</note> is correct: and therefore I did not hesitate to fuse into one the two words which were previously read as separate.

3. *So that they themselves should need these things.*] The word *autoi* <note>themselves</note> is correct, although previously *autōn* was read, which was also in the Bodleian and Meermann manuscripts. For *deōntai* <note>they might need</note>, which is also in the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts, it was previously published as *deontai*. This is also acceptable, although it fights against the rules of the Grammarians. The sentiment itself—that God does not stand in need of our gifts—he frequently introduces in these books. Others also frequently introduce it. Compare <term>Kortholt</term> <note>Christian Kortholt (1633–1694), a Lutheran theologian</note> on *Justin's Apology I, page 9.*

<summary>Porphyry argues that since sacrifice is a gift of "first-fruits" of one's own food, it is illogical and unholy for vegetarians to sacrifice animals to the gods. The scholarly notes debate the specific Greek phrasing of "first-fruits" and the theological concept of divine self-sufficiency.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument that sacrifice should reflect the lifestyle of the worshiper. Since the philosopher abstains from meat, their offerings to the gods should likewise be bloodless. This section begins to transition into the Neo-Platonic hierarchy of worship, distinguishing between the supreme God and lesser divine powers.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

...among men, back when they did not touch animal food, they did not offer sacrifices from living beings either. [4] But from the time they first tasted meat, they also began offering first-fruits <note>original: "ἀπαρξαμένων" (aparxamenōn) - the practice of dedicating the first portion of a meal or harvest to the gods</note> from animals. Therefore, even now it is surely fitting that the person who abstains from those creatures should make offerings from the things which he actually handles.

§ 34. [1] We, too, shall therefore sacrifice; but we shall sacrifice, as is fitting, different sacrifices to different powers. [2] To that God, indeed, who is over all—as a certain wise man <note>Likely referring to the Pythagorean philosopher Apollonius of Tyana</note> said—we shall offer nothing that is perceptible to the senses, neither burning incense nor even calling him by name. [3] For there is nothing material that is not immediately "impure" to an immaterial being. [4] For this reason, even the spoken word, produced by the voice, is not appropriate for Him...

<column-break/>

...we find this custom: that when they did not eat from living things, they did not perform sacred rites from them either; instead, they offered first-fruits from that which they ate. For which reason it is fitting, even now, that he who abstains from animals should make offerings from those things which he touches.

§ 34. We shall therefore sacrifice as well; but we shall sacrifice, as is appropriate, different sacrifices, seeing as we are offering to different powers. To the God who is truly above all, as a certain wise man says, we offer nothing that is sensible <note>Meaning "perceptible to the physical senses"</note>, neither burning incense nor naming Him. For there is nothing material which does not immediately become impure when brought to the immaterial. For this reason, not even the word which is expressed by the voice is suitable for Him.

---

<margin>
4. **"From the time they tasted."** Reiske <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note> suggests the Greek should read "from the time they indeed tasted" or "from the time they tasted," referring specifically to the animals or animal food. The Meerman manuscript reads: "from the time he touched."
</margin>

<margin>
5. **"Which he touches."** The Greek words for "touching" and "handling" are used particularly for the contact with foods one eats. Similar terms—"touch, taste, handle"—were grouped together by St. Paul in Colossians 2:21 regarding forbidden foods. Our author uses "touch" and "handle" in Book IV, 17, and "to handle food" in III, 18. Julian <note>The Emperor Julian, known as "the Apostate"</note> says in Oration VI, "nothing prevents handling." Sophocles uses "touch" similarly in *Oedipus Rex*, line 1464.
</margin>

<margin>
1. **"We too, then, shall sacrifice..."** Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father</note> uses these words, up to the phrase "but to his offspring," in his work *Against Julian*, Book II. Shortly after, the author speaks of "different sacrifices," just as the ancients everywhere command that different types of worship be offered to the gods according to their different conditions. Read Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries*, I, 15 and V, 18. We saw what these "powers" are called in section 2.
</margin>

<margin>
2. **"To the God indeed..."** You may read these words and what follows until the end of the paragraph also in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IV; and again up to "to his offspring" in *Proof of the Gospel*, Book III. Nothing should be said here regarding the rank and dignity of the gods. However, compare what we remark regarding the "God over all" at section 37. In the margin of the Meerman manuscript, this scholarly note was read: "Note: what kind of sacrifice should be brought to the God over all." Shortly after, instead of "things perceptible to the senses," Cyril writes "a sensible thing," but Eusebius confirms our reading in both places. In another place, "burning incense" is written as "sacrificing."
</margin>

<margin>
3. **"Which is not to the immaterial immediately..."** The most learned R.W. <note>Possibly Thomas Gale or another contemporary editor</note> praises these words to illustrate those of Hierocles in *The Golden Verses*: "For what would you bring to such a one from the..." but he writes "immaterial" <note>Greek variant: anylō vs. aylō</note>. It is also published this way in Cyril. I must provide for you one hilarious French interpreter to laugh at, who took our word in Book I, 41, to refer to "flutes."
</margin>

<margin>
4. **"Therefore not even the word..."** Eusebius in *Proof of the Gospel* writes: "Therefore neither the word to him, nor that according to the voice... nor..." but in another place he follows our text and Cyril; though here, instead of "defiled," he has "polluted."
</margin>

<summary>Porphyry argues that the highest, immaterial God should not be worshiped with material offerings or even spoken words, as the material world is "impure" compared to the divine essence. This page features extensive scholarly commentary linking Porphyry's Neoplatonism to early Christian writers like Eusebius and Cyril of Alexandria.</summary>

...nor that which is within, if it has been defiled by a passion of the soul. But with a pure soul and pure thoughts concerning Him, we worship Him. It is necessary, therefore, that having been joined with Him and made like Him, we should offer the elevation of our own mind as a sacred victim to God; which same act is both a hymn and our salvation. In a contemplation of the soul free from passions, the sacrifice to this God is perfected. But for those born from Him—the intelligible gods <note>In Neo-Platonic thought, "intelligible gods" are divine entities that exist in the realm of pure thought/intellect, rather than the physical world.</note>—a hymn expressed in words is now also added.

...nor that which is within, whenever it has been defiled by a passion of the soul; but through pure silence and pure thoughts about Him, we worship Him. It is necessary, then, that having been joined and made like Him, we should bring our own elevation as a sacred sacrifice to God, this same thing being both a hymn and our salvation. In the passionless contemplation of the soul toward this God, this sacrifice is completed. But to His offspring—the intelligible gods—one must now also add the singing of hymns from the spoken word.

5. *Through pure silence.*] The formula for commanding silence was well known in the sacred rites of the ancients. The Pythagoreans and Egyptians especially honored God with silence. See *our author* <note>The commentator is referring to Porphyry's other work</note> in *The Cave of the Nymphs*, p. 266; and *Iamblichus* in *On the Mysteries*, VIII, 3. And to whom is their Harpocrates <note>The Egyptian god of silence, often depicted with a finger to his lips.</note> unknown? *Proclus* in *Platonic Philosophy*, II, 11: "But with silence, to hymn that which is inexpressible, and which is cause-less before all causes." I wonder whether that sacred silence should be illustrated by those things read in *Psalm 65*, 2 <note>In the Hebrew tradition, this is Psalm 65:1. The Latin Vulgate/Septuagint tradition often translates the opening as "To you, silence is praise."</note>. If you further observe that our author thereafter opposes this silence to "the singing of hymns from the spoken word," and that the common reading is found the same way in two places in *Eusebius* and *Cyril*, you will perhaps judge it sufficiently asserted, even though *Felicianus* read it as "of the soul" <note>original: "ψυχῆς" (psychēs)</note>, which uniquely pleased Gale in his notes on *Iamblichus*, *On the Mysteries*, VIII, 3. Those who understand the nature of sacred rites know that this does not contradict what *Iamblichus* commands in *On the Mysteries*, VII, 4—that "words akin to the gods must be used"—or that the Pythagoreans prayed even with a clear voice, as *Clement of Alexandria* teaches in *Stromata*, Book IV.

However, since it is read this way in the printed versions, that manuscript does not differ from the author's reading, as in the three variations that follow; it agrees with the printed *Eusebius*. For on the second page it has "offspring," and in the third "first-fruit" <note>original: "ἀπαρχὴ" (aparchē)</note> in the nominative case, which I think is more true. Likewise, "He holds the essence together in being," with great variety, which I approve of. <term>VICTORIUS</term> <note>Pietro Vettori, a 16th-century Italian scholar.</note>. *Cyril* also has "we worship." But the same later says "it is necessary then." This is an excellent precept, which our author and others often emphasize. R. W. collected testimonies for *Hierocles* in *The Golden Verses*, p. 30. We know that the divine man <note>The Apostle Paul</note> commends "rational worship" <note>original: "λογικὴν λατρείαν" (logikēn latreian)</note> in Romans 12:1.

7. *Elevation.*] The transfer of our souls, being called away from decaying things toward divine and immortal ones. Commonly called "the elevation of the heart to God" and "abstraction." <term>REISK</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note>. See *Budaeus*, and those things from him in *Stephanus* in his *Thesaurus*; and the things that *Gale* disputes against *Iamblichus* on this passage in *On the Mysteries*, V, 22. *Cyril* has "guidance," then "to bring to," and likewise *Eusebius* in *Preparation for the Gospel*, but not in the other passage. For "being a hymn," *Cyril* has "hymning."

These should be corrected from this source. There are also things similar to this passage which are read in the same *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book III, p. 122, C. Furthermore, the word "the" before "God" is not used by *Eusebius* or *Cyril* or...

2. *To encounter them through offerings.*] I suggest it should read *names* <note>original: *onomasin*</note>. Eusebius: *Preparation for the Gospel* v. 8. In the word *encounter* <note>original: *tynchanein*</note> is understood "calling upon," or "obeying," or "befriending," or something similar. REISKE: The celebrated Abresch suggested *invocations* <note>original: *anaklemasi*</note> or "addresses." Suidas: *anaklesis* means "calling upon." Likewise, "to encounter the gods" means "to find them gracious." Clarified in Thucydides p. 19 and similarly page 167. Aeschylus in *The Suppliants*: "not to encounter the Olympian gods."

3. *To the gods indeed within the heaven, wandering etc.*] LIPSIUS: *in the heaven*. These matters pertain to the theology of Pythagoras, which is the same as the doctrine of the Egyptians. He held the sun, the moon, and the other stars as gods, all of whom are "intellectual living beings and gods." Hierocles says their whole consists of the incorporeal and the body: see his *Commentary on the Golden Verses* p. 284.

<column-break/>

R. W. Plato is also said to have distinguished divinities into the *unbegotten god and those who have come to be in the world of heaven, both the planets and the fixed stars*. See Cuper: *Observations* III, 16. Gale on Iamblichus: *On the Mysteries* I, 17. and others.

Plotinus, if I am not mistaken, or Plato. But the former is more likely. REISKE. Instead of "we might kindle," Valentinus had rewritten "kindling" without necessity. We often come across the opinion of the Theologian which he adds. In Plato: *Laws* VI. p. 875. C. and others. We see often now that Pythagoras and others taught these things. His maxim is well known: "do not sacrifice without meal," which Lomeier, in *On Purifications* ch. 24, compares with the Jewish saying "without flour there is no Law."

6. **"Nor from a blood-stained hearth..."**] We spoke above concerning the bloodless altar of Pythagoras. Let the Grammarians teach what an *eschara* <note>Greek: $\dot{\sigma}\chi\acute{\alpha}\rho\alpha$, a hearth or low altar</note> properly is. Albert in his notes on Hesychius, Valckenaer in his *Animations on Ammonius*, and the Scholiast on Euripides' *Phoenician Women* (line 647), with the note of that most elegant man, treat this abundantly. Instead of "from" <note>$\dot{\alpha}\phi'$</note>, Valentinus had corrected it to "upon" <note>$\dot{\epsilon}\phi'$</note>, and for "outside" <note>$\stackrel{\prime}{\epsilon}\xi\omega$</note> he corrected it to "goes out" <note>$\dot{\epsilon}\xi\grave{\iota}$</note>; both are incorrect.

7. **"But he knows, being concerned with piety..."**] In the three verses that follow, three variations of the writing are found in the same author <note>Eusebius</note>, who cites them in his fourth book; I judge these should be preferred to this reading. For first, "he of piety" is read there: yet our manuscript does not differ from the printed one in this, and as it were applies itself to the author's reading, although it is clearly disturbed in this part, for it has: "he knows that when of piety," and below "but to daemons," "but either to the good." At the very end, "of those needing them." **VICTORIUS.** See Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IV, p. 153 C, where Viger writes that our "that" <note>$\stackrel{\prime}{o}\tau\iota$</note> can be approved instead of "since indeed" <note>$\stackrel{\prime}{\alpha}\tau\epsilon$ $\delta\grave{\eta}$</note>. But that which is in Eusebius is uniquely true, for it is also thus in the Leipzig Codex. To those words "not to gods is it sacrificed, but to daemons," Abresch had well added this from the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 10:20: "But that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils <note>daemons</note>, and not to God." See also what our author says below in section 58. Those words "and to others" I cannot digest. Eusebius is correct; the "the" <note>$\tau\grave{\alpha}$</note> in "transcribe" had erroneously fallen out in the Meerman manuscript.

8. **"And of those, how far..."**] I cannot explain these things.

<column-break/>

The sense seems to require: "and how far it is necessary for those needing their help to proceed." <note>Latin: *& quo ad progredi deceat eos, qui eorum ope egeant.*</note> **REISKE.** Victorius gave the reason. "Of him" <note>$\alpha\dot{\upsilon}\tau o\tilde{\upsilon}$</note> could indeed stand, namely "to sacrifice." However, I have greater faith in Eusebius. Compare Viger there, who preferred: "and how far, of those needing the same things." For the Theologian knew not only whose part it was to sacrifice to them, but also "how far," namely "the sacrificing is." To what extent they ought to proceed in sacrificing.

9. **"Let it be laid down as 'blessed'..."**] A marginal note in the Meerman manuscript: "In the Ionic dialect, instead of 'auspicious' <note>$\epsilon\stackrel{\prime}{\upsilon}\phi\eta\mu\alpha$</note>, and they say 'to pray' <note>$\epsilon\dot{\upsilon}\xi o\mu\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\nu$</note> instead of 'to speak auspiciously' <note>$\epsilon\dot{\upsilon}\phi\eta\mu\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\nu$</note>." We have "let it be laid down as blessed for me" according to Herodotus in Plutarch, from where Theodoret excerpted it in his *Discourse on Oracles*, p. 625; and it is frequent in others, for it was like a proverb. See the learned men on Magister Thomas under "To pray," and Wesseling on Herodotus II, 171; they have spoken of it abundantly.

He has "unblamable" <note>$\dot{\alpha}\nu\epsilon\mu\acute{\epsilon}\sigma\eta\tau o\nu$</note> instead of "in the middle" <note>$\dot{\alpha}\nu\grave{\alpha}$ $\mu\acute{\epsilon}\sigma o\nu$</note>, but agrees on "to indicate" <note>$\mu\eta\nu\acute{\upsilon}\epsilon\nu$</note>, for which either "he indicates" or, as Reiske preferred, "he will indicate" or "he is able to indicate" should have been said, unless this is Porphyrian brevity. "Setting forth... to indicate," namely "it is necessary," etc.

11. **"Setting forth..."**] Perhaps "having been set forth." **REISKE.**

# P O R P H Y R Y

...I believe I must put forward their explanation. For they speak in this way:

§ 37. The first god, being incorporeal <note>existing without a physical body</note>, immobile, and indivisible, and not being within anything else, nor even bound within himself, stands in need of nothing external, just as has been said. Indeed, not even the Soul of the World <note>the 'Anima Mundi,' the spirit that animates the physical universe</note> needs any external thing. Although she possesses three-dimensional extension and is naturally self-moving, she is designed by nature to choose to move herself and the body of the world in a beautiful and orderly way according to the highest principles. She has received the body of the universe into herself and embraced it, even though she herself is incorporeal and free from all passion. 

<column-break/>

I think I should put forward their explanation. For they speak in this manner:

§ 37. The first god is indeed incorporeal, immovable, and indivisible; he exists neither in any place nor is he bound within himself, and he requires no external thing, just as was stated. Moreover, the Soul of the World itself requires no external thing: for she possesses within herself the capacity to be complete in three dimensions and to move naturally from within herself. By her nature, she intends and chooses to move herself and the body of the world in a good and orderly fashion according to the best reasons; she has admitted the world's body into herself and embraced it, though she is considered incorporeal and free from every external influence. 

<column-break/>

As for the remaining gods—the world itself, and the fixed and wandering stars <note>the planets</note>—which consist of soul and body and are visible gods, thanks must be returned to them in the manner already mentioned, through inanimate <note>bloodless</note> sacrifices. What remains for us, then, is the multitude of invisible beings,

<column-break/>

As for the rest of the gods—the world, and both the wandering and non-wandering stars—which consist of soul and body and are visible gods, thanks ought to be given to them in the manner stated, by means of inanimate sacrifices. What remains is the multitude of invisible beings,

---

<margin>1. **The first god is incorporeal, etc.** This is the one they call "the one who is first over all and the father and king of all" <note>original Greek: τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι πρῶτον τε ὄντα καὶ πάντων πατέρα καὶ βασιλέα</note>. Plato calls him the "greatest of the gods" <note>original: μέγιστον τῶν θεῶν</note> and "the helmsman of the universe and the greatest spirit" <note>original: τὸν τοῦ παντὸς κυβερνήτην καὶ μέγιστον δαίμονα</note>. Other gods and spirits <note>daemons</note> of a lower order are substituted under him. See what Eusebius argues on this matter from the theology of the ancient Greeks in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book III, page 141, concerning the nature, distinctions, duties, and deceptions of spirits; our author [Porphyry] speaks at length on these, but I say nothing because it has been discussed by many. Those treasures or storehouses are open to anyone, and therefore they should not be plundered <note>i.e., repeated unnecessarily</note> here. They had Plato as their guide. See Gale on Iamblichus's *Mysteries* I, 5 and II, 1, and Cuper’s *Observations* III, 16.</margin>

<margin>2. **Neither... nor.** I have a hundred examples at hand in which these particles vary; sometimes "neither... nor" <note>original: οὐδὲ, οὔτε</note> and sometimes "nor... neither" <note>original: οὔτε οὐδὲ</note> is said. The same logic applies to the words *mēde* and *mēte*. The notes by D’Orville on Chariton VIII, 8 will be sufficient. A little later, Valentinus correctly changed "the [thing] well" <note>original: τοῦ καλῶς</note> to "the beautiful [thing]" <note>original: τὸ καλῶς</note>.</margin>

<margin>3. **And for the rest of the gods.** I read "But for the rest..." <note>original: τοῖς δὲ λ. θ.</note>. I have Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note>, Lipsius, and the Meerman manuscript as my witnesses; and soon from the same Cyril, "thanks should be returned" <note>original: ἀντευχαριστέον</note>.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s discussion of the hierarchy of divine beings. Having previously described the "First God" and the "Soul of the World," he now moves down the scale to "daemons"—spirits that occupy the space between gods and mortals.</meta>

### On Abstinence, Book II.
Y 2

...whom Plato called daemons without distinction <note>original Greek: "adiastolōs," meaning generally or without specific categorization</note>. Among these, those who have been named by men receive honors equal to the gods and other forms of worship among various peoples. Others, for the most part, have not been given specific names, but receive both a name and veneration obscurely from certain people in villages or specific cities. The rest of the multitude is called by the common name of "daemons." Regarding all of them, however, people are convinced that if they become angry because they are neglected or deprived of their established worship, they will inflict harm; conversely, they believe these spirits will benefit those who have made them favorable through vows, supplications, sacrifices, and other such acts.

§ 38. But since the understanding of them is confused and leads to much calumny <note>misrepresentation or false accusation</note>, their nature must be distinguished in this discourse...

<column-break/>

...whom Plato called daemons without distinction. Among these, some have been named by men and obtain honors equal to the gods and other service among each people; others, for the most part, have not been named at all, but by some in villages or certain cities, they obtain both a name and worship in an obscure manner. The rest of the multitude is thus addressed by the common name of daemons. There is a conviction concerning them all: that they might indeed do harm if they are angered by being overlooked and not obtaining the customary service, and again, that they might be benefactors to those who appease them with prayers, supplications, sacrifices, and the things that follow.

§ 38. Since the concept of them is confused and moves into much slander, it is necessary to distinguish...

---

<column-break/>

<margin>4. *“Called daemons without distinction”*] Fogeroll and G. Cuper (Observations III, 16) read this as *specific daemons* <note>original: "idiosolous"</note>; for one is called *idiosolos* who is sent to protect or perform some specific thing. Felicianus and Marcilio Ficino seem to have read it as *without distinction* <note>original Latin: "indistinctos"</note>, for both rendered it as such. I, therefore, should attempt nothing against the faith of the manuscripts. It says that Plato calls those who are distinguished from the gods he had just listed "daemons" in a general sense, or indiscriminately, and we see immediately that this is true. This is confirmed by what follows: *“The rest of the multitude is thus addressed by the common name of daemons.”*</margin>

<margin>5. *“God-like honors.”*] Thus we find *god-like honors* <note>original Greek: "timai isotheoi"</note> in Diodorus Siculus (I, 90) and others. Learned men have most diligently illustrated this style of speaking in notes on Paul’s letter to the Philippians (II, 6). However, it does not always signify honors equal to the divine in every respect, as in that fragment of Menander (p. 238): 
> Law prescribes to allot god-like honors to parents
as the learned man observes there.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>6. *“The rest of the multitude.”*] In the Leipzig manuscript, the word “but” is missing, and shortly after, “only” is written instead of “daemons.” both are errors.</margin>

<margin>7. *“With prayers.”*] Read as *those* <note>correcting the Greek grammar</note>. Be careful not to refer *those* to *themselves*, for it refers back to *those being appeased*. REISKE. Thus they established that daemons did not ward off the evils they had brought upon cities and peoples until they had been appeased. Read what Gale noted on Iamblichus’s *On the Mysteries* (I, 13). We also find the phrase *“to appease the gods”* in Plutarch (Vol. I, p. 176 B) and Aristides (Vol. I, p. 18).</margin>

<meta>catchword: lai</meta>

# PORPHYRY

...by reason of their nature. For perhaps it is necessary, as they say, to reveal the source from which error concerning them has arisen among men <gloss>1</gloss>. We must therefore make a division in this manner. Those souls which, having sprung from the whole, govern great parts <gloss>2</gloss> of the regions below the moon <gloss>3</gloss>, leaning upon a spirit <term>pneuma: a subtle, airy substance or "spirit-body" that connects the soul to the physical world</term> but ruling over it according to reason—these must be considered good daemons <note>original: "daimones". In the ancient world, a daemon was a mediating spirit, not necessarily evil like the modern "demon."</note> who manage everything for the benefit <gloss>4</gloss> of those subjects under their care <gloss>5</gloss>, whether they preside over certain animals, or assigned fruits, or even those things that exist for the sake of these, such as moderate rains and winds...

<column-break/>

...we must distinguish. For perhaps it is necessary, they say, that the source from which error concerning these beings has fallen upon men should be made manifest. Therefore, a division must be used in this way: Whosoever souls, having arisen from that universal whole, govern the great parts of the places which are below the moon, leaning indeed upon a spirit, but themselves ruling over it according to reason: these are to be esteemed as good daemons, and those who procure all things for the utility of those whom they preside over: whether they preside over certain animals, or certain fruits, or those things which exist for the sake of these: of which kind are rains and winds.

---

<column-break/>

1. *Concerning them, to reveal.*] The translator whom we have followed distinguishes the text well here, differently than was previously customary.

2. *Of the regions below the moon.*] They commonly assign this tract of space to the daemons: *between the highest ether and the lowest earths, positioned in that intervening space of air (divine middle powers) through which both our desires and our merits pass to the gods.* Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*, p. 101. Who, on p. 103 of the same work, says the Daemons were allotted the regions of air bordering the earth, and no less confined by heaven. Learned men have brought together many things of this kind from the decrees of the Jews and Philosophers to illustrate Paul’s letter to the Ephesians 2:2, where the evil genius is called the *ruler of the power of the air*. *Sextus Empiricus:* other souls also *inhabit the region below the moon*. On which matter see *Needham* on Hierocles’ *Golden Verses*, p. 437.

3. *Leaning upon a spirit.*] This passage is very obscure; from p. 82, 18 it appears that for the Platonists, *pneuma* (spirit) is the principle of evil, madness, and blindness. Almost nothing occurs to me in my haste that fits the matter, unless we think this is something: *resisting that spirit.* *Resisting that spirit which rushes blindly.* Then the word

<column-break/>

*antereidos* (resisting) would be derived from *eris* (strife). —REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a famous German physician and philologist.</note>. I understand it as that subtle, spiritual *pneumatic* body which they attributed to Daemons, concerning which see § 39 and 42. Just as *daemons having acquired a spirit* are mentioned by *Tatian: Oration to the Greeks, 20*, and at the end of this section, *to rule over the continuous spirit*. *Marsilio Ficino* <note>The famous Renaissance Neoplatonist who translated Plato and Porphyry into Latin.</note> in his version retained the Greek word *apereidomenai* and translated it as *leaning upon*, or *clinging to*, or *placed upon the spirit*. Similarly, *images flowing from all things* in *Synesius:* whenever they encounter the psychic spirits — they lean upon these, and rest as if upon a perch. *On Dreams*, p. 138. In the *Leipzig Manuscript* it was *which things we saw in the spirit*.

4. *Benefit of those coming.*] Perhaps *of those praying*, or *of those approaching*, or finally *of those offering first-fruits*. —REISKE. *Valentinus* had corrected it to *of those being ruled*. Not bad. *Felicianus* also seems to have read it this way, and the following words could confirm it. *Marsilio Ficino read the common version, translating it as "to procure all things for the utility of those things which are done."*

5. *Whether presiding over certain animals.*] *Origen: Against Celsus, Book VIII* says that not Daemons but angels preside over the produce of fruits and the offspring of animals. *See Gale on Iamblichus: On the Mysteries, V, 17.* Like other things, they received these ideas from the Platonists.

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK II.
-> Y 3 <-

...moderate winds, clear skies, the seasonal temperatures of the year, and other things that contribute to these. Likewise, if they preside over the arts—both those pertaining to music and all education, as well as medicine, gymnastics, and similar pursuits. For it is in no way possible that these beings should both supply benefits and be made the authors of harm in those same matters. Among these must also be numbered those who, as Plato says, are "conveyors," <note>original: "πορθμεύοντας" (porthmeuontas) - literally ferrymen or messengers</note> announcing deeds from men to the gods and from the gods to men. For they bring our prayers to the gods as if to judges,

<column-break/>

...moderate winds, clear skies, the seasonal temperatures of the year, and other things that contribute to these. <gloss>6</gloss> They also serve us in matters of music, all education, <gloss>7</gloss> medicine, gymnastics, or anything similar to these. For it is impossible for these same beings to both provide benefits and again be the <gloss>8</gloss> causes of harm in those same matters. Among these must be numbered <gloss>9</gloss> those who are "conveyors," as Plato says, announcing the things from men to the gods and the things from the gods to men; bringing our prayers to the gods as if to judges, and...

---

...the ancient Christians did this, though it greatly displeased Jerome. Read the Distinguished Scholar on the *Shepherd of Hermas* in Cotelier’s *Apostolic Fathers*, Volume I, page 83, and on Origen’s *Commentary on Numbers*, page 323. Regarding that ministry of Daemons, when Apuleius said in *On the God of Socrates*, page 102: "all these intermediate powers obey <note>original: "obediunt"</note> between men and gods," one should immediately rewrite "perform" or "traverse" <note>original: "obeunt"</note> instead.

6. **They also serve us, etc.**] The Leipzig manuscript reads: "they serve us in the arts and those things pertaining to music." If we follow the traces of this reading, it leads us toward the truth. For it seems Porphyry wrote that they "lead us in the arts and those things pertaining to music." That is, these beneficent minds are our guides and teachers of both the illiberal and the liberal arts over which the Muses preside. Having first spoken of the needs of farmers, he then adds: "to us ourselves, who devote effort to the arts." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a renowned German physician and philologist</note>. This passage was foully corrupted, but we can heal it with the help of the manuscripts; for as it is in the Leipzig manuscript, so it is in the Bodleian and Meerman manuscripts. The word for "arts" <note>Greek: "τεχνῶν" (technon)</note> is so certain that nothing is more certain. But instead of "to us," <term>FELICIANO</term> <note>Giovanni Bernardino Feliciano (c. 1490–1552), an editor and translator of Porphyry</note> seems to have read "on the one hand," which <term>DAVIES</term> adopted in his notes on Lactantius, chapter 28, and which the celebrated <term>RUHNKEN</term> advised in his most kind letters.

7. **Medicine and gymnastics.**] Read on this

<column-break/>

matter Iamblichus’s *On the Mysteries*, Section III, 28, and the notes made there by <term>GALE</term> <note>Thomas Gale (1635–1702), an English classical scholar</note>.

8. **Causes of [harm].**] Instead of "causes" in the dative <note>Greek: "αἰτίοις"</note>, read "causes" in the accusative <note>Greek: "αἰτίας"</note>. <term>VALENTI</term>. Or use "guilty" as an adjective, or rather "authors" <note>Greek: "αἰτίους"</note>. <term>REISKE</term>. The latter was also preferred by the famous <term>ABRESCH</term>, and rightly so.

9. **And those who are conveyors...**] Plato in the *Symposium*, page 1194 A, describes the nature of Daemons as "interpreting and conveying to the gods the things from men, and to men the things from the gods." Following Plato, Aristides (Volume II, page 106) and Apuleius in *On the Doctrines of Plato* write: "They believe Daemons—whom we may call Spirits and Household Gods <note>original: "Genios & Lares"</note>—to be ministers of the Gods, guardians of men, and interpreters if men want anything from the Gods." And in *On the God of Socrates*, page 101, he says: "He calls daemons the carriers of prayers from here [earth] and gifts from there [heaven] between the inhabitants of heaven and mortals." More on this matter can be found in <term>CUPER</term>, *Observations* III, 16, and <term>NEEDHAM</term> in his notes on Hierocles’ *Golden Verses of Pythagoras*, page 369. Thus, there is no need to explain this as the celebrated man did in his notes on Chariton VI, 2, regarding the persuasion of the ancients who believed one divinity could be turned and moved to mercy through another. What the Platonists attribute to Daemons, the Christians contribute almost entirely to the Angels, whom the divine man [St. Paul] says are sent for a pious ministry in...

# PORPHYRIUS
-> Page 174 <-

<column-break/>

...their exhortations and warnings, bringing them out to us along with prophecies. <margin>10</margin> But those souls which do not control the conjoined <term>spirit<note>The word used here is "pneuma," which in Neoplatonic thought refers to a "spirit-vehicle" or subtle body that connects the immaterial soul to the material world.</note></term>, but for the most part are even controlled by it, are led and carried away excessively whenever the rages and desires of the spirit gain momentum. These souls, though they are also daemons, would rightly be called evildoers.

§ 39. And all these, as well as those of the opposite power, are <margin>1</margin> invisible and completely imperceptible to human senses; for they are not <margin>2</margin> clothed in a solid body, nor do they all have one form, but...

<column-break/>

...their counsels and warnings through prophecies they explain to us. But the souls which do not rule over the spirit joined to them, but are mostly even overcome by it, and are thence driven and carried violently whenever the rages and desires of the spirit have gained incitement: these indeed are also themselves daemons, but are rightly called malicious daemons.

§ 39. And indeed all these, and those who are endowed with contrary power, are altogether invisible, and of such a kind that they can in no way be perceived by human senses, for they do not have a solid body wrapped around them: nor do they have one form all...

---

<margin>Epistle to the Hebrews 1:14. *Elsner on Paul, 1 Corinthians 11:11.*</margin>
10. *But those souls etc.*] <note>original: "Ὅσαι δὲ ψυχαὶ &c."</note> The following sixteen verses are placed by the same author <note>Eusebius of Caesarea</note> in the same book. However, the writing in these places differs from what is now found in the author. The phrase "because of this" <note>original: "διὰ τοῦτο"</note> is used with the middle word removed. For whereas before these words in the printed version of Pamphilus it says "they are greatly mastered" <note>original: "πολὺ κεκράτηνται"</note>, in the manuscript copy it says "and they are controlled" <note>original: "καὶ κρατοῦνται"</note>, as in Porphyry below "and they themselves" <note>original: "καὶ αὐταὶ"</note>. Likewise "but only in shapes" <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ἢ ἐν σχήμασι"</note> is a small part of the speech added. And immediately: "and their forms characterizing their spirit." <note>original: "καὶ χαρακτηρίζουσαι τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτῶν αἱ μορφαί."</note> What is read in the printed version, "that which is by the souls" <note>original: "τὸ δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν ψυχῶν"</note>, is faulty, and as here, it ought to be read in the dative case "to the" <note>original: "τῷ"</note>, as I found it written in the manuscript of Eusebius. That phrase "and to be changed" <note>original: "καὶ τρέπεσθαι"</note> is correct, and it is necessary to correct Porphyry accordingly. Just as in these words, with the two names kept more intact: "those who assign more to the passible part [of the soul] the region near the earth, [saying] that nothing of the evils etc." <note>original: "οἱ πλεῖον τῷ παθητικῷ νέμοντες τὸν περίγειον τόπον, οὐδὲν ὅτι τῶν κακῶν &c."</note> in the following verse, "having" <note>original: "ἔχοντες"</note>, which was faulty in the author's text. Since what follows has been varied in the same author...

...in the printed book, and it is read there: "and having been removed from the natural happiness derived from the better [sort]" <note>original: "ἐξηρημένων τε τῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ κρείττονος φυσικῆς εὐδαιμονίας"</note>, I do not think it ought to be accepted; nor do I think that reading should in any way be preferred to ours. VICTORIUS. <note>Pietro Vettori, a 16th-century Italian philologist.</note> The passage from *Eusebius* is *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IV, page 171, C. Soon, instead of "and these" <note>original: "καὶ αὗται"</note>, Abresch rightly corrected it to "and themselves" <note>original: "καὶ αὐταὶ"</note>. Lipsius wrongly suggested "to act wickedly" <note>original: "κακοεργεῖν"</note>.

1. *Invisible and completely imperceptible.*] <note>original: "Ἀόρατοι καὶ τελέως ἀναίσθητοι."</note> *Eusebius* [reads]: "both invisible and completely." Iamblichus in *On the Mysteries*, Section I, 20, is so similar to our author that he seems to have taken it from him: "For the daemons are both invisible and in no way graspable by sense." <note>original: "οἱ μὲν γὰρ δαίμονες ἀόρατοί τέ εἰσιν καὶ οὐδαμῶς αἰσθήσει περιληπτοί."</note> Apuleius teaches the same in *On the God of Socrates*, page 106, who says the bodies of Daemons are not visible to anyone at random, unless they present an appearance of themselves by divine will.

2. *Clothed in a solid body.*] <note>original: "Στερεὸν σῶμα περιβ."</note> Exactly as many of the Christians attributed "subtle bodies" to Angels, concerning which see the note to § 42. Soon a distinction is made in *Eusebius* after "in many" <note>original: "πλεῖοσιν"</note>: "their forms being molded and characterizing their spirit, now this way—now that." <note>original: "ἐκτυπούμενοι δὲ καὶ χ. τ. π. αὐτ. αἱ μορφαὶ, τοτὲ --- τοτὲ."</note> Earlier editions of *Porphyry* had "being molded" (feminine) <note>original: "ἐκτυπούμεναι"</note>, and so also the *Meerman Manuscript*. If however after that word...

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s discussion on the nature of demons (daemones), specifically their physical composition and how they differ from divine beings. The previous section likely established that demons possess a form of "spiritual body."</meta>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->**On the Nature of Demons**<-

...but rather impressed with many figures. Moreover, the forms which characterize their spirit itself sometimes appear, and at other times withdraw from sight, becoming obscure. Sometimes those among them who are of the worse sort even change their forms. And indeed, their spirit, insofar as it is corporeal <note>original: "corporeus"; referring to the "pneumatic" or airy body of the demon</note>, is subject to passions and is corruptible. Yet, because it is so bound by their souls that their appearance persists for a longer time, it is nevertheless not eternal; for it is likely that something is constantly flowing away from it and that it admits of nutrition. The bodies of the good demons are established in equal proportion, not unlike the bodies of those things which are visible. Those of the evildoers, however, are unequal—

<column-break/>

—but rather modeled in many shapes. The forms characterizing their spirit sometimes appear, and sometimes are invisible. Sometimes they even change their forms, at least those who are worse. The spirit, in that it is corporeal, is passive and perishable; but by being thus bound by the souls, so that their form remains for a longer time, it is nonetheless not eternal. For it is likely that something flows from it continuously, and that it is nourished. Now, the bodies of the good are in symmetry, just like the bodies of things that are seen. But those of the evildoers are asymmetrical, not more—

***

<margin>
If we wish to distinguish the [textual] difference, as was usually done, it is necessary to restore "modeled" <note>Greek: ἐκτυπούμενοι</note>, which *Valentinus* therefore received into the text. You could also read "modeled forms" <note>Greek: ἐκτυπουμένας μορφάς</note>, so that it refers to "all," but *Viger* preferred this for *Eusebius*. *Gale* on *Iamblichus' Mysteries p. 208* notes "imprinted forms" <note>Greek: ἐντετυπωμένας μορφάς</note> is used by *Eusebius* in *Preparation for the Gospel Book III*. But *Eusebius* also says "demons imprinted in many shapes" in *Book IV*, referring to this very passage. Therefore, one should read it the same way in both places. For "sometimes" <note>Greek: τοτὲ</note>, the *Bodleian Manuscript* had "at some time" <note>Greek: ποτὲ</note>. In earlier editions it was "then" <note>Greek: τότε</note>, but what I have given is from *Eusebius* and is uniquely true. *Abreschius* also saw this beautifully. Finally, compare this passage with what *St. Paul* says in *1 Corinthians 11:14* concerning Satan, who "transforms himself into an angel of light," where scholars find many things of that kind.
</margin>

3. **For it is likely that something flows... and is nourished.** *Eusebius* reads "and is changed" <note>Greek: καὶ τρέπεσθαι</note>, and *Viger* and *Victor* wished to correct it here in that way. To me, it seems *Eusebius* should be amended from our author [Porphyry]. He attributes "not eternal" to the demons because something flows away and admits nutrition. Demons, there-

<column-break/>

-fore, are not everlasting <note>Greek: αἴδιοι</note> because they require food, as *Aristotle* says. Just so, our author [Porphyry] says below that their spiritual nature "is fattened and strengthened by the steam of sacrifices." "To flow away" <note>Greek: ἀποῤῥεῖν</note> is a common word in this matter. *Iamblichus* in *Mysteries V, 10*, speaking on the same subject—though not entirely agreeing with Porphyry—says: "For if there is any body surrounding the demons, which some think is nourished by sacrifices, this is unchangeable and impassive, so that nothing flows from it, etc." See *V. Gale* on this. I notice what might be said in favor of "changed" <note>Greek: τρέπεσθαι</note>, but he who reads the preceding will not expect "it is likely to be changed" here. The learned know those words are often confused. The words from "it is likely" up to "the bodies" are missing in the *Bodleian Manuscript*; *Eusebius* also poorly reads "those of the good."

4. **Not more—** In *Eusebius* 4.22 it is read "those who are more." The learned interpreter translates it thus: *this genus of Demons... as it dwells more willingly and frequently in places nearer to the earth for the sake of fulfilling desire, etc.* VALENTINUS. Perhaps "the greater part is asymmetrical," being mostly inconstant on account of desire and the mutability of passions, and it inhabits the regions bordering the earth. Those neuter—

# PORPHYRY
## On Abstinence, Book II

->**The Nature and Influence of Spirits**<-

...assigning more to the passionate part <note>referring to the irrational part of the soul or spirit</note>, they occupy the region near the earth. There is no evil, therefore, that they do not attempt to perform. For having a character that is entirely violent and treacherous, and being deprived of the protection that comes from the superior spirit <note>original Greek: "daimonion"</note>, they make, for the most part, vehement and sudden attacks like ambushes—sometimes trying to remain hidden, and sometimes using force. For this reason, the sufferings caused by them are sharp; but the cures and the corrections which proceed from the superior spirits seem to be slower. For everything that is good, being both tractable and smooth, proceeds with order and does not overstep what is necessary. If you think in this way, you will never fall into that most absurd opinion of supposing that evils come from the good, or

<column-break/>

...are vulnerable; hence, being more subject to passions, they occupy a place near the earth. There is no evil, therefore, which they do not attempt to bring about. For they have entirely violent and subdolous <note>deceitful or crafty</note> habits; and when they have been deprived of the guardianship of a better spirit, they make vehement and sudden assaults as if from an ambush. At times they strive to remain hidden, and at other times they bring open force. Thus, the evils that proceed from them are swift; but the remedies and corrections which are managed by the better spirits seem for that reason to be slower. This is because everything that is good, since it is easily directed and consistent, proceeds in an orderly fashion and does not miss the proper opportunity. If you are of this opinion, you will never fall into that most absurd sentiment, as to believe either that evils come from the good, or that goods come from the evil

---

The neuter terms "the asymmetrical" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἀσύμμετρον</note> and "assigning" <note>original Greek: νέμον</note> depend on a preceding "the" <note>original Greek: τὸ</note>, where "thing" or "affair" is understood, as is well known. However, it seems rather that something is missing. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note>. You could also read "the greater part" <note>original Greek: τὸ πλεῖον</note>. "To the passionate part" <note>original Greek: τῷ παθητικῷ</note>, that is, "because of the passionate nature," as was favored by the learned man. I believe it is safer to follow *Eusebius* <note>The Church Father Eusebius, who quoted Porphyry extensively</note>. *Viger* saw the point there: with whom, however, it is not therefore necessary to restore "nothing that" <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν ὅ, τι</note> in this place. Regarding the dwelling place of the spirits, it has already been discussed above. That they inhabit thick, dark air close to the earth after being cast down from the ethereal seats was also the opinion of *Origen* <note>an early Christian theologian</note>, whom many other Christians followed. See *Wetstein* on *Origen: Exhortation to Martyrdom*, p. 303.
5. **Having a character.** <note>original Greek: Ἔχοντες ἦθος</note> The *Florentine* edition is wrong, as is the *Leiden* edition which followed it, reading "and having a character" <note>original Greek: ἔχον τε ἦθος</note>. As *Valentinus* has it, so also *Eusebius*, the *Leipzig*, and the *Meerman*—

<column-break/>

—**manuscript.** The things that follow in *Eusebius*, "deprived of the natural happiness from the superior," ought to be corrected from our text.
6. **Vehement... like ambushes.** <note>original Greek: Σφοδρὰς ---- οἷον ἐνέδρας</note> Perhaps "as if from ambush" <note>original Greek: οἷον ἐξ ἐνέδρας</note>. <term>REISKE</term>. Likewise "vehement" <note>original Greek: σφοδρὰς</note>, as in "a more vehement blow" in *Eunapius* <note>a Greek sophist and historian</note> and elsewhere. See *D’Orville* on *Chariton*, V, 2, p. 438.
7. **Sharp indeed are the sufferings.** <note>original Greek: Ὀξέα μὲν τὰ ἐπ’ ἐκ. π.</note> What are called "acute passions" <note>referring to sudden-onset diseases</note> by physicians and lexicographers is well known. For "upon" <note>original Greek: ἐπ’</note>, *Valentinus* had corrected it to "from" <note>original Greek: ἀπ’</note>. It seems it was "by" <note>original Greek: ὑπ’</note>, which is in the *Leipzig* text. The word "cures" <note>original Greek: ἀκέσεις</note>, which he uses immediately, is not unknown to others either, and was correctly rendered in *Hierocles* <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> on the *Golden Verses of Pythagoras*, p. 210. See *Needham* there.
8. **Being tractable.** <note>original Greek: Εὐήνιόν τε ὂν</note> *Suidas* <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> defines "tractable" as "obedient" or "well-reined." Hence a "tractable man" in *Plutarch*.

# PORPHYRY
## On Abstinence, Book II

->**The Deception of Malicious Spirits**<-

...you should think such an opinion exists. For the absurdity of the matter does not consist only in this; rather, it also happens that most people, having conceived the most wicked opinions about the gods, spread them to all other men.

§ 40. For this must be established as one of the greatest harms inflicted by malicious spirits <note>original: "maleficis daemonibus." In the Neoplatonic tradition, daemons were intermediate spirits between gods and humans, capable of being either good or evil</note>: that although they themselves are the cause of the calamities that occur around the earth—such as pestilences, famines, earthquakes, droughts, and other things of that kind—they persuade us that the authors of these things are actually those who are responsible for the exact opposites, that is, for fertility and prosperity. In doing so, they remove themselves from the blame for these calamities. Their first priority is to remain hidden as the ones who cause the offense; then, they lead us to offer supplications and sacrifices to the benevolent gods, making it appear as if it were the gods who were angry. These and similar acts they perform...

<column-break/>

...and [they attribute] good things to the causes of evil. For the argument is not only absurd in this regard, but many people, adopting the most base assumptions about the gods, pass them on to the rest of mankind.

§ 40. For indeed, this must be counted as part of the greatest harm caused by evil-working spirits: that <gloss>1</gloss> they themselves, being the causes of the sufferings around the earth—such as plagues, crop failures, earthquakes, droughts, and the like—persuade us that those who are the causes of the most contrary things (namely, of abundance) are responsible. They exempt themselves from the blame and make it their primary business to escape notice while doing wrong. After this, they turn us toward prayers and sacrifices to the good-working gods, as if they were the ones who were angry. <gloss>2</gloss> These things and similar things they do...

<margin>
1. **They themselves being the causes, etc.** *Origen, Against Celsus, Book VIII, page 765:* "But if one must dare to say, if these are indeed the works of spirits, we shall say that famines, and infertility... and droughts, and even the corruption of the air... all these things spirits perform themselves." He then, on page 785, attributes the care of such matters to angels. You may read other things of the same kind in *Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book V, chapter 4*. But I remember that I have already spoken of these matters above.

2. **These things and, etc.** The twenty-one verses that follow are likewise cited by the same author <note>Eusebius</note> in the same book, not far from the end, and, unless I am mistaken, in a more corrected form. I will therefore indicate the variations. Where it says here "turning toward themselves" <note>original Greek: "ἐπ’ ἀ. ἐπισρ."</note>, in that text it is "upon themselves" <note>original: "ἐφ’ ἑαυτοὺς"</note>. And below, "by means of inflaming such desires," which I think is more accurate. In the following verse, "vanities" <note>original: "κενοδοξίαις"</note>, which I also approve of. For "strange glory" <note>original: "ξενοδ."</note> is clearly a mistake, although in the printed code of Eusebius it is perversely read in the genitive case, singular number, as "of vanity." After "they persuade also regarding the gods," in the verse that follows, "by which they are disturbed." On the second following page, "hearing those who seem wise." And a few words later, "even more about the gods..." However, in the manuscript, as in Porphyry, it is "still more." These words are not read in the example from Plato in Book VII. Nor soul...

# PORPHYRY

They act thus because they wish to turn us away from a correct understanding of the gods and toward themselves. For they delight in all things done so inconsistently and incongruously; and as if putting on the masks of the other gods <note>original: "personas subeuntes"</note>, they take advantage of our lack of wisdom. They win over the masses by inflaming human desires with passions, and with longings for wealth, power, and pleasures, as well as with empty vanity <note>original: "inani gloria"; the Greek text notes "xenodoxiais" (hospitality/strange opinions) but the Latin and notes suggest "kenodoxiais" (vainglory)</note>, from which seditions and wars grow, and things akin to these. And what is the most serious of all...

<column-break/>

...it is not the property of cold to heat, but of its opposite <note>original: "ψυχρότητος τὸ θερμαίνειν"</note>, which are found there. Since that most learned writer was not content with that one example, but added another, he brought in something different from the former and passed on to other matters, if we wish to trust the opinion of the author himself. However, so that the whole matter and where the error remains may be more easily perceived, I will cite the whole passage from Plato: *For I do not think it is the work of heat to cool, but of its opposite. Certainly. Nor of dryness to moisten, but of its opposite. Quite so. Nor indeed is it the work of the good to do harm, but of its opposite.* <note>Quoting Plato's Republic, Book I, 335d</note> Therefore, either Porphyry thought it sufficient to place the former, or if he also cited the later example, which is more likely (for the end of the later part, differing in no way from the end of the former, could have provided an opportunity for a scribe to err), one must consider whether he varied the words and the opinion of the author, or the example; and, as it came to mind, added something suitable for proving the same point. For there are also other variations from the reading of Plato in this testimony taken from there. Moreover, the passage is taken from the first book of the *Republic*: below, *most just indeed... since it would not even be divine.* With two tiny changes, which I nevertheless did not want to omit indicating, and this also remains in the written copy of Eusebius: the word "but" <note>Greek: "δὲ"</note> is placed where it is in Porphyry. <term>VICTORIUS</term> <note>Pietro Vettori (1499–1585), a famous Italian philologist</note>.

<column-break/>

3. **For in all these things etc.**] Those words of Minucius Felix in chapter 27 concerning Daemons harmonize excellently: *They disturb life, they disquiet sleep; creeping also into bodies secretly, they terrify minds and distort limbs, so that they may force men to worship them; so that, fattened by the steam of altars or the sacrificial victims of cattle, they may seem to have cured what they had previously constricted.* See more on those snares of the daemons there. Compare also Gale to Iamblichus II, 10; III, 31; and V, 20, who irrigated his own fields from our author <note>meaning he drew heavily from Porphyry's work</note>, having much to say about the fraud of spirits, how they put on the appearance of better deities and lie that they are those whose form they bear.

4. **To inflame the desires of men with passions etc.**] I have seen to it that "to inflame" <note>Greek: "ἐκκαίειν"</note> is printed instead of "he inflames." For "hospitality" <note>Greek: "ξενοδοξίαις"</note>, Eusebius reads "vainglory" <note>Greek: "κενοδοξ."</note>. For "the" <note>Greek: "ὁ"</note> I had restored "which" <note>Greek: "ὃ"</note>; I later found it thus in Eusebius. <term>VALENT</term> <note>Likely the scholar Henri Valois (Henricus Valesius)</note>. It is most certain that "to inflame" is correct, which Eusebius protects in two places, as do the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts. It is elegantly said "to inflame desires with passions." Indeed, "to desire" and "desire" are used particularly of Venusian [sexual] longing, as has often been observed. However, love is well distinguished from lust: *Let us say this man desires, but does not love* (Maximus of Tyre, XXVII, 4).

5. **With longings for wealth.**] Good Spirits are also "givers of wealth" (Hesiod, *Works and Days*, 146), to which he refers...

**On Abstinence, Book II.**

Z 2

...is the most serious thing; having proceeded from these, they also persuade people of similar things regarding even the greatest gods, to such an extent that they subject even the best god to these accusations—claiming, as they say, that he throws all things into total confusion <note>original: "sursum ac deorsum conturbant," literally "upside down"</note>. This happens not only to the unlearned, but also to many of those who are engaged in philosophy; and this occurs through a mutual cause. For even those practicing philosophy who have not withdrawn from the common course of the masses fall into the same errors as the multitude; and conversely, when the multitude hears things that agree with their own opinions coming from those who appear to be distinguished, they are even more confirmed in holding such views about the gods.

->§ 41.<-

<column-break/>

...the most terrible thing of all; they ascend from these points and persuade others of similar things even concerning the greatest gods, to the point of bringing even the best god under these accusations—by whom, they say, all things have been turned upside down. This has been experienced not only by private citizens, but by not a few of those who spend their time in philosophy. The cause has become mutual; for even those of the philosophers who do not stand apart from the common current <note>original: "κοινῆς φορᾶς" (koines phoras)</note> have ended up with the same views as the masses. And again, when the masses hear things in harmony with their own beliefs from those who seem to be authoritative, they are further strengthened to think even more in this way regarding the affairs of the gods.

->§ 41.<-

***

Plutarch cites this in Volume II, page 417. But also below in Section 42, as others do, he says the desire for riches proceeds from them. For "strange opinions" <note>original Greek: "ξενοδοξ." (xenodoxiais)</note>, we should undoubtedly refer to "vainglory" <note>original Greek: "κενοδοξίαις" (kenodoxiais)</note> based on Eusebius.

6. **And concerning the &c.**] This is well-stated by Valentinus and agrees with Eusebius. Earlier editions had "and the things concerning the gods," where "the things" <note>original: "τὰ"</note> was incorrectly repeated from a previous part. Moreover, the Leipzig manuscript incorrectly had "to these accusations" <note>original: "τοῦ τοῖς ἐγκλ."</note>. I have also restored "by whom" <note>original: "ᾧ"</note> from Eusebius, instead of which "he who" <note>original: "ὁ"</note> was being published. Then "up and down" <note>original: "ἄνω καὶ κάτω"</note> was found in the Pamphilus manuscript, which Vigerus approves.

7. **Happened through one another.**] The learned Abresch had noted a passage from Aristides, Volume I, page 7: "to do... through one another."

8. **From the common current.**] Elsewhere he calls the "common current" <note>term: "κοινὴν φορὰν" (koines phoran) — a phrase referring to the prevailing flow of popular opinion</note> the common opinion of men. See Book IV, sections 9 and 16. It is used no differently in this place to mean that common impulse by which men are usually carried along. It is therefore not necessary to derive this from the meaning of "abundance" or "multitude" and thus take it to mean the "common crowd," as Fabricius does in his notes on Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Logicians*, Book VII, page 379. Regarding what follows, "they ended up with the same," Abresch illustrated this with a line from Aeschylus' *Libation Bearers*, line 208: "to come to the same point with others."

9. **Again, the masses.**] Previously it was read as "again themselves" <note>original: "πάλιν αὐτὰ"</note>. But they must be read separately <note>original: "πάλιν αὖ τὰ"</note>, as I have cared to publish. Eusebius and the Meermann manuscript are correct. Very often in this formula, "again" <note>original: "αὖ"</note> has merged with the following "the" <note>original: "τὰ"</note> through the fault of scribes. See Markland's notes on Maximus Tyrius, XXVI, who also restores it in this place. I doubt, however, whether it should be rewritten thus in Longinus, *On the Sublime*, II, 5, where they want "again the" instead of "themselves." This formula is also corrupted in our author below in Book III, section 22; see there.

10. **Of those who seem.**] "Of those who seem wise" appears twice in Eusebius, page 172 D and page 173 D, which might seem to have arisen from a gloss, for "those who seem" <note>term: "οἱ δοκοῦντες" (hoi dokountes) — an idiom for people of high reputation or social standing</note> is also said simply of those who are in high esteem or distinguished by authority. See many examples in the notes on Paul’s *Letter to the Galatians*, II, 2. Elsewhere, however, Malchus [Porphyry] is accustomed to add what kind of "seeming" people are understood. Furthermore, after "concerning," the word "the" <note>original: "τὰ"</note> ought to be deleted, as Eusebius does not recognize it. A similar error was driven out a little earlier. From the same source, you could read "still" <note>original: "ἔτι"</note> instead of "upon" <note>original: "ἐπὶ"</note>.

# P O R P H Y R Y

<column-break/>

->§ 41.<-

For the art of poetry has further inflamed the misconceptions of men, using a style of speech designed to cause astonishment and wonder, capable of casting a spell and instilling belief in things that are most impossible. <margin>1</margin> Yet we ought to be firmly persuaded of this: that the good never harms, nor does the evil ever benefit. For it is not the property of heat, <margin>2</margin> as Plato says, to cool, but rather its opposite; likewise, it is not the property of the just to cause harm. Surely the divine is by nature the most just of all things, <margin>3</margin> otherwise it would not even be divine. Therefore, this power and portion [of harming] must be cut away from the beneficent <term>daemons<note>In this context, Porphyry refers to "daemons" as intermediary spirits between gods and humans. Unlike the modern word "demon," these could be good, neutral, or deceptive.</note></term>. For a nature that is prone to and desirous of harming is the opposite of one that does good; and opposites can never exist within the same thing. While these [harmful spirits] ruin the mortal race in many ways, and sometimes in great matters, <margin>4</margin> individually there is never a time when the good ones do not attend to their duties, but they also give forewarning—

<column-break/>

§ 41. For poetic eloquence has additionally set fire to the opinions of men, since it employs a style of speaking adapted to induce admiration and stupor, and is of such a kind that it can soothe minds and create faith in things that are the least possible of all. Yet we ought to hold it as a firm persuasion that the good never harms, nor does the evil ever help. For it is not the nature of heat, as Plato says, to make things cold, but of its opposite; thus it is not the nature of the just to inflict any injury. Moreover, the divine power is certainly by nature the most just of all things; otherwise, it would be nothing. Therefore, this power and lot [of harming] must be severed from the well-doing daemons. For a faculty which is accustomed by nature to harm, and wishes to do so, is undoubtedly contrary to the well-doing one, and opposites can in no way exist in the same subject. Since, therefore, those [harmful ones] injure the mortal race of men in many respects, and sometimes in the greatest, the good daemons never cease their individual offices: but dangers—
