# On Abstinence, Book II.

They demonstrate to us, as far as they are able, the dangers hanging over us from evildoers, showing them through dreams, through a divinely inspired soul, and through many other signs. Thus, if someone were capable of distinguishing the things signified, they would recognize and guard against every fraud. For they signify to all, but not all perceive what is signified; nor can everyone read what is written, but only those who have learned their letters. Nevertheless, all deceptions <note>original: "praestigiae" / "γοητεία" (goēteia) - referring to sorcery or illusions</note> are performed through the contrary demons. For those who procure evils through sorceries and charms especially venerate these demons and the one presiding over them.

<column-break/>

-> § 42. <-

...unless, as *Abresch* <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch (1699–1782), a Dutch philologist</note> preferred, you wish to read "there is not when" instead of "not indeed."

5. **Hanging over... dangers.** *Valent.* following *Fogerolles*, corrected the Greek to "encountered." I would prefer "impending" <note>original: "ἐπηρτημένους" (epērtēmenous)</note>. Among the Greeks, this is commonly used for impending danger, punishment, and similar things. "To hang fear over" occurred to us above in Book I, chapters 2 and 9.

6. **Showing through dreams.** They believed the highest God was "all-seeing" <note>original: "παντοδῆ" (pantodē)</note> and signified future things to men through demons. See *Davies* on *Maximus of Tyre*, Dissertation 19. This also happened through dreams. *Apuleius* in *On the God of Socrates*: "as a province is assigned to each, even for the confirming of dreams," etc. See also *Justin Martyr*, Apology I, 17. Likewise, the Jews believed certain dreams proceeded from demons, on which matter see the best interpreters on *St. Paul* to the Ephesians 2:2. Next, "to distinguish" <note>original: "διαιρεῖσθαι" (diaireisthai)</note> means to discern or judge with the mind. See *Bos*, Critical Observations, chapter 6, and the learned discussion on this word by *D'Orville* on *Chariton*.

7. **To know every [danger].** It would be better to read "everyone would know," as I have restored. **VALENT.** The former was very true (and the first hand had given it so in the *Meerman* manuscript), but instead of "would know" from the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* codices, I read "might know." *Abresch* had beautifully attempted to reach the truth by conjecture; however, the *Meerman* manuscript wrongly gives "might guard against."

8. **Nevertheless, through the contrary [demons] etc.** *Eusebius* <note>Early Christian historian</note> has these words up to the end of § 42 in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IV. *Cyril* <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note> has the same, and a little more, in *Against Julian*, Book IV. *Theodoret* also uses most of these in his *Sermon on Angels and Demons*, but he praises these as if taken from *Porphyry’s* books *On the Philosophy from Oracles*. This happens quite often, that he mixes different passages of Porphyry together. For example, in the *Sermon on Sacrifices*, he praises certain things from the books to which we have devoted this work, which in the *Sermon on Oracles* he says were drawn from the books *On the Philosophy from Oracles*. However, it could sometimes happen that the same things were said in different places. In *Theodoret*, "sorcery" <note>original: "γοητεία" (goēteia)</note> ought to be restored from our author in place of "need."

<column-break/>

Many have handed down this idea, and it is clear from *Isaiah 1:11* <note>The verse where God asks, "To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? ... I delight not in the blood of bullocks."</note> and other places that the Jews themselves were infected by this foolish opinion about God. See *Havercamp on Tertullian's Apology, 22.* It is a much more recent doctrine that not the Gods, but only the Demons—and the worse ones at that—delight in such food. This opinion pleased many of the "Fathers," as we call those ancient Theologians; there were even some who claimed that the persecutions pressing upon the Christians were caused by the Demons noticing that, as the Gospel grew stronger, they were being deprived of those delicacies. See *Wetsten on Origen: Exhortation to Martyrdom, Vol. I, p. 303.* Yet that same sentiment was very convenient for the Christian cause, since they could show even from the Platonists <note>The followers of Plato, like Porphyry himself.</note> that victims benefited only evil spirits, not the gods. Therefore, when those [pagan] philosophers saw that this dogma was bringing more harm than benefit to their cause, they rejected it. It is no wonder, then,

<column-break/>

that Iamblichus <note>A later Neoplatonist philosopher who disagreed with Porphyry and defended the use of ritual and sacrifice.</note> and others depart from our author on this matter. Read *Mosheim on Cudworth, Vol. II, p. 1087* and *R.W. on Hierocles’ Golden Verses, p. 52.*

2. **It is nothing to us.** That is, it does not *pertain* to us; see what we said above regarding Book I, § 52.

# PORPHYRIUS

We exert every effort to become like God and those beings who surround Him. This likeness is achieved through <term>impassibility</term><note>original: "apatheia" – a state of being undisturbed by passions or emotions</note>, a clear and distinct understanding of those things which truly exist, and a life directed toward those same realities. Conversely, we strive to become unlike evil men and demons, and generally unlike anything that delights in what is mortal and material. Therefore, in accordance with the words of Theophrastus, we too shall offer sacrifice. With this, the <term>theologians</term><note>Porphyry likely refers to ancient priestly authorities or Orphic/Pythagorean writers</note> have also agreed, knowing that to the extent we neglect the purification of the soul’s passions, to that same extent we are joined to a wicked power; thus, it becomes necessary to appease even that power. For as the theologians say, for those who are bound by external things and do not yet rule over their passions, it is necessary to turn away the malice of this power; otherwise, they will never find rest from their labors.

§ 44. Thus far, let the matters pertaining to sacrifices be explained. Now, regarding what we said from the beginning—that it is not necessary to assume that if animals must be sacrificed, they must also be eaten—we shall demonstrate that one must not eat of animals, even if it is sometimes necessary that they be sacrificed. For all the theologians agree in this: that one must neither touch

<column-break/>

We exert every effort to become like God and those who are around Him, so that we may be made similar to Him: this occurs through impassibility, and a distinct perception of those things which truly are, and a life tending toward these very things: but that we may turn out dissimilar to evil men and demons, and altogether to everyone rejoicing in mortal and material things. Therefore, according to those things which were said by Theophrastus, we also shall sacrifice. With whom the Theologians also have agreed, since they have known that as much as we have neglected the cleansing of the affections of the soul, so much are we joined to a depraved power: so that it is necessary for us to soften even that power. For just as the Theologians say, for those who are bound to external things, and do not yet master their affections, it is necessary for them to avert the mischief of this power also. Otherwise, they will never cease from their labors.

§ 44. Up to this point, however, let those things which pertain to sacrifices be explained. Now, because we said from the beginning, it is not necessary that if animals are to be sacrificed, we should immediately think they are also to be eaten: we shall demonstrate that one must not eat from animals, even if sometimes it is necessary that they be sacrificed. For all theologians agree in this—

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK II.
Aa
<meta>catchword: ce-</meta>

...agree, that from sacrifices which are performed for the sake of averting evils, nothing is to be tasted; rather, they assert that expiatory purifications must be used. For they say that no one should return to the city, or enter a private home, unless they have first cleansed their garments and body in rivers or springs. For this reason, they even command those to whom they have permitted the act of sacrificing to abstain from the animals sacrificed; and before they sacrifice, they must purify themselves through fasting, and especially through abstinence from the flesh of living creatures. For they say that purity and <term>chastity</term><note>The Latin 'castimonia' and Greek 'hagneia' refer to a state of ritual and moral purity, not just sexual abstinence.</note> act as a guard to prevent harm: like a divine symbol and seal, so that a person suffers no evil from those beings whom he approaches while making atonement. For when he is in a state of being contrary to the nature of the things he is doing—and more divine, because he is clearly purer in respect to both the body and the passions of the soul—he remains unharmed, with purity set before him like a defensive wall.

->§ 45.<-

<column-break/>

...[one must not] taste of the things sacrificed in the <term>averting sacrifices</term><note>original: "apotropaiois thysiais" – sacrifices meant to turn away evil spirits or bad luck</note>, and one must use purifications. For they say that no one should go into a city, nor into a private house, without first cleansing garments and body in rivers or a spring. So, they also commanded those whom they allowed to sacrifice to abstain from these sacrificed things, and to sanctify themselves beforehand by fasting and especially by abstinence from living things. For they say that purity is a guard for caution, like a divine symbol or seal, against suffering anything from those beings whom one approaches and appeases. For being in a state contrary to the things he does, and more divine, because he is purer in body and in the passions of the soul, he remains unharmed, having purity wrapped around him like a fortress.

->§ 45.<-

***

<margin>1. *And one must use purifications.*] A <term>purification</term><note>original: "Katharsion"</note>, specifically a "sacred rite," is called an "expiatory lustration." See D'Orville on Chariton VIII, 1. The custom itself—that when they had performed those sacred rites, they did not return home before they had purified their clothes and body with water from either a river or a spring—is known from those who have written about the purifications of the ancients, and Casaubon on Theophrastus, ch. 15, p. 292. Indeed, the "averting" victims were believed to pollute those who touched them. Marsham (Chronicus Canon, Section IX, p. 208) discusses these established sacred rites according to his own judgment.</margin>

<margin>2. *Like a divine symbol or seal.*] Abresch preferred the reading "And like a symbol." He rightly calls the purity of the mind by this name, just as Psellus established that there are "divine symbols in souls" which would put demons to flight. Compare the notes by Elsner on the Revelation of John IX, 4. Casaubon (on Athenaeus III, 32) excellently explained the nature and use of the word. Those words "caution like ... those" are missing in the Meerman manuscript.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>3. *Than the things he does.*] The word "Than" <note>original: "ē"</note> seems as though it should be deleted. He exists in a condition much different than the things he is now doing. For he is occupied with killings <note>referring to the animal sacrifice</note>, and therefore also in the company of evil spirits who delight in slaughter; but he himself is most alienated from all these things. It can also be read as "disposed in the things he does." REISKE: "He is most alienated from these spirits in those very things which he then does." I understand this to refer to those evil spirits of whom he had spoken. To "do" <note>original: "drân"</note> is a technical term for performing sacred rites.</margin>

<summary>This page discusses the strict ritual requirements for "averting" sacrifices, emphasizing that participants must not eat the meat and must undergo rigorous purification to protect themselves from the evil spirits they are appeasing. Porphyry argues that ritual purity—abstaining from meat and fasting—acts as a "divine seal" or "fortress" that shields the soul from harm during these dangerous interactions with the supernatural.</summary>

# P O R P H Y R Y

<column-break/>

§ 45. Hence, even among sorcerers <note>Greek: goēton; Latin: praestigiatores — individuals who perform magic through trickery or demonic invocation</note>, the necessity of such a precaution seems established. However, it cannot be effective for them indefinitely; <gloss>1</gloss> for it is for the sake of licentiousness that they trouble evil spirits. Thus, <term>purity</term><note>Greek: hagneia; Latin: castimonia — ritual and moral cleanliness</note> does not belong to sorcerers, but to divine and god-wise men; it brings a safeguard everywhere to those who use it, through a close connection with the divine. Would that sorcerers also used it always! For then they would not desire to perform sorcery, being blocked by this purity from enjoying those things for which they act impiously. Hence, <gloss>2</gloss> being full of passions, and only abstaining from impure foods for a short time—while still being filled with impurity— <gloss>3</gloss> they pay the penalty for their lawlessness against the whole of nature, partly by those very beings whom they provoke, and partly <gloss>4</gloss> by that Justice which oversees all mortal things—both deeds and thoughts—which is...

<column-break/>

§ 45. From this, the necessity of this kind of precaution extends even to tricksters and sorcerers. Yet it does not always have power in them, because they invoke evil demons for the sake of crimes and lust. Therefore, <term>chastity</term><note>Latin: castimonia</note> does not belong to sorcerers, but to divine men imbued with divine wisdom. This purity, through reconciliation with the gods, is accustomed to bring protection to those who practice it. Indeed, would that sorcerers also practiced it constantly! For they would no longer wish to pursue their deceits, since they would be drawn away from enjoying those things for which they act impiously. Hence, as they are full of disturbances, and after abstaining from impure foods for a little while they are filled again with uncleanness, they suffer the penalties for the crime they commit in their entire operation—partly from those very spirits whom they provoke, and partly also from Justice, who [watches] all mortal deeds and works...

---

<margin>...to say, *to perform sacred rites* <note>original: sacris operari</note>. This manner of speaking is well known, illustrated a hundred times in both languages [Greek and Latin]. See § 59. *Athenaeus, Banquet of the Learned, XIV, 23*: "the ancients called sacrificing 'doing' <note>original: drān</note>."</margin>

1. *For it is for the sake of licentiousness—*] The translator gave "of crimes and lust" <note>original: flagitiorum & libidinis</note>. Indeed, <term>licentiousness</term><note>Greek: aselgeia</note> has a very broad meaning and encompasses every lack of self-control in the soul. Philologists have dealt with this word most diligently in the Epistle to the Romans 13:13 and D'Orville on Chariton 5:6.

2. *Being full of passions, filled.*] Paul also joins these in Romans 1:29: "being filled with all unrighteousness... full of envy" etc. where see Kypke. "Full of passions" and similar phrases occur a hundred times. Compare D'Orville on Chariton 5:8, p. 480, who did not forget Porphyry.

3. *They pay the penalty.*] To pay the penalty <note>original: dikēn tinein</note> properly means *to pay a monetary fine*, and from there it is transferred to other things, signifying to give or endure any punishment. Examples are found everywhere, but were diligently collected by the Learned Man <note>Latin: V. D. — Vir Doctus</note> on Paul's Second Epistle to the Thessalonians 1:9.

4. *By Justice... who oversees all—*] *Hesiod, Works and Days 254*:
> For there is the virgin Justice, born of Zeus,
> Honored and revered by the gods who hold Olympus, etc.

where Graevius says much about that avenging Goddess, who was called Nemesis and was believed to sit by the throne of Jove. That she is said by our author to watch over all mortal works agrees with those things in *Eusebius, On the Praise of Constantine*.

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->**A a 2**<-

...observes both deeds and counsels. Therefore, the purity of a divine man is both internal and external. Just as he strives to abstain from the passions of the soul and from those foods that incite the passions, so he enjoys the food of divine wisdom. He reconciles himself to the likeness of God through right thoughts concerning Him. He is one who is consecrated by an intellectual sacrifice <note>original: *intellectuali sacrificio*; referring to a mental or spiritual offering rather than a blood sacrifice</note>, approaching God with a white garment—which is truly the bright purity of the soul’s freedom from passion <term>impatibilitatis; the state of being unaffected by worldly suffering or emotion</term> and the lightness of the body. He does not approach God burdened by foreign and external juices in the body or by disturbances in the soul.

§ 46. For surely, it is not the case that in temples dedicated to the gods by men...

<column-break/>

...justice. Therefore, the purity of a divine man is both internal and external. He strives to be "fasting" from the passions of the soul and "fasting" from those foods that stir the passions, while "feeding" upon divine wisdom. He makes himself like God through correct thoughts about the Divine. He is a man consecrated by the intellectual sacrifice, approaching God with a white robe—the truly pure state of the soul’s freedom from passion—and with a lightness of body, not burdened by alien and foreign juices <note>original: *χυμῶν* (chumōn); referring to the bodily humors or fluids affected by diet</note> or by the passions of the soul.

§ 46. For surely, if in the temples set apart for the gods by men...

### [Critical Commentary]

<columns>2</columns>

*Eusebius* in his *Praise of Constantine* says the eye of Justice is the overseer of human affairs. I see these and other points already praised by *Kuster* in his notes on *Suidas* regarding the "Eye of Justice." *Synesius* in *On Kingship*, p. 19: "The justice of God sees all and hears all."

5. **Fasting from...** The phrase "fasting from passions" (for the word "from" seems unnecessary to remove) may be compared with that famous and solemn maxim of Pythagoras, if I am not mistaken: "to fast from wickedness." *Reiske* <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note>. *Caelius Rhodiginus* thought this a great and divine saying of Empedocles. To "feed on wisdom" and similar phrases are well known from the Lexicographers.

6. **A man being consecrated.** The form *hierōmenou* is more common, from the verb "to be a priest." It seems the word "man" should be removed as it was placed just above. *Reiske*. Grammarians note a distinction between *hierasthai* and *hierousthai*: the latter is used for things being consecrated, the former for those performing the office of a priest. See *Duker* on *Thucydides* V, 1. I thought *Thomas Magister* meant that *hierasthai* and *hiereuesthai* are said of sacrifices, but only *hierasthai* is said of priests. But interpreters contend the reading there is corrupt. *Eusebius*, perhaps regarding this, says in *Demonstratio Evangelica* I, p. 29: "those consecrated to the God over all, not with cattle-sacrifices... but with right dogmas of true piety." Our author and others repeat this so often that there appears no reason to think he received this from *Paul* in *Romans* 12:1.

7. **A white and pure garment.** Compare the observations at § 19. The white garments of those performing sacred rites are very well known. *Clement of Alexandria* rightly says in *Stromata* IV: "External adornment and purification happen for the sake of a symbol." Thus, white clothes are fitting for priests, according to *Artemidorus* in *The Interpretation of Dreams* II, 3. The *Meermann* manuscript reads "of the body," but then incorrectly reads "winter" instead of "juices."

8. **Burdened.** The Florence and Leiden editions read *bebarumenou*. It comes to the same thing. Both *bareisthai* and *barunesthai* commonly mean to be weighed down, to be sluggish, or to languish; it is attributed to the soul which becomes sluggish through immoderate food, drink, cares, etc. Such is that passage in *Luke's Gospel* 21:34: "lest your hearts be weighed down." On which many learned men have commented.

1. **For surely...** This entire paragraph...

# P O R P H Y R Y

<columns>
And <gloss>2</gloss> one must have clean and unstained sandals on one's feet; yet in <gloss>3</gloss> the temple of the Father—which is this world—is it not fitting to preserve <gloss>4</gloss> the final and outermost "tunic of skin" <note>original: χιτῶνα τὸν δερμάτινον (chitōna ton dermatinon); a Neoplatonic metaphor for the physical body, referencing the "garments of skin" given to Adam and Eve</note> as holy, and to dwell in the temple of the Father with a holy garment? For if the danger lay only in its being defiled, perhaps one could overlook it and be careless. But now, since every sensible body carries the effluence of material demons <term>material demons; in Neoplatonism, lower spirits associated with matter and physical desires</term>, along with the impurity resulting from flesh and blood, a power that is <gloss>5</gloss> friendly and welcoming to this impurity is present due to similarity and kinship.

§ 47. Whence correctly the theologians...

<column-break/>

...we ought to wear pure shoes, free from every stain; but in the temple of the Father, which is this world, should no care be taken that our outermost tunic of skin be preserved pure, and that we enter with it pure and shining? For if the danger consisted only in its defilement, it might perhaps be allowed to neglect it. But since every sensible body carries with it certain flows of material demons, it happens that, along with the impurity which exists from the eating of flesh and blood, a power friendly and familiar to it is also present through similarity and kinship.

§ 47. Wherefore correctly the theologians [abstaining]...

</columns>

### [Critical Commentary]

<columns>
1. Cyril [of Alexandria] took this from our author in *Against Julian, Book IX, page 310*. Instead of "by men" he uses "from men." "Consecrated"... "To set apart" <note>original: ἀφορίζεσθαι (aphorizesthai)</note> is properly said of those things designated and dedicated to God, as particularly of a portion of land which was separated from the rest of the field for divine use. Exactly as land consecrated to God is "set apart land" <note>original: γῆ ἀφωρισμένη (gē aphōrismenē)</note> by the *Alexandrian elders* <note>the translators of the Septuagint</note> in Leviticus 27:21. Hesychius: *Sacred precincts: temples, groves, or places set apart in honor.* See Salmasius on Solinus, page 767, cited by the learned man in his notes on Paul's Letter to the Romans 1:1.

2. **Clean on the feet... unstained sandals.** Who is ignorant of the ancients' sacred rite of walking barefoot <note>original: nudipedalia</note> and Pythagoras's precept: "Sacrifice and worship barefoot"? It is believed to have been taken from the Hebrews. See *Moses* in Exodus 3:5 and the *Book of Joshua* 5:15. The same custom existed among certain ancient Christians, concerning which see *Bingham's Antiquities of the Christian Church, Vol III, page 342*; nor has it fallen into disuse today among the Indians and other nations. Suidas explains "unstained" as "spotless" or "pure." On this matter, see *Synesius, Letter 105*: "It is fitting for a priest to be unstained in all things."

3. **In the temple of the Father, the world...** The *Leipzig Manuscript* uses the Attic form for "temple." Our author did not strictly follow those rules, and a little later uses the common form. However, he uses the Attic style below in § 54. Heraclitus beautifully illustrates the matter in a letter: "Do you not know that God is not hand-made, nor does He have a base from the beginning, nor a single enclosure? But the whole world is His temple." In the sacred scriptures, this whole universe is also viewed as the temple of God. The prophet *Malachi* (1:11) signifies this.

4. **The final and outermost tunic.** I spoke of this above (I, 31). *Seneca, Letter 92*: "What I said about clothing, think that I say the same about the body: for nature has also surrounded the soul with this as a kind of garment; it is its covering." A little later, *Cyril* reads "it was possible even to overlook."

5. **A friendly and welcoming power.** These terms are well joined, as below in § 53. "Friendly and welcoming" appears in *Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book I*. "Welcoming" <note>original: προσήγορον (prosēgoron)</note> signifies that which is joined and friendly, whence it is opposed to "hostile," as Markland teaches in his notes on Maximus Tyrius. This sheds light on our author.

</columns>

...they should apply the chief care of abstinence: and the **Egyptian** <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: Αἰγύπτιος (Aigyptios); referring to Plotinus, Porphyry's teacher</note> revealed these things to us, offering a most natural cause which he had proven through experience. For since a base and irrational soul, <gloss>2</gloss> which has deserted the body after being violently snatched away, remains present with it—since indeed the souls of men who perish by a violent death <gloss>3</gloss> are also accustomed to linger near the body itself: a fact which <gloss>5</gloss> forbids anyone from violently casting themselves out of the body <note>This refers to the Neoplatonic prohibition against suicide</note>. Since, therefore, the violent slaughter of living beings forces the souls to delight in those [bodies] <gloss>6</gloss> which they have deserted; and the soul is by no means prohibited from being in that place where something kindred <term>kindred; referring to the physical remains or "blood" which still holds an attraction for the lower soul</term> draws it: for which reason many [souls] have also been seen to lament; <gloss>7</gloss>

<column-break/>

...they took care of abstinence. And the **Egyptian** <gloss>1</gloss> declared these things to us, giving a most natural cause, which he had tested by experience. For since a base and irrational soul <gloss>2</gloss>, which left the body, having been **stripped by force** <gloss>3</gloss>, remains with it, <gloss>4</gloss> where indeed even the souls of those men who died by force are held near the body (which is also a deterrent <gloss>5</gloss> against leading oneself out by force). Since then the violent slaughter of animals forces the souls to take pleasure in those which they leave <gloss>6</gloss>, and the soul is in no way barred from being there, where its kindred drags it down, whence also many were seen lamenting. <gloss>7</gloss> And those of the unburied...

</columns>

---

### [Critical Commentary]

<columns>
1. **The Egyptian.**] This is Plotinus. REISKE. He certainly had his homeland in Lycopolis in Egypt; since there were two cities of this name, the one located in the Thebaid seems to be meant. *Fabricius, on Our Author, in the Life of Plotinus, Greek Library IV, 26.*

2. **For since the soul.**] The adverb *since* <note>original: ἐπεὶ (epei)</note> in a period that is quite long-winded and ambitious, is repeated twice for the sake of restarting the speech—as if a travel guide for a reader about to go astray—once in verse 26, then again in verse 37. Immediately after, instead of "the body" <note>original: ἡ τὸ σ.</note>, the Leipzig manuscript has "or," but he intended "if," which is the true reading. REISKE. *The Meerman manuscript also has "or."*

3. **Violently stripped.**] It was previously published as *syllēphtheisa* [seized], but I have restored *sylētheisa* [stripped]. The Leipzig and Meerman Codices did well to preserve the true writing for us, which is confirmed by Felicianus and Marsilio Ficino, who gave "exspoliata" [plundered/stripped]. Many authors illustrate this very doctrine which our author introduces concerning the unhappiness of the souls of those men who perished by violent slaughter. See *Fortunio Liceti, On the Secret Lamps of the Ancients, Book III, ch. 7.*

4. **Where.**] This is an indication of an argument brought forth to demonstrate the truth of the proposed opinion: soon a verb is missing before "and are held"...

<column-break/>

...for example: they flee, they roam, they wander, or something similar, or "and" should be deleted. REISKE.

5. **The [sentence] of not...**] It was more correctly read previously as "the also of not." And thus it was in the Leipzig and Meerman Codices. "To lead out by force," "to lead oneself out," "to lead oneself out of life," etc., are phrases they use for those who take their own life by force. Indeed, "the soul is the true man," as he says in section 47. See: *Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus III, 33; and V. D. on Xenophon of Ephesus, New Miscellaneous Observations, p. 52.* Our author rightly refutes this opinion, though he himself had once thought of killing himself, as we know from the *Life of Plotinus, ch. 2.* Pythagoras forbids "departing from the guard and station of life without the command of the general, that is, God." *Cicero, On Old Age, ch. 21.* This is contrary to what seemed right to the Stoics [men of the Porch], so to speak, and others, although even they did not think death should be hastened rashly. But regarding the dogma of Pythagoras, read *Holstenius in the Life of Porphyry, ch. 8; and V. D. on Hierocles in the Golden Verses, p. 260.*

6. **In those which they leave.**] Namely, "bodies," which I am not sure should be added. REISKE.

7. **And those of the unburied remain, etc.**] Concerning the soul...
</columns>

The souls of the unburied also remain beside their bodies; sorcerers <term>venefici: those who use potions or magic</term> abuse these souls for their own service, compelling them by detaining either the whole body or some part of it. Since, therefore, they observed the nature of a wicked soul, and the kinship <gloss>8</gloss> and pleasure it is accustomed to have toward the bodies from which it was torn away, they rightly avoided the eating of flesh. They did this so that they might not be disturbed by the presence of foreign souls—violently snatched away and <gloss>9</gloss> impure—which are attracted to what is kindred to them. They feared being hindered from approaching God alone while being troubled by the presence of demons <note>original: "daemonum"; in this context, Porphyry refers to lower spirits or restless souls rather than "demons" in the modern sense</note>.

§ 48. <gloss>1</gloss> For experience has taught these men in many instances that the nature of a kindred body is a lure for attracting the soul. Indeed, those who wish to take into themselves the souls of prophetic animals <gloss>2</gloss> swallow the most vital parts, such as the hearts of crows...

<column-break/>

The souls of the unburied also sit beside their bodies: sorcerers abuse these, forcing them into their service by the detention of either the whole body or some part. Because they had noticed both the nature of a depraved soul, and the kinship and pleasure it usually has toward the bodies from which it was torn; they not unjustly avoided the eating of meat: lest they be thrown into disorder by foreign souls, violently snatched and impure, being attracted to things kindred to them, and lest they be hindered from approaching God alone, being interrupted by the presence of demons.

§ 48. For experience in many cases taught them that the nature of a kindred body is an enticement for drawing the soul. For those who desire to receive into themselves the souls of prophetic animals, [swallow] their chief members, the hearts...

<column-break/>

<margin>On depraved and unpurified souls, see *Plato* in the *Phaedo*: page 61. D. "Such a soul is weighed down and dragged back again into the visible world... wandering, as is said, around monuments and tombs." <note>original: "ἡ τοιαύτη ψυχὴ βαρύνεταί τε καὶ ἕλκεται..."</note> So also the souls of those who perished by a violent death; hence the necromancers <term>nekromanteis: those who consult the dead</term>, who consulted souls about the future, were accustomed to spend the night in sepulchers. See *Elsner* on *Matthew VIII*, 28. It was believed those souls retained the remains of their old filth, on which matter see *Gale on Iamblichus*: *On the Mysteries* II, 5. and many others. Lawgivers prudently made use of this persuasion—that such souls do not rest before the corpses are buried—for their own purposes, so that murders would not be committed safely and easily: a point beautifully handled by the learned *Warburton* in *The Divine Legation of Moses*, Book II. page 368.</margin>

<margin>8. *And has pleasure.*] Thus our manuscripts have it. *Valentinus* had inserted "which" after "pleasure," and rightly so. Since two syllables of the same sound followed each other, one absorbed the other. This happens a thousand times to Greek and Latin authors.</margin>

<margin>9. *Impure.*] By a fault of the typesetters, I believe, the Florentine edition had "uninstructed" <note>original: "ἀκατάρτοις"</note>, which not only the Leiden edition followed, but the Cambridge edition also wished to be seen. You do not lack authority in a manifest matter. *Lipsius* and *Meermann* are correct.</margin>

<margin>1. *For that [it is] a lure...* etc.] See *Psellus*: *On Demons* and *Gaulmin's* notes page 142. VALENTINUS.</margin>

<margin>2. *Swallowing, as it were, the hearts of crows...* etc.] Swallowing...</margin>

§ 49. Rightly, therefore, the philosopher—the priest of the God who is above all—abstains from every meat of living creatures. § 49. <margin>
Iamblichus says in *The Mysteries* (III. 14) that certain drinks bring the power of prophecy; see Gale’s notes there. Regarding the parts of animals believed most useful for divination, read the same author on III, 22; they thought that the spirit entered into crows, hawks, and other birds. Eusebius touches upon the futility of this in *Demonstratio Evangelica* Book V, p. 209; see also him *Against Hierocles*, p. 918. They primarily ate the heart because it was a symbol of the soul. Read what the celebrated Michaelis learnedly argued in his *Dissertation on the Heart and Brain*. Otherwise, the word "most important" was omitted in the Meerman manuscript.
</margin>

</margin>

<margin>
1. "Philosopher, and priest of God."] Just as pious and holy men are often called "priests of God" in sacred scripture. The Stoics used to say that only the wise man is a priest. This is a very well-known matter.
</margin>

<margin>
2. However, "to God" is suggested by what preceded: "to approach God alone," and what follows in § 52: "he himself... approaching God through himself." I would almost believe these words strike at the Christians. For the Lord Jesus is the priest who saves those "approaching God through him," as it says in the Epistle to the Hebrews VII, 25. Porphyry had undoubtedly read this passage.
</margin>

</margin>

# PORPHYRY

...as a priest of a specific deity is skilled in the installation of his statues, and his secret rites, initiations, purifications, and the like; so too the priest of the God who is over all is skilled in the fashioning of His image <note>original Greek: "ἀγαλματοποιΐας" (agalmatopoiia). While this usually refers to making physical statues, Porphyry uses it here to describe the philosopher's task of shaping their own soul into a "divine image" or likeness of the Supreme God</note>, and in the purifications and other practices by which he is joined to God.

§ 50. <gloss>1</gloss> Now, if the priests and diviners <term>hieroskopoi|priests who inspect sacrifices to discern the will of the gods</term> of the gods in this world command both themselves and others to abstain from graves, <gloss>2</gloss> from unholy men, from menstruating women, from sexual intercourse, and <gloss>3</gloss> even from shameful or mournful sights, or from hearing anything that stirs the passions—for it often appears, even because of the impure people present, that the diviner is disturbed; which is why they say that sacrificing at the wrong time brings greater harm than profit—<gloss>4</gloss> surely then the priest of the Father will not allow himself to become a tomb for dead bodies?

<column-break/>

...of his statues, and of sacrifices, and ceremonies, and expiations, and similar things he is skilled: so the priest of the God presiding over all things is experienced in the knowledge of His images, expiations, and all other things by which they are joined to Him.

§ 50. But if the priests and sacrificers of those gods who are here command both themselves and others to abstain from burials, and profane men, and menstruating women, and sexual intercourse, and even from shameful and mournful spectacles, as well as from hearing those things which move the passions: because it often appears, on account of even the impure people present, that something disturbs the sacrificer and the soothsayer: whence they also say that to sacrifice out of season brings greater loss than gain: will he, who is the priest of the highest Father, endure to become himself a tomb of dead bodies?

---

<column-break/>

<margin>Reiske suggests "priest of a part of the temples." He speaks of "a certain god," meaning local deities, as opposed to "the priest of the God over all." Just below, the Meerman manuscript reads "merchant" incorrectly instead of "skilled."</margin>
<margin>1. **If the priests of the things here.** Reiske suggests "priests of the temples here." For "If," the Meerman manuscript reads "But."</margin>
<margin>2. **Unholy men, and menstruating women, etc.** Those polluted by such things were barred from sacred rites among the ancients. Compare what is said at Book IV, 16. These might seem to touch upon the laws of Moses. Indeed, a note in the Meerman manuscript says: "I believe he means the divine Moses."</margin>
<margin>3. **A shameful sight—and hearing.** Just as the Emperor Julian <note>Julian "the Apostate," the last pagan Roman Emperor, who tried to reform the priesthood along Neoplatonic lines</note> instructed the priest whom he wished to approach in worship of the Gods: "neither saying nor hearing anything shameful." See Gale's notes on Iamblichus: *On the Mysteries*, I, 11.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>4. **Surely he will not endure to become a tomb.** The scholar Abresch rightly notes: "surely much less... will he endure." This latter reading was also preferred by Reiske, and the translator agrees. Note this beautiful turn of phrase, frequent in writers of both languages <note>Greek and Latin</note>. Regarding a man torn apart by wild beasts, Lucretius says in Book V:
> He provided living food for the wild teeth to swallow,
> Seeing his living guts buried in a living tomb.
These and many other examples are found in Gataker's notes on Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, VI, 21: "he is buried in the bodies of those who are fed." Elegantly, Dandamis says in Palladius regarding...</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->**B b**<-

...himself full of defilement, while he strives to be an associate of the superior being? <note>original: "cum praestantiore" / "τῷ κρείττονι". This refers to the Divine or the gods.</note> Is it not enough that we take the portions of death into this life of ours through the fruits of the earth? But it is not yet the place to treat of these things. For we must return to a more exact distinction of those matters which pertain to sacrifices.

51. For someone might say that we would be doing away with a great part of divination—that which is customarily performed through the entrails <term>exta: the internal organs of a sacrificial animal, used for omens</term>—if we abstain from the slaughter of animals. But such a person might as well kill human beings, since the future is seen even more clearly, so they say, in their entrails; and many among the barbarians practice divination through human entrails <note>original: "aruspicianam" / "σπλαγχνεύοντες"</note>. But just as it was a mark of injustice and cruelty <note>original: "immanitatis" / "πλεονεξίας"</note> to kill one’s own kind for the sake of divination, so it is unjust to slaughter an irrational animal for the sake of prophesying. Now, whether the gods show these signs, or spirits <term>daemones: in the Greek sense, intermediary spirits between gods and humans</term>, or the soul as it departs from the animal through...

<column-break/>

<note>The following section translates the scholarly annotations provided at the bottom of the original page.</note>

---

<column-break/>

Concerning the Brahmans: page 43. *“And you become walking tombs of dead animals.”* <note>A famous Pythagorean sentiment regarding meat-eating.</note>

5. **The superior being.**] Felicianus translates as *with the more excellent*. I suspect, however, it is better rendered as *with God*. The term *superior* <note>Greek: "κρείττον"</note> is used for a *divine power*, but most especially in the plural <note>Greek: "κρείττονες"</note> they are the *Gods*. See *Bos: Animadversions on Lucian, chapter 15.* Presently, the Leipzig Manuscript omitted the word *the*; then Abresch preferred the phrase *from the fruits*.

1. **Divining through humans.**] Abresch suggests *through human beings*. I believe the manuscripts that have the form *they practice divination* <note>Greek: "σπλαγχνεύονται"</note> hold the true hand of the Author, though I know how the common reading can be defended. Note the "anthropomancy" <term>divination by human sacrifice</term> of certain nations, or the custom of divining through human victims. Concerning the Gauls, see *Diodorus Siculus, Book V, 31.* Concerning the Lusitanians and others, see *Olearius on Philostratus’s Life of Apollonius of Tyana, Book VIII, 15*, where you will see that Elagabalus, that most foul of bipeds, also established this practice. Nor were Christians treated any better by the Roman Emperors. Concerning Julian, see the *Scholiast on Gregory Nazianzen, Invective II, page 61.* For others, see the Learned Men on *Justin’s Apology I, 24.*

2. **Injustice and cruelty.**] Felicianus gave *Injustice and cruelty* <note>Latin: "Iniustitiae & immanitatis"</note>, in which sense the word *greed/cruelty* <note>Greek: "πλεονεξία"</note> is also used elsewhere in Porphyry. These terms are well joined, because *to be greedy* is *to inflict injury*...

<summary>Porphyry argues that using animal entrails for divination does not justify their slaughter, noting that if utility were the only metric, one might just as easily justify human sacrifice. The commentary provides historical context on "anthropomancy" (human sacrifice) among ancient cultures and the Roman Empire.</summary>

# P O R P H Y R I U S

...whether the divine responds to an inquiry through signs in the entrails <term>exta: the internal organs of a sacrificial animal, used for omens</term> is not the concern of the present discussion to investigate.

§ 52. As for those whose lives revolve around external matters, we allow them to be carried away where they are already going, having once acted impiously toward themselves. But for the person we describe as a philosopher—one who holds back from external things—we rightly claim they will not trouble the spirits <term>daemones: intermediary spirits between gods and humans</term>, nor will they have any need for seers or the entrails of animals. Indeed, they have made it their study to distance themselves from the very reasons why divinations are usually performed. They do not look toward marriage or commerce in such a way as to trouble a seer about them; they do not seek counsel regarding a servant, or a promotion, or any other such human vanities <gloss>4</gloss>.

<column-break/>

...whether the divine responds to an inquiry through signs in the entrails, it is not within the scope of this present dispute to inquire.

§ 52. However, for those whose life is devolved to external things, we permit them—once they have taken up impiety against themselves—to be carried where they are accustomed to be carried. But the one we describe as a philosopher, who abstains from external things, we rightly assert will bring no business to the spirits, nor will they have any need for prophets or the entrails of animals: especially since they study to abstain from those things for which divinations are customarily made. For they do not look toward marriage or trade, so as to be about to question a seer concerning these things: they do not consult regarding a servant, or fortunes, or the increase of honor, or other such human ambitions—

1. **But the one we describe as a philosopher, etc.**] *Eusebius* also takes testimony from here in the same book. These are the variations in reading: in that text, "to the seer" is written in the dative case <note>original: "τῷ μάντει"</note>, and in the following line, it reads "concerning theft" <note>original: "περὶ κλοπῆς"</note> rather than "concerning advancement" <note>original: "προκοπῆς"</note> as it is here. Furthermore, where "he has studied" <note>original: "μεμελέτηκεν"</note> appears above, the reading there is "it has been a care" <note>original: "μεμέληκεν"</note>, which is erroneous. This is also confirmed by the authority of the manuscript of *Eusebius*. VICTORIUS. Up to those words at the end of § 52, "and instead of a seer," etc. *Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IV, page 166, section D.

2. **To trouble the seer.**] *Eusebius*, as just mentioned, uses the dative case. *Heraldus* also cites this from our author in his notes on *Arnobius*, page 233, but he had read it in *Eusebius*; for he also cites other errors in *Eusebius* that are not in *Porphyry*, such as "it has been a care" and "theft."

<column-break/>

Our author constructs this in both ways: with the accusative case in Book I, 49 and Book II, 45, and with the dative just a moment ago in "to trouble the spirits" <note>original: "ἐνοχλήσειν δαίμοσι"</note>. You might find it both ways a hundred times. See the celebrated *Alberti* on *Hesychius* under the letter E. The same logic applies to "to harass." *Luke* in Acts 15:19 joins it with the dative, while others use both.

3. **Of advancement.**] The word "theft" in *Eusebius* has already been corrected by learned men. Perhaps the error arose because minor Greek grammarians think this word "advancement" <note>original: "προκοπή" / "prokope"</note> is unapproved; however, it has long been shown by scholars that they are gravely mistaken, and that it signifies any kind of "increase." It is well known that "to advance" <note>original: "προκόπτειν"</note> is specifically said of those who *make progress in the study of virtue*. *Jens* in his *Literary Harvest*, page 41, and *Alberti* on 2 Timothy 3:9, investigate the origin of this figure of speech. Instead of "other," the *Meerman Manuscript* incorrectly has "to others."

4. **Of vainglory.**] Regarding the word "to hunt for glory" <note>original: "δοξοκοπεῖν"</note>, see the note on Book I, 38. *Suidas* defines "vainglory" <note>original: "δοξοκοπία"</note> as "empty glory." The same author, under "to court the people," says that "vainglory" is also called "demagoguery."

# O N   A B S T I N E N C E   B O O K   I I.

...divination is for them. But regarding the things he seeks, neither any seer nor any animal entrails can indicate their certainty. Instead, as we have said, the philosopher himself, approaching God through his own self—the God who is established within his own true entrails <note>The "true entrails" is a metaphor for the philosopher's soul or conscience, contrasted with the physical guts of a sacrificed animal</note>—receives guidance concerning eternal life. He is drawn entirely toward that divine realm, desiring to become, in place of a seer, an interlocutor of great Jove <note>original: "Iouis alloquutor." Porphyry refers to a Homeric description of King Minos, who was said to have conversed directly with Zeus (Jupiter/Jove).</note>.

§ 53. For even if some necessity should press upon him, there is no lack of good spirits <term>daemones: intermediary beings between gods and humans</term> who come to meet such a man who lives in this way and is an intimate of God, providing guidance through dreams, and through signs, and—

<column-break/>

—concerning the things he seeks, no seer, nor the entrails of animals will reveal the truth; but he himself, as we say, approaching the god who is established in his true entrails, will receive the instructions concerning eternal life, having flowed entirely there, and instead of a seer, praying to become a companion of great Zeus <note>original: "Διὸς μεγάλου ὀαριστὴς"</note>.

§ 53. And if indeed some matter of necessity should urge him, there are those spirits who attend the one living thus as a servant of God, both through dreams and signs, and—

---

<margin>They choose consuls based on military reputation, Lucius; and from demagoguery, Terentius. And so again in *Courting Popularity*. These are taken from Appian’s *Hannibalic Wars*, p. 559, who adds "promising them many things from his customary courting of popularity," which latter parts I believe should also be attributed to Suidas. For those earlier parts have nothing to do with the word *doxokopia* <note>Greek: "δοξοκοπία," the pursuit of popular glory</note>. I also wish that the word *doxokopia* in Appian had not been suspected by that learned man, for Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Lucian, and many others use it frequently.</margin>

5. **Will reveal the truth.** Thus "clear" <note>Greek: "σαφὲς"</note> is used for "accurately and truly" in Pindar. And "clear Phoebus" <note>The god Apollo</note> in Sophocles is used instead of "truthful," as the ancient critics explain. See Albert on Matthew 20:31 and Suidas. Shortly after, instead of "we say," it should be read as "we were saying" <note>Greek: "ἐλέγομεν"</note> from Eusebius and the Meermann manuscript, for it refers back to what was said above.

6. **In the true [entrails], etc.** To better understand the meaning of this word, it helps that a memory aid was written in the margin of the Leipzig manuscript: "that God is established in the entrails of the one living according to virtue." It seems to refer back to page 90, line 23. (Reiske). The same scholarly note was written in the Meermann manuscript. The ancients used to say God was "in the entrails" because they believed He signified the future through them, as if there were a certain sign in them called "God," and if it appeared whole, it showed a propitious Deity. Therefore, he refers to this when he says God is "established in the true entrails of the wise man." See Olearius on Philostratus 8.15. Gataker rightly compares these with "the spirit established within, in the depths" in Marcus Aurelius 3.16; just as the Apostle Paul wishes our bodies to be temples of God. And "the Word of God dwelling in the true entrails" is said in Eusebius’s *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IV, p. 170 D, who certainly refers to this passage.

7. **Companion of great Zeus.** He took this from the "Prince of Poets" <note>Homer</note>, where Minos is called this in the *Odyssey*, Book 19, line 179:
-> Companion of great Zeus. <-
These words are praised and explained by Plato in the *Minos*, p. 568, and Strabo, Book 10, p. 328. In the Florence edition, it was "conversation," which is out of place here. A little before, in our author [Porphyry] as quoted by Pamphilus, "entirely there" <note>Greek: "ὅλως ἐκεῖ"</note> should be restored for the printed "wholly there."

1. **If some of [necessity]...** The Leipzig manuscript has "if some of." Incorrect. However, it is clear from this that one should read "if indeed some of..." (Reiske).

2. **Through dreams and signs and omens.** I have restored to Malchus <note>Porphyry’s original name</note> his own words, for all manuscripts agree on this reading. Only the Valentinus manuscript had neglected "and signs." Only the Valentinus notes a certain divine instinct by which humans are instructed, from which comes "to forebode" and in the Attic dialect "to take an omen" by a certain secret instinct...

# PORPHYRY

and through omens <note>original: ὄττης (ottēs). Porphyry refers to divine signs or voices</note> good spirits <note>original: δαίμονες (daimones). For one must only depart from evil, and recognize that which is most precious in the universe, and consider everything good in the universe to be a friend and approachable. Furthermore, even if one accepts the ritual of sacrifice for the sake of foreknowing the future, it does not follow from this that it is necessary to eat and accept flesh, just as a sacrifice performed in any way to either gods or spirits does not introduce the eating of meat. ->## On Abstinence, Book II.<-
->Bb 3<-

Theophrastus recorded this, and moreover he handed down many other things to memory concerning the sacrifice of humans, which the ancients used; yet it is certainly not established that humans ought to be eaten for that reason.

**§ 54.** Since these instances are indeed many and varied, I think these few which I subjoin will be sufficient to prove this. For in Rhodes, on the sixth day of the month of Metageitnion <note>Original Latin: "pridie nonas Iulias" (the day before the Nones of July); Greek: "Metageitniōn." This was a summer month in the Athenian and Rhodian calendars</note>, a human was sacrificed to Saturn <note>Original Greek: "Kronos." The Romans identified their god Saturn with the Greek Titan Kronos</note>. And when that custom had persisted for a long time, it was later changed in a more humane manner. They would detain someone condemned to death by public judgment in prison until the Saturnalia <note>Original Greek: "Kronia," the festival of Kronos</note>; and when the solemn day arrived, they led the man outside the gates opposite the shrine of Aristobula <note>Aristobula means "Best Counselor," an epithet often associated with the goddess Artemis</note>

<column-break/>

Theophrastus mentioned this, but he also handed down the memory of many other instances, how the ancients even sacrificed humans; but surely for this reason humans are not to be eaten.

**§ 54.** $^1$ And that we do not say these things simply, but because history is full of them, these examples too are sufficient to present. $^2$ For in Rhodes, on the sixth day of the beginning of the month of Metageitnion, a human was sacrificed to Kronos. This custom, which had long prevailed, was changed. For they held one of those who had been publicly condemned to death until the Kronia; $^3$ when the festival was at hand, they led the man outside the gates opposite the [shrine] of $^4$ Aristobula—

***

1. **And that these &c.**] In the same book <note>referring to Eusebius</note> are read the twenty-three verses which follow here in succession; I shall note what variations there are in them. The first distinction is small, for "giving wine to drink" <note>original: "oinon potisantes"</note> is written there in the genitive case, and so forth. In the following verse is "Coronea" <note>original: "Korōneia," a town in Boeotia</note>, in which the diversity of reading remains, since he later makes mention of this town again in the same book. In the penultimate line of this page is "they sacrificed" <note>original: "ethyon de"</note>. Likewise in the second line of the following page, for the same reason, it is "they sacrificed," not "they were sacrificed" <note>original: "ethyonto"</note>, as it is in both places here. However, where it is read below "and the Dumatii of Arabia," it is written there as "Dumates. Those of Arabia." In the last verse, "Latiarius" is written with a changed letter, not "Latiarius." I believe this is an error, for the written book of Eusebius agrees with Porphyry. VICTORIUS. Eusebius transcribed almost to the end of § 56 (page 155), whom you should also see "On the Praises of Constantine the Great" (page 255). Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note> in the cited book, and Theodoret in the "Sermon on Sacrifices," all use these passages from Porphyry. But also Clement of Alexandria in the "Protrepticus" (page 27) and many others deal with that dreadful kind of sacrifice. But those things may be true

which he says: that although they are sacrificed, it does not follow from this that humans are also to be eaten. Nevertheless, you may observe that these things were generally joined together. Compare Fabricius on Sextus Empiricus, Book III, 24 (page 178).

2. **For he was sacrificed &c.**] Eusebius also relates these and the following things in "On the Praises of Constantine" (page 533) and Theodoret in the "Sermon on Sacrifices" (page 389), but there it is read "it was changed into a custom." 3. **When the festival was at hand—**] Note the custom that when a festival day approached, they would execute those guilty of crimes, for it was not permitted during the festival itself. Note also that the punishment was inflicted "outside the gates," which was a very frequent custom in ancient times. Compare the Learned Man on the "Epistle to the Hebrews" (Chapter XIII, 12). The most honorable Cuper teaches the same concerning the Romans and indicates the reason for the matter in "Observations," Book IV, 19.

# OF PORPHYRY

...of [best] counsel, and after giving them wine to drink, they slaughtered them. $^6$ In what is now called Salamis <note>An ancient city-state on the eastern coast of Cyprus</note>, but was formerly named Coronis, in the month known to the Cyprians as Aphrodisios <note>The month of Aphrodite, the goddess of love; roughly corresponding to April/May</note>, $^7$ a human used to be sacrificed to Agraulos, the daughter of Cecrops and the nymph Agraulis. This custom persisted until the times of Diomedes <note>A hero of the Trojan War, later worshipped as a god in various locations</note>. Later it was changed, so that the human was sacrificed to Diomedes. $^8$ Within a single enclosure <note>original: "peribolos"</note> were contained the temple of Athena, and that of Agraulos and Diomedes. $^9$ The one being sacrificed was led by the youths and ran three times around the altar. Then the priest struck him with a spear in the stomach <note>The Greek "stomachon" and Latin "guttur" suggest the throat or upper chest area</note>, and thus—

<column-break/>

—offered him as a drink-offering of wine, they slit his throat. In that place which is now Salamis, but was previously called Coronis, a human was slaughtered in sacrifices to Agraulos, daughter of Cecrops and the nymph Agraulis, during the month following the Cyprian custom of Venus <note>The Roman equivalent of Aphrodite</note>. This custom indeed persevered until the times of Diomedes; then it was so changed that a human was sacrificed to Diomedes. For within one and the same circuit of walls, the shrines of Minerva <note>The Roman equivalent of Athena</note>, Agraulos, and Diomedes were enclosed. The one who was to be immolated, having been led out by the youths, first ran around the altar three times; then he was struck by the priest with a spear driven into the throat; and so...

---

...by their example, Themistocles built a temple at Athens to Diana <note>The Roman name for Artemis</note> "of the Best Counsel" <note>original: "tēs Aristoboulēs"</note>, regarding which see *Meursius* in *The Piraeus*, chapter 9.

5. *Having given wine to drink.*] Following the custom of the ancients, which commentators illustrate by the "posca" <note>A mixture of vinegar/sour wine and water</note> which the soldiers gave to the Lord Christ, in *Matthew 27:48* and *Mark 15:36*.

6. *In what is now Salamis, etc.*] *Meermann* incorrectly writes "Koronidion," where the "on" became attached from the following syllable. In *Eusebius* it is "Koroneia." See *Viger* there; as our author writes, so does *Cyril*; see also *Theodoret*, *Sermon on Sacrifices*, page 589. *Stephanus of Byzantium* writes that "Korone" is a part of Salamis. But that the city was called this in antiquity, which Teucer later enlarged and named Salamis after his fatherland, is shown by *Meursius* in *Cyprus* I, 20. Regarding the Cyprian month *Aphrodisios* and others, read the same author, chapter 24.

7. *A human was sacrificed to Agraulos, daughter of Cecrops, etc.*] I wish the illustrious man <note>Likely referring to the scholar Joseph Scaliger</note> in *Chronological Canons*, Section VIII, had proven that Cecrops introduced human sacrifice <note>original: "anthrōpothusian"</note> to Cyprus. Certainly, you cannot conclude it from this passage. And I remember others hand down much milder traditions regarding the sacrifices of Cecrops. For "Agraulos" he reads "Aglauros," and soon for "Agraulidis" he reads "Aglauridis"—see *Barnes* on Euripides' *Ion*, line 23. But those names are everywhere confused with each other. *Alberti* on *Hesychius* has spared us the effort regarding the entry "Agraulos." On the matter itself, read *Meursius*, *Attic Lectures* VI, 3, who corrects the error of those who confuse Agraulos, the daughter of Cecrops, with Minerva [Athena], who was also surnamed *Agraulos* or *Aglauros* by the Athenians. Porphyry calls the wife of Cecrops *Agraulis*, others call her *Agraulos*. See *Meursius* on the *Athenian Kingdom* I, 11. For the phrase "so that to Diomedes," *Meermann* reads "as to Diomedes."

8. *Under one enclosure, etc.*] The word is used specifically for the perimeter of a temple. The Greeks properly called a *peribolos* <note>An enclosure or sacred precinct</note> a certain measure of land that was vacant around temples and enclosed by a wall. The Latins called this the *conseptum* <note>A fenced or enclosed space</note> of the temple. From this it began to be used more broadly to refer to the temple itself. See *Salmasius* on *Solinus*, page 8, and *Clarus Stosch*, *Antiquities of Thyatira*, Book I, 7, 20. For "times" just above, in *Cyril* it is "seasons," and for "human" he has "man."

9. *Being sacrificed.*] The earlier editions of *Eusebius* and the *Leipzig Manuscript* all use the word *sphagiazomenos* <note>Being slaughtered for sacrifice</note>. In *Cyril* it is *sphazomenos* <note>Being slain</note>. *Meermann* mistakenly has *sphagiazomenos* [with an accentual variant].

# On Abstinence, Book II.

§ 55. Diphilus, the King of Cyprus, who lived in the times of Seleucus the "Theologian" <note>original: *theologus*; here referring to a writer on divine genealogies or a mystic</note>, abolished this custom, changing the sacrifice to the immolation of an ox. The deity <note>original: *daemon*; in the Neoplatonic sense, a spiritual being or tutelary spirit</note> accepted the ox in place of the human, signifying beyond doubt that the power of both acts is of equal value. Likewise, in Heliopolis of Egypt, Amosis abolished the law concerning the slaughter of humans: as in the li—

<column-break/>

—thus he would offer him as a whole burnt offering upon the constructed pyre.

§ 55. Diphilus, the King of Cyprus, abolished this decree, having lived during the times of Seleucus the Theologian, changing the custom to the sacrifice of oxen. And the deity accepted the ox instead of the human. Thus, the deed is of equal value. Amosis also abolished the law of manslaughter <note>referring here to ritual human sacrifice</note> in Heliopolis of Egypt. To whom <insert>the catchword "To whom" indicates the start of the next section</insert>

***

10. *Burned as a whole offering on the pyre.*] *Eusebius:* in both places, both in *Preparation for the Gospel* and *On the Life of Constantine*: "constructed" <note>original: νηθεῖσαν</note>. *Cyril:* "kindled" <note>original: ἀφθεῖσαν</note>. In the other passage *Eusebius* has "they burned whole," but in the *Oration in Praise of Constantine*, as here in the singular: "he burned whole." *Cyril* also has this. He uses the word again below in Book IV, § 15. It could have been "he sacrificed whole," which pleased the illustrious Abresch, as above in § 26. For "Diphilus," *Eusebius* incorrectly has "Diiphilus."

1. *In the times of Seleucus the Theologian.*] Concerning Seleucus the Theologian, or magus (for he seems to have been the same person), read *Fabricius, Greek Library, Vol. I, p. 77.* Reiske notes that in the Meerman manuscript it is "against Seleucus." There were several of this name. See *Gale on Iamblichus' Mysteries, p. 297* and *Viger on Eusebius*, to whom in *Preparation for the Gospel, Book V, p. 203*, he is called a "wonderful theologian and an initiate of secret mysteries." Such men were formerly called Orpheus, Linus, and others; and following their example, even more recent figures were so named, on which matter see *Fabricius on Sextus Empiricus, IX, Against the Physicists, p. 593.* The Meerman manuscript incorrectly has "nation" <note>original: ἔθνος</note> for "custom" <note>original: ἔθος</note>; the same manuscript deletes the word "the" before "human."

2. *He abolished the law.*] Thus, immediately, "to abolish a decree." "To break customs" appears above in § 33, which can be added to a hundred other examples collected by the learned man on *Matthew 5:17.* In *Eusebius* it is "and also in Heliopolis," and it is the same in the Meerman manuscript.

3. *Of Egypt, concerning the slaughter of humans.*] *Herodotus* denies that the Egyptians sacrificed human victims, but others affirm it along with our author. See *Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus, I, 88.* Indeed, we know from *Athenaeus, Book IV, ch. 21* that Seleucus wrote *On Human Sacrifice among the Egyptians*.

<column-break/>

However, Gale notes on *Iamblichus' Mysteries, p. 278* that they did not observe this dire custom except in the most severe calamities; and perhaps it did not pervade all of Egypt, but held sway in only one or two cities. For why would Amosis not have removed it everywhere his empire extended? Certainly Manetho, and our author following him, who speak only of Heliopolis, would not have been silent on this. *Plutarch, however, Vol. II, p. 380*, reports from Manetho that living humans were also burned in the city of Idithya. There, for "Idithya," I rewrite "Ilithyia," otherwise called "Eileithyia." *Stephanus of Byzantium* says: "Eileithyia, an Egyptian city." Nor is it necessary to conclude from this that they disagree because *Plutarch* indicates these rites were made to Diana, while our author says to Juno, a matter which will be discussed immediately.

4. *Amosis.*] In *Eusebius' Praise of Constantine*, it is rendered "Amoses." Elsewhere it is also "Amasis." There is variation everywhere in these names. See the *Translators of Diodorus Siculus, I, 60*, and the one who elegantly shows how it happened that this name is reported so diversely, *Bos, Animadversions on Josephus, 27*. Nor is there less variation in the name of that Amosis in whose reign the Hebrews are believed to have exited Egypt. See *Perizonius, Egyptian Origins, 18.* Our author here is called "Amasis" by *Philostratus in Life of Apollonius, V, 42*, where he is called a "lion" because he joined gentleness with a royal nature, being the one who authorized the removal of human sacrifice, as *Olearius* writes there.

# P O R P H Y R Y

5. To this Manetho bears witness in his work *On Antiquity and Piety*. 6. They were sacrificed to Hera and were examined, just as the pure calves that are sought out and marked with a seal. 8. Three were sacrificed each day, in whose place Amosis ordered an equal number of wax images to be placed upon the altar. 9. They also used to sacrifice a human being in Chios to Dionysus the "Raw-Eater" <note>original: ὠμαδίῳ (Omadios)</note> by tearing them apart, and in Te—

<column-break/>

—Manetho testifies in his book *On Antiquity and Piety*. They were slaughtered for Juno <note>The Roman equivalent of the Greek Hera</note>, and they were inspected no differently than pure calves, which were accustomed to be investigated and marked with a sign. And indeed three were sacrificed in a day, in place of which Amosis ordered as many wax images to be substituted. In Chios also they offered a human being in sacrifice to Bacchus the "Raw-Eater" <note>original: Omadio Baccho</note> by tearing him apart; and also in Te—

***

5. *To which Manetho bears witness.*] I would prefer, based on *Eusebius*: "As Manetho bears witness." In *Plutarch* he is called "Manethon," and by others "Menethos." Learned men know that this name is pronounced in various ways, though "Manethon" is generally approved by them. See *Fabricius: Greek Library III, 20, 1*, where much is said about him and about the book *On Antiquity and Piety* cited here, in the same place, section 5.

6. *They were sacrificed to Hera.*] Our author and others indicate these sacrifices were made to Juno, as many speak of that Egyptian Goddess. And yet *Herodotus (II, 50)* testifies that Juno was entirely unknown to the Egyptians; but he is speaking of the Juno of the Greeks, whom the Egyptians truly did not know, while others speak of the Juno of the Orientals, who was often confused with Venus. Compare the celebrated *Jablonski in Egyptian Pantheon I, 1, 4*. From *Plutarch*, as I was just saying, you might gather these sacrifices were offered to Diana, but she who is Eileithyia <note>Goddess of childbirth</note> among the Greeks is Lucina, Diana, and Juno to the Romans. Thus our author could explain Eileithyia by the name Juno, on which matter see the same *Jablonski (Book III, 3, 7)*.

7. *Pure calves and marked with a seal.*] From this the priests were called "Sealers" <note>original: σφραγισταὶ (sphragistai)</note>, who marked the ox to be sacrificed by pressing a seal upon it. See *Plutarch, Vol. II, p. 363*, and what will be said below in Book IV, 7. The celebrated *Wesseling* uses this passage so that in his edition of *Herodotus (II, 38)* he may restore the phrase "pure male oxen."

8. *Three were sacrificed daily.*] That three men were sacrificed each day to Juno at Egyptian Heliopolis is also handed down from our author by *Theodoret in Sermon on Sacrifices, p. 589*, and *Eusebius in In Praise of Constantine*. For the word "to place upon" <note>original: ἐπιτίθεσθαι (epitithesthai)</note>, *Viger* (in his notes on *Eusebius, p. 11*) preferred "to substitute" <note>original: ὑποτίθεσθαι (hypotithesthai)</note>, to be put

<column-break/>

in place of the living. This is incorrect. *Eusebius* in both passages defends the common reading: "to be placed upon," namely, upon the altar.

9. *They sacrificed — to Dionysus the Raw-Eater.*] "And they also sacrificed" is found in *Eusebius*. For "Raw-Eater" <note>original: ὠμαδίῳ (omadiō)</note>, the *Leipzig Manuscript* has a slightly different spelling. *Eusebius* in another passage is exactly like our author, and so again in *Preparation for the Gospel, p. 163*, except that there he adds "tearing them limb from limb." But in the *Oration in Praise of Constantine*, he writes "to Dionysus the Raw-Eater." *Cyril (p. 129)* does not add this epithet. I do not doubt that "Omadius Dionysus" is the same as "Omestes," the consumer of raw flesh. For to him they sacrificed living men, as *Apostolius* says in *Proverbs XXI, 13*. Indeed, we have examples in *Plutarch (Vol I, p. 119, 289, and 324)*. Just as in this passage, he says this cruel sacrifice was performed for the "Raw-Eater." He was indeed believed to delight in raw flesh. Below in Book IV, 19, he calls them "the raw-eating feasts of Zagreus." It is therefore no wonder that the Bacchantes <note>female followers of Dionysus</note> were also accustomed to feed on raw flesh, a matter discussed by *Barnes on Euripides' Bacchae, 139*. *Arnobius (Book V, p. 212)* mentions "eating of raw flesh" <note>original: ὠμοφαγία (omophagia)</note>, and *Clement of Alexandria* says "the Bacchantes celebrate Dionysus with the eating of raw flesh." See *Meursius, Greek Festivals, Book VI*. This epithet is also used by our author in the *Orphic Hymn 51, 7*, and as the Distinguished Men <note>original: V. D. (Viris Doctis)</note> rightly judge, in *Hymn 29, 5*, where it is published as "ormadios." In both places, a famous man translates it as "porter" <note>original: baiulum</note>, but I think it means "raw-eater," which can also be gathered from the following verse: for in the rituals mentioned there, we see that solemn feasts of this kind occurred. Nor do I understand by what right that title "Porter" fits Bacchus, whom we see described as delicate.

1. **But the Phoenicians in great, etc.**] In place of "they were sacrificed" <note>original: ἐθύοντο (ethuonto)</note>, *Eusebius and Cyril* read "they sacrificed" <note>original: ἔθυον (ethuon)</note>, and here "voting" <note>original: ψηφίζοντες (psēphizontes)</note> instead of "decreeing by vote" <note>original: ἐπιψηφίζοντες (epipsēphizontes)</note>. is understood to be the Sun. Certainly, the arguments Porphyry <note>The text here uses "Malchus," which was Porphyry's original Syrian name meaning "King"</note> discussed above regarding the origin of sacrifices easily prove that human sacrifice did not extend back to that early age. # PORPHYRY

...translated into the Greek language and arranged into eight books. Moreover, Ister, in his collection of Cretan sacrifices, says that the Curetes <note>Ancient Cretan priests or demigods associated with the infant Zeus</note> were accustomed in ancient times to sacrifice boys to Saturn. Pallas, who best collected the mysteries of Mithras <note>A Persian sun-god whose cult was popular in the Roman Empire</note> during the reign of the Emperor Hadrian, says that human sacrifices were abolished among almost all peoples. For in Laodicea in Syria, a virgin used to be slaughtered every year for Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena</note>; now, a doe is accustomed to be sacrificed. <column-break/>

<margin>
Porphyry greatly admired Sanchoniaton. Note in passing the error of *Cyril*, who in Book VI *Against Julian*, page 205, says the history of Sanchoniaton was translated from the Phoenician idiom into Greek by Josephus the Jew, and cites *Clement of Alexandria* as a witness. Both are false. Other scholars have long seen the error of the prelate. *Compare Fabricius: Greek Library I, 28, 2.* *Huet* observes in *Demonstratio Evangelica IV, 2* that Philo allowed himself much liberty, so much so that just as Sanchoniaton interpolated Moses, Philo interpolated Sanchoniaton.
</margin>

4. **In eight books.**] *Eusebius* disagrees, who in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book I, page 31 D, attributes nine books to him. Learned men enter upon different paths to reconcile these accounts. Read *Fabricius* in the place cited.

5. **Moreover, Ister—**] *Viger* spoke concerning Ister in his notes to *Eusebius*, page 11. Most identify the Curetes with the Idaei and Corybantes; others distinguish them. See *Meursius* in *Creta I, 4*.

6. **Among all.**] After "all," the *Leipzig Manuscript* has a minor punctuation mark, which I approve of. For the words "were abolished" seem to belong to Ister as far as "all," not to Pallas. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a 18th-century German scholar</note>. The *Meerman manuscript* punctuates in the same way.

7. **Pallas, who best—**] *Eusebius* writes "who [collected] the most accurately concerning..." Below in IV, 6: "Pallas in his writings on Mithras." *Ibid.* "History of the mysteries of Mithras." So I read there from the *Leipzig Manuscript*, and more will be said. These sacred rites

<column-break/>

were not performed without a human victim; that this indeed ceased by a law passed by Hadrian is observed from our author by *Casaubon* in his notes on *Lampridius' Life of Commodus, 19* (where the emperor *polluted the Mithraic rites with actual murder*).

8. **Under the Emperor Hadrian.**] *Pliny* in *Natural History XXX, 1* says that both cannibalism and human sacrifice had already been abolished by Roman laws; not only is it not enough to be eaten, but it is even most healthy <note>Pliny's ironic comment on the "benefits" of Roman law</note>. *Fabricius*, in his notes on *Sextus Empiricus, Pyrrhonic Outlines III, 24, p. 180*, shows from *Petit's* *Attic Laws* that from the time of Hadrian it was forbidden by Roman law to kill children. However, *Marsham* in *Chronicus Canon, Sec. XI* observes from *Procopius* that this lasted among the Blemmyes <note>An ancient nomadic people of Nubia</note> until the time of Justinian. Indeed, among other nations that cursed custom lasted long after; it is far from the truth, as some wish to claim, that human sacrifices ceased everywhere after the birth of the most mild Savior. Read *Fabricius: Library of Antiquities, ch. XI, 3*.

### On Abstinence, Book II.

...[Iphicrates] abolished <note>This refers to Iphicrates, a famous Athenian general of the 4th century BCE, who reportedly convinced the Carthaginians to stop human sacrifice</note>. I omit the Thracians and Scythians.
