Finally, the learned *Viger* <note>François Viger (1590–1647), a French Jesuit scholar</note> was hopeless in this matter. I thought it would be too difficult for a "little man" like myself to resolve a matter that such a "Giant" was not sufficient to explain. VALENT. <note>The initials of the commentator</note> Nor could I figure out what business a very famous Athenian general had with the Carthaginians. *Viger*, in his notes to *Eusebius* (page 12), notes that others attribute this abolition of human sacrifice <note>original: "ἀνθρωποθυσίας"</note> to Gelon, the Prince of Syracuse. *Thirlby*, in his notes on *Justin Martyr’s Apology II* (page 128), writes that human sacrifice was forbidden by Iphicrates and others, yet it was always being renewed. In the *Leipzig Manuscript*, the name is spelled "Ephicrates," and shortly before, the *Meerman Manuscript* reads "the same sacrifice," which is not a bad reading.

**11.** Dumatii.] Perhaps it should be "Dumathioi," as it seemed also to *Viger* and *Abresch*. *Stephanus of Byzantium* <note>A 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary</note> writes "Dumatha: a city of Arabia; the citizen is a Dumathan." In *Eusebius’s Oration in Praise of Constantine*, *Valesius* prefers "Dumathenes."

**12.** Which they use as a cult statue.] *Maximus of Tyre* <note>A Greek rhetorician and philosopher</note> in *Dissertation VIII, 8* says: "The Arabs worship a god, though I do not know which one. But I saw the image; it was a square stone." This is the "Dysares" of Arabia mentioned by *Tertullian* in *Apology, chapter 24*; not Mars, as it seemed to *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> under the heading "The God Ares," but Bacchus. *Huet* in *Evangelical Demonstration IV, 3* thinks it was an image of Moses. Even today, the Arabs at Mecca worship a black stone, which *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and orientalist</note> in *On the Syrian Gods II, 4* says he does not know if it is that same square stone mentioned by *Maximus*. But see the arguments *Bochart* raised against this opinion in *Phaleg II, 19*. Certainly in this passage, the most distinguished *Cuper*, in his notes on *Lactantius’s On the Deaths of the Persecutors* (page 11), rightly judged that the same stone of Bacchus is meant, since that altar served as a cult image, and the shape of an altar fits well.

<column-break/>

**13.** Phylarchus indeed, etc.] In *Eusebius* (*Preparation for the Gospel*, pages 156B and 164A), "Philarchos" is incorrectly printed. Then, in the other *Eusebius* passage, *In Praise of Constantine*, it says "before going out to wars." In the *Leipzig Manuscript*, it is written "enemies." Moreover, in both that manuscript and the *Meerman*, this scholium <note>An ancient marginal note or commentary</note> was added: "that the Bulgarians also did this before receiving holy baptism."

**14.** Killed the daughter of Erechtheus and Praxithea.] *Eusebius* in *In Praise of Constantine* says: "The Athenians remember the daughters of Leos and the daughter of Erechtheus being slaughtered," where see *Valesius*. *Cyril* in *Against Julian* (page 128) and many others record that Erechtheus himself sacrificed his daughter to demons. But these accounts are not in conflict. It is also well-known that some testify that the girl (indeed, some say two offered themselves) voluntarily offered herself to be slaughtered. See *Meursius* in *Kingdom of Athens II, 13*, who also discusses the name. As for the testimony of Demaratus in *Stobaeus’s Sermon 38*, where she is called Proserpina, since I see that name attributed to her nowhere else, I suspect the author wrote "sacrifice to Persephone" <note>original: "Περσεφόνη θύσῃ"</note> rather than the printed "sacrifice Persephone" <note>original: "Περσεφόνην θύσῃ"</note>. For *Clement of Alexandria* in the *Exhortation to the Greeks* (page 27) says she was sacrificed to "Pherephatta" <note>Another name for Persephone</note>.

**15.** But even now.] "But even now at least." Thus read *Eusebius*, the *Leipzig*, and the *Meerman Manuscripts*.

**16.** The Great City.] See de la Cerda on *Tertullian’s On the Spectacles*, note 93. VALENT. He understands "The Great City" to be Rome, according to the custom of his age. See *Valesius* on *Eusebius*, page 256. It is a solemn epithet, regarding which see *Vitringa* on *Revelation 17:18* and *Fabretti* on the *Theodosian Code*, Vol. VI, page 292. We know that several cities were designated by this title...

# On Abstinence, Book II.

->Cc 3<-

Finally, when all other food had been consumed, they turned upon one another and by lot ate their fellow soldiers who were drawn. When Hamilcar <note>Hamilcar Barca, the Carthaginian general</note> finally defeated them and took them into his power, he had them trampled to death by elephants; he judged it a violation of divine law for such men to ever mingle with other human beings again. Nor did he himself ever admit the eating of humans simply because some had dared to do it; nor did his son Hannibal, when someone advised him as he led his army into Italy to accustom his troops to eating human flesh so that they might never be overcome by a lack of food. Therefore, just because famine and wars were the cause of our beginning to use other animals for food, it does not follow that the same should be practiced for the sake of pleasure. In the same way, we have never accepted the eating of human flesh. Nor, because they sacrificed animals to certain powers <note>original: "potestatibus" / "δυνάμεσι" — referring to spiritual or divine entities</note>, should they therefore be eaten. For even those who sacrificed humans did not, for that reason, also [eat] their flesh—

<column-break/>

—and they even rushed upon one another, eating their fellow soldiers by lot. But Hamilcar, having taken them captive, trampled them under his elephants, as it was not holy for them to mix with other men any longer. And neither did he accept it because some had dared <gloss>3</gloss> cannibalism <note>original: "ἀνθρωποφαγίαν"</note>, nor did his son Hannibal, to whom someone suggested while he was campaigning in Italy that he should habituate the army to cannibalism so they would not lack nourishment. Therefore, since <gloss>4</gloss> famines and wars have been the causes of eating other animals, one ought not to accept this practice for the sake of pleasure, just as we did not welcome cannibalism. Nor, because they sacrificed <gloss>5</gloss> animals to certain powers, was it necessary to eat them. For those who sacrificed humans did not taste the flesh for that reason—

3. *Cannibalism.*] The *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts incorrectly read "human-slaughter" <note>original: "ἀνθρωποσφαγίαν"</note>. And so again a little later, "to habituate the army to human-slaughter," and then "we welcomed human-slaughter."

4. *Famines and wars.*] The *Bodleian* manuscript reads "plagues and wars" <note>original: "λοιμοὶ κ. π."</note>. It is noted elsewhere that these words are frequently confused. Here, what we have given is the only true reading. There are many examples of those whom the extremes of war, dire circumstances, and the long poverty of a terrible siege forced to protect their lives with human flesh, as Juvenal says of the Vascones in *Satire XV, 95*. Strabo affirms the same regarding the Celts, Iberians, and others in *Book IV, page 39*. The same advice of Critognatus is found in Caesar's *Gallic Wars, Book VII, chapter 77*. Athenagoras says this happens "according to some most bitter calamity" in *On the Resurrection of the Dead, page 63*, where Rechenberg indicates what the interpreters of natural law determine on this matter. A little later, for "human" <note>original: "ἀνθρωπίνων"</note>, the *Meerman* manuscript has "man-like" <note>original: "ἀνθρωπείων"</note>. See the note on Book I, 9.

5. *To certain powers.*] So again a little later he mentions "the powers in the universe." But see the note at section 34.

§ 58. 3. *We shall conclude the book.*] To a learned man commenting on <term>Diodorus</term>, page 5, it seemed that the word "we shall finish" <note>original: "παραγράψομεν"</note> should be used. For "paragraphein" means to circumscribe or finish. However, "perigraphein" <note>the word in the text</note> means to cross out or circumscribe with marks, indicating that what is enclosed by those marks should be deleted. Nor would I deny that one of these words has occasionally taken the place of the other by mistake; the learned <term>Abresch</term> will give examples in *Diligences on Thucydides*, page 367. Nevertheless, the metaphor is drawn from those things which we define by circumscribing them.

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK II.
D d

VALENT[IUS]. "Five" is a dull and absurd conjecture in this place. "Everything" <note>original: "πάντα"</note> is correct. It means "thousands of each," such as a thousand oxen, as many sheep, likewise pigs and goats, and so on. REISKE. Felicianus rightly says: "thousands of whichever you please." "Everything" <note>original: "πάντα"</note> means of every kind. This is exactly like "to sacrifice a hundred of everything" <note>original: "πάντα θύειν ἑκατόν"</note>, which Strabo (Book III, p. 107) and Athenaeus (Book IV, 10) praise from Pindar. For what is here written as "he will believe himself to act unjustly" <note>original: "ἀδικήσειν ὀνήσεται αὐτῷ"</note> is undoubtedly correct, whereas in that other place it is read corruptly in the plural: "of them" <note>original: "αὐτῶν"</note> in the genitive case. Our reading here is also confirmed by the written manuscript. Further down, "but the best first-offering to the gods" <note>original: "θεοῖς δὲ ἀρίση μὲν ἀπαρχὴ"</note>. And in the last line, "at the reclining-couches" <note>original: "κατακλίσεσιν"</note>, with only one letter varied in the middle syllable of that word. This, however, changes the meaning significantly and makes it better: and immediately followed by "the giving of contributions" <note>original: "συντάξεων δόσεσιν"</note>. VICTORIUS.

<gloss>6. And of the others —]</gloss> In earlier editions it is "and in those of the others" <note>original: "καὶ ταῖς τῶν ἄλ."</note>, which is also preferred by the Leipzig and Meermann Codices. Furthermore, it is true that in Eusebius' *Preparation for the Gospel* (p. 152 D), it reads "how could he ever be willing" <note>original: "ποτ’ ἂν ἑκών"</note>.

<gloss>7. All would.]</gloss> In place of "all would" <note>original: "πάντ’ ἂν"</note>, I later found "how would" <note>original: "πῶς ἂν"</note> substituted, and in Eusebius "how could he ever" <note>original: "ποτ’ ἂν"</note>. VALENT[IUS].

Philological notes discuss variations in the text compared to other ancient sources like Eusebius.</summary>

8. *They have no need, etc.*] See what we said in section 33. He said in section 15 that <note>original: "Deum τὸ τῶν θυόντων ἦθος, ἢ πρὸς τὸ τῶν θυομένων πλῆθος βλέπειν"</note> "God looks at the character of the sacrificers, rather than the quantity of things sacrificed." You have often observed that the word "to approach" <note>original: "προσίεναι"</note> carries the meaning of obedience, veneration, and religious worship. The Meermann manuscript incorrectly gives "of the greatest things" <note>original: "μεγίσων"</note> instead of "greatest" <note>original: "μεγίστην"</note>. In the margin it was read: "Note that God looks to the character of the human, and not toward the victim."

9. *How not temperate, holy, and just.*] Just as below he joins "prudently and temperately and holily," Book IV, 21. Exactly as here "temperate, just, holy," St. Paul in Titus 1:8. Wetstein compares these with the current passage, as well as the following with the Gospel of John 4:24. "Temperance, justice, and holiness" <note>original: "σωφροσύνη, δικαιοσύνη & ὁσιότης"</note> are joined this way by Plato in the *Lysis*, page 494.

1. *It is also fitting to offer moderately.*] I thought it ought to be read "as you see" <note>original: "ὠικείων"</note>, and therefore translated it "as you see." Now, having been informed by Eusebius, who also has "fitting" <note>original: "οἰκεῖον"</note>, it can better be rendered: "it would also be consistent for the Gods to take a libation from other things moderately." VALENTINIUS. Previously it was read "of moderate things" <note>original: "μετρίων"</note>. Neither did the Eusebius, Lipsius, or Meermann manuscripts differ. I think it was "moderate."

2. *For honors should be similar.*] Perhaps it should be "for it is necessary for honors to be similar" <note>original: "ἐοικέναι γὰρ δεῖ"</note> (which is also in the Lipsius manuscript). REISKE. I also preferred "it is necessary" <note>original: "δεῖ"</note> instead of "indeed" <note>original: "δὴ"</note>, and Elsner had already led the way in his notes on Paul's 2 Corinthians 9:7. The Meermann manuscript is no different. In Eusebius, "indeed" is published.

3. *Rising and sitting down.*] The Eusebius manuscript has "rising up and sitting down... not the giving of contributions." VALENTINIUS. The Lipsius manuscript correctly has "sitting down" <note>original: "κατακλίσεσι"</note> from "to lean" <note>original: "κλίνειν"</note>. But on "requests" <note>original: "δεήσεσιν"</note> it incorrectly agrees with the common version. The translator correctly conjectured "gifts" <note>original: "δόσεσιν"</note>. "Contributions" <note>original: "συντάξεις"</note> are taxes written for each person, which everyone pays unwillingly. REISKE. These are read foolishly, but they can be corrected with a little work from Eusebius. Compare these notes with the celebrated Wetstein on the Gospel of Matthew 23:6. The Meermann manuscript agrees with the Lipsius manuscript.

But God is not satisfied by these things. Wherefore Plato says that it is fitting for the good man to sacrifice and to always converse with the gods with prayers and offerings and sacrifices, and with every service; but for the evil man, his great labor concerning the gods is in vain. For the good man knows what must be sacrificed, and from what he must abstain, and what things must be brought forward, and from what things the first-fruits must be given; but the base man, bringing honors to the gods out of his own disposition and from the things he himself has been eager about, is impious rather than pious. 4. *If you remember &c.*] Grotius translated this in *Excerpts from Valent.* p. 911, whom [the editor] has followed. For *Philinus, a favor from you*, it previously read *To love: exchange a favor*. From which the writing of the *Leipzig Manuscript* does not depart much: *I have long since received [it], you love [me], exchange the favor*. I am not ignorant of where a pretext for these readings might be sought; however, I prefer the common reading. The *Meerman Manuscript* gives *curse the favor* instead of *long since*, and the *Bodleian Manuscript* gives *again*.

5. *For it was for this reason &c.*] The earlier editions wrongly had *before you I deposited*. *To deposit a favor with someone* is used as if for a *deposited gift* (for that is the proper meaning of *katatithenai*, whence a favor deposited in this way is elegantly said by the Greeks *to be laid up*). We have this usage in *Luke, Acts of the Apostles 24:27*, see the interpreters there, and *Wolf on Libanius, Epistle 215*. But in those examples, it is constructed with the dative case. Just as our author [uses it] in *Demosthenes against Neaera p. 864 B*: *to deposit a favor with the woman herself*. Likewise *On the Liberty of the Rhodians p. 145 B*: *to deposit a great service with him*. Which Aristides said as *unto someone* (Vol. I, p. 38) and Chariton (IV, 5, p. 72), where D'Orville diligently illustrates this manner of speaking. Reiske advised that in the upper verse, the article *the* before *favor* should be adopted from the *Leipzig Manuscript*, and that in this verse the meter requires the form *heneka* [because of].

6. *Satisfied by these things.*] A question mark should be placed after *these things*. For it is a speech in the form of a negative question. —REISKE.

7. *But the base man—*] Often *base men* are opposed to *good men*, but as to what Jeremiah Markland concludes from this in his notes on *Maximus Tyrius VIII, 3*, there instead of *dei* [it is necessary]—

### P O R P H Y R I I

[...should] associate with others, the philosopher thinks: for this is neither pleasing to the gods nor useful to men. Instead, he wishes for the philosopher to try to change others for the better; but if that is not possible, he must not let himself sink into their evil habits. He believes one must proceed along the straight path, taking no account of dangers from the many, nor of any other slander that might arise. For it would truly be a terrible thing if the Syrians would not taste fish, nor the Hebrews swine, nor most of the Phoenicians and Egyptians female cattle—indeed, though many kings have tried to make them change, they chose to endure death rather than the transgression of their law—while we [philosophers] [betray] the laws of nature and divine commands out of fear...

<column-break/>

...believes the philosopher ought to dwell among others. Since this would be neither pleasing to the gods nor useful to men, he wants the philosopher to take care that men are changed to a better state. But if he is less able to do this, he does not want the philosopher himself to slip into their bad customs. Rather, he judges that the philosopher must progress by the straight way, regardless of any danger or any infamy from the common crowd. For it would certainly be an absurd thing if, while the Syrians will in no way taste fish, and the Hebrews swine, and most of the Phoenicians and Egyptians female cattle—but when many kings applied force, they proposed to undergo death rather than violate their ancestral institutions—we [should abandon] the laws of nature and divine precepts because of terrors...

<margin>Where "cowardly" <note>original: δειλαῖς</note> is written, perhaps it should be read as "worthless" <note>original: φαύλοις</note>, since "good" follows; yet it may be seen otherwise. For "cowardly" is often the same as "bad" or "evil," even with no respect to war, as in Theognis: in *Sentences* 105 and 108. The Pythagoreans are accustomed to use that word in this way, as the Learned Man <term>V. D.: Vir Doctus, a standard abbreviation for a learned scholar</term> testifies regarding the *Golden Verses of Pythagoras*, 21. Immediately observe the elegant metaphor in "associating with" <note>original: συμπεριφέρεσθαι</note>, taken from ships that are tossed by the winds. We find "being carried about" <note>original: περιφέρεσθαι</note> used this way in the Epistle to the Ephesians and to the Hebrews. A little later, the Bodleian manuscript <note>A famous manuscript at Oxford</note> very poorly has "love-charm" <note>original: Φίλτρον</note> instead of "friend/pleasing" <note>original: φίλον</note>.</margin>

# PORPHYRY THE PHILOSOPHER
### ON ABSTINENCE FROM ANIMAL FOOD
### BOOK THREE.

# PORPHYRY
### ON ABSTINENCE FROM ANIMAL FOOD
### BOOK THREE.

#### SUMMARY.

In this third book, Porphyry proves that animals ought not to be killed because, since they participate in reason, justice can and should be extended even to them. § 1. 2. He shows that they do not lack reason from the fact that they use speech. § 3, etc. to § 7.

<summary>Porphyry concludes Book II by arguing that philosophers must remain steadfast in their dietary laws like the Jews and Egyptians, then opens Book III by arguing that animals deserve justice because they possess reason.</summary>

# PORPHYRY

->That animals direct themselves by internal reasoning, possess sensation, and are formed and affected in the same manner as we are. ### Section I.
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial N inside a square frame with floral and geometric patterns.</image-desc>
We have demonstrated in the two previous books, O Firmus Castricius, that the eating of animals contributes neither to temperance and parsimony, nor to piety, which are most conducive to the contemplative life, but rather is opposed to them. And Socrates indeed, against those who asserted that pleasure was the highest good, said that he would never believe it, even if all pigs and goats should prove it, in—

# On Abstinence, Book III.
<meta>catchword: δια- (Greek: "through" or "across")</meta>

...he said <note>referring to Socrates, mentioned on the previous page</note> that our happiness was situated in pleasure, provided that the intellect remained dominant in all things. We, however, even if all the wolves and vultures were to praise the eating of meat, will never concede that they speak of what is just, so long as man remains harmless by nature and abstains from procuring pleasures for himself through the injury of others. Therefore, let us move on to the discussion of justice. And because those who contradict this decree <note>referring to the decree of abstinence</note> assert that justice only extends toward beings similar to ourselves, and for that reason they exclude irrational animals from any legal or moral right in relation to humans: come, let us now put forward the true and simultaneously Pythagorean opinion on this matter. We shall demonstrate that every soul which participates in sensation and memory is also rational. For if this is demonstrated, it will be established—even according to their own opinion—that justice pertains to all animals. We shall relate what has been handed down by the ancients in summary form.

### Section 2.
Since, therefore, reason (or speech) is twofold according to the opinion of the Stoics—the one being internal—

<column-break/>

...that our happiness is situated in pleasure, so long as the mind rules in all things. But we, even if all wolves or vultures approve of meat-eating, will not grant them that they speak of justice, as long as man is by nature harmless and keeps himself from providing pleasures for himself through the harm of others. Moving then to the discourse on justice—since those who speak against us say that this must extend only toward similar beings, and for this reason <margin>4</margin> they strike the "irrational" animals from the account—come, let us provide the true and Pythagorean doctrine together, <margin>5</margin> demonstrating that every soul which shares in sense-perception and memory is rational. For if this is shown, we shall reasonably extend justice to every living being even according to their own terms. We shall speak by briefly summarizing the findings of the ancients.

### Section 2.
Since there are two types of <term>reason</term> <note>original: "logos"</note> according to the Stoics, <margin>1</margin> the one being internal—

***

<margin>4. **They strike the animals from the account.** <note>original: "Διαγράφουσι τῶν ζώων"</note> To "strike through" (diagraphēin) means to draw a transverse line through something, and thus to erase it or remove it from consideration. See what the illustrious **Reiskius** discusses regarding the nature of this metaphor in his excerpts on **Polybius**, page 766, and **Casaubon** on **Athenaeus**, Book II, chapter 22.</margin>

<margin>5. **Every soul, etc.** <note>original: "Πᾶσαν ψυχὴν"</note> This was indeed the foundation of the Pythagorean "abstinence" (apochē), and is therefore frequently emphasized by our author. Hence, in the *Life of Pythagoras*, he says that "all things produced with souls are of the same kind," as we have seen in another place.</margin>

<margin>1. **The internal, and the expressed.** <note>original: "Τοῦ μὲν ἐνδιαθέτου, τοῦ δὲ προφ."</note> This is a very common distinction in the writings of the philosophers and the ancient Christians. <term>Internal reason</term> <note>original: "logos endiathetos"</note> or "thoughtful reason" and <term>expressed reason</term> <note>original: "prophorikos"</note> or "speech." The ancients placed Mercury in charge of both, on which subject see **Toll's** *Italian Journey*, page 153.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument from Section 2 of Book III. He is currently challenging the Stoic definition of "reason" (logos) to show that if animals are excluded from justice because they "lack reason," the definition used by the Stoics is unfairly narrow and would exclude most humans as well.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

->**Book 3, Section 2**<-

...internal, the other external; and again, one being perfected <note>The Stoic term *katorthoma* refers to a perfectly right action performed by a wise person</note>, the other faulty. It is fitting to distinguish which of these they deprive the animals of. Is it only the right reason, or is it reason in the absolute sense? Or is it completely all reason, both that which is internal and that which proceeds outward? They certainly seem to attribute to them a total deprivation of all reason, not only of that which is perfected. For otherwise, these other animals would not be "irrational," but would still be "rational" beings, in the same way that almost all humans are regarded by them. For according to their view, there have been only one or two "Sages" <note>The Stoic ideal of a perfectly wise person</note> in whom alone "right reason" is seen; all others are base or "foolish"—even if some are making progress, while others are held in a flood of baseness. Nevertheless, all these humans are nonetheless considered rational by them. Therefore, the Stoics, led by an excessive self-love <note>original: *philautia*</note>, claim that all other animals are—

<column-break/>

...one internal, that is, *internal reason* <note>original: "ἐνδιαθετος" (endiathetos)</note>, which is arranged in the mind; the other external, which is expressed by the voice; and one right, the other depraved. It seems a distinction must be made as to which of these they deny to animals. Do they say that animals lack only right reason, and not reason in an absolute sense? Or do they say they lack all reason entirely, both that which is within and that which proceeds without? They certainly seem to attribute a total deprivation of all reason to them, not only of the perfected kind. For otherwise, the rest of the animals would not be "irrational," but would be considered "rational," just as almost all humans are according to their own standards. This is because, in their opinion, only one or two Sages are found in whom alone "right reason" is perceived. All the rest are base, even if some make a little progress and others are detained, as it were, in a flood of depravity. Yet all of them are nonetheless rational according to the Stoics. Thus, the Stoics, induced by an excessive love of their own kind, claim all other animals are—

they call them "irrational," wishing to express by this name "irrationality" that which is entirely deprived of reason. But if the truth must be told, not only is reason <note>original: "ratio" / "logos"</note> observed absolutely in all animals, but in many of them, reason is seen to be of such a kind that it displays indications approaching toward perfection.

§ 3. Since, therefore, reason and speech are twofold, as we have said—one consisting in the disposition of the mind, the other in outward pronunciation—we shall begin first with that which is uttered and consists in the voice. If, then, outward speech is a vocal sound which signifies and expresses through the tongue the affections that are within and in the soul (for this is the common definition, not yet attached to any specific sect <note>The author refers to philosophical schools like the Stoics or Peripatetics.</note>, but one which declares the simple notion of speech): what, I ask, is lacking from this in the other animals that are endowed with a voice? Do they not also first experience an affection in the soul, and think before they express it with the voice? Thought—

<column-break/>

—all the others, wishing to indicate the complete deprivation of reason through the term "irrationality." And yet, if one must speak the truth, not only is reason contemplated simply in all living beings, but in many of them it even <gloss>5</gloss> possesses approaches toward the perfect.

§ 3. Since, then, it was twofold—one in utterance, the other in disposition—let us begin first from the uttered kind, and that which is ordered according to the voice. If uttered speech is a vocal sound through the tongue signifying the internal passions and those according to the soul (for this is the most general definition, <gloss>1</gloss> and not yet adhering to any sect, but only to the conception of speech), what of this is absent from those creatures that utter sounds? And why do they not <gloss>2</gloss> also experience something first, and think before they say what they intend? I say indeed—

<margin>
5. *Possessing approaches.*] Perhaps *epibolas* <note>original: "ἐπιβολὰς"</note>: opportunities, approaches, entrances, protections. REISKE. I would prefer *hyperbolas* <note>original: "ὑπερβολὰς" meaning "excellences"</note>. He says that reason is not only found in living beings, but is found in such a way that it is much more excellent in some than in others. Indeed, in the following sections, he disputes at length for that reason, to show that it is stronger in some beasts than in others, and even more so than in humans. "Prosphora" was wrongly put for "prophora" <note>utterance</note> in the Meerman manuscript.

I think Felicianus expressed it well: *hairesis* is "choice" or "option," as Demosthenes and others join "choice and judgment," on which matter see Stephanus in the *Thesaurus*; otherwise it is defined as an "inclination toward doctrines." See Casaubon on Diogenes Laërtius I, 20. Soon after, the Leipzig and Meerman codices have "of those animals that utter sounds."
</margin>

<margin>
2. *Experience something first.*] For *tē* <note>the</note> read *ti* <note>something</note>. <meta>This page continues Porphyry's argument that animals possess "uttered reason" (speech), even if humans cannot interpret it. It draws a parallel between animal vocalizations and foreign human languages.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

-> P O R P H Y R I I <-

<meta>catchword: an- / te-</meta>

...thought is that which is spoken within the soul in silence. Therefore, regarding that which is voiced by the tongue (in whatever way it may be voiced, whether in a foreign manner, or in Greek, or like a dog, or like an ox), since it is indeed speech, those animals that are vocal partake in it. Men speak according to human laws <note>Greek: nomous; here meaning social conventions or linguistic rules</note>, while animals speak according to the laws which each has received from the gods and Nature. And if we do not understand them, what of that? For the Greeks do not understand the language of the Indians, nor do those raised in Attica understand the Scythians, Thracians, or Syrians. Rather, the sound of one group strikes the ears of another just like the "clangor of cranes." Yet to those speaking, their own language is literate and articulate, just as ours is to us; but to others—

<column-break/>

—for I call that "thought" <note>original: "tionem" from "cogitationem"</note> which is spoken in the soul through silence. Since, therefore, whatever is brought forth by the voice through the tongue is speech—whether it is expressed in a foreign way, or in Greek, or like a dog, or like a horse <note>The Latin translation here uses "equine" where the Greek used "ox-like"</note>—all other animals that possess a voice are capable of it. However, while men speak by human law, other animals speak by that law which has been granted to each by the gods and nature. If we truly do not understand, what does it matter? For the Greeks do not perceive the language of the Indians, nor do those educated in Attica understand the Scythians, Thracians, or Syrians. Instead, the sound of one voice is accustomed to strike the other no differently than the "clangor of cranes," even though each one's own voice is literate and articulate to themselves, just as ours is to us; to them—

---

<margin>Instead of "d", as was previously read incorrectly, both versions read "ha". The truth is "d". No less certain is "mellei", which is supported by the authority of the Leipzig and Meerman Manuscripts.</margin>

3. **"Whether like a dog, or like an ox."** That which is called "ox-like" (*boikōs*) here is called "to speak in the manner of an ox" (*boisti lalein*) in the *Life of Pythagoras*, chapter 24: see Holstenius's notes there. To speak "in the manner of a human" (*anthrōpikōs phthengesthai*) is discussed below in section 4. Reiske preferred the phrasing "vocal animals" (*ta zōa ta phōnētika*), and rightly so; the Meerman Manuscript prefers the same.

4. **"According to the laws which from—"** As is said of Plato in Clement of Alexandria's *Stromata*, Book I, page 338, C: "It is said that there are also dialects of irrational animals, which those of the same species understand." See more on this matter there. The Meerman Manuscript reads "as he received" (*hōs eilēchen*). It often happens in that manuscript that a syllable of the preceding word is repeated by mistake.

5. **"We do not understand, etc."** Exactly as our author does, Sextus Empiricus <note>A skeptical philosopher</note> in Book I, 14, page 20, says: "Even if we do not understand the voices of the so-called irrational animals, nevertheless—

<column-break/>

—it is not unlikely that they are conversing, though we do not understand. For even when hearing the voice of foreigners, we do not understand, but we think it is monotonous." The celebrated Fabricius provides more on this point there. Our author signifies this frequently in the following passages.

6. **"What of this?"** Namely, "What great thing is this?" or "What does this matter to the present case?" as seen below in Section 4. This is a common formula in interrogations. See Demosthenes, *On the False Embassy*, page 306, C: "If the Phocians are not present, what of it?" and others often. After "the language of the Indians," Fogerolles ineptly supplied "understood" (*synetoi*). "Understanding the tongue" is easily understood from the general sense. Then, the Leipzig Manuscript reads "nor that of the Scythians."

7. **"Literate to others."** Understand the word "being" (*ousa*), though it would be better if it were added. Perhaps "just as" (*hōs*) should follow immediately.

...[al]tered and inarticulate <note>original: "terata uero & inarticulata"; likely a continuation of a word meaning "distorted" or "strange"</note> is the speech of the Syrians, if we happen to hear it, or that of the Persians, just as the voice of all other animals strikes all men. For just as we perceive only a certain sound and noise, being unskilled in the speech of—for example—the Scythians, so that they seem to us to give a shriek and to explain nothing articulately, but rather to use a single sound, now longer, now shorter; and that variety of sound carries no meaning at all for us, yet for them their own speech is easy to understand and provides much distinction. It is the same way with other animals. Indeed, to them, the voice of each is clear and perceptible according to their specific kind; to us, only an empty sound, lacking all meaning, is heard. This happens because none among us, being learned in their tongue, has been able to explain to us—through an interpreter—what is being said among the other animals. Nevertheless, if we are to believe the ancients, and those who lived in our age and that of our ancestors—

—and inarticulate and unlettered is the speech of the Syrians, for instance, or the Persians, just as the voice of animals is to everyone. # PORPHYRY

...among those who are said to have listened to and possessed an understanding of the utterances of animals. Such were Melampus <note>A legendary seer of Greek mythology said to have learned the language of birds after snakes licked his ears.</note> and Tiresias <note>The famous blind prophet of Thebes.</note> among the ancients, and others of that kind; and not long ago, **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher and miracle-worker of the 1st century AD.</note>. Concerning him, it is said that while he was with his companions, a swallow <note>The Greek text says swallow, though the Latin and later notes discuss a sparrow.</note> flew over and made a sound; he said that the swallow was informing the others that a donkey had fallen down before the city, carrying a load of grain, which was now scattered on the ground because the beast of burden had fallen. Moreover, a certain friend of ours used to relate that he had been fortunate in a young servant boy who understood all the utterances of birds, and that they were all prophetic, and—

<column-break/>

—among our own people there have stood forth those who are said to have perceived and understood the speech of other animals. Just as in the memory of the ancients there were Melampus and Tiresias, and others of this sort: and not much before, Apollonius of Tyana: of whom indeed it is reported, that when he was in the company of friends, and a swallow had flown to them and chirped something or other, he said it was announcing to the others that they should hurry, because a donkey laden with a bundle of grain had fallen outside the city, and that it lay scattered across the ground. Indeed, a certain friend of ours used to tell us that he happened to have a servant boy who perceived the speeches of birds extremely well, all of which were prophetic, and—

---

<margin>
*Vossius* writes in *On Idolatry*, Book II, chapter 44, that these things either proceeded from human fraud or [deception]. On the other hand, certain peoples are mentioned who, ignorant of speech, screech rather than speak, as seen in *Pliny*: V, 8; *Solinus*; and *Fabricius* in his notes on *Sextus Empiricus*: I, 14, page 20.
</margin>

11. **Apollonius of Tyana.**] *Philostratus*, in his life of Apollonius, narrates the same thing as our author, except that Porphyry puts a swallow in place of a sparrow, and says a donkey with a load fell instead of grain being spilled by a boy. In this matter there is nothing inconsistent <term>asystaton: logically incompatible</term>, and thus he is undeservedly blamed by *A. Delrio* in *Magical Investigations*, II, 19. See: *Vossius* on *Idolatry*, III, 44. However, grain suits a sparrow better than a swallow. Regarding this wisdom of Apollonius, see also *Eusebius*: *Against Hierocles*, page 518, C.

12. **To say.**] Perhaps it should read "he said" <note>original: "εἶπεν"</note> because of the preceding "that" <note>original: "ὅτι"</note>. REISKE. Either "he said," or the second "that" is vacant, as it is often pleonastic <note>redundant</note> when an infinitive follows, as if that particle had not preceded at all; on this matter see the Learned Man on *Luke, Acts of the Apostles* XXVII, 10 and *Gronovius* on *Arrian's Expedition*, II, 16. Instead of "having sat upon" <note>original: "ἐπισάσης"</note>, *Abresch* elegantly conjectured "having flown to" <note>original: "ἐπιπτάσης"</note>. The common word for things that appear suddenly and can be seen by all is frequent. Instead of "under whom" <note>original: "ἐφ’ οὗ"</note>, the *Meerman* manuscript has "from whom" <note>original: "ἀφ’ οὗ"</note>; and instead of "uttering" <note>original: "φθεγγομένης"</note>, that manuscript has "to those uttering" <note>original: "φθεγγομένοις"</note>. Often the letters *eta* and *oi* are mixed up in that Codex. Also, "of the meal" <note>original: "ἄσεως"</note> is wrongly written for "of the city" <note>original: "ἄστεως"</note>.

13. **The beast of burden having fallen.**] *Lucian* and others use this term in matters of porterage, as *Jungerman* notes on *Pollux*, VII, 130.

14. **Understood all.**] Perhaps "he was understanding" <note>original: "ξυνίη" or "ξυνίει"</note>. REISKE. Or with *Abresch*, "he understood." It is confused a hundred times in compound verbs derived from "to be" and "to go." For "understanding," the *Leipzig Codex* has "having understood" below in section 5. *Gataker* on *Antoninus* <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, Book V, section 7, contends that "to be with" is used for "to understand," but see what *D’Orville* opposed to him on *Chariton*, Book V, 7, page 467; though by his own admission, confusion in the compounds of those verbs cannot be entirely avoided. A little later, instead of "he might send," one should read "they might send"; the *Meerman* manuscript is incorrect here.

<margin>
Scholiast on Euripides: snakes having come and licked the openings of the ears, made them so sharp-hearing that they alone heard the counsels of the gods and were the highest diviners. More other things on this matter can be read in Bochart: *Hierozoicon* I, 1, 3. and Olearius on Philostratus: *Life of Apollonius of Tyana* I, 20.
</margin>

4. **Provoke to battle.** <note>original Greek: Προκαλῆται εἰς μάχην</note> Porphyry speaks in full here. Elsewhere the term "to provoke" is used simply and everywhere when the talk is of a challenge to a contest or war. I only point out Kühn on Aelian: *Various Histories* I, 24. A little before, the word "to" <note>original Latin: "eis"</note> before "food" was wrongly omitted by Meermann.

5. **But when to one another...** <note>original Greek: Ὅταν δὲ πρὸς ἄλληλα φθ.</note> The Leipzig manuscript adds "not" after "but." Without doubt the particle for "indeed" <note>original Greek: μὲν (men)</note> lies hidden in it. Often those two—"indeed" and "not"—are exchanged for each other in transcriptions. If that is admitted, the passage could be reformed thus:

<column-break/>

"as many things as they indeed <note>original Greek: μὲν (men)</note> utter to one another are clear (that is to say, they are) and distinct." With this assumed, the word "if" <note>original Greek: εἰ (ei)</note> can hold its place before "appear." But if we set the passage thus: "but when they utter to one another clear things"—then "if" must be removed. It matters not which path you follow. — REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a famous German scholar and physician known for his editions of Greek texts.</note>. Meermann and the translator also expressed the reading of the Leipzig manuscript. Correctly so, in my opinion. But the Leipzig MS errs a little before, when it omits "and" before "raven," as does Meermann, who again confuses the Greek letters *eta* and *oi*, writing "of the one having laid down." Wetstein compares with these the "distinct speech" mentioned by Paul in 1 Corinthians 14:9.

6. **Crows indeed and magpies etc.** Persius in the prologue to his *Satires*, line 8:
> Who made the parrot so ready with its "hello,"
> And taught the magpies to attempt our words?

# On Abstinence, Book III.

->**On the Speech of Animals**<-

Both redbreasts <note>original: "erithaci"</note> and parrots imitate human beings; they remember what they hear, and while being taught, they listen to and perceive the instructor. Indeed, many of these birds have even pointed out and revealed those committing crimes within a house by using the words they had learned. Furthermore, the Indian hyena, which the natives call the *corocotta* <note>A mythical or semi-mythical creature often identified in antiquity as a hybrid of a hyena and a lioness or dog, famed for its mimicry.</note>, speaks in such a human-like manner even without a teacher that it is accustomed to frequent houses and call out to anyone it recognizes can be easily overpowered. For it imitates the voice of the person's dearest friend, or someone whom the person called would absolutely obey; the result is that the Indians, although they know of this trick, are deceived by the similarity, and obeying the voice, they go outside and are consumed and perish. Now, if not all animals—

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the original Greek text of the passage translated in the first column.</note>

Both redbreasts and parrots imitate humans and remember whatever they hear; when being taught, they obey the teacher, and many have reported those doing wrong in the house through the things they were taught. And the Indian hyena, which the locals call the *Krokottas*, speaks so humanly even without a teacher that it even visits houses and calls whoever it sees is easy for it to master; it imitates the voice of the person's most beloved, and whoever the one called would entirely obey. Thus, even though the Indians know this, they are deceived by the likeness and are destroyed as they go out and obey the voice. But if [it] does not imitate all—

<margin>Where he speaks of other birds of this kind and the singular cleverness of certain ones.</margin> **Casaubon:** Not forgetting our own. 7. **The Indian hyena which they call the Corocotta.** The *Corocotta* is a species of hyena which some write is born from a dog and a wolf, others from a hyena and a lioness. See **Wesseling** on Diodorus Siculus, Book III, 35. Some distinguish between these animals, yet both attribute to them that cunning malice which our author mentions. See **Aelian**, *On the Nature of Animals*, VII, 22. Most report that the hyena is not entirely ignorant of human speech, but they attribute the imitation of the voice especially to the *crocuta*. There are many testimonies to this matter, but **Vossius** in *On Idolatry*, Book III, 59, argues they are false. The **Leipzig Manuscript** has *korottan*, and it is also written this way in the small index added to the margin: "concerning the Indian hyena, which is also called the *korokotta*." **Meermann** has the same, except in the margin it is "concerning the I. H. or *korokotta*," and this should not be rashly rejected. For although the word is commonly pronounced with three syllables, **Aelian** (in the place cited) also calls it *korottan*. **Felicianus** also gave *Corocottam*, and **Salmasius** observed (on Capitolinus in *Antoninus Pius*, ch. 10) that it is almost always found written this way in Latin books of better quality.

8. **Speaks humanly.** <note>original: "Φθέγγεται ἀνθρωπικῶς"</note> **Diodorus Siculus** (III, 35) called this "imitating the dialect of humans." Above in section 3, we encountered "to speak like a dog or an ox."

9. **It imitates.** The **Leipzig Manuscript** has "to imitate" <note>original: "μιμεῖσθαι"</note>. This is poor and ambiguous, so that you do not know whether he wanted "it imitates" or "to imitate." But "to imitate" seems preferable. **REISKE.** <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a famous German physician and philologist.</note>

# P O R P H Y R Y

And if not every animal is <gloss>11</gloss> apt at learning our speech, what of it? For not even every human being is apt at learning or good at imitation—not only failing to mimic the sounds of animals, but not even mastering <gloss>12</gloss> five of the dialects found among men. Some animals perhaps do not speak because they are not taught, or because they are hindered by the physical organs of their voice. We ourselves, at least, <gloss>13</gloss> while in Carthage, raised a tame partridge that had flown to us. As time went on and familiarity turned it into a creature of great tameness, we perceived it not only fawning upon us, attending to us, and playing with us, but even answering back to our voice and, as far as it was able, responding. It did this in a different way than partridges are accustomed to calling one another; it was not silent, but when I spoke, it would call back in return.

<column-break/>

They imitate us, and if not all are fit for learning our speech, what does it matter? For neither are all men teachable, or fit for imitating the voices of other animals, nor even any five of the languages that exist among men. I might also mention that some animals perhaps do not speak either because they are not taught, or because they are hindered by the unsuitability of their vocal instruments. Indeed, when we were at Carthage, we raised a certain tame partridge that had flown to us; in the course of time it was brought to such a state of tameness that it not only played, fawned, and acted charmingly, but even cried out in turn at our voice, and as far as was possible, it even answered—in a different manner than partridges are usually accustomed to calling to one another. For it did not do this while I was silent, but while I was speaking and calling, it emitted its voice in turn.

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK III.

§ 5. It is likewise recorded that among animals lacking a human voice, some have followed their masters’ commands so promptly that no man could do better. For Crassus the Roman <note>original: "Crassi... Romani"</note> had a lamprey <note>original: "Muraena," a type of eel-like fish highly prized by Romans</note> so accustomed to him that it would come to him whenever it was called by name. He was so affected by its obedience that although he had previously borne the loss of three sons with moderation, he mourned for the fish when it died. Many have also handed down to memory that the eels in Arethusa <note>A famous spring in Syracuse, Sicily</note> and the *saperdas* <note>a type of small fish, possibly a perch or herring</note> around the Maeander River <note>A river in Asia Minor</note> listen to those who call them. Therefore, the internal thought <note>original: "imaginatio," translates the Greek "phantasia"</note> of the speaker, whether it issues forth into the tongue or not, is undoubtedly the same. I do not see, then, how it is not absurd to insist that only human speech should be called "discourse" <note>original: "orationem," translates "logon"</note> simply because it is perceived by us, while we reject the voices of all other animals. For it is just as if crows were to judge that only their own speech was truly discourse, and considered us irrational because we do not speak in a way that is clear to them; or as if the Athenians believed that only the Attic dialect was speech...

<column-break/>

§ 5. It is related that even among the voiceless <gloss>1</gloss> there are those who obey their masters as readily as any <gloss>2</gloss> man among his acquaintances. For instance, the <gloss>3</gloss> lamprey of Crassus the Roman, when called by name, would approach Crassus; and it so affected him that he mourned its death, though he had previously borne the loss of three children with composure. <gloss>4</gloss> Many have also recorded that the eels in Arethusa and the *saperdas* near the Maeander obey those who call them. Is not, then, the mental impression the same as that of the speaker, whether or not it reaches the tongue? How, then, is it not unreasonable to say that only human voice is "speech" <note>original: "logon"</note> because it is intelligible to us, but to reject that of other animals? For this is similar to if crows claimed that theirs was the only voice, and that we were irrational because we do not utter sounds that are clear to them; or if the Athenians said that only the Attic dialect was speech, and that all oth...

# PORPHYRY

->On Abstinence from Animal Food<-

...they considered others to be "irrational" <note>Greek: *alogous*, meaning both "without speech" and "without reason"</note> simply because they lacked the Attic dialect. And yet, an inhabitant of Attica would sooner understand the meaning of a crow than that of a Syrian or a Persian speaking in their own hissing and Persian tongues. But surely it is absurd to judge what is rational or irrational based on whether a speech is easily understood, or based on silence and voice. For by that logic, one might say that the God over all things, and the other gods, are not rational because they do not speak in this human way. Yet the gods signify their will while remaining silent; and the birds understand them more quickly than humans do. Having understood, they report these things as best they can, acting as heralds for the various gods to mankind. Of these, the eagle belongs to Zeus, the hawk and the crow to Apollo, and the stork to Hera...

<column-break/>

<margin>
See Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals*, Book 8, Chapter 4. Note the variations in the Meerman manuscript regarding the word for "calling" or "speaking." Abresch suggests a correction regarding the phrase "upon the tongue," which is confirmed by the Meerman codex.

<note>Scholarly Commentary on the Text</note>

5. **By not speaking.**] Reiske suggests the reading: "By speaking nothing," or rather, "one might say they are not even rational because they do not speak." The Meerman manuscript uses "thus" instead of "so." The Leipzig codex had a slight error in the particle used here.

6. **And understanding, etc.**] The Leipzig and Meerman codices use the form "having understood." As I mentioned above, birds were believed to be aware of the future and to be the heralds and interpreters of the gods. Indeed, these and other animals have a closer fellowship with God, and they teach humans those things which God has revealed to them—as Celsus says in Origen’s *Against Celsus*, Book 4, where more is written on this subject. Hence, a bird is called a "messenger"

<column-break/>

in Apollonius Rhodius, Book 3, line 1111. Euripides calls them "heralds of the gods." See also Plutarch and Spanheim’s notes on Callimachus’s *Hymn to Jove*. After the word "can," the Meerman manuscript adds: "now that he pursues, now that he has captured, and of the wanderer, that he wanders." These words appear again in their proper place shortly after, though the first part is omitted there.

7. **Of which the eagle is Zeus’s.**] Valentinus suggests "as" would be more suitable than "of which." While "of which" can be defended, I suspect it arose from the ending of the preceding word. It was fitting to consecrate the eagle to Jove; it is a truly royal bird. Diodorus Siculus writes: "The Thebans honor the eagle because this animal is thought to be kingly and worthy of Zeus."

8. **And to Apollo the hawk and the crow.**] Just as the eagle is to Zeus, so these birds were sacred to Apollo (or the Sun) among the Egyptians and other nations. From coins...

### On Abstinence, Book III.

Ff 2

...the stork <note>Latin: *ciconia*; Greek: *pelargos*</note>; the corncrake and the owl are sacred to Minerva; the crane to Ceres; and others to various other gods. Furthermore, those among us who are observant, and who spend their lives in the company of certain animals, recognize what their voices mean. For instance, a hunter, by the different qualities of a dog's barking <note>The OCR reads *laratus*, a likely error for *latratus*</note>, perceives whether it is seeking a hare, has found one, has caught it, or is merely wandering aimlessly. Likewise, a cowherd understands by the varying lowing of an ox whether it is hungry, thirsty, tired, aroused for mating, or searching for its calf. The lion also expresses threats through its roar, just as the wolf indicates its distress with a howl. Even by their bleating, shepherds can perceive what their sheep need.

§ 6. Nor does the human voice escape their understanding, whether we are angry or speaking kindly,

<column-break/>

...the stork; and for Athena, both the corncrake and the owl; for Demeter, the crane; and so others for other gods. Indeed, those of us who pay close attention, and those who are raised with them, recognize their utterances. A hunter, for example, knows from the "acting" <note>Greek: *hypokrisis*, referring here to the tone or delivery of the sound</note> of a barking dog whether it is now searching for the hare, now has found it, now is pursuing it, now has caught it, or, when the dog is lost, that it is wandering. And the cowherd knows whether the cow is hungry, thirsty, weary, in heat, or seeking its calf. The lion, by roaring, shows that he threatens; the wolf, by howling, that he is in a bad state; and the bleating sheep do not fail to make the shepherd understand what they require.

§ 6. Therefore, the voice of humans does not escape those animals either,

9. **As others for others.**] It seems that "as" <note>Greek: *hos*</note> should be deleted, and then one should read "others" in the plural <note>Greek: *alla* instead of *allo*</note>. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist</note>. Or, as *Abresch* preferred, "as others [people] for others [animals]." <term>MEERMAN</term> <note>The Meerman Codex</note> deletes "and" before "of us."

10. **A hunter, for example —**] *Sextus Empiricus* argues for the same cause in *Outlines of Pyrrhonism*, Book I, 14, page 21: "and we hear dogs uttering one voice when they are defending themselves, another when they howl, and another when they are beaten, and a different one when they wag their tails."

11. **Acting.**] <note>Greek: *Hypokrisis*</note> In this passage, it refers to a certain composition and modulation of the voice, varying according to the affection of the mind. <term>REISKE</term>.

12. **Whether the cow is hungry.**] Either "now" <note>Greek: *nyn men*</note> should be deleted, or if it is kept, one should read "that the cow is hungry, and now that it is thirsty, or weary." ### P O R P H Y R Y

...not as if they are merely reacting to anger, or friendliness, or being called, or being chased, or asked for something, or given something—not simply one of these, but they are seen to obey all such voices appropriately. This could happen in no way unless a similar intelligence <note>Original: "συνέσει" (synesei) / "intelligentia". Porphyry argues that for an animal to understand a human, there must be a shared "like" faculty of reason.</note> responded to its like. Furthermore, deer, bulls, and other animals are soothed by certain melodies, and are rendered tame from their wild state. <gloss>1</gloss> Even those very people who judge other animals to be irrational <gloss>2</gloss> assert that dogs are, in a way, capable of dialectics <note>The art of logical investigation and reasoning.</note>. <gloss>3</gloss> Specifically, they claim dogs use what is called the "syllogism of multiple choices" when they reach a three-way crossroads while tracking prey. For they say the dog reasons thus: "The beast went either this way, or that way, or the other way; but it went neither this way nor that way; therefore, it fled the third way." Once they have gathered this conclusion, they are accustomed to dash off in that remaining direction. Although a response is ready for those critics—that dogs have these traits by an internal nature because no one taught them—it is as if we ourselves were not also allotted reason by nature, <gloss>4</gloss> even if...

<column-break/>

...whether they [humans] call, or chase them away, or wish to seek or give something: but they are seen to obey all such voices appropriately. Which could in no way happen unless a like intelligence responded to a like. Also deer, bulls, and other animals are mitigated by certain modulations <note>Musical rhythms or tones.</note>, and from wild are rendered tame. Add that even those who judge other animals to be irrational assert that dogs are in some way capable of dialectics, especially in that proposition which they call "disjunctive from several," when in tracking they come upon a certain three-way crossroads. For they say they [the dogs] reason thus: "The beast went either this way, or that way, or that other way; but neither this way nor that way: therefore it fled that way." When they have gathered this, they are accustomed to throw themselves into the run that way. Although a response can be ready for them [the critics], that the dogs have these things innate by nature, because they were taught by no one: as if forsooth we also [were not naturally rational]...

---

<margin>1. "From wild etc." <note>Original: "Ἐξ ἀγρίων &c."</note>] Clarius noted this. Abresch notes the passage is in Eustathius’s commentary on Homer’s *Iliad* Book I, page 284, at the end. A little before this, the phrase "not the one asking" is wrongly missing in the Leipzig Codex.</margin>
<margin>2. "Of dialectics themselves" <note>Original: "Διαλεκτικῆς μὲν αὐτοὶ"</note>] The Leipzig manuscript gives "For of dialectics themselves," which I would not reject; and so also Meerman.</margin>
<margin>3. "And to use the [syllogism] through several disjunctions etc." <note>Original: "Κεχρῆσθαί τε τῷ διὰ πλ. διεζ. &c."</note>] This is taken from Plutarch, where you may also read these things in Volume II, page 969 A. Concerning the traces of reason found in brute animals, many authors have written much. See those whom Fabricius praises in his notes on Sextus Empiricus, Book I, chapter 14. There is more on this matter at paragraph 7; see also Meerman.</margin>

<margin>
He calls their history <note>Aelian: Various History IV, 19.</note> a well-known title of Aristotle's work, "The History of Animals," or "Inquiries on Animals." On this matter, see Perizonius's notes on Aelian in the cited place.

8. **That which participates in reason.** <note>original: "Τὸ μετέχον τοῦ λόγου"</note> Perhaps it should read "that which participates in their spoken reason," because of what follows. The verb "to grasp" <note>original: "ἑλεῖν"</note> is drawn from the language of hunting. *Reiske.* "The reason" <note>original: "Τὸν λόγον"</note> in the Lipsian and Meerman manuscripts is an error. "To grasp" means to hold an opinion or to judge. Philosophers are accustomed to using this for the dogma they follow. See *Stephanus’s Thesaurus*.

<margin>
1. **One must also demonstrate the [reason] within them, etc.** There are many among the ancients who thought that reason was common to animals and humans, including some among the Jews and, what you might find surprising, Christians, as is clear from Lactantius and others. See Scheffer's notes on Aelian, *Various History* I, 6. Among more recent writers, not a few have established the same thing. Wolf, in his notes on the *Philosophical Origins*, chapter 9, praises many who took it upon themselves to elaborate on this argument. More recently, the most excellent scholar S. H. Reimarus has most sagaciously disputed the ingenuity of beasts. The famous Mosheim explains Porphyry’s dogma in his notes on Cudworth’s *Intellectual System*, page 1159, where there is more on this matter. However, what that distinguished man says—that Porphyry judged the minds of brute animals to be equal to human minds—should not be taken too strictly. At any rate, he felt with his mentor Pythagoras "that all things which are born with souls ought to be considered of the same kind" <note>original: "ὁμογενῆ"</note>, as he says in his *Life of Pythagoras*, 19; or "that all ensouled beings participate in the rational," as seen below in § 23. He therefore thought the souls of animals were of the same essence <note>original: "ὁμοουσίους"</note> as ours, not indeed in terms of their physical substance, but according to the "more and less" of their participation in reason, as Holstenius correctly notes on the former passage of our author. This is what he explicitly signifies in this place.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the argument that animals possess both physical and mental similarities to humans. Porphyry is now moving into a physiological proof, arguing that because animals share our biological structures and suffer from the same diseases, they must also share our internal mental capacities.</meta>

### On Abstinence, Book III. ###

P

...that almost no one does not grant that other animals are disposed no differently than us regarding the rest of the instrumental organization <note>The physical "tools" or structures of the body</note>, both of the sensory parts and of the whole flesh. For they share a similarity with us not only in the natural affections and movements that exist within them, but there is also a great communication <note>original: "communicatio," meaning a shared experience or likeness</note> between us and them in those things which occur contrary to nature and are morbid. Nor should any right-thinking person assert that they are devoid of reason and speech simply because of the diversity of their physical habit and form; for among humans, too, one sees much variety of this kind according to the diversity of races and peoples, and yet he grants that all are nonetheless rational beings. The donkey, then—to come to the point—is accustomed to be seized by a dripping of phlegm <note>original: "pituitae destillatione," likely referring to catarrh or a respiratory infection</note>; if this flows down into the lungs, it is consumed by the illness and dies just like a human. The horse becomes suppurated <note>afflicted with pus or abscesses</note>, and just like a human, it is consumed and wastes away. Likewise, stiffness <note>rigor</note> invades the horse, and—

<column-break/>

—almost everyone has conceded that they are disposed similarly to us in their instrumental organization, both in terms of their senses and <margin>3</margin> according to their flesh. For they share with us not only the natural passions and movements through these parts, but even those things observed in them that are contrary to nature and diseased. A person of sound mind would not say they are incapable of a rational disposition because of the difference in their bodily state, seeing that even among humans there is much variation in state <margin>4</margin> according to races and nations, and yet he concedes that all are rational. The donkey is certainly seized by catarrh, and if the disease flows into its lungs, it dies just like a human. <margin>5</margin> The horse also becomes full of pus and wastes away, just like a human. And <margin>6</margin> tetanus seizes the horse, as do gout, fever, and rabies...

...Indeed, stags no longer shed their horns, but retain them, just as eunuchs retain their hair <note>A reference to the observation that those castrated before puberty do not go bald</note>; however, if they are still without horns when they are castrated, they never produce them thereafter, just like those who are made eunuchs before they have grown a beard. It is certainly not the case that only human taste perceives flavors <note>original: χυμῶν (chymōn)</note>, sight perceives colors, smell perceives odors, hearing perceives sounds, or touch perceives hot and cold and other such tactile qualities, while other animals do not perceive them likewise. Indeed, it cannot be said that other animals lack senses.

one must go out to find a boar or a deer: indeed, the state of the air affects us slowly, but is felt immediately by other animals, so that we take from them the signs of coming storms. Furthermore, they possess such an exact distinction of flavors that they discern what is morbid, healthy, and poisonous better and more exquisitely than any human physician is able. Now, Aristotle <note>referring to Aristotle's "History of Animals" or "On the Soul"</note> asserts that those beings endowed with more vigorous senses are also more prudent. The diversity of bodies may indeed cause one to be affected easily or with difficulty, or to possess a reason that is more or less ready; but it cannot change the soul in its essence, since it has neither changed nor entirely taken away the senses or the passions. Therefore, it must be conceded that the difference lies in being endowed with more or less reason or speech, not in being utterly devoid of them; nor that we possess it while they do not. For just as in one and the same

<column-break/>

9 <note>original Greek: οἱ διελθεῖν ἐπὶ σῦν ἢ ἔλαφον</note> ...to go out after a boar or a deer; and the state of the air touches us late, but other animals immediately, so that these are used as evidence of what is to come. 10 They know the distinction of juices <note>or "flavors/humors"</note> so as to be precise about both the diseased, the healthy, and the poisonous, 11 as not even the physicians among men can do. Aristotle says that those with better senses are more prudent. Differences of bodies can make them easily or hardly affected, and have reason more or less at hand, but they cannot alter the soul in its essence, since it has not turned the senses 12 nor the passions, nor made them entirely departed. Therefore, let a difference be granted in the "more and less," not in a total deprivation; nor in one having it absolutely and the other not; but as in a single genus...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the intelligence of animals and the relationship between the soul and the body. The catchword "non" from the previous page leads into the Latin translation of the Greek text.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

...one body is, <gloss>13</gloss> so to speak, healthier, and another less so, and in disease likewise there is a great difference; and just as there are <gloss>14</gloss> natural aptitudes and lack of aptitudes <note>original: "εὐφυΐαις καὶ ἀφυΐαις" — terms usually referring to innate talent or physical disposition</note> in bodies, so it is in souls: one is good, another base; and of the base, one is more so, another less. Even among the good there is not the same equality; Socrates, Aristotle, and Plato were not good in the same way, nor is there identity even among those of the same school of thought. Therefore, even if we possess more intellect than the other animals, we must not for that reason strip the animals of their intelligence. Just as partridges are not to be deprived of the power of flight because hawks fly better than they do; nor are other hawks to be thought lacking flight because the <gloss>15</gloss> dove-killer <note>original: "φασσοφόνος" — likely the peregrine falcon or a similar raptor</note> excels them and all others. One might grant, then, that the soul sympathizes with the body, and is affected by it whether it is in a good or bad state, but that the soul changes its own nature—that is impossible.

<column-break/>

...in the same class of bodies, both in the fitness for health or the susceptibility to disease, there is a great diversity: so in souls also, some are found good, others wicked: and of the wicked, some are more so, others less so, and in the good also there is not the same parity. For Socrates, Aristotle, and Plato are not good in a similar way. Furthermore, not even in those who hold the same opinion is there an entirely identical conformity. Therefore, if we also understand more than the rest of the animals, the intelligence of the rest of the animals must not be taken away for that reason. Just as partridges are not to be deprived of flight because hawks fly more powerfully than they; nor are other hawks to be judged to lack flight because the one called the "dove-killer" stands out above them and all others. Someone might therefore concede that the soul has a certain consensus with the body, so that it is indeed affected by the body being well or ill-disposed, but its nature nevertheless [does] not [change].

---

<margin>13. *As a healthier body.*] Either "as" <note>original: "ὡς"</note> should be deleted, or it should read "so to speak, healthier" <note>original: "ὡς εἰπεῖν, ὑγιεινότερον"</note>. As if to say, or rather thus: .. in each one, so to speak, in its kind, one is healthier. — REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist</note>.</margin>
<margin>14. *Natural aptitudes and lack of aptitudes.*] These pertain to the habit and nature of the body. Elsewhere they are usually transferred to the soul, whence Plato and others called the excellence of character "good natural aptitude" <note>original: "εὐφυΐαν"</note>, and he who was strong in it was called "well-endowed" <note>original: "εὐφυὴς"</note>. The opposite is "lack of aptitude" <note>original: "ἀφυΐα"</note> and "unfit" <note>original: "ἀφυὴς"</note>. So our author in the *Life of Pythagoras*, chapter 1, where see Holstenius: but I spoke of this word above at Book I, section 11.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>15. *The dove-killer of all.*] Homer: *Iliad* Book 15, line 238:
- - - - - - - - - - - like a hawk
swift, the dove-killer, which is the swiftest of winged things.
From there the Author of the *Life of Homer* took it, in Gale’s *Opuscula Mythologica, Physica et Ethica*, page 320. So the hawk is called the "lightest of winged things" in *Odyssey* Book 13, line 87. Regarding the speed of these birds, Bochart has much in *Hierozoicon* II, 29. Aelian calls it the "dove-slayer" <note>original: "Φασσοφόντην"</note> in *History of Animals* XII, 4. A little after, "as" <note>original: "ὡς"</note> before "instrument" <note>original: "ὀργάνῳ"</note> is missing in the Leipzig edition.</margin>

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK III.

G g 3

...does not change. But if the soul is only affected in conjunction with the body, and uses the body as an instrument, it will be able to perform many actions through that instrument—if it is organized differently than ours—which we ourselves are unable to do. At the same time, though the soul may be affected by the body’s condition, it does not change its own essential nature.

§ 9. We must therefore demonstrate that the rational power of the soul is also present in other animals, and that they do not lack prudence <note>original: "prudentia" / "φρονήσεως" — referring to practical wisdom or foresight</note>. First, indeed, every animal knows best whether it is weak or strong: and for this reason, it guards against some and uses others for its own defense. The leopard indeed protects itself with its teeth; the lion with its claws and likewise its teeth; the horse with its hooves; the ox with its horns; the cock with its spur; and the scorpion with its sting. But the Egyptian serpents defend themselves with spit—for which reason they are also called <term>ptyades</term> <note>original: "πτυάδες" — "spitters"</note>—and with it, they aim for and blind the eyes of those who attack them. Thus, it is clear that different animals use different means to preserve their own safety. Furthermore, those animals that are brave and strong graze and live far away from humans; whereas the weaker and more cowardly creatures, on the contrary, live far from other fiercer be-

<column-break/>

...us. But if the soul only sympathizes with the body, and uses it as an instrument, it might perform many things through it (if the instrument is organized differently than ours) which we are incapable of performing; and it would sympathize with the body's state, yet it would not truly change its own nature.

§ 9. Therefore, it must be shown that the rational element is within them, and they are not deprived of prudence. First, each animal knows if it is weak or strong, and so it guards against some things and makes use of others: as the leopard uses its teeth, the lion its claws and teeth, the horse its hoof, the ox its horns, the cock its spur, and the scorpion its sting. Those serpents in Egypt defend themselves with spit (whence they are also called "spitters") and they blind the eyes of those who approach. 3. **As much as it knows what is for its advantage.**] The Leipzig manuscript has "as much as is advantageous," without the word "for." This is correct. One could also read "everything which it knows to be advantageous (or suitable) for itself." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and philologist known for his textual criticism.</note>

# On Abstinence, Book III.

...there was never a time when it was irrational; but as soon as it existed, it also existed as rational; and nothing could prevent it from being so, since it did not acquire reason through any training. But in animals, just as in humans, there are many things that nature has taught; others are later acquired through training. For they learn certain things from one another, and some, as has already been said, even from humans; and they are endowed with memory, which is the principal part of the acquisition of reason and prudence <term>prudence: here translating "phronesis," a type of practical wisdom or intelligence</term>. # P O R P H Y R Y #

...if he were a vine-dresser planting a vine, he would not do so unless he applied his mind to it; yet almost all men procreate while drunk. But the other animals do not act this way. They bring forth life for the sake of offspring, and for the most part, once they have made the female pregnant, the males do not attempt to mount her, nor does the female allow it. In this matter, the degree of human insolence and lack of self-control is clear. Among animals, the mate recognizes the labor pains and often shares in the suffering <note>The text suggests a form of sympathetic labor, where the male feels the female's pain</note>, just as roosters do; some even help hatch the eggs, as male pigeons do. They also take care to find a place where they are to give birth. And when each has given birth, it cleans the newborn and itself. If someone observes carefully, they will see that everything proceeds with order and reason. For they also run to meet their provider with wagging tails, recognize their master, and point out an intruder.

§ 11. Who is ignorant of how social animals maintain justice toward one another? Take, for instance, the ants—

...if he should cultivate a field or plant a vine, he would not do so unless he turned his mind specifically to that task; yet almost all men are at leisure for procreating children while drunk. In which matter, there is no doubt how much human insolence and intemperance exists. Furthermore, in other animals, one mate even recognizes the labor pains of the other; and many even experience labor together, as do roosters; some even incubate eggs together, like pigeons; and they take care to seek out the place where they are to give birth. Likewise, each one, when it has produced its offspring, cleanses both itself and the fetus brought into the light. In these things, if anyone observes correctly, they will notice that all things proceed by order and reason. For they even run to meet their parent by fawning, recognize their master, and indicate the traps of strangers.
