-># On Abstinence, Book III.<-

...is most clearly evident in bees and other similar creatures. Who is ignorant of the chastity of wood-pigeons <note>original: "palumbium"</note> toward their mates? For if they happen to be pressed by an adulterer, and the mate discovers it, they strike him down and kill him. Who has not observed the justice of storks <note>original: "ciconiarum"</note> toward their parents? For a certain proper virtue excels in each animal, for which it has been made fit by nature; so that neither the nature nor the stability of these virtues ought to take away from them their rational power. For that point <note>that they lack reason</note> could perhaps be proved if the works of virtue and rational skill <note>original: "rationalisque solertiae"</note> were not clearly seen. Although we do not understand how these things are done, because we are unable to penetrate into their thoughts, they are not therefore to be condemned by us in such a way that they are thought to be entirely lacking in reason. For since we cannot penetrate into the mind of God in any 
way...

<column-break/>

...each of these, and this is also true of bees and similar creatures. And who is unheard of <note>unaware of</note> the temperance <note>original: "σωφροσύνην" (sophrosynen)</note> of wood-pigeons toward those they live with—who, if they are even victims of adultery, kill the one who committed the adultery if they catch them—or the justice of storks toward those who gave them birth? For in each animal a certain specific virtue stands out toward which it is naturally inclined; therefore, neither nature nor the constancy of these traits removes reason from them. For one would have to prove that their works are not those of virtue and rational dexterity <note>original: "λογικῆς ἐντρεχείας" (logikes entrecheias)</note>. But if we do not understand how these things are practiced because we cannot enter into their reasoning, we shall not for that reason accuse them of irrationality. For no one is able to penetrate into the mind of God...

---

1. ...which seems to be later. <term>Reiske</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and philologist.</note> It often happens among the ancients that they join an adjective or pronoun of a different gender to a substantive. This seems to have arisen because another word expressing the same thing was being observed in the writer's mind. This matter has been insisted upon so many times that I would not wish to add even a single example from Greece or Latium. In this place, "race" <note>original: "γένος" (genos)</note> or something similar can be understood.

2. *The temperance of wood-pigeons, etc.*] "Of temperance" <note>genitive case</note> because of the following word "unheard of." <term>Reiske.</term> <term>Fogerolles</term> <note>François de Fogerolles, a 17th-century physician and translator of Porphyry.</note> had also corrected it thus: rightly so, unless you wish to repeat "who is ignorant" from the previous lines. For then it seems one should read "or who is unheard of... regarding the storks." <term>Aelian</term> discusses the chastity of wood-pigeons in *On the Nature of Animals*, Book III, 44, who also records that they punish adultery with death. More on this matter in <term>Samuel Bochart</term>, *Hierozoicon*, part II, Book I, chapter 4.

<column-break/>

3. *Or that of the storks...*] Rather, "or who [is unheard of] regarding the storks," as was just said. <term>The Celebrated Abresch</term> <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch (1699–1782), a Dutch philologist.</note> agrees with me. The ancients everywhere proclaim the piety of the stork. "Regarding storks, then, it is a common story among many that they are fed in return [by their young]," to speak with <term>Aristotle</term>, *History of Animals*, Book IX, chapter 13. A little later, "we take away" is erroneously written in the *Leipzig Manuscript* instead of "being taken away."

4. *Rational dexterity.*] "Rational dexterity" <note>original: "λογικὴ ἐντρέχεια"</note> is rational—if I may put it so—skill, or the use of reason. It often denotes skill mixed with some malice, yet not always, but is also taken in a good sense. Thus <term>The Celebrated D'Orville</term> <note>Jacques Philippe d'Orville (1696–1751), a Dutch classicist.</note> explains the passage we have at hand in his notes on Chariton, Book II, chapter 6, page 195.

<margin>See Romans 11:34: "For who has known the mind of the Lord?" On this point, Johannes Alberti cites secular authors; Porphyry often regards God as unsearchable to the human mind. See Job 11:4, 1 Corinthians 2:10-11, etc.</margin>

6. **The works of the sun, etc.**] It should rather be read "of God" <note>original: "θεοῦ" (theou)</note>. However, "of the sun" <note>original: "ἡλίου" (heliou)</note> can be tolerated, though it is not as suitable a reading. —VALENTINUS. <note>The editor, Conrad Gesner or similar, citing an earlier commentator.</note> Pythagoras, Plato, and others held the sun and other celestial bodies to be Gods, which they believed to be rational and endowed with a mind, as has been said in another place. Plato calls the sun and moon "great gods" in *Laws, Book VII, p. 901.* Julian the Apostate says in *Epistle 51*: "The Great Sun, the living image, both ensouled and intelligent, and a benefactor from the intellectual Father." Therefore, although the Pythagoreans (from whom the Stoics received this) believed God was diffused through all nature, they nevertheless held the sun and other celestial bodies to be the primary image of Him. "For the whole rational order, along with its inherent incorruptible body, is an image of the whole Creator," as I might say with Hierocles in his *Commentary on the Golden Verses of Pythagoras, p. 18.*

The word "sharing" <note>original: "κοινωνούντων" (koinonounton)</note> is from a correction by the same ancient hand.

2. **Extending [to those] to whom.**] That word "to whom" <note>original: "οἷς" (hois)</note> has no value; therefore it seems it should be deleted. —VALENTINUS. "To whom" should be deleted as a faulty repetition of the last syllable of the preceding word "extending" <note>original: "ἐκτείνοντας" (ekteinontas)</note>. —REISKE. Only someone with a stomach for stones could tolerate these things as they were previously published. The word "to whom" used to be connected with the preceding "extending." If you place a mark of distinction after that word, the sense becomes convenient: "For just as among humans, to whom life vanishes if society is removed, so it is for those animals." It has often been said that our author [Porphyry] loves these types of transpositions.

3. **In need of humans [he] placed...**] Perhaps it should be "he placed both humans in need of them, in the use..."

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument from Book III of "On Abstinence." In the preceding section, Porphyry argued that animals and humans share a social bond. ### On Abstinence, Book III. ###

Hh 2

...and it seems that nature has established humans in this state of need for this very reason: so that a common right <note>original: "commune ius" — implying a shared moral or legal standing</note> might be generated both for them toward us, and for us toward them. If there are some animals that act fiercely toward humans, it is not surprising. For what Aristotle says is true: he claims that if a supply of food were available to all, animals would not exercise any ferocity toward each other, nor toward humans. Indeed, all their friendships and enmities arise for the sake of food—however meager and necessary—and for the sake of their dwelling place. For if humans were reduced to that same scarcity of necessities that oppresses other animals, how much more fierce and monstrous must we think they would become, even compared to those creatures that currently seem "wild"? War demonstrates this, for in war men do not even abstain from devouring one another. Furthermore, even without war or famine, they do not hesitate to kill and eat the tame animals that live among them.

<column-break/>

...making humans feel the need for them, [Nature] implanted justice <note>original: "τὸ δίκαιον" (to dikaion) — natural justice or right</note> in them toward us, and in us toward them. But if any act wildly toward humans, it is nothing to wonder at; for the saying of Aristotle was true: that if all possessed an abundance of food, they would not behave wildly toward one another or toward humans. For it is for the sake of this [food], even if it is necessary and cheap, that their enmities and friendships exist, and also for the sake of their territory. But if humans were so completely shut into want as animals are, how much wilder would they have become even than those that seem wild? This is shown by war and famine, where men do not even spare tasting one another; and even without war and famine, they devour the very animals that are tame and reared alongside them.

# PORPHYRY

§ 13. But someone might say that while animals are indeed rational, they have no relationship <note>original: "σχέσιν" (schesin) - a technical term for a moral or social connection</note> toward us. And yet, it was by first assuming they were irrational that people denied this relationship; they made them out to be irrational, and then they derived our lack of community with them from their own needs <note>i.e., the human desire to use animals for food or labor</note>, rather than from the nature of reason itself. Our goal, however, was to demonstrate that they are rational, not whether they have made formal agreements with us. For even among humans, not everyone enters into a contract with us, yet no one would call a person "irrational" simply because they have not made such an agreement. Furthermore, many animals have even served humans, and as someone rightly said, although they serve through the ignorance and injustice of men, they have—through their own wisdom and justice—turned their masters into their own servants and caretakers. <note>Porphyry suggests that by being useful, animals compel humans to feed, shelter, and protect them, effectively making humans their "stewards."</note> Moreover, their vices are clearly visible, and it is from these that their rational faculty is most clearly revealed; for—

<column-break/>

§ 13. But indeed, someone might say that they are rational, yet they have no regard for us. First, they made them irrational, and from the fact that they were irrational, they asserted that they had no relation to us. Then, they claim that our fellowship with them is based on the utility we perceive in them, not on reason. But our purpose is to show that they are rational, not whether they have any pact with us; since even among men, not all are joined to us by a pact, and yet no one would say those who do not agree with us are therefore irrational. But many of them have even served men, and as a certain person said quite rightly, although they served out of the ignorance and injury of men, they themselves, out of wisdom and justice, rendered their masters their own ministers and managers. And indeed, their vices are plain to see, from which the rational faculty shines forth. For and in—

1. *Then from the need &c.*] Instead of "which they attach" <note>original: "ἣν ἀναπτόντων"</note> I would gladly read "they attached themselves." **VALENTIUS**. Something seems to be missing here; perhaps the passage may be patched up thus: *Then, being refuted, they deny that there is a treaty between us and them. But this belongs to those who trace our community with them back to necessity and utility, not to reason.* **REISKE**. I would prefer: "they made them irrational" (previously a major punctuation mark was placed there) "since from the need—" He is responding to those who did not deny reason to animals, but maintained they had no relation to us. But in truth, he says, they removed that relationship because they considered them incapable of reason, as that suited their purposes. There were, of course, those who called animals "outcasts and excluded from community" (Book I, § 4). However, he had taught in the preceding sections that a community exists between them and humans.

2. *But to us, if [they are] rational—*] **Valentius** had also fixed a small star <note>a marginal mark for a query or correction</note> to this place, which **Reiske** rightly observes is sound, if it were distinguished in the way we have followed. Previously, it used to be done otherwise. *If* <note>original: "εἰ"</note> here means *that* <note>original: "ὅτι"</note>.

3. *As serving.*] The "As" <note>original: "Ὡς"</note> should be deleted as a mistaken repetition from the nearby "rightly" <note>original: "ὀρθῶς"</note>. **REISKE**. A little later, for "they are jealous" <note>original: "ζηλοτυποῦσιν"</note>, the **Meerman manuscript** reads "they emulate" <note>original: "ζηλοῦσιν"</note>.

# P O R P H Y R Y

...they refrain and depart; indeed, some even mock and urinate upon the trickery of men. Others, however, yielding to greed and gluttony, though they are not unaware that they will be captured, nevertheless—no differently than the companions of Odysseus <note>The Greek text refers to Odysseus; the Latin uses the Roman name, Ulysses.</note>—do not hesitate to expose themselves to death as they gorge themselves and eat. And some have argued, not without merit, that animals are much more prudent than we are, based on the very regions they were allotted to inhabit. <margin>2</margin> For just as those dwelling in the aether <note>The highest, purest part of the atmosphere, where the stars and gods were thought to reside.</note> are rational, so they say that those inhabiting the region immediately following it, such as those in the air, and then the aquatic, and finally the terrestrial, differ in degree according to their distance. We inhabit the very <margin>3</margin> dregs <note>original: "ὑποστάθμην" (hypostathmēn) – literally the sediment or dregs that settle at the bottom of a liquid.</note> of these regions. For surely superiority of rank based on location is not something to be considered only in the case of <margin>4</margin> the gods, while for mortals we refuse to apply the same logic.

<column-break/>

...abstain and depart; indeed, they sometimes insult and urinate upon the fraudulent devices of men. Others, truly succumbing to desire and gluttony, though they do not ignore that they must be captured, nevertheless, just like the companions of Ulysses, do not hesitate to expose themselves to death as they gorge and eat. Some, however, are not wrong to attempt to demonstrate, from the places which they have been allotted, that they are much more prudent than us. For just as those who inhabit the aether are rational, so they say are those who occupy the next adjacent place, such as those who spend their lives in the air; and to these are joined the aquatic, and to the aquatic the terrestrial, in proportion to their distance. We inhabit the lowest region of these. For obviously, excellence is not to be considered based on location only among the gods, while among mortals the same is not to be done.

<margin>2. *For just as those dwelling in the aether are rational.* ----]</margin> Perhaps the text should read "most rational" <note>original: "λογικώτατα" (logikōtata)</note>. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a famous 18th-century philologist.</note>. Elsewhere, living beings <note>original: "ζῶα" (zōa)</note> are commonly divided into those of the land, the sea, and the heaven. See <term>Casaubon</term> on <term>Strabo</term> page 2. The ancient philosophers taught that all regions of the world—the aethereal, the aerial, the aquatic, and the terrestrial—produce, nourish, and foster living beings of their own kind, as is evident from Aristotle and others. See <term>Gataker</term> on <term>Antoninus</term> <note>Marcus Aurelius.</note> Book XII, 24, and <term>Casaubon</term> on <term>Athenaeus</term> Book VIII, 13. Our author, I believe, is imitating <term>Plato</term> in the *Phaedo*, page 81. D: "and that these are the dregs, always flowing together into the hollows of the earth."

# On Abstinence, Book III

<columns>2</columns>

§ 15. Since they <note>referring to non-human animals</note> even acquire skills—and human ones at that—learning to dance, to drive chariots, to engage in gladiatorial combat, and to walk on tightropes; and furthermore to write and read, to play the flute and the lyre, and even to shoot arrows and ride horses: can you still doubt whether they possess that faculty which receives such knowledge, when the knowledge received is clearly visible within them? For where do they receive it, if there is no underlying reason <note>original: *ratio* / *logos*</note> in which these skills can exist? For they do not hear our voices as mere noise, but they also have a perception of the diversity of signs, which arises from rational understanding. But, they say, they perform these human tasks poorly. Yet not even all humans perform them well; otherwise, it would be in vain that some are victors in contests while others are defeated. But they do not deliberate, they say, nor do they hold assemblies, nor sit in judgment—

<column-break/>

§ 15. When they take up skills, and human ones at that, learning to dance and to drive chariots, to fight as gladiators and to walk on ropes, and now even to write and to read, to play the flute and the lyre, to shoot arrows and to ride horses, will you still dispute whether the animal possesses the receptive faculty, when that which has been received is observed in them? For where does it receive these things if **1** reason <note>original: *logos*</note> were not present, in which skills are established? For it does not hear our voice as a mere sound, but there is in them a perception of the differences between signs, which already proceeds from rational intelligence. **2** But, someone says, the animal performs human tasks badly. Well, not even all humans do them well. **3** Or else it would be in vain that there were victors and vanquished in a contest. But they do not deliberate, they say, nor hold assemblies,

---

<columns>2</columns>

**1.** *Reason were present.*] Thus I have restored the text from the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts, which the translator confirms. Previously it was read ridiculously as *reason to speak*. For which *Valentini* had substituted *was in*. Anyone can see how easily these words could be confused.

**2.** *But, someone says.*] This is correct. Namely, *the opponent*. Many have written much about this formula, and, if I am not mistaken, *Bentley* among them in his notes on *Horace*. However, the plural *they say* can also be approved, because it follows immediately after. REISKE. <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 1716–1774, a noted German classicist.</note> The singular *says* is often used without an explicit "someone" when it is meant to indicate that someone is raising an opposing argument. See *Reiske* on *Dio Chrysostom* p. 187, and *Richard Bentley* on *Horace* (Satires I.4.79), who teaches that the Latins speak in the same way. Therefore, *Valentini* should not have substituted the plural *they say*.

<column-break/>

**3.** *Or else in vain a contest and victors...*] *The celebrated Abresch* (in *Dilucidationes Thucydideae Auctarium* p. 390) reads *well indeed and by...* <note>original: *καλῶς ἂν καὶ μὰ τὴν*</note>. It is certainly an ingenious conjecture. For as for what *Bos* thought (in *Animadversiones* ch. 3), that the formula *by the...* <note>feminine oath</note> is not found among the Greeks like the masculine version, I would not say that. See *Hemsterhuis* on *Aristophanes' Plutus* p. 120. If you prefer the common reading, the meaning is this: if both parties performed the task well, victors and vanquished could not be produced in the wrestling school. To "win a contest" <note>original: *νικᾶν ἀγῶνα*</note> is used also by *Epictetus* (Enchiridion 25), just as "to win a battle," "a song," and similar phrases, regarding which see *Wesseling* on *Diodorus Siculus* XI.26 and XIII.74.

nor do they exercise judgment. What is so strange about that, when not even all humans do so? Do not many act before they have consulted? How else can it be shown that other animals do not consult? Indeed, no argument exists for this thing that can be brought forward: on the contrary, many arguments exist, supplied to us by those who have written individual accounts about animals. The rest of the things they keep declaiming against them are truly stale. Cities, they say, they have none: But neither do the Scythians, who wander about in wagons: nor even the gods. 4. *Nor do they sit in judgment.*] I would prefer the word for *they seek justice for themselves*. They experience the law; then follows *they deliberate* in the subjunctive. <term>REISKE (Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century philologist).</term> <term>MEERMANN (Gerard Meerman, Dutch jurist)</term> incorrectly prefers *they wish*.

5. *For tell me, do all humans.*] Rather, it should be *Or indeed—all*, as <term>ABRESCH (Friedrich Ludwig Abresch, classicist)</term> preferred. That formula *tell me* is elegant in a challenge, when we want the person we are dealing with to prove something, as it were, and confirm it with examples. The Latins say *Speak*, and *Tell me*. See <term>the celebrated BURMAN (Pieter Burman the Elder, Dutch scholar)</term> on *Ovid's Heroides XVI, 341.*

6. *Is declaimed against them.*] The term *to speak rhetorically* is often used, like the Latin *rhetoricari*, for frivolous and wordy chatter. See the materials gathered by <term>D'ORVILLE (Jacques Philippe d'Orville, philologist)</term> on *Chariton VI, 1. p. 503*, who did not leave these Porphyrian passages untouched. It can be clear from this by what right a Distinguished Man thought, regarding <term>MAXIMUS TYRIUS (Platonic philosopher)</term> *Dissertation IX, 5*, that *battles and rhetorical displays* could not be correctly joined, since the quarrels and contests of boys over their toys can be called nothing less than *rhetorical displays*.

7. *That they have no cities.*] In a slightly different way, <term>CELSUS (2nd-century philosopher)</term> in <term>ORIGEN (Early Christian theologian)</term> Book IV, p. 369, said that if humans 

<column-break/>

seem to differ from beasts because they inhabit cities, use laws, and appoint magistrates and leaders for themselves, that reasoning is entirely vain, for both ants and bees do the same.

8. *Wagon-dwelling Scythians.*] This matter is well enough known from other sources. Hence they are called "wagon-dwellers" by <note>original: *hamaxoikoi*</note> <term>STRABO (Greek geographer)</term> Book VIII, p. 208. <term>MELA (Pomponius Mela, Roman geographer)</term> expressed it in Latin in Book II, 1: *because they have wagons instead of feet, they are called Hamaxobii*. If I consider that custom, I think nothing should be changed in <term>JULIUS CAPITOLINUS (one of the authors of the Augustan History)</term> in *Life of Maximinus 13*: *others he would present with Scythian vehicles*. Certainly, I cannot stomach <term>SALMASIUS's (Claude Saumaise, French scholar)</term> *dry vehicles*. *Scythian vehicles* is correct, because placed in vehicles they were forced to journey day and night, as is said in <term>HERODIAN (Roman historian)</term> VII, 3.

9. *Nor among humans, as long as prosperous.*] The Leipzig Manuscript reads *For neither among...* which is not bad. For he speaks that way a little before as well. Regarding the matter itself, see the observations made in Book I, § 8.

10. *Apis is said to be the first...*] In the Leipzig Manuscript, this marginal Scholion <note>an ancient or medieval explanatory note</note> is added: *that Apis was the first lawgiver among the Greeks, being King of the Argives.* To be sure, this refers to Apis the king of the Argives, who is usually held to be the son of Phoroneus. However, in <term>AESCHYLUS (Greek tragedian)</term> in *The Suppliants 270*, he is said to be a stranger.

For Apis is said to have been the first among the Greeks to establish laws, at the time when they first required them.

§ 16. To men, indeed, on account of their voracity and gluttony, other animals seem to possess no reason. But to the gods and to divine men, they are held in veneration no differently than sacred ministers. For when the God <note>The Oracle of Apollo at Delphi</note> gave a response to Aristodicus of Cyme, he said that the sparrows were his own ministers. Socrates also used to swear by them, and before him, Rhadamanthus.

<column-break/>

And Apis is said to have been the first to legislate among the Greeks, when they had need of it.

§ 16. To men, then, because of their gluttony, animals do not seem to have reason; but by gods and divine men they are honored equally with <gloss>1</gloss> sacred suppliants, and the <gloss>2</gloss> god, in giving an oracle to Aristodicus the Cymaean, said the sparrows were his own suppliants. <gloss>3</gloss> Socrates also swore by them, and even <gloss>4</gloss> before him, Rhadamanthus.

---

<column-break/>

...is said, and the son of Apollo, who, since he was a physician, bound the land of Argos to himself by a distinguished benefit. I add these things because light is shed here upon *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, in whose work, under the entry for Apis, it is said: "Apis the Egyptian was the first to transport the art of medicine into Greece." On this, *Kuster* <note>Ludolf Kuster, an 18th-century scholar</note> noted that he had not read in any ancient writer that Apis came to Greece from Egypt. It is well known among all that the Egyptian Apis is often confused with the Argive one. As for our author attributing the first laws to him, others ascribe this to his father Phoroneus. See *Clement of Alexandria* in his *Exhortation*, page 67. D. and *Tatian's* *Address to the Greeks*, 60. For he [Phoroneus] was the one who "first gathered men into a community," as is said by *Pausanias* in his *Description of Greece (Corinth)*, page 112. However, *Theodoret* in his *Cure of Greek Affections*, IX, agrees with our author, as praised by *Fabricius* in his *Greek Library*, Vol II, page 546.

1. **They are honored as sacred suppliants.**] In the Leipzig manuscript it is "to the priests, suppliants." This is certainly an error. Yet in that reading there is a hint of the true one, which seems to be "to the priests and suppliants." <term>Reiske</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist</note>. They can be called "sacred suppliants" because in ancient times the greatest regard was held for suppliants, which is why *Hesiod* compares them to guests in *Works and Days*, line 327:
"It is an equal sin for him who harms a suppliant or a guest."
Hence, in Homer, we find "Zeus of the Suppliants" <note>original: *Zeus Hiketesios*</note>. See *Le Clerc* on verse 333, and *Perizonius* on *Aelian's* *Various History*, III, 26.

2. **The god to Aristodicus, etc.**] Read *Herodotus*, Book I, chapter 159, and *Wesseling* there. Indeed, sparrows who were "suppliants" were accustomed to be treated with great religious care. Compare what will be said below in Book IV, chapter 14.

<column-break/>

3. **Socrates also swore by them.**] Concerning Socrates, Apollonius says in *Philostratus*, VI, 19: "He swore by these things not as gods, but so that he might not swear by the gods." See *Olearius* there; our author also indicates this a little further on. Moreover, he correctly wrote "he swore by them" <note>original: *omnyen kat’ auton*</note>. Therefore, there is nothing unusual in that passage in the *Epistle to the Hebrews*, VI, 13: "He had no one greater to swear by" <note>original: *kat’ oudenos eiche meidzonos omosai*</note>. *Wetstein* compares this passage with ours, as well as verse 16: "They swear by one greater." I have said more about this construction in my *Monday Lectures*, II, 20.

4. **Before him, Rhadamanthus.**] Who especially compelled the Cretans to swear oaths by living things, as he [Porphyry] writes below. Sosicrates, in the Scholia <note>ancient commentaries</note> on *Aristophanes' Birds*, line 524, says: "Rhadamanthus seems..." etc. *Suidas* brought these into his own collections under the word "Lampon." See him also under "The Oath of Rhadamanthus" and "to swear by the goose," and what *Kuster* says there. To *Huet* in his *Demonstratio Evangelica*, IV, 12, Rhadamanthus is the same as Moses, among whose laws was that no one should use the name of the Lord in vain; therefore, he wished men to swear by the goose, etc. It is well known how the genius of the learned Bishop [Huet] luxuriates in these matters. The celebrated *Jablonski*, in his *Egyptian Pantheon*, Book V, chapter I, section 5, opines that this Rhadamanthus was either Egyptian by birth, or after traveling there, brought back the worship of certain gods to his home; therefore, he swore by these animals which were sacred to the Egyptians. At any rate, it was not because they were sacred to the gods, or symbols of the gods, that the Cretans swore by them, but other reasons for the practice are brought forward.

# PORPHYRY

The Egyptians also regarded these animals as gods, whether because they truly believed them to be gods, or because they intentionally fashioned the forms of the gods with the faces of oxen, birds, and other creatures, so that people might abstain from them just as they do from human beings, or perhaps for other more mystical reasons. In the same way, the Greeks attached the horns of a ram to the statue of Zeus <note>original: "Iouis" / "Διὸς"; the text refers to Jupiter Ammon</note>, and the horns of a bull to that of Dionysus <note>original: "Bacchi" / "Διονύσου"</note>. They composed Pan from a man and a goat, and they gave wings to the Muses and the Sirens; according to—

<column-break/>

The Egyptians, moreover, referred these same animals to the gods, whether because they truly thought they were gods, or because they purposefully assigned the faces of oxen, birds, and other animals to the gods, to warn that one must abstain from them no differently than from humans: or perhaps led by some other more hidden cause. Thus also the Greeks applied the horns of a ram to the statue of Jupiter, and those of a bull to the image of Bacchus: likewise they composed Pan from a man and a goat. They had equipped the Muses with wings, and the Sirens as well.

---

See *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> book I. *Socrates*, a not-uncelebrated writer of Cretan history whom an eminent man praises, is unknown to me. *Zenobius* and the *Scholiast on Aristophanes*: they have often misled learned men, in whose corrupted manuscripts "Socrates" is read instead of "Sosicrates." Compare *Kuster on Suidas* and *Fabricius, Greek Library* Book II, 23. p. 827.

5. **Whether because they truly believed them to be gods etc.**] That the Egyptians did not truly hold those animals to be Gods, but only as images and symbols of them, is shown among others by *Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel* Book III, p. 117 and *Plutarch, Volume II* p. 379. Nevertheless, they held the same honor for the symbol as for the Divinities, on which matter see *Cuper, Harpocrates* p. 42. Soon *Meermann* reads *the forms of the gods*, omitting *the*.

6. **And of others.**] Perhaps it should read *and making others with similar faces*. And soon *that of them* (line 6.) REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century philologist</note>.

7. **Or for other reasons.**] Differently than other nations, the Egyptians worshipped not illustrious men, but animals with divine honors. This is indeed well-attested, but from where the practice took its origin is not so certain or explored. Both ancient and modern writers disagree greatly. *Diodorus Siculus* I, 86; *Mosheim on Cudworth’s Intellectual System of the Universe* p. 418; *Jablonski in the Prologue to the Egyptian Pantheon* § 35; *Warburton in The Divine Legation of Moses* Book IV, 4. etc. have dealt with this argument so at length that nothing ought to be added. Reiske rightly deleted *from* before *them* a little earlier; Abresch wanted the same.

8. **They attached the horns of a ram.**] Concerning Jupiter, or Ammon, *ram-faced* <note>original: "κριοπροσώπῳ"</note>, all things are well known, since the ancient theologians so often reproach the pagans for it. Read the *Learned Man on Minucius Felix* ch. 21. But you may wonder that this is attributed to the Greeks in this passage, which elsewhere is attributed to the Africans. *Suidas* indeed, under *Ammon*, says it is the *name of a Greek god*, but there Kuster thought one should read *Libyan* or explain it as *national*. But in truth, not only by Africans but also by Greeks was Jupiter worshipped as *ram-faced*. Spanheim discusses this beautifully in *On the Use and Excellence of Coins, Dissertation VII*.

9. **And of a bull to Dionysus.**] No one is ignorant of the horns of Bacchus. Hence he is called *bull-horned* and the *bull-horned god* <note>original: "ταυρόκερως"</note>, concerning which name see *Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus III, 64*.

10. **And Pan—**] *Minucius Felix in Octavius* ch. 28: *You also dedicate gods mixed from a goat and a man, and gods with the faces of lions and dogs.* Where the interpreters have much on this matter. Compare *our author* <note>Porphyry</note> below, IV, 9.

11. **They gave wings to the Muses and the Sirens.**] They establish wings as common to the Sirens and the Muses (the daughters of one of them, as most relate). See *Spanheim, On the Use and Excellence of Coins, Dissertation V*. On the winged Sirens, Broukhuis writes most elegantly on *Tibullus V, 1, 69*. No one is unaware of the feathers of *Victory* and the others mentioned here.

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK III.

Ii 2
<meta>catchword: Not-</meta>

In a similar way, they depicted Victory and Iris, as well as Cupid <note>original: "Cupidinem" / "Ἔρωτα" (Eros)</note> and Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium" / "Ἑρμῆν" (Hermes)</note>, with wings. Pindar, indeed, in his odes, introduced all the gods—at the time they were being pursued by Typhon—not in the likeness of men, but in the forms of other animals. They assert that Jupiter <note>original: "Iouem" / "Δία" (Zeus)</note>, captured by love for Pasiphae, took the form of a bull; at other times, the myths say he became an eagle or a swan. By all these means, those ancient people displayed the honor they believed should be shown to animals. This is even more evident when they say that Jupiter was nursed by a goat. Furthermore, among the Cretans, there was a law of Rhadamanthys <note>A legendary king of Crete known for his wisdom and justice</note> which commanded that all animals be included when swearing an oath.

<column-break/>

In the same way, they depicted Victory, Iris, Eros, and Hermes with wings. 12 Pindar, in his processional songs, portrayed all the gods—when they were being chased by Typhon—not as having been made like men, 13 but like other animals. They say that 14 Zeus, having fallen in love with Pasiphae, became a bull, and at other times an eagle and a swan. Through these stories, the ancients demonstrated their honor toward animals, and even more so when 15 they say a goat finished nursing Zeus. Among the Cretans, there was a law of Rhadamanthys 16 to bring all animals into an oath.

---

<column-break/>

12. *Pindar in his processional songs.*] The oldest editions have *prosodiois* <note>original: "προσοδίοις"</note>; I would not have changed this, as the manuscripts of many writers offer both spellings. See *Seber on Pollux: IV, 53*. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> says under the letter V: *Prosodia are poems by lyric poets intended for the festivals of the gods.* But the same author also says: *Prosodion: a hymn.* In the entry for *Pindar*, he attributes to the poet *prosodia* and *parthenia* <note>Maiden-songs</note>, which terms should perhaps be joined there and understood as the *partheneia* <note>original: "παρθένεια"</note> that Plutarch <note>Volume II, page 1136 F</note> attributes to Pindar.

13. *But like other animals.*] The great scholar <note>referring to a previous commentator, likely Valesius or similar</note> in his notes on Diodorus Siculus <note>Book I, 86</note> cites "But like irrational animals," though I have not found this in the manuscripts. Many recount the myth he touches upon here; regarding this matter, see the *Excellent Man* <note>a common scholarly epithet for a contemporary</note> and the interpreters of Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* <note>Book V, 321</note>. However, the claim made by that celebrated man—that the shameful figures of the Egyptian gods were born from this myth—is not without controversy.

14. *To have become now indeed...*] These things are unknown to no one who reads the mythographers. I will only cite *Theodoret in his Sermon on Sacrifices*, because he often reflects our author and also joins these things: *and even the father of the gods, being likened to an eagle, a bull, and a swan,* etc. It seems we should read "to have become now indeed," as 

<column-break/>

*Abresch* <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch, an 18th-century philologist</note> advised. For others are accustomed to speak this way, as is our author above in section 5, although in the latter place it is only used once. See *Reiske* <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a noted German scholar</note> there.

15. *They say [a goat] nursed Zeus.*] I have restored the word "the" <note>original Greek: "τὸν"</note> to its place, from which it had been expelled by *Valens* <note>an earlier editor</note>, who published it as "the [feminine]". The earlier editions and the Leipzig Manuscript support this. *Minucius Felix in Octavius, chapter 21*: *And what are the rites of Jove? The nurse is a she-goat, and the infant is stolen from the greedy father so he is not devoured.* Many learned men discuss this matter in that place.

16. *To bring all animals into an oath.*] This expression is well-formed: to bring upon oneself, that is, to bring forward in one's own cause, every kind of living creature, so that they may be an <term>horkos</term> <note>an oath or a thing sworn by</note>—that is, a religious obligation sanctioned by swearing. *Reiske*. *Valens* had marked the passage with an asterisk as suspect to him, but the distinguished *Reiske* rightly defends it. From this comes the <term>epaktos horkos</term> <note>an "imported" or additional oath</note> in Isocrates' *To Demonicus, page 12*, about which expression the grammarians disagree. Suidas says well: *An epaktos horkos: one to which another person is led.* Just as they call the aid of foreigners and those sought from elsewhere <term>epakton dynamin</term> <note>an external force</note>. See *Casaubon on Aeneas Tacticus, page 1736*. *Epaktos ploutos* refers to a dowry in Euripides' *Melanippe, verse 49*. Other examples of this kind are found in *Alberti's* notes on Hesychius under the word *Epakton*. This very subject occurred to us a little earlier.

# PORPHYRY

<meta>Catchword at bottom right: 2. </meta>

17 Nor did Socrates joke when swearing by the dog and the goose, 18 but he made his oath according to the law of the son of Zeus and Justice <note>referring to the judge Rhadamanthys</note>. 19 Nor was he joking when he called swans his "fellow servants" <note>Socrates considered himself a servant of Apollo, to whom swans were also sacred</note>. The myth also hints that they share the same soul as us, 20 and that by the wrath of the gods they changed from humans into animals; having changed, they are thereafter pitied and loved. 21 For such are the stories told about dolphins and halcyons <note>kingfishers</note>, and nightingales and swallows.

§ 17. And each of the ancients also boasts that his vision was fortunate from...

<column-break/>

Neither did Socrates, while he swore by the dog and the goose, do so as a joke: but he swore solemnly according to the ordinance of the just son of Jupiter <note>original: "Iovis" / Zeus</note>: nor did he through a jest call the swans his fellow servants. Indeed, even the myths—which claim that a transformation from humans into animals occurred through the indignation of the gods, and that the gods therefore followed them with mercy and loved them thereafter—seem to signify that other animals are endowed with the same soul as we are. For of such a kind are those things which are handed down concerning dolphins, halcyons, nightingales, and swallows.

§ 17. Likewise, each of the ancients who [received] a happy upbringing from animals...

---

<margin>Hence the Cretans also swore by divine names, and by all kinds of living creatures. See *Meursius* in *Crete*, Book IV, ch. 1.</margin>

17. **Nor did Socrates etc.** Socrates swore by those things, not as if they were gods, but so that he might not swear by the name of God; this was mentioned above. *Tertullian, Apology, ch. 14: "I am silent about the philosophers, content with Socrates, who in contempt of the gods, swore by the oak, the goat, and the dog."* See *Havercamp* there and *Menage* on *Diogenes Laërtius II, 40.*

18. **But according to the [son] of Z. and J.** "But according to the son of Zeus and Justice." This follows the example of Rhadamanthys, who was born of Zeus and Justice <note>original: "Dice"</note>. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note>. The celebrated Jablonski in *Egyptian Pantheon I, 5, 5* corrects this to "the son of Zeus and Maia." He thinks Socrates meant the Egyptian Anubis, or, as the Greeks interpret it, Mercury (Hermes), whom they held to be the son of Jupiter and Maia. I should say, these ideas stray too far from the literal text; if the dog signified Mercury, what of the goose, the goat, etc.? Nor does the word "according to" <note>original: "κατὰ" (kata)</note> usually mean this when constructed this way. Since Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Aeacus are called "children of the god" by our author in his *Life of Plotinus*, and Rhadamanthus is the son of Zeus and Europa in *Plato's Minos p. 367 D*, and he became most famous for the praise of his justice, as is known from *Meursius* in *Crete III, 15* and others, I have decided nothing should be changed. For *poieito* <note>he was making</note>, read *epoieito* from the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts.

19. **Nor joking, fellow servants ----** *Plutarch, Volume II, p. 975 B: "Specifically, Socrates says he makes himself a fellow servant of the swans."* *Pausanias in Attica p. 58:* The night before Plato was to become his student, Socrates saw a dream of a swan flying into his lap. Perhaps for this reason Socrates said he made himself a fellow servant of the swans, as *Spencer* writes in his notes on *Origen, Against Celsus, Book VI, p. 635.* But this is of no consequence and is refuted by our author, for he held swans and geese in the same regard.

20. **And by wrath.** Either something is missing before "and," or in its place one should read "saying," or a similar participle. Soon after, read "having changed" <note>plural</note>. <term>REISKE</term>

21. **For such things &c.** Concerning the Halcyon, turned into a bird by the anger of Zeus, see *Didymus* on *Homer's Iliad I. 558.* Concerning the swallow and the nightingale, see the *Most Learned Man* on *Aelian, Various History XII, 20*, where *Perizonius* notes from Pausanias what gave occasion to the myth.

1. **The vision was fortunate.** Perhaps read "as each one" <note>original: "ὡς τις" (hos tis)</note>. <term>REISKE</term>

# On Abstinence, Book III.

-> Ii 3 <-

...happily attained [greatness], they did not boast of their parents so much as they did of those who nursed and raised them. One spoke of a she-wolf, another of a deer, another of a goat, and another of a bee. Semiramis <note>The legendary Queen of Assyria</note> spoke of doves, Cyrus of a dog, and the Thracian of a swan—from which he even took his name <note>original: "Thrax... a nutriente etiam nomen obtinuit," likely referring to Cycnus, whose name means swan</note>. Indeed, Hecate is more likely to hear a prayer if she is addressed as a bull, a dog, or a lioness. But if, because they sacrifice animals and eat them, they say—in order to absolve themselves of the crime—that animals are irrational, then in the same way those who [eat] pa-

...from being raised by animals, they did not [honor] their fathers as much as those who reared them. From this also come the epithets of the gods: for Dionysus <note>Bacchus</note>, "of the kid"; for Apollo, "wolf-like" and "of the dolphin"; for Poseidon <note>Neptune</note>, "of the horse"; and for Athena <note>Minerva</note>, "of the horse." <margin>2. *One a she-wolf — a deer — a goat etc.*] Read *Diodorus Siculus II, 4; Justin XXIII, 4; and Aelian, Various History XII, 42 & 45.* I would prefer the word "hind" (female deer) for *elaphon*.</margin>

<margin>3. *Dionysus, "of the kid."*] As if it were *eriphiotes* <note>from 'eriphos', meaning kid/young goat</note>. See *Fabricius, Letters p. 57, Reiske.* Excellent. This has nothing to do with the Bacchus whom the *Orphic Hymn XLVII* calls "loud-roaring" or "sewn-in-the-thigh" <note>original: "eiraphiotes" or "merorrhaphes"</note>, as corrected by the celebrated *Lennep* in his *Notes on Coluthus III, 2*; regarding which see *Barnes on Euripides' Bacchae, 286.* Therefore, *Felicianus* rightly translates it as "fawn." The *Etymologicum Magnum p. 302* says: "or from the kid, for they say he was raised by kids." In *Clement*, Bacchus is called by this form of the name, as noted by the illustrious *Hemsterhuis on Pollux X, 17.*</margin>

<margin>4. *Wolf-like and of the dolphin.*] Regarding the first surname of Apollo, see *Bergler on Alciphron I, 26.* The same author explains why he is called "of the dolphin" in *Etymologicum Magnum and V. <margin>5. *Hecate: bull, dog, lioness.*] Because she had three heads placed on one body, the Greeks call her "three-faced," "three-formed," and "three-necked." See *Cuper, Ancient Monuments p. 206.* She is called "three-headed" and "three-formed" by *Virgil* and others. *Orpheus, Argonautica 974*, attributes to her the heads of a horse, a human, and a dog. Our author [Porphyry] below in Book IV, 16, gives her the horse, bull, and lioness. From the bull's head she was called "bull-faced," just as the ancients commonly attribute cows to the Moon, on which see *Cuper on Harpocration p. 12.* Because she delighted in dogs, she was also depicted with a dog's head, as the same author teaches on p. 198. But our author says in another place that Hecate commands demons, and that those demons are signified by dogs. See *Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel p. 175.* She is not wrongly called a lioness, just as the lion was a symbol of Apollo or the Sun, regarding which more later.</margin>

§ 18. Through these points and others which we shall mention in order as we review the opinions of the ancients, it is demonstrated that other animals are rational beings. # DE ABSTINENTIA LIB. III.

...no one would consume fish as food unless they had been killed by force. In this practice, there is undoubtedly much injustice. Furthermore, as Plutarch also remarks, the fact that our nature requires and uses certain things does not mean we should immediately extend injury to all things. It is conceded that harm may be inflicted to a certain extent out of necessity; indeed, taking anything from plants is a form of harm, even if they remain alive. However, to seize and destroy other things out of arrogance and to indulge our pleasures seems to be the height of cruelty and injustice, especially since abstaining from them does not hinder our ability to live or to live well. For if, just as with air, plants, and fruits—without which life cannot be sustained—so [murder...]

<column-break/>

...which we also destroy by force, no one would partake of. Thus, there is a great deal of injustice in these matters. To begin with, as Plutarch says, simply because our nature needs some things and we use them, we should not extend injustice to everything and toward every creature. For nature <note>The Greek text implies a personified Nature or the natural order</note> grants and allows harm only up to a point for the sake of necessity (if indeed it is harm to take something from plants, given that they remain alive). But to enjoy and destroy other things out of superfluity <note>original: "ἐκ περιουσίας" (ek periousias), referring to luxuries or things beyond basic survival</note> and for the sake of pleasure would be an act of complete savagery and injustice. Abstaining from these things does not diminish our life or our ability to live well. For if, just as with air and water, plants and fruits—without which it is impossible to live—so [murder...]

7. **Out of superfluity.** In common speech, this refers to "things whose presence is not necessary," as Suidas says in his Lexicon. Diodorus Siculus, Book XX, 59 says: "they used all things out of superfluity <note>meaning abundantly or luxuriously</note>." From there the phrase is gracefully transferred to other contexts, about which there is a great Commentary. Sometimes it is also said of things acquired easily and without labor; see Casaubon on Strabo, Book III, p. 60. Our author <note>Porphyry</note> seems to have had in mind the words of Aristotle in *Topics* III, 2: "To live well is a matter of superfluity [a luxury]; but living itself is a necessity."

8. **To enjoy for pleasure.** "To destroy" or "to lose" was created from the letter "A" by the scribes; these two letters are often swapped. REISKE. A clever conjecture, though I have preferred the common reading.

# PORPHYRY

...if we were in need of the slaughter of animals and the eating of flesh for the sake of our lives, nature would have a necessary entanglement with this injustice. But if many priests of the gods, and many kings of the **barbarians** <note>original: "βαρβάρων" (barbarōn); here referring to non-Greek peoples, often used by Porphyry to denote the Egyptians or Indians who practiced asceticism</note> live in purity, and countless races of animals live without ever touching such food at all, and they attain their natural end, how is he not absurd who commands that, if we are forced to be at war with some, we should not even live peacefully with those with whom it is possible? Does he think we must either live by practicing justice toward none, or not live at all by practicing it toward all? Just as among men, he who for the sake of his own safety, or his children, or his country, either takes away the money of some or crushes a region and a city, has necessity as a **pretext** <note>original: "πρόσχημα" (proschēma); a legal or moral excuse</note> for his injustice; but he who does these things for the sake of wealth, or satiety, or luxurious pleasures—

<column-break/>

...so if we also needed the slaughter of animals and the eating of flesh, our nature would necessarily be bound to this injustice. But if indeed many priests of the gods and kings of the barbarians lead a life piously and chastely—furthermore, if innumerable kinds of animals are not frustrated in reaching their natural end and good even though this kind of food is never tasted at all—how is he not absurd who, if we are forced to wage war with some, does not bid us live peacefully even with those with whom it is permitted? Or does he judge that we must either live by using justice toward none, or not live by using it toward all? Therefore, just as among men, he who for the sake of his own safety, and his children, and his country, either seizes the money of others or oppresses a region and a city, has a necessity which in some way excuses the injustice; but he who [does so] from the insolence of riches and pleasures, not—

<margin>
*To enjoy* <note>original: "Ἀπολαύειν" (Apolauein)</note> refers to pleasure, whether honorable or depraved and luxurious; hence *Hesychius* says: "He enjoys; he lives luxuriously." See *Alberti* on this. Hence *enjoyable things* <note>original: "ἀπολαυστικὰ"</note> are sometimes the same as *pleasurable things* <note>original: "ἡδονικὰ"</note>, just as men of this kind are called *pleasure-seekers* <note>original: "ἀπολαυστικοί"</note>, and their life is called a *life of enjoyment* <note>original: "βίος ἀπολαυστικὸς"</note>. See *Gataker* on *Antoninus* <note>Marcus Aurelius</note> III, 6. Thus there is a pregnant sense in those words of Paul in the First Epistle to Timothy VI, 17: "God provides *all things richly for enjoyment*."

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK III.
->K k<-
<meta>catchword: καὶ</meta>

...not led by any necessity, he does the same, he is considered unjust, incontinent, and wicked. Thus, God grants humans the use of plants, the consumption of fire and water, the shearing of sheep, their milk, and the yoking of oxen; and since they use these for their own safety and preservation, He pardons them. But to slaughter animals, and to eat them cut into pieces and full of slaughter and blood—not for the sake of nourishment and satiety, but for the sake of pleasure and gluttony—that indeed is unjust and wicked beyond measure. For is it not enough that we use them to the point of exhaustion, even though they should not be oppressed with any labors?

<column-break/>

...and providing for the fulfillment of unnecessary desires, he seems to be antisocial, incontinent, and wicked. Thus, God grants pardon for the damage done to plants, the consumption of fire and streams, the shearing of sheep and their milk, and the taming and yoking of oxen for the safety and survival of those who use them. But to lead animals to slaughter and to cook them, filling oneself with murder—not for the sake of food or satiety, but making pleasure and gluttony the goal—is monstrously lawless and dreadful. For it is sufficient that we use those who labor on our behalf <note>original: "προκάμνουσι" (prokamnousi); those who toil in our place</note>, even though they ought not to suffer.

<margin>
12. <term>Antisocial</term> <note>original: "Ἄμικτος εἶναι δοκεῖ"</note>] An elegant expression. *Amiktoi, anepimiktoi, aprosmiktoi, dysepimiktoi*—these are all terms for those who exclude foreigners from the right of commerce and refuse their association and approach, as <term>Wesseling</term> rightly notes on *Herodotus* I, 25. Therefore, "antisocial, incontinent, and wicked" are rightly joined together, as in <term>Lucian</term>, *True History* I, 35: "harsh, heavy, antisocial, and wild." Below, the term "difficult to associate with" will occur for us in Book IV, 6.

See <term>Plutarch</term>, *On the Cleverness of Animals*. <term>VALENTINUS</term>. "Laboring on our behalf" is correct. *Prokamnein* means to labor in place of another, and by one's own previous work to relieve the successor's work of a great part of the trouble. But then one should read: "and they toil, the teams of horses and donkeys." For the verse is an iambic senarius of <term>Aeschylus</term>, also frequently recited by <term>Plutarch</term>. <term>REISKE</term>. Earlier editors end the sense after "laboring on our behalf," and join the word "labors" <note>original: "μόχθους" (mochthous)</note>—which does not seem to belong to <term>Aeschylus</term>—to the following words. Yet our author could have said "the labors of horses... as slave-substitutes," just as in the same <term>Aeschylus</term>, *Prometheus Bound* 463, they are called:
> Successors to the greatest toils for mortals.

The lines that follow from the same author are praised by <term>Plutarch</term> (Vol. II, p. 98 and p. 964), but in a different way. In the first place:
> Giving the teams of horses and donkeys, and the offspring of bulls, 
> As gifts in return and as receivers of toils.

In the other place, he has "a team," "slave-substitutes," and "receiver." Therefore, in both <term>Plutarch</term> and our author, "slave-substitutes" <note>original: "ἀντίδουλα"</note> should be read instead of "gifts in return" <note>original: "ἀντίδωρα"</note> in the first passage. <term>Pauw</term>, on the Fragments of <term>Aeschylus</term>, would undoubtedly have asserted this from <term>Porphyry</term> against <term>Xylander</term>, if he had remembered our author.
</margin>

§ 19. But as for the one who deems that we should not use the ox for food, nor destroy spirit and life to create seasonings for our gluttony and decorations for our table—what thing necessary for safety, or what thing beautiful for virtue, does he take away from life? Indeed, to compare plants to animals is altogether forced and unnatural. For animals are by nature capable of sensation: they feel pain, they experience fear, and they can be harmed; therefore, they can also be wronged. But for plants, there is no sensation; thus, nothing is foreign to them, nor is there evil, nor any injury or injustice. For the origin of all kinship and alienation is sensation. # On Abstinence, Book III.
->Kk 2<-

Likewise, there are those who, in cruelty, anger, and insolence, surpass even the most horrible wild beasts—murderers of parents, the wicked, and tyrants. Regarding these men, we assert that we have a right <note>original: "ius"; here meaning a legal or moral standing to judge or punish</note> to act against them. But regarding the ox that plows, the dog that lives in our home, and the flocks that nourish us with milk and clothe us with their wool, can we say we have no right of justice?

§ 20. But that argument of Chrysippus <note>A famous Stoic philosopher who argued animals were made solely for human use</note> is likely persuasive to those men: that we were made for our own sake and for the sake of the gods, but all other animals were made by the gods for our sake. Thus, horses were made to carry out war alongside us, and dogs to hunt with us; leopards, bears, and lions were made to provide us with manly exercise. As for the pig—

<column-break/>

—again, those who have surpassed the most fearsome of beasts in rawness, temper, and greed: child-killers and parricides, <gloss>2</gloss> tyrants and the servants of kings. Toward these men, we <gloss>3</gloss> think we have a standing; but toward the plowing ox, the companion dog, and the livestock that nourish us with milk <gloss>4</gloss> and adorn us with their fleece, how is it not the height of irrationality to say we have no bond of justice?

§ 20. But by Zeus, that point of Chrysippus might be persuasive: that the gods made us for ourselves and for one another, but made the animals for us—horses to fight alongside us, dogs to hunt with us, and panthers, <gloss>1</gloss> bears, and lions for the practice of courage. And the <gloss>2</gloss> pig, <gloss>3</gloss> [was born for nothing else but to be sacrificed...]

<column-break/>

<gloss>2. Tyrants and the servants of kings.]</gloss> These things ought to be explained according to the custom of those who, living in liberty, held the name of "king" in hatred. For since free kingdoms easily devolved into tyranny, they attacked that vice as if it were inherent to kingship. Hence the phrases *to live like a king* or *to act kingly and cruelly* and similar terms among the Latins; by the word "king," lack of self-control and tyranny itself are expressed, as *Schulting on Seneca's Controversies II. 15* shows. "King" and "tyrant" are usually joined for this same reason by *Demosthenes* and others.

<gloss>3. Think we have a standing.]</gloss> I have supplied the words "a right of justice" <note>original: "to dikaion"</note>. For the sense of the words demanded it. —VALENTIUS. Perhaps "think we have some kinship (or justice)." —REISKE. The *Lyons Edition* had already noted "justice" in the margin, and the matter itself speaks to the fact that the sense must be filled in that way.

<gloss>4. Adorn us with their fleece.]</gloss> The word *thremmata* <note>Greek for "nurslings" or "creatures"</note> denotes *livestock* in this passage; those who strive to assert the same meaning in the *Gospel of John 4:12* use this. Compare *Wetsten*: I agree with those who understand it there as *domestic animals*.

<gloss>1. And bears.]</gloss> In the *Leipzig Manuscript*, it was written *arkous* by the first hand, which a more recent hand corrected to *arktous*. He could have skipped that effort, for *arkos* was used no less than *arktos*. —REISKE. The *Meermann manuscript* also gives *arkous*.

> ...and the pig is thought to be
> the first victim to have deserved to die.

Elegantly, *Clement of Alexandria, Miscellanies II. p. 405 D.*: "It is said, at least, that one of the philosophers, etymologizing the word for pig (*hys*), said it was so named as being fit only for sacrifice (*thysis*) and slaughter." *Varro, On Agriculture II, 4*: "The pig is called *hys* in Greek, formerly called *thys*... for the beginning of sacrificing seems to have first been taken from the swine species." Where for *thyfus* I rewrite *thys* following Clement. Nor do I doubt that the Philosopher whom *Clement* mentions, and whom *Scaliger* says he does not know in his notes on *Varro*, is *Cleanthes*, whose testimony will be produced immediately. Regarding pigs, *Aesop* speaks charmingly...

...truly, for here indeed the most delightful of favors resides: [the pig] was created for no other purpose than to be sacrificed. 3. <term>For here is the sweetest of favors.</term>] Indeed, it has long been believed that the meat of the pig is sweeter than all others, as Aelian says in *On the Nature of Animals*. It is well known how rudely the Jews were once treated because they abstained from pork. I will add here the saying of Antiochus to Eleazar: <note>Antiochus IV was a Hellenistic king who tried to force Jews to eat pork; Eleazar was a martyr who refused.</note> "Why do you loathe the eating of this animal's flesh, which Nature has granted as most beautiful? For it seems foolish not to enjoy those things which are pleasant without shame, and it is unjust to turn away from the favors of Nature." (Found in Josephus, *On the Maccabees*, chapter 5).

4. <term>Mixed the soul like salt.</term>] A saying of Cleanthes <note>A Stoic philosopher and successor to Zeno.</note>: "They have a soul instead of salt, so that the meat does not rot," cited in Clement's *Miscellanies*. Cicero also says <term>the soul was given to that beast in place of salt, lest it should putrefy</term> in a passage cited by Sylburg and Rittershusius in their notes on Porphyry's *Life of Pythagoras*.

5. <term>And sea-nettles.</term>] This is a better spelling than <term>akalyphe</term>, which others use; on this matter, see Johannes Alberti's notes on Hesychius.

<column-break/>

6. <term>Not from elsewhere.</term>] This passage is sound, though a little obscure. "Not from elsewhere" is the same as saying "for no other cause." It was not for any other reason but as if God himself had devoted a great part of his care to this. That is, as if God had voluntarily directed a great part of his concerns here, and in forming this universe, had primarily aimed to supply man with the greatest possible abundance of pleasures. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774) was a noted German scholar and physician known for his editions of Greek texts.</note>

7. <term>Turning into sweetness.</term>] I punctuate it this way: "turning toward sweetness, surpassing nurses" in the zeal of our mind to gratify ourselves by piling up the delights of things. The word "surpassing" is in the aorist tense. <term>REISKE</term>. However, I would prefer the word "nourishing" [threprsas], an idea which also pleased the illustrious Abresch. These words are often confused because the letters look similar.

8. <term>Will say to that argument.</term>] Plato says in the *Sophist* (p. 168): "one must consider what he will answer to the question asked." This seems to be a phrase borrowed from legal language.

...should respond to that argument of Carneades. <note>Carneades (c. 214–129 BCE) was a Skeptic philosopher known for systematically attacking the dogmatic beliefs of the Stoics.</note> He says that every thing produced by nature attains a "benefit" when it reaches the end for which it was naturally made. However, "benefit" must be understood here in its more common sense of "good use," or what those men <note>The Stoics.</note> call "serviceability." Now, the pig was made for this very purpose: to be slaughtered and eaten. Therefore, when the pig is eaten, it reaches its natural end and is thus "benefited." But if God produced animals for the use of humans, for what use are we to have flies, mosquitoes, bats, beetles, scorpions, and vipers? ...is said of those who respond to an opponent's arguments but have nothing effective to offer in opposition. *Lucian, in "Jupiter the Tragedian":* "What then will you say to these things?" A little earlier, the Leipzig Manuscript has "how" instead of "to whom," and omits "something" after "it seems"; both are poor readings.

9. **The benefit which they call serviceability.** The celebrated Abresch says this is better: "the matter of benefit." The Stoics called indifferent things "useful" or "serviceable," but not "beneficial" <note>original: *ōphelima*. In Stoic ethics, only virtue is truly "beneficial"; other things are merely "preferred" or "useful."</note>. *See Galen, To Antoninus VI, 45.*

10. **But the pig.** Perhaps it should be "But indeed." This is the beginning of a refutation based on absurdity. He concludes thus: if what Carneades said is true, and if what you Stoics assert is also true (that animals were created for your sake), it follows that it is in the pig's own interest to be slaughtered. But this is absurd; therefore, your decree is false. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774) was a prominent German physician and philologist.</note>

Who among us has ever eaten a lion, a viper, a vulture, a stork, a kite, or the little worms that crawl upon the shore?"

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 263, where Porphyry addresses the Stoic and Peripatetic claim that nature requires a balance of opposites (mortal/immortal, rational/irrational).</meta>

# PORPHYRY

### BOOK III, SECTION 21

They claim that the irrational must exist in opposition and as a counterpart. They say this pairing of opposites should not be left incomplete or maimed <note>original: *πεπηρωμένην*, referring to a lopsided philosophical category</note>. As if we were denying this, or as if we did not demonstrate that a great deal of the irrational is found among existing things! For surely, a great and abundant irrational force presents itself in all things that lack a soul; thus we require no other category from elsewhere to serve as the opposite to the rational. Since everything inanimate, being inherently devoid of reason and mind, stands in opposition to that which is endowed with reason and mind. 

Even if there is someone who considers nature not in a general sense, but specifically considers "animated nature" <note>i.e., the world of living things</note> to be such that one part is endowed with imagination and the other lacks it, or one part is sensible <note>capable of sensation</note> and the other insensible—so that nature might maintain these oppositions of habits and privations within the same genus as a kind of balance—this is surely absurd. For it would be absurd if someone wanted one part of living creatures to be sensible and another part to be insensible.

<column-break/>

They argue that the irrational must exist as an opponent, and that this yoking of opposites must not be left defective. As if we were to deny this, or were not showing that many irrational things are found in reality. For a great and copious irrational power offers itself in all things that lack a soul: so that nothing else needs to be sought from elsewhere to be opposed to the rational. Indeed, since everything inanimate is immediately devoid of reason and mind, it is opposed to that which is endowed with reason and mind. 

Even if there were someone who did not judge nature in a common sense, but judged animated nature to be that which has one part endowed with imagination and another lacking it, and one part sensible, another insensible: so that nature might obtain the oppositions of these habits and privations within the same genus as a kind of equilibrium: that would certainly be absurd. For he would be absurd who wished that among living beings, one should be sensible and another insensible.

---

I interpose the word "not" <note>original: *μὴ*</note> based on conjecture. <term>VALENTINUS.</term> <note>The scholar Lucas Holstenius</note> On the contrary, these preceding words are already those of <term>Plutarch</term>. I said so immediately.

2. *And maimed.* <note>original: *Καὶ πεπηρωμένην*</note>] This is correctly stated; and it is found thus in <term>Plutarch</term>: it was previously read incorrectly as "filled" <note>original: *πεπληρωμένην*</note>. Therefore, our author rightly restored this, as did <term>D'Orville</term> in his notes on *Chariton, II, 9*, where more is said concerning this word.

3. *Or much of the irrational.* <note>original: *Ἢ πολὺ τὸ ἀλ.*</note>] <term>Valentinus</term> interposed "not" <note>original: *μὴ*</note>, and before him <term>Fogerolles</term>; <term>Plutarch</term> also suggests this. The repetition of the same letter deceived the scribe, unless we suppose "not" <note>original: *μὴ*</note> was originally there instead of "or" <note>original: *ἢ*</note>.

<column-break/>

4. *But animated nature.* <note>original: *Ἀλλὰ τὴν ἔμψυχον Φ. ἔ.*</note>] Previously it was read as "innate" <note>original: *ἔμφυτον*</note>, but this has now been corrected. <term>Plutarch</term> has it in a slightly different way: "If anyone thinks nature should not be mutilated, but that animated nature should be..."

5. *These and opposite...* <note>original: *Ταύτας καὶ ἀντιθέτους*</note>] The Florence edition and the Leipzig and Meerman codices read "to these" <note>original: *Ταύταις*</note>. <term>Valentinus</term> correctly restored "these" <note>original: *ταύτας*</note> from <term>Plutarch</term>. In place of "productions/qualities" <note>original: *ποιήσεις*</note>, the same scholar preferred "privations" <note>original: *σερήσεις*</note>, which <term>Reiske</term> also preferred; the common people call these "qualifications" in a barbaric tongue. A little after, the Florence and Leipzig editions have "if indeed absurd."

# On Abstinence, Book III.

one, another that uses imagination, and another that does not. For every living being that possesses sensation is, by its very nature, immediately capable of imagination. Thus, no one can justly demand that among living beings, one should be granted to be rational and another irrational—especially when arguing against those men who believe that nothing partakes of sensation which does not also partake of intelligence <note>original: "intelligentiae"</note>; and that there is no animal that does not also possess some form of opinion and reasoning. This is because every sensation and every impulse exists according to nature. For Nature—which they rightly say does all things for the sake of something and toward some end—did not make the animal endowed with sensation merely so that it might simply experience and feel; rather, since many things are suitable and advantageous to it, and many are foreign <note>or harmful</note>, it could not exist for even a brief moment unless it had learned to avoid the latter and join itself to the former. Nature therefore bestowed the knowledge of both upon each creature by providing sensation in a similar manner. Those things which follow from sensation are the pursuit and grasping of useful things, as well as the repelling and fleeing of destructive and painful things.

<column-break/>

and one partaking of imagination, the other without it; because every living being, being sensitive, is by nature immediately capable of imagination. Nor 6 would he thus reasonably demand that one part of living beings be rational and the other irrational, when speaking to men who think that nothing partakes of sensation which does not also partake of understanding, nor that there is any animal in which there is not some opinion and reasoning, 7 since all sensation and impulse are present according to nature. For nature, which they rightly say does all things for the sake of something and toward some end, did not make the animal sensitive for the 8 bare purpose of experiencing and perceiving, but because there are many things familiar to it and many things foreign, 9 it would not be possible to survive for even a moment without learning to guard against some and to go along with others. Sensation, therefore, provided the knowledge of both to each alike, while the actions following sensation—the takings and pursuits of the beneficial, and the thrusting away and flights from the deadly and painful—

<column-break/>

6. *Thus indeed nothing so reasonably.*] This was the previous reading in the *Florentine &amp; Lyon* editions; what you see now is from *Plutarch*, to whom however he restored "this man" <note>original: "οὗτος"</note>. *Reiske in Observations p. 547. Leipzig &amp; Meerman Manuscripts:* "For thus not even this man reasonably."
7. *Since all sensation.*] Perhaps it should be punctuated and read thus: "reasoning. Since (for, indeed, because) it is present in all sensations and impulse according to nature." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note>. Instead of "since all," *Plutarch* has "just as." And a little before: "thinking not even one thing ---- which not also."
8. *Experiencing and.*] *Plutarch:* "to the one experiencing." But there *Reiske* restored "experiencing something" in *Observations p. 547.* "To experience" <note>original: "τὸ πάσχειν"</note> is in the *Meerman* manuscript.
9. *Possible to survive without learning.*] *Plutarch:* "it was possible to survive for the one not learning." And better, presently: "sensation provides ---- to the sensation."

# P O R P H Y R Y

-> L l <-

...nor is there any <gloss>10</gloss> possible way for these faculties to be present in those who are not naturally disposed to reason, judge, and pay attention. For if you were to entirely strip away expectation, memory, <gloss>11</gloss> purpose, preparation, hope, fear, desire, and indignation, you would leave no use for the eyes or the ears, nor for any other sense or imagination. If these senses do not have a mind to use them, it would be better to be rid of them entirely than to suffer, feel grief, and experience pain <gloss>12</gloss> while lacking the ability to ward these things off in the absence of thought. Indeed, there is an argument by Strato the Physicist <note>Strato of Lampsacus (c. 335 – c. 269 BCE), a philosopher who headed the Peripatetic school and focused on natural science</note> which demonstrates that it is impossible to perceive anything at all without the presence of intelligence. Often, when our mind is focused on other things, <gloss>13</gloss> letters that meet our eyes and words that fall upon our ears go unnoticed and escape us. Then he returned again...

<column-break/>

...the means of escape can in no way be present, except in those things which are so constituted by nature that they are able to reason, judge, remember, and turn their attention toward something. For if you utterly take away expectation, memory, attention, preparation, hope, fear, desire, and indignation, you will leave no use for the eyes, ears, or other senses that are present. Indeed, if the senses and imagination have nothing to utilize them, it would be better to lack them than to struggle and grieve without any faculty to drive away these annoyances. Furthermore, there is the reasoning of Strato the physicist, by which he demonstrates that no one can perceive anything at all without intelligence. For both letters meeting the eyes and speeches falling upon the ears frequently remain hidden from us and are accustomed to escape us when we have our mind intent on something else.
