### On Abstinence, Book III.
-> Ll 2 <-

Then again, where the mind returns and recurs, it follows each of the things previously mentioned by recollecting them. For this reason, it has also been said: **“The mind sees, and the mind hears; all other things are deaf and blind.”** <note>original Greek: "Νοῦς ὁρῇ καὶ νοῦς ἀκούει· τ’ἄλλα κωφὰ καὶ τυφλά." This famous line is attributed to the Sicilian poet and philosopher Epicharmus (c. 524–435 BCE).</note> This is because the physical impression occurring around the eyes and ears does not produce actual perception unless the thinking faculty is present. On this point, it is also told that King Cleomenes, <note>Cleomenes I, a King of Sparta (r. 524–489 BCE).</note> when a singer was being praised at a banquet and he was asked whether he also found the man excellent, ordered the others to judge that, for he said his own mind was currently in the Peloponnese. <note>Cleomenes was preoccupied with military or political matters back home, illustrating that without focus, the ears do not "hear."</note> Therefore, it is necessary that intelligence be present in all beings that possess sensation.

§ 22. But even if we were to grant that sensation does not require the mind for its own specific function—whenever it is concerned with...

<column-break/>

...then it pursues and follows each of the aforementioned things, gathering them up. <gloss>14</gloss> For which reason it is said, "The mind sees and the mind hears, but other things are deaf and blind," as the physical state of the eyes and ears does not produce perception if the thinking part is not present. Wherefore King Cleomenes, <gloss>15</gloss> during a drinking party when a performance was being highly regarded, being asked if it did not seem excellent, bid those men to look to it; <gloss>16</gloss> for he said he had his mind in the Peloponnese. From this, it follows of necessity that in all things where there is the capacity to sense, <gloss>17</gloss> there is also the capacity to think.

§ 22 But let it be that sensation does not need the mind for its own work, yet whenever it concerns that which is proper to...

---

Let us hold this. Soon after "follows each of the things previously mentioned" appears in *Plutarch*.

14. **“For which reason it is said: The mind... ”** <note>original: "Ἧι καὶ λέλεκται. Νοῦς ----"</note> Lipsius corrected this very poorly as "the mind hears the heavens." There was a note written in the margin: "I think Heraclitus says this," which is also false. It belongs to **Epicharmus**. <note>A Greek dramatist and philosopher often cited for his pithy observations on nature.</note> See above, Book I, 41. Maximus Tyrius also understands him in this way in Dissertation XVII, 10, attributing it to the Syracusan poet (who was Epicharmus). Davies reviews many who praise this verse here (except some who mistakenly give "light" instead of "deaf"):
**“The mind sees, and the mind hears; everything else is deaf and blind.”**
To these add Julian’s Oration VIII, and those cited by Heinsius for Clement of Alexandria’s *Stromata* II, and Hemsterhuis for Aristophanes’ *Plutus*. From this, it seems the text should be corrected in our author's *Life of Pythagoras*, number 46, to read "deaf and blind" rather than "lame," as it is currently published. However, Pythagoras is credited there, and he may have changed it slightly. Plutarch and others correctly use the word "sees" <note>original Greek: "ὁρῇ"</note> rather than "looks" <note>original Greek: "ὁρᾷ"</note>, for Epicharmus used the Doric dialect.

15. **“A performance being highly regarded.”** <note>original: "Εὐδοκιμοῦντος ἀκροάματος."</note> The latter word is missing in the Leipzig Manuscript, but a new hand supplied it—the same hand that, without cause, corrected "himself" in verse 12. The first hand correctly gave "himself." <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and philologist known for his editions of Greek orators.</note>

16. **“For he himself in the Peloponnese...”** The earlier editions and the Meerman Manuscript have what I have provided, and therefore it ought to be restored, for the word "said" is elegantly suppressed. Valentinus had adopted "him" from Plutarch, but there too "himself" should be read. The same reads "if it did not seem excellent, he ordered." Theophrastus, in *On the Senses*, correctly says: "Often when we have our mind on other things, we neither see nor hear."

17. **“And to think.”** The Leipzig Manuscript deletes the "and." Shortly after, Plutarch writes "whenever the animal [is concerned] with..." and then "and even when things are not present."

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument regarding the rational capacities of animals, specifically focusing on memory, preparation, and conceptual thought. It draws heavily on Stoic terminology and compares readings with Plutarch.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

Once perception has internalised the difference between what is familiar and what is foreign, and has departed from the immediate experience, what is it that then remembers? It is that which fears things that cause pain, longs for things that are beneficial, and, when they are not present, devises ways for them to be provided. It prepares points of attack, refuges, <gloss>1</gloss> and snares; and again, it provides ways for those who have been caught to escape their attackers. Or <gloss>2</gloss> do not even those [the Stoics] <note>Porphyry is likely referring to Stoic philosophers, who often denied reason to animals while using these very technical terms.</note> wear us out by repeating these things in their introductions at every turn? They define "purpose" as the <gloss>3</gloss> marking of a completion; "approach" as an impulse before an impulse; "preparation" as an action before an action; and "memory" as the comprehension of a past proposition, the presence of which was first grasped by perception. For there is nothing among these things that is not rational, and they all belong to all living beings. Just as, of course, <gloss>4</gloss> is the case regarding "intellections" <note>original: *noeseis* (νοήσεις) — formal acts of the intellect.</note>, which, when stored away, are called "conceptions" —

<column-break/>

— and when they are set in motion and agitated, they are called "discursive thoughts" <note>original: *dianoeseis* (διανοήσεις) — the process of reasoning from one point to another.</note>. When a creature works out the difference between the advantageous and the alien, it already possesses the faculty of memory. It fears those things that bring trouble and desires useful things even when they are absent, taking care that they might be present. It prepares a method for pursuing and hunting, and conversely, for fleeing and avoiding those things which have attacked. Indeed, they themselves [the Stoics] also hammer these points home everywhere in their introductions to the point of boredom. They define "purpose" as the seal of perfection; "aggression" as the incitement before the incitement; "preparation" as the action before the action; and "memory" as the comprehension of a past thing which the sense had perceived as present. Truly, there is none of these things which is not rational, and all are present in all animals. This is clearly what they do regarding intellections, which, when stored, they call *conceptions* <note>original: *ennoias* (ἐννοίας) — innate or stored ideas.</note>, and while they are being moved and driven, they call *discursive thoughts*.

---

<margin>1. **And snares.** ---] Instead of "and snares, and again for those caught, escapes from attackers," the text in Plutarch reads: "and snares, and again for those about to be caught, and escapes from attackers." If Porphyry’s reading is better, I would rather translate it as --- *and nets, and again for themselves escapes from those who have captured them.* VALENTINI. <note>Federico Valentini, a 16th-century editor.</note> Nay, the reading of Plutarch is not only much better, but the only true one. Therefore, I did not hesitate to restore it to the "received text." It happened here, as we have seen happen often above, that two words *au tois* [again for them] were wrongly merged into one, *autois* [themselves]. Regarding the formula "again," we spoke at Book II, 40.</margin>
<margin>2. **Or do not even those wear us out.**] *Plutarch* reads "and these things indeed." But there some manuscripts read "and yet." And so Reiske <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German philologist.</note> restored it in his *Observations*, p. 548. Furthermore, *apoknaiein* means to *blunt* someone with annoying chatter, which the Greeks also call "wearing out the ears" or "the hearing." The use of the word was very skillfully explained by the celebrated Ruhnken <note>David Ruhnken (1723–1798), a head librarian and scholar at Leiden.</note> in his notes on *Timaeus' Lexicon*, p. 30, not forgetting our author, or rather Plutarch.</margin>
<margin>3. **The marking of a completion.**] Reiske writes "upon completion" as two words in his *Observations on Plutarch*, p. 548. I prefer "of completion" as one word. The old editions held it thus, and the Meerman manuscript alone; Valentini had pulled it apart.</margin>
<margin>4. **And regarding intellections.**] *Plutarch* reads "and the things regarding intellections," which Valentini and Reiske followed—</margin>

# THE WORKS OF PORPHYRY

...nor to feel fear, nor to plan ahead, nor to remember; instead they say it is "as if" <note>original: *hosanei*</note> the bee remembers, "as if" the swallow plans, "as if" the lion is angry, and <margin>10</margin> "as if" the deer is afraid. I do not know what they would say to those who claimed animals do not even see or hear, but only "as if" see and "as if" hear; or that they do not make sounds, but only "as if" make sounds; or that they do not live at all, but only "as if" live. For such claims are no more justified than the others, and are equally contrary to plain evidence, as any fair-minded person would be convinced. However, when one compares the lives, actions, and habits of animals with human character, <margin>11</margin> and sees much that is base, and of virtue— <margin>12</margin> for which purpose reason exists— <margin>13</margin> none of the animals...

<column-break/>

...neither fear, nor prepare, nor remember, but they say the bee "as if" remembers, the swallow "as if" prepares, the lion "as if" is angry, and the deer "as if" fears. I do not know what they would answer to those who might say animals neither see nor hear, but "as if" see and "as if" hear, nor emit a voice, but "as if" emit a voice, nor live at all, but "as if" live. A fair listener would easily notice that these things are said against all evidence, no less than the previous claims. But indeed, if in comparing the lives of other animals to human character, actions, and diet, I were to see much depravity in them, and no clear leaning toward virtue (at which reason <note>original: *ratio*</note> chiefly aims), no...

# On Abstinence, Book III.

->**On Abstinence, Book III.**<-

...perfection, no appetite: I would certainly wonder why nature gave a beginning to those things which could not reach any end. But even to those very men <note>The Stoic philosophers, who argued that animals lack reason.</note> this does not seem at all absurd; for although they establish that love toward offspring is the beginning of society and justice in us, and they see that this love is powerful in other living creatures, they nevertheless judge that there is no justice or society shared with them. Furthermore, although mules lack none of the reproductive organs—for they have both a penis and a womb and use these with pleasure—they nevertheless do not achieve the end of generation <note>Mules are sterile, yet possess the biological drives and organs for reproduction; Porphyry uses this as an analogy for "imperfect" reason.</note>. In addition to this, does it not seem ridiculous if they say that the likes of Socrates, Plato, and Zeno behave no better than any common slave, but are in a similar way unwise, intemperate, and unjust; and then, because beasts do not conduct themselves exactly and exquisitely according to virtue, they ascribe this to a total privation <note>A complete lack of the faculty.</note>, rather than to a depravity or weakness of reason?

<column-break/>

...of animals, neither a clear aim, nor progress, nor appetite, I would be at a loss as to how Nature gave the beginning to those unable to reach the end. Or rather, this does not even seem strange to those men. At any rate, while they posit that natural affection toward offspring <gloss>14</gloss> <note>original: "philostorgia"</note> is the beginning of society and justice among us, and they see it present in great and strong measure in the animals, they say they do not, and should not, have a share in justice. Mules are not deficient in any of the generative parts; for having both genitals and wombs and the use of these with pleasure, they do not reach the end of procreation. Consider it another way: is it not ridiculous to claim that the likes of Socrates, Plato, and Zeno <gloss>15</gloss> are involved in a condition no lighter than that of any chance slave, but are equally foolish, licentious, and unjust, and then to blame the lack of purity and precision toward virtue in the beasts as a privation, rather than a defect...

---

§ 23. <margin>1</margin> But to claim that because a creature is not naturally fit to achieve the "rectitude" of reason, it does not possess reason at all, is first of all no different than claiming that a monkey does not naturally partake in ugliness, or a turtle in slowness, simply because they are not capable of beauty or speed. # On Abstinence, Book III

->Mm 2<-

...than a lion <note>Continuing the sentence from the previous page: "as a deer is more cowardly than a lion."</note>, we certainly do not say. For just as among those things that lack all motion, one is not said to be "slower" than another, nor among those that have no voice can one be endowed with a "thinner" voice than another: so too nothing is called more cowardly, nor more sluggish, nor more incontinent, where the faculty of understanding is not also present in all. Since this faculty is present in some in one way and some in another—either more or less—it has produced these kinds of differences which are observed in animals. In this matter, it should bring us no wonder that man excels other animals by such a great interval in docility, and cleverness, and other things which pertain to justice and common society. For many of those animals also far surpass all men, both in the size of their body and in swiftness, as well as in the sharpness of sight and the keenness of hearing. Nor for that reason, however, is man judged "deaf," or "blind," or "weak." But we also run, although more slowly than deer; and we also see, although not so...

<column-break/>

...than a lion <note>original Greek: "ἔλαφον λέοντος"</note>. 12 Or just as among the motionless one is not slower than another, nor more small-voiced among the speechless, so neither is anything more cowardly, nor more sluggish, nor more incontinent, where the power of thinking is not present in all by nature; but being present in different ways in different beings, according to the "more" and "less," it has created the differences we see. But it is not a thing of wonder how much man differs from the animals in readiness to learn and shrewdness, and in matters concerning justice and society. For many of those animals have left all men behind, some in size and swiftness of foot, others in the strength of sight and accuracy of hearing; but man is not for this reason deaf, nor blind, nor powerless. But we also run, even if more slowly than deer, and we see, even if worse... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "χεῖ-" (chei-), likely completing the word "cheiron" meaning "worse."</note>

# PORPHYRY

->Book III<-

...worse than hawks. Nature has not deprived us of strength and size, even though we are as nothing in these regards when compared to the elephant or the camel. Therefore, let us not say that beasts do not think or reason at all—or that they do not possess reason—simply because they think more sluggishly and reason more poorly [than we do]. Rather, we should say they possess reason in a weak and turbid state, just like a dim and troubled eye.

§ 24. If many examples had not already been collected and described by many authors, I could have brought forward ten thousand more to demonstrate <margin>1. On the natural talent <note>original Greek: εὐφυΐας</note> of animals. *Plutarch:* our author [Porphyry] diverges from him here; Plutarch does not have these words. What "natural talent" <note>original Greek: εὐφυΐα</note> properly is, we have discussed in another place. He rightly mentions the natural talent of animals, just as man himself is called a "talented animal" in *Diodorus Siculus, Book I, chapter 8.*</margin> the natural talent of animals. But there is another point to consider: it appears that whatever part or power is naturally suited to receive something according to nature <margin>2. "To receive something." I have restored the text this way because all manuscripts and printed editions require it. *Valente* [an earlier editor] had used "the receiving." The following words "being maimed... to fall into" are missing from the *Meerman Codex*.</margin>, it is also of such a nature that it can fall into a state contrary to nature if it is maimed or diseased. Just as it happens to the eye to fall into blindness, the leg into lameness, and the tongue into stammering—and to no other parts. For blindness cannot exist in what is not naturally suited to see, nor lameness in what is not naturally suited to walk, <margin>3. "And stammering..." Reiske [a scholar] suggests: "Nor stammering."</margin> nor stammering...

<column-break/>

...as sharply as hawks. We are not entirely deprived of strength and size by nature, although if we are compared to the elephant and the camel, we seem to be nothing in these respects. In a similar way, therefore, it must not be said that beasts do not think or understand at all simply because they understand more sluggishly and think worse than we do, and that they are endowed with no reason. Rather, they too possess reason, though it is weak and turbid, just as one might have a dull and clouded eye.

§ 24. There are innumerable things I could produce in proof of the intelligence of animals, if many authors had not already collected and recorded these things for memory. This also is worthy of consideration: it seems to belong to the same part or faculty which receives something according to nature that it can also fall into that which is contrary to nature, when it is corrupted or diseased. Just as the eye incurs blindness, the leg lameness, and the tongue stammering—nothing else can suffer these. For blindness does not belong to that which cannot see, nor lameness to that which is not naturally fit for walking...

# On Abstinence, Book III.

->Mm 3<-

Neither can anything be called lisping, or stammering, or mute, which does not possess a tongue. In the same way, therefore, you would not call anyone delirious, or out of their mind, or insane, for whom thinking, reflecting, and reasoning were not a natural state. For it is impossible for anyone to be affected by a condition unless they are first endowed with the faculty of which that condition is either a deprivation, a crippling, or some other defect. But have you never encountered rabid dogs? Or even horses? Some say that even oxen and foxes go mad. But it is enough to consider dogs, for this is beyond dispute; it testifies that the animal possesses reason and a mind of no mean sort, for the condition called rabies and insanity is a disturbance of that very mind. Indeed, we see that neither their sight nor their hearing is altered. Just as someone who, observing a man in a state of melancholy or delirium, would be absurd if they did not recognize that his power of understanding, reasoning, and remembering had been displaced and corrupted—

<column-break/>

<note>The Greek text here mirrors the Latin on the left, providing the original source for the argument regarding animal madness.</note>
—lisping, or mute, or stammering among those who have no tongue. Nor would you call one <note>original: "παραπαίοντα ἢ παράφρονα" - delirious or out of one's mind</note> delirious or frantic, or even insane, if the capacity for wisdom, thought, and reasoning did not belong to them by nature. For it is not possible to be in a state of suffering <note>original: "πάθει" - a passive state or affection</note> without possessing the power of which that suffering is a deprivation, a mutilation, or some other malady. But truly, I have encountered rabid dogs, and also horses, and some say even oxen and foxes go mad. The case of dogs is sufficient; for it is indisputable, and it bears witness that the animal possesses reason and intellect of no small degree, of which the so-called rabies and madness is a disturbed and confused state. # PORPHYRY

<meta>catchword: 2.</meta>

...is; (for common usage also makes this charge against those who are out of their minds, that they are no longer "with themselves," but have "fallen away from their reasonings,") likewise, anyone who thinks that rabid dogs have suffered something else, and not that the faculty naturally meant for thinking, reasoning, and remembering has been filled with turmoil and has fallen away—causing them to fail to recognize their dearest faces and to flee their accustomed dwellings—seems either to overlook what is evident, or if he does see what is happening, he chooses to struggle against the truth out of sheer contentiousness. Such are the things said by Plutarch in many books, written in response to the followers of the Porch <note>The Stoics, who famously denied that animals possessed reason.</note> and the Walk <note>The Peripatetics, the followers of Aristotle, who also generally separated animal instinct from human reason.</note>.

§ 25. 1. Theophrastus also uses an argument of this sort. Those who are born from the same parents, I mean both father...

<column-break/>

...asserts the faculty, is absurd: for it is a matter of common custom that we say those who are delirious are not "with themselves," but are "driven out of their mind and judgment." Thus, he who thinks rabid dogs have suffered something else, and not that the part which is suited by nature for understanding, reasoning, and remembering has been driven out and displaced—so that they do not know their dearest companions and flee their usual haunts—he seems either not to notice what is clearly apparent, or if he does notice, he wishes to struggle against the truth. And indeed, those things that Plutarch wrote in various books against the Stoics and Peripatetics are of this kind.

§ 25. Theophrastus truly also uses this reasoning. Those, he says, who are born of the same, namely father and mother...

<margin>ἐσιν. <note>original: "ἐσιν. prius itaque δὲ post ἔνιοι Porphyrio reddidi..."</note> I have restored the word *de* [but] after *enioi* [some] in Porphyry, which Valentinus had removed against the consensus of other editions and manuscripts. *The matter of the dogs* from the Meerman and Leiden manuscripts.</margin>

<margin>6. <note>original: "Οὐχὶ τοῦ φρονεῖν πεφυκότος"</note> Not that which is by nature capable of wisdom. In the Florentine Edition it was *pephykotōs* [naturally], but Fogerolles corrected the typesetter's error as if on his own authority. In the text of Plutarch <note>of Chaeronea</note> it is *all’ ouchi tō phronein pephykoti kai l.* [but not to that which is naturally capable of thinking and reasoning]. A little earlier, Meerman has *atopon* [absurd] instead of *atopos* [an absurd man]. Incorrectly. But later he better reads *tauta ge katēg.* [accuses these things at least].</margin>

<margin>7. <note>original: "Καὶ παραπτωκότος"</note> And having fallen away. One could certainly think of *parapepaikotos* [having been struck aside/delirious], because one is said *parapaiein* [to strike awry/be crazy]. However, I see no sufficiently grave reason why the common reading should be abandoned. REISKE. <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a notable German physician and philologist.</note> Yet the Author whose words these are uses that very voice, though in a slightly different way: *anapeplēsmenous tarachēs kai parapepaikotas* [filled with turmoil and having been struck delirious].</margin>

<margin>8. <note>original: "Τὰς διαίτας"</note> Their dwellings. Feliciano gave *solita diuersoria* [accustomed lodgings]: for *diaita* signifies to the Greeks both a "way of life" and a "place." Plutarch is fuller here: *tas syntrophous diaitas* [their familiar haunts].</margin>

<margin>9. <note>original: "Τὸ γιγνόμενον"</note> The happening. The comma should be removed. *To gignomenon ex autou* means that which flows from the premise taken above, and follows from it. REISKE. This opinion is confirmed by the punctuation in Plutarch; but there it is published as *mē synorōn to gignomenon* [not seeing the consequence], where the *mē* [not] must be changed to *ē* [or] according to our Author.</margin>

<margin>1. <note>original: "Θεόφρασος"</note> Theophrastus. Reference seems to be made to Theophrastus's books *On Animals*, which the ancients often mention. Regarding these, see Menage on Diogenes Laertius, Book V, 44; and Fabricius, Greek Library, III, 9, 17.</margin>

# PORPHYRIUS

...but rather like seed, flesh, and the kind of fluids that are innate to living beings. And if what is said is true—that the origin of their character is of such a kind—then all tribes of animals possess understanding, though they differ in their upbringing and in the temperaments <note>original: "krasis," referring to the mixing of bodily humors</note> of their primary elements; thus the race of other animals would be entirely kindred and related to us.

<column-break/>

...but concerning the seed, the flesh, and that kind of humor which is implanted in animals. It is much more so because the souls within them do not differ from one another, namely in their desires and angers, as well as in their considerations, and most of all in their senses. However, just as with their bodies, so too with their souls: some animals have them more exquisite and perfect, others less so, yet by nature the principles are the same for all. This is declared by the likeness and affinity of their affections. If it is true, as is said, that the generation of character is of this sort, then all kinds of animals are wise and understand, but they differ nevertheless in their educations and in the various temperaments of their primary elements: the race of other animals must be considered altogether affine and cognate to us.

<meta>Catchword: mo- / κα-</meta>

...manner. For since all nourishment is the same for all of them, and they possess breath—as Euripides says—as well as the flow of red blood:

> All animals, as if to show they have
> Parents common to all, the heavens and the earth.

§. 26. Therefore, since they are so closely related, if they are also seen to have been allotted the very same soul—as Pythagoras used to believe—then any person might rightly be judged impious for not abstaining from doing injury to their own kin. Nor indeed should the right of kinship be considered broken simply because some of them are wild. For among men, no fewer (and indeed often more) are found to be evildoers toward other men, driven by a certain spirit of their own nature and depravity to inflict harm on those they meet. Though we certainly believe such people should be removed and put to death, we do not for that reason break off all social bonds with those who are gentle toward us. In the same way, then, if there are some among the animals that are fierce and wild, those should be

<column-break/>

...the race of animals. For indeed, all their foods are the same for all of them, and they have breath, as Euripides says, and all animals have streams of crimson blood; thus he shows that the parents of all are the heavens and the earth.

§ 26. So, since they are kindred, if it should appear—according to Pythagoras—that they have also received the same soul, one might justly be judged impious if they do not refrain from injustice toward their own relatives. It is certainly not the case that because some of them are wild, the kinship is therefore cut off. For no less, but even more, some humans are evildoers toward their neighbors and are carried away toward harming whomever they encounter, as if by some blast of their own nature and wickedness. # On Abstinence, Book III.

->Nn 2<-

If one abstains from all living beings, even if they contribute nothing to one's own society, he will be much more careful to avoid inflicting harm upon those of his own kind. For if he loves the genus <note>the broad category of "living beings"</note>, he cannot pursue a specific species with hatred; rather, the wider the genus of animals extends, the more he will preserve the same sense of right even toward a part of it. For he who establishes a kinship toward animals in general will not treat any specific animal with injustice. But he who circumscribes all right and law only within the human sphere is like one shut within very narrow boundaries, and can easily cast aside his caution against injustice. Hence, the Pythagorean "seasoning" is far sweeter than the Socratic one. For Socrates used to say that hunger was the seasoning for food <note>original Latin: "cibi opsonium esse famem"</note>, but Pythagoras thought that the sweetest seasoning of justice for one's meal was the fact that no injury was being inflicted. ### P O R P H Y R Y

<columns>2</columns>

It was an escape from the injustices surrounding food. For God did not make our survival an impossibility without the mistreatment of another being; otherwise, He would have implanted a principle of injustice within our very nature. Perhaps those people also seem to be ignorant of the specific character of justice—those who think it should be introduced only from our kinship toward other humans; for such a thing would merely be a form of "philanthropy" <note>original Greek: "philanthropia," meaning a love for fellow humans</note>. But true justice consists in restraint and harmlessness toward anything whatsoever that does not harm us. And this is how the "just man" is understood, and not in the other way: justice extends even to living beings, as it is founded upon harmlessness. Therefore, the very essence of justice lies in the rational part of the soul ruling over the irrational part, while the irrational part follows. For when the rational rules and the irrational obeys, it is an absolute necessity for the human being to be harmless toward every thing. For once the passions are contracted and—

<column-break/>

—we also undoubtedly avoid the injuries that occur regarding food. For it must not be thought that God brought it about that we are in no way able to preserve our health and safety without the insult and injury of others. For in that way, He would have given us a nature that existed as a principle of injustice. Add to this that those people also seem to me to be ignorant of the property of justice, who think it must be established from kinship toward humans alone. For in that case, it would be called a certain humanity and kindness toward humans. But justice is not of that kind: rather, it consists in abstinence from the injury of anything that does not itself harm. And in this way also, the notion of the "just" is held, not in the other way: so that since justice is established in never inflicting injury on anyone at all, it seems it must be extended even to the rest of the animals. Whence also its essence is said to lie in the dominion of reason over the irrational part, and the obedience of the irrational <note>The "irrational part" refers to the part of the soul driven by instincts and emotions rather than logic</note>. For while the former commands and the latter obeys, it is necessary for a man to be innocent toward all things. For since, with the disturbances calmed—

---

<columns>2</columns>

—by adding "HARM NO ONE" <note>original Latin: "NEMINEM LAEDERE"</note> (remember, or it is necessary), he not only added a side-dish to the bread, but even a seasoning to the side-dish itself. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar noted for his work on Greek texts.</note>. "Justice" <term>Meermann</term> <note>Refers to the Meermann manuscript collection.</note> as well.

11. **So that [justice] extends ----]** Perhaps "it is he who extends." And immediately after, "if they also remain in harmlessness," meaning, if they themselves also remain innocent, so to speak. That is, if they also refrain from bringing damage and—

<column-break/>

—inflicting injuries. <term>REISKE</term>. The <term>Leipzig Manuscript</term> could confirm this conjecture, as it has "and to remain" instead of "consisting in." However, because it was said similarly above that "justice consists in harmlessness," I will attempt nothing here. "So that it extends" (namely, it is necessary). Instead of "rational" <note>original Greek: "logistikon"</note>, <term>Meermann</term> has "logical" <note>original Greek: "logikon"</note>. A little before, the same manuscript has "they thought in this way." And then it omits the word "is understood." Both are poor readings.

<summary>Porphyry argues that true justice is a universal restraint from harming any non-harmful being, rather than a social contract limited to humans. He defines the essence of justice as the internal mastery of reason over the irrational passions.</summary>

### On Abstinence, Book III.

<columns>2</columns>

Once the disturbances and desires are calmed, and anger has been settled, reason holds its dominion, and immediately the likeness to a more excellent nature <note>original: "praestantiorem naturam," referring to the divine or universal intellect</note> shines forth within us. Now, the most excellent nature in the universe is the most innocent toward all things. Indeed, because of its power, it is the preserver of all things, and it is a benefactor to all, standing in need of nothing.

But we, while innocent toward all things because of justice, are in need of necessities because of our mortality. However, the taking of necessities brings no harm: not to plants, when we take from them those things which they cast off; nor to fruits, when we use them after they have already died; nor to sheep, when we benefit them more through shearing, and by providing them our care, we in turn become participants in their milk. Therefore, the just man appears,

<column-break/>

and <gloss>12</gloss> when the desires and angers have withered away, and reason holds its proper rule, immediately follows the likeness to that which is better. That which is better in the whole universe was entirely harmless; by its power it is the preserver of all, and <gloss>13</gloss> the benefactor of all, and in need of nothing. But we, through justice, are harmless to all, yet through mortality, in need of necessities. 

The taking of necessities harms <gloss>14</gloss> neither plants, when we take what they cast off, nor fruits, when we use the fruits of those that have died, nor sheep, when through shearing we help them more, and share in their milk, providing them our own care in return. Therefore <gloss>15</gloss> the just man appears <gloss>16</gloss> as—

</columns>

<margin>12. **When the desires and angers have withered away.**] It might be doubted whether "orgai" <note>Greek for angers or passions</note> here meant intense inclinations of the soul, as the poet Alcman says: "among men, ten thousand heavy angers." Compare Duker’s notes on Thucydides, Book I, 140. But above in § 25 and Book II, 38, "angers" and "desires" are joined together. They are said to "wither" by an elegant metaphor. Exactly as Dionysius of Halicarnassus says: "until the angers of the many wither away." (Book VII, p. 445). Clement of Alexandria says this beautifully: "One must check both pleasures and desires, and wither away the impulses and increases of the flesh." (Stromata, Book II, p. 411 C).</margin>

<margin>13. **Beneficent toward all.**] Pollux condemns this word, as well as the related word for "beneficence," but he does so wrongly, as we saw in Book II, § 12. Hesychius defines "Doers of good" as "beneficent" and "just." See more on the word "beneficent" in Henri Estienne’s *Thesaurus* <note>A famous 16th-century Greek dictionary</note>.</margin>

<margin>14. **Nor fruits, when—**] Here he means all those kinds of grains and fruits that the earth bears in fields, woods, gardens, and vineyards, while they still stand firm or hang green on their stalks and trunks. But he immediately means the same kinds when already reaped, plucked, or fallen; if this is not observed, the speech will seem inconsistent. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske was a 18th-century German scholar known for his editions of Greek texts</note>. See Book III, § 18 and the arguments for this same cause in Book II, § 13. Meermann wrongly neglected the last syllable in the Greek word for "they cast off."</margin>

<margin>15. **The just man appears**] Perhaps "gentle"; the just man seems to someone who looks at him cursorily and judges without careful consideration to be almost injurious to himself. <term>REISKE</term>. Fogerolles had also corrected this word. The manuscripts agree on the common reading, which can be defended by my notes on Book II, 4.</margin>

...it happens that we are made like unto God, as far as is possible, when innocence is preserved toward all. In what way, then, does the man led by his passions practice innocence only toward his children and his wife, while he despises and harms all others? For since the irrational part of the soul dominates him, he is moved toward mortal things, admiring and being stunned by them. But he who is guided by reason conducts himself innocently even toward his fellow citizens, and toward strangers as well—indeed, toward all men. Because he keeps his irrational faculty in subjection, he is more rational than the former man, and more divine. Thus, he who does not limit the boundaries of innocence to humans alone, but extends them even to all other animals, is more similar to God; and if he were able to extend them even unto plants, he would preserve that image and likeness even further. Because he cannot do this, from that point our nature—

<column-break/>

...becoming like God <note>original: ὁμοιοῦσθαι θεῷ (homoiousthai theo)</note> being the goal, as far as is possible, innocence <note>original: τὸ ἀβλαβὲς (to ablabes), meaning "harmlessness" or "non-injury"</note> is preserved in all things. In the same manner, then, as the man led by passions is harmless only toward his own children and wife, but is contemptuous and greedy toward others—since the irrational part rules within him, he is roused toward mortal things and is struck with awe by them—so the man led by reason maintains innocence toward a citizen, and even more toward strangers, and toward all men. He holds his irrationality in obedience, and is himself more rational than those others, and for these reasons more divine. Thus, the man who has not only established innocence among humans, but has extended it even to the other animals, is more like God; and if it were possible to extend it as far as plants, he would preserve that image even more. If not, then at least from this point the [flaw] of our nature—

Moreover, poverty acquires for itself safety and ornament from external things, from which we received our existence. He, therefore, who requires more external things is more "glued" to poverty. # On Abstinence, Book III.

-> O o <-

Even if a man possesses all the acres of the earth, since he is addicted to want, he is without doubt poor; and for that reason he is also unjust, and impious, and estranged from God, and finally liable to every vice. The nature of this vice was introduced by the soul’s sliding into matter <note>original: "delapsio animae in materiam"</note> through the deprivation of the Good. Therefore, all things are trifles as long as one has wandered from the first principle; likewise, every person is in need of all things as long as they do not look toward fullness <note>The Latin uses "satietatem" (satiety/fullness), translating the Greek "koron."</note>; and one indulges the mortality of their own nature as long as they do not truly know themselves. Moreover, injustice is quite skilled at employing persuasion upon itself and at judging those who are held under its power, because it maintains a <unclear>familiarity</unclear> <unclear>habit</unclear> with its foster-children and associates.

<column-break/>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument regarding the superiority of the rational life over the irrational one. # P O R P H Y R Y

Just as in the choices of different ways of life, a more accurate judge is the one who has experienced both, rather than the one who has experienced only one of the two; so also, in choosing or avoiding what is necessary, a more reliable judge is the person who looks down from a higher state to judge the lower, rather than someone judging from a lower state those things set above him. **17** Therefore, the one who lives according to the mind is a more precise judge of what should be chosen or avoided than the one who lives by irrationality; for the intellectual man has also passed through the irrational life, having been familiar with it from the beginning. But the person who has no experience of the things of the mind merely persuades those similar to himself—**18** like a child babbling among children. "But if everyone," they say, **19** "were to be persuaded by these arguments, what will happen to us?" **20** Isn't it obvious that we would be happy, with injustice banished from humanity and justice governing...

<column-break/>

...dwells with pleasure among his own habits. Just as in the choices of life paths, he is accustomed to judge more correctly who is experienced in both, than he who has been an expert in only one: so also, in the choices and avoidances of those things which are required, the judgment of him who discerns the lower from the higher is more certain than his who judges from the lower those things placed before him. For this reason, he who establishes his life based on the mind and intellect can more correctly and exquisitely define those things which are to be sought or fled, than he who is accustomed to live by the irrational faculty. The former has indeed passed through the irrational life, inasmuch as he was bound to it from the beginning: but the latter, being inexperienced in those things which proceed from the mind, easily persuades his own kind—a child among children babbling trifles. "But if all," they say, "should assent to these reasons, what would come to us from there—"

<note>The following notes are scholarly commentary on the text above, likely from an 18th-century editor.</note>

...had corrected. I will change nothing, since all agree on the word *to judge* <note>original: "δικάζειν" (dikazein)</note>. This is confirmed by what follows, when he opposes the more equitable judge—who establishes his life by mind and intellect—to that one who is accustomed to act from the irrational faculty. To "judge those placed under" is therefore to "give the law, or to have them as subjects."

16. **Choices of lives.** <note>original: "Βίων αἱρέσεσιν"</note>] Plutarch calls these "the classes into which lives are divided" in Volume 1, page 91. Indeed, "life" <note>original: "βίος" (bios)</note> signifies a type and manner of living. We have seen this above; see also Hemsterhuis on Pollux, IX, 33.

17. **The things set before.** <note>original: "Τὰ προκείμενα"</note>] For "the things set before," I would prefer "the things set above" <note>original: "ὑπερκείμενα" (hyperkeimena)</note>, so that it stands in opposition to "from below." **VALENT.** Moreover, Reiske preferred "what must be chosen" <note>original: "αἱρετέον" (aireteon)</note> instead of the common "what is chosen."

18. **A child babbling among children.** <note>original: "Παῖς ἐν παισὶ φλυαρῶν"</note>] Elegantly said. "Child" <note>original: "παῖς" (pais)</note> is used everywhere regarding character, and is applied to those who are children in mind, as words of this kind are used in both languages <note>Greek and Latin</note>. I add nothing to those things which the celebrated Alberti noted regarding Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians 4:14.

19. **What will happen to us?** <note>original: "Τί ἡμῖν ἔσαι"</note>] This too is a beautiful way of speaking. "What reward shall we carry back?" Exactly as Peter says, "What then will there be for us?" in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 19:27. On this, see Kypke, and join him with Raphel on Mark 11:24.

20. **Is it not clear that we shall be happy etc.** <note>original: "Ἢ δῆλον ὡς εὐδαιμονήσομεν"</note>] This refers to the opinion of the ancients that Justice, because of the crimes of men, left this earth and migrated into heaven. But just as Aristides asserts that Justice and modesty returned to men during the reign of Marcus <note>the Emperor Marcus Aurelius</note>, so clearly the same will happen...

# On Abstinence, Book III.
Page 291
Sig. Oo 2

...will happen? This, without a doubt: that we will be happy. For injustice will be banished far from humanity, and justice will dwell among us just as it is in heaven. But as it stands, the situation is as if the Danaids <note>In Greek mythology, the Danaids were fifty sisters punished in the underworld by being forced to carry water in leaky jars forever—a symbol of futile, unending labor.</note> were to ask what kind of life they would lead if they were freed from that service of drawing water in perforated jars. For they [our opponents] ask and wonder what would happen to us if, being established in and for the sake of things necessary, we were to find rest by indul...

<column-break/>

...also among us, just as it is in heaven. But now it is similar to if the Danaids were at a loss as to what life they would live, once released from the service <gloss>21</gloss> concerning the leaky jar through the sieve. For they wonder what will be if we should cease piling things into our passions and desires, through which everything flows away <gloss>22</gloss> in an absence of evils, while we are content with a life based on necessities and for the sake of necessities <gloss>23</gloss>.

---

Our author means: "if the human race could be brought back to a simple and harmless way of life." See: *Gataker on Marcus Aurelius*, Book V, § 33.

21. <term>Concerning the leaky jar.</term> <note>original Greek: Περὶ τὸν τετρημένον πίθον</note>] A well-known fable. From this is derived the phrase <term>to draw water with a sieve</term> <note>original: κοσκίνῳ ὕδωρ ἀντλεῖν</note> in Theodoret’s *Sermon on Matter and the World*, p. 531; and <term>to draw into a leaky jar</term> <note>original: εἰς τετρημένον πίθον ἀντλεῖν</note> in his *Dialogues*, I, p. 18. Others also call it a "worn-out jar," as the illustrious Wesseling shows on Diodorus Siculus, I, 97. But our author said "leaky jar" following the example of his Plato in the *Gorgias*, p. 336 D. He took these things from Plutarch, Vol. II, p. 160, as my dearest friend Abreschius opportunely reminded me.

22. <term>In an absence of evils —</term> <note>original: Ἀπορίᾳ τῶν κακῶν</note>] The Leipzig manuscript correctly gives "the [life] upon" and then "the necessary [life]," which I approve so far as to read "and not beyond what is necessary." All of this perishes and vanishes when we lack evils (which it is necessary to endure when seeking a luxurious and sumptuous diet), if we find contentment in a life that stays within necessities and does not exceed them. <term>The life focused on necessities</term> <note>original: ὁ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀναγκαίοις βίος</note> is the life led with a supply of things only strictly necessary, on the condition that nothing superfluous is desired or sought after. I also wonder whether it might be better to read "inexperience" <note>original: ἀπειρίᾳ</note> instead of "absence" <note>original: ἀπορίᾳ</note>, since we are free from the experience and knowledge of troubles. I would not want to guarantee that nothing is missing after the word "evils." Finally, "and for the sake of necessities" could be defended, and the rest of the passage could seem sound, provided that "the" <note>original: τὸν</note> is admitted in line 20 instead of "of the" <note>original: τῶν</note>. We have said what the "life focused on necessities" is—namely, that which rejoices in the necessities at hand

<column-break/>

and is lived on the condition that it is content with them. It remains to be said what the life "for the sake of necessities" is; namely, that which labors only to acquire necessary things. **REISKE.** The Meerman manuscript also reads "Necessary." I will speak on this immediately.

<term>Of evils, etc.</term> <note>original: Τῶν κακῶν</note>] It seemed it should be read as "of the good things" <note>original: τῶν καλῶν</note>, and that this is the meaning of the passage. *We always try to satisfy our desires, but in vain: because we do not seek the truly good things, which would fill the gaps and cracks of our soul better than those things which seem most necessary among external matters.* For I read "loving" <note>original: σεργόντων</note> instead of "bearing" <note>original: φεργόντ.</note>. **VALENTIN.** That last part is foolish. The illustrious Reiske excellently defends the common reading, and therefore I have restored "the" to its place, as Fogerolles had already emended. Felicianus accepted it no differently. Nevertheless, I contend it should be read thus: "in the inexperience of the good things, while we are content with a life focused on necessities." Do not wonder how I have become so authoritative: Plutarch, whom our author imitates here, says the same thing in the same words in the place cited. From this, you should have no doubt about the restoration of "the." "Evil" and "Good" are often confused. We saw examples in Book I, § 9; D’Orville on Chariton, VIII, 4, will give more.

23. <term>While we are content with a life.</term> <note>original: Στεργόντων ἡμῶν βίον</note>] Valentin foolishly reads "holding" <note>original: σεγόντων</note>, although those words are sometimes confused, as in Diodorus Siculus, XI, 29. I have already noted that this is Plutarch's. "To be content with a life" is said like "to be content with things present," "with fortune," and similar things, about which see Wesseling on Diodorus.

<summary>Porphyry argues that a life of abstinence and justice leads to happiness, comparing the pursuit of excessive desires to the eternal, futile punishment of the Danaids. The accompanying scholarly notes debate the correct Greek terminology for a life focused on necessities versus one plagued by the pursuit of luxuries.</summary>

# PORPHYRY

"What then shall we do?" you ask, O man. Let us imitate the Golden Race <note>original: "χρυσοῦν γένος" — the first and best age of mankind in Greek mythology</note>; let us imitate those who have been set free. For with them, Shame, Indignation, and Justice walked together, because they were content with the fruits of the earth.

> For the grain-giving earth bore fruit for them
> Spontaneously, in great and plenteous abundance. <note>A quotation from Hesiod's *Works and Days*</note>

And those who have been set free now provide for themselves the very things they once provided while serving their masters. In no other way, then, shall you also—having been released from the slavery of the body and from the service to the passions caused by the body—nourish yourself. Just as you used to nourish that body in every way with external things, so now you shall nourish yourself in every way with internal things, justly reclaiming what is your own, and no longer taking away the property of others by force.

<column-break/>

...to cease indulging in disturbances and desires, from which all fruit flows away and perishes due to a lack of honorable things. What then are we to do, you ask? We shall imitate that Golden Age; we shall imitate those who have been asserted into liberty. For with them, Shame, Indignation, and Justice were familiar, because they were content with the fruits of the earth. *For the fertile Earth bore fruit for them of its own accord.* But those who have been gifted with liberty henceforth acquire for themselves those things which they previously prepared by ministering to their masters. In no other way shall you also—if you are freed from the slavery of the body and from that ministry which you exhibit to the passions—nourish yourself inwardly in various ways, just as you used to nourish that body outwardly. In this matter, your own things will justly be available to you, so that the things of others need no longer be taken by you through violence.

See Gataker: on *Marcus Aurelius VI, 44*, who teaches that "to love" is used in the same sense in § 49. Eusebius in *Demonstratio Evangelica III, p. 119 B* says "having loved a hardy and laborious life."
</margin>

24. **Those who have been set free.**] "To set free" <note>original: "Ἐλευθεροῦν"</note> specifically means *to claim into liberty*, and is said of manumitted slaves. Our author [Porphyry] beautifully applied this from Plutarch to the liberty of the soul. Read the Learned Man <note>referring to a previous commentator</note> on those words of *John in the Gospel VIII, 32: "The truth shall set you free."*

25. **Shame and Indignation —**] He seems to be looking back at those words of Hesiod, whom Shame and Indignation <note>original: "Αἰδὼς καὶ Νέμεσις"</note> are said to have abandoned only in the Iron Age. *Works and Days, 198.* In this passage, Indignation and Justice are also well distinguished; for it is understood that this is not that "Nemesis" who was also called "Justice."

26. **For the fruit —**] *Hesiod: Works and Days, 117.*

<column-break/>

- - - - "and the grain-giving earth bore fruit." He uses this again in § 2 of the following book; see there.

27. **They provide in no other way.**] This is correct. *Without any doubt, without controversy, more certain than certainty.* Reiske, Fogerolles, and Valentinus had rashly corrected it to "for others." However, I have punctuated it differently than was previously done, as the major mark of distinction used to be placed after "in no other way." *Plutarch: "the things they used to do while serving their masters, these they now do for themselves and by themselves."* So the soul... if it should be released from service, etc.

28. **And you.**] An elegant formula, and therefore frequently used by others. See: *Markland on Maximus Tyrius, Dissertation XVII, 11*, who was not forgetful of this passage. Shortly after, instead of "you shall nourish him [the body]," the *Meerman manuscript* has "you shall nourish her [the soul]."

### ON ABSTINENCE FROM ANIMAL FOOD
### BOOK FOUR.

# PORPHYRY
## THE PHILOSOPHER
### ON ABSTINENCE FROM ANIMAL FOOD
### *BOOK FOUR.*

->SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT<-

*The fourth book is divided, like the preceding ones, into three parts: the first of which contains the preface to Firmus Castricius <note>A student of Porphyry to whom this work is dedicated</note>. The second part confirms, through the examples of the ancients, that abstinence from animals was practiced by great men—such as legislators, philosophers, and the high priests of sacred rites—while, conversely, it was cruel and impious men who used them for food. Examples of abstinence are drawn from the laws and customs of various nations: the Spartans (§ 3), the Egyptians (§ 6), the Jews (§ 11), the Syrians and Cypriots (§ 15), the Persians (§ 16), and the Cretan priests (§ 19). The exhortation <term>paraenesis: a speech or text intended to provide moral advice</term>, which occupies the third place, encourages the chastity of the body, the purity of the mind, and the sanctity of both.*

§ I. <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial A featuring floral and geometric patterns.</image-desc> Against almost all the excuses of those who, since in truth for the sake of lack of self-control and plea-

<column-break/>

§ I. <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial P featuring floral and geometric patterns.</image-desc> Against almost all the excuses of those <gloss>1</gloss> who, in truth, for the sake of lack of self-control and indulgence

---

<margin>1. In truth.] The *Leipzig Manuscript* <note>Cod. Lips.</note> gives "on the one hand, in truth." Similarly in line 8, it reads "the practice of meat-eating for them," with the rest omitted. It appears the passage is corrupt, which anyone will easily perceive who pays attention to the phrase "in truth," which lacks a corresponding phrase in the sentence. It seems the author wrote something like this: "On the one hand, in truth, for the sake of their own lack of restraint and indulgence, yielding to their desires... but on the other hand, providing themselves with shameless excuses for meat-eating out of necessity." REISKE <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a noted German physician and classical scholar</note>. In truth.</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

Among those who have accurately collected the history of Greek affairs is the Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> Dicaearchus. In recounting the ancient life of Greece, he asserts that those early people—who by their antiquity stood closest to the gods, were of the best possible nature, and led such holy lives that their era was considered a "Golden Age" compared to our own, which is composed of adulterated and most wicked matter—were not accustomed to killing any animal. He says the poets also bear witness to this when they speak of that golden race of men: "To whom," as they say, "all good things were present, and the fruit was borne freely."

> The fertile earth bore much in lavish crops;
> They themselves, at peace and in quiet, 
> Enjoyed their own will amidst many blessings.

<column-break/>

Among those who have accurately collected the history of Greek affairs is also the Peripatetic <gloss>1</gloss> Dicaearchus, who, in describing the ancient life of Greece, [says] that the ancients, having been born near to the gods by nature, being the best by nature and having lived the best life, were considered a golden race when compared to those of today, who exist of a debased and most foul matter; [and] that they murdered no living thing. This is what the <gloss>2</gloss> poets represent <gloss>3</gloss> when they name it the golden race. "All good things," they say,

> Belonged to them, and the grain-giving earth bore fruit
> Spontaneously, both much and unstinting; and they, 
> Content and at peace, tended their works amidst many good things.

---

<columns>2</columns>

<gloss>1. Dicaearchus ---- the ancients, etc.</gloss> *Jerome: Against Jovinian, Book II, Chapter 13.* <note>original: "Hieron: II. Adv: Iovin: c. 13." Jerome was a Church Father who often quoted Porphyrius.</note> (In these books he expresses our author <note>Porphyrius</note> throughout, as has been said more often.) *Dicaearchus, in his books of Antiquities and his description of Greece, reports that under Saturn—that is, in the Golden Age—when the ground brought forth all things, no one ate meat, but everyone lived on the fruits and produce which the earth produced of its own accord.* Regarding Dicaearchus, of which name there were several, see *Suidas under the letter D, and Fabricius: Greek Library, Book III, Chapter 11.* Our author also praises him in the *Life of Pythagoras*, numbers 18 and 56, but there he seems to mean the books *On Lives*, which many confuse with the one he called *The Life of Greece*, mentioned here, of which a splendid fragment survives. See *Menagius on Diogenes Laertius III, 4,* who, in calling it a geographical book, perhaps confuses this work with Dicaearchus's geographical poem called *The Description of Greece*. Now, because *Varro, in On Agriculture II, 1,* excerpted the same things from Dicaearchus as our author, I ought to add them here: *It is necessary that human life descended by degrees from the highest memory to this age, as Dicaearchus writes; and the highest degree was the natural one, when men lived from those things which the earth brought forth untouched and of its own accord; from this life they descended into the second, the pastoral life, etc.*

<column-break/>

<gloss>2. The poets represent.]</gloss> The word "representing" <note>original: "παρισάντας"</note> is not in the *Leipzig Manuscript* from the ancient hand. For the person who, within the memory of our fathers, wrote "passing over" <note>original: "παρασάντας"</note> above the line, seems either to have been ignorant or to have forgotten the difference between "representing" and "passing over." I will not condemn "passing over," but it could be absent without damage to the meaning. For the word "which" <note>original: "ὃ"</note> often denotes the same as "wherefore." "Which" can also refer to "race." In either way of explaining, that word "representing" can be dispensed with. —REISKE. Shortly before, the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts erroneously had "debased" (plural) and "existing of the matter."

<gloss>3. Named the golden race ----]</gloss> *The Golden Age—*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the philosopher Dicaearchus’s account of the "Golden Age," transitioning from the moral character of the first humans to a naturalistic explanation of their diet, health, and lack of technology.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

Which things Dicaearchus, in his explanation, says: that the life in the time of Cronus <note>The Greek Titan, known as Saturn to the Romans, who ruled during a legendary "Golden Age" of peace and plenty.</note> was of this kind—if one must accept it as having actually happened and not as a story told in vain. Leaving aside the excessively mythical parts, we should reduce it to a natural explanation through reason. For it is reasonable that all things grew spontaneously. For they themselves produced nothing, since they did not yet possess agriculture as a skill, nor indeed any other art at all. This was also the cause of their leisure, and of their passing time without toil or care; and if we must follow the mind of the most elegant physicians, it was also the cause of their not falling ill. For one could find no greater rule for their health than not producing waste products <note>The Greek term *perittomata* refers to metabolic residues or undigested food, which ancient doctors believed were the primary cause of disease.</note>, of which...

<column-break/>

Indeed, Dicaearchus, explaining these matters, says such a life existed in the times of Saturn. If only we admit that it truly existed and was not celebrated in vain: and once those things which are quite fabulous are set aside, the matter must be brought back to a natural consideration. For all things were born spontaneously by merit: because, clearly, they themselves performed no labor, since they had not yet discovered agriculture or any other art. This was also the reason why they lived in leisure, without any care and without any labors; and if we are to agree with the opinions of the most elegant physicians, it was also so that they did not get sick. For there is no precept of theirs which contributes more to health than when they advise that effort must be given so that as few waste products <note>original: "excrementa"</note> as possible are produced—

---

<margin>
*Who does not know the ages of the King?* <note>A poetic reference to the era of Saturn/Cronus.</note> These verses are from *Hesiod, Works and Days, 116*: 
->all good things<- 
->belonged to them. Fruit<- 
which also occurred at the end of the previous book. I have left them as I found them, as if the hexameter were complete, although the meter is inconsistent; perhaps the Philosopher <note>Porphyry.</note> was not concerned with this. *Homer says this:* 
->But these things [grow] unsown and unplowed<- 
->All things grow<-

### ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK IV.

...waste products are produced: from which they certainly kept their bodies forever purged. For they did not take food that was stronger than the nature of their bodies, but rather food that their nature was stronger than; nor did they take more than was moderate simply because it was available, but rather, for the most part, less than was sufficient because of its scarcity. Furthermore, there were neither wars nor seditions among them, since there was no prize proposed in their midst <note>original: "ἆθλον... ἐν τῷ μέσῳ," a common idiom for a prize of competition available to anyone</note> of such a kind that anyone would wish to undertake a great contention to acquire it. Thus, the summary of their whole life was nothing other than leisure, and rest from the labor of providing for their necessities, as well as health, peace, and friendship. Therefore, to later generations, who had fallen into many evils because they had desired greater things, a life of this sort naturally appeared desirable. The meager and improvised diet of those first men, which required no elaborate preparation, is sufficiently declared by the proverb that was spoken later: "Enough of the oak." <note>This famous Greek proverb (Halidrys) marks the transition from the "primitive" diet of acorns to the "civilized" diet of grain. It implies "we have had enough of the old ways" or "the age of simple survival is over."</note>

<margin>
6. *For there was no prize... lying in their midst.*] Terence says in the prologue to *Phormio*, verse 17: "The palm [of victory] was placed in the middle." Our author uses the common expression "a prize lying before them." Aristotle uses it in *Politics* VII, 10: "It is better that a prize be set before all slaves." Plotinus in *Enneads* III, Book 2, page 25: "The prizes of virtue are set before us." In Appian's *Civil Wars* I, page 645 and Homer's *Iliad* X, verse 163, the prize is said "to lie." In the same way, a "contest" is said to "lie before us," as the interpreters of the *Epistle to the Hebrews* XII:1 illustrate with many examples. Moreover, "to lie in the middle" is almost proverbial among the Greeks for things that are exposed to all. Heliodorus uses our same compound word for this in Book IV, page 169: "and things lying in the middle for whoever wants them."
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
7. *Leisure.*] In this context, it signifies an honorable rest, just as the word "to be at leisure" <note>original: "ῥαθυμεῖν"</note> in Polybius means to relax the mind with rest. See Suidas <note>The Suda, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> on this word. Otherwise, it is usually a vice of a mind devoted to worthless things, as we have seen above.

### On Abstinence, Book IV.

...they finally arrived at the cultivation of fields. These are the accounts Dicaearchus <note>Dicaearchus of Messana (c. 350–285 BC) was a student of Aristotle who wrote a history of Greek civilization titled *Life of Greece*.</note> records when recounting the ancient history of the Greeks, praising the blessed life of those early people. To this life, abstinence from living creatures contributed perfection no less than other virtues. Consequently, there was no war then, as it was entirely free from all injustice. Later, however, alongside the injustice committed against animals, war and the struggle to possess more than others <term>greed: the Latin "plus habendi" and Greek "pleonexia" refer to the desire to take more than one's fair share</term> crept in. For this reason, many types of injustices were banished from Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>. For who would have wanted to steal, or to receive as a bribe, or to snatch away things which were neither easy to hide nor glorious to possess—and which, if they were broken into pieces, would offer no utility? At the same time, useless arts were also cast out along with these things, since the products of such labors could not be sold. it possessed such little power; so that an exchange of ten minae required a large storehouse in a house, <margin>5</margin> even when a team of oxen brought it. Once this was ratified, many kinds of crimes fell away from Lacedaemon. For who was going to steal, or take bribes, or defraud, or plunder that which was neither possible to hide, nor enviable to possess, but not even <margin>6</margin> profitable to break up? And useless trades were also destined to be driven out with these, <margin>7</margin> as their works had no market. For the iron cargo was not exportable to the other Greeks, nor did it have value, being mocked; so that it was not possible to buy any foreign <margin>8</margin> or petty wares, nor did a cargo of merchants sail in.

5. *Even when a team of oxen brought it—*] <note>original: "Καὶ γευσοῦ ἀγαγόντος"</note> Reiske <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note> corrects this to "And a team of oxen bringing it, which being ratified..." Nothing is more absurd than what is currently read, in which the manuscripts nevertheless agree. Fogerolles and Maussac ridiculously interpreted it as "acting concerning taste." Our author <note>Porphyry</note> should be amended by Plutarch, and he in turn by the former: in Plutarch it is "and a team of oxen bringing it, this having been poured over." Those earlier words are to be restored to Porphyry. Then indeed one must read "which being ratified." Thus, with no letter changed, we have the true hand of the author. But also that last word in Plutarch ought to be restored: where it is published as "poured over." Xenophon, in *The Constitution of the Lacedaemonians* p. 682 D, says this: "for first, as for currency... it would require a large space and a wagon for transport." A little later, "nor enviable to possess" is in Plutarch and Meerman.

6. *Profitable to break up.*] The man from Chaeronea <note>Plutarch</note> adds: "For by quenching the edge of the red-hot iron in vinegar, he took away its use and power for other things, as it became weak and difficult to work." Iron could not receive an inscription or be forged if it were dipped in vinegar while glowing. Hence Lycurgus is said to have given "currency of iron spoiled by fire" in Plutarch Vol. I, p. 354 A. Felicianus translates, *if indeed they had been broken into pieces.* "To strike/cut currency" <note>original: "κόπτειν νόμισμα"</note> is said everywhere, but in this passage it does not mean to mint or engrave, but is mostly used for larger coins where weight gave the value, on which matter see Sperling, *On Uncoined Money*, chapter 28. Those things which follow are expressed by Plutarch in a slightly different way.

7. *As their works had no market.*] Translate: *with the works having no sale*, that is, *the works being unsellable.* Thus D'Orville on Chariton III, 3, who excellently cites the use of this word. Indeed, it is very widely applicable, as many have taught. But we have not assigned this labor to Plutarch.

8. *And petty wares.*] This scholium <note>marginal note</note> was added to the Leipzig Manuscript: "Petty wares: things of no value. For *rhopos* is all kinds of small or light freight, but also a mixture of color. From which also a *rhopopoles* is one who sells these things." You may read similar things in Suidas under the entries *Rhopos* and *Rhopikos*.

# PORPHYRY

no merchant ship reached the ports, and no sophist <note>A professional teacher of rhetoric or philosophy.</note> who sold his words, no wandering diviner, no keeper of harlots, nor any craftsman of gold or copper ornaments set foot in Laconia, since there was no currency there. Thus, being gradually deserted of those who fueled and nourished it, luxury withered away of its own accord. There was no advantage for those who possessed many things, since their abundance of wealth had no path to the public, but remained walled in and idle. For this reason, common and necessary items—couches, chairs, and tables—were crafted by them with the greatest skill. And so luxury, stripped of all its fuels and nourishment, wasted away by itself. There was no greater convenience for those who possessed much, since the abundance of riches had no doorway through which it could break out, but lay entirely buried and idle. Hence, those household goods which are readily available and serve a necessary use, such as dining couches, chairs, and tables, were manufactured by them with excellent workmanship. For the craftsmen, having abandoned useless works, displayed the excellence of their skill in necessary items.

§ 4. When he decided to suppress luxury even further and remove the admiration for wealth, he introduced a third and most beautiful institution: that of the common messes and shared banquets. This was so that people, gathering in a public place, would dine together on common and prescribed portions of meat and food. They were not to recline at home on sumptuously upholstered beds at tables prepared by the hands of designers and cooks, indulging their bellies in the shadows; nor should they gorge themselves like voracious animals, corrupting their very bodies along with their morals through every kind of desire and gluttony.

<column-break/>

the waters being drunk, which were offensive to the sight, were hidden by the color; and as the mud was obstructed and held back by the rims <note>original Greek: "ambōsi"</note>, that which was drunk approached the mouth cleaner. The lawgiver was the cause of these things as well, as Plutarch says. For the craftsmen, being freed from useless things, demonstrated their artistic skill <note>original Greek: "kallitechnian"</note> in the necessary ones.

§ 4. And planning to attack luxury even more, and to take away the zeal for wealth, he introduced the third and finest political institution: the arrangement of common meals <note>original Greek: "syssitiōn"</note>. Thus, they would dine with one another, coming together for common and appointed meats and foods. They were not to live at home, reclining on expensive bedding and tables, provided for by the hands of craftsmen and cooks, as if they were <note>marginal note suggests a correction here from "impoverished" to "being fattened"</note> gluttonous animals in the dark. Such a life destroys the body along with the character, leaving it abandoned to every desire and excess.

---

<margin>
From Plutarch; Valckenier had already corrected it, and the Lipsian and Meerman manuscripts agree. Soon after, he [Plutarch] says "obstructing within and..."
15. **Rims.** <note>original Greek: "Ambōsi"</note> But see Casaubon’s commentary on Athenaeus: Valckenier.
1. **Gluttonous animals.** <note>original Greek: "Adēphaga zōa"</note> Reiske writes it with a double "d". Previously it was incorrectly edited as "gluttony" <note>original Greek: "adēphagia"</note>, which is itself found in some manuscripts of Plutarch. The spelling varies throughout. See Alberti on Hesychius and the learned editors on Moeris the Atticist, page 89. A little before, Plutarch writes "to live, or bedding... in the hands," etc.
2. **Impoverished.** <note>original Greek: "Penomenous"</note> This word will undoubtedly find defenders, for it has means to protect itself. I believe, however, that Plutarch's true word was "being fattened" <note>original Greek: "pianomenous"</note>, which Valckenier had substituted. Shortly before "abandoned" <note>original Greek: "aneimena"</note>, previous editions and the Lipsian manuscript had "being let loose."
</margin>

# PORPHYRY

-> ...requiring long periods of sleep, hot baths, much rest, and a kind of 4 sedentary nursing of the sick. 5 This was indeed a great achievement; but even greater than this was making wealth "unenviable," as 6 Theophrastus says, and "unwealthy" through the communal nature of the dinners and the frugality of the diet. For there was no use for it, nor any enjoyment, 7 nor even any sight or display of all that preparation, since the rich man went to the same dinner as the poor man. Thus, that famous saying was fulfilled: 8 "In Sparta alone is Wealth <note>The god Plutus</note> seen to be blind," lying there like a painting, soulless and motionless. For it was not permitted for those who had already dined at home to go to the communal meals... <-

<column-break/>

...excessive: since satiety requires long sleep, hot baths, much rest, and a sort of medical treatment for the ill. This was a great thing in itself, but far greater was that which, as Theophrastus says, rendered riches both inglorious and impoverished by the community of meals and the parsimony of living. For there was no use for them, nor could anyone enjoy them: indeed, there could be no sight or ostentation of any great apparatus at all, since both the rich and the poor man approached the same table. Thus, that which is common in the proverb was seen: that in Sparta alone is Wealth blind, lying like an inanimate and motionless picture.
