3. *Long periods of sleep ----*] Such are those of whom *Julian* speaks, citing Homer in *The Beard-Hater* <note>original: *Misopogon*</note> p. 342. D.
-> *They prefer warm baths and beds* <-
accepting these instead of what is holy.

4. *Sedentary nursing of the sick.*] *Plutarch* writes *nosēleias* <note>nursing/illness</note>. Many words of this kind are usually pronounced not only with the diphthong *ei*, but also with a simple *iota*, as we saw in Book I, § 14. From that source, however, I confidently restore the reading *kathēmerinēs* <note>daily</note>; I wonder if *Eiusdem deomenōn* <note>of those in need</note> might be better. Our text conveniently refers back to *plēsmonēn* <note>satiety/fullness</note>.

5. *This was indeed a great ----*] The word *Oun* <note>therefore/indeed</note> was omitted in the *Cambridge Edition*, but against the evidence of all others. *Plutarch* continues: "but greater was making wealth invulnerable <note>original: *asylon*</note>, or rather unenviable and unwealthy."

6. *Theophrastus says.*] *Meursius* thought this referred to Theophrastus's books *On Wealth*. Others contend the books *On Lives* are meant. *Fabricius* in *Greek Bibliography III, 9, 17* suggests the books *On Lawgivers*, mentioned by *Diogenes Laertius V, 45.* These matters are so uncertain...

<column-break/>

...that even those illustrious men are inconsistent with themselves. *Menage* in his notes on *Diogenes V, 42* notes that *Meursius* thought the books *On Lives* were referenced; but as *the same author* writes at V, 47, he actually thought it was the book *On Wealth*. *Fabricius* in the place cited on p. 246 says it is from the books *On Lives*, but on p. 251 of the same work, they seemed to be taken from those *On Lawgivers*. Therefore, I determine nothing.

7. *Sight.*] This is correctly found in *Plutarch*. In *Vettori's* edition it was *opsas*, which was propagated into subsequent editions. Soon after, instead of *holēs* <note>whole</note>, *the same author* has *pollēs* <note>much</note>, and *tauto* instead of *to auto* <note>the same</note>.

8. *In Sparta alone ----*] Not only in Sparta is Wealth <note>Plutus</note> described as blind, but he is so described among others as well. See *Spanheim* on *Aristophanes' Plutus, 13.* In Plato, Wealth is numbered among the lesser goods—not the blind Wealth, but the one who sees most acutely, provided he follows Prudence as a guide. *Laws, Book I, p. 773. C.*, a passage excerpted by *Theodoret* in *Discourse on Divine Providence, p. 567.*

## ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK IV

### Qq

...to arrive <note>Continuing from the previous page: "filled at home"</note>: for the others, diligently observing those who did not drink and eat with them, were accustomed to condemn them as if they were incontinent, seeing as they rejected the common fellowship. For this reason, they also called these banquets *Phiditia*: either because they were the cause of mutual friendship and kindness—so that *Phiditia* <note>original: Φιδίτια</note> were named as if they were *Philitia* <note>original: Φιλίτια</note>, with the letter "d" taken for the letter "l," which you might interpret as "amiable gatherings"—or because they accustomed men to utility and parsimony, and thus were called *Phiditia* as if "parsimonious gatherings" <note>original: Φειδίτια, related to the Greek word for thrift</note>. Moreover, they were accustomed to go together in groups of fifteen, or a few more or less. Each person brought every month one modius <term>modius: a Roman dry measure, about 2 gallons or 9 liters; the parallel Greek text specifies a "medimnus," which is significantly larger (about 12 gallons)</term> of meal, eight choes <term>chous: a liquid measure, roughly 3 liters or 3 quarts</term> of wine, five pounds <note>original: *libras*</note> of cheese, five heminae <term>hemina: a unit of volume, roughly half a pint</term> of figs, and in addition to these, a very small amount of money for purchasing relishes <term>opsonia: savory additions to the basic grain diet, like meat or vegetables</term>.

§ 5. Rightly, therefore, the children of those who dined so thinly and temperately also frequented these communal meals, as if they were being led to a school of temperance. There they would hear civic discourses—

<column-break/>

...satiated <note>original: συμπεπληρωμένους</note>, but the rest, diligently watching the man who was not drinking or eating with them, would revile him as one who was lacking self-control and becoming soft toward the common way of life. For this reason they called these *Phiditia*: either as being the causes of friendship and friendliness, taking the "delta" instead of the "lambda," or as things that accustom one to frugality and thrift. They came together in groups of fifteen, and slightly fewer or more than this. Each of the mess-mates brought monthly a medimnus <term>medimnus: a large Greek dry measure, approximately 50 liters</term> of barley-meal, eight choes of wine, five minas <term>mina: a Greek unit of weight, about 430 grams or roughly 1 pound</term> of cheese, five half-minas of figs, and in addition to these, some small amount of coinage for buying relishes.

§ 5. It was reasonable, then, since they dined so simply and temperately, that the children also attended the communal meals, as if being brought to schools of temperance; they would listen to political—

9. **Satiated.**] *Plutarch:* "filled." And soon after: "observing." For "becoming soft," *Meermann* reads "softened things" and "tithia" for "Phiditia." *Plutarch:* "becoming faint." But what follows there, our author did not include in his own work.
10. **Either as Friendship ----**] In *Plutarch* it is: "either as being the causes of friendship and kindness." And he brings forth another reason for the name besides. In *Lipsius*, "of philosophic-kindness" is written incorrectly. Then, for "accustoming" <note>original: συνεθιζόντων</note>, it should be read as "accustomed" <note>original: συνεθίζοντα</note>. The common reading arose because in *Plutarch* "being" <note>original: ὑπαρχόντων</note> preceded it; when our author wrote "being causes" <note>original: ὑπάρχοντα αἴτια</note>, Plutarch’s "accustoming" was nevertheless retained. *The same author then writes "and briefly."*
11. **Of the communal meals.**] The author of these [notes] wrote "of the mess-halls" <note>original: συσσιτίων</note>, where others say "of the mess-mates" <note>original: συσσίτων</note>, and the translator expressed this. Each of the guests therefore contributed these things monthly. And so it is not defined whether these Phiditia were celebrated for only one month, or for every month. Compare: *Meursius, Lacedaemonian Miscellany, Book I, chapter 10.* Soon after, *Reiske* corrected the text to "a small bit of money" by omitting the "and." And so it is in *Plutarch*.

# PORPHYRY

...political [matters], and they looked upon <gloss>1</gloss> liberal education. They were accustomed to both playing and joking without buffoonery, and when they were the subject of jokes, they did not take offense. For this also seemed to be very much a Spartan trait: to endure a joke; but for one who could not bear it, it was permitted to ask for it to stop, and the one joking would cease. Such was the simplicity of the Spartans regarding their diet, even though it was legislated for the common people. For this reason, those who were raised under this form of government are recorded to have been manlier, more temperate, <gloss>2</gloss> and more concerned with what is right than those from other states, <gloss>3</gloss> who were corrupted in both their souls and their bodies. And it is clear that total abstinence is suited to such a government, while gluttony is suited to those that are corrupted. But if we turn to other nations, as many as [possess] good laws and civility...

<column-break/>

...they heard and observed liberal play. They themselves were accustomed both to joke and to speak with wit without scurrilousness, and not to be indignant if they had been touched by some such sharpness of speech. For to tolerate a witty remark said against oneself seemed to be truly Spartan. However, if anyone did not bear it, it was permitted to refuse, and the other would immediately desist from the mockery. And indeed, the thinness of the Spartans' diet, although it had been instituted for the people, was of this kind. Whence also they are recorded by history to have been stronger and more temperate, and more eager for what is right, those who set out from this republic, than those from others, which were corrupted in both mind and body. It is evident that abstinence was peculiar to this state, but luxury of diet to the others. Now truly, if we turn to other nations as well, among whom [there was] justice, gentleness, and piety...

<margin>**1. Liberal education.** <note>original: Παιδείας ἐλευθερίας</note> This same author elsewhere uses "liberal educators." It is well known what "liberal educations" <note>the education befitting a free citizen</note> are. Otherwise, Valentinus' suggestion of "play" <note>original: παιδιᾶς, a common pun or scribal error with παιδείας, "education"</note> is not bad. Soon after, instead of "they were accustomed" <note>original: ἠθίζοντο</note>, Plutarch has "they accustomed," but some manuscripts have "they were accustomed." Then, in the same place, "he had ceased," though other manuscripts prefer "they had been stopped" or "it has ceased." At the word "buffoonery" <term>bomolochia: a Greek term for crude or vulgar jesting; literally "one who waits by the altar" to steal meat</term>, it is noted in the Meermann margin as "the flattery of a jester’s joke." It is said to be derived from "lurking" at the "altars" <note>original: βωμοῖς</note> to take from the sacrifices.</margin>

<margin>**2. And of the right.** <note>original: Καὶ τοῦ ὀρθοῦ</note> I do not know what that [erroneous reading] "of the dung" <note>original: ὄνθου (*onthou*)</note> is meant to mean. Perhaps it should read "of the common" <note>original: κοινοῦ</note>. VALENTINUS. In the Leipzig manuscript it is "filth" <note>original: ὄνθρου</note>. REISKE thinks he meant "of the right" <note>original: ὀρθοῦ</note>. Without doubt Meermann also wanted "right," though he gave "dawn" <note>original: ὄρθρου</note>. This is so true,</margin>

<column-break/>

that, lest that "dung" wound your nostrils any longer, I have ejected the possession of "dung" [from the text], nor would I have done so had not Felicianus also found that [word, "right"] which we have given. In Hesychius, indeed, under "beetle-pastries," it is "to season with dung," from which you might conclude it was a type of condiment. But that, even if you contend the writing there is intact, does not belong here. Soon after, Meermann erroneously has "apple" <note>original: μῆλον</note> instead of "clear" <note>original: δῆλον</note>.

<margin>**3. Corrupted in their souls.** Above, Book III, section 24, from Plutarch: "the faculty of thought and reason has been corrupted." He could also have used the accusative case, for it is usually constructed both ways by the Greeks. Compare the learned gentleman on those words of Saint Paul in 1 Timothy 6:5: "men corrupted in mind." See also Horreus' Observations on Herodotus, chapter 9.</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

-> Qq 2 <-

...the care shown toward the gods was of primary importance, clearly perceiving that it contributes to the safety and benefit of cities that the precept of abstinence should apply, if not to all, then certainly to some: those who, by offering sacrifices and the remaining worship to the gods on behalf of the city, might atone for the sins of the people. For just as in the mysteries the one called the "child from the hearth" <note>original: "puer qui a Vesta dicitur" / "ὁ ἀφ’ ἑστίας παῖς." This refers to a youth chosen by lot to perform specific rituals in the Eleusinian Mysteries to win the gods' favor for the whole community.</note>, by exquisitely performing all things that have been commanded, appeases the divinity on behalf of all those being initiated: so in nations and cities the priests do the same, while they sacrifice for everyone, and through religion and piety implore the divinity to protect the safety of their people. To the priests, therefore, whether you look at the custom of the Greeks or the barbarians, it is commanded that some abstain from all animals, and others entirely from the eating of certain ones.

<column-break/>

...and if the record of piety toward the divine were inscribed, it would be clear that the command of abstinence was ordained for the safety of cities and for their advantage—if not for everyone, then at least for some—and that those sacrificing to the gods and serving them on behalf of the city were appeasing the sins of the many. For just as in the mysteries the so-called "child from the hearth" appeases the divine on behalf of all the initiates by accurately performing the things commanded, so throughout the nations and cities the priests are able to do this by sacrificing on behalf of all, and by drawing the divine to their guardianship through piety. To the priests, then, it has been commanded to abstain from food—to some from all animals, and to others from certain ones—whether...

4. *Inscribed.*] The Leipzig Manuscript <note>Latin: "Lips. Cod."</note> wrongly has "copied." To "turn one's attention toward something" <note>Greek: "ἐπιστρέφεσθαί τινος"</note> is to turn one's care toward something, or to take account of some matter. As Anacreon says in Longinus, Section 31: "I no longer turn my mind to Thracian matters," where see Tollius. The opposite is "not turning toward," concerning which see the illustrious Bast, *Critical Observations*, chapter 23.
</margin>

<margin>
5. *The safety.*] I do not see what great difference there is between "safety" <note>Greek: "τὴν σωτηρίαν"</note> and "the advantage." The word "safety" is usually written in mixed manuscripts in such a way—as it is also written in the Leipzig Porphyry manuscript—as "holiness" <note>Greek: "ὁσια.."</note>. Should we then read "holiness" and "to the sanctity of the city, and to its other benefits"? REISKE. After "cities," both in the earlier editions and in the Leipzig Manuscript, there was the word "being," which was doubtless born from the preceding syllable.

6. *And if on behalf of the city.*] The Leipzig Manuscript reads "those who [sacrifice] on behalf of the city."

"From" <note>Greek: "ἀπὸ"</note> here corresponds to the Latin *a*, when it indicates the care and ministry of some thing, such as "from the feet" <note>a footman</note>, "from letters" <note>a secretary</note>, "from the silver plate" <note>a steward</note>, etc. A little earlier one should read "just as." <meta>This page continues Porphyry's argument from Book IV, where he defends the practice of ritual abstinence. Having established that priests act as mediators who purify themselves to intercede for the state, he now introduces the testimony of Chaeremon the Stoic regarding the ascetic lives of Egyptian priests to prove that such abstinence is a mark of high philosophy, not a burden to society.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

<columns>
...whether you look at **Greek custom** <note>original: "Ἑλληνικὸν ἔθος"</note> or that of the barbarians, you will find things handled differently by different people. The result is that if one were to consider all these various groups as a single body, they would appear to be abstaining from all animals. If, therefore, those who preside over the safety of cities, and those to whom all piety and religion toward the gods has been entrusted, abstain from the flesh of animals, who is so shameless that they would not fear to condemn this kind of abstinence as if it were "useless" to the state?

§ 6. Furthermore, writing about the Egyptian priests, Chaeremon the Stoic—who says they were even regarded as philosophers among the Egyptians—relates that they chose the temples as the place to dwell and practice philosophy. For since they were drawn toward the total desire for the contemplation of the divine...

<column-break/>

...And this is practiced differently among different people: so that if someone considers all those who are everywhere as if they were one, they all seem to abstain from all things. If, therefore, those who preside over the safety of many, and to whom all piety and religion toward the gods is committed, abstain from the eating of animals: who is so impudent that they do not fear to condemn abstinence of this kind as if it were useless to the state?

§ 6. Furthermore, writing about the Egyptian priests, Chaeremon the Stoic—who says they were even considered philosophers among them—relates that they chose the temples for themselves, in which they might spend their lives and practice philosophy. For indeed, since they were drawn toward the universal appetite for the contemplation of the gods...

</columns>

---

<margin>
9. **Greek custom.** <note>original: "Ἑλληνικὸν ἔθος"</note> I would prefer "Greek nation" <note>original: "ἔθνος"</note>. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and celebrated philologist known for his editions of Greek orators.</note>

10. **Presiding over the cities.** <note>original: "Τῶν πόλεων προεστῶτες"</note> This is exactly like those who take care of the sacred rites of others, called **presiders** <note>original: "προϊστάμενοι"</note> in the New Testament and **those standing before** <note>original: "προεστῶτες"</note> among the ancient Christians, and **Presidents** <note>original: "Praesidentes"</note> in the works of **Tertullian**. See **Kortholt** on **Justin Martyr's First Apology, p. 42**. **Felician** <note>An earlier editor/translator</note> seems to have read "of the many" <note>original: "πολλῶν"</note> instead of "of the cities" <note>original: "πόλεων"</note>.

11. **Entrusted with piety.** <note>original: "Τὴν εὐσέβειαν ---- πεπιστευμένοι"</note> A turn of phrase used by others and frequent in our author [Porphyry]. See the note on the **Life of Plotinus, chapter 18**, in **Fabricius’s Greek Library, Book IV, chapter 26**. Who is ignorant of that passage of St. Paul to the **Romans 3:2**, "that they were **entrusted with the oracles of God**," <note>original: "ὅτι ἐπιστεύθησαν τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ"</note> where examples "as numerous as the dust" <note>original: "ὅσα κόνις"</note> have been gathered by interpreters. Parmenion, in the works of **Diodorus Siculus**, is said to be "**entrusted with the king's treasures**." Consult **Wesseling** on **Book XIX, chapter 59**.

1. **The Priests, Chaeremon the Stoic, etc.** You may also read these things in **Jerome, Against Jovinian, Book II, 13**: "Chaeremon the Stoic, a most eloquent man, narrates concerning the life of the ancient Egyptian priests, that having set aside all the business and cares of life, they were always in the temple, and contemplated the natures of things, the causes, and the systems of the stars; they never mingled with women, nor did they ever see relatives or neighbors, not even their own children, etc." But the judgments of the ancients concerning Chaeremon vary considerably. See the end of section 8. The celebrated **Jablonski** <note>Paul Ernst Jablonski (1693–1757), a scholar of Coptic and Egyptian antiquities.</note> gathered from this fragment that Philo the Jew took the things he discussed regarding the **Therapeutae** <note>A Jewish ascetic sect in Egypt</note> from Chaeremon, though he changed certain things and transposed them with skillful artistry. See the Illustrious **La Croze’s Treasury of Letters, Vol I, p. 180**. Regarding the Egyptian priests and the rule of life they followed, read more in **Herodotus, Book II, 37**.

2. **To be supposed... he relates.** The **Leipzig Codex** gives "to have been supposed," which Reiske rightly preferred. Meermann orders the same. Then "he relates" <note>original: "ἐξηγεῖται"</note>, not "to relate" <note>original: "ἐξηγεῖσθαι"</note>, as was previously published; an error which both **Fogerolles** and **Valentin** had already corrected. The manuscripts, however, show no variation here.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the description of the lifestyle of Egyptian priests as recorded by Chaeremon the Stoic, emphasizing their seclusion in temples and their status as "sacred" figures within society.</meta>

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK IV.

...it seemed kindred to their nature to dwell beside the statues of the gods. This made them secure through divine veneration, as everyone honored these philosophers as if they were certain sacred animals. It also brought them peace, because they only had to deal with crowds during public assemblies and festivals; at almost all other times, the temples were not accessible to others. Indeed, it was not permitted for anyone to approach the temples unless they had purified themselves and abstained from many things. This is, as it were, a common law of the temples of Egypt. Having renounced all other trades and human labors, they dedicated their entire lives to the contemplation and inspection of divine matters. From this inspection, they derived honor, protection, and piety; and from...

<column-break/>

...of contemplation <gloss>3</gloss> it was kindred to dwell beside their statues. This provided them with safety arising from divine respect, as everyone honored the philosophers like sacred animals. They were also at peace, since their interaction with others occurred only during public gatherings and festivals. For the rest of the time, the temples were almost inaccessible to others <gloss>4</gloss>; for it was necessary to approach only after having been purified and having abstained from many things, and this is like a common ordinance of the temples in Egypt. Having renounced all other work and human means of profit <gloss>5</gloss>, they devoted their whole life to the contemplation <gloss>6</gloss> and vision of divine things. Through this, they provided for themselves what is honorable, secure, and pious, and through...

<margin>3. **It was kindred.** <note>original: "Συγγενὲς ἦν"</note> That is, "it was appropriate." The scholar Abresch cited a passage from Aeschylus's *Agamemnon*, line 841: "for this is kindred to few men." Regarding what they called *Aphidrumata* <note>Shines or cult images established in a specific place</note>, see Book I, section 35. Soon after, instead of "public assemblies" <note>original: "πανηγύρεις"</note>, the Meerman manuscript reads "for the public assemblies."</margin>

<margin>4. **For it was necessary for those having been purified...** You see that those priests did not even wish to mix with their own countrymen unless they had undergone certain purifications. And so, a little later, he relates that during the time of their purifications, lest they be defiled, they separated themselves from the company of friends and even from priests who were not clean. This custom was very frequent both today and in the past, that others, and especially priests, do not engage in commerce with foreigners, and restrain citizens from meeting and living with outsiders. There is nothing strange in this regarding the Egyptians, who so despised other nations and were accustomed to eat and converse with "those outside" <note>original: "τοῖς θύραθεν," meaning non-priests or foreigners</note> only very rarely. Something of this sort seems almost engraved in human nature itself. Hence, this illustrates what is read in Moses, Genesis 43:32 <note>The biblical passage where Egyptians refuse to eat with Hebrews because it was an "abomination" to them</note>, and it shows that nations before the Law was given already had a custom of certain impurities and, consequently, purifications to resolve them. See Spencer, *On Ritual Laws*, Book III, Dissertation 3. The word *thesmos* <note>meaning a divine law or ordinance</note> is discussed below.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>5. **They devoted their whole life.** You might prefer "gave over" <note>original: "ἐπέδοσαν"</note>, which Abresch rightly favored. Thus: "they gave their lives for the safety of the Greeks," from Diodorus Siculus, Book XI, 11, where Wesseling says more. These compound verbs are often confused. See Book II, 30.</margin>

A learned friend wanted "knowledge" <note>original: "γνώσει"</note>, but I defend the common reading. These words differ just as "to contemplate" and "to behold," or "spectator" and "observer," about which...</margin>

# P O R P H Y R I U S

...of contemplation, and knowledge. Through both of these, they acquired a certain hidden and **ancient-seeming** <note>original: ἀρχαιοπρεπῆ</note> discipline of character. For to be always engaged in divine knowledge and inspiration removes one from all greed, restrains the passions, and awakens the life toward understanding. They practiced simplicity and restraint, self-control and endurance, and in all things justice and freedom from avarice. Their **lack of social interaction** <note>original: τὸ δυσεπίμικτον</note> also rendered them venerable. Indeed, during the actual time of their so-called purifications, they hardly mixed even with their closest kinsmen and fellow tribesmen, nor were they seen by anyone else, except...

<column-break/>

...knowledge through trial: from both they prepared for themselves a certain hidden exercise of character, befitting ancient dignity. For to be always occupied in divine cognition and inspiration excludes one from all greed and insolence, represses the affections, and excites the mind toward intelligence. Likewise, they practiced parsimony, thinness of diet, continence, and tolerance, and justice and equity in all things. They were also rendered venerable by the fact that they mingled very little with others. For in the very time of chastity and purification, they did not even associate with those most closely related to them or their peers; nor were they seen by any other...

***

On which matters *Valckenaer* disputes beautifully in *Animadversions on Ammonius, Book II, ch. 3.*

$^7$. **Ancient-seeming.** <note>original: Ἀρχαιοπρεπῆ</note> This word is also ignored by the most copious treasury of the Greek language <note>The translator refers to the lack of this word in standard dictionaries of the time.</note>. It is also used by *Aeschylus in Prometheus, line 408.*

$^8$. **Divine knowledge and inspiration.** <note>original: Θείᾳ γνώσει καὶ ἐπιπνοίᾳ</note> It seems that "reflection" or "meditation" <note>original: ἐπινοίᾳ</note> might better suit this passage. **REISKE.** These words could very easily be confused, as happened in *Marcus Aurelius's Meditations I, 17* and others. Here I would change nothing. Thus we find "inspiration of the gods" in *Iamblichus, On the Mysteries III, 9*; "divine inspirations" in the same, chapters 6 and 21; and "daemonic inspirations" in chapter 7. Those priests, after certain sacrifices were duly and lawfully performed, were persuaded that they saw the god and received his breath, or that mysteries were revealed to them by him; on which matter see the celebrated *Jablonski, Egyptian Pantheon, Book V, 5, 12.*

$^9$. **Restrains the passions.** <note>original: Καταστέλλει δὲ τὰ πάθη</note> *Represses, settles.* He uses the word well, as it is primarily applied to those who are tumultuous and seditious, whence those who are *settled and modest* are called "katestalmenoi." See

<column-break/>

*Kypke on Luke, Acts of the Apostles XX, 36.* For whom, in *St. Paul’s First Letter to Timothy, ch. II, 9*, "katastole" is correctly defined as *modesty or restraint in clothing, gestures, gait* and other things falling under the senses, where more is said on this meaning. And I understand this in our author a little later through "katastole" (which word the *Meerman Codex* wrongly omits there), not as *thinness of diet*, as *Felicianus* gave it. Thus Pythagoras is said to have adorned himself with "reverence of soul and restraint of body" in *Iamblichus, Life of Pythagoras, ch. II, no. 10*; also regarding character in *Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, Book VI, p. 659*: "unto the ordering of character and restraint."

$^{10}$. **Lack of social interaction.** <note>original: Τὸ δυσεπίμικτον</note> This word also escaped the diligence of the Lexicons. Among others, we have it in *Strabo, Book XI, p. 340*: "Nomads who are difficult to mix with others." The "lack of easy mixing" is mentioned *ibid. p. 346.* I have said more on related words *at Book III, 18.*

$^{11}$. **Nor seen by others.** <note>original: Οὐδὲ ἄλλων τῶν θεωρ.</note> In the *Leipzig Codex* it is "nor seen by others." It seems Porphyry wrote "nor otherwise seeing" or "being seen." That is, they were not seen in any other condition...

### On Abstinence, Book IV.

...were seen, except when the necessary needs of those who were purifying themselves together required it: for they inhabited the inner sanctuaries <note>The "penetralia" or "adyta," the most sacred, restricted parts of a temple</note> which were inaccessible to impure and unpurified men, and were holy for the purpose of sacrificing. For their gait was moderate, and their look was so composed, that...

...except for necessary needs while purifying together, or they were assigned to inner sanctuaries as places of purification for those not yet purified, and holy for sacred rites. # PORPHYRY

...whenever they wished, they would not blink their eyes at all. Laughter was quite rare, and of such a kind that it did not go beyond a cheerful expression. Their hands were always kept tucked inside their clothing. Moreover, there was even a specific mark for each individual which signified their rank and status—for there were several different levels—which each person had been allotted within the temples. They lived on a meager and simple diet. For of wine, some [drank] none at all, while others...

<column-break/>

...whenever they wished, they would not blink their eyes at all: laughter was quite rare, and of such a kind that it did not progress beyond the cheerfulness of the face: their hands were always kept inside their clothing. Moreover, there was even a mark for each which signified the rank and status of each (for there were several), which each had been allotted in the temples. They used a meager and simple diet. For of wine...

---

...you see those two things are also joined. See there the notes of the learned gentleman. The Greeks elsewhere use "eyes" and "face" <note>original: ὄμματα & πρόσωπον</note> with a different sense, as the celebrated D'Orville shows in his notes on Chariton, Books III and V, who was not unmindful of our author.

17. **As when they wished not to blink.** <note>original: Ὡς ὅτε βουληθεῖεν μὴ σκαρδαμύττειν</note> Our colleague Abresch suggested correcting this to: "As when they did *not* wish to blink." To "blink" <note>original: σκαρδαμύττειν</note> means to look intensely throughout and never close the eyelid, as I might say with Heliodorus. Thus Synesius, in his *Praise of Baldness*, says that the "healers of the divine" <term>Therapeutae</term> in Egypt could not even tolerate hair on their eyelids (a word which could be added to Henri Estienne’s collection). Lexicographers and the commentator on Aristophanes' *Knights* explain our word similarly. The details added there regarding the meaning of the word "unblinking" <note>original: ἀσκαρδαμυκτεῖν</note> agree beautifully with our author in his *Life of Pythagoras*, section 10; from this comes "to look with unblinking eyes" <note>original: ἀσκαρδαμυκτὶ βλέπειν</note>, a sign of boldness and strength, which Bentley explains elegantly in his notes on Horace.

18. **Laughter... limited to a smile.** <note>original: Γέλως δὲ ---- μέχρι μειδιάσεως</note> Just as Isocrates forbade "loving reckless laughter," a "smile" <note>original: μειδιᾷν</note> properly refers to gentle laughter. See the celebrated Lennep’s observations on Coluthus. It is therefore well contrasted with "laughing" <note>original: γελᾷν</note>. Aelian says that Anaxagoras was never seen laughing or even smiling. The word for "smiling" <note>original: μειδίασις</note>, which Estienne writes occurs in lexicons without any specific author, is found in Pollux.

19. **Hands within the garment.** <note>original: Ἐντὸς τοῦ σχήματος χεῖρες</note> This too was a sign of modesty and shame. It was no different among the ancient Greeks and Romans. See Casaubon on Diogenes Laertius regarding the Romans, and Seneca in his *Controversies*: *Among our ancestors, those who*

<column-break/>

*were beginning their public careers thought it a sin to extend the arm outside the toga.* I see these points have already been addressed by the learned gentleman in his notes on Valerius Maximus.

20. **There was a symbolic mark... of the rank, etc.** <note>original: Σύμβολόν γε ἦν ---- τῆς τάξεως</note> Regarding the priests of the Egyptians, Diodorus Siculus says: "they go about the cities and the countryside with their own unique signs." These "ranks" <note>original: τάξεις</note> can be compared with the priests of the Hebrews, who were assigned to several "classes" or families, a term used by Saint Luke in his Gospel, chapter 1, verses 8 and 9; the famous Abresch had noted this passage.

21. **A meager and plain diet.** <note>original: Δίαιτα δὲ λιτὴ καὶ ἀφ.</note> These things can also be compared with the institutions of the Jews. See Marsham’s *Chronicus Canon*, Century IX. Instead of "plain" <note>original: ἀφελὴς</note>, the Meermann Manuscript gives "safe" <note>original: ἀσφαλὴς</note>, but not quite correctly.

22. **For of wine, some [drank] none at all...** <note>original: Οἴνου γὰρ οἱ μὲν οὐδ’ ὅλως ---</note> Just as with the Kings (most of whom were chosen from the priests), there was a "fixed measure of wine" according to Diodorus. Wesseling explains this from our author; it was a common practice among all Oriental priests and philosophers to detest wine as if it were brought forth for the destruction of mankind, a belief that flowed to others as well. Read Jablonski’s *Egyptian Pantheon*. Hence, while it was the custom for some Pythagoreans to "use wine," others who were more rigid would "drink no wine at all"; thus two passages of Iamblichus in the *Life of Pythagoras* are well reconciled. Wetstein compares our text with the precept of Saint Paul in 1 Timothy 5:23, and Grotius compares it with the divine law in Leviticus 10:9.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

->R r<-

some [drank] nothing at all, others very little, on account of the damage it might do to the nerves <note>original: "nervorum laesionem"</note> and the filling of the head <note>congestion or "brain fog"</note>, which would be a hindrance to contemplation; also because it would incite the desires of Venus <note>sexual urges</note>. For this reason, they also behaved with great caution regarding other things they consumed: for they never tasted bread during their periods of ritual purification <note>original: "castimoniis"</note>, but when it was not a time of abstinence, they were accustomed to eat it crushed with hyssop; for they said the hyssop blunted the strength of the bread for the most part. Most of them abstained from oil generally, and many always: but if anyone used it occasionally with vegetables, he used very little, only as much as might slightly soften the taste.

§ 7. Furthermore, it was not lawful for them to touch those foods and drinks which were produced outside of Egypt; and thus they kept a great deal of room for luxury excluded.

# P O R P H Y R Y

...place. $^1$ Among those in Egypt itself, they abstained from all fish, and from all quadrupeds $^2$ that were solid-hoofed, or multi-cloven, or without horns; and of birds, they avoided those that were carnivorous. Many of them abstained from all living creatures entirely; and during times of ritual purification <note>original: "hagneiais"</note>, all of them did so, at which time $^3$ they would not even permit an egg. Furthermore, they made a rejection of other things $^4$ that was not free from a certain malicious scrutiny <note>original: "asykophanteton," implying a scrupulous or even slanderous level of pickiness</note>; for example, they rejected $^5$ the females among cattle, and of $^6$ the males, those that were twin-

<column-break/>

Indeed, all those who were in Egypt abstained from fish, and likewise from all quadrupeds which were solid-hoofed, multi-cloven, or not horned; and also from birds which fed upon flesh. Many also abstained from all animals whatsoever, and during times of purification, all of them abstained: for they judged that at those times nothing [living] at all should be eaten by them. Furthermore, there was much observation of other things among them. For they rejected the females of the cattle for food: and the males also, if they were tw- <note>The Latin catchword "ge-" suggests "gemini" (twins).</note>

---

<margin>
Salt was their seasoning <note>original: "opson hales"</note>, which the more refined among them seasoned with hyssop. They received this practice from the *Egyptians*.
1. *Among those in Egypt... they abstained from fish.*] That all Egyptians formerly used fish, as the river supplied a great abundance of them, you may gather from *Diodorus Siculus*, Book I, 43. But later, some abstained from some types, and others from others. "But the priests abstain from all," as *Plutarch* says in *Moralia* vol. II, p. 353 C. Compare also *Julian*: Oration V, p. 176 and *Clement of Alexandria*: Book VII, p. 718 D, who also inquire into the reasons why they had to abstain from them either perpetually or at least during ritual purifications <note>original: "en tais hagneiais"</note>. On this matter, see also the *Learned Man on Horapollo*, Book I, ch. 15. From here, therefore, the practice was derived by the Pythagoreans. See *Athenaeus* VII, 16 and *Plutarch, Symposiac Questions* 8. *Iamblichus* almost seems to disagree in *Life of Pythagoras* n. 98, where he says they "seldom used sea-foods." In that passage, one should either rewrite it with *Kuster* as "with sea-foods," or rather with the learned *Koen on Gregory Pardus regarding Dialects* p. 122 as "used the flesh of sea animals as a side-dish," unless "to use foods" was said in the same way as "to eat of meats" or "to drink of wine" and similar phrases; but *Iamblichus* is not accustomed to use that style. Therefore, the former refers to the more rigid practitioners, or signifies that they did not use every kind of fish, just as the philosopher in our author's *Life of Pythagoras* 45 prescribes "to abstain from almost all sea creatures." In the same way, Pythagoras is said to have "seldom used sea-creatures" by *Diogenes Laertius* VII, 19, who in the same place, section 34, prescribes "not to touch those fish which are sacred." A little before this, *Abresch* corrected "thus" <note>original: "houtos"</note> to "a certain great" <note>original: "polys tis"</note> in the *Leipsic and Meerman Manuscripts*.
</margin>

2. *Those that were solid-hoofed or multi-cloven.*] He says below in section 14 that this was also forbidden to the Hebrews; it is a known law of *Leviticus XI*. Many others have long ago noted those related institutions of both nations, such as *Huet* in *Demonstratio Evangelica* IV, 11, 1. *Spencer* in *On Ritual Laws* I, 5, learnedly discusses the Jews and Egyptians abstaining from certain animals for the sake of religion, but observing different customs and laws in choosing and rejecting them. To see how ancient theologians explain these things, read *Cotelerius on the Epistle of Barnabas*, Vol. I, *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 36.

3. *They would not even permit an egg.*] The Jewish teachers tell similar things about the High Priest. See *Spencer: On Ritual Laws* III, 5.

4. *Not free from malicious scrutiny.*] I wish that "not" <note>original: "ouk"</note> were deleted. VALENTIUS. He calls the pride of the Egyptian priests in the selection of victims and the severity of their religious rites "not without malicious scrutiny" <note>original: "ouk asykophanteton"</note>; this is a quality that can hardly be freed from the mark of intemperance and malice, by which they even rejected those things which no one else would ever have marked as a vice. And they acted as "sycophants" <note>informers or false accusers</note> in religion, even plucking apart and condemning things that were holy and harmless, whether by a certain error of will or judgment—just as slanderers harass the most holy and upright men with frivolous and unworthy accusations. REISKE.

5. *The females among cattle.*] See *on Book II, section 11*.

I understand it to refer to those brute animals that were raised in sacred enclosures, to whom greater honor was certainly shown than to others. They are called such throughout *Plutarch*, Volume II, page 359, and elsewhere.

I once thought it meant "it departed from custom" or "departed from the usual," meaning it deviated from the accustomed mode of nature; but I do not attribute much to this conjecture myself. I would not dare to affirm for certain whether the simple word for "departing" was once used to mean "departing from the usual," but it almost seems so. <term>REISKE.</term> Certainly, these words are "sick" <note>A scholarly way of saying the manuscript text is corrupted</note>. There was one to whom "likeness" was attractive, which I do not approve of because of the preceding word "likeness." What if "should be" is read instead? This is a gentle remedy and supplies the sense which otherwise must be

<column-break/>

supplied by that same word. He says, therefore, that they abstained from all those animals which were similar to "honored" ones, or were, as it were, images of any thing—for instance, of the Gods or of the virtues, of which they were accustomed to be symbols. The word "or" could also be referred to those things which preceded: "similar to those honored in any way," etc. The Lexicons are ignorant of the word for "likeness" used here. *Hesychius* explains "likenesses" as "similarities." The author of the *Book of Wisdom* (13:10) calls the Gods of the Egyptians "likenesses of animals," as it seems. This word is found more often in *Plato*.

10. **Observations.**] He uses this word well, for "observations" <note>original: "paratereseis"</note> are properly scrupulous and attentive sightings, just as "observing" was used above in III, 5 and 10. *Plutarch* (Volume II, page 363) speaks of "making a precise observation." The force of the word was excellently asserted by the most learned *Kypke* in his notes on *Luke's Gospel* 17:20. The second to last syllable was omitted in the *Meermann Manuscript*.

# PORPHYRIUS

The **sealers of calves** <note>original: "μοσχοσφραγιστῶν" (moschospragistōn)</note>, whose duties extend even to the composition of books. They are even more meticulous regarding birds; for instance, they do not eat the **turtle-dove**. For they say that the **hawk** <note>original: "ἱέραξ" (hierax)</note>, having captured this creature on many occasions, lets it go free, granting its life as a reward for their mating. Therefore, lest they should unknowingly happen upon such a bird <note>i.e., one that had mated with a sacred hawk</note>, they have chosen to abstain from the entire species. These are some of the common religious observances, but they differ according to the classes of priests and are specific to each god. However, the **purifications** <note>original: "ἁγνεῖαι" (hagneiai)</note> of them all involved cleansing...

<column-break/>

The **sealers of calves** <note>original: "μοσχοσφραγισταὶ" (moschospragistai)</note>, that is, "calf-men" or "those who mark calves with a seal," are so named: a practice which proceeded even to the writing of books. This they do even more carefully regarding birds. For they believe that the turtle-dove, to cite this as an example, must not be eaten by them. For they say the hawk often, when it has caught that bird, lets it go unharmed, granting safety as a reward for sexual union. Lest, therefore, they should fall upon any such bird from among them, they judged that they must be forbidden from the entire genus. And indeed, there are some common rites.

---

They used sacred objects, for the sealing of which according to a certain ritual priests were employed, whom they thereafter call **sealers of calves**; the knowledge itself is called **the art of sealing calves**. See *Wesseling* on *Diodorus Siculus*: I, 70, and what we said regarding Book II, 55. I would not dare to strike out "proceeding" <note>original: "προάγουσα" (proagousa)</note>. Truly, it refers to the "observation of the art," as in another matter above in III, 25.

13. **"For instance, not to eat the turtle-dove."**] Which for others is among the delicacies of the table, as is clear from *Plautus' Mostellaria* I, 1, 43 and *Athenaeus* IV, 1. We read, however, that the Tartars and other nations abominate their use. The Egyptians, out of a superstitious suspicion of impurity, drove them away from tables and altars, as *Spencer* writes in *Ritual Laws* I, 5, 3. Our author assigns another cause for the matter: lest they should by chance happen upon a turtle-dove released by a hawk (a bird sacred to them), just as their young sometimes escape, as *V. Aldrovandi* explains in *Ornithology* Book XV, 10, p. 245; which I learned from *Slichter's Dissertation on the Turtle-dove*, for that book is not at hand. But Porphyry indicates more closely the reason why the hawk releases the turtle-dove.

14. **"Giving back safety as a reward for mating."**] Those lines of *Flaccus* <note>Horace</note> in *Epode* XVI, 31 come to mind:
> *A wondrous love! It pleases that tigers lie with deer,*
> *And the dove is defiled by the kite.*
"Mating" <note>original: "Μίξις" (mixis)</note>, "to be mixed," and similar terms regarding sexual intercourse

<column-break/>

are quite frequent, and not only regarding a man who has a matter with a woman, as *M. Thomas* thought, but also regarding a woman with a man; even the **most Attic** <note>original: "Ἀττικωτάτοις" (Attikōtatois) - referring to the purest Greek style</note> writers employ that word, as was rightly observed by *Bosius* in response to *Thomas*. However, you will mostly find it in the former way. The Latin *miscere* (to mix) is very well known. The peoples of the East and others speak in the same way, for among most nations, with nature as the guide, the word has taken on that usage. Otherwise, the chastity of turtle-doves is common knowledge; those curious about nature report that they have one mate and do not admit another. See *Bochart: Hieroz:* II, I, 4.

15. **"They avoided."**] <note>original: "Περιΐξαντο" (Periixanto)</note> They shun, they beware of. *D'Orville* clearly brings out the force and power of the word in his notes on *Chariton* I, 13. The *Learned Men* <note>original: "V. D." (Viri Docti)</note> also have much to say for illustrating *Paul's* Second Letter to Timothy II, 16. Presently, the word "but" <note>original: "δὲ" (de)</note> after "classes" is missing in the *Meerman* manuscript.

16. **"They were purified of all things."**] The passage is correct. The meaning is that although religions were diverse according to the diversity of places, nevertheless all priests, wherever they were, when they performed their **purifications** <note>original: "ἁγνείας" (hagneias)</note> or "acts of chastity," then "they were purified" <note>original: "ἐκαθάρευον" (ekathareuon)</note>; what this "being purified" was, he explains a little later. *Reiske* says: "Excellent." *Valckenaer*, with poor judgment, had changed "of all things" <note>original: "πάντων" (pantōn)</note> into "altogether" <note>original: "πάντως" (pantōs)</note>, and had thrust that into the text itself against the consensus of everyone.

17. **"And this time..."**] Namely, of the purifications then when... — for those purifications...

None were the same: others were different according to the class of priests and suited to the individual gods. However, **purifications** and **cleansings** were observed among all. The time for these was when they were about to perform some service in the sacred worship, defined by a number of days—sometimes forty-two, sometimes more, sometimes fewer—yet so that it never fell below the number seven. At that time, they abstained from all living creatures: from all garden herbs and legumes <note>Specifically referring to pulses like beans or lentils, which were often considered "heavy" or "impure" in ancient ritual diets</note>, and primarily from sexual intercourse with a woman; for they avoided the company of males at all other times as well <note>This implies a permanent rule of celibacy regarding same-sex relations for these priests</note>. Three times a day they washed in cold water: when they rose from bed, when they were about to eat lunch, and when they went to bed. If it happened by chance that they were polluted by a discharge in their sleep, immediately

That time was consecrated when they wished to perform the fixed sacred rites. And they preceded those days of fixed rites by undertaking those purifications we mentioned through other days, 42 etc. There is nothing faulty in this passage. "The purifications of all..." etc. is the same as saying "all [were] in their own purifications." And "the time of the purifications was a preceding number of so many days" is the same as "the purifications began before the day of the general sacrifice, by so many days." REISKE. <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and philologist known for his work on Greek texts.</note> Further on, "of two" <note>original: "δυεῖν" (dyein)</note> the Meerman and Cambridge manuscripts had "two" <note>original: "δύο" (dyo)</note>, but the older ones had "two" <note>original: "δυοῖν" (dyoin)</note>. In expressing the dual form, the ancients are not consistent with themselves; for sometimes they write it one way, sometimes the other, and it does not seem that this should be attributed everywhere to the negligence of scribes. See Duker on Thucydides, Book IV, 8, and Wesseling on Diodorus, Selections, page 531.

18. **Never falling below seven.]** From this, therefore, some conclude that the weekly cycle of days among the Hebrews was taken from mathematical discipline and the innermost storehouse of Egyptian antiquity. See Marsham, *Chronicus Canon*, Century IX. <note>John Marsham (1602–1685), an English writer on chronology who suggested Egyptian influence on Hebrew law.</note>

<margin>

What "legumes" <note>original: "Ὄσπρια" (Ospria)</note> were, see Book II, 6. Further on, Valentinius foolishly stuffed "and" before "intercourse." "To associate" <note>original: "ὁμιλεῖν" (homilein)</note> and "association" <note>original: "ὁμιλία" (homilia)</note> are used a hundred times for sexual intimacy. See below, section 18.

But there was also one who read "thrice" there. Compare Wesseling, who was mindful of this passage. Herodotus is more complete there than our author here; the ellipsis is very common.

# PORPHYRY

...they stayed awake for the sake of learning, as they had no concern for acquiring wealth and were set free from that cruel master, luxury. Truly, their tireless labor and constant perseverance bear witness to their character, and their lack of desire demonstrates their self-restraint. They considered it a great impiety to sail away from Egypt, as they were wary of foreign luxuries and customs; for it seemed holy only to those who were forced to travel due to royal duties <note>original: "βασιλικὰς χρείας" (basilikas chreias) – official government business or service to the Pharaoh</note>. They were also deeply concerned with remaining true to their ancestral traditions. If they were caught transgressing these rules even slightly, they were expelled. And indeed...

<column-break/>

...they kept watch with a zeal for literature, as people who had no concern for any income and were free from the slavery of that troublesome mistress, luxury. Tireless and constant labor manifests their endurance, and the absence of all desires manifests the self-restraint of these men. Since they avoided foreign customs and luxury, they judged it a peak of impiety to depart from Egypt. For it seemed permissible only to those who were compelled to handle royal business; yet even these men had such a great concern for their ancestral institutions that if they were caught violating them even in the slightest, they were cast out. And...

---

<margin>Even the wealthiest people neglect this. See Pollux: Book I, section 71.</margin>

8. <note>original: "Πόνος ἀτρυτος" (Ponos atrytos)</note> **Tireless labor.** An elegant epithet. Look into the *Suda* <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, which I see has already been cited by the illustrious Alberti, who provides another passage from Herodotus regarding Hesychius under the letter V.

9. <note>original: "’Απομαρτυρεῖ" (Apomartyrei)</note> **Bears witness.** This means "bears witness sufficiently," as the prefix *apo-* <note>the Greek preposition for "from" or "away"</note> often functions in compound words. See the notes on Book II, section 30.

10. <note>original: "Βασιλικὰς χρείας" (Basilikas chreias)</note> **Royal duties.** The word "duties" is missing in the Leipzig manuscript, which is a mistake. Unless other books read "according to royal marketplaces" or "according to royal commands," as Reiske suggests. "Duty" <note>Greek: "chreia"</note> means business, office, or a task, specifically one where the industry of others is necessarily required. Just as our author does, Josephus attributes "royal duties" to those who manage the king's business in his *Antiquities* (Book 16, 8, 3). Read more in the best commentators on the Acts of the Apostles 6:3.

11. <note>original: "’Απηναγκασμένοις" (Apenangkasmenois)</note> **Being compelled.** This must be explained by a notable Greek custom. You have here not so much a compound word (which you would search for in dictionaries in vain, but which Eunapius also uses in his life of *Maximus*, page 102) as a simple word where the full meaning must be sought from the context. Greek writers often omit certain words for brevity, indicating them via a preposition which, because it cannot stand alone, they prefix to the verb. When you supply the missing parts, the preposition moves back to its proper place. In Porphyry, "being compelled" <note>starting with the prefix apo-</note> is the same as if it read "compelled *to sail from* Egypt," referring to the phrase that came before. This passage can therefore throw light on that difficult verse in the Gospel of Luke 6:35: "lend, hoping for nothing in return," which means "hoping to receive back from the one to whom you lend." The learned Abresch beautifully explained this regarding Matthew 22:5.

12. <note>original: "Λόγος ἐμμεῖναι τοῖς πατρίοις" (Logos emmeinai tois patriois)</note> **A concern to remain in ancestral ways.** The passage seemed corrupt and mutilated. Therefore, Valentin supplied and corrected it to "concerning the remaining." I wish he had not. He thought *logos* here meant "speech" or "word" when it actually means "care" or "concern," as in the phrase "to take account of" or "to care for" used by Lucian in *Hermotimus* 23 and others. Nevertheless, I have restored the word "to remain" <note>Greek: emmeinai</note> to the author from the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts, whereas it was previously published in a different tense. "To remain in ancestral ways" is used elsewhere as "to remain in the law" or "in faith," as noted in Book II, section 25. A rarer usage is found in Euripides' *Medea* 753: "to abide by what I hear from you."

13. **And indeed...** The discussion here concerns the Egyptians...

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

The true method of philosophizing was indeed preserved among the prophets, the sacrificers, and the scribes, as well as the time-keepers. The remaining multitude of priests, temple-wardens, and attendants also live purely and abstinently, though not with such exacting diligence as the former group. These are the things recorded concerning the Egyptians by a man who was a lover of truth and accurate in his study—one who philosophized among the Stoics not in a vain way, but with great solidity.

->§ 9.<-

...the truth was sought by those who philosophized among the prophets <note>original: "προφήταις" (prophētais)</note>, the sacred robe-keepers <note>original: "ἱεροσολισαῖς" (hierostolistais)</note>, and the sacred scribes, as well as the time-keepers. The rest of the multitude of priests, shrine-bearers <note>original: "πασοφόρων" (pasophorōn)</note>, temple wardens <note>original: "νεωκόρων" (neokōrōn)</note>, and assistants to the gods, live in a state of purity likewise, yet certainly not with such a degree of precision and self-restraint. Such are the testimonies concerning the Egyptians by a man who loves truth and is accurate, having philosophized most practically among the Stoics.

->§ 9.<-

---

...and other ministers of the sacred rites. Regarding these, see Causin’s *Observations on Horapollo’s Hieroglyphics*, 37 & 39, and Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book VI, p. 456. **VALENTINI:** Many orders and families of priests there cared for the worship of the Gods and all its rituals. These were the **prophets**. Others occupied themselves with functions of lesser dignity, whom our author mentions immediately after. The celebrated Jablonski explains these most diligently in his *Egyptian Pantheon*, Prolegomena § 38.

14. **Sacred robe-keepers and sacred scribes.**] The former are called *stolistai* <note>original: "σολισαὶ"</note> by Plutarch, Volume II, p. 366. E. Others are also called **sacred scribes**, acting as writers for the sacred rites or for the holier literature expounded in the sacred books. Among their number, Jannes and Jambres <note>Traditional names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note> are included according to Eusebius. See Gale on Iamblichus' *On the Mysteries*, p. 183, and Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus, II, 16.

15. **Time-keepers.**] These are the "hour-watchers" <note>original: "ὡρέσκοποι" (hōreskopoi)</note> mentioned by Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VI, p. 633, who adds that they held a "horologium" <note>An instrument for measuring time, like a sundial or water clock</note> in their hand. Those prelates are mentioned in that passage in a nearly inverted order, but that is because the text describes the order in which they proceeded during ceremonies. He says the first to proceed is the **singer** <note>original: "ᾠδὸς" (ōdos)</note>, whom our author does not mention here, but below in § 9, where he will be discussed.

16. **Shrine-bearers and temple wardens.**] They were called **shrine-bearers** <note>original: "πασοφόροι" (pasophoroi)</note> or "bearers of the sacred objects" because they carried the *pasoi* <note>original: "πασοῖς"</note>—the inner chambers or small shrines of the Gods. On this subject, see Cuper in *Harpocrates*, p. 129. For this name, Causin attempted to foist a new term, *pasophronous*, upon writers, but this was met with

<column-break/>

indignation from the assembly of scholars. See Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus, I, 29. There is more than one opinion among the learned regarding their dignity. Since they carried the **shrines** or small temples on their shoulders, and since our author joins them with the temple-wardens, and since Clement of Alexandria commemorates them in the last place, and finally, since Diodorus indicates they were nearly equal to the Athenian **heralds** <note>original: "κήρυκας" (kērykas)</note>, I hardly doubt they were ministers of a lower rank. I am aware that F. Boerner, in *Egyptian Medical Antiquities* § 40, collects entirely contrary evidence from the passage in Clement, but he fails to persuade me that they were the most eminent in dignity, especially since Clement himself in *The Instructor* III, 2, indicates they were attendants. *Apuleius, in the Metamorphoses Book X, p. 719, says this was the name of a "most holy college," and on p. 776 he indicates it was a "venerable college." But even so, they could be called this by Apuleius primarily because they practiced medicine and took care of the human body, as Clement of Alexandria teaches. Physicians, it seems, belonged to the "clergy," as they call it. Recently, instead of "assistants" <note>original: "ὑπουργῶν" (hypourgōn)</note>, the Leiden and Meerman editions have "sub-assistants" <note>original: "ὑπεπουργῶν"</note>, as do the oldest editions.*

17. **By a man who loves truth...**] This seems otherwise to many, for the judgments of the ancients regarding Chaeremon are quite discordant. See the notes at § 6. Strabo and others certainly report things in a different manner. It is believed that Dionysius of Alexandria was his disciple and succeeded him in the School of Alexandria. See the *Suda* under "Dionysius of Alexandria" and...

# PORPHYRY

§ 9. 1 Starting from this spiritual discipline and their intimacy with the divine, they recognized that the divine did not pass through man alone, nor 2 did the soul dwell upon the earth in man only as its tabernacle; rather, nearly the same soul has passed through all living beings. 3 Therefore, in their representation of the gods, they included every living creature, and 4 in a similar way they mixed together the forms of wild beasts and humans, and again the bodies of birds—

<column-break/>

§ 9. Proceeding, therefore, from this exercise and conjunction with God, they learned that divinity did not pass through man alone, nor did the soul obtain a tabernacle on earth in man alone: but that the same soul, as it were, passes through all animals. Whence also, for the fashioning of the gods, they assumed every animal along with man: in which they mingled the bodies of both cattle and man, and likewise of birds and man. Each—

***

Gale on Iamblichus: *The Mysteries*, p. 303, besides those whom I cited above.

1. **Starting from this—** Eusebius brought this entire passage into the third book of the same work <note>original: "Praeparatio Evangelica"</note>. These are the variations in the reading: the fourth verse from this one is changed by two words: *and in a similar way they mixed wild beasts and humans*, which is pleasing; likewise a little after, *bodies and of humans*. Below, *another the Cynopolite* <note>City of the Dog</note>, not *Lycopolite* <note>City of the Wolf</note>, although a district in that land was also named after the wolf, which Plutarch mentioned in his commentary *On Isis and Osiris*; but in another place later: in the edition of Pamphilus, the words *of God* are equally absent from the printed and written text. However, at the beginning of the following section, where the sense is not yet complete, the letter *η* in the printed version is clearly a mistake, and it ought to be read as the plural genitive *ὧν* <note>of whom/which</note>, as it is written in the author and the Pamphilus manuscript. As for what immediately follows there, *they worship water and fire, the most beautiful of the elements*, it differs in many ways. Regarding the first change of the word, though not the sense, they use *they worship* below for the same reason. The latter variation, which changes the meaning significantly, must be carefully noted. To me, the author's reading is certainly more approved. After this, *more than these they revered those as if upon...* with two variations, both of which I approve. In the part that follows, *all such animals since...* The following is likewise changed in several ways: for *of these is sacrificed* is read there, although the written Pamphilus copy agrees with Porphyry’s reading. And after, *but he, after a little while, might eat his own things, prepared for him as if for a man.*

<column-break/>

VICTORIUS. Up to those words near the end of the paragraph, *and generally according to each*, etc., Eusebius transferred all these into his own work in the place already indicated, p. 93. D.

2. **Soul—dwelled as in a tabernacle.** <note>original: "κατεσκήνωσεν"</note> Beautifully said in John the Evangelist 1:14, *the Word dwelt among us* <note>original: "ἐσκήνωσε"</note>, where the interpreters say much about the style of speaking, but those points do not belong here. Our author speaks according to the custom of the Platonists, by whom the body is frequently called a *tent* <note>original: "σκῆνος"</note> or *tabernacle* <note>original: "σκήνωμα"</note>. Compare Davies on Maximus Tyrius VIII, 3: "the earthly tent" in Plato. See Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies* V, p. 593. D., with which they compare the passage of Paul: 2 Corinthians 5:1; whether rightly, I doubt. Indeed, as our author signifies here, they use the term even regarding beasts. See Fabricius on Longinus, p. 174, to which I refrain from adding more.

3. **In their representation of the gods, they included every living creature.** <note>original: "Εἰς τὴν θεοποιΐαν παρέλαβον π. ζ."</note> We have already touched upon these things in the preceding pages, and we spoke of the reasons why the Egyptians followed living creatures with divine worship. However, Iamblichus, acting as the advocate for the Egyptians, subverts this doctrine, as Gale notes on *The Mysteries* VI, 1. Warburton, in *The Divine Legation of Moses*, Book IV, 4, took it upon himself to refute this opinion of Porphyry, and he also warns that Iamblichus does not depart much from him. No one will wonder that the Indians even today attribute some form of religion to certain animals, if he considers the ancient Indians to have been colonists of the Egyptians, which is the opinion of La Croze, *Christian History of the Indies*, Book VI, p. 426, 355. Pollux condemns the word *theopoïia* <note>original: "θεοποιΐα" - the making or representation of gods</note> in I, 13.

4. **In a similar way they mixed...** Read from Eusebius *in a similar way somewhere* <note>original: "ὁμοίως ποῦ"</note>. VALENTINUS. Perhaps *and towards...*

# On Abstinence, Book IV.
Ss 2
<meta>catchword: Bu-</meta>

For the throats <note>original: "gulae"</note> among their statues of the gods exhibit a human appearance even up to the neck, but they have the face of a bird, or a lion, or some other animal imposed upon it; or conversely, they show the body of another animal placed beneath a human head. From these things, it is clearly signified that, according to the judgment of the gods, these beings have a fellowship <note>original: "societatem"</note> with one another: and that animals, both tame and wild, are kindred to us, not without some divine purpose. Hence also the lion is worshipped as a god: and a certain part of Egypt, which they call a pasture <note>original: "pascuum," translating the Greek "nomos"</note>, is named the Leontopolite <note>City of the Lions</note> after the lion, another after the ox

<column-break/>

...forms and of man; for one might see among them a figure that is human-like as far as the neck, but possessing the face of a bird, or a lion, or some other animal. And again, there is the human head, with the parts of other animals placed sometimes beneath it and sometimes above it. Through these symbols they show that, according to the mind of the gods, these creatures also share in a common society, and that even the wild among the beasts are our companions and tame ones, not without some divine will. Whence also the lion is worshipped as a god, and a certain part of Egypt, which they call a "nome" <note>original: "nomon," a Greek term for an administrative district</note>, is named after the lion as the Leontopolite, and another...

***

<margin>
**They mixed beasts and humans in the likeness of the god.** <note>or "joined together"</note> Or more briefly: **and in the likeness of a god.** They mixed beasts and humans for the *assimilation* (that is, the image) of the deity: that is, they composed the image by which they wished to represent the God from a human image coupled with a bestial one. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note>. I also follow *Eusebius*: **the likeness of the god and humans.** Then he says **and of humans.** The Roman historian *Tacitus* signifies this same thing among others in *Histories, Book 5*: *The Egyptians venerate many animals and composite images.* The early Christian writer *Minucius Felix* in chapter 28 says: *gods mixed from both goat and man, and the faces of lions and dogs dedicated as gods.* The author *Tertullian* well calls this a **biform deity** in his *Apology*, chapter 16. Even today, on the monuments of the Egyptians, the heads of various animals are seen, either alone or placed upon other bodies. See the very learned *Shaw* in his *Geographical Observations on Syria, Egypt, etc., chapter 5, page 112.*
</margin>

5. **Wild among the beasts.** One could also read "and the wild ones," which would fit well with what follows; then "companions" <note>original: "syntropha"</note> should be understood in a broader sense, as if he were speaking of every kind of living creature: *all living things were divided into tame and wild,* as the philosopher *Plato* says in his *Statesman* <note>original: "Politicus," p. 532. D.</note>; but nothing should be changed against the evidence of the manuscripts.

6. **Worshipped as a god and—** There were certain animals that all Egyptians worshipped collectively, and there were also those worshipped separately. Besides our author, the geographer *Strabo* in Book 17 and others teach this. The Egyptians called their divisions "Nomes" <note>original: "Nomous"</note>, according to the major parts of Egypt, as *Proclus* says. See *Wesseling’s* notes on *Diodorus Siculus*, Book I, 73. Only *Lipsius* correctly has *nomon* here, which you see restored. Translators often fall into error by neglecting the distinction between *nómos* (law) and *nomós* (district), a matter discussed by *P. Leopardus* in his *Emendations*, VII, 18.

7. **Leontopolite, another the Ox, another the Lycopolite.** *Jerome* says in *Against Jovinianus*, II. 7: *Almost every city in Egypt venerates beasts and monsters*, whence cities among them are also named from the words for animals: *Leonto* (Lion), *Cyno* (Dog), *Lyco* (Wolf), *Busiris* (Ox-Osiris), *Thmuis*, which is interpreted as *he-goat*. There were therefore many cities of this type which primarily worshipped those animals from which they took their name. # PORPHYRY
### On Abstinence, Book IV
<meta>catchword: dit,</meta>

...the Busirite district, and another the Lycopolite <note>City of the Wolves</note>. 8. For they worshipped the power of God, which extends through all things, by means of the companion animals that each of the gods had assigned. 9. They revered water and fire most of all the elements, as these are the most essential causes of our preservation. They displayed these in their temples and sacred rites, just as even now 11. in the "opening" of the holy Sarapis <note>Serapis, a major Greco-Egyptian deity</note> the service is performed through fire and water, 12. while the hymn-singer pours out the water and the fire.

<column-break/>

...the Busirite, and another is called the Lycopolite after the wolf. For they thus venerated the force and power of God, which is diffused into all things, through the companion animals which each god had exhibited. But especially of all elements they worshipped water and fire, as these were the primary causes of our safety; and they showed them in the temples and sacred rites. Just as even until now, in the opening of the holy Sarapis, the worship is performed through fire and water. For he who sings the hymns also pours out the water drop by drop...

***

<margin>
**the Busirite.**
<note>original: "δὲ Βουσειρίτην"</note>
Added to Leontopolis in *Diodorus Siculus* I, 84. *Eusebius* calls it "Busiriten." It is pronounced both ways, as is common in these variations. Instead of "Lycopolite," the same author uses "Cynopolite" <note>City of the Dogs</note>. It matters little, for there was a Nome <note>an administrative district</note> of each name. But the Lycopolite district should not be confused with the other Lycopolis in the Sebennytic Nome. This one of ours seems to have been the homeland of Plotinus <note>the famous Neoplatonist philosopher</note>. Read *Fabricius* on our author in the *Life of Plotinus* (*Bibliotheca Graeca* IV, 26, p. 92). *Meermann* incorrectly reads "another the Busirite."
</margin>

<margin>
**8. For the [power] over all—]**
<note>original: "Τὴν γὰρ ἐπὶ —"</note>
Perhaps it should read: "For they worshipped the universal power of God (namely, that which reaches through all things) by means of companion animals, and the partial powers (namely, specific divine forces) through those animals which each of the gods exhibited." They venerated the universal power of God, which pertains to all things and remains everywhere, in domestic and tame animals, etc. <term>REISKE</term> <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, a 18th-century German scholar</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
**9. Which each of the gods [provided].**
<note>original: "Ὧν ἕκαστος τ. θ. π."</note>
In *Eusebius* it is "which [singular] each of the gods provided." The learned Vigerus translates the whole sentence thus: *For indeed, they are accustomed to worship the supreme power of God over all things through the living beings naturally joined and connected with Him, which the individual gods declared.* I have rendered it as if "companion animals" <note>original: "sunnomon"</note> signified the animals reared in the individual "Nomes" <note>provinces</note>, each of which presented a certain god. For just as one province provided a lion and another a wolf, etc., so the variety of divine power was represented by the various animals of these prefectures. I believe the words can be best read as: "That power which the individual gods showed, they worshipped under the images of various animals." <term>VALENTIUS</term> <note>Benedictus Valentius, an earlier commentator</note>. The common reading is fine, as rightly noted by *Victorius* and *Vigerus* in their notes on *Eusebius*. Valentius had ineptly corrected the text itself to "each god."
</margin>

<margin>
**10. Water and fire.**
<note>original: "Ὕδωρ καὶ πῦρ."</note>
See *Causin* on Hieroglyphics, Book I, 41. <term>VALENTIUS</term>.
</margin>

<margin>
**11. In the opening—]**
<note>original: "Ἐν τῇ ἀνοίξει —"</note>
This is the same ceremony that they still use in Egypt today, calling it <note>original Arabic: "Wafaa el-Nil" or "the Abundance of the Nile"</note>, when they open the Nile canal that is led through the city of Cairo, after the dam is broken. There is no one who has published an account of their journey to Egypt who does not mention this ceremony. <term>REISKE</term>. See the most accurate *Shaw* (*Geographical Observations on Syria, Egypt, etc.*, chapter 5). Moreover, "Sarapis" is the same as "Serapis," as is well known. Compare *Vives* in his notes on *Augustine's City of God*, XVIII, 5.
</margin>

<margin>
**12. The hymn-singer.**
<note>original: "Τοῦ ὑμνῳδοῦ."</note>
The "hymn-singers" are the same as those elsewhere called "Oidoi" <note>Singers</note>, whose duties are described by *Clement of Alexandria* (*Stromata* VI, p. 663). They were also called "Paianistai" <note>Paean-singers</note>, such as the "Paean-singers of Zeus Helios Sarapis in Rome," found in *Reinesius* (*Inscriptions* II, 68). We know that hymns were very frequent in the sacred rites of the ancients. Consult *Spanheim* on *Callimachus's Hymn to Jove*, 1, and on the types of hymn-singers of other nations, see *Kuhn* on *Pollux*, I, 36.
</margin>

# On Abstinence, Book IV.
-> Ss 3 <-

...and shows the fire, when standing on the threshold he awakens the god in the native language of the Egyptians. <note>original: "Aegyptiorum uoce deum excitat"</note> These things, therefore, they worship above all others, as being those which most participate in the sacred rites. They would not, therefore, a little while later eat those things which are held in the same honor as a human being. Add to this that from their surpassing wisdom, and the intimacy which they have with the gods, by which gods...

...showing the fire, whenever standing <gloss>13</gloss> upon the threshold, in the native language of the Egyptians, he awakens the god. <note>The following section contains critical apparatus and commentary in two columns.</note>

13. **Upon the road.**] In Eusebius: *threshold*. <note>original: "ουδοῦ"</note> Truly much better. See Scaliger on Tibullus: Book I, Elegy 3. Kircher in *The Pamphilian Obelisk*: Interpretation page 491. VALENTINI. Nothing is more true: what had been an error of the workmen in the *First Edition*, was ridiculously transcribed into the following ones as "upon the road." <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ"</note> Meerman: *standing upon the threshold*. Regarding the matter itself, see Cuper in *Harpocration* page 52. Moreover, the phrase "to awaken the god" <note>original: "ἐγείρειν τὸν θεὸν"</note> is a proper expression, and not unknown even to our own sacred rites. Iamblichus: *On the Mysteries* V, 23: *he awakens the gods*. Where see Gale. The Leipzig Manuscript gives "may he awaken."

14. **The participants.**] Perhaps "the providers," <note>original: "τὰ πάροχα"</note> and especially the more... when they worshipped those things, they then worshipped the deities from whom those things had proceeded, and those deities all the more, as they had found those things more numerous and fruitful for life. REISKE. Eusebius: *they worship the participants and especially more of the...* — The sense is clear enough, provided that it is punctuated as has now been done. They worshipped those things which were participants in the divine nature, and since these were many, they especially venerated those which participate most in the divine nature.

15. **They worship a human in Anubis.**] In Eusebius: *Anabis* page 94 and page 117 *Anamis*. VALENTINI. Not otherwise in the *Victorian Edition*, whose wandering typesetter the later editors rashly followed, for which reason I restored *Anabis* instead of *Anubis*. And so it is in the Leipzig and Meerman Manuscripts. Theodore of Gaza <note>original: "Theodor: de Ang."</note> writes that this happens in the village of Anabis. Minucius Felix chapter 29: *The Egyptians certainly choose a human for themselves whom they may worship, him alone they propitiate, him they consult about all things, to him they slay victims*, where see more from Learned Men and on Clement in Cotelerius page 670. The matter was different among the Greeks, by whom "good men" <note>original: "ἄνθρωποι ἀγαθοὶ"</note> were not worshipped unless after they had been translated into "the higher powers." <note>original: "τοὺς κρείττονας"</note> Next, poorly in Eusebius: "of these is sacrificed." The same later more correctly: "is burned up." However, "is burned" <note>original: "κάεται"</note> is also in the Leipzig and Meerman Manuscripts.

16. **Which indeed a little later he might eat...**] Eusebius: *But he might eat a little later those things prepared and set before him as his own, as if for a human.* This reading is to be preferred. The translator renders the passage thus: *But he, a little later, eats only those things which have been prepared and set before him from his private larder, just as for a human.* Those things which Porphyry has in the same place concerning the Hawk and the Beetle are illustrated by Causin in his notes on Horapollo, etc.
