# PORPHYRY
### On Abstinence, Book IV

...they discovered that certain animals are more beloved to some of the gods than humans are: 17 for example, the hawk is sacred to the Sun. They say its entire nature consists of blood and spirit, yet it takes pity on man, and mourns over a human corpse whenever it happens upon one, 18 and it sprinkles earth into the eyes, in which 19 they believe the solar light dwells. And they have observed that it indeed lives for many years; 20 but when it has departed from life, it obtains the power of divination; once it has been freed from the body, 21 it is most rational and a presager of future things. 22 Indeed, they assert that these birds even consecrate the statues of the gods and move the temples.

<column-break/>

...they discovered which animals are more pleasing to the gods than humans: such as the hawk to the Sun; they say its entire nature consists of blood and spirit. It takes pity on man, and mourns over his corpse whenever it happens upon one, and sprinkles earth into the eyes, in which they believe the solar light inhabits. And they have observed that it indeed lives for many years; but when it has departed from life, it obtains the power of divining, and once it has been freed from the body, it is most rational and a presager of future things. For they assert that they even complete the statues of the gods and move the temples.

---

And Kircher in *The Idea of Hieroglyphics*. VALENTIUS suggests: *Perhaps all those things are burned which they themselves do not eat in small portions. The others...* <note>original: "κάεται ὅλα ὅσα μὴ αὐτοὶ μὲν ὀλίγα φάγοιεν. τὰ δ. κ."</note> they burn the victims except for those few small parts which the sacrificers themselves devour; some parts are also set out as prepared for the god Anubis. REISKE corrected the phrase to *which they might eat a little later*; Gale, in his notes on Iamblichus' *On the Mysteries* (p. 278), says that Felicianus corrupted this passage. The reading in Eusebius seems more true, except that I believe the word "through" <note>original: "διὰ"</note> arose from the particle "indeed" <note>original: "δὴ"</note>.

17. **A hawk for the Sun.**] Eusebius reads: *sacred things and*, <note>original: "ἱερὰ καὶ"</note> which ought to be corrected from our author. We have already seen above that the hawk was a bird sacred to the Sun. Our author and others bring forward various reasons for this. See the discussions by the most distinguished Cuper in *Harpocrates* (p. 72).

18. **And heaping up earth.**] Eusebius reads: *heaping up* (in the neuter plural), <note>original: "ἐπαμώμενα"</note> which is incorrect. But see Viger’s notes there. Kuhn, in his notes on Aelian’s *Various History* (X, 4), illustrates from this the once very common custom of throwing a bit of dust upon a dead person, which was a form of burial.

19. **The solar light dwells...**] Aelian, in *On the Nature of Animals* (X, 14), says: *For hawks alone of all birds see easily and without pain while looking directly into the rays of the sun, and are not at all blinking; they fly the highest path, and the divine flame does not hurt them at all.* It is therefore no wonder that the Egyptians consecrated this bird to the Sun, which is why Aelian (VII, 9) mentions the <term>hieroboskoi</term> <note>literally "priests who feed the sacred animals"</note> as Priests of Apollo.

20. **But after life...**] Because it was sacred to Apollo <note>Apollo was frequently identified with the Sun/Helios</note>, the Egyptians attributed a fatidical <note>prophetic</note> power to this bird, which the license of superstition maintained would last even after death. Read Diodorus (I, 87) and the notes there by Wesseling, as well as Gale on Iamblichus’ *Mysteries* (VI, 3).

21. **Released from the body.**] In the same manner of speaking, the phrase "to release the soul from the body" <note>original: "ψυχὴν ἀπολύειν τοῦ σώματος"</note> is used below in sections 10 and 18. Others say "to release from living," "from the bonds of the body," or simply "to release." Many scholars have used this to illustrate the Gospel of Luke (2:29). <note>The "Nunc Dimittis": "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace."</note>

22. **And most prescient.**] Perhaps it should read *most prescient and most suitable for consecrating statues.* It refers to possessing the greatest power for instructing small seals or images (commonly called <term>talisman</term> <note>original Arabic: "طلسمان"</note> or talismans) with <term>telestic</term> <note>the ancient "science" of animating statues or making them ritually active</note> power—that is, a power which, in hidden ways, can ward off certain evils from any person or place, or can forewarn of the future—and "to move temples," that is, those small shrines in which they were displayed.

# On Abstinence, Book IV

An ignorant person, unaware of divine matters, will despise and loathe the **scarab beetle**; but the Egyptians venerate it as a living image of the Sun. For the scarab, being believed to be of the male sex only, emits its seed into the dung, and once it has shaped it into a ball, it rolls it with its hind legs, just as the sun moves the heavens. It follows a cycle of twenty-eight days, which corresponds to the lunar month. In a similar way, they philosophize about the ram, the crocodile, the vulture, and the ibis, and indeed about every single animal; so that from their insight and divine wisdom, they proceeded to the veneration and worship of these animals as well. But the ignorant man does not even notice how those people do not follow the common way of men...

<column-break/>

...and to move the temples. 24 An ignorant person would be revolted by the **scarab beetle**, being unacquainted with divine things. <margin>The hidden statues of the gods are situated there, animated by a prophetic power. <term>REISKE.</term> <note>original Latin: "abscondita sunt sita deorum simulacra animata vi fatidica."</note></margin> But the Egyptians revered it as a living image of the sun. 25 For every scarab is male, and discharging its seed into the mire, and having made it spherical, it rolls it back with its hind feet, just as the sun moves the heaven. It waits for a cycle of twenty-eight days, which is lunar. Thus they also philosophize something about the ram, and something else about the crocodile, and about the vulture, 26 and the ibis, and generally about each of the animals; as if from prudence and excessive divine wisdom they arrived at the worship even of animals. But the ignorant man did not even suspect this very thing, 27 how they do not by the common...

---

23. **And to move the temples.** <note>original Greek: "Καὶ ναοὺς κινεῖν"</note>] One might read "to adorn" <note>original Greek: "κοσμεῖν"</note>. It was the custom for both men and the vestibules of temples to be decorated with the beak of a hawk, a custom mentioned by the celebrated **Wesseling** in his notes on **Diodorus**, Book I, 87. But I attempt no change to the text.

24. **But the ignorant [despises] the scarab.** <note>original Greek: "Κάνθαρον δὲ ἀμαθὴς"</note>] This passage is also cited elsewhere. The first variation is in the first word, where the genitive case "of the scarab" <note>original Greek: "κανθάρου"</note> is read there. However, this is incorrect, for the manuscript of **Eusebius** uses the same case as **Porphyry**. As for the history and this "absurd" Egyptian custom, it was also recorded by **Pliny** in Book 30, chapter 11. He asserts that the explanation given here by Porphyry was actually devised by **Apion** <note>A Greek-Egyptian grammarian and commentator</note> to excuse the rituals of his nation. Pliny himself thinks this arose from the same folly by which many such superstitions flourished in their minds. The mention of "twenty-eight days" is absent in that other version, which suggests it might be a scholarly note <note>original: "scholion"</note>. Likewise, it differs below where it is written "as if from prudence" <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἐκ φρονήσεως"</note>. **VICTORIUS.**

<column-break/>

**The Scarab, etc.** <note>original Greek: "Κάνθαρος &c."</note>] Many authors signify what our author says, including **Plutarch** and others. See **Jablonski’s** *Egyptian Pantheon*, IV, 2, 21. On the word "mire" <note>original Greek: "τέλμα"</note>, see **Suidas** and **Tollius’s** notes on **Longinus**, IX, page 68.

26. **And of the ibis.** <note>original Greek: "Καὶ ἴβεως"</note>] I have restored the spelling to *ibeos*. **VALENTIUS.** Correct. It is so in the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts. Therefore, that silly reading *hybeos* <note>original: "ὕβεως", which can imply "excess" or "insolence"</note> should no longer occupy the text. Many describe this bird as beneficial. See **Wesseling** on **Diodorus**, I, 87. **Plato** writes in the *Phaedrus* (p. 1240 A) that it was dedicated by the Egyptians to the spirit **Thoth**. It was an image of the Moon, as **Plutarch** (Vol. II, p. 381) and **Clement of Alexandria** (*Stromata*, V, p. 567) maintain. Next, I prefer Eusebius’s "as" <note>original Greek: "ὡς"</note>, unless it was "so that" <note>original Greek: "ὥστε"</note>.

27. **How not by the common movement —** <note>original Greek: "Ὅπως οὐ τῇ κοινῇ φορᾷ"</note>] Perhaps it should read "these people" <note>original Latin: "ouito"</note>. Lest he even suspect that these Egyptians, originally carried away by a common impulse of error, had gone astray; but having overcome the foolishness of the common people, they finally began to worship those things which...

# PORPHYRY

->On Abstinence from Animal Food<-

...carried away by a common current that perceives nothing, they clearly wandered into the path of ignorance themselves. However, having surpassed the ignorance of the masses—which is the first thing everyone encounters—they deemed those things worthy of veneration which to the many were of no value.

§ 10. In addition to what has been said, there was another factor that led them toward a belief in this veneration of animals: they understood that the soul of every animal, once released from the body, is rational <note>original: λογικήν (logikēn)</note>, possesses foreknowledge of the future, is capable of delivering oracles <note>original: χρηματιστικήν (chrēmatistikēn)</note>, and is effective in all the same ways as a human soul is when released from the body. Therefore, they rightly honored them and, as far as possible, abstained from them.

<column-break/>

...following a certain flux which perceives nothing, they themselves wandered into the way of folly. But having overcome the ignorance of the common people, into which every person first falls, they judged those things worthy of divine worship which were held in no esteem by most.

§ 10. It is added that, no less than the other things mentioned above, this also induced them to this cult of animals: that they had perceived the soul of every animal, when it had been released from the body, to be both rational and possessing foreknowledge of the future and the power of prophecy, and to be the achiever of all things which even a human being, free from the body, could perform. Whence they deservedly held them in honor, and from the eating of them, as far as was pos— <note>The Latin text cuts off at "fie-", matching the catchword "fie-" from the previous page's metadata.</note>

---

<margin>Which to most people seem worthy of contempt and ridicule. REISKE. On the "common current," see the notes on Book II, 40.</margin>

28. *Ignorance.*] I have restored "ignorance" <note>Greek: ἄγνοιαν</note> in place of "purity" <note>Greek: ἀγνείαν</note>. VALENTIUS. Most truly. The translator, as well as the Leipzig and Meerman Codices, agree; therefore, the lost reading rightly recovers its possession. It seems, however, that "first" <note>πρώτῃ</note> should be read, which I have given, as it does no violence to the Author; previously it was read as "the first" <note>πρώτη</note>, from which you could also read "the first [ignorance] which encounters everyone." Regarding the following phrase "deemed worthy of veneration," *Wetstein* compares Luke in the Gospel, 20:35.

This also has respect to other things in which Egyptian religion was occupied in worship. REISKE. Or "of the animals," as was said a little before, "to come to the veneration even of the animals." Or "into,"

<column-break/>

which was inserted by *Valentius*; because it had immediately preceded, it fell out. A little before, the Translator rightly read "it is added" <note>προσγέγονε instead of προγέγονε</note>.

2. *Of every animal, rational, etc.*] See *Kircher*: Oedipus Aegyptiacus: Hieroglyphics: p. 312. VALENTIUS.

3. *Foreknowledge of the future.*] This passage is perfectly sound, though the *Cambridge Edition* fruitlessly placed a small star <note>a mark of suspected corruption</note> before it. To "chrematize" <note>χρηματίζειν</note> is properly to transact business, especially public business, whence it is attributed to those who give responses to ambassadors; from there it means to declare divinely or to reveal by oracle. It is well <unclear>erg</unclear> <note>likely "ergo" (therefore)</note> transferred to the power of prophesying in this place. Next, the *Meerman* manuscript has "they honored as," omitting the "and."

5. *A human being, released.*] See the notes on § 10.

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK IV.

<margin>6. *When they embalm.*] The Egyptian <term>taricheutai (embalmers)</term> and the preservation of bodies are very well known, even from the Sacred Scriptures. The custom was so frequent that even sacred animals had their own embalmers: hence the "mummies," as they are called, which physicians of our age and the previous one have examined most diligently and explained the method of curing and embalming. See *Wesseling* on *Diodorus Siculus I, 91* and *Herodotus II, 86*.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the translation of the Egyptian funeral prayer recorded by Porphyry. The previous page established the setting: the embalmers remove the internal organs (the "belly") and place them in a chest, addressing the Sun god to declare the deceased’s innocence.</meta>

# PORPHYRY
->P.<-
<meta>catchword: as-</meta>

...receive me, and deliver me to dwell among the eternal gods. For I have continued to worship the gods whom my parents showed me, for as long a time as I held my life in that age <note>original: ἐκείνῳ αἰῶνι (ekeinō aiōni) - likely referring to the deceased's time on earth</note>; and those who generated my body I always honored. Of other men, I neither killed any, nor did I defraud anyone of a deposit <note>A legal term for property entrusted to another’s care</note>, nor did I commit any other incurable evil. If, however, I committed any sin during my life by eating or drinking what was not lawful, I did not sin through myself, but through these things—pointing to the chest in which the belly was kept. And having said these

<column-break/>

things, he would cast the chest into the river. Then the rest of the body, as—

---

*Wesseling: on Herodotus Book I, p. 100.* This speech contains many points concerning the worship of the Gods, the honoring of parents, etc., which seem to regard the Table of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> and the so-called Noahide laws <note>The Seven Laws of Noah, considered universal moral laws in Jewish tradition</note>. Other things are also worthy of note: the immortality of the soul is asserted; the sun is said to receive souls; and mention is made of *that age*, all of which S. Le Moyne illustrates with much light from the antiquities of the Hebrews (*Dissertation on Jeremiah XXIII, 6*), though he is not equally solid everywhere as he is ingenious. The phrase *those who gave life to the [deceased]* is missing from the *Leipzig Manuscript*, and for *receive* the *Meerman Manuscript* has *to receive*, but that scribe frequently confuses the Greek letters *e* and *ai*.

10. *To the eternal Gods.*] Was Herodotus then mistaken, along with many others who report that the Egyptians believed the souls of men migrated into beasts? Shall we say they taught that the soul, having fallen from its seat, passes for a time through humans and animals until it returns to its original place? This is the opinion of the celebrated Iablonski (*Egyptian Pantheon I, 2, 3*). Or was Egyptian theology perhaps not the same throughout the entire kingdom? Did those priests whom Herodotus visited invent the circuit through various bodies, while others believed the minds of the good were immediately admitted into the council of the Gods? This

<column-break/>

view is elaborated by the excellent Mosheim (*on Cudworth's System, Vol I, p. 366*). It is also possible that their theology was changed in this regard by the lapse of time. Finally, a distinction can be made, as with the most ancient philosophers, between the "ethereal mind," which shares in reason, and the "corporeal spirit," or the sensing soul; the former did not migrate into humans and beasts, while the latter did. An eminent man <note>referring to the scholar Mosheim</note> noted at page 1042 that the difficulty could be removed by this observation. I cannot be too laborious here. Furthermore, the *Leipzig Manuscript* does not have the words *the* and *whom*.

11. *In that age.*] I have already advised that these things are illustrated by Hebrew antiquities, which oppose *that age* to *this age*. This is commonly noted by interpreters on *Matthew 12:22, Luke 20:35,* etc. See also Huet (*on Origen’s Matthew, p. 497*). For *that [age]*, the *Leipzig* and *Meerman* manuscripts read *of those [ages]*.

12. *Defrauded of a deposit.*] *To defraud* <note>Greek: ἀποστερεῖν (aposterein)</note> is to cheat or circumvent someone in any way. It is joined here with *to seize* (above in section 3) and the word *to steal*, as in *Gospel of Mark 10:19* and *Xenophon, On the Constitution of the Lacedaemonians, p. 685 B.* "Defrauders and thieves" appears in *Plato’s Republic, p. 583 A.* It is said specifically of those who deny having received a deposit. Plato uses this very phrasing in *Republic IV*.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

...as if it were pure. And so they believed they needed to offer an excuse to the gods for those things which they had eaten or drunk, and for that reason, they judged that the belly should be treated with this manifest indignity <note>original: "uentrem manifesta hac contumelia afficiendum" - referring to the Egyptian practice of removing the intestines during mummification and casting them away as the source of sin</note>.

§ 11. But truly the Jews—before their institutions were first undermined by Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king who attempted to Hellenize Jerusalem</note>, and later nearly destroyed by the Romans, when the temple in Jerusalem was captured and trampled by all those to whom it had been inaccessible, and the city was utterly overturned—they used to abstain from eating many other animals, but especially from the flesh of swine, a practice they observe even to this day. There were considered to be three sects of those who practiced philosophy among them: one of the Pharisees, another of the Sadducees, and a third of the Essenes, which was seen to be the most venerable of all—

<column-break/>

—having spoken [a prayer], he casts it into the river. The rest of the body, as being pure, he embalms. Thus they thought they required a defense before the Divine for what they had eaten and drunk, and because of these things, they committed an indignity <note>against the entrails</note>.

§ 11. # PORPHYRY

...to be, the Essenes. These third ones established such a way of life for their community, as Josephus has recorded in many parts of his treatises. 4 For he mentions them in the second book of the *Jewish History* <note>original: "Iudaicae historiae" or "Ἰουδαϊκῆς ἱστορίας" - this work is more commonly known today as *The Jewish War*</note>, 5 which he completed in seven books; also in the eighteenth book of the *Antiquities*, which he composed in twenty books; and in the second book of his work 6 *Against the Greeks* <note>original: "πρὸς τοὺς Ἕλληνας" - today known as *Against Apion*</note>, which consists of two books. 7 The Essenes are, therefore, Jews by race, but they are "Lovers of one another" <note>original: "Philalleloi"</note> even more than the others. These men turn away from pleasures as if they were a vice, but they consider self-restraint and not succumbing to the passions to be a virtue. They hold marriage in low regard among themselves, but they take in the children of others

<column-break/>

who are still tender and receptive to instruction, and they treat them as their own kin. These third ones conducted their life in this manner, as Josephus testifies in various books. For in the second book of the *Jewish History*, which he finished in seven books, and in the eighteenth book of the *Antiquities* which he followed through in twenty books, and in the second book *Against the Greeks* (and these are the two books), he makes mention of them. The Essenes are therefore Jews by race, who pursue one another with mutual love more than the rest. They avoid pleasures as if they were a fault, but think that self-control and not yielding to the emotions is a virtue. Indeed, they do not admit marriage, but receiving the children of others while they are still young for training, they [consider them] their own relatives.

<margin>
* Essenes. See *Spanheim* on Josephus: *Antiquities* XV, 10, 5. It is no wonder they are greatly praised by our author [Porphyry], for, as Josephus says there: "It is a race that follows a way of life used among the Greeks that was established by Pythagoras." <note>Pythagoras was a Greek philosopher known for asceticism and communal living</note> Just as the Sadducees are usually compared with the Epicureans <note>Philosophers who denied divine providence and sought peace of mind</note>, and the Pharisees approached very closely to the sect of the Stoics <note>Philosophers who emphasized duty and control over emotions</note>, see Josephus's *On His Own Life*, chapter 2. That they had many things in common with the Pythagoreans has been demonstrated by the dedicated work of learned men. However, what *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century scholar</note> thought—that Pythagoras adopted their principles—seems far from the truth, since that sect [the Essenes] only emerged much later; they therefore could receive from him, but he could not receive from them. But others have dealt with this more than enough. See *Fabricius*: *Greek Library* II, 12. 2. and *Brucker*: *History of Philosophy* Vol. II, page 759. Regarding the Essenes, many things which agree with our author are found in *Philo* in the book *That Every Good Man is Free*, and *On the Contemplative Life*, and from him in *Eusebius*: *Preparation for the Gospel* VIII, 379. Philo and Josephus do indeed disagree on some points; truly no one will wonder at that who has weighed those things that were observed regarding Book II, § 26.

->neither humility should appear, nor any excellence of wealth; but from the possessions of each individual mixed together, there should be one single estate for all, just as if they were brothers. For they consider it a beauty to be unwashed, and to always wear white garments. ->neither humility nor any excellence of riches is seen: but from the combined possessions of individuals, a single resource is available to all, just as to brothers. ***

<note>The following section contains scholarly annotations regarding the text above.</note>

...lived among themselves with such charity. Such were the Essenes, Pythagoreans, ancient Christians, and even many today. See *Holstenius* on our author’s *Life of Pythagoras* 20. For "matter" <note>original: πράγματι</note> *Meermann* reads "matter" <note>original: πράγματι</note>—foolishly.

9. **And if he is anointed.**] "Anointed" <note>original: Ἀλειφῇ</note> in *Josephus*: "was anointed" <note>original: ἀλειφθῇ</note> in *Eusebius*: Whichever you choose, I don't care a straw. <note>A Latin idiom meaning "I don't care at all."</note> But *Meermann* wrongly reads "war" <note>original: πούλεμον</note> instead of "the oil" <note>original: τοὔλαιον</note>.

10. **For to be unwashed—**] Since some trace the origin of Christian monks to these Essenes, the Jewish ascetics, it is no wonder that they once attracted such filth, a practice which has not yet fallen into disuse. See *Salmasius* on *Tertullian's On the Mantle*, page 68.

11. **And to wear white.**] There is a dispute regarding the Therapeutae <note>A similar ascetic group in Egypt.</note> as to whether they were Pagans, Jews (which is most likely), or Christians made from Alexandrian Jews. Certainly they led an ascetic life not much different from the Essenes. I will therefore add a passage from *Philo* saying the same thing with the same word: *On the Contemplative Life*, page 695 D: "whenever they come together, they are bright in their white garments."

12. **Administrators of common affairs.**] "The administrators" <note>original: Οἱ ἐπιμελ.</note> in *Eusebius*: This refers to the treasurers, about whom *Philo* speaks in the same way in *Eusebius's Preparation for the Gospel*, page 380 A: "each receiving their wages from such different tasks, they give it to the one elected treasurer."

<column-break/>

"and he, having received it, immediately buys the necessities, and provides abundant food, and the other things which human life requires."

13. **Undistinguished for—**] *Vigerus* explains what these words mean in his notes on *Eusebius*, though I do not think the word "into" <note>original: εἰς</note> should be deleted with him. The word "elected" <note>original: αἱρετοὶ</note> might be tempting, which is in the *Leiden Manuscript of Josephus*, but nothing should be changed against the consensus of so many others. The word "for" <note>original: πρὸς</note> can be construed with "elected." Indeed, he says the treasurers were created by common vote.

14. **But not one—they dwell as sojourners in each.**] Thus our author is correct, and *Eusebius* following him. *Josephus* has "they inhabit" <note>original: κατοικοῦσι</note>, but I would wish it rewritten in his text as well. Those words differ, and "to dwell as a sojourner" <note>original: μετοικεῖν</note> is properly said of inhabitants who do not enjoy the rights of citizenship, and hence it is applied to those who live in some city for a time, later to migrate elsewhere. See *Plato's Laws VIII*, page 919 E. By this observation, I believe the very serious controversy that occupies the Learned can be resolved: how *Josephus* can be brought into harmony with *Philo*, for whom (in the book *Every Good Man is Free*, page 678) the Essenes "dwell in villages, avoiding the cities." For they did not have a fixed domicile in any one city, but preferred to live in the fields; yet even so, when circumstances required, they were accustomed to stay and travel through cities for a time.

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK IV.

many of them live together; for those arriving from elsewhere, provided they are members of the same sect, access is open to all. And those who first see them recognize them just like old friends. Hence, whenever they travel, they are accustomed to bringing nothing with them for expenses. They never change their shoes or clothing unless they are either completely torn or worn out by age. They neither buy nor sell anything; but each person gives what he has to those in need and receives in return what will be useful to him. Indeed, it is permitted to take what is needed from whomever they wish, without any such repayment.

§ 12. Regarding the divinity, they certainly practice piety in a particular way. For before the sun rises, they speak nothing profane, but [offer] certain ancestral prayers—

—many live, and for those coming from elsewhere who are members of the same sect, the homes of others are thrown open, and those seeing them for the first time recognize them as if they were familiars. Therefore, they travel without carrying anything for the sake of expenses. They change neither clothing nor shoes until they are first completely torn or consumed by time. They neither buy nor sell anything, but each person, giving what he has to the one in need, receives in return what is useful from that person; and without this exchange, they are permitted to partake of what they wish from whomever they choose without hindrance.

15. *To those coming who are members of the sect.*] In *Josephus*, "chosen ones" <note>original: αἱρεταῖς</note> is read less correctly; however, our "sect-members" <note>original: αἱρεσιώταις</note> can be approved, as *Viger* notes regarding *Eusebius*. It is now published as "sect-members," and *Victor* already read it this way; but the manuscripts vary considerably. This word is certainly used twice by our author from Josephus in § 13.

16. *They know them as if they were familiars.*] *Eusebius* has "they enter" <note>original: εἰσίασιν</note>, which *Viger* approves if it were changed to "they go out" <note>original: ἐξίασιν</note>. I would change nothing, and I think "they know" <note>original: ἴσασιν</note> was almost certainly there as well. "They enter" is indeed in *Josephus*, but our author [Porphyry] deviates a little from him here, for there it also has "to them" <note>original: αὐτοῖς</note> instead of our author’s "among each other" <note>original: ἀλλήλοισι</note>, for which "among others" <note>original: ἀλλήλοις</note> is better in *Eusebius*: and there are several more things there which are not read here. It seems, therefore, that *Porphyry*, and *Pamphilus* after him, expressed only the general sense. Certainly all the manuscripts agree on the common reading; wherefore I do not know from where *Hudson* drew the note that "they enter" <note>original: εἰσίασιν</note> is read in our author. He says that as soon as they had seen one of their own—

<column-break/>

—they recognized them as familiars <note>original: συνήθεις</note>. These things agree beautifully with what they tell of the fellowship of the "Freemasons" <note>original: Francs Maçons</note>, as they are called. The curious reader will find other things in the institutes of the Essenes which he will think are not foreign to these customs: "they give a small spade to those about to join the sect" <note>original: σκαλίδα διδόασι τοῖς μέλλουσιν αἱρεσιώταις</note> etc. And perhaps more if someone initiated into those sacred rites should stumble upon these. Compare also *Reiske* at the end of § 12. Soon after, *Josephus* has "garments" and "before they were torn," and a little later, instead of "that which is with himself" (which is missing in the Leipzig manuscript), *Eusebius* has "that which is with himself," while *Josephus* has "the things from him."

# PORPHYRY

<column-break/>

...as if entreating [the sun] to rise, they pour forth prayers to it. Once this is done, each man is dismissed by the overseers <gloss>2</gloss> to practice the various crafts he knows. Having worked strenuously until the fifth hour <note>roughly 11:00 AM</note>, they gather again in one place. Girded with linen coverings, they wash their bodies in cold water. After this purification, they enter a private building where no one of a different sect <note>original: "heterodoxōn," meaning those of different beliefs or schools</note> is permitted to enter. Being pure themselves, they proceed into the dining hall <note>original: "coenaculum," often used for a communal dining room or upper chamber</note> as if into some holy sanctuary. When they have sat down in silence, the baker sets out loaves of bread in order, and the cook sets before each person a single vessel containing a single dish.

<column-break/>

...as if entreating it to rise, they pour out [prayers] to it. When this has been done, they are dismissed by the presiding officers to the crafts each knows how to practice. Having worked there strenuously until the fifth hour, they are all gathered together again in one place: in which, girded with linen coverings, they wash their bodies with cold waters. After this purification, they come together in their own dwelling. No one is permitted to enter there who belongs to another sect. They themselves, being pure, go into the dining room as if into some holy temple. In which, when they have all reclined in silence, the baker, observing the order, places bread, and the cook places for each one a single small vessel of one dish.

---

...are called. Just as he most learnedly examines the other customs of the Essenes, so also the celebrated *Brucker* <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), a pioneering historian of philosophy</note> in his *Critical History of Philosophy, Vol. II, p. 768*, interprets this [ritual] very mildly as being "on account of or in" [the sun], so that they recited prayers composed for or because of the sun's rising, so that its light might happily shine upon them. Indeed, this could not be done more absurdly than if a Christian were to compose a song to the sun and praise that most excellent work [of God]. And there are things of this kind in the Sacred Scriptures, as was noticed by *Aldrovandi in his notes on Josephus*. Those men used to wait impatiently for the sun's rising, and therefore they could ask in a solemn formula, like suppliants, for it to put forth its light, just as they withdrew themselves with difficulty after its setting. *Philo*, as quoted in *Eusebius, p. 379: "But before the sun rises, they turn to their accustomed [tasks], and after it sets they barely return."* There is a remarkable passage from *the same author [Philo] in On the Contemplative Life, p. 698, concerning the Therapeutae* <note>An ascetic Jewish sect in Egypt, similar to the Essenes</note>: *"Having stood with their eyes and their whole body toward the dawn, when they see the sun rising, they stretch their hands to heaven and pray for prosperity and truth."* Or perhaps in this way

<column-break/>

they nevertheless seem to have thought more grandly of the sun than was proper. See [the note] at II, 26 and below at 13 regarding "calling it God" <note>original: "ton theon vocare"</note>. Nor is there any reason to wonder, if you consider that many of the Hebrew teachers, along with Pythagoras, believed the celestial spheres to be endowed with soul and intellect; for this reason, some think the Jews were called "heaven-dwellers" <note>original: "caelicolae"</note> by the Roman emperors. See *Spencer in his notes on Origen's Against Celsus, p. 344.* As was just said, the Essenes had many other things in common with him [Pythagoras]. Why? Is it absurd to attribute this to them, when even those who formerly wished to be considered Christians were not free from this stain? On which matter see *Cuper's Harpocrates, p. 112.* Indeed, this seems to have been propagated from Oriental philosophy. *Thomas Hyde*, in his *Religion of the Ancient Persians, chapter 1*, shows that it was not uncommon in the East, neither then nor today, for people to receive the rising sun reverently and with a bowing of the body.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

Before the food is taken—which is chaste and pure—the priest offers a certain prayer, and it is not lawful for anyone to taste the food before this. After the meal, prayers are likewise offered by the same man. For they believe they must honor God both when beginning and when finishing. Afterward, laying aside these garments as if they were sacred, they return again to their labors. Having applied themselves to these until evening, they return and dine in the same manner, with guests also sitting at the table if any happen to have arrived. No shouting or tumult ever defiles the house. Instead, they grant one another the turn to speak or remain silent so modestly that to those on the outside, the silence of those within appears like some wonderful mystery. The cause of this is the constant sobriety of the men, who measure out their food and drink only to the point of sati-

<column-break/>

-faction for each. <note>The text here transitions from Latin to the original Greek source material being discussed.</note> The priest offers a prayer before the food, as it is holy and pure; and it is unlawful for anyone to taste it before the prayer. After they have dined, he prays again. Both at the beginning and at the end, they honor God. Then, laying aside their garments as sacred, they turn again to their works until evening. Returning, they dine <note>original: πίνουσι, literally "they drink," but used here for the evening meal</note> in the same way, with guests sitting with them if they happen to be present. Neither shouting nor noise ever defiles the house, but they yield to one another the turn to speak in an orderly fashion. And to those from the outside, the silence of those within appears as a formidable mystery. 3. *Anyone before the—*] *Josephus* says "someone before," but there also the *Leiden Manuscript* has "before." *Eusebius* also has "someone." </margin>

<column-break/>

that passage of *Cicero: Letters to Friends IX. 24. We have given "neither," following the faith of the Hebrew and the Christian, although I am not unaware that no necessity compels us to reduce these particles to the same form. The *Leipzig* has "not noise," and so it is in the oldest *Editions*. The *Meerman* has "thurybos" <note>a misspelling of 'thorybos' (noise)</note>, by a perpetual confusion of letters.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

-> V v 2 <-

...will support the just, and will show loyalty and obedience to all, but especially to those who rule; for leadership does not fall to men without the will of God. If he himself should rule, he will never use his power insolently: he will not surpass his subjects in clothing or any other more splendid ornament: he will always embrace the truth and prefer it to a lie: he will keep his hands pure from theft, and his soul from unjust gain: neither will he hide anything from his fellow members, nor [reveal] to others anything e-

<column-break/>

1 to fight alongside the just, to offer loyalty to all, but especially to 2 those in power; for without God, the right to rule does not come to any. And if he 3 rules, never to abuse his authority, nor to outshine those subject to him with clothing or any greater decoration. To love the truth always, and 4 to expose those who lie; 5 to keep his hands from theft, and his soul pure from unholy gain. And neither to hide anything from the fellow-initiates, nor...

---

<margin>1. *To fight alongside the just.* <note>original: Συναγωνίζεσθαι τοῖς δικ.</note>] Eusebius: *to be wronged with*. Josephus: *to fight along with*. Learned men use this to illustrate Saint Paul's letter to the Romans 15:30. A little before, those other two authors use the simple verb *to keep* <note>original: φυλάξειν</note> instead of the compound form.</margin>
<margin>2. *To those in power, for not without God—*] Paul to the Romans 13:1: *for there is no authority except from God*, where see the most diligent interpreters. In that place, by "authority" <note>original: ἐξουσίαν</note> (a word our author uses immediately after), the office itself seems to be understood, and thus the form of the empire or Republic, which certainly has God as its author. So "royal authority" etc. is usually said; "all beginnings and authorities" <note>original: πᾶσαι ἀρχαὶ καὶ ἐξουσίαι</note> include all forms of empire, as in Plato’s *Alcibiades* page 450 B. Others thus say "those exercising authority" <note>original: ἐξουσιάζοντες</note> in Luke 22:25 and "authority" or "authorities." "Those in power" <note>original: κρατοῦντες</note> are those who possess the state, as is often seen. See Markland on Euripides' *Suppliants* 18. For "to some" <note>original: τισι</note> Josephus and Eusebius have "to someone" <note>original: τινι</note>. Josephus, a little before, says "always loyal to all."</margin>
<margin>3. *If he rules, never to abuse authority.*] Josephus: *if he rules, never to be insolent.* Eusebius also uses the form *if he rules*, which seems to be the correct reading, though the grammar allows for both, as discussed by Bergler in his notes on Alciphron Book II, Letter 58. It is truer that Eusebius wrote *to be insolent*, for which Valentinus had given *to act insolently*. For so it is in the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts, and the edition by Victorius (for I attribute the spelling there, *ἐξυβρῦσαι*, to a printer’s error, which Fogerolles followed, as he often did). Thus they tolerated legitimate magistrates, but they did not want them to be proud of their dignity or to exalt themselves above others, for they were great haters of the "servile condition." This is what Philo means in Eusebius's *Preparation for the Gospel* page 382 A: *They condemn masters not only as unjust for violating equality, but also as impious for destroying the law of nature, which gave birth to all equally* etc. He soon uses the word "to be subject" <note>original: ὑποτάσσεσθαι</note> well, which is specific to this context. From this, the words of the Divine Man in the Epistle to the Romans 13:1 can be illustrated.</margin>
<margin>4. *To expose those who lie.*] Victorius correctly defends the common reading; Markland gives more examples of this meaning in his notes on Maximus Tyrius 36, 2. Josephus has: *to rebuke and expose*, where the "and" was omitted.</margin>
<margin>5. *Hands from theft and soul—*] He joins "hands and soul," much like James joins "hands and heart" in chapter 4:8, which I wonder if it can be illustrated from here. Certainly, if "men pure of hand" are understood as those who are *not greedy*, Raphel correctly notes that they are specifically called this. The Apostle might seem to touch on three commandments of the Decalogue here: verses 4, 8, and 11. However, I would prefer to interpret it more broadly, for "pure hands" in both languages usually denotes innocence and integrity of life.</margin>

# PORPHYRY

-> [The Essenes] will reveal nothing to others, even if one were to be tortured unto death. In addition to these things, <note>original: ἑτέροις αὐτῶν τι μηνύσειν / nunciaturum</note> he swears to transmit the doctrines to no one in any other manner than he himself received them; to abstain from robbery; and to likewise preserve the books of their sect and the names of the angels. <note>original: τῶν ἀγγέλων ὀνόματα / angelorum nomina</note> Such are their oaths. But those who are caught [in sin] and expelled perish by a miserable fate. For being bound by their oaths and customs, they are not even able to partake of food from others; so, eating grass and having their bodies wasted by hunger, they perish. Wherefore many... <-

<column-break/>

-> ...[the Essenes], moved by mercy, [receive back]... <-

***

6. *To reveal something to others.*] The *Meerman* manuscript <note>A famous 18th-century collection of manuscripts</note> incorrectly reads "to companions" (*hetairois*); these words are often confused, as shortly after "in another way" (*heteros*) is confused for "to companions" (*hetairos*). It was a very common custom among many peoples to take diligent care that the secrets of sacred rites not become known to the uninitiated. <note>original: τοῖς ἀμυήτοις</note> The Essenes held these things in common with the Pythagoreans, and received them from the Egyptians, about whom there is much testimony. This flowed down to the Christians, who did not betray the mysteries of religion to infidels; on which matter see *Milles* on *Cyril of Jerusalem, Preface p. 9.*

7. *He swears — than he himself received.*] *Josephus* writes: "In addition to these things they swear," and the *Meerman* manuscript reads "to transmit to no one." Then *Josephus* uses "partook of" (*metelaben*) instead of "received" (*parelaben*). But our reading is more emphatic. For "to receive" (*paralambanein*) is properly to receive a doctrine handed down by parents or teachers, just as to propagate it is "to hand down" (*paradidonai*). Saint Paul joins both in this way in 1 Corinthians 11:23: "For I received from the Lord that which I also delivered unto you." Our author and others do this a hundred times.

8. *The names of the angels.*] The word "the" is omitted by *Meerman*. *Scaliger* and others use this passage of *Josephus* to suggest that St. Paul in Colossians 2:18 condemns the "worship of angels" among the Essenes.

<column-break/>

On the contrary, many come forward and clear the other Jews of that age of this crime. Whether they are right, I do not inquire. *Origen in John p. 212* certainly seems to signify the opposite. But our author here says nothing about worship, only that they diligently guarded the names, which is not surprising in men devoted to superstition, since various ranks <note>original: τάξεις</note> of angels were believed in. Therefore, nothing should be changed against the will of the manuscripts of *Josephus*, *Porphyry*, and *Eusebius*, despite the Illustrious Man who conjectured the word "vessels" (*angeion*) instead of "angels" (*angelon*) in *Josephus*. <margin>† This word passed from the Jews and Christians to the Platonists, Hierocles, our author, and others. From this it is clear by what right the Learned Man <note>original: V. D. / Vir Doctus</note> noted in *Porphyry's Introduction ch. 3* that whenever that word occurs in our author, it is corrupt and the word "God" should be substituted. On the matter itself, compare *the celebrated Brucker: History of Philosophy Vol. II. p. 769.*</margin>

9. *But those who are caught.*] *Josephus* is more complete: "those caught in noteworthy sins." Our author departs a little from him in what follows.

10. *Eating grass.*] *Josephus* says: "eating grass and his body wasting away with hunger, he perishes." So too our Porphyry, except that "the body" is missing. It is more correctly edited there even now as "eating grass"—

<margin><insert>+ Haverkamp. see Odè on Angels p. 941.</insert></margin>

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK IV.
V v 3

[The Essenes] received those placed in the direst necessities, judging that they had given sufficient penalty for their sins by having been afflicted with calamities even unto death. Moreover, they are accustomed to give a trowel <note>original Latin: *sarculum*; a small tool for digging</note> to those who are to be admitted into the sect for this reason: because otherwise they do not sit down to relieve themselves unless they have dug a trench a foot deep and covered themselves with a cloak, lest by seeking the splendor of light they might inflict some insult upon the gods. <note>The Essenes viewed the sun’s rays as a manifestation of the divine.</note> So great, however, is the thinness and scarcity of their food that on the seventh day—which they have dedicated entirely to hymns to God and to rest—they have no need for the evacuation of excrement. From which exercise they have achieved such great endurance...

<column-break/>

...taking pity on many in their final extremities of need, they took them back, <note>The Greek text here uses *elabon* (took), but scholars suggest it should be *anelabon* (took back/recovered).</note> believing that the torment even unto death was a sufficient punishment for their sins. They give the small hatchet <note>original Greek: *skalida*</note> to those who are about to join the sect. For they do not otherwise sit to relieve themselves <note>original: *thakeuousin*</note> without having dug a pit a foot deep and covering themselves with a garment, so as not to insult the rays of God. So great is the simplicity and scarcity of their diet that on the seventh day they do not require emptying [the bowels], which day they are accustomed to keep for hymns to God and for rest. Those of this discipline have made their endurance so great...

***

<columns>2</columns>

...suggests they were previously "grass-eaters" <note>original: *poēphagountes*</note>. Here too, the later editors foolishly followed a defect of the typesetters that had crept into the First Edition, which gave the word as "grass-eaters."

11. *In necessities they took.*] I retain "necessities" (*anagkais*), but I think "they took back" (*anelabon*) should be attributed to Josephus. REISKE. <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note> And so *Eusebius* writes: Josephus says "they recovered them in their final gasps." 13. *They sit to relieve themselves.*] Well said by *Hesychius*: "They sit for their needs." Many things are noted there by the Learned Man.

14. *To insult the rays of God.*] An Excellent Man <note>Referring to the scholar D'Orville</note> preferred "to such things" instead of "rays" in his notes on *Chariton* IV, 2, not considering that these things are to be restored from *Josephus*. Nor is it different in *Eusebius*: therefore there is no reason why we should

<column-break/>

*change* the word "to insult" <note>original: *enybrizein*</note>, which Valentinus had turned into the subjunctive "they might insult." In *Josephus*, he had found "they would insult" (*hybrizoien*). The *Leipzig Codex* gives "insult the gods" in the plural. Since the other editions and *Felicianus* also recognize this last part, I would not have dared to proscribe it. *Porphyry* spoke in the manner of the Greeks [using the plural 'gods']. However, the construction better allows for "of God" [in the singular]. For it seems to be spoken somewhat at length, whether you translate with *Felicianus*, or as: *lest by the splendor (or through the splendor) they inflict an insult upon the gods*, while they strike their splendor. Regarding the reverence which the Essenes showed to the Sun, it was discussed above.

15. *On the seventh day.*] D'Orville corrects this to "on the Sabbath day," not the "whole week." *Eusebius* has "on the seventh day," which comes to the same thing. Certainly, the Sabbath day, or the seventh, is signified. It is called *hebdomas* by the Greeks, for it only later took on the meaning of a "week" [seven days], on which matter see *Salmasius* in *Plinian Exercises*, page 431.

16. *Those of [this] discipline.*] Rather "from this discipline," as *Eusebius*, the *Leipzig*, and the *Meerman* codices correctly have it. Soon after follows "being bent" <note>original: *lygizomenoi*</note>, a word derived from...

# PORPHYRY
### Book IV

...[endur]ance, so that even when they are twisted on the rack, bent, burned, and passed through every instrument of <margin>17</margin> torture, they will neither blaspheme their lawgiver nor eat any forbidden food. They clearly demonstrated this in the war against the Romans. For they would not stoop to flatter their tormentors, nor did they allow themselves to weep; instead, smiling in their pains and <margin>18</margin> mocking those who applied the tortures with irony, <margin>19</margin> they cheerfully surrendered their souls, as if they were to receive them back again. For this belief is firmly rooted among them: that while bodies are corruptible and their matter is not permanent, souls remain immortal forever; and that <margin>20</margin> they are entwined [with the body], having descended from the thinnest aether, drawn down by a natural force...

<column-break/>

...they have acquired for themselves, so that they would rather endure being tortured, scorched with flames and fire, and finally afflicted with every kind of torment, than either wish to speak ill of their lawgiver or eat anything that is contrary to their custom. This was especially seen in the war against the Romans: when they would neither permit themselves to flatter those who tortured them, nor shed any tears, but smiling in their torments and using irony against those who brought the punishments, they surrendered their souls with alacrity as if they would receive them back. For the settled opinion among them is that, just as bodies are subject to corruption and consist of unstable and decaying matter, so souls are immortal and last forever; and when, wandering from the thinnest aether...

---

<margin>The term for "bending and twisting" passed into the meaning of "torturing." See the notes to Book I, 33 and Kuster’s notes on the *Suda* <note>The *Suda* is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note>. For the word "burned," Josephus writes *kaiomenoi*.</margin>
17. "Instruments of torture" — This is a fuller expression, whereas other authors often omit the noun, as D'Orville <note>Jacques Philippe d'Orville (1696–1751), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> observes in his notes on Chariton, Book IV, 2. Furthermore, Josephus and Eusebius write "so that they might neither blaspheme..." The former [Josephus] writes that they would suffer "neither of the two," but Eusebius agrees with our author, saying "they endured to suffer anything rather than do either." However, he also adds "anything" before "of the forbidden foods." Therefore, "so that" should be inserted before "blaspheme" (for which the Leipzig manuscript incorrectly reads *blasphemoisi*), or it must be supplied mentally. Immediately following in Eusebius is "since they did not flatter," which is corrected to "because."

18. "Mocking with irony." In the Leipzig manuscript, this Scholium <note>An ancient or medieval marginal note.</note> is added: "high-minded, acting a part, but now pretending." None of these is sufficiently apt or clear. —REISKE. <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a German physician and celebrated Hellenist.</note> The same Scholium is added to the Meermann manuscript.

# PORPHYRY

-> Concerning Cyprus and Phoenicia, these are the facts. For at first, no living creature was sacrificed to the gods; nor was there any law concerning this, because it was forbidden by natural law. But they tell a story that at certain times <note>original: "ὑπὸ δέ τινας καιροὺς"</note> they first sacrificed a victim, asking for a soul in exchange for a soul <note>This refers to the concept of "life for life" or substitutionary sacrifice</note>. Then, after this had occurred, they would burn the sacrificed animal whole. Later, while a victim was being burned, a piece of flesh fell to the ground; the priest, picking it up and being burned by it, unintentionally brought his fingers to his mouth to soothe the burn. Having tasted the fat and juices <note>original: "κνίσσης" - the savory aroma or steam of burnt fat</note>, he desired it and did not abstain, but even shared it with his wife. When Pygmalion <note>The legendary King of Cyprus</note> learned of this, he [ordered] both him and his wife to—

<margin>
4. *At certain times.*] Perhaps it should read "by some occasion" and "being asked." Often the word *kairos* <note>time/occasion</note>, like the Latin *tempus*, signifies a calamitous and mournful condition of affairs, as I have explained at length in my notes on Polybius. They were forced to begin by some sinister and unlucky time demanding a soul, by which satisfaction might be made for another soul — REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note>. A little later Meermann's manuscript says: *to burn the sacrifice whole*. Various accounts are handed down regarding the occasion on which mortals first began to use meat. See Castellan, *On the Eating of Flesh*, Book I, chapter 1. This much is certain: in the most ancient times, meat-eating <note>original: "κρεωφαγίαν"</note> was unknown, since victims were only slaughtered in honor of the Gods. Afterward they did indeed begin to use meat, but sparingly at first, and almost never unless it had been sacrificed. Not far from our author are the words of *Athenion*, that some wise man slaughtered a victim and roasted the meat over fires; and since it seemed sweeter than human flesh, they roasted cattle sacrificed to the Gods:
> Since they once had
> some experience of the pleasure, from that beginning
> they increased the art of cookery to the greatest extent.

<margin>How much it defies the meter! But the grammatical logic of the language requires it, because "the feet" <note>original: τοὺς πόδας</note> preceded it. Otherwise, the article "the" <note>original: τοὺς</note> should be omitted there as well. And indeed, the meter allows "the" <note>original: τοὺς</note> no more than "the" <note>original: τὴν</note>. Perhaps the line should be: "swelling in their two feet and their belly due to their lack of control, they took up sackcloth, then sat by the road" <note>original: ἀκρασίαν αὐτῶν τῷ πόδε καὶ τὴν γασέρα οἰδοῦντες, ἔλαβον σάκκον, εἶτ’ εἰς τὴν ὁδὸν ἐκάθισαν αὐτοὶ</note> of their own accord, voluntarily, with no one ordering them. LIPSIUS. "They swell up, then they took up a small sack, then by the road." REISKE. The earlier editions and the Meermann Manuscript gave "the belly" <note>original: τὴν γασέρα</note>. If you remove the article in both places, the meter will hold together beautifully. Instead of "of them" <note>original: αὐτῶν</note>, Menander has "of them" <note>original: αὐτῶν</note>. These matters pertain to the Syrian belief that a crime committed by the throat <note>meaning gluttony or eating forbidden foods</note> is punished by swellings, wasting away, and other diseases. Martial understands those swellings in Book IV, Epigram 43: "I swear to you by the Syrian swellings." See Scaliger on Manilius, page 344.</margin>

11. **Then a small sack** —] "Thereupon" <note>original: Ἔπειτα</note> is published in Menander's text. "They swell up then they took a small sack then by the road." Earlier editions and the Meermann Manuscript gave this reading. Many have explained the custom that in mourning and after serious crimes they would wrap themselves in small sacks or <term>cilicia</term> <note>garments made of coarse haircloth, often goat hair, worn as a sign of penance</term> and defile themselves with dust, or sit in filth or on a dung-hill. Regarding the Phoenicians, who are being discussed here, see Wesseling on Diodorus Book XIX, 106, who did not forget this testimony. Concerning them—

<column-break/>

—the Holy Scriptures also testify. Read Ezekiel 27:30 and Luke’s Gospel 10:13.

12. **They sat.** —] "They were seated" <note>original: Ἐκάθησαν</note> was given by earlier editions and the Meermann Manuscript. "To sit" <note>original: καθῆσθαι</note> or "to seat oneself" <note>original: καθίζειν</note>, which we have here, meant to sit on the ground, which was characteristic of mourners and those dressed in sacks, as Kypke teaches on Luke 1:1 and Alberti on Matthew 4:16. But, what is most relevant here, it was also characteristic of <term>suppliants</term> <note>people making a humble or earnest plea to a god or authority</note>. See those cited by the illustrious Klotz on Tyrtaeus, page 144.

13. **They appeased [for the purpose of]** —] Some take this to mean that they appeased the Syrian Goddess—that is, Venus, who had been changed into a fish <note>referring to the myth of Atargatis</note>—so that she might remove those swellings which she had sent, and that this is the meaning of "to humble" <note>original: ταπεινῶσαι</note> in this place. See Scaliger on Manilius, page 344, and Selden on the *Syrian Gods*, Book II, chapter 3. One should then read "of the humbling" <note>original: τοῦ ταπ.</note>, a reading in which all the manuscripts of Porphyry agree. However, a different sense emerges if you read "by the" <note>original: τῷ</note>, for in that way it refers to the suppliants themselves. And it is published thus in Menander. I would prefer that, both because of the word "humble" and because of the addition of "greatly."

1. **For this signifies** —] Among others, Apuleius says the same in the *Apology*, Book I, page 147: "for if, as I read in most authors, a Magus in the Persian language is what a priest is in ours..."

2. **Darius the son of Hystaspes.** —] Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXIII.

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

...he took care to have it inscribed that he had been a teacher of the magical arts <note>original: "magicorum doctor"</note>. These men were divided into three classes, as stated by Eubulus <note>The OCR reads "Symbolus," but the marginal notes correctly identify this as Eubulus, a writer on the Mithraic mysteries</note>, who composed a history of Mithra in many books. Of these, the first and most learned neither ate nor killed anything with a soul <note>meaning animals</note>, but persevered in that ancient abstinence from living creatures. The second class did eat meat, but they would not kill any of the tame <note>domesticated</note> animals. The third class, however, did not refrain from any, but laid hands on all animals just as other men do.

<column-break/>

3. ...on his monument, among other things, that he had also become a teacher of the magical arts. 4. These were divided into three classes, 5. as Eubulus says, 6. who recorded the history of Mithra in many books. Of these, the first and most eloquent neither eat anything with a soul, nor do they kill, but they abide by the ancient abstinence from animals. The second use them, yet they do not kill any of the tame animals. Nor do the third, in the same manner as others, lay hands on all—

---

<column-break/>

<margin>XXIII. Near the end. *Zoroaster added much knowledge from the secrets of the Chaldeans, and then Hystaspes, a most wise King and father of Darius.* In which it is false that he calls Hystaspes "King": certainly if he means the parent of Xerxes, it is no other Hystaspes. But these matters are not clearly settled, whether that most ancient Magus Hystaspes was the same as the father of Darius or not. Persian writers, as Thomas Hyde has shown, consider him the same as Darius himself, the father of Xerxes. See Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Book I, chapter 14, 2.</margin>

<margin>3. On the monument — that [he was a teacher] of the magical arts —] The Most Distinguished Cuper says in *Observations* III, 30, that other editions have "of the Magi" <note>Greek: μάγων</note>, and he prefers that. To me, it is not clear: all my copies agree on "of the magical arts" <note>Greek: μαγικῶν</note>. Indeed, it is not surprising, since magic was taught among the first royal duties, as Apuleius says in *Apology* I, p. 148. For it was expedient for Kings to claim the guardianship of religion for themselves. "Teacher of the magical arts" here denotes not so much a teacher of magicians as an Arch-magus or sacred pontiff, as Brucker observes in *Critical History of Philosophy*, Vol. I, p. 159. Cuper, in the place cited, as well as Felicianus, takes this as if Darius ordered these things to be inscribed on *his own* monument. However, it seems it should be understood as his father's monument, for he, as was said, had deserved very well of the magical doctrine. Even so, it would better agree with the testimonies of the Persians, as we have seen.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>4. Divided — into three classes.] Just as they were described in three classes, so these and other things are common with the ancient Persians and Indians. Indeed, many Persians formerly settled in this region. It is therefore no wonder that Pausanias calls Isidore and the philosophers "Magi." Read La Croze, *Christian History of the Indies*, Book VI, p. 439.</margin>

<margin>5. As Eubulus says.] Instead of "Symbolus," it should be read as "Eubulus." See Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*. VALENTINUS. Lambecius confirms that "Eubulus" must be read in *Prodromus of Literary History*, p. 277; compare below, p. 253. REISKE. Most true. Thus also Fabricius restored it in *Greek Library* IV, 27, p. 205, and the Learned Gentleman in his notes on Jerome, who expressed our author's meaning in *Against Jovinian* II, 14: *Eubulus also, who explained the history of Mithra in many volumes, relates that among the Persians there are three classes of Magi, the first of whom, being the most learned and eloquent, take nothing more for food except flour and herbs.* Tollius thinks he is the same Eubulus mentioned in the fragments of Longinus, p. 246.</margin>

<margin>6. Who [wrote] the [history] of Mithra —] LIPFIUS: "he concerning." Correct. For it should be read either "he concerning the history of Mithra" or "he concerning the history of Mithra." REISKE. So a little later, "Pallas in the [writings] concerning Mithra," and above II, 56, "concerning the [rites] of Mithra." However, the common reading is defended by Jerome.</margin>

# PORPHYRY

...of all. 7. For it is a doctrine held by all the ancients that there is a transmigration of souls <note>original: "metempsychosis"</note>. This is also what they seem to indicate in the 8. mysteries of Mithra; for hinting at our commonality with the animals, they are accustomed to designate us by the names of animals. Thus, they call the men who participate in these same rites "lions," the women "hyenas," and those who serve "ravens." And regarding the fathers—

<column-break/>

For a decree is held among the first <note>the most ancient authorities</note> concerning the transmigration of souls into different bodies. This they also seem to signify in the mysteries of Mithra. For, to suggest that we share a common nature with the other animals, they have made it a custom to indicate us by the names of other animals; while they call those who are participants in the same sacred rites "lions," the women "lionesses," and the attendants "ravens." And among the fathers in a similar fashion—

---

<margin>
7. *For it is a doctrine of all —*] The phrase "of the first" <note>original: "tōn prōtōn"</note>, if it is correctly recorded, signifies "a doctrine of the first and most ancient teachings." However, I have sometimes suspected that it should read "of those previously mentioned" or "of the Persians." That is, "of all the aforementioned" (namely the Magi) or "of all the Persians." REISKE. If you take it in the former sense, everything is clear. The translator did not follow Porphyry's intent. The error arose from the fact that he had said the third class of Magi laid hands on all things indiscriminately, which might suggest that they did not use the animals indiscriminately in their religious rites. Those who have written on the religion of the Persians explain this doctrine more extensively. That which Porphyry calls "metempsychosis" <note>transmigration of souls</note> is described in various ways by the ancients, regarding which the celebrated Irkov wrote: *On the Palingenesis of the Ancients*, Book I, 1.
</margin>

<margin>
8. *In the mysteries of Mithra.*] There is a difference between "Mithra" and "Mithras"; the latter is the *Sun*, the former *Venus*. They performed their sacred rites in hidden caves, so that, always submerged in the gloomy foulness of darkness, they might not see the grace of the splendid and serene light, as Julius Firmicus says in *On the Error of Profane Religions*, page 414. Some think Isaiah 45:19 refers to these things. But those whom Reinesius praises in *Syntagma of Inscriptions* I, 48, and Mosheim in his notes to Cudworth’s *Intellectual System*, page 328, have examined these matters with such admirable erudition that to attempt anything after them might seem like "a voyage of daring, but not of mind" <note>original: "plous thrasous, all’ ou phrenos"</note>, as the saying goes. Since both here and in *The Cave of the Nymphs* and among other authors, the whole apparatus is described in such a way that these things seem to have pertained solely to physical and astronomical reasoning, not—
</margin>

<column-break/>

—yet has the illustrious man persuaded us that Mithra was a robust man, or a King and Hunter, who freed the province from robbers and beasts, and thus earned these honors. The *Meerman Codex* gives: "which also seems to be revealed."

<margin>
9. *To call them lions.*] —] I have translated this as "lionesses" <note>original: "leaenas"</note> on the authority of Kircher, whom I would wish you to consult, whoever wishes to understand more fully the things that follow concerning the mysteries of the Persians. VALERIUS. "They call the women lionesses." In the *Leipzig Codex* it is "hyenas" <note>original: "hyainas"</note>. REISKE. Nothing is more certain; and thus Felicianus correctly writes. Salmasius writes in his commentary on Lampridius, chapter 9, that certain things were even called *hyainai* because they called the women hyenas, just as they called the men lions; but he seems to have been deceived by a faulty reading of this passage. Certainly, I do not remember reading it in any other author. Note in passing that humans of both sexes undertook those sacred rites, as we know was also practiced among others.
</margin>

<margin>
10. *Ravens. And regarding the fathers —*] Those who were initiated into the rank of "Patricians" were called "Fathers," hence "Fathers of the unconquered Sun God" appears on inscribed stones; this title denoted eminence over the rest of the priests, and it is from this that they are nicknamed "Eagles" and "Hawks." A similar reasoning applies in the "Raven-rites" <note>Coracica</note> and "Lion-rites" <note>Leontica</note>, from which they call them "ravens" and "lions." An inscription in Gruter also joins these: "Leontica, Coracica, and Patrica." Those rites were also called "Hierocoracica" <note>Sacred Raven rites</note> and the ministers were called "hierocoraces" <note>sacred ravens</note>. Read Reinesius, *Syntagma of Inscriptions* I, 48. You see, therefore, by what right the Honorable Man in *Ancient Monuments*, page 236, explains "regarding the fathers"—
</margin>

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK IV.

...manner. For these are called eagles and hawks. And he who assumes the lion-like rites puts upon himself all various forms of animals. Regarding the cause of these things, Pallas, in his treatises on Mithra, says it is the common opinion that these things are to be referred to the nature of the Zodiac circle; but in truth, they signify certain secrets concerning human souls, which they claim are contained within diverse bodies. For even certain Latins <note>The Romans</note> in their own language call people "boars," "scorpions," "bears," and "blackbirds." Moreover—

<column-break/>

...these are addressed as eagles and hawks. And he <gloss>11</gloss> who takes up the lion-like rites <gloss>12</gloss> invests himself in all kinds of animal forms. Giving the reason for these, Pallas, in his works on Mithra, says <gloss>13</gloss> that the common view is to think they refer to the course of the Zodiac circle; but the true and accurate understanding hints at human souls, which they say are encompassed by all kinds of bodies. For indeed, some of the Latins in their own <gloss>14</gloss> dialect call people "boars," "scorpions," "hares," and—

---

...within the memory of our fathers, in more ancient times.

11. **Taking up the lion-like rites.**] See Porphyry, *On the Cave of the Nymphs*. VALENTINIUS: Those who were initiated into the "Leontic" <note>Lion</note> grade were said to "take up the lion-like rites" in the Mithraic ceremonies. Just as one is said to "undertake the Eleusinian mysteries" or similar phrases among the Latins. See Casaubon on Lampridius' *Life of Commodus*, chapter 9.

12. **Invests himself in all kinds—**] Such a person is described in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* Book XI, page 748: *“A precious cloak hung from my shoulders, and from whatever side you looked, I was marked out by animals embroidered in various colors. Here were Indian dragons, there Hyperborean griffins”*—the initiates call this the "Olympic" stole (though Reines preferred the term "Leontic"). Montfaucon and others display an image found excavated at Zurich, Switzerland <note>Tigurum</note>, showing a man girded in such wild beast skins alongside signs indicating Mithra. Indeed, even after the introduction of the Christian religion into Gaul, the custom persisted for a long time that on the Kalends of January <note>New Year's Day</note>, which were formerly sacred to Mithra, men would run about dressed in the skins of beasts; learned men believe this custom flowed from the Mithraic rites. See the great Mosheim, in the place cited, page 331. Just as with other things by which they wished to signify a kinship with animals, I am persuaded that the Persians received this also from the Egyptians. There is a notable passage in Diodorus Siculus, Book I, chapter 62: *“For it is the custom among the rulers of Egypt to place upon their heads the foreparts of lions, bulls, and dragons as signs of their authority.”*

<column-break/>

13. **The common—**] Perhaps it should read: "the common *natural* opinion is that they refer to the course of the sun through the circle of the Zodiac." REISKE. See the notes on Book II, section 40.

14. **In their dialect "boars" and "scorpions"—**] I do not know, to be honest, what the word *lapourous* <note>a corrupted Greek transliteration of a Latin name</note> is meant to be. The French translator rendered it as "lizards" <note>Lacertos</note>; I would have done the same if that name were found among the Romans. VALENTINIUS: The meaning is clear: many Roman names are derived from animals. For certain illustrious Roman families use the name "Aper" (Boar), others "Caprus" (Goat), others "Taurus" (Bull), others "Merula" (Blackbird). But *lapourous* causes trouble; I find no such name in Roman families. It occurs to me to suspect that Porphyry wrote *lakertas* (lizards), and when someone wrote *sauros* or *sauras* above it, a faulty reading was formed, reflecting neither a Greek nor a Roman name, but parts of both. REISKE. Cotelerius thought we should read *scrophous* (sows) and *lapous* (hares), so that—

# PORPHYRY

...to call them *meruli* <note>original: μερούλους; likely referring to blackbirds</note>. And they also addressed these creator gods in this way: **Artemis** <note>the goddess of the hunt</note> as a she-wolf; the **Sun** as a lizard, a lion, a dragon <note>or serpent</note>, and a hawk; **Hecate** <note>goddess of magic and crossroads</note> as a horse, a bull, a lioness, and a dog. Most theologians say the name of **Pherephatta** <note>a title for Persephone/Proserpina</note> <gloss>18</gloss> comes from "feeding the wild dove" <note>Greek: *pherbein ten phattan*</note>. For the wild dove is sacred to her. For this reason, the priestesses of **Maia** dedicate this bird to her. <gloss>19</gloss> And Maia is the same as Persephone, insofar as she is both a midwife and—

<column-break/>

—they even call these creator gods by such names, naming Diana a she-wolf; the Sun a lizard, a lion, a dragon, and a hawk; and Hecate a horse, a bull, a lioness, and a dog. Most theologians interpret the name of Proserpina—that is, *Pherephatta*—as being from "feeding the wild dove" <note>Greek: *apo tou pherbein ten phattan*</note>, because the wild dove is sacred to her. Whence also the priestesses of Maia themselves dedicate it to her. Moreover, that Maia is the same as Proserpina is a matter of doubt to no one: inasmuch as she [is called] *maia* <note>midwife/mother</note>—

***

But first, let the surname be *Schrofa* <note>Sow</note>, and *Laros* be said instead of *Lartes*. But *Thomasf:* preferred the conjecture of *La Croze* (Treasury of Epistles, Vol. I, p. 343), though what that was is not indicated. I suspect **Porphyry** wrote "boars and wild swine" <note>original: ἄπρους καὶ κάπρους</note> (which word could very easily have turned into *skoprous*) ... from which *ourous* was born when the letter sigma fell out; since the scribe did not notice this, he added *la* at the beginning, just as *de-leaenan* was written for *leaenan* <note>lioness</note> just below. *Fel.* also reads "Bears," but instead of *skoprous*, he reads *skorpious* <note>scorpions</note>, though this name is not so frequent. Note in passing that names were given to men from animals, just as we have seen done to the Gods themselves and will be discussed shortly. Conversely, we read of names of men given to animals. See *Cuper*: Ancient Monuments, p. 236 & 293. *Meerm.* wrongly has *melourous* for *meroulous*.

15. **Artemis as a she-wolf.** Just as her brother is "Wolf-like" <note>Apollo Lykeios</note>. See Book III, 17. Thus the name *Lykeia* was given to Diana. *Pausanias* investigates the cause of this in his *Corinthiaca*, p. 144.

16. **Lizard, lion—** Instead of "lizard" <note>sauros</note>, I believe it should read "bull" <note>tauros</note>; for I could prove with many examples, if it were worth the effort, that the Sun was sometimes called that. It is not yet clear to me that he was called a "lizard." **VALENT.** He rightly calls the sun a "lion," since that animal is dedicated to the sun and is its symbol among many nations. See *Cuper*: *Harpocrates*, p. 10. The **serpent** <note>draco</note> is also sacred to him for a specific reason, on which see the same, p. 62. Regarding the hawk, the matter is well known from earlier sections. "Bull," which fits better here than "lizard," also has a relationship to the sun, on which see *Cuper*: Book I, p. 12 and the *Scholiast on Statius* at the end of Book I; however, it relates more to the moon, as will be seen shortly.

17. **And Hecate etc.** I did not wish to change anything relying solely on conjecture. I will now advise what I suspect, however. I think "bull, lioness" should be read, with the particle *de* deleted as idle or rather disturbing the sense. **VICTORIUS.** In the first edition, it is foolishly read as *deleaenan*, which is nonetheless also in the Leipzig and Meermann Manuscripts. He speaks of Hecate in the same way in Book III, § 17; see there.

18. **From feeding the wild dove.** See *Voss*: *On Idolatry*, Book II, 54, who would prefer "to carry" <note>pherein</note> instead of "to feed" <note>pherbein</note>, which is not strictly necessary. From this is named the *Pherephattion*, a temple of Proserpina at Athens, concerning which see *Meursius*: *Attic Miscellany*, Book II, 16. More on this name shortly.

19. **Maia is the same as Persephone.** Proserpina was also called Maia. See *Cuper*: *Observations* III, 10. I am surprised that he interprets *phattan* as a turtledove. If turtledoves were offered in the worship of the Gods—which we know was frequent among the Hebrews—it must have happened very rarely [here]. Certainly, in this passage, it is not said; turtledoves and wild doves are entirely—
