# ON ABSTINENCE, Book IV.
->Y y<-
<meta>catchword: thne-</meta>

...that is, she is the nourisher of all. Indeed, she is a goddess of the earth, who is also **Ceres** <note>the Roman name for Demeter, goddess of agriculture</note>. To her they also consecrated the rooster. From this it follows that her priestesses abstain entirely from domestic birds. For it is also commanded in the **Eleusinian Mysteries** <note>the most famous of the secret religious rites of ancient Greece</note> that they abstain from domestic birds, fish, beans, apples, and pomegranates. By touching the stems of these, they are defiled just as if they had touched a dead body.

<column-break/>

...and being a nourisher. <gloss>20</gloss> For she is the goddess of the earth and the same as **Demeter**. And they dedicated the rooster to her. For this reason, those initiated into her mysteries <gloss>21</gloss> abstain from domestic birds. For it is commanded even at **Eleusis** to abstain from domestic birds, <gloss>22</gloss> fish, and beans, <gloss>23</gloss> as well as pomegranates and apples; and they are equally defiled <gloss>24</gloss> by touching the stem as by [touching] a dead— <note>original: θνη- (thne-), likely part of thnesidion, "a dead thing"</note>

***

...they differ entirely, as is clear from those who have written about animals. For **Pherephatta** <note>Persephone</note>, *Meermann* reads *Persephone*, as it is rendered above in Book I, 25. *Moeris the Atticist* (p. 396) says: *Pherephatta* is the Attic form; *Persephone* is used by the Greeks. Sometimes it is also called *Phersphatta* and *Persephatta*. See *Pierson* there.

20. **For she is the goddess of the earth—**] In ancient monuments, the names of **Ceres** and her daughter **Proserpina** <note>Persephone</note> are often used interchangeably. See *Spanheim* on Callimachus' *Hymn to Ceres*, 133. It is singular that he says the rooster was consecrated to this goddess, as we know the ancients primarily sacrificed it to **Mars** <note>god of war</note> and **Aesculapius** <note>god of medicine</note>. However, *Ovid* in *Fasti* I, 455 says:
> At night, the crested bird is slain for the Goddess of Night.

21. **Domestic birds.**] He uses the term "indoor birds" <note>original: enoikidion</note> exactly as *Pollux* does in Book X, 156; shortly after he calls them "household birds" <note>original: katoikidious</note>, as others often do. See *Jungermann* on Pollux, who teaches that these are chickens, which are also simply called "birds." See *Casaubon* on Athenaeus I, 15. The Latins call them *aves* <note>birds</note>, as seen in writers on rural affairs like *Columella* (VIII, 5) and others.

22. **Fish and beans.**] Who has not commented on "abstaining from beans" and "not tasting fish," which were among the symbols of **Pythagoras**? No one will be surprised that these Eleusinian decrees are related to the teachings of Pythagoras, if they remember they were derived from the same source. For "at Eleusis," *Lipsius* mistakenly gives "Eleusin."

23. **Pomegranates and apples.**] See *Julian's* Oration 5 for the Mother of the Gods. *Valentin* notes: Grammarians distinguish between the pomegranate tree <note>rhoia</note> and its fruit <note>rhoa</note>, though this distinction is not 

<column-break/>

constant. See *Ammonius* and the notes by *Valckenar* and *Oudendorp* on *Thomas Magister*. They are also joined by the Comic poet in *The Wasps* (line 1259): "instead of an apple and a pomegranate," which ancient critics explain as "abundant delicacies." *Spanheim* (in *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, Dissertation VI) shows that this fruit was held as a mystical object among the ancients, and they abstained from it in the **Thesmophoria** <note>a festival held in honor of Demeter and Persephone</note> and other sacred rites. There were also pomegranates in the chests that women carried in the Eleusinian rites. Read *Meursius* on Eleusis, chapter 25.

24. **Touching the stem—**] For "not" <note>original: ou</note>, we should read "the" <note>original: to</note>. *Valentin.* Perhaps it should read "and the touch of a woman in childbirth defiles equally as that of a corpse." *Reiske.* Similarly, *Gale* on Iamblichus' *Mysteries* (Section IV, 11) notes that Pythagoras, according to *Diogenes Laertius*, kept himself pure "from mourning and from eating dead things" <note>original: thnesidion</note>, where you see those two things joined. The illustrious *Abresch* comes even closer to the common text, reading "and that of a woman in childbirth." Indeed, a *lecho* is a woman who has recently given birth, as *Hesychius* says; I do not know why *Spanheim* (on Callimachus' *Hymn to Jove*, 14) wants this word changed. It is well established that women in childbirth were once considered impure. See *Casaubon* on Theophrastus' *Characters*, p. 290. The **Mosaic Law** <note>the laws of Moses in the Bible</note> is the most well-known example. *Spencer* (on *Ritual Laws*, I, 8) thinks this opinion originated with the Egyptians or the children of Noah. It is therefore no wonder that these ideas were approved by Pythagoras and his followers. There is a similar logic regarding menstruation, mentioned above in Book II, 5. If one wishes to defend the common reading, nothing is easier than changing "not" <note>ou</note> to "of the" <note>tou</note>.

### PORPHYRY

...dead things. <note>original: θνησιδίων (thnesidiôn), referring to animal carcasses</note> Whoever has investigated the nature of those apparitions <note>original: φασμάτων (phasmatôn), or spirits that can be seen</note> knows the reasoning why one must abstain from all birds—especially when one strives to be released from earthly things and to be established among the heavenly gods. But wickedness—as we often say—is quite capable of advocating for its own cause, especially when it addresses its arguments to those who are ignorant. For this reason, those who are only moderately wicked consider such a prohibition to be "vain babbling" and, as the proverb goes, "old wives' tales." Others consider it a form of superstition. But those who have progressed further in their own depravity are ready not only to speak blasphemy against those who advise and point out these things, but even to slander the pure man as a charlatan...

...had touched dead animals. Whoever has a clear understanding of the nature of those visions which are called **Apparitions** <note>original: Φάσματα (Phasmata)</note>, knows the reason why all birds must be avoided: particularly when one desires to be freed from earthly bonds and to be moved toward the celestial gods. But wickedness—something we have already said many times—is marvelously suited to defending itself, especially when it speaks among those who are unacquainted with the facts. For this reason, it happens that those who are only moderately wicked think such warnings are a form of vanity—or, as the proverb says, "old wives' tales"—while others think it is superstition. However, those who have progressed further in their own depravity are not only prompt and ready to attack with insults those who give this advice and instruction, but they even go so far as to slander the chaste and abstinent man as an arrogant charlatan...

<margin>25. **Dead things.**] He calls them *thneseidia* above in Book III, chapter 8; see that passage. While our author says that all corpses cause pollution, others restrict this rule only to the human body; on this matter, see the notes of *Thomas Gale* on *Iamblichus: On the Mysteries: Section VI, chapter 1.*</margin>
<margin>26. **Such a prohibition.**] This term is well-suited here, meaning a "discouragement," "forbidding," or "pleading against," as when we wish not to dare or use something. **Reiske** <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar</note> had corrected this to *parainesin* [advice/exhortation], which **Felicianus** also seems to have read. The famous **Wetstein** compares our author’s "vain babbling" <note>original: ματαιολογίαν</note> with *Saint Paul’s First Letter to Timothy, chapter 1, verse 6*.</margin>
<margin>27. **Old wives' tales.**] **Meermann** <note>Gerard Meerman, a Dutch book collector and scholar</note> incorrectly wrote *huthlôn* [with an omega], as he often confuses the short 'o' and the long 'ô'. The phrase is found in Plato’s *Theaetetus*, page 129, B: "For these things are what is called old wives' tales." *Suidas* <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> says: *Old wives' tales* is a proverb applied to those who babble in vain. See the writers of proverbs.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Next, the word *epidosis* signifies **increase** or **progress**. Read *Alberti* in his notes on the dictionary of *Hesychius* under the letter V.</margin>
<margin>28. **They are ready** not only.] That is, the word "they are" is implied. You will find this word used in this manner in many places. Consult the famous *D'Orville* in his notes on *Chariton*, Book I, chapter 4, who cites our specific passage. **Meermann** incorrectly wrote the singular form *hetoimon*.</margin>
<margin>29. **Pure.**] Perhaps the text should read *hagneian* [purity], and then "to themselves first" [referring to their own conscience]. — **Reiske**.</margin>
<margin>30. **To slander as sorcery.**] An elegant Greek idiom. When a noun is used with the preposition *eis* [into/as] and joined to verbs like "to slander," "to insult," and similar words, it indicates the thing that brings hatred upon someone, or the specific vice with which they are being reproached. They do not hesitate to slander [the holy men] as impostors and charlatans. <margin>
The Meerman manuscript incorrectly reads *ektainontes* [stretching out] instead of *ektinontes* [paying a penalty], and then *aute* [by it].

1. *For since the Indians &c.*] I think *Theophrastus* speaks of these in *History of Plants, Book IV, ch. 5*: "And the wise and abstaining men of the Indians use [this] food." *They translate this as: "the wise men of the Indians, who live naked, use this food." Indeed, those who are "wise but not abstaining" stop there. They cannot both eat and abstain,* says *Scaliger*: but *the "abstaining ones,"* those who are such by excellence, of whom our Author speaks, did not eat of that fruit. These Indians had many things in common with the Egyptians, and *La Croze* derives this from the idea that they were colonies of the Egyptians, as we observed above. However, that opinion is pressed by many difficulties, which can be read in *Brucker* in the *Treasury of Letters of La Croze, Vol. I, p. 70.* But if you think they migrated from India into Egypt instead, it would be because *Philostratus* places the Gymnosophists in Ethiopia near the Nile river. Compare *Ludovicus Vives on Augustine’s City of God, XIV, 17.* But they could also have received these customs through the Persians, to whom our Author joins the Indians here, and we have seen elsewhere that they had more things in common with the Egyptians. For the Persians, Arabs, and other northern Asian nations once enriched India with inhabitants, on which matter see *Illustrious La Croze, Book VI, History of Christianity in India.* Indeed, *Clearchus* says in *Diogenes Laertius's Prooemium* that the Gymnosophists *are descendants of the Magi.*

<column-break/>

2. *To call them Gymnosophists.*] *Jerome* expressed these things in Latin in *Against Jovinian, II, 14*: "Bardesanes, a man of Babylon, divides the Gymnosophists among the Indians into two dogmas, one of which he calls Brahmans, the other Samanaeans; who are of such great continence that they are nourished either by the fruits of trees near the Ganges river, or by a common meal of rice or flour." Regarding the reason for the name, and in what sense they were "naked," see the arguments of *Wolf on Origen’s Philosophy, ch. 24.* On the philosophers of the Indians, see also extensively *Diodorus Siculus, Book II, ch. 40*, where *Wesseling* has made many excellent observations.

3. *Brahmans — Samanaeans.*] The Meerman manuscript neglected the first syllable in *proistantai* [they preside] and immediately gives *hiereteian* [priesthood]. Concerning the Samanaeans, more a little later. Countless authors have dealt with the Brahmans; see as many as possible cited by *Wolf on Origen’s Philosophy, ch. 24*, regarding both those ancient ones and those of today.

# PORPHYRY

...saying, "If everyone imitates you, what will become of us?" Yet human affairs have not been thrown into confusion because of these people. For neither did everyone imitate them, nor were those who did imitate them the cause of confusion among the nations; rather, they were the cause of <term>eunomia</term> <note>original: εὐνομία; a state of well-ordered government or "good law."</note>. Furthermore, the law did not compel them, but while permitting others to feed on meat, it allowed these people to be autonomous, and it revered them as being better than itself. It did not subject them to the legal penalties it imposes as if they were initiators of injustice; rather, it subjected the others. To those, however, who ask what would happen if everyone imitated such people, one must reply with the saying of Pythagoras: for he says that if everyone became kings, life would be difficult to navigate, yet surely kingship is not to be shunned because of that. And if everyone were <term>virtuous men</term> <note>original: σπουδαίων; literally "serious" or "excellent" men who strive for moral perfection.</note>, it would be impossible to find a way to manage a state that maintains a dignity appropriate to such excellence; yet surely no one would be so mad as to not [wish this] for all—

---

<margin>
**To say.** He seemed to say something not entirely to be looked down upon. <term>Reiske</term> <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century classical scholar.</note>
</margin>

11. **Rather, of Good Order [Eunomia].** <term>Diogenes Laertius</term> <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> defines "Good Order" beautifully in Book III, 103: "Good order is divided into three parts. First, if the laws are excellent, we say there is good order. Second, if the citizens abide by the established laws, we also call this good order. Third, if, in the absence of laws, they govern themselves well through customs and practices." Thus, <term>Suidas</term> <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist.</note>, putting the effect in place of the cause, defines "Good Order" as "peace."

12. **Left them autonomous.** That is, "the law is not laid down [for the righteous]."

<column-break/>

—if they all imitate us, what will happen to us? Human affairs have not been thrown into disorder on account of these people. For not everyone has imitated them: and those who did imitate them have stood as the cause of order and tranquility for peoples, rather than confusion. But indeed, the law brought no necessity upon these men; rather, since it permitted others to eat flesh, it left these to be of their own right, and honored them as if they were superior to itself. For it did not subject these men, as if they were perpetrators of injustice, to the punishment it inflicts, but rather others. To those, however, who inquire what would happen if all were to imitate such a way of human life, one must answer with that saying of Pythagoras. For if all were kings, he says, the result would be that life could only be led with difficulty, yet kingship is not to be fled for that reason. So too, if all were upright, no way of managing and arranging the republic would be found in which its own dignity could be preserved for their uprightness. But no one would be so insane as not to [desire this] for
->all<-

---

<margin>
**It is not laid down.** See above at Book I, section 8. The Philosopher speaks well in Diogenes Laertius, Book VI: "The wise man should not live according to established laws, but according to the law of virtue."
</margin>

13. **If all should imitate.** For the Philosopher did not dictate this norm of living to everyone indiscriminately, which is why he emphasizes this more often. See at Book I, 27.

14. **If all were virtuous.** Perhaps "if all were being virtuous." <term>Reiske</term>. The dictionaries I am consulting lack the word "excellence" <note>original: σπουδαιότης; meaning moral gravity or diligence.</note>. <term>Diodorus</term> also uses it.

<summary>Porphyry argues that vegetarianism and philosophical abstinence do not cause social chaos; instead, they represent a higher moral order that the law respects but does not mandate for everyone. He uses a Pythagorean analogy to show that even if a virtuous lifestyle makes traditional governance difficult, it remains a goal worth pursuing.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument regarding the ethical necessity of a vegetarian diet for the philosopher, comparing the philosopher's self-imposed discipline to the sacred laws governing priests and the social expectations of honorable men.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

The law does not forbid one from spending their life in taverns <note>original: καπηλίοις / cauponis. In antiquity, taverns were often associated with low social status or vice.</note>, and yet such a thing is a reproach to a man of moderate character. Something similar is evident regarding diet. One should not concede to the best men that which is permitted to the masses. A philosopher, above all, should prescribe for himself those sacred laws which the gods, and men following the gods, have defined. Now, sacred laws have appeared throughout nations and cities which command purity and forbid the eating of living things <note>original: ἐμψύχων / animatorum. Literally "things with a soul."</note> <gloss>21</gloss> to those engaged in sacred rites, and <gloss>22</gloss> even forbid the multitude from certain foods, either for the sake of piety or because of some harm arising from the nourishment. Therefore, one must either imitate the priests or obey all the legislators; for in either case, the man who is perfectly law-abiding and pious must abstain from all [flesh]. For if some people abstain from certain things in part for the sake of piety, then the man who is pious toward all things will surely abstain from all things.

->§ 19.<-

***

<margin>Notes on the ancient passages. See Perizonius on Aelian: Varia Historia, Book III, 14.</margin>

21. **To those in sacred rites already.**] So I read and punctuate: "forbidding the priests, and even now..." — REISKE. <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, an 18th-century scholar.</note> Excellent! The celebrated Abresch <note>Friedrich Ludwig Abresch, a Dutch philologist.</note> desired the same, and it is clearly confirmed by the following words, "therefore one must either imitate the priests." The phrase "already and" or "already but also" means "furthermore." "Already" <note>original: ἤδη</note> in this formula is a particle of emphasis. Raphel <note>Georg Raphel, a German theologian.</note> has many examples in his notes on the Gospel of Matthew, chapter III, 10, to which I now only add Aelian: Varia Historia, XIII, 1.

22. **To the multitude.**] Felicianus <note>Giovanni Bernardino Feliciano, a 16th-century translator.</note> interprets this in the same sense

<column-break/>

as above in section 5, where he gave "to the people." Thus it would be: "even now forbidding the eating of certain things in great quantity."

Bentley <note>Richard Bentley (1662–1742), an influential English classical scholar.</note> argued that this belongs to the latter type, followed by Barnes, who in his edition of *Euripides* (page 478) ensured that verses 6, 8, 9, 10, and 11 were published according to Bentley's emendations. In Euripides, one also finds "roofs" and "by the Chalybian [iron]."

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

<column-break/>

They believed that the removal of souls <note>original: "ψυχῶν" - referring here to the departure of life or the dead</note> brought defilement upon the living; and much more so when a body that had possessed sensation was deprived of it, <gloss>3</gloss> and being dead, was brought into contact with the sensation of a living being. Therefore, in all things, sanctity and purity consist in the setting aside and abstinence from the many <gloss>4</gloss> and the contrary things, and in the isolation and reception of those things which are kindred and appropriate. For this reason, sexual acts also defile; for they are a union of female and male. Whether the seed is conceived, it brings defilement to the soul through its association with the body; or if it is not conceived, <gloss>5</gloss> it defiles through the "death" <note>original: "νεκρώσει" - referring to the loss of vital seed</note> of that which was offered. <gloss>6</gloss> Furthermore, the union of males with males contaminates doubly: both because it is spent in what is "dead" <note>i.e., non-reproductive</note> and because it exists contrary to nature. And in general, sexual acts and nocturnal emissions pollute because the soul is mixed with the body and is dragged downward toward pleasure. The passions of the soul also defile <gloss>7</gloss> through their entanglement, and <gloss>8</gloss> because the irrational part <note>the emotional or animalistic side of the soul</note> causes the internal male <note>the rational, governing principle</note> to become effeminate. For indeed, every <gloss>9</gloss> man who...

<column-break/>

<margin>3. And dead.] Perhaps "and having been deadened," and soon after "with the sensation of the living," according to Reiske.</margin>
<margin>4. And of contraries, isolation.] It should rather be read "by the isolation of contraries, and the reception of kindred things," according to Valent. The word "isolation" <term>monosis: a philosophical state of being alone or singular</term> is also used below and by others. See Spanheim on Josephus's Antiquities, Book II, 4.</margin>
<margin>5. By the death of that which was offered.] "Death" <note>nekrosis</note> is the proper term in this matter. It is exactly as used by Saint Paul in Romans 4:19, "a body having been deadened," with which Kypke rightly compared this passage.</margin>
<margin>6. Furthermore, the [union].] I have rewritten this based on the authority of the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts; previously it was read as "he who," but it refers back to either "union" or "intercourse."</margin>
<margin>7. Through the entanglement and.] The "and" after "entanglement" seems redundant, according to Valent.</margin>
<margin>8. The irrational part being made effeminate.] Since the female sex was considered weaker, philosophers were accustomed to compare the irrational part of the soul to a woman; on which matter see the illustrious Irhovius, "On the Transmigration of Souls," III, 5, 4.</margin>

9 <gloss>9</gloss> Defilement and pollution signify the mixing of one thing with another of a different kind, especially when it becomes difficult to wash away. Hence, even in the case of dyes—which are created through mixtures where one substance is intertwined with another—they say it "stains" <note>original: "μιαίνειν" (miainein)</note>.

12 <gloss>12</gloss> "As when a woman stains ivory with Phoenician purple." <note>A famous line from Homer’s *Iliad* (4.141) comparing a wound to dyed ivory.</note>

Conversely, painters call such mixtures "corruptions" <note>original: "φθοράς" (phthoras)</note>. In common usage, however, that which is unmixed and pure is called "incorruptible," "unadulterated," and "undefiled." For even water mixed with earth is corrupted, and is no longer unadulterated. The...

<column-break/>

...is diminished. For the names of defilement and pollution also signify, in a certain way, the mixing together of things of different kinds, especially when a certain "infection" of this sort follows which can only be wiped away with great difficulty. Hence, even in the case of dyes, which arise from mixture, when one species is confounded with another, they call it "staining." Just as a woman, says Homer, stains ivory with Tyrian purple. Furthermore, painters call mixtures "corruptions." Common custom likewise dictates that what is unmixed and pure is called "incorrupt," "sincere," and "unpolluted." For water mixed with earth is corrupted, and [no longer] sincere...

---

9. <gloss>9. Defilement, etc.</gloss> I ought to record the notable passage from *Plutarch* which our author refers to (Volume II, page 393, section C): "For defilement is the mixture of one thing with another. As Homer says somewhere, ivory made red with dye is said to be 'stained.' And the dyers call the mixing of colors 'corrupting,' and they call the mixture itself a 'corruption' <note>original: "φθοράν" (phthoran)</note>." Just as painters used to call the mixture of colors "corruption," philosophers call the mixing of any thing with another by that name, as is said immediately following. Compare Gataker’s notes on Marcus Aurelius, Book VI, section 30.

10. <gloss>10. Becomes difficult to wash out.</gloss> The terms "hard to wash out" <note>original: "δυσέκπλυτοι"</note> and "hard to wipe away" <note>original: "δυσέκνιπτοι"</note> are joined together in Aelian (*History of Animals*, Book I, 48). Our word is elegantly used by Plato regarding opinions that are pulled out with difficulty (*Republic*, Book II, page 605, section A). The stain of sin is called by Stobaeus a "hard-to-wipe-away dreg," by Philo a "hard-to-wash-out impression," and by Chrysostom an "unwashable blot." You may read these and others in Gataker (Book XI, *Adversaria*), whom I see is already praised by Wolf in his notes on Origen's *Philosophumena* (chapter 19). To these can be compared the Hebrew word *rachats* <note>original: "רחצ"</note>, which they translated as "to wash out" in Isaiah 4:4.

11. <gloss>11. They say "to stain".</gloss> This is the first and proper 

<column-break/>

meaning of the word: to mix or to dye. See Bos (*Critical Observations*, chapter 30). It is therefore rightly attributed to painters, just as the Latins use the words *inficere* <note>meaning both to dye and to infect</note> and *inquinare* <note>meaning to stain or pollute</note>. The passage of Plutarch just cited is significant.

12. <gloss>12. As when someone—</gloss> The Poet in the *Iliad*, Book 4, verse 141. Plutarch refers to this, as I was just saying. Virgil imitates this in the *Aeneid*, Book XII, line 67:
> As if someone had stained Indian ivory with blood-red purple.

13. <gloss>13. Painters call them "corruptions".</gloss> Because a thing which is mixed with another is in some way corrupted and loses its natural power, painters call the mixture a "corruption," as Plutarch speaks in the place cited. From there the term passed to the philosophers. To the notes, add Kuster on Aristophanes' *Plutus*, line 530.

14. <gloss>14. Unadulterated and undefiled.</gloss> Porphyry also uses the first term in Book I, 54, and the adverb "unadulteratedly" in section 40, which the Scholiast on Thucydides (Book II, 52) explains, where Hudson notes an error by Dionysius of Halicarnassus. "Undefiled" is also a good term and follows the usage of the ancients. See the notes on Book III, 27. Elsewhere it is called "unmixed and undefiled" in Theophrastus' *On the Senses* (page 502) and the passage of Plutarch cited above—from which our author had taken certain things—"and always unmixed..."

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK IV.
->A a a<-

...no longer exists. But that which flows, and is carried along with a swift course, casts back the earth it encounters—which, as Hesiod says, *flows clear, trickling from an eternal spring* <note>original Latin: "fluit illimis manans e fonte perenni"</note>. For because it is incorrupt and unmixed, it provides a healthful drink. In the same way, a woman who has admitted no male exhalation or mixture into herself is called "incorrupt." Therefore, corruption and defilement consist of the mixture of an opposite. This is why the injection of dead things into animals—and specifically the insertion of things that once lived with sensation into living beings, and of dead flesh into living bodies—rightly brings about a pollution and defilement of our nature. Just as...

<column-break/>

...flowing and escaping, it thrusts aside the earth that is brought near, whenever, 15 as Hesiod says, it flows from an eternal and ever-running spring, which is also untroubled. And the drink is healthy, 16 because it is uncorrupted <note>The printed text uses "distinct" (diaphoron), but scholars suggest "uncorrupted" (adiaphthoron).</note> and unmixed. And a female who has not received the exhalation of seed into herself, 17 is called incorrupt. Thus, both corruption and defilement are the mixture of the opposite. 18 If, then, there is a placement of dead things into living animals, and 19 of those things that lived according to sensation into living beings, and of dead flesh into living ones, it reasonably brings a stain and 20 a defilement to our nature, just as...

---

<margin>15. **Hesiod says:** *Works and Days*, line 595: "From an eternal and ever-running spring, which is also untroubled." Regarding "eternal rivers and springs" <note>original Latin: "Aénaoi fluvii & fontes"</note>, as the Latins call them "aeterni" (eternal), the celebrated Burman beautifully demonstrates their proper naming in his notes on Rutilius, I, 109. Sophocles calls a spring "ever-flowing" <note>original: "aeirryton"</note> in *Oedipus at Colonus* 465, where the Scholarly commentator explains it as "eternal" <note>original: "aennaon"</note>. See also the learned Goens in his notes on our author's *Cave of the Nymphs*, p. 101.</margin>

<margin>16. **Because it is distinct:** <gloss>Uncorrupted</gloss>. REISKE. This is the best reading. Abresch also corrected it this way, as "uncorrupted water" is used correctly shortly after. First, a careless scribe corrupted the word into "indifferent/distinct" <note>original: "adiaphoron"</note>, then another, even more careless, tried to make sense of it by writing "distinct/excellent" <note>original: "diaphoron"</note>. These words are often confused, as in Diodorus Siculus, where Wesseling successfully restored "corruption" <note>original: "diaphthoras"</note> in place of "difference" <note>original: "diaphoras"</note>.</margin>

<margin>17. **Is called incorrupt:** Just as an "uncorrupt woman" <note>original: "adiaphthoros gynē"</note> refers to one who has not prostituted herself in Diodorus I, 59. Conversely, regarding sexual violation, Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Book II, p. 96) says: "considering corruption the beginning of a lack of self-control, and drunkenness the beginning of corruption." The Greek verbs "to ruin" <note>original: "phtheirein"</note> and "to corrupt" <note>original: "diaphtheirein"</note> are very common in this context. The Latins use the terms "corrupters" and "to corrupt a virgin," on which see Taubman’s notes on Plautus’s *Casina* I, 3.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>18. **If then, toward the—:** This is how I read and punctuate this passage: "If then toward animals (one must understand 'it brings a stain' from the following) the insertion of dead things..." That is: if, therefore, the grafting of dead things into living beings brings some contamination—even if that grafting involves things that once seemed to live and feel—it is necessarily consistent that the intrusion of dead flesh into living flesh pollutes. REISKE.</margin>

<margin>19. **Lived according to sensation:** This same expression is found in Aristides (Vol. III, p. 674) and Plato (p. 423 C). These passages were noted by the celebrated Abresch.</margin>

<margin>20. **To our nature:** It appears that in some manuscripts the word was "Nature" <note>original: "physei"</note> and in others "Soul" <note>original: "psychē"</note>, from which the faulty reading "Natural" <note>original: "physike"</note> emerged. It should be read "and a defilement to our soul," which the following words prove. REISKE. Valente corrected it to "Nature," and the previous translator seems to have followed that, unless it was "the natural [part]," which my friend preferred.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s philosophical argument regarding the purification of the soul through abstinence from meat, specifically addressing how physical contact with bodies causes spiritual pollution.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

When the soul <gloss>21</gloss> is embodied, it is defiled. Therefore, <gloss>22</gloss> he who is born causes pollution through the mixture of the soul <gloss>23</gloss> with bodies; and he who has died, when he leaves behind a dead body, leaves something of a different nature and foreign to the living. The soul is also contaminated by anger, desires, and a multitude of passions, for which the diet is also in some way a contributing cause. Just as water flowing through rocks <gloss>24</gloss> is more pure than that which goes through marshes, because it does not pull along much mud; so also the soul, when it administers its own affairs through a dry body—one not irrigated by the juices of foreign flesh—is better, more incorruptible, and more ready for understanding. For they say that even for bees, the driest and most pungent thyme produces the best honey. Therefore, the intellect—or rather, the one who exercises intellect—is defiled when it is mixed with the faculties of imagination or opinion, and with their activities. <gloss>25</gloss> The

<column-break/>

In the same way, the soul also, when it is joined to the body, is stained. Whence also he who is born contracts pollution from the mixture of the soul with the body, as does he who dies, because he leaves behind a dead body which is foreign and different from the living. Likewise, the soul is contaminated by anger, and lusts, and a multitude of disturbances, of which the manner of living <note>original: "uictus"; referring here to diet and lifestyle</note> is also accustomed to be a cause in some way. For just as water which flows through rocks is more incorrupt than that which runs through marshes, inasmuch as it does not drag much mud; so the soul which administers its own affairs through a dry body, not through a flow of the juices of foreign flesh, is better, and more incorrupt, and more ready for intelligence. Indeed, they say that for bees also, the thyme which is driest and endowed with the greatest sharpness brings the best honey. Therefore, even thought—or rather the thinker—is stained when it is combined with the powers and operations of either imagining or opining.

---

<margin>21. **Is embodied.**] Either *ensomatoutai* <note>present tense</note> or *ensesomatotai* <note>perfect tense</note>. REISKE. Certainly one of the two is true. *Abreschius* also saw this. Instead of "is defiled" <note>memolytai</note>, the *Leipzig* and *Meermann Manuscripts* wrongly have the plural.</margin>
<margin>22. **He who is born.**] Perhaps "he who is being begotten" <note>gennomenos</note>, as pleased the Learned Man? But "to be born" <note>genesthai</note> is frequent enough. I add nothing to those things which *Alberti* noted regarding Paul's letter to the Galatians 4:4.</margin>
<margin>23. **Of the [soul] to the bodies.**] The word "of the" <note>tes</note> seems to have arisen from the last syllable of the word "soul" <note>psyches</note>, and thus one should read "of the soul to the body" or "by the mixture of the soul with the body." I also suspected</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>that this sentence was missing: "for souls are foreign to bodies." REISKE. I would believe that former suggestion to be most true. The *Meermann Manuscript* agrees beautifully, which has: "pollutes by the mixture of the soul with the bodies."</margin>
<margin>24. **Incorrupt of—**] After "incorrupt," the word "better" or "healthier" is missing. REISKE. Unless "more" is understood, which is familiar enough to our author, though rather harsh in this kind of structure. A little later also "and incorrupt," where *Reiske* prefers the comparative "more incorrupt" or "more so." The *Meermann* reading "incorrupt" is poor.</margin>
<margin>25. **The [connections] of this.**] Namely, of the intellect.</margin>

### On Abstinence, Book IV.

->Aaa 2<-

...is mixed. Purification and holiness, however, are a separation from all these things, and a state of solitude; it is the nourishment that preserves each thing in its own essence. For in this way you would correctly call the "nourishment" of a stone that which is the cause of it persevering in its own form; and for a plant, that which preserves it in growing and fruiting; and for the body of a living creature, that which maintains its constitution. For it is one thing to nourish and provide necessities, and another to supply luxuries. Therefore, according to the diversity of things being nourished, the nourishments are also diverse. And indeed, all things must be nourished: yet effort must be given so that those things which are primary in us are nourished and made fat. Thus, there is also a nourishment for the rational soul, which preserves it as rational: and that is the <term>Mind</term><note>Original: "Mens" / "Nous". In Neoplatonic philosophy, the "Mind" or "Intellect" is the highest part of the soul, connecting humans to the divine.</note>. Therefore, the soul must be nourished by the mind: and we must strive more to fatten the soul with the mind than the flesh with foods. For the mind preserves eternal life for us. But the body, having been fattened... <note>catchword: fa- (the start of "fattened")</note>

<column-break/>

...be mixed with them. But purification <gloss>26</gloss> is the separation from all these, and holiness is solitude, and nourishment is that which keeps each thing in its being. For in this way you might speak of the "nourishment" of a stone as the cause of its staying together, and of its <gloss>27</gloss> remaining in its state. And for a plant, that which preserves it in growth or fruit-bearing; and for the body of a living creature, that which preserves its constitution. But it was one thing to nourish, and another to fatten; and one thing to give what is necessary, and another to <gloss>28</gloss> provide luxuries. Therefore, nourishments are different, <gloss>29</gloss> according to the difference of those being nourished. And it is necessary to nourish everything, but to strive to fatten what is most sovereign within us. And so the nourishment of the rational soul is that which preserves it as rational. And this is the Mind. Thus, it should be nourished by the mind; and one should strive to fatten [it] <gloss>30</gloss> from this rather than [fattening] the flesh from foods. For the one sustains eternal life for us, but the body, being fattened, <gloss>31</gloss> [fat...] <note>catchword: λί- (the start of "lipos," meaning fat)</note>

---

<margin>For "these things" refers back to the imaginative and opinionative power. I would also prefer the active verb "should mix," referring to the one who thinks. REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske was a prominent 18th-century German scholar of Greek texts.</note></margin>

26. *The separation from these.* Either "the" should be deleted entirely, or it should be placed before "all." REISKE.

<margin>27. *Remaining in its state.* T. Gataker <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654) was an English scholar who wrote extensively on Marcus Aurelius.</note> beautifully explains what "state" <term>Hexis</term><note>A technical term for the "holding-together" force in inanimate objects.</note> is in these matters in his notes on Marcus Aurelius, Book VI, § 14. He thought that in this place we should read "and of staying in its state," and not without merit.</margin>

28. *Provide luxuries.* This is correct in the first editions and the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts. The Valentinian edition wrongly gave "nourishments," unless it was an error of the printers, for the editor interpreted it well.

<margin>29. *And the difference.* Rather indeed "according to some difference," or "according to the difference," as it is in the Leipzig and Meerman manuscripts; the translator expressed it no differently.</margin>

30. *From this rather than.* "Not from the [flesh]..."—namely, the "not" was lost because of a similar sound at the end of the previous word, and "k" was swapped with "e," which often happens in manuscripts. REISKE. It seems "rather" should be understood here, as we have seen often in this sentence structure elsewhere.

The text includes scholarly annotations by Reiske and Gataker regarding the correct Greek phrasing.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s discourse from Book IV of "On Abstinence from Animal Food." On the previous page, he established that the "Mind" or "Intellect" is the true nourishment of the rational soul, and that we must strive to "fatten" the soul with divinity rather than the body with meat. Here, he explores how physical indulgence drags the soul down and uses the magnet as a metaphor for divine attraction.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

->37.<-

...it <note>Referring to heavy or excessive food mentioned on the previous page</note> causes the soul to starve for the blessed life, and increases our mortal nature—which, when it becomes unrestrained, acts as an obstacle to the immortal life. It stains the soul as it becomes bound to the body, dragging it down into a nature that is alien to it. Now, the magnet stone <note>original: "Magnes lapis"</note> gives a kind of "soul" to iron when it is placed near it; thus the heaviest iron is made light, running toward the stone, lifted up by the stone's spirit. If this is so, should someone who is suspended from the incorporeal and intellectual God worry much about the kind of food that only fattens the body—the very body that stands in the way of the mind? Would he not instead contract the body's necessities into something small and easily obtained, nourishing himself by clinging to God even more than iron clings to a magnet? For if it were possible, we would abstain even from the nourishment provided by fruits to avoid the trouble of it, if only our corruptible nature did not require it.

<column-break/>

<margin>31. **Starving the soul.** <note>original: "Limōttein tēn psychēn"</note> Read what was discussed regarding this matter above in Book I, 29, and what Philostratus <note>A 3rd-century Greek scholar</note> says in Book VIII, 12, where Olearius <note>Gottfried Olearius (1672–1715), a scholar who edited Philostratus</note> also mentions our author. Instead of "starving" <note>limōttein</note>, the editor Fogerolles had given "plaguing" <note>loimōttein</note>, though I do not know where he got that. We have noted elsewhere that these words are often confused, but here the former is the only true reading.</margin>

<margin>32. **Taking away.** <note>original: "Parairoun"</note> Perhaps it should read "holding in suspense" <note>paraōroun</note>, as in keeping something elevated. REISKE <note>Johann Jacob Reiske (1716–1774), a famous German classicist</note>. Certainly the letter "o" <note>omega</note> could very easily have dropped out, as has often happened. I would not, however, want Markland <note>Jeremiah Markland (1693–1776), an English classical scholar</note> to have corrected John the Evangelist (Chapter 10, verse 24) in that way, changing "you take away" to "you keep in suspense," as he did for Euripides' *Suppliants* 89.</margin>

<margin>33. **Running toward.** <note>original: "Prosanatrechōn"</note> This word is also missing from Henri Estienne's very extensive *Thesaurus* <note>The *Thesaurus Graecae Linguae*, the most famous Greek dictionary of the Renaissance</note>.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>...it does occur quite often, however, as the examples collected by the celebrated Wesseling <note>Peter Wesseling (1692–1759), a Dutch scholar</note> in his notes on Diodorus Siculus (Book IV, 60) will show you.</margin>

<margin>34. **Toward the mind.** <note>original: "Pros noon"</note> The Lipsiensis and Meermannus manuscripts read "mind" <note>noun</note>. Reiske preferred "toward that which thinks" <note>pros to nooun</note>.</margin>

<margin>35. **Without trouble.** <note>original: "Aneu pragmatōn"</note> *Pragmata* here refers to business, labor, or nuisances, as used above in Book I, section 46, and by Gataker <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), an English scholar</note> in his notes on Marcus Aurelius (I, 12).</margin>

<margin>36. **If only it were not so.** <note>original: "Ei mē tout’ ēn"</note> This second "if" <note>Ei</note>, like the first and third, is a sign of a wish. "Oh, that this inclination of our nature toward decay and ruin did not cling to us!" REISKE.</margin>

The margins contain dense philological debates by Enlightenment-era scholars regarding the correct Greek terminology for "starving," "suspense," and "trouble."</summary>

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

For if, as Homer says, we required neither food nor drink so that we might truly be immortal: for this was rightly stated by the poet <note>Homer, Iliad 5.341</note>, to signify that nourishment has brought about the occasion not so much for living, but also for dying. If, therefore, we had no need of this kind of nourishment, we would be as much more blessed as we were more immortal. But now, since we exist in a mortal state, we ignorantly render ourselves even more mortal (if it may be said so) by clinging to it: since the soul, as Theophrastus says, does not merely pay a small rent for its habitation in the body, but adds its whole self besides. But would that it were possible to lead that life spoken of in fables, entirely lacking hunger and thirst: so that each person, having restrained the flux of the body, might in the shortest time—

<column-break/>

For if, as <gloss>37</gloss> Homer says, we did not need food or drink, so that we might truly be immortal. The poet presented this well, showing that food was a <gloss>38</gloss> provision <note>original: "ephodion"</note> not only for living, but also for dying. If then we did not need this, <gloss>39</gloss> how much more blessed we would be, by as much as we were more immortal. But now, being in a mortal state, we make ourselves even more mortal, if one must say so, through our ignorance, <gloss>40</gloss> by the addition of this [mortal nature]; the soul <gloss>41</gloss> paying to the body not a great rent for its dwelling in it, as Theophrastus says somewhere, but adding its whole self. Would that it were easy to possess that fabled life free of hunger and thirst, so that one, having checked the <gloss>42</gloss> flowing away of the body, might quickly be among the best things,

They hate first themselves, and the one who truly fathered them <note>Likely referring to the Divine or the "One" in Neoplatonic philosophy</note>, and then they hate those who remind them of the truth and exhort them to <gloss>44</gloss> sober up from their drunkenness. <gloss>45</gloss> Therefore, perhaps it is best to leave such people aside and move on to the remaining questions of our inquiry.

**Notes on the Text:**

<gloss>43.</gloss> **Being.** <note>original Greek: "on"</note> The scholar Lipsius preferred the reading "being" <note>original: "ōn"</note>, which is undoubtedly correct and is read in the Meermann manuscript. Valerius saw this, but by poor judgment gave "o" in the text. The French edition followed him, and here, as is his habit, is a typographical error from the Florentine edition.

<gloss>44.</gloss> **To sober up from drunkenness.** <note>original Greek: "tēs methēs ananēpsai"</note> The term "to become sober again" <note>original: "ananēphein"</note> is used everywhere for those who recover themselves from fear, anger, love, etc. See D’Orville on Chariton, Book 3, Chapter 1, who also illustrates that passage of Saint Paul in 2 Timothy 2:26 <note>"...and that they may recover their senses and escape from the snare of the devil..."</note>, where philologists have gathered a harvest of examples. Specifically in this place, it means *to return to oneself* from intoxication, as in Lucian’s *Hermotimus* 83: "sobering up from drunkenness," and many others whom I see have already been cited there. It is the same as "to become sober" in 1 Corinthians 15:34, where Alberti notes it. The Meermann manuscript corruptly reads "to remain."

<gloss>45.</gloss> **Wherefore never—** The word "never" <note>original Greek: "mēpote"</note> can be defended. The word "see" is understood—as in, "see whether we should move on." However, Reiske preferred "now at last." You could also use "certainly at last," which was favored by the celebrated Abresch. The Greeks are accustomed to omit the words "to see," "to look," or 

<column-break/>

"to consider" before this particle. It could also be translated simply as: "therefore perhaps it will be necessary" or "it will be better." See what the learned Alberti discusses regarding the use of this little word in the unfairly criticized passage of Matthew 25:9 <note>The parable of the ten virgins: "Lest there be not enough..."</note>.

<gloss>1.</gloss> **Bringing forward the Nomads—** This refers to the objections raised above in Book 1, Section 5. Saint Jerome expressed this in *Against Jovinianus*, Book 2, Chapter 7: *“The Nomads and Troglodytes, and Scythians, and the new ferocity of the Huns, eat half-raw meat.”* Furthermore, the **Fish-eaters** <note>Ichthyophagi</note>, a people wandering on the shore of the Red Sea, roast fish on rocks glowing with the heat of the sun, and they live on this food alone. Diodorus Siculus writes in Book 3, 32: *“The Troglodytes are called Nomads by the Greeks, having a nomadic life from their herds.”* Regarding this, the "Great Commentator" <note>likely referring to a specific 16th or 17th-century editor</note> observes that the Beklenfes [Blemmyes] occupy the seat of the Troglodytes in our time, and they follow the same way of life.

<gloss>2.</gloss> **They are ignorant—** Regarding this passage, there was a note written in the margin of the Leipzig manuscript—I do not know if it was a scholarly explanation or a different reading: <margin>the nature of the land</margin>

### On Abstinence, Book IV.

...land which is so sterile and covered with rocks and sands that it does not even produce any herbs; they were led to this by the necessity of finding nourishment. A proof of this is that they cannot even use fire due to the lack of fuel and wood, but instead they roast fish on rocks glowing in the sun and in the sand. And these people indeed live this way because they are compelled by necessity. But if certain nations are found who are of a monstrous and savage nature, it is not fitting for a fair judge of things to bring a slander against the entire human race because of them. For in that way, not only the eating of other animals, but also the eating of men—and every other kind of ferocity—would become a matter of dispute. <meta>This page continues the discussion of diverse and often violent funerary customs among ancient peoples, specifically focusing on the Massagetae, Tibareni, and Hyrcanians. It maintains the scholarly tone of the previous entries, citing various classical authorities.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

...the most wretched are those who die by a natural death. Therefore, they anticipate this by sacrificing and feasting upon those of their dearest kin who have grown old. 10 The Tibareni, however, cast down their nearest elderly relatives from cliffs while they are still living. The Hyrcanians and Caspians—some of them expose the living, others the dead, to be devoured by birds and dogs. The Scythians [bury] the living...

<column-break/>

...that this custom has now been abolished is stated by *Theodoret in his Sermon on Laws, p. 615, and Eusebius in Preparation for the Gospel, Book I, p. 11.* It was attributed to the institutions of the Romans by *Pliny, Book XXX, ch. 1.* However, the things written by the *learned Pelloutier in History of the Celts, Book II, ch. 3* to excuse the Scythians (whose <term>anthropophagy</term> <note>original: "ἀνθρωποφαγία" - the eating of human flesh</note> is noted everywhere) deserve to be read. Since nothing is more desirable than to depart by the fate of nature, you might rightly marvel at that insane love of violent death among some nations. That they themselves hastened their own fate can indeed be attributed to a zeal for glory. *For all cause for light is placed in arms, and to live for peace is condemned, as Silius Italicus says of the Cantabrians in Book III, 320.* The Cimbri and Celtiberians used to exult with joy in the line of battle, as if they were about to depart life gloriously and happily; they would lament in sickness, as if they were to perish basely and miserably. *Valerius Maximus, Book II, 6, 11.* But as for why they took the lives of their own people, it was from that persuasion by which they believed those who perished in such a manner would be more fortunate and blessed after this life. Concerning the Thracians, *Solinus in ch. 10* says they all agree on voluntary death, while some of them think the souls of the dying return, and others think they are not extinguished but become more blessed. Compare also *Pelloutier, as cited above, Book III, 18.*

9. **They feast upon those of their dearest kin who have grown old.** <note>original: "Ἑστιῶνται τῶν φιλτ. τοὺς γεγηρ."</note> *Sallust, in On the World, ch. 9*, also says the Massagetae "eat" their parents. If they reached extreme old age, they would slaughter and devour them; if they were extinguished by disease, they would hide them in a mound. Compare the *Learned Man on the Fragments of Pythagoras in Gale’s Mythological, Physical, and Ethical Works, p. 713.* Note also the word <term>to sacrifice</term> <note>original: "καταθύειν"</note> which he uses significantly, for he wishes it to be understood that those old men were slaughtered like sacrificial victims. For <term>to sacrifice</term> is to offer victims to the Gods on an altar, a part of which was eaten. See *Perizonius on Aelian, Various History, Book IV, ch. 1.* For "anticipating" <note>original: "φθάσαντες"</note>, the Meerman Codex has "those who anticipated."

10. **The Tibareni, however, [cast down] the living...** Such were the Cantabrians in *Silius Italicus, Book III, 318:*
> *A strange love possesses the people: when sluggish age turns grey,*
> *To anticipate the years already unfit for war with a stone.*

Those who are called *Tibareni* by our author are called *Tibari* by *Eusebius*. *Theodoret* calls them *Tibareni*, and they are usually expressed in that way, as in this place in the Meerman manuscript, although the codices vary everywhere on that name. See the *Learned Man on Stephanus of Byzantium and Wesseling on Diodorus, Book XIV, 30.* However, *Jerome* translated this poorly: *The Tibareni hang the old men they have loved on gallows*, when he ought to have said *they cast them down*, as *Cotelerius on the Recognitions of Clement, Vol. I, p. 584, and others* have noted. Nevertheless, those words are often confused. Certainly the simple *krēmnāō* and *krēmnēmi* are sometimes the same as *kremāō*, "I hang," on which matter see *Kuhn on Diogenes Laertius, Book VI, 50; Barnes on Euripides’ Heracles, 520; and others.* At any rate, among the Scythians, it was considered a blessed burial for the dead to be fixed to a cross or a stake, as *Plutarch, Vol. II, p. 499 C*, teaches among others. The Colchians hang those sewn in skins from trees, according to *Aelian, Various History, Book IV, ch. 1*, which however *Apollonius of Rhodes, Book III, 208*, suggests should be understood only of the men. Nor was it unusual for the Germans, the offspring of the Scythians, to end their lives with a noose, as *Bardesanes teaches in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book IV, p. 277 D.*

11. **Some to birds and dogs...** Many have noted that cruelty of the Hyrcanians. See *Menage on Diogenes Laertius, Book VI, 79.* *Theodoret, p. 615*, says the Hyrcanians and Caspians feed themselves on the corpses of men, which differs a little from...

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK IV

->§ 22.<-

<column-break/>

...together they bury them, and upon the funeral pyre they slaughter those whom the deceased especially loved. The Bactrians throw those who have grown old alive to the dogs. When Stasanor, a prefect of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note>, attempted to abolish this custom, he nearly lost his command. But just as we do not believe that humanity toward men should be discarded based on the example of these people, so we ought not to follow those nations that eat meat out of necessity. Instead, we must imitate those who conduct themselves piously and lead a life more devoted to the gods. For to live badly—not prudently, temperately, and holily—Democrates <note>Possibly the philosopher Democritus; see note 16 below</note> used to assert was not "living badly," but "dying for a long time."

->§ 22.<-

<column-break/>

...the dead. 12 The Scythians bury the living along with them, and slaughter upon the pyres those whom the deceased loved most. And the Bactrians, indeed, cast the elderly alive to the dogs. When Stasanor, the governor under Alexander, attempted to abolish 13 this, he nearly lost his office. But just as we did not abolish kindness toward men because of these people, so we will not imitate the nations that eat flesh out of necessity, but rather those who are pious and 14 more devoted to the gods. For as for 15 living badly and not prudently and temperately and holily, 16 Democrates used to say that this was not "living badly," but "dying for a long time."

<margin>
*Our Author*. Indeed, our same author immediately affirms this regarding both the Hyrcanians and the Bactrians, and many attribute no other type of burial to the *Oritae*. Compare *Wesseling* on *Diodorus Siculus, Book XVII, ch. 105.* Regarding the Persians, *Theodoret* also indicates this in his *Sermon on Laws, p. 614.* *Eusebius* refers to these nations in *Demonstration of the Gospel, Book IV, p. 161 and Book V, p. 205.*
</margin>

12. **The Scythians —** Above, in Book III, 17, the Scythians are said to "eat their fathers." But as the name was applied very broadly, so their customs were also diverse among them. For it is established that among the Scythians, as well as the Indians and other nations, it was a custom to eat their own people; on which subject see *Perizonius* on *Aelian's Various History, IV, 1.* Our author just spoke of this regarding the Massagetae and Derbices.

13. **Stasanor, the [governor] of Alexander —** This refers to Stasanor, one of the friends of Alexander the Great, who after Alexander's death was assigned a province; regarding him, see *Strabo*, *Diodorus Siculus*, and others. See *Meursius* in *Cyprus, Book I, 25 and Book II, 31.* In *Justin, Book XIII, 4*, he was incorrectly called "Statanor," but the translators have now restored the true name. In *Fabricius'* notes on *Sextus Empiricus' Outlines of Pyrrhonism, Book III, 24, p. 179*, "Nicanor" is cited from *Jerome*.

<column-break/>

14. **More devoted to the gods.** A well-known turn of phrase. Everything that is vowed or dedicated to the Gods is said to be <term>devoted to the gods</term> <note>original: "ἀνακεῖσθαι θεοῖς"</note>. So says *Sallust the Philosopher* in *On the Gods and the World* found in *Gale’s Mythological, Physical, and Ethical Opuscules, p. 248*, and others. *Clement of Alexandria* explains: "it was only permitted to the consecrated to enter—that is, to those devoted to God." *Stromata, Book V, p. 555.*

15. **To live badly and not prudently —** Just as above, "temperate," "holy," and "just" are joined together. Book II, § 60, see there. *Casaubon* in his notes on *Persius, Satire V, 152*, and *Gataker* on *Marcus Aurelius, Book IX, § 2*, have excellently illustrated this sentiment, and they did not forget this passage.

16. **Democrates.** Perhaps *Democritus*. I personally do not know this Democrates. *Reiske.* These names are indeed often confused by the carelessness of scribes. We have the *Golden Sentences* of the Pythagorean Democrates in *Gale's* work, and *Fabricius* lists several of this name in *Greek Bibliography, II, 13.*

§ 22. Finally, let us bring forward a few testimonies of individual men concerning abstinence; for this was also one of the points of accusation <note>referring to those who criticized the practice of abstinence</note>. Among the lawgivers of Athens, we have received the tradition that Triptolemus <note>A legendary figure in Greek myth who was taught the craft of agriculture by Demeter and spread it across the world</note> was the most ancient. <gloss>1</gloss> Regarding him, Hermippus <note>A Greek biographer and philosopher</note> writes the following in his second book *On Lawgivers*: "They say that Triptolemus also established laws for the Athenians. And of his laws, three still <gloss>2</gloss>—so the philosopher Xenocrates <note>The third head of Plato’s Academy</note> asserts—remain standing at Eleusis <note>The site of the famous Eleusinian Mysteries</note>, namely these: <gloss>3</gloss> **Honor your parents.** **Glorify the gods <gloss>4</gloss> with the fruits of the earth.** **Do not harm <gloss>5</gloss> animals.**" Regarding the first two, it is said they were rightly established; for we ought to honor our parents, since they have become our benefactors...

<column-break/>

§ 22. It remains for us to offer a few testimonies of individual men regarding abstinence. For this was another point that was being objected to. We have heard that Triptolemus was the oldest of the Athenian lawgivers: about whom Hermippus writes in the following manner in his second book *On Lawgivers*: "They say that Triptolemus also ordained laws for the Athenians. Xenocrates the Philosopher asserts that three of his decrees still survive at Eleusis: **To honor parents: To worship the gods with fruits: To not harm animals.**" And he says that two were indeed rightly instituted. For we owe honor to our parents, seeing as they have deserved the best from us...

---

<column-break/>

<margin>1. **Regarding him, Hermippus in the second—]**</margin> In the same way, he is cited by *Diogenes Laertius* in his life of *Pythagoras* regarding the second book *On Lawgivers*. *Origen* praises Hermippus in the first book of *Against Celsus*, p. 333, regarding the first book *On Lawgivers*. There were several men of this name. *Vossius* in *On the Greek Historians* (I, 16) attributes that book on lawgivers to the *Smyrnaean* Hermippus; however, in another place, he attributes it to Hermippus of *Berytus* <note>Modern Beirut</note>, who lived in the time of the Emperor Hadrian. Regarding this error, see *Spencer*’s notes on the previously mentioned passage of *Origen*. Consult also *Fabricius*, *Greek Library*, Book II, 14, 17.

<margin>2. **Xenocrates the Philosopher.**</margin> There were also different men of this name, and among them Xenocrates the physician from Aphrodisias, who wrote *On the Utility of Animals*, or, as it is called by *Clement of Alexandria* in the *Stromata* (Book VII, p. 717), *On Food from Animals*; regarding him and others, read *Fabricius*, *Greek Library*, Book III, chapter 3. *Jerome* <note>St. Jerome, the Latin Church Father</note> translates these words in Book II of *Against Jovinian* (14): "Xenocrates the Philosopher writes that concerning the laws of Triptolemus among the Athenians, only three precepts remain in the temple of Eleusis: *parents must be honored, the gods must be venerated, and meat must not be eaten.*" This last part is not quite correct, as will be explained shortly.

<column-break/>

<margin>3. **Honor your parents.**</margin> You could also link this as "but to honor parents," as seen in the *Meerman* and *Marsham* manuscripts: *Chronicus Canon* (Sec. IX), which compares this with the Hebrew commandments. *Euripides* says beautifully in his *Antiope* (fragment 42):
> There are three virtues you should practice, my child:
> To honor the Gods, and the parents who raised you,
> And the common laws of Greece.
A learned man thought that Menander had this law in mind in his *Fragments* (p. 238):
> Law assigns to parents honors equal to the gods.
But this precept is extremely common among most peoples.

<margin>4. **Glorify with fruits.**</margin> The word "Glorify" <note>original: ἀγάλλειν (agallein)</note> often expresses the worship we owe to the Supreme Being or others, and thus it was translated correctly enough by *Jerome*. However, *Salvini*, in his notes on *Petit's Attic Laws* (I, 1, p. 68), preferred the translation "Let them gladden the gods with fruits," a version which *Wesseling* excellently defended in that same place.

<margin>5. **Do not harm animals.**</margin> *Jerome* gave "meat must not be eaten." These words have a broader meaning. Indeed, animal sacrifices are forbidden. The matter is clear from those things which follow shortly after, regarding the command to use fruits—lest they should become...

# On Abstinence, Book IV.

-> Bbb 2 <-

deserved well of me, to return the favor in turn according to my strength; and to offer the firstfruits to the gods from those things useful for life which they have bestowed upon us. Concerning the third law, he <note>The philosopher Xenocrates</note> thinks we must inquire what Triptolemus intended when he commanded that one must abstain from animals. Was it because he thought it altogether unworthy that kindred beings should be killed? Or because he perceived it happened that the most useful animals were being taken for food by men? Since he wished, therefore, to make the life of men mild, he took care that those animals which lived among men, and were especially tame, should be preserved. Unless perhaps, because he had commanded that the gods be honored with fruits, he judged that this worship would be more firmly established if sacrifices to the gods were not made from animals at all. While many other causes for this decree are brought forward by Xenocrates—though these are not particularly precise—it is enough for us from these accounts that this institution is seen to have originated from Triptolemus. From which point, those later acting lawlessly, when they touched the eating of animals—

<column-break/>

—to return the favor as far as possible; and to make firstfruits <note>original: ἀπαρχὰς (aparchas)</note> to the gods from the useful things they gave us for life. Regarding the third, he wonders what Triptolemus was thinking when he commanded to abstain from animals. For he asks whether it was because he thought it a terrible thing to kill a kindred creature, or because he saw that it happened that the most useful animals were being destroyed for food by men; wishing therefore to make life civilized, he tried to preserve those animals that live with men and are especially tame. Unless it was because he brought people to honor the gods with fruits, supposing that this honor would better endure if sacrifices were not made to the gods by means of animals. Although Xenocrates gives many other reasons that are not entirely accurate, it is sufficient for us from what has been said that this was legislated by Triptolemus. Whence later, those acting lawlessly, when they touched the animals—

*Sacrifices to the gods by means of animals.* Compare *Wesseling* on *Petit's* Attic Laws, Book II, 4. p. 245.
6. *To make firstfruits.*] A most ancient custom, that they should venerate the Gods and Goddesses by offering the firstfruits of the crops. Which the Illustrious Man <note>likely referring to the scholar Wesseling</note> also shows from *Our Author* <note>Porphyry</note> regarding *Diodorus Siculus* Book I, 14. The sacred records teach that the same was practiced among the Hebrew people, and *Spencer* in *Ritual Laws* III, 9, serving his hypothesis, derives this from that most ancient custom of offering firstfruits.
</margin>

<margin>
7. *To abstain from animals.*] Triptolemus did not wish that living creatures should be entirely not killed, nor that they should not be used for human nourishment, but he only wished that those which were useful for assisting in rural labor should not be cut off and exterminated. Therefore this example seems misplaced. REISKE. <note>Johann Jakob Reiske, an 18th-century critic</note>
8. *To preserve.*] Up to this point are the words of Hermippus; the following are those of Porphyry. REISKE.

# P O R P H Y R Y, etc.

...out of great necessity and involuntary errors, as we have shown, they fell into this custom. Since even a law of Draco <note>Draco was a 7th-century BCE Athenian legislator known for his harsh legal code, though the laws cited here focus on religious piety.</note> is remembered as such: "An eternal ordinance for those inhabiting Attica, valid for all time. To honor the Gods and local Heroes in common, following ancestral laws, and privately according to one's power, with auspicious words and firstfruits of crops, and annual cakes <note>original: πελάνους (pelanous) — a mixture of meal, honey, and oil offered to the gods</note>." Of the law commanding to honor the divine with firstfruits of crops, which man uses, and with cakes.

<column-break/>

...they proceeded with much necessity and involuntary sins, as we have shown, falling into such a custom. For a law of Draco is also handed down to memory in this way: "An eternal law for those inhabiting Attica, which is to be held valid for all time. That the Gods and indigenous heroes be held in veneration in public, following ancestral laws, and privately according to one's strength, with a good omen of words, and firstfruits of the harvest, and annual cakes." Where the law commands the divinity to be worshiped with the firstfruits of the crops which man eats, and with cakes.

---

<margin>
There were those among the Leiden and Cambridge editors who had omitted the word "to honor" <note>original: τιμᾷν (timan)</note>, which I have restored to its place as was done in the first edition, and the Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts. Abresch also saw this beautifully. A little after, the word "this" <note>original: τοῦτο (touto)</note> before "had been legislated" was missing in the Leipzig manuscript.
</margin>

10. **An eternal ordinance.** In Athens, laws were called *thesmoi* <note>term: θεσμοί — specifically the ancient, sacred laws established by early legislators like Draco</note>, but specifically these laws of Draco, because they began with this word. Read the learned man on Aelian: *Varia Historia* VIII, 10, and Meursius on *Solon*, ch. 13.

11. **To honor the Gods and local heroes.** As the ancients often mention "local gods" and "following." See Cuper: *Observations* Book III, 16. They also often join "local gods and heroes," on which matter see Duker on Thucydides IV, 87. Since Draco ordained these things, Maximus Tyrius (*Dissertation* IV, 10) writes with little accuracy that neither Solon nor Draco's laws handed down "what the divine is, or how it must be honored."

12. **Following ancestral laws.** Petit reads "under penalty" <note>original: ἐμποινίμοις (empoinimois)</note> and in the penultimate line "and annual cakes." See *Attic Laws* at the beginning. I would prefer "accordingly" <note>original: ἑπομένως (hepomenos)</note>. VALENTINUS. Petit’s reading seems to have been approved even by the Distinguished Cuper (*Observations* III, ch. 16), but was rightly refuted by Wesseling in *Attic Laws* p. 69, who restored "following" <note>original: ἑπομένους (hepomenous)</note>, or rather "accordingly." The Leipzig and Meermann manuscripts give "following" <note>original: ἑπομένοις (hepomenois)</note>, and thus Davis restored it on Cicero's *On Laws*...

<column-break/>

...p. 36, as the illustrious Abresch advised; I have made a place for this word in the text. For that ridiculous "under penalty" <note>original: ἐμποένοις (empoenois)</note> which was read before was derived from a foolish error of the Florentine typesetter into subsequent editions, when he should have given what you see now. He correctly says "ancestral laws" <note>original: πατρίους νόμους (patrious nomous)</note>, which others call "inherited." See Book I, § 20. The ancients strove for nothing so much as that laws of this kind should not be neglected. I will add only Socrates’ response in Xenophon, because it seems to refer to this law of Draco. Being asked whether it was permitted for anyone to worship the gods at their own discretion, he replied: "No, but there are laws according to which one must do this." See Marcilius on the *Golden Verses of Pythagoras*, p. 344.

13. **Annual cakes.** Nay, rather "and with annual cakes" <note>original: καὶ πελάνοις (kai pelanois)</note>, or "with annual cakes," as has long been emended by learned men: J. Meursius in *Attic Themes* I, 1; P. Petit, followed by G. Cuper (*Observations* III, 16), and others. However, the Leipzig manuscript offers no help, but the Meermann perhaps intended it, for it usually expresses not only "ous" but sometimes "ois" as well, in the manner done here. For what "cakes" <note>term: πέλανοι (pelanoi) — sacrificial cakes often used as bloodless offerings</note> were, see Book II, 6.

14. **And with cakes.** Not a few things are missing at the end of this book, namely examples of illustrious men from all Greek and Roman antiquity who abstained from meat, together with the concluding speech. REISKE.

### Letter I.

->*To the Most Reverend Man*<-

## URBAN GODOFREDUS SIBER,

->*Sends Fondest Greetings*<-

## JOHANN FRIEDRICH THOMAS.

I do not need to seek far for reasons to explain at length to you, Most Reverend Sir, why I have taken the liberty of sending this present writing as an obscure man not even known to you by name. Both the fame of your merits in literary as well as ecclesiastical affairs, and the renown of your singular kindness—by which you wonderfully adorn and assist the study of higher learning and its noble practitioners—have encouraged me. Relying on that goodwill of yours toward all, I send this small letter to you to modestly set forth my requests. As I am working on an edition of Porphyry’s work <term>On Abstinence from Animal Food</term> <note>original: "περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων" (peri apoches empsychon). Porphyry was a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher; this work is one of the earliest defenses of vegetarianism.</note>, I intend to prefix to the work a dissertation on the life and philosophical method used by Porphyry. I shall take up for particular treatment the vexed question of *Porphyry’s Apostasy* <note>The historical debate over whether Porphyry was originally a Christian who later abandoned the faith to become a fierce critic of Christianity.</note>, which is commonly believed even by Great Men such as *Fabricius*, *de la Croze*, and others; it is regarding this that I urgently and earnestly beseech you to write back your opinion to me. Concerning the *Porphyrians*—the name by which, as you know, the *Arians* <note>Followers of Arius, whose theological views were declared heretical at the Council of Nicaea. The Emperor Constantine ordered their books to be called "Porphyrian" to associate them with the pagan enemy of the Church.</note> were once designated—I am not yet sufficiently certain. For the opinions of both *Sandius* in his *Core of Ecclesiastical History* and *Godofredus* in his commentary on *Philostorgius* regarding them are displeasing to me. Likewise, the conjecture of *Cudworth*, which he puts forward in his excellent *Intellectual System of the Universe* on page 594, seems to me more subtle than true. Permit me, therefore, to learn the more correct view from you. Your love for and merits in historical investigations, which are well-celebrated, do not allow me to doubt that I shall experience your benevolence and favor in this matter; although I acknowledge myself plainly unequal to repaying it, I shall nonetheless do enough in proclaiming and cherishing it. Indulge my requests, therefore, Most Distinguished Man, and if any other materials are available to you which might be of use to my endeavors, even in illustrating the Work itself, allow yourself to be persuaded to grant them liberally. Farewell. Written at Schweidnitz in Silesia <note>original: "Suidnicii Silefiorum", modern Świdnica, Poland.</note>, the 14th day before the Calends of October, 1715 <note>September 18, 1715.</note>.

<summary>Johann Friedrich Thomas writes to the scholar Urban Gottfried Siber seeking academic guidance for his upcoming edition of Porphyry's treatise on vegetarianism. He specifically asks for Siber's opinion on Porphyry's alleged apostasy from Christianity and the historical labeling of Arians as "Porphyrians."</summary>

### Letter II.

->To the Illustrious and Most Distinguished Man,<-

# JOHANN FRIEDRICH THOMAS,

->of Schweidnitz in Silesia,<-

->Sends Fondest Greetings<-

# URBAN GODOFREDUS SIBER.

->*Most Distinguished, Most Noble Man, Patron to be honored with all respect,*<-

Since I am accustomed to place great value on the conversations of learned men—from which not only does friendship grow, but also various benefits often flow for the public good—I cannot help but praise your kindness, by which you address me so charmingly, though I have been neither seen nor heard by you; indeed, you even seek my opinion on a "vexed question" <note>A "vexed question" refers to a long-standing, difficult scholarly debate that has caused much disagreement.</note>. I thank you, Most Distinguished Sir, and likewise ask that, although your estimation of me may be too high, you nevertheless maintain a benevolent spirit toward me, and you may promise yourself every kind of service from me. 

Furthermore, as it pertains to your efforts, they are indeed to be praised in the highest degree. For such a business cannot be criticized, in which men of such stature as Holstenius <note>Lucas Holstenius (1596–1661) was a celebrated German humanist and geographer who wrote a foundational biography of Porphyry.</note> once moved with such great labor and diligence. Truly, I think that regarding the life of Porphyry, scarcely anything more accurate can be produced than what Holstenius has already published on that matter, being a man most well-versed in all literature and libraries. While I say this, I would not wish to interrupt your own industry here, since it can happen that new worlds may be discovered by excellent minds, and those things may be examined which we are surprised to find were either not seen or neglected by others.

Regarding the Apostasy <note>original Greek: "Αποστασίᾳ" (apostasia). In this context, it refers to the historical claim that Porphyry was a Christian before becoming a critic of the faith.</note> of Porphyry, you first ask and call it into doubt; and I think you do this not entirely without reason, since the older writers of Church History offer no sign that Porphyry was ever a member of the Christian fellowship; indeed, they rather consider him a sworn enemy of the holy Religion. Sozomen <note>A 5th-century historian of the Christian Church.</note> is the first who relates that Porphyry, having been beaten by a Christian and seething with a desire for revenge, defected from the faith. Theophanes <note>Theophanes the Confessor (c. 758–818), a Byzantine monk and chronicler.</note> copies this on page 45, bringing Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos (c. 1256–1335), the last of the Greek ecclesiastical historians.</note> into the same company. The authority of these three men might seem so great to some that Porphyry would indeed appear to have once embraced Christianity...
