<meta>This page continues the response from Urban Gottfried Siber to Johann Friedrich Thomas. The previous page ended mid-word; the full thought concludes here as "could [not] be proven." Siber is weighing the conflicting historical accounts of the philosopher Porphyry’s relationship with the early Christian church.</meta>

page 387
Ccc 2

...could <note>The text likely completes a word like *nequeat* (could not) from the previous page.</note>. Nevertheless, he could have been a **Catechumen** <note>A "Catechumen" was a convert to Christianity receiving basic instruction before being baptized; they were permitted to hear the scriptures but not to participate in the full liturgy.</note>, in whose rank even those who were held by a true zeal for our sacred rites used to remain for a long time. He could also have been delighted by the reading of the divine Oracles <note>A common term for the Holy Scriptures.</note> alone; that he did this is sufficiently testified not only by the testimonies of the Church Fathers, but also by the very Porphyrian refutation consisting of fifteen books <note>Refers to Porphyry’s famous work *Against the Christians*, which was later banned and burned by imperial decree.</note>. Perhaps, therefore, he approached with the intention of embracing Christianity if the reasons pleased him, but departed as an enemy, since a mind accustomed to the logical demonstrations of the wise was irritated even by the offenses of those whose life disagreed with the heavenly rule. But if we grant that he stood only on the boundary of Christianity and Paganism, and did not truly enter the camp itself, it must be established that Sozomen, Theophanes, and Nicephorus <note>These are prominent early Byzantine church historians.</note> interpreted the term **apostasy** <note>original: *ἀποστασίας* (apostasias)</note> too broadly, and that Porphyry was not stained with that infamy by a clearly accurate reasoning.

I, however, would not wish such things to be discussed too laboriously—namely, lest the authority of the Ecclesiastical Writers collapse if we should overturn those things which have been believed for so long and established by those to whom, as if to the stewards and treasurers of antiquities, we are accustomed to turn. Nor indeed does it harm the Christian cause that a Christian should play the **Apostate**, since we acknowledge that even perfections and heavenly spirits <note>A reference to the fall of the rebel angels.</note> deserted the Deity itself. Furthermore, Most Distinguished Man, you ask from where the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father; they were considered heretics by the orthodox church.</note> received the name of "Porphyrians" as a term of shame? Do you recognize that what Gothofredus said in his *Observations on Philostorgius* (page 420) is not sufficient for your accuracy? To these things I reply that, to me at least, in the Letter of Constantine the Great—provided that it is indeed Constantine's own—most abundant reasons were given: namely, that the Arians were doing the same thing that Porphyry did. Now the efforts of Porphyry, like those of Celsus and Philostratus <note>Earlier pagan critics of Christianity.</note>, aimed only at this: that they might recognize nothing of the divine in Christ, or if any such thing appeared, they would destroy it. Since the Arians did this even more strongly, and perverted the very words testifying to his divinity by an unheard-of **distortion** <note>original: *στρεβλώσῃ* (streblōsei)</note>, they were most aptly and fittingly called Porphyrians.

I have indeed thought that any evil thing was called **porphyrion** <note>original: *πορφύριον* — a play on the name Porphyry and the Greek word for purple/darkness.</note> by the Greeks, and I remember that at one time a sea monster ravaging the shores and long hostile to fishermen was marked with the name of "Porphyry" <note>This refers to a famous whale, nicknamed Porphyrios, that harassed ships in the waters near Constantinople for over fifty years in the 6th century.</note>; but I do not determine whether that monster did not draw its name from Porphyry the Apostate. Certainly the reasons of Constantine so pleased posterity that Emperor Theodosius, in a second edict for burning the books of Porphyry, repeated them or changed them a little, yet at the same time indicated that the Arians had acquired that name from a madness equal to that of Porphyry.

Thus I think my respect for you, Most Distinguished Man, has been declared; if it does not satisfy your accurate intellect—which I already perceive—consider that in that vast Ocean of Ecclesiastical History, I prefer to avoid the rocks and seek the wealth that may benefit the multitude. Meanwhile, I ask with all effort that you keep for me the friendship you offered, and introduce me to the notice of your other friends, from whom I shall not cease to give and seek mutual signs of benevolence. May God preserve you. 12 October 1715.

->To the Most Great, Reverend, and Distinguished Man<-

### URBAN GOTTFRIED SIBER,

->*Professor of Theology and Sacred Antiquities*<-

->Sends Fondest Greetings<-

### JOHANN FRIEDRICH THOMAS.

Your reply brought me great joy, filled as it was with all kindness and erudition. You very benevolently indicated that my previous letters were not entirely unwelcome, and you remarkably declared your goodwill toward me. I certainly offer you the greatest thanks I can for your singular kindness, which was greater than my hope and expectation; I earnestly and zealously beseech you to preserve this favor toward me forever. 

Regarding the subject matter—the reason I so eagerly sought your friendship—I confess indeed that your ingenious conjecture pleases me greatly. In order to keep the tradition of the Church Fathers regarding Porphyry’s <term>Apostasy (falling away from the faith)</term> intact, you maintain that Porphyry was a <term>Catechumen (a convert under instruction but not yet baptized)</term>. Or, if this should displease anyone, you advise that the word "apostasy" <note>original: "ἀποστασίας"</note> ought to be interpreted a little more broadly, which seems to me the best course of all. 

But truly, since I still desire more certain proofs for this opinion of yours (which has a great appearance of truth), and since I do not think anything can easily be brought forward to this effect from the ecclesiastical writers or others who have handed down anything concerning Porphyry, you will not take it poorly if I choose "to withhold judgment" <note>original: "τὸ ἐπέχειν," a Skeptic philosophical term for suspending assent</note> here. Instead, I shall propose to you my own "divination" <note>meaning a scholarly guess or hypothesis</note> on this question, to be determined by your judgment. 

To be sure, the authority of the Church writers is sacred to me; however, I revere it in such a way that I have always thought the account of truth must be held in higher regard. Since those writers were very often stirred by a "gadfly of passions" <note>meaning they were often driven by intense emotion or bias</note>—as you yourself will acknowledge—and since they saw with resentment that Porphyry’s name was held in high esteem among his own people for his sharpness of mind and great store of learning, they certainly could not brand his reputation with a greater mark of shame than by passing on to their own and to posterity a story of Porphyry’s apostasy received from others. I could easily believe this story arose from our Philosopher’s familiarity with Origen Adamantius <note>A famous early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) whom Porphyry met in his youth</note>. 

As for the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, whose views on the nature of Christ were declared heretical</note>, it is well that you write that the most abundant reasons why they were called "Porphyrians" were noticed by you in the letter of Constantine; but it is better what you add: "if only that letter is truly Constantine’s own," about which there is still reason to doubt...

<summary>Johann Friedrich Thomas writes to Urban Gottfried Siber, debating whether the philosopher Porphyry was truly a Christian convert who later committed apostasy. Thomas suggests the story might be a biased invention by Church Fathers intended to discredit a formidable intellectual rival.</summary>

--- Page 433 ---
<meta>This page continues Thomas's argument regarding the philosopher Porphyry. In the previous page, Thomas expressed skepticism about Siber’s theories regarding Porphyry’s status as a Christian convert (catechumen) and now transitions into a discussion of Porphyry’s reputation and the practicalities of editing his works.</meta>

In this, I understand great men to be involved. I also think it difficult to demonstrate from the writings of Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher known for his work "Against the Christians."</note> that he acknowledged nothing divine in Christ, or that if he saw anything resembling divinity, he sought to destroy it. Indeed, many rather praise this in Porphyry: that nowhere did he say anything insulting against Christ himself. 

Next, this also makes me very doubtful: that the Holy Fathers who disputed against the <term>Arians (followers of a belief that Christ was not fully divine)</term> never charged them with following the impiety of Porphyry. Such a charge certainly would have made the Arians much more hated. Instead, it is well known that the Arians so thoroughly embraced the dogmas of Plotinus <note>Porphyry’s teacher and the founder of Neoplatonism</note> that they should have been called Plotinians by a better right than Porphyrians. 

Furthermore, the observation you add regarding the word *porphyrion* <note>original: "πορφύριον"</note> is elegant; you think that any evil thing was designated by this word by the Greeks. To that end, you cite Procopius regarding the sea monster distinguished by the name "Porphyry." <note>Procopius of Caesarea recorded a famous whale named Porphyrios that harassed ships near Constantinople for 50 years.</note> Unless I am entirely mistaken, I remember reading this same history in Michael Glycas, in the fourth part of his *Annals*, page 270. To this one might also relate, in a certain way, the explanation of Porphyry’s nickname, "the Bataneote," <note>original: "τοῦ βατανεώτου," a reference to Porphyry's likely Syrian or Palestinian origins</note> which Stephanus le Moyne gave on page 607 of his *Various Sacred Matters*. But I confess that this specific meaning of the word *porphyrion* is unknown to me, and I would very much desire it to be proven from Greek authors. 

With your permission, I have chosen to point these things out—not because I wish to take anything away from your opinion, but solely because I intended to invite you to further reflection on this matter. 

In the work of illustrating Porphyry’s writings itself—to add this as well—I have been especially concerned with the <term>Collation (the line-by-line comparison of different manuscript copies to find the original text)</term> of manuscripts. With their help, the true reading, which is lacking in many places, might be restored. Nor did my prayers fail to produce some result. For the illustrious Prefect of the Library of Vienna, Gentilotto ab Engelsbrun, procured for me not just a comparison, but a complete description of the Vatican manuscript. And, to provide an even greater abundance of his favor toward me, he most kindly promised a comparison of the Florentine manuscript, with the observations of the distinguished Salvini added, as well as the unpublished notes of Holstenius on the manuscript, which were only recently sent over. Likewise, the distinguished Lederlin gave a specimen of various readings from the Royal Codex of Paris, with a full collation of that manuscript to follow soon. 

Therefore, it has been my long-held desire to obtain a comparison of the Leipzig Codex, which your "Pauline Library" <note>The library of the University of Leipzig</note> preserves. I explained this to several distinguished men who reside in Leipzig, and not long ago to the Magnificent Mr. Boerner. I now gather the sum of these requests again and pour them into your bosom: please take charge of this business and make room for my petition—which I think is honorable and will benefit the public good—and help my efforts through your work. I beg you to forgive this audacity of mine, which assigns such a burden of undertaking to you, a man very busy with other things; however, from this, comfort shall come to me, and the fruit of glory to you. 

I truly have no way to repay your leaning toward me in goodwill; nevertheless, I shall strive and endeavor as much as I can to prove all my diligence, which is placed in both piety and respect, and looks especially toward your honor and esteem. 

Farewell, Most Distinguished Sir, and—as I uniquely pray—preserve your benevolence toward me forever. 

Written at Świdnica, Silesia, on the 13th day before the Kalends of December, 1715. <note>November 19, 1715</note>

<meta>This page continues the correspondence between Johann Friedrich Thomas and Urbanus Gottfried Siberus regarding the 3rd-century philosopher Porphyry. On the previous page, Thomas argued that Porphyry was never a Christian and that the "Apostate" label was a later invention. ### Letter IV.

->To the Most Distinguished and Learned Man<-

## JOHANN FRIEDRICH THOMAS,

->of Schweidnitz,<-

->sends many greetings.<-

## URBANUS GOTTFRIED SIBERUS,

->*Professor of Theology and Sacred Antiquities and Priest at the Church of St. Thomas.*<-

To defend Porphyry of Tyre—that Phoenician who was indeed a supreme philosopher but the worst of Christians, and thus a deserter—from the stain of <term>apostasy (the abandonment of one's religious faith)</term>, and to draw me toward agreement, you use numerous arguments. These are probable, but not true, and I shall review them here in summary. First, you think that: 1) Christian writers were driven by a frenzy of emotions; 2) kindled by envy, they fruitlessly reproached Porphyry with that crime; 3) the Letter of Constantine, in which he wished <term>Arians (followers of Arius who denied the full divinity of Christ)</term> to be called "Porphyrians," appears to be a forgery; 4) Porphyry’s Christianity was "sculpted" merely out of his familiarity with Origen <note>A prominent early Christian scholar and theologian</note>; 5) it cannot be demonstrated that Christ’s divinity was attacked by him; 6) nor were any insults against Christ spoken; 7) the Church Fathers never charged the Arians with "Porphyrianism." Before I weigh or discuss these points according to your demand, I myself declare once again that it matters little to me—or perhaps even to the entire Christian society—whether Porphyry acted the part of an apostate or not. Nevertheless, lest I seem to have made light of your reasons, or to be insufficiently attentive to the duties of my office, I respond and uphold that most widely accepted affirmation of the Fathers concerning Porphyry's apostasy. First, I plainly deny that the ecclesiastical writers, from whom that tradition has come down to us, were driven by a frenzy of emotions—or, what is the same thing, the stings of hatred and fury—to invent such a thing about Porphyry. For the more I look upon the modesty and <term>self-restraint (original: *χαλιναγωγίαν*, literally "bridling")</term> of those ancient men in their writing, the more I discover their supreme tranquility in accusing the pagans. Indeed, I would assert that Suetonius, Tacitus, and other secular writers lashed out far more strongly against the crimes of their own people. On the contrary, even when peace was granted to them, they thought a law was given to them that no <term>loose-tongued remarks (original: *ἀθυρόγλωσσα*, literally "words without a door")</term> should appear, but rather they should check the intemperance of the tongue, <term>the lack of restraint of the tongue (original: *τὸ ἀκρατὲς τῆς γλώσσης*)</term>,

<summary>Urbanus Siberus begins his formal rebuttal to Johann Friedrich Thomas, listing seven points Thomas used to argue that the philosopher Porphyry was never a Christian. Siberus defends the integrity of the Church Fathers, arguing they were characterized by linguistic restraint rather than hateful invention.</summary>

<keywords>Porphyry of Tyre, Johann Friedrich Thomas, Urbanus Gottfried Siberus, apostasy, Church Fathers, Arians, Constantine the Great, Origen, polemics, historical accuracy</keywords>

--- Page 435 ---
<meta>The previous page likely discussed the initial accusations against Porphyry and the nature of his departure from the Christian faith. The catchword "in-" suggests the text continues onto the next page with a word like "incited" or "inflamed."</meta>

They held it to be the <note>original: "νοσημάτων αἴσχισον" (nosēmatōn aischiston)</note> **most shameful of diseases**. (*) This is quite evident from the first public writings of the Christians, their *Apologies*, in which, while they were pleading against the crimes charged to them, they nevertheless spoke with great verbal chastisement regarding the vices of the Deities whom [the pagans] worshipped and the crimes of mortals; nor did they publish anything unless it was plainly certain and common knowledge. And what gain, I ask, would the Christians have had if they had charged Porphyry with **Apostasy** <note>The act of renouncing one's religious faith.</note> out of mere madness, when his efforts against Christianity were going to be equally worthless whether he acted as a Philosopher or as a treacherous Christian? Certainly, the Christian Republic was not so helpless or ignoble that, because of one man being denied access, they would break the reins of Christian moderation and hurl falsehoods at those who had wandered astray.

And I use the same argument against your second reason: as if the Christians, looking upon the fame of Porphyry with envious eyes, had fabricated the charge of Apostasy? Certainly, they had no reason to envy the Greeks for such a man, who—whatever he knew in the human or philosophical arts and sciences, or wrote with greater sobriety—he had drawn from the company of Christians and his familiarity with **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note>, and from there he had amended the dogmas of the other Philosophers. This is asserted by **Augustine** in Book 10 of *The City of God*, chapter 30, and by Baltus in *Platonism Defended by the Fathers*. If he [Porphyry] misused these things against his Masters, they had weapons, displayed from heaven and strengthened by a divine edge, with which they could overthrow and defeat entire cohorts of Porphyrys. This was indeed done, since at that time more than one person endowed with Porphyry's talent was attempting to undermine the Church. **Arnobius**—whose disputations against the heathens Ciacconius claims were born chiefly from Porphyry’s Apostasy—beautifully says in Book 3 of *Regarding the Church*: *She [the Church] is content with her own strengths and rests upon the foundations of her own truth; nor is she stripped of her power, even if she has no defender: indeed, even if all tongues speak against her and strive against her, and conspire with the animosity of a united consensus to abolish faith in her.* From this it is clear that the Christians burned with no envy toward Porphyry; however, this will be even more abundantly clear if you look closely at the citations made here and there by the Fathers. These are so far from breathing envy that they sometimes seem to exhale praise instead, except when the truth had to be sacrificed for. **Eusebius**, in his books on the *Preparation for the Gospel*, commends his talent; and **Cyril**, in his books against Julian, spoke with a most composed mind only those things which, if Porphyry had survived until Cyril’s time, he would not have wished said otherwise. In Book 1 against Julian, Porphyry is said to be <note>original: "ἐπὶ παιδείᾳ κοσμικῇ δόξαν ἔχων παρ’ ἐκείνοις οὐκ ἀγεννῆ" (epi paideia kosmika doxan echōn par’ ekeinois ouk agennē)</note> **having a reputation among them for worldly learning that was not ignoble**. I ask, where is this "envy" attributed to the Fathers? Did Cyril deal as kindly with the schismatics Nestorius, Theodore, or Ibas as he did with Porphyry? In the same book, he refers to him among the most select writers of Greece, among <note>original: "ἑτέρους τῶν παρ’ αὐτοῖς λογάδων" (heterous tōn par’ autois logadōn)</note> **others of the elite among them**. In Book 8, page 270, among those who are <note>original: "πανάρισοι καὶ σοφοὶ" (panaristoi kai sophoi)</note> **all-excellent and wise** and have received a <note>original: "λαμπρὸν καὶ διαβόητον ὄνομα" (lampron kai diabōēton onoma)</note> **bright and famous name**, he places Porphyry in the first rank—and this without envy, which otherwise might have [incited] the distinguished Prelate...

Now as pertains to your third reason—that the letter of **Constantine**, in which it is ordered that the name of 'Porphyrians' be imposed upon the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who held a controversial view on the nature of Christ; Constantine sought to insult them by linking them to the pagan philosopher Porphyry.</note> as a mark of ignominy, is a forgery—I ask that you allow me to clear away my earlier suspicions. I do not deny that I was once swept away into those quicksands <note>original: "Syrtes," a classical reference to the dangerous sandbanks off the coast of Libya, used here as a metaphor for intellectual doubt.</note> of doubt, questioning whether the Letters and Edicts presented under Constantine's name were truly his or not. And it seemed likely that a Prince overseeing so many kingdoms would hardly have had so much leisure as to preach at such length as is done in those monuments. Nor indeed was it unusual for Emperors, both contemporary with Constantine and older, to commit speeches written by others to memory and subsequently recite them in public ceremonies.

<meta>This page continues the argument that Porphyry was a former Christian who abandoned the faith. ...[he] frequented the open Catechetical Lectures <note>Basic religious instructions for those preparing for baptism.</note> at Caesarea, but having abandoned them out of irritation, he finally acted as a deserter.

Fifthly, you think that his apostasy <note>The abandonment of one's religious faith.</note> cannot be proven from Porphyry's own writings for the reason that he said nothing against the divinity of Christ. To this I reply that the writings witnessing to Porphyrian Impiety no longer exist because Christians, according to solemn custom, consigned them to the pyre and boasted of such a fire. I recall that in the work of Ciampini, an image engraved in bronze was discovered in the Church of Ravenna, in which the books of heretics are carried away by flames. Even if those mad writings no longer exist, will you deny credit to Cyril? He describes the "bitter words" <note>original: "λόγους πικροὺς"</note> written by Porphyry as "fighting against the glory of God" <note>original: "τῇ θεοῦ δόξῃ μαχομένους"</note>, "loose-lipped" <note>original: "ἀθυροστόμους"</note>, and "dancing in mockery" <note>original: "κατορχουμένους"</note> of it. It was enough to overthrow the divinity of Christ that he—following a custom which the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note> thereafter adopted—introduced subsistences <note>A theological term for the distinct persons of the Trinity.</note> that were subordinated and subjected to one another. He showed "the subsistence of one from the other, beginning from the King, and the descent and diminishment of those after the first; but to those who follow the thinking of Arius, he divides and establishes them equally, introducing the subsistences as subordinate to each other, and he thinks that the Holy and Co-essential Trinity consists of three gods divided" <note>original: "Δεδήλωκε τὴν ἐξ ἀλλήλων ὑπόστασιν... τὴν ἁγίαν καὶ ὁμοούσιον." This describes how Porphyry's Neoplatonic hierarchy of "emanations" was viewed as a precursor to the Arian heresy.</note>. To this may be added what Augustine brings forward in *The City of God*, Book 10, Chapter 23, concerning him, since he had established two principles: "As for what he says are the 'Principles' as a Platonist, we know he means God the Father and God the Son, whom he calls in Greek the 'paternal intellect' <note>original: "paternum intellectum"</note>:" regarding the Holy Spirit, he says either nothing or nothing clearly. And he said this as he could, or as he wished: "For philosophers use free words." Soon in Chapter 24, Augustine refutes this further.

How much he departed by that assertion from "the precision among us" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς παρ' ἡμῖν ἀκριβείας" — referring to orthodox Christian doctrine.</note> was declared by the praised Cyril in Book 8, pages 270 and 271, and by Augustine in *The City of God*, Book 10, who in Chapter 29 called those words "undisciplined." Besides Cyril and Augustine, Theophylactus exposed the sophistries of Porphyry against the divinity "of the Word" <note>original: "τοῦ λόγου" (tou Logou)</note> in his *Exposition of the Gospel on the Nativity*, which I have read only in Latin in the collection of Combefis, Volume 1, page 351. These things must be carefully collected with others, lest you defend the enemy and adversary of Christ too kindly.

For even if it could be demonstrated that he not only did not insult the divinity of the Savior, but even granted him "something divine" <note>original: "θεῖόν τι" (theion ti)</note>, that would still not be enough to defend him. For "something divine" was attributed even to excellent philosophers and craftsmen according to Plato, who called such people—especially if they were involved in reforming the Republic—"probing gods" <note>original: "θεοὺς ἐλεγχτικοὺς" (theous elenchtikous)</note>, a role which Porphyry took up. "Porphyry maintains that there is a certain race of gods, whom he says occasionally transform into humans, acting as it were like those among us who play." <margin>(*) Cyril, Book 8, page 287.</margin> <note>original: "Πορφύριος δὲ γένος εἶναί τι θεῶν... ἀθύροντας μὲν."</note> However, since Christians were not concerned with acknowledging merely *something* divine in Christ, but rather "all the fullness of the Godhead," it was enough to accuse him of apostasy if he once acknowledged and then denied His full divinity, as we confess in the Creeds following the lead of Scripture.

# IV.

Nor indeed is the stain of **apostasy** <note>original: *ἀποστασίας* (apostasias)</note> washed away even if the slanders spread by him against Christ cannot be demonstrated, although the testimonies of Cyril sufficiently declare that he acted otherwise. But if you should disregard those, it must be known that Christ had adversaries of different kinds: some who insulted him in a common, vulgar manner—which was done in the theaters both before Julian and during the reign of that treacherous prince—and others who, with more learned reasoning, desired to see His Majesty overthrown. These were the Philosophers, whose **dignity** <note>original: *σεμνότης* (semnotēs)</note> and credibility would have perished if they had betrayed any lack of restraint in their speech. Thus Julian usually restrained himself from speaking too impudently; his Satire was poured out only so far as to contemptuously call Christ a "Galilean" and the "son of a carpenter," although Cyril <margin>(*) Cyril, Book I, p. 38.</margin> called these very words **ill-omened voices** <note>original: *παλιμφήτους φωνὰς* (palimphētous phōnas)</note>. However, the moderation of these men was all the more dangerous because, under the appearance of **impassivity** <note>original: *ἀπαθείας* (apatheias)</note>, they won all the greater applause for themselves, which Augustine graphically describes in *The City of God*, Book XIX, chapter 23. Indeed, what would you say if you read through the Quran? Although no one denies it was written to prostrate the divinity of Christ, is there any railing against Christ present there? You will find scarcely a shadow of detraction, but rather many praises and other things that can be turned to his glory. Will these things truly persuade you, most learned Sir, to free the Author and his followers from the crime of Apostasy?

Finally, it will be of little use if you assert that the Fathers rarely charged the Arians with "Porphyrian arts." It is enough that Arius, in the first birth of his heresy, followed the dialectical arts of Porphyry—which Rufinus so greatly reproached Jerome for—and that he held the same hypotheses as Porphyry, as Cyril taught a little earlier. It is enough that the Arians imitated the **ways** <note>original: *τοὺς τρόπους* (tous tropous)</note> or manners of Porphyry (which are the words of Constantine), and **changed like chameleons** <note>original: *ὡς χαμαιλέοντες μετεβάλλοντο* (hōs chamaileontes meteballonto)</note>, and thus expressed both of Porphyry's crimes: his disputations and his Apostasy. Later writers, when they saw that Porphyry had been surpassed in many ways by Arius and his followers, thought it more advisable to call the abominable heresy by its own Author, or by the principal heads of its errors, rather than referring back to Porphyry. This was especially true since the successors of Arius had peculiar marks by which they were distinguished from Porphyry, just as it seemed better to the Church to call the Nestorians by their own name rather than by the name of Simon Magus, even though Theodosius had commanded this with the same severity as Constantine had commanded the name "Porphyrians."

With your opinions discussed in this manner, I should think you must look for stronger arguments if you require even a mere probability that Porphyry was not an Apostate. Therefore, I repeat again and again that the authority of the Ecclesiastical Writers is not only not to be despised, but rather every stone must be turned to ensure it remains sound and protected. For that reason, I urge you to weigh carefully: First,

# IV. c. 11.

"When I, having been summoned to Bithynia <note>A Roman province in modern-day Turkey.</note> to teach the art of oratory, happened to be there at the same time that the temple of God was being overturned, two men arose in that place who insulted the fallen and rejected truth, I know not whether more proudly or more impudently; one of whom professed himself a *High Priest of Philosophy*." This was Hierocles, as all learned men agree. Lactantius continues: *"The other described the same material more bitingly; he was then among the number of the judges, and was a primary author of the persecution that was to be carried out. Not content with this crime, he also pursued with his writings those whom he had afflicted. For he composed two small books, not 'against' the Christians, lest he should seem to pursue them as an enemy, but 'to' the Christians, so that he might seem to advise them humanely and kindly. In these books, he attempted to prove the falsehood of Holy Scripture as if it were entirely contradictory to itself; for he set forth certain chapters that seemed to conflict with one another, enumerating so many and such intimate details that at times he seemed to have been from that same school of discipline."* 

Thus far are the words of Lactantius. Regarding these, I warn of a disagreement among the learned, who have sometimes confused these two philosophers with one another, such that they referred to Porphyry what pertained to Hierocles, and attributed to Hierocles what pertained to Porphyry. This is what Theophilus Raynaud did when, in his book *On Judas the Traitor*, Chapter 15, Section 7, he spoke thus: *"Hierocles and Porphyry, in the same year that Diocletian <note>The Roman Emperor who launched the last and most severe persecution of Christians.</note> was overseeing the destruction of the churches of the Christians and the burning of books at Nicomedia, having previously professed the Christian religion, became traitors to the faith whose name they had taken and the Sacrament they had received, and thus represented Judas the traitor."* I have used the words of Lactantius in part, and although he mentions neither by name while reviewing their venomous writings against the Christian religion, nevertheless from the circumstances he relates, he sufficiently suggested who they were. He clearly noted Hierocles when he said the title of the two small books written by him (who was one of the judges and an instigator or even author of the persecution against the Christians) was *Philalethes*, or *The Lover of Truth* <note>original: *Philalethes veri amator*</note>. We learn that all these details apply to Hierocles from Eusebius, who wrote a refutation of that work by Hierocles. 

That Porphyry, however, is the philosopher and enemy of the Christians mentioned in the same place is a conjecture made by Baronius from the circumstances in the Year of Christ 302. Moreover, it is established from Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian.</note> Book 3, Chapter 9, that he was a deserter of Christianity. Therefore, both are rightly numbered among the close kin of the traitor Judas, as I reported was done by Lactantius. Thus says Raynaud, though I personally think the latter description <note>original: *Prosopographiam* (a description of a person's appearance or character)</note> by Lactantius pertains rather to Porphyry. But before that is determined, let us meanwhile embrace the opinion of the great Bishop Pearson, who, in his *Prolegomena to Hierocles*, thinks Lactantius was dealing with these two philosophers. Although I know he is contradicted by Holstenius, and that those same contradictions are repeated and approved by Needham <margin>(*) Needham's Preface to Hierocles, page 14.</margin> in his notes to Pearson's *Prolegomena*, you will see, most illustrious sir, that Holstenius's reasons are of no great weight, and by an accurate measure of chronology and a correct reconstruction of Porphyry’s biography...

can be very easily overturned. For how will they prove that in the nineteenth year of Diocletian <note>303 AD, the start of the Great Persecution.</note> and the 303rd year of Christ, Porphyry had passed the sixty-ninth year of his age? Or, even if that premise is granted, how can they prove he had not become a man of ninety or a hundred years, since he is called by the singular surname "The Old Man"? Indeed, it adds much to the weight of accepting Lactantius's words and applying them to Porphyry that Jerome likewise, and all others, testify to these same writings by Porphyry. Furthermore, Cyril, in his books against Julian, seems to have translated Lactantius's words about Porphyry into the Greek language when he expressed his impudent insult with the word *mocking dance* <note>original: "τῆς κατορχήσεως" (tēs katorchēseōs), a term implying a triumphant or insulting dance over a fallen foe.</note>, which is always, according to Strabo, joined with *shamelessness* <note>original: "ἀναιδείᾳ" (anaideia).</note>.

Furthermore, the account of Eusebius of Caesarea <note>A 4th-century bishop and the "Father of Church History."</note>—that Porphyry, unable to endure insults, returned to the camp of the pagans—must not be brushed aside. Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century Church historian.</note> drew this from Eusebius's own books written against Porphyry, although those books have long since been lost. By what reasoning can you render that account void? One would have to accuse Socrates of fiction and overthrow his entire credibility. No one fails to see how much danger this poses to historical truth. But if you believe that Socrates took those details from Eusebius, you must simultaneously believe Eusebius; no one would claim that Eusebius was ignorant of the events that took place in his own Church unless they intended to wrongly insult such a great man.

Added to this is the Emperor's Edict regarding Porphyry's name being held in ignominy. This was primarily due to his *Apostasy* <note>The formal abandonment of the Christian faith.</note>, since such a stigma was burned into none of the other philosophers for mere paganism alone. Now, that edict, held as genuine and repeated by Theodosius, was never challenged as a forgery by Jacques Godefroy (*) or any other learned men. This is a certain sign that those who approved the edict also believed the reasons that brought such disgrace upon Porphyry. Now, where will you dismiss Socrates (**), who by fixed purpose relates that Apostasy from the books of Eusebius? Relying on such a great man as Eusebius was, Socrates could assert the same with total confidence. If you think he was mocking the world, you might as well strike down everything else he left to memory in an instant. In that case, Hardouin <note>Jean Hardouin (1646–1729), a scholar famous for claiming many ancient works were medieval forgeries.</note> and his followers, who have long tried to undermine the authority of the Ancients, would triumph securely. But if your mind is otherwise, Socrates will surely please you all the more because he soon compares Julian the Apostate with Porphyry, establishing that both fell into the same impiety: *“Both therefore, having acted impiously with knowledge of their sin, bear the penalty”* <note>original: "ἀμφότεροι οὖν δυσσεβήσαντες ἐν γνώσει ἁμαρτίας τὸ ἐπιτίμιον ἔχουσιν"</note>. Departing from the interpretation of Valesius, I translate these words as follows: they shall be struck with a greater punishment because, having been better and more rightly instructed, they wandered from the true path against their own conscience. Nor did Socrates alone do this, but even the orator Libanius, who linked Porphyry and Julian because of that desertion—a fact which Nicephorus (***) rightly observed. In the manner of Cyril, he even called Porphyry the *father and teacher* of Julian, specifically regarding his Apostasy.

calling him by name. A little while later, joining the two together again, he says: *Julian leaned toward the madness of Porphyry, and both, having chosen impiety with full knowledge, are abominable, paying the penalty for their voluntary sin.* <note>original Greek: Ἰουλιανὸς πρὸς τὴν Πορφυρίου λύσσαν ἀπέκλινεν...; the author is quoting Nicephorus Callistus</note> Johannes Langus translates this as: *Julian in the same manner declined into the rage of Porphyry. Both are to be detested, since they embraced impiety while being prudent and knowing, and they therefore hang under the punishment of a voluntary and deliberately admitted sin.* Very well put indeed. For from this we see 1) an equality between the two, 2) knowledge, namely of sound doctrine, and 3) a voluntary sin <note>original Greek: ἑκούσιον ἁμαρτίαν</note>, and thus a perfect apostasy <term>apostasy: the formal abandonment of a religious belief</term>. This is what moved Nicephorus to call them both "abominable" <note>original Greek: ἀποτροπαίους</note>, that is, according to the testimony of Stephanus: to be averted, detested, horrendous, terrible, and abominated. Nor would I wish to scorn the authority of Nicephorus, since he follows Cyril and Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, the church historian</note>, and doubtless many others besides, who with unanimous consent recognized that apostasy. And I conveniently join to them Theophanes, who, since he collected his Chronology from the most excellent writers, gives us confidence that this was the belief among all the writers of his nation. After Theophanes comes Elias of Crete in his commentary on the 4th Oration of Gregory Nazianzen, where he called him "the Apostate" without any veil over his speech in number 69. Almost alone among all the Greeks is Theophylact, though he is somewhat negligent in Ecclesiastical History; he calls Porphyry a "gentile philosopher," looking toward the later period of the Apostate's life, yet he did not deny the crime that had gone before.

Indeed, the greatest and most influential part of the learned Latin writers have likewise recognized this apostasy. Jerome joined him with Julian, and in this followed the Greeks most closely, in Chapter 16 on Hosea: *The mouth of fools bubbles over with folly, such as were Porphyry and Julian, who poured out floods of their own folly against the teachers of the Church.* Rufinus, in his invective against Jerome, says: *Brother, you have made a bad omen in that your introducer is Porphyry. Where does that Faithless one lead you? If to that place where he himself is, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth; for there the Apostates, and the enemies of God, and perhaps the perjurers dwell.* <margin>(*) Rufinus said these things having stayed a long time among the Greeks both in Alexandria and in Palestine and Caesarea, so that he was able to know well whether these things were being tossed about truly or falsely concerning Porphyry. Nor would he have dared to do so, having such an adversary as the man from Stridon <note>Jerome, who was born in Stridon</note>, who, if Rufinus had used fables as a weapon, would have quickly crushed that "leaden fig."</margin> Furthermore, Augustine must certainly be brought forward, by whom many things have been preserved from the books which Porphyry wrote against Christ after his apostasy. He himself indicates several times that the Philosopher, just as he was about to approach the Religion, recoiled from its simplicity. *If you had truly and faithfully loved the Wisdom of Christ, you would have known the power of God and Wisdom, nor would you have recoiled, puffed up in your usual way, from his most wholesome humility.* <margin>(**)</margin> These words prove: 1) there was a time when Porphyry loved that Wisdom, 2) but that love was not constant, 3) and thus he recoiled.

---

(*) Jerome, Volume 4 of his Works, page 146.
(**) Book 10, chapter 25 <note>of Augustine's City of God</note>.

<meta>This page continues the argument for Porphyry’s status as an apostate, transitioning from the testimonies of Greek historians to the evidence found in the works of Saint Augustine and Cassiodorus, before concluding with a letter regarding manuscript variants for a forthcoming edition of Porphyry’s work.</meta>

### Page 398
### I N-

from the faith, to which he had crossed over. Indeed, he even adds (*) that after his apostasy from the Faith, he did not even adhere sincerely to Paganism <note>The author uses "Gentilismo," referring to the polytheistic religions of the Roman Empire</note>, but was trembling, pretending, and as if blushing with shame, in chapter 24. Recent editors of Augustine have seen that the Holy Prelate <note>Referring to Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo</note> was aware of the philosopher’s apostasy, and for that reason, they added that he was first a Christian, and later a deserter. The more closely I examine the Prelate's writings, the more I suspect the primary incentives for Porphyry's desertion—namely, the Incarnation of Christ and the Resurrection, of which he believed the former was unbecoming and the latter was barely possible. Let Cassiodorus follow Augustine; he confirms this very point, being a man skilled in Greek literature and preserving those things which he had learned from the Greek Fathers. But if all that number of witnesses still seems too small to you to confine Porphyry among the apostates, remember: 1) in the age of Porphyry, the term "apostate" was not yet quite customary; 2) nor was <term>apostasy</term> <note>original Greek: ἀποστασίαν</note> considered ignominious among philosophers, unless you except the followers of Pythagoras; 3) out of prudent reason, one's mind and judgment occasionally had to be hidden, as Lactantius records when he says: *For the sake of the times, Christians were sometimes silent.* See the Valesian Edition, p. 573.

I think these points will suffice to convince you, Distinguished Sir, that you should not think more of your own guesswork than of the manifest evidence of such great men, whom I can scarcely—or not at all—persuade myself were fed on fables and dreams. Regarding your other requests, I am sending you various readings excerpted from the Leipzig Manuscript Codex, which the Illustrious Boerner <note>Christian Friedrich Boerner (1683–1753), a German theologian</note> very kindly shared with me. However, you will need to compare them with the French edition from Lyons by Fogerolles <note>François Fogerolles, who published a Latin translation of Porphyry in 1613</note>, against which I ordered the Codex to be collated. The manuscript book is of paper, neatly written, not very old, and not of such a quality that I think much trust can be placed in it. Sometimes several lines that appeared in Fogerolles were omitted; occasionally syllables were neglected. Meanwhile, however, I hope those readings will not be entirely useless to you, but that "grapes may be gathered from these thorns" <note>A biblical allusion to Matthew 7:16, suggesting that even a flawed source can yield valuable information</note>. May God prosper your efforts in editing Porphyry, and make your other labors happy and auspicious with a large harvest of good fortune. Leipzig, December 28 <note>original Latin: "d. V. a. Cal. Januarii," the 5th day before the Calends of January</note>, 1716.
